s1.text:
"Look at Kolo," says Captain Nalei. "He is doing something nobody taught him."

The little mynah bird hops across the path, a seed in his beak. He drops it into the dark soil. He pats it down with his foot. Then he tilts his head at you, as if to say, well?

"What is he doing?" you ask.

"Planting," says Nalei. "Every green thing on this island arrived by traveling. By wing, by wave, by wind. Kolo is just helping."

You look around. The jungle is so thick here you cannot see the ground, let alone rock. Vines hang like ropes. Birds you cannot see are shouting at each other in the canopy. It is hard to imagine this place as anything other than what it is.

Nalei crouches beside you. "This island is the oldest of the whole chain," she says. "An archipelago — that is the word for a family of islands. And this family has a secret. Under the sea, far below our boat, there is one hot spot in the earth. It never moves. But the sea floor slides over it, slow as a fingernail growing. So the hot spot builds an island, and the floor carries it away, and the hot spot builds another. One fire, making island after island after island."

Kolo hops closer, head tilted the other way now.

"The youngest island is bare black rock," Nalei says. "Nothing alive on it at all. Not one leaf."

"Nothing?" you say.

"Nothing yet."

She stands and looks out at the water, where other islands fade in a line toward the horizon.

"I could show you," she says. "Sail the chain backward, oldest to youngest, and watch the jungle come off like a coat. By the end of the week you would stand on the newest rock in the world, and you would know exactly how it begins."

Kolo gives one short chirp, and flutters to the boat's rail.

"He wants to come," says Nalei. "So. Shall we?"

s2a.text:
The anchor splashes down in water so clear you can see the shadow of the boat on the sand below. "Toes off," says Nalei, and you wade ashore onto a beach that glitters like spilled pepper.

The sand is warm under your feet. Not warm like a beach at home, warm like bread just out of the oven. You dig your toes in and the warmth goes deeper.

A green sea turtle sleeps at the high edge of the beach, flippers tucked, looking like a boulder somebody polished. Kolo hops toward it, stops a respectful hop away, and tilts his head.

"She knows something we don't," Nalei says. "Sea turtles only rest where they feel safe." She scoops up a handful of sand and lets it fall through her fingers. The grains are sharp, not smooth like the sand at home. "When the hot lava hit the cold ocean," she says, "it cracked into a million pieces. The waves have been tumbling those pieces ever since, grinding them smaller and smaller."

You hold out your hand. The sand sticks to your wet palm, black and shining. Kolo pecks at a sparkle near your thumb, gentle as a question.

"So the beach is just the mountain," you say, "crumbled up?"

"The mountain, the waves, and a hundred years of patience," says Nalei. The turtle sighs in her sleep, a long breath that ruffles the sand beside her shell.

s2b.text:
The boat rolls over deep blue water, and Nalei taps a screen bolted beside the wheel. "Look here," she says. "The mountain's other half."

The screen shows a green slope dropping away under the boat. Down and down it goes, past numbers you have to count twice, until the line flattens into darkness.

"That is how tall the volcano really is," Nalei says. "Taller than the biggest building you have ever seen. Taller than the hill behind your school. Most of it has been underwater the whole time."

You grip the rail. The island behind you suddenly looks like a hat on a giant's head.

Kolo balances on the bowsprit, feathers ruffled by the wind. Ahead, a splash of silver leaps from the water — flying fish, their wings catching the sun before they splash back. Kolo watches them go, head whipping from side to side.

"Travelers," says Nalei, pointing at a line of white birds wheeling toward the next island. "Just like the first ones. Seeds stuck to their feathers, or in their bellies. They land on bare rock and leave life behind."

The next island rises ahead, green and cloudy at its peak. Kolo gives one short chirp, as if he recognizes it. The boat rises on a swell, and you feel the whole mountain moving beneath you, slow and steady as a sleeping breath.

s3.text:
Kolo flies ahead of us the whole way, island to island, as if he is checking his work.

By the third morning the jungle is thinning. The vines let go. The trees shrink. And then we step out onto bare black lava that clicks under our shoes, and the only green is pale crusty lichen spreading over the rock like the island's first freckles.

"Lichen," says Nalei. "The first colonists. Anything that can live on bare rock and make soil for whoever comes next."

In the cracks, ferns are unrolling. A little ohia tree holds on sideways, its red flower the brightest thing for a mile. Kolo hops from crack to crack, inspecting every one. He drops his seed beside the ohia and pats it down.

"Same as before," you say. "Every island, he plants."

"He is showing you the whole story," Nalei says. "Look back."

Behind us the islands stand in a line, green to grey to black, like footprints walking away across the sea.

"But why does the line go that way?" you ask.

Nalei kneels. She lights a candle and holds a paper plate above the flame, and slides the plate slowly sideways. The flame never moves. The burn mark does.

"One hot spot," she says. "The plate of earth slides over it, slow as a fingernail growing. The hot spot stays. It builds an island, the floor carries it off, it builds another."

You stare at the burn mark. Then at the line of islands.

"So the youngest one—" you say.

"Is straight ahead," says Nalei. "Still being built. What did you find back there? Keep it close. The new rock is where it all starts."

s4a.text:
We climb into the clouds.

Mika the volcanologist leads, and Kolo rides her shoulder, feathers flat in the wind. The path is old lava, ropey and grey, and it crunches under our shoes. "Feel that?" Mika says. "Sharp edges. Young rock. Up top it is older, smoother. The island has been sitting here longer."

Then the cloud breaks, and we are standing on the crater rim.

Below us the bowl drops away, red-brown and enormous, quiet as a held breath. This is where it began. One hot spot, far below, pushing rock up through the sea until it broke the waves and became an island.

Mika crouches and touches the rim. "You can read lava like a book," she says. "Red-brown and rough, that is old. Black and shiny, that is young. This rim has been resting a long time."

Kolo hops to the very edge and tilts his head at the bowl, at us, at the sky. A gust takes one of his feathers. It spins, lands at my feet, and I tuck it into my pocket.

"Look out," Mika says softly.

On the horizon, beyond the haze, more islands stand in a line. Grey, green, ghostly. The chain keeps walking away across the sea, past what we can see, and every single one began in a bowl like this one.

"How far does it go?" you ask.

"Further than anyone has ever followed it," Mika says. "Footprints across the sea."

Kolo chirps once, sharp and bright, and flutters to your shoulder. In your pocket the feather lies light as a whisper. Somewhere far below, the hot spot is already building again.

s4b.text:
The new shore is black and bare, and it hums.

Mika the volcanologist walks ahead, slow and careful, across ropey lava that looks like giant braids of dark taffy. "Only a few years old," she says. "The youngest land on Earth. Feel through your shoes."

You stop. The rock is warm. Not hot, just warm, like bread an hour out of the oven. The whole island is still cooling.

Kolo hops across the braids, feet quick, head tilting at every crack. Nothing grows here. No lichen, no ferns. Just black rock and the sea and us.

"Stay where I step," Mika says, easy as anything. "The safe crust sounds hollow. The thin places sound different. Listen." She taps the rock with her stick. Tok. Tok. Solid and sure.

Then the light begins to change.

Dusk comes down purple and soft, and where the lava meets the water, the sea glows faint orange. It hisses like a giant kettle. Plumes of steam rise and curl, and the glow pulses, slow, like something breathing.

"It is still going," you whisper.

"Always," says Mika. "Look out there."

She points past the glowing water, out to the dark swells. "Under those waves, a brand-new island is climbing toward the sunlight. It has been growing for thousands of years. Someday it will break the surface, and birds will come, and seeds, and it will be the youngest of the chain."

Kolo flutters to a warm rock and stands very still, watching the orange water.

On the black sand at your feet, something glints. A smooth piece of sand glass, the sea has already begun to polish. You pick it up. It is warm.

"The chain is still growing," Mika says. "You are standing on the newest page."

Kolo gives one soft chirp, and the sea hisses back, and the glass in your pocket holds the warmth of a brand-new world.

c1.question: "First stop, explorer. Do you want to dig your toes into the black sand beach and meet the turtle, or ride the deep water and see the mountain hiding under the sea?"

options.label: Stop at the middle island's black sand beach
Sail the deep water and watch the depth finder

c2.question: "Here's the youngest island, and you get to choose how to meet it. Climb with me to the crater rim and look down into where it all began — or walk the new shore where the lava is still warm and the next island is growing under the waves?"

options.label: Climb to the crater rim above the clouds
Walk the warm youngest shore at dusk

stories.title: Grandma Nell and the Dawn Chorus

s1.text:
Grandma Nell turns off the lamp beside her chair.
"Listen a minute," she says.
We are sitting on the rug at her feet, you and me, with the window open a hand's width and the evening coming in cool over the sill. Out in the hedge the birds are shuffling about, getting comfortable. One of them keeps saying the same short thing over and over. Then it stops.
"There," says Grandma Nell. "That is them going to sleep. When I was your size, birds woke me up instead."
She has a lapful of yellow wool, needles crossed on top.
"My bed sat right under the window. Every morning, before the sun, the sky went the grey of dishwater. And then, from the fence post, one chirp. Always the same robin, round as an apple, red down his front, one black eye on me."
We call him {robin_name}.
"When {robin_name} started, the others woke and joined on, one and one and one, until the whole garden was singing. The dawn chorus. And then one morning there was something underneath it."
She pinches a thread of the wool and holds it up.
"A voice about that thick."

s2a.text:
"So I watched him," says Grandma Nell. "Nothing else. Just him."
She puts her needles down and does not pick them up for a while.
"He stood on the very tip of that post and puffed his red front out until he was nearly a ball. And when he sang, the whole of him shook with it. Beak to tail feather. Chirp, chirree, chirree."
"Then the blackbird came in off the chimney, low and easy, and then the sparrows all at once, arguing inside the hedge. Song landing on song, the way blankets go on a bed in winter."
"I pushed my window up a crack. Only a crack, because the cold came straight in off the wet grass. And then I did a bold thing. I hummed."
She hums it for us now. Two notes, hardly there.
"{robin_name} turned his head. One black eye, straight at me, and he did not go anywhere. That is the way with a robin. Keep your hands on the sill and keep still, and he will let you stay."
She picks her needles up again.
"And under all of it, that thin voice. Still going. Still waiting to be found."

s2b.text:
"So I looked into the hedge," says Grandma Nell. "Right in deep, where the leaves are thickest. That is where the robins kept their nest, and I had watched them build it in the spring."
"That is how I found out what a beak is for. A robin's beak is a tool, like a little pair of tweezers. He picked up one straw at a time, just so, and carried it in, and tucked it exactly where he wanted it. Round and round he went. Twigs. Moss. More moss. Until it was a bowl, a proper little bowl, lined inside with soft grey feathers."
She smooths the yellow wool flat over her knee.
"That morning I could just make out the rim of the nest through the leaves. And the rim was wobbling. Something in there was hopping about. Something small was trying out a pair of brand new wings."
"My tummy went fizzy with waiting. I did not go down the garden and I did not part the leaves to look, because whoever it was would come out when they were ready."
"And then the thin voice came again, straight out of that bowl of twigs."

s3.text:
"And then out he came," says Grandma Nell. "Out of the hedge and onto a low branch. A fluffy scrap of a thing, soft as a dandelion, with wings too short to be any use yet."
"He hopped along that branch. Hop. Wobble. Hop. Then he flapped hard and got himself up onto the fence post, right beside {robin_name}."
She stops. Out in the hedge the birds have gone quiet.
"The whole garden hushed like that. Even the sparrows. And the baby opened his yellow beak as wide as it would go, and out came one small scratchy chirp. Not much of a song. Nothing like a song, if I am honest."
"But {robin_name} tipped his head back and answered him with the biggest chirree of his life."
"So the baby had another try, a bit stronger."
"Big song, small song. Big song, small song. Back and forth the two of them went, and behind them the sky was going pink along the bottom."
She holds up her thread of yellow wool again, and this time she pulls it out longer.
"You could hear it getting ready."

s4a.text:
"I stayed still as a stone," says Grandma Nell. "Not a toe. Not a finger."
"That baby filled his chest right up. And out it came. His first whole song. Wobbly at the front, then all at once clear, and going up at the end like a question."
"{robin_name} sang the high parts and the baby sang the small parts, and the blackbird and the sparrows wrapped themselves round the pair of them. Then the sun came up over the hedge and poured itself gold all across my blanket."
"I clapped. Only with my fingertips, so as not to spoil it. And he fluffed himself up on that post, as pleased as anything."
Grandma Nell picks up the yellow row where she left it.
"That was a great many mornings ago. But I still open this window before the sun, every day of my life. Some mornings there is a robin on that same post."
She nods at the dark garden.
"I like to think it is his family, still teaching the little ones the first song of the day. Open yours tomorrow. See if they got as far as your house."

s4b.text:
"I went down to the kitchen on my toes," says Grandma Nell. "I took the crusty end of yesterday's loaf and I crumbled it up small, small, small. Then I laid the crumbs along my windowsill and knelt down well back from the glass, because he would never come while I was leaning over it."
"{robin_name} saw them first. Down he came onto the sill, one little tap of his feet. Peck, peck, peck, quick as a needle going through cloth."
"And then he did the loveliest thing. He turned to the fence and chirped, the way you call somebody in for their dinner."
"Over flapped the baby, all wobble, and landed beside him with a bump. {robin_name} nudged a crumb along the sill towards him. And that baby had his first breakfast right there in front of my nose. Peck, peck, hop. Peck, peck, hop."
Grandma Nell reaches over and taps a jar on the windowsill. It is half full of crumbs.
"I have kept one of these ever since," she says. "They sing for their breakfast, and I get the best seat in the house."

c1.question: Grandma Nell puts one needle down. "Now then," she says. "If it was you at that window, where would you look? At the robin up on the fence post, or into the hedge where the nest was? Robin, or nest?"

options.label: The robin singing on the fence post
The nest hidden in the hedge

c2.question: "The sun was nearly up," says Grandma Nell. "And I had a think. Stay where I was, still as anything, and listen? Or go down to the kitchen and fetch the bread? Listen, or crumbs?"

options.label: Stay still and listen to the baby's first song
Fetch the bread and lay crumbs along the windowsill

robin_name.role: the robin who sings first every morning

s1.text:
Low tide. The sea has walked backwards and left the black rocks bare, and we come down over them the way we always do.
Our pool is the third one along.
It is smaller than our bath. The water is clear as a window, and the sun lays wobbly gold rings on the sand at the bottom.
"Morning," we say.
One arm spills up over a stone and waves at us, slow and friendly. It is {octopus_name}. We wave back with our whole arm, octopus style.
"Eight arms," grumbles the hermit crab from the far side. "Who needs eight of anything."
Then a shadow slides across the pool. Only a seagull, going by.
And when we look down again the pool is empty.
No arms. No {octopus_name}. Just water, and sand, and one lumpy grey rock, and a big empty spiral shell wedged in the corner.
We put our hands on our knees and leave them there, because reaching in would only cloud the water.
"She is in there," we say. "She has to be."

s2a.text:
We crouch down beside the hermit crab.
"You said you watch everything," we whisper.
He hauls himself up tall in his shell, which is not tall at all. "I am a professional," he says.
"So where did she go?"
He thinks about it for a very long time. "I saw eight arms," he says. "Or seven. Possibly eleven. Numbers are hard when they wiggle."
"What colour was she?"
"Ah. That part I have got." He taps his shell. "Pinky orange, she was, like the inside of a peach. Then, quick as a blink, speckly grey, like a wet stone. And then, poof."
He points. It is the wrong claw. He notices, folds it away, and points again with the other one, right at the middle of the pool.
So she never left. She only changed.
An octopus can go almost any colour she likes, faster than we can say it, and she can change her bumps as well, rough as rock or smooth as sand.
"Watching is thirsty work," says the crab, and pops inside.

s2b.text:
We stay where we are and look at the water instead. Still as two herons.
Nothing moves. So we stop looking for movement and start looking for the small things.
"There," we whisper.
A puff of sand near the middle of the pool, curling up and settling back down. Something pushed off from that spot.
Beside it lies a broken sand dollar, tipped on its side. We lean closer. Under the edge is a dip in the sand the size of an egg cup.
"Too small," we say. "Nobody fits in that."
Except an octopus has no bones at all, not one, anywhere in her. She is all squish, and the only hard part of her is a beak the size of a bean, and wherever that beak fits, the rest of her pours through after it, like honey off a spoon.
So a gap the width of a straw is plenty.
We look at the pool again.
"It is not empty," we whisper. "Look at it. It is stuffed with places to hide."

s3.text:
Two clues now.
The first is that {first_clue}. The second one is right in front of us.
A line of tiny sand puffs runs along the bottom of the pool, puff, puff, puff, like footprints made out of dust, and they go into the corner.
In the corner there are two things. The lumpy grey rock, bumpy all over. And the big empty spiral shell, pale as milk, wedged between two stones.
The hermit crab comes hurrying up sideways.
"That shell is mine," he says. "Well. It is going to be mine. I have been growing into it for weeks."
We look at the rock. We look at the shell.
Then something happens that makes us hold absolutely still.
Out of the mouth of the shell comes one small puff of water. Just one.
Shells do not breathe.
Rocks do not breathe either. But that rock has an awful lot of bumps for a rock.
We lean out over the pool, close enough to see our faces in it.

s4a.text:
We lean right over and look in at the round mouth of the shell.
Two golden eyes look back at us.
"Hello, {octopus_name}, we found you."
Out she comes, in no hurry at all. First one arm curls over the lip, then a second, and then all the rest of her pours out through a hole no bigger than a bottle cap and puffs round again on the sand.
Her whole self. Through a bottle cap.
Her suckers take hold of the bottom, tap, tap, tap, hundreds of tiny hands.
That is the entire trick. No bones. Just squish.
The hermit crab arrives at top speed, sideways, and climbs into the empty shell. It is enormous on him. He wobbles. He tips slowly over.
"I will grow into it," he says from inside, with great dignity.
{octopus_name} goes bright pink all over, which is exactly what laughing looks like on an octopus. She waves one arm, and we wave back with our whole arm.
Behind us the sea comes sliding up over the rocks to fill her pool again.

s4b.text:
We sit back on our heels and go quiet. Quiet as the rocks.
Waiting is hard, so we count our own breaths. Nine. Ten.
Then the shell tips, just a little.
One arm slides out over the sand, testing. Then another.
Then {octopus_name} pours out of the shell like milk out of a jug and walks across the pool on the tips of her arms, her suckers taking hold and letting go.
As she walks, she changes. Over the pale sand she goes sandy. Over dark stone she goes dark. Over a patch of pink weed she goes pink, and stays pink, and looks straight up at us.
"Pink means hello," we whisper. "Hello."
In the middle she stops, reaches one long arm behind her, and shoves the empty shell. It rolls all the way to the hermit crab's feet.
"For me?" he says. "Truly?"
He climbs in and turns round twice. It fits him like a hat that was waiting.
Then the sea slides up over the rocks and fills the pool, and we walk home saying hello to every colour we pass.

c1.question: "Well," says the hermit crab. "You could ask somebody who watches this pool all day long. Me. Or you could stare at that water until your eyes go funny. Crab, or look?"

options.label: Ask the hermit crab what he saw
Look at the pool ourselves for clues

sets_slots.first_clue: she poured herself into somewhere small

c2.question: "Get on with it," says the hermit crab. "Peek right in at her. Or sit back on your heels and wait her out. Peek, or wait?"

options.label: Peek inside the spiral shell
Wait quietly for her to come out

octopus_name.role: the little octopus who plays hide and seek

first_clue.role: the first clue we found about where she went

s1.text:
Ocho the octopus lived in a cozy den beneath a rocky ledge, where the tide pool shone like a coin in the sun. All around him sat his collection: jars of every shape, every one of them opened. Pickle jars. Jam jars. A jar that once held eighteen pickles and now held exactly one very proud octopus memory. Ocho was a problem solver, you see. Give him a lid, and his eight arms would get to work like a thinking machine—twisting, pulling, testing, until pop. Open.

Today, something new gleamed at the edge of the pool. A glass jar, washed in by the morning tide. And inside it, the outline of something round and golden. A sleeping crab cake, still dreaming.

Nib the hermit crab scuttled sideways out from behind a shell, clicking his claws so fast they sounded like tiny castanets. Click-click-click. "A jar! A jar! And it's sealed! Ocho, it's sealed!"

"I see it," said Ocho.

He wrapped one tentacle around the glass. Cool. Smooth. He wrapped another around the lid and gave it a twist.

Nothing.

He tried the other way. Nothing again. His eight arms settled around the jar like a huddle of thinkers, each one holding a different part, waiting for a plan.

"Well?" said Nib, practically vibrating inside his borrowed shell.

"This lid," Ocho said slowly, "is not like the others."

And that was when his eyes lit up—because a new kind of lid meant a new kind of puzzle, and a new kind of puzzle was Ocho's favorite thing in the whole tide pool.

s2a.text:
"Pull," said Ocho. "Good old pull."

He planted himself on the sand and wrapped all eight arms around that lid—one over the top, two on the sides, the rest wherever they fit. A huddle of thinkers with one single idea. He pulled. He pulled harder. His suckers gripped, squeaked, and slipped. Squeak-slip. Squeak-slip. The smooth glass would not hold them, not even for a moment.

"Pull! Pull!" clicked Nib, dancing sideways in a circle.

Ocho gave one last mighty tug, and his suckers popped off all at once—pop, pop, pop-pop-pop—like a row of little corks. He tumbled backward into the sand, arms over head over arms, and lay there blinking up at the tide pool sky.

Nib hurried over and peered down at him. "Ocho. Your arms are all knotted."

"I noticed," said Ocho.

He sat up slowly, sand sliding off his head, and looked at the jar again. It had not moved even a whisker. But now, up close, he saw something. The lid had ridges—little bumps running round and round in a spiral.

Nib tapped one with his claw. Tink. "These aren't for pulling," he said. "These are for turning. See how they wind? Like my shell. Like a path that goes around and around."

Ocho ran one tentacle along the spiral ridge, following it with his sucker tips, and his eyes went wide and bright. "It's not a pop-top," he whispered. "It's a twist-top. And I tried to yank it straight off."

"We all make mistakes," said Nib kindly, patting Ocho's arm with one small claw. "Even thinking machines."

s2b.text:
"Squeeze," said Ocho. "Like a stubborn clam."

He wrapped his tentacles around the whole jar—around and around and around, the way he did with clamshells on good days, when one strong hug was all it took to pop them open. His eight arms settled over the glass like a net, and he began to press.

The jar pressed back.

"Tighter!" clicked Nib, hopping from foot to foot. "Tighter, Ocho!"

Ocho squeezed tighter. And then he heard it. A tiny sound, so small he almost missed it. Tink. A thin, bright line had appeared in the glass, right where his strongest arm was pressing. A crack.

Ocho stopped. His whole body went still. Slowly, gently, he unwound his arms, one by one, and set the jar down on the sand as carefully as a mother setting down a sleeping baby.

"Did it open?" said Nib, scuttling closer.

"No," said Ocho. "And it very nearly broke. This jar is not a clam, Nib. It's fragile. It needs a gentler touch than that."

He sat back on his arms and looked at the jar, and the jar sat there looking back, still sealed, still whole, but only just. Nib crept up beside it and tapped the lid with one claw. Tink. Then he tapped the ridges—those little bumps running round and round in a spiral.

"Look at these," said Nib. "They wind like my shell. Around and around. I don't think this lid wants squeezing. I think it wants turning."

Ocho touched one ridge with the tip of a tentacle, and his eyes lit up. "A spiral," he breathed. "It's a twist-top. And I nearly crushed it."

"But you didn't," said Nib. "You listened. That's what thinking machines do."

s3.text: Nib clicked his claws, quick as rain on a tin roof. "Well? What did you find? Tell me everything." Ocho ran one tentacle along the lid, slow and sure, feeling every bump and groove. "This lid doesn't want to be pulled," he said. "And it doesn't want to be squeezed. It wants to turn. Like a wheel. Like the slowest, most patient wheel in the sea." He wrapped one strong arm around the lid itself, just for grip. His other seven arms settled around the glass below, holding the jar steady, each one doing its own quiet job. Eight arms, thinking together, like a thinking machine. "Ready?" said Ocho. "Ready," said Nib, holding his breath inside his shell. Ocho turned. Not fast. Not hard. Just slowly, steadily, the way you turn a door handle when you're trying not to wake anyone. The lid resisted. Then it gave. Click. The tiniest sound, but Ocho felt it travel up his arm like a small spark of triumph. He kept turning. Click-click. And then, with a soft, satisfied pop, the lid came free. A smell rose out of the jar, warm and golden, and drifted through the tide pool like a invitation. Nib's eyes went wide. "You did it," he whispered. "You actually did it." Ocho held the open jar gently, like something precious. "We did it," he said. "Eight arms. One jar. And one very good clue."

s4a.text: Click-click-click. Nib froze. A shadow slid over the pool, wide and slow, turning the water gray. "Shark," he whispered. Ocho didn't run. He dropped flat against the bottom, and his skin changed. The rusty red faded. Speckles of sand bloomed across his back, brown and gold and gray, until there was no octopus at all. Just sand. Just shadow. Just a jar sitting on the ocean floor like it had always been there. Nib tucked himself into his shell, one eye peeking out. The shadow circled. Once. Twice. Ocho stayed so still that a tiny fish landed on his arm, thinking he was a rock. He didn't even blink. Then the shadow grew thin, and thinner, and was gone. Nib burst out clicking. "You vanished! You actually vanished!" "Eight arms," said Ocho, his color washing back like a sunrise, "and one very patient octopus." They carried the jar home between them, and there in the den they split the crab cake, half for a crab, half for an octopus, and it tasted like triumph. Afterward, Ocho set the empty jar on the shelf with the others. "That one," said Nib, curling up beside it, "is my favorite." "Mine too," said Ocho, and all eight arms settled in, like a thinking machine at rest.

s4b.text: Click-click-click. Nib froze. A shadow slid over the pool, wide and slow. "Shark!" Ocho grabbed the jar with two arms and looked at the rocks. There. A crack, narrow as a pencil. Too small for a shark. Just small enough for an octopus. He pushed one arm in. Then two. Then he poured himself through, soft as soup through a sieve, all eight arms pulling and folding and squeezing. His body flattened like dough under a rolling pin. Nib scuttled in sideways behind him, shell and all. Pop. They were through, into a hidden pocket of rock, dark and safe and barely big enough for two friends and a jar. Outside, the shadow cruised past. It circled the crack. It was much, much too wide. Nib pressed against Ocho in the dark, and they listened to the water go quiet. "You fit," Nib whispered, amazed. "No bones," said Ocho. "It's my best trick." When the shadow was long gone, they squeezed back out and hurried home. They split the crab cake in the den, half for a crab, half for an octopus, and it tasted like a door only they could open. Ocho set the empty jar on the shelf. "A tight squeeze and a good friend," he said. "Best kind of day."

c1.question: "Click-click! The lid won't budge, Ocho. Will you pull it with all your might, or squeeze it like a stubborn clam?"

options.label: Try pulling the lid straight off with all eight arms
Try wrapping and squeezing the jar like a clamshell

c2.question: "Click-click! A shark! Quick, Ocho—will you vanish into the sand, or slip through the rocks?"

options.label: Change colors to blend into the sandy bottom
Squeeze through a narrow gap in the rocks

stories.title: Old Marta and the Island That Was Not There

s1.text:
Old Marta is mending her net on the step, and she gives us the needle to hold.
The sea has gone flat and pink. Marta looks out at a green hump of an island and half laughs.
"That one there," she says. "That island was not there when I was a girl. Sit closer.
"One summer the sea out that way began to steam. All autumn it threw up black stones. Then one morning there was land, warm and bare and brand new.
"When the steaming stopped I rowed out. I pulled my boat up past the wet line and looped the rope round a rock, because a boat left at the edge goes exploring without you.
"Then I looked round. No grass. No trees. Not one footprint anywhere, so the first footprints that island ever had were mine.
"So I gave it a name. I called it {island_name}."
Marta looks up.
"And on a warm rock sat a small orange lizard. 'You came,' she said. 'Somebody came at last. I am {companion_name}.' Then she looked out at the water. 'Nothing has ever arrived here, and something will. Stay until the light goes.'"

s2a.text:
"I walked the water's edge with my shoes in my hand," said Marta. "Down there the sand was cool and firm. Higher up, where the sun had been all day, it was warm as a bed.
"And it was black. Every grain of it was a crumb of the island itself, ground up small by the waves. It squeaked under my feet. That squeak and the sea were the only sounds in the world.
"Then I found a thing that sat me down in the sand. A seed. A hard round seed, brown as a hazelnut, rolled up on the beach in a rope of seaweed. It had floated there from somewhere, and I never did learn where from.
"I dug a dip with two fingers, tucked it in, and patted the sand down over it.
"'What will it be?' said {companion_name}.
"'Nobody knows yet,' I said. And she patted it too, with the tip of her tail, very seriously, as if we had just planted a whole garden."

s2b.text:
"I climbed," said Marta. "It was not much of a hill. Twenty steps and I was standing on the top of the whole island.
"{companion_name} rode up on my shoulder and held on to my ear like a handle.
"From up there I could see all of it at once. One black island, round as a loaf. Sea all the way round it. No path. No harbour. No smoke, because there was no chimney to make any.
"Only warm rock under my bare feet, and one small pool of rain.
"Far off, low and blue, I could see my own island, with my mother in it and her lamp lit.
"'Is that where you live?' said {companion_name}.
"'That is where I live,' I said.
"The sun went down behind it, and the sea turned copper, then rose, then grey. The wind came over the hill, and I heard the wind itself, because there was nothing up there for it to rustle. Not one leaf. Not one blade of grass.
"I sat down on the warm stone and let it hold me."

s3.text:
"By the time the light went I was sitting with my back against a rock," said Marta. "It was still warm from the day, the way a wall stays warm long after the sun has gone.
"{companion_name} curled up against my knee and shut both eyes.
"The sky went peach. Then plum. Then almost dark. One star came out over the water. I was tired and happy and thinking about nothing at all.
"And because I was so still, two things happened at once.
"The first was right beside my foot. In a crack in the rock, where a little ash and rainwater had gathered, there was a thread of green. A shoot. A stem no taller than my finger, with two leaves on it.
"The first green thing that island ever grew.
"The second was far out over the water. A white speck, coming closer. A seabird, flying straight in at my little island.
"{companion_name} opened one eye. 'Told you,' she said.
"It was nearly dark. I could lean down to the one, or hold still for the other."

s4a.text:
"I got down on my elbows in the black sand," said Marta. "Two leaves, no bigger than my thumbnail, holding themselves up out of a crack.
"A seed had come from somewhere, on the wind or in the water, the way everything arrives out there. It had found one crack with a spoonful of ash and one sip of rainwater in it, and decided that was plenty.
"The wind came over the hill and the little thing shivered. So I put my two hands round it, like this, to keep the wind off, and stayed like that a long while.
"Then I built it a wall of black pebbles, a ring the height of my finger, and {companion_name} patted the ash flat all round it."
Marta lays her mending down.
"I have been back many times since," she says. "That island is green all over now. Bushes. Grass. Birds shouting at each other in the morning. Somewhere in the middle of all that green are the great grandchildren of my one shoot.
"And I still keep a black pebble in my coat pocket. Here. Feel how smooth it has got."

s4b.text:
"I did not move," said Marta. "Not one finger. I sat as still as the rock behind me and watched it come.
"It circled twice, low and slow, the way you look round a room you have never been in.
"Then it put its feet down on the warm stone, folded its wings, and stood there. White chest. Yellow beak. Perfectly at home already.
"It looked at me, and then at {companion_name}. It decided we were nothing to worry about.
"Then it made one small call, out over the dark water.
"That was the first voice that island ever heard."
Marta smiles at the net in her lap.
"It stayed the night, and in the morning it was gone," she says. "But it came back the next year, and it brought others. Birds carry seeds home in their feathers without meaning to and drop them wherever they land, so the green came a little at a time.
"Every island you can see out there began the same way. Bare, and quiet, and then a visitor."
Marta looks out at the green hump in the water.
"Goodnight, {island_name}," she says. "Sleep well."

c1.question: Marta stops with the needle in the air. "Now you tell me what I did first," she says. "Walk the black sand along the water, or go up the little hill and see the whole island at once. Sand, or hill?"

options.label: Walk the black sand along the water's edge
Climb the little hill to see the whole island

c2.question: "You choose again," says Marta, and she holds the net still in her lap. "Lean down to the little green shoot, or hold quite still and let the seabird land. Shoot, or bird?"

options.label: Lean down to the first green shoot
Hold still and let the seabird land

island_name.role: the young island with no name yet

s1.text: You wake up in a soft grass nest. You are a round yellow puff. Your feet go wiggle, wiggle, wiggle. They want to go! Mama Duck stretches up tall. "Quack, quack," she says. That means follow me! You peep. "Peep, peep, peep!" You tumble out of the nest. Slap, slap, slap go your little feet. You are the last one in line. The littlest one. Mama waits. She looks back at you. "Quack," she says. Come along, little one. Today is the day! Today we walk all the way to the pond.

s2a.text: Slap, slap, slap. Past the red barn we go. Then — plip! A rain puddle! Little things wiggle in it. Wiggle, wiggle, wiggle, like tadpoles do. "Peep, peep, peep!" you say. What is THIS? "Quack," says Mama. Baby frogs. Swimming before they can hop! You lean in close. But your shadow falls — splish! They all scatter! You wait. You hold still. One little tadpole comes back. Dot, dot, dot. You dabble your beak in. Hello, little swimmer!

s2b.text: Slap, slap, slap. Past the cozy coop we go. Then — cheep, cheep! Tiny cheeps! Mama Hen fluffs her wing wide. Underneath is dark and warm. A feather house! "Peep, peep, peep!" you say. What is THIS? "Quack," says Mama. Baby chicks, all tucked in. You lean in close. It is rumbly in there. You count the cheeps. One, two, three! Then one little chick peeks out. It looks at you. "Cheep!" it says, beak to beak. Hello, little one!

s3.text: Through the meadow gate we go. The tall grass tickles our fluff. Tickle, tickle! A lamb bounces over. "Baa!" it says. And far across the field, its mama turns her head that very second. "Baa!" she calls back. Every mama knows her own baby's sound. Just like Mama knows our peep. Under the willow tree, a mama robin feeds her nestlings. Little beaks open wide, like tiny flowers. Then the path ends. The pond! Big and shiny and new. A frog says, "Ribbit." Plop! Mama slides into the water. "Quack, quack," she calls. That means: your turn, little one.

s4a.text: You put one foot in. Slap! The water lifts you up! Babies float! "Peep, peep!" you cry. "Quack," says Mama. I knew you could. You paddle behind her. Slap, slap, slap go your feet. A frog swims beside you. "Ribbit," it says. Hello, neighbor. You bob past the lily pads. You are swimming! At the muddy edge you climb out. Shake your fluff. One wet footprint stays on the mud. Yours. You are a swimming duckling now.

s4b.text: You stay at the warm muddy edge. You dabble. Peep, peep, peep at the ripples. Peep at your own wobbly face peeping back. Plop! goes the frog. Plop, plop, plop from pad to pad. Mama floats close. "Quack," she says, soft. I am here. You press your fluff against her warm side. The sun sprinkles gold on the water. The pond knows your peeping face now. Tomorrow you will swim. Today you dabble with Mama.

c1.question: "Quack quack, little one — shall we visit the wiggly swimmers in the puddle, or the cheeping chicks under the hen's wing?"

options.label: Stop at the rain puddle to meet the tadpoles
Stop at the coop to peek under Mama Hen's wing

c2.question: "Quack quack, Peeper — will you put a foot in and float with me, or shall we dabble together here at the warm muddy edge?"

options.label: Put a foot in and paddle across the pond behind Mama
Stay at the muddy edge and explore the ripples with Mama

s1.text: Pip was squeezed. Not hugged. Squeezed. Her shell had been a fine shell once, roomy as a big coat. Now it pinched like a shoe one size too small, and her soft curled back end, the part that went round and round like a question mark, had nowhere left to go. “Scritch-scritch-scritch,” went the shell, dragging across the rock of the tide pool. Scritch. Scritch. It was low tide. The water sat still and clear, and Pip tugged her too-tight shell sideways past a starfish who was doing absolutely nothing, and doing it very well. Then something came wobbling around a stone. It was a hermit crab wearing a bright red bottle cap. It tipped. It righted itself. It beamed. “Behold,” said the Bottle-Cap Crab, “the Cap House! Light! Stylish! Nearly waterproof!” It tipped over again. Pip watched it wobble past, pincers waving like a tiny inventor taking a bow. On the warm flat rock, the shore crab lay stretched out in the sun, lazy as a cat in a window. “Why the fuss?” it yawned. “A shell’s a shell. Or a cap.” Pip did not answer. Because just then, a shadow swept over the tide pool. Wide wings. A gull. It circled once, then flapped off toward the far end of the beach. It would be back. Pip tucked her question-mark tail in as far as it would go, which was not far at all. “Right,” she said, mostly to herself. “I need a bigger shell. Now.”

s2a.text: Pip went sideways, fast as her too-tight shell would drag her. Scritch-scritch-scritch. On the far side of the tide pool, half-buried in sand, sat a shell so beautiful she stopped moving just to look at it. It curled round and round like a question mark, striped cream and brown, big as a teacup. "That one," Pip whispered. "That is the one." The Bottle-Cap Crab tipped over with excitement. "A palace!" it announced. "Try it! Try it!" Pip backed out of her old shell. The cool water touched her soft curled tail. She wiggled backward into the new shell, round and round, deeper and deeper. It fit. It fit perfectly. "It fits!" she shouted. She took one sideways step. The shell did not move. She pulled harder. The shell tipped, slow as a falling tree, and rolled her onto the sand. Her soft belly flashed up at the sky. Above the pool, a wide shadow swept across the water. The gull. Back already. Pip kicked her legs in the air. "Not now," she squeaked. "Not now!" The Bottle-Cap Crab pushed at her with both pincers. "Out! Out!" Pip popped free, scrambled sideways, and squeezed back into her old too-tight shell just as the shadow slid past. The gull circled once. It flapped off. Pip lay very still, her heart going thump-thump-thump against the rock. "The palace," said the Bottle-Cap Crab sadly, "is too heavy." "The palace," said Pip, "is a terrible palace." But her tail still pinched. And the gull would be back.

s2b.text: Pip went sideways, quick as she could. Scritch-scritch-scritch. Behind a flat green stone she found it: a pale shell, light as a leaf, sitting open like a little boat. "Light!" said the Bottle-Cap Crab, tapping it with one pincer. "You could run in that!" Pip backed out of her old shell. Cool water touched her soft curled tail. She wiggled backward, round and round, and the new shell slid on easy as a sock. She took a sideways step. Then another. She was fast. She was nearly skipping. "Look at me!" she shouted. "I am a racing crab!" She zigged. She zagged. The Bottle-Cap Crab cheered and fell over. Then Pip felt it. A thin line of cold water, trickling down her soft belly. She twisted her eye-stalks around. There, right down the side of her beautiful light shell, ran a crack. Long as a blade of grass. Wide as her own leg. Above the pool, a shadow swept the water. The gull. Back already. Pip froze. Through the crack, her soft question-mark tail showed pink against the pale shell. The shadow circled. "Out!" squeaked the Bottle-Cap Crab. Pip popped free and scrambled under the flat green stone, her heart going thump-thump-thump. The gull landed on the rock above them. It looked at the Bottle-Cap Crab. It looked at the ridiculous red cap. It looked away. The cap had no crack. The gull flapped off. Pip breathed out, long and slow. "The light shell," she said, "has a hole in it." "A window," said the Bottle-Cap Crab. "Very stylish. Very nearly waterproof." Pip did not laugh. Her tail was bare. And the gull would be back.

s3.text: Pip ducked under the ledge of the warm flat rock, heart going thump-thump-thump like a tiny drum. She thought. The heavy shell had been the right size, but far too heavy. The cracked shell had been the right weight, but broken. Nothing on this beach was right. "You worry too much," said the shore crab, still stretched out in the sun. "Just pick one and stop fussing." "Easy for you," said Pip. "Your shell grows with you." Then she saw it. Across the tide pool sat a big hermit crab in a beautiful spiral shell, roomy as a house with an extra room. And at the shell's opening, the big crab's soft curled back end was poking out, squeezed tight, tucked away like a question mark with no room to finish its curve. Pip knew that feeling. She scuttled sideways over, scritch-scritch-scritch, and tapped gently on the spiral shell with one pincer. Tap-tap. That was how hermit crabs asked to trade. The big crab pinched back. Not hard. Just firmly. No. "Worth a try," said Pip, backing away sideways. But she was not squashed. Not even a little. Because now she knew something worth knowing. That big crab was outgrowing its shell too. And a crab who is outgrowing a shell will not keep it forever. Somewhere behind her, the Bottle-Cap Crab tipped over with a clatter. "Did it work?" it called. "What did you find?" "Patience," said Pip, and she settled in to watch.

s4a.text: Pip tucked herself into the crack beside the big crab. It was a thin crack, a nothing crack, and her soft curled back end folded into it like it had been made for exactly this. The question mark had a hiding place after all. "Scritch," went her shell, once, and then she held still. The big crab did not look at her. It was busy. It had found a shell half-buried in the sand, a wide pale shell, and it was turning it over, tapping it, peering inside. "Come on," Pip whispered. "Come on, come on." The big crab slid out of its spiral shell, quick as a wink, and into the new one. Gone. And there it sat. The old shell. Empty. Roomy. Waiting. Pip did not wait one second more. She scooted out of the crack, sideways, fast, and backed straight into the spiral shell. It was a little tight. It was a little lopsided. It was whole, and it was light, and it was hers. Then the shadow came. Wide wings, sweeping over the tide pool. The gull. Pip pulled herself in, every leg, every pincer, and the gull's shadow passed over a shell on a rock, nothing more, and moved on. Around the stone came a wobble and a clatter. The Bottle-Cap Crab tipped, righted itself, and stood very still, staring at Pip in her new shell. "Behold," it said softly, like an inventor whose terrible machine had finally, finally worked. "The waiting machine. You sit. You hide. You win." It tapped the spiral shell with one pincer. "Finest engineering I have ever seen. And I have seen a bottle cap."

s4b.text: Pip tucked herself into the crack beside the big crab. It was a thin crack, a nothing crack, and her soft curled back end folded into it like it had been made for exactly this. The question mark had a hiding place after all. "Scritch," went her shell, once, and then she held still. The big crab did not look at her. It was busy, turning over a wide pale shell half-buried in the sand, tapping it, peering inside. "Come on," Pip whispered. "Come on, come on." The big crab slid out of its spiral shell, quick as a wink, and into the new one. Gone. And there it sat. The old shell. Empty. Roomy. Waiting. Pip scooted out of the crack, sideways, fast, and backed straight in. A little tight. A little lopsided. Whole, and light, and hers. Then the shadow came. Wide wings, sweeping over the tide pool. The gull. Pip pulled in every leg, every pincer, and the shadow passed over a shell on a rock, nothing more, and moved on. On the warm flat rock, the shore crab was watching. It had not moved all day, but it had seen everything. "Hm," it said. "What?" said Pip. "That crack," said the shore crab slowly. "I could not have fit in that crack. Too hard. Too wide." It stretched, lazy as ever, but its eyes stayed on her. "So. A soft back end." A pause. "Has its uses." Pip felt her question-mark tail curl, deep inside her new shell, all the way to the end of its curve for the very first time. On the way home she picked up a scrap of seaweed in one pincer and carried it sideways, like a sandwich, for later.

c1.question: "Two shells, little crab!" the Bottle-Cap Crab announces, tapping one with each pincer. "This one is big and beautiful. This one is light as a feather. Which do you try first?"

options.label: Try the big beautiful spiral shell
Try the light easy-to-drag shell

c2.question: "The big crab will move soon," the shore crab says, clicking its hard shell. "Do you want to wait right here where you can see it, or tuck into that crack and wait where the gull can't see you?"

options.label: Wait in the open where you can watch the bigger crab
Tuck into the crack and wait where the gull can't see you

s1.text:
Dad seahorse wrapped his curly tail around a blade of seagrass and held on tight. His body was swollen and glowing. Then he pumped. And jerked. And out burst a cloud of seahorse fry, smaller than grains of rice, tumbling like living confetti into the green water. One of them was {hero_name}. He spun head over tail, too tiny to steer, and stared at everything. Sunlight poured down in golden ribbons through the meadow. The seagrass swayed. Dad's tail gripped the grass like it was the safest thing in the world.

"What was that?" a voice said. A pipefish zipped in, long and thin and curious. "I'm Zephyr. How did you all fit in there? What's a brood pouch? Why do you curl?"

{hero_name} blinked. He didn't know anything yet. He just wanted to stay close to the grass where he was born, and see every single thing in this enormous world.

Far above, a dragonfly skated across the bright skin of the water, quick as a skipped stone.

But the current was pulling. Quietly, gently, it tugged at the cloud of fry. Some drifted one way. Some drifted another. {hero_name} reached out his own small tail, but he did not know how to hold on.

"Where are you going?" Zephyr called.

s2a.text:
"Fight it!" {hero_name} squeaked. He stood tall in the water, the way Dad stood, and fluttered his tiny back fin as hard as it would buzz. Bzzzz. Bzzzz. He pushed toward the green meadow. He pushed with everything he had.

"Look at that fin go!" Zephyr cried, arrowing alongside him. "How does it move so fast? It is just a blur! Does it ever get tired?"

{hero_name} did not answer. He was too busy swimming. But the current was stronger than his little fin. It tugged him sideways. It tumbled him backward. He kicked and fluttered, but the seagrass grew smaller and smaller behind him.

"You are going the wrong way!" Zephyr called, zipping in a circle. "The water is winning! How can something so soft be so strong?"

{hero_name} stopped. He was breathing hard. His fin ached. He looked at the open blue water all around him, so big and so empty. He was farther from home than ever. And he was all alone.

s2b.text:
"Hide!" {hero_name} whispered. He stopped fighting the current. He dropped down, down, down to the pale sand below. He went perfectly still, the way he somehow knew seahorses do. He did not move a muscle. He did not blink an eye.

"What are you doing?" Zephyr asked, hovering above him. "Why are you just lying there? Is this a game?"

{hero_name} stayed quiet. He waited for the sea to forget him. But the sand was white, and he was brown, and there was no green seagrass to hide him. His small shadow lay plain on the bright sand, dark as a drop of ink.

"I see you!" a voice chirped. A young fish named Snapper darted toward him, quick as a blink.

{hero_name} gasped. He fluttered his fin and shot up into the drifting murk, just as Snapper's mouth snapped shut on empty sand. He hung in the cloudy water, heart pounding. Stillness had not saved him. There was nothing here to match, nowhere to blend in. He was still out in the open, and still alone.

s3.text: The water shoved. {hero_name} tumbled, and his tail lashed out and caught a strand of drifting weed. He held on with everything he had. But the weed was not holding on to anything. It was wandering, and now so was he, lost and moving at the same time. "Where is this going?" Zephyr cried, zipping alongside. "Why are you riding it? Can you steer?" {hero_name} could not steer. Then the weed brushed against something tattered and brown, and the tattered thing opened one ancient eye. "Little fry," it said, slow as settling sand. "You are holding a leaf that cannot hold you." It was Grandmother Weed, and she was not a leaf at all. She was a seahorse, her tail corkscrewed deep around a grass blade rooted in the meadow floor, her body the exact green of the swaying grass. Snapper glided past, close enough to touch, and did not see her at all. "How did you vanish?" Zephyr breathed. "Is it camouflage? How does your skin know what colour to be?" Grandmother Weed's eye crinkled. "My tail holds what holds the earth. My colour wears what the meadow wears. That is the whole secret, and it is not a secret." {hero_name} looked at his own small tail, then at the rooted grass below. "Will you show me?" he asked. "Show me everything you just found out," said Grandmother Weed, "and then let us begin."

s4a.text:
{hero_name} stopped fighting. He let go of the wandering weed, and the current carried him gently down to the first rooted blade of grass. His tail corkscrewed around it, just like Dad's had. Then his skin did something wonderful. It turned slowly, slowly seagrass green.

"You're doing it!" Zephyr whispered. "How does your skin know?"

Snapper glided past. His eyes slid right over {hero_name}, over one more leaf in the green forest. {hero_name} held his breath and held on. Snapper was gone.

"Now," said Zephyr, "blade by blade. Quiet as a leaf."

They moved through the meadow, tail to grass, grass to tail, until {hero_name} saw him. Dad. Still gripping the same stem, right where the world began.

"You came back," Dad said.

"I held on," said {hero_name}.

And there, caught in the grass beside Dad's tail, was a tiny curled shell no bigger than a tear. {hero_name} tucked it close. His tail knew, at last, what to hold.

s4b.text:
{hero_name} stopped fighting. He gripped the first rooted blade he reached, and his skin turned slowly, slowly seagrass green. Then he waited.

While he waited, tiny shrimp drifted past his nose. His snout went slurp. Slurp-slurp-slurp. He was aiming like a straw, and the shrimp simply vanished inside. It was the first meal he had ever caught all by himself.

"Did you just drink a shrimp?" Zephyr cried. "Through your snout? Like a straw?"

"Like a straw," said {hero_name}, and his belly felt warm and full.

Fed and steady, he worked his way home along the rooted blades, tail to grass, grass to tail, with Zephyr zipping beside him. And there was Dad, still gripping the same stem.

"You came back fed," Dad said.

"I learned the slurp," said {hero_name}.

As he spoke, one green scale-fleck drifted loose from his brand-new camouflage and caught in the grass. {hero_name} tucked it close. Proof he was a real meadow seahorse now.

c1.question: "Little cousin, the water is pulling you away! Will you fight it — flutter that fin and swim straight home? Or will you hide — drop down, go still, and let the sea forget you?"

options.label: Swim straight back against the current
Drop to the sand and stay perfectly still

c2.question: "You hold and hide like an old one now, little cousin. But home is far and the water is wide. Will you wait for the calm and slip home quiet as a leaf? Or will you stay and hunt — learn the slurp, fill your belly, and swim home fed and strong?"

options.label: Hold on, stay hidden, and slip home when the water calms
Stay gripped and learn to slurp up drifting shrimp first

hero_name.role: The seahorse fry's name, spoken by Dad, Zephyr, and Grandmother Weed throughout

s1.text: The pool is quiet this morning. Just us, and Grandpa Joe, and the big basket of toys. Pip digs right to the bottom. "This one," says Pip. A bright yellow duck. "Dabble," says Grandpa Joe. "A fine name." On the shallow step, he pushes Dabble under. Blub. Up it pops. "Full of air," says Grandpa Joe. "That is why it floats." He hums his little bubble-tune. Pip watches Dabble bob. "I want to float like that," says Pip. "On my back." Grandpa Joe holds out his hands. Pip leans back. Lifts one foot. Lifts the other. Down goes Pip's bottom. Splash. "Ker-plop," says Grandpa Joe. Pip tries again. Feet up. Bottom down. Splash. "Ker-plop."

s2a.text: "Bubbles first," says Pip. Grandpa Joe hums his bubble-tune. Pip puts just their lips in the water. Blow. Blub-blub-blub. The bubbles tickle Pip's nose. It rumbles funny, like a purring cat. Pip giggles. Snort! Water goes up. "Too big," says Grandpa Joe. "Soft and slow, little fish." Pip tries again. Soft. Slow. Blub-blub-blub. A long stream of bubbles dances up. Then Pip takes a big breath. Their chest puffs up, round and full of air. Just like Dabble's round yellow belly. "Look," says Pip. "I'm full of air too." Grandpa Joe smiles. "That you are," he says. "That you are."

s2b.text: "Chase the duck," says Pip. Grandpa Joe tosses Dabble out. Ker-plop. Pip lies on their belly. Grandpa's hands hover close. Pip kicks stiff legs. Splash, splash. Nowhere. "Floppy feet," says Grandpa Joe. "Like a frog." Pip flops. Kick, kick, kick. The water pushes back. Pip scoots forward. One whole glide. The water holds Pip up the whole time. It feels like a big soft hand. Pip reaches. Gotcha. Dabble bobs in Pip's arms. "You floated," says Grandpa Joe. "On your belly." Pip hugs the wet yellow duck. "Again," says Pip. "Again."

s3.text: Grandpa Joe turns Dabble upside down and pushes him under. Blub. Up he pops, right side up, bobbing. "Air inside," says Grandpa Joe. "That is the secret." He hums his little bubble-tune. Then he scrunches his hand into a ball. Down it dips, low in the water. He spreads his fingers wide, flat like a star. Up it floats. "See?" says Grandpa Joe. "Big breath. Loose body. Wide like a starfish." Pip looks at Dabble. Pip looks at the star-hand. "Like that?" says Pip. "Just like that," says Grandpa Joe. "Show me what you found." Pip takes a big, big breath. Arms out. Legs out. Grandpa Joe's warm hand rests under Pip's back. The water lifts. The water holds. Pip's feet leave the bottom. "I'm floating!" says Pip. "Ker-plop," says Grandpa Joe, softly. "No splash at all."

s4a.text: Pip takes a big breath. "One finger," says Grandpa Joe. Off comes one. "Two." Off comes two. Pip's cheeks puff out. Pip's toes wiggle above the water. Off comes the last finger, and Grandpa Joe's hand hovers close, not touching. The water lifts. The water holds. "I'm doing it!" says Pip. "All by myself!" Grandpa Joe hums his little bubble-tune. The lifeguard smiles and gives a thumbs-up. Dabble bobs beside them, bright and yellow. "Ker-plop," says Grandpa Joe, softly. "No splash at all." Then Pip stands up, laughing, and scoops Dabble close. Home they go, wrapped in the warm towel. And at bedtime, Dabble sits by Pip's pillow, ready for the story.

s4b.text: "Let's glide," says Pip. Grandpa Joe sets Dabble on the far step, bright and yellow, waiting. Pip leans back. Big breath. Arms out. Legs out. "One long, slow ker-plop," says Grandpa Joe. "Ready?" Pip kicks. Splash, splash, splash. The water lifts. The water holds. Pip glides on their back, right across the shallow step. "I'm moving!" says Pip. "I'm really moving!" Grandpa Joe hums his little bubble-tune, walking beside. Then — bump. Pip's fingers touch the step. "You made it!" says Grandpa Joe. Pip sits up, laughing, and grabs Dabble tight. Home they go, Dabble riding on Pip's tummy in the warm towel, still smelling of pool water.

c1.question: "Well, little fish, Dabble here floats easy as pie. Shall we practice our bubble-blowing first, or shall we chase this rascal duck across the water?"

options.label: Practice blowing gentle bubbles that tickle your nose
Lie on your belly and kick after the duck

c2.question: "You're floating, Pip, you're really floating! Now then — do you want to let go of my fingers one by one and float all by yourself, or shall we kick-glide on your back, nice and slow, all the way to Dabble?"

options.label: Let go one finger at a time and float solo
Kick-glide on your back across to the duck

stories.title: Ravi and the Blue Marble Ride

s1.text:
"Ravi! Come quick." Astronaut Bea is waving from the big round window, the one at the end of the space station corridor. {hero_name} runs. Socks on a metal floor, so it's more of a slide, really. Bea catches him by the shoulders and points. "Look. Right there."

Outside the glass, the whole Earth hangs below them. Blue. Huge. The kind of blue that makes you forget what you were about to say. A long coastline curves along the edge of a continent, and a river winds across the land like a silver ribbon someone dropped.

"It's like a marble," {hero_name} whispers. "A giant blue marble rolling in sunlight."

Bea grins. "Wait till you see it from out there."

Something small and silver zips past the window. It loops back. It hovers right outside the glass, blinking a tiny green light.

"That's Pip," says Bea. "A satellite. He orbits the whole planet, and he has been asking all morning if someone wants to ride along."

A crackly little voice pipes through the speaker on the wall. "Ooh, look at THAT one! That is a very good coastline. You should see it from my side. Hop in, hop in!"

A small hatch opens on Pip's side. A pod, just the right size for one kid.

{hero_name} looks at Bea. Bea looks at {hero_name}. "Well?"

He climbs in.

s2a.text:
"Clouds! Good pick!" Pip tips his whole silver side, and the pod tips with him, and the world swings up to meet them.

Below, the ocean is dark blue and busy. And there — a giant pinwheel of cloud, spinning slow over the water. Arms of white curl around and around, like the swirl on top of a milkshake, only bigger than a country.

"Ooh, look at THAT one!" Pip chirps. "That is a storm doing its exercises. Round and round. It never gets dizzy. I get dizzy just watching, and I do not even have a tummy."

{hero_name} laughs, and then he sees it. Where the deep blue stops, there is a wiggly border — tan sand, then white foam, then blue again. A coastline, curving like a line someone drew with a very good pencil.

"The line," he breathes. "It's like the river. It bends the same way."

He presses his finger to the glass and traces it, up and around and down. The glass is cold. The line slides away under his fingertip, because Pip's orbit never stops, not for anyone.

"Wait — I'm not done!"

"No taking it home!" says Pip. "But hold on. I know a trick."

He slows, just a little, just enough, and the coastline lingers one more long lovely second while {hero_name}'s finger finishes the curve.

s2b.text:
"Islands! Excellent!" Pip flips his silver nose toward the open ocean, and the pod glides after, smooth as a spoon through pudding.

At first there is only blue. Then — dots. One, two, three, a whole scatter of dark green islands rising out of the water, and they are not sprinkled any old way. They make a line. A long, curved line, like the dots on a dot-to-dot page.

"Count them, count them!" Pip chirps. "I always lose count. I get to nine and then I see a good cloud and have to start again."

{hero_name} counts, slow, out loud. "Ten. Eleven. Twelve." Around each island the water turns pale turquoise, soft and milky, like someone stirred cream into the blue.

"Ooh, look at THAT!" says Pip. "Those pale bits are the shallows. Down under there are coral reefs — whole underwater gardens, busy with fish. We are too high to see the fish. But the reef shows itself anyway, if you know where to look."

{hero_name} leans close to the glass. "Pip. The islands make the same line as the coastline. The same bendy one."

"They DO," Pip says, delighted. "The Earth draws that line everywhere."

The turquoise shapes fade behind them. The orbit pulls on.

s3.text:
Pip's orbit swings them over land now, and the light is turning slow and golden.

"Ooh, ooh, look down!" Pip chirps. "What did you find back there? Tell me everything."

Before {hero_name} can answer, Pip gasps. "Wait. Look at THAT one first."

Below them, a big river winds across the land like a shiny brown ribbon, curling from the mountains all the way toward the sea. It bends. It loops. It never once goes straight.

"Another curvy line," {hero_name} breathes. "It's like the coastline. It's collecting them."

"Everything curvy is my favourite," says Pip, spinning a happy little loop. "Where does it end? Where does it end?"

"The sea," says {hero_name}. "Can we follow it? All the way?"

"Hold on to your socks."

Pip tips, and the river slides beneath them, bend after bend after bend. Then the edge of night rolls over the land — and one by one, golden lights begin to blink on below. Clusters of them. Long strings of them, like someone spilled a jar of stars along the ground.

"City lights," Pip whispers, suddenly quiet. "Every dot is a home."

{hero_name} presses his forehead to the glass. The river ribbon glints ahead, heading for the dark coastline — and the lights keep multiplying, sparkling awake as night spreads.

"So," says Pip, his green light blinking. "Do we chase the river to the sea, or go count those lights?"

s4a.text:
"The lights," says {hero_name}. "Let's find the brightest clump."

"Ooh, yes. Hold on to your socks."

Pip tips, and they dive their eyes down toward the dark. Below, whole cities are switching on. Golden dots sprinkle across the black, then clump, then glow — bright clusters where a million homes hum at once.

"That one!" Pip chirps. "Look at THAT one!"

It spreads like spilled honey, thick and shining, with thin bright strings running out of it — roads, {hero_name} realizes. Roads made of light.

"Every dot is somebody's kitchen," he whispers. "Somebody's cat. Somebody's cocoa."

Pip goes very quiet, the way he does when something is beautiful. Then: click. "Got it. A photo. I'm signing it."

"You don't have hands."

"I'm signing it in my heart."

The station swings around the curve of the world, growing bigger, and there is Bea at the round window, holding two mugs. Pip docks with a soft bump.

"Well?" says Bea.

{hero_name} climbs out, the photo warm in his pocket — a curving coastline of light, signed by a satellite. "Pip," he says, "everything curvy is my favourite too."

s4b.text:
"The edge," says {hero_name}. "Let's race the edge."

"Ooh, fast one. Hold on to your socks."

Pip tilts, and they chase the line where night meets day. It slides beneath them, slow as a page turning — and then, right along the curve of the world, something appears.

A skinny blue halo. Glowing. Hugging the planet all the way around, thin as the skin on warm milk.

"The air," {hero_name} breathes. "That's the air. All of it."

"All of it," Pip whispers. "Every breath everybody ever breathed, in one thin curvy line."

It shimmers — blue fading to gold where the sun catches it. Another curving line, the curviest one yet, wrapped around everything.

"It's going," says Pip. "The edge is moving."

Click. "Got it. A photo. For your pocket."

The halo slips away behind them, and the station swings around the curve of the world, growing bigger. There is Bea at the round window, holding two mugs. Pip docks with a soft bump.

"Well?" says Bea.

{hero_name} climbs out, the photo warm in his pocket — one thin glowing line, holding the whole world. "Bea," he says, "the air is a ribbon too."

c1.question: Pip chirps, "Quick, Ravi — shall we chase the giant spinning clouds, or hop over to the island dots?"

options.label: Chase the giant white cloud spiral over the ocean
Glide over the volcanic island chain and turquoise reef hints

c2.question: Pip hums, "Last look before home, Ravi — do we hunt the brightest city lights, or race to the glowing edge of the air?"

options.label: Hunt the brightest clusters of city lights in the dark
Race to the thin glowing rim of air along Earth's edge

hero_name.role: the child hero riding with Pip

s1.text:
{hero_name}'s pink flowers grew in a pot by the back door, and they were the best flowers in the garden. {hero_name} had watered them every morning for a week.
A bee came past {hero_name}'s ear, close enough to move the air.
It did not stop.
Another came, and then three more, and then too many to count. They all came up out of the two white boxes at the bottom of the garden, and they all went the same way. Over the grass. Over the far fence. Gone.
Barnaby watched them go. Barnaby was a very large and very serious old dog, and he went wherever {hero_name} went.
"They ignored us," he said. He took it personally. He took most things personally.
{hero_name} crouched down by the pot. The pink flowers stayed wide open and empty, every single one of them.
"Barnaby," said {hero_name}. "How does every one of those bees know where to go?"

s2a.text:
The bee on the lavender was working the way {hero_name} works a bowl of cereal. Head down. No time for talking.
{hero_name} knelt in close.
On each back leg the bee had a fat little pocket of yellow, packed on tight, like butter pressed onto a knife. She shoved into one purple flower and came out yellower. She shoved into the next one and came out yellower still.
"Pollen," said {hero_name}. "Barnaby, look at her legs. She is taking it home."
Barnaby leaned in to see. His nose came so close that the bee walked round to the other side of the flower and carried on.
"Rude," said Barnaby.
Then up she went, over the grass, over the fence, one small bee with her legs full, going exactly where all the others were going.
Every bee knew. Nobody had told {hero_name}.

s2b.text:
{hero_name} turned the bucket upside down and stood on it to see over the fence.
The bees had made a road in the air.
Going out, they crossed at the same spot every time, just above the wobbly post. Coming home, they used the air lower down, sliding along over the grass towards the white boxes. Out along the top, back along the bottom, like the two escalators at the shops.
"They are all doing the same thing," said {hero_name}. "Barnaby. Every one of them is doing exactly the same thing."
Barnaby sat down on {hero_name}'s foot, which was how he agreed with things.
One bee came home so low and so heavy that she nearly parted his ears. She lifted at the last moment, landed on the white box, and walked in through the little door.
Whatever they were fetching, it was worth the whole long way.
Every bee knew the road. Nobody had told {hero_name}.

s3.text:
Ada keeps the two white boxes. She was down at the bottom of the garden with her sleeves rolled up, watching the bees come and go.
"Ada," said {hero_name}. "Not one of them will come to my pink flowers."
{hero_name} told her about {first_clue}.
"Good noticing," said Ada. "That is half of it already. Come and stand by me. Still hands, slow feet. Then they go round us the way water goes round a stone."
So {hero_name} stood still beside her. A bee landed on {hero_name}'s wrist, walked two steps, and lifted off again. Barnaby stood still too, and held his breath, just in case.
{hero_name} put an ear near the wood. The box hummed like the fridge at night. In there, in the dark, were thousands of them.
"They are not ignoring your flowers," said Ada. "They found somewhere better. And then somebody told them where it is."
"Told them?" said {hero_name}. "Bees tell each other things?"

s4a.text:
Ada slid back a small wooden shutter. Under it was a window of glass, and under the glass was the dark.
{hero_name}'s eyes took a moment. Then the dark filled up with bees, hundreds of them, walking about on a wall of yellow comb. One came in with two yellow pockets on her legs and pushed them off into a hole in the comb.
"Watch this one," whispered Ada.
One bee was doing something nobody else was doing. She walked a short straight line, shaking her back end so fast that it blurred. Then she curved round and walked the very same line again. And again.
The bees near her pressed in and touched her all over with their feelers.
"The straight part tells them which way," said Ada. "A long shake means far. She has been somewhere good, and now the whole house knows."
One by one, the bees who had touched her turned round, went out of the door, and crossed the fence exactly the way she said.
Ada put a drop of honey on {hero_name}'s finger. It tasted of clover.
Barnaby licked the finger clean and did not apologise.

s4b.text:
Out at the corner gate, the field on the other side had gone white. Clover. All the way across, more clover than anybody could pick in a week.
{hero_name} stopped to listen. The whole field was humming, low and busy, the way the kitchen sounds through the door when everyone in there is making lunch.
"There it is," said Ada. "It opened on Tuesday. Every hive for a mile knows."
The bees were rolling about in the little white heads and coming out dusty. {hero_name} watched one pat the yellow dust into the pockets on her back legs, fatter, fatter, and then she was up and away home, low over the grass.
Barnaby lay down in the clover and let a bee walk right across his paw without moving one hair, which for Barnaby was an enormous thing to manage.
They followed that bee home. Just inside the little door of the white box, where the light stopped, she walked a short straight line and shook her back end at everyone.
"That is her telling them," said Ada. "Which way. How far."
{hero_name} picked one clover flower for the kitchen table.

c1.question: "Two things worth looking at," said Barnaby, pointing his nose. "That one on the lavender, doing something with her legs. Or the whole lot of them, crossing the fence in a line. Legs, or fence?"

options.label: Look close at the one bee on the lavender

sets_slots.first_clue: the two fat pockets of yellow on the bee's back legs

options.label: Follow the line of bees over the fence

sets_slots.first_clue: the road the bees had made in the air over the fence

c2.question: "Two ways to find out," said Ada. "There is a little window in the side of this box, and through it you can watch them tell each other. Or we can walk out to the corner and see the place they were told about. Window, or field?"

options.label: Watch them tell each other through the little window
Walk out and see the place they were told about

hero_name.role: the child in the garden who works the mystery out

first_clue.role: the clue the child chose to follow in the garden
first_clue.default: the two fat pockets of yellow on the bee's back legs

s1.text: Grandma's porch chair creaks like a contented cat when she sits down, and that is how we know evening has properly begun. "Look up, {hero_name}," she says. "First star." But it is not a star. We know stars. Stars twinkle, like they're shivering. This one does not shiver. It hangs over the garden fence, steady and silver, and it looks... wrapped up. Warm. Like it is wearing a blanket we cannot see. "Why does it shine so warm?" we ask. Grandma rocks. The chair purrs. "That," she says, "is Venus. And it has the thickest, cosiest, most backwards blanket in the whole sky." Backwards? We pull our own blanket tighter. How can a blanket be backwards? Grandma just smiles. "Ask it," she says. So we do. We lean out over the porch steps, and we whisper, "Venus, why are you so warm?" And the strangest thing happens. The light seems to wink. Not twinkle. Wink. Like it heard us. Like it has been waiting all evening for someone to ask.

s2a.text: We build the fort right there on the living room rug. Three chairs, two sofa cushions, and the big patchwork quilt. "In," we say. We pull {friend_name} under with us. It is dark and squishy and smells like laundry soap. "Now we wait," we whisper. "If the blanket holds our heat in, we will get toasty. Just like Venus." We hold very still. We listen to our own breathing. Slowly, slowly, the air gets thick. It gets heavy. It gets warm. "It is working!" {friend_name} says. "I am sweating!" We push the quilt up and tumble out, gasping. Grandma is waiting on the porch. The chair creaks. "Well?" she asks. "The blanket holds the heat close," we say. "It never lets it go." Grandma nods. "Venus wears a golden quilt of clouds," she says. "Thick as porridge, thick as jam. It never comes off. The whole planet stays toasty." We look up. The silver light winks again. Warm. But something still feels odd.

s2b.text: We run to the playground. {friend_name} is already there, hanging off the merry-go-round. "Push me!" they shout. "But push me backwards!" We grab the bars. We run the wrong way round. The world spins backwards. The trees slide past in reverse. {friend_name} giggles so hard they nearly fall off. "It works!" they shout. "It feels funny, but it works!" We spin and spin until we are dizzy. We flop onto the grass. Grandma is waiting on the porch. The chair creaks. "Well?" she asks. "Backwards works," we say. "It feels strange, but it works." Grandma rocks. The chair purrs. "Venus spins backwards too," she says. "All the other planets go one way. Venus goes the other. As if something bumped it, long ago, and turned it round." We look up. The silver light hangs steady. Backwards. But why would a planet do that?

s3.text: Back on the porch steps, we are buzzing. Grandma holds up a hand. "Tell me," she says, her eyes twinkling like proper stars, "what did you find?" We tell her everything, all in a tumble. She listens, and the chair creaks, and the chair purrs. "Then it is time," she says, "for the blanket trick." From her sewing basket she brings out an old globe and a flashlight. She hands us the light. "You be the sun." We click it on. Grandma wraps the globe in her thick yellow shawl, fold over fold, till it looks like a lumpy golden quilt. "Venus wears clouds," she says, "thicker than any blanket. The sun's warmth slips in... and cannot slip back out." The shawl feels warm already. Then Grandma does the funniest thing. She spins the globe. The wrong way round. Slow, slow, backwards, like a top that changed its mind. "Long ago," she says, "something gave Venus a great big bump, and ever since, it turns the other way. On Venus, the sun rises in the west." We stare at the glowing quilt turning backwards in her hands. Warm blanket. Backwards spin. One strange, wonderful world. "So it is backwards," we say, "and it is proud of it."
