Grandma laughs, and the porch chair purrs.

s4a.text: We pull the golden blanket around our shoulders, and it smells of wool and Grandma's lavender soap. "I am Venus," we say, stepping into the garden where the grass is cool. "The Evening Star with my thick cloudy coat." We wrap it tighter, fold over fold, just like the shawl on the globe. "You look like a lumpy quilt," Grandma says from her chair. Creak. Purr. "A beautiful, backwards lumpy quilt." We stand very still, feeling the warmth trapped close, while above us the real Venus hangs steady and bright. "Do you feel it?" we whisper up. "The warm staying in?" The light seems to soften, like a friend tucking in their own blanket. We are small on the porch steps, wrapped up and different, and the night air cannot reach us. "It is not so strange," we say, "being backwards." Grandma rocks. "No," she says. "Just warm." We keep the blanket on. It is ours now.

s4b.text: "Spin with me!" {friend_name} shouts, already on the merry-go-round. We climb on, and the metal is cold under our hands. "Backwards," we say. "Like Venus." We push off with our feet, slow, slow, the wrong way round. The world tilts. Grandma's porch light trails behind us, then the fence, then the garden, all sliding backwards past our eyes. "Wheee!" {friend_name} yells, hair flopping into their face. "We are Venus!" We spin and spin, dizzier than a top that changed its mind, and the chair creaks from the porch. Purr. Purr. "Careful!" Grandma calls, but she is laughing. We are not careful. We are backwards and silly and exactly right. Finally we wobble to a stop, the world still turning inside our heads. "Did you see?" we gasp. "We were the backwards blanket!" {friend_name} nods, eyes crossed. "Best way to be," they say. We lie back on the metal, looking up at Venus, and we are still smiling.

c1.question: "Should we test how blankets trap heat first, or shall we find out why Venus turns the wrong way?"

options.label: Build the blanket fort to test the warmth
Go to the merry-go-round to feel the backwards turn

c2.question: "Now that we know Venus's secrets, do you want to wrap up tight like its cloudy blanket, or spin slow and backwards like its turn?"

options.label: Wrap in the golden blanket on the porch
Spin backwards on the merry-go-round

s1.text: Grandpa's kitchen table smells like toast. It is Saturday morning, and Grandpa has been drawing something on a big piece of paper for a whole hour, with his tongue sticking out the corner of his mouth like it does when he is concentrating very hard. "Look at this," he says, and slides the paper across to us. It is a maze. A proper one, with walls and corners and long skinny passages. Grandpa calls it {maze_name}. "I drew it just for you," he says. "And at the finish, I hid a treasure. A real one." He taps the very middle of the maze with one finger. Right there, he says, is {surprise_at_finish}. We put our pencil at the start. Easy, we think. We begin to draw. The line goes forward, turns left, turns right. But the closer we get to the middle, the more the maze seems to giggle at us. Dead end. Dead end. Another dead end. We are so close we can almost taste that treasure, and we cannot get there. Grandpa leans back in his chair and smiles. "Why do you think it gets harder," he says, "the closer you get?"

s2a.text: "The clues," we say. "We want to hunt for clues." Grandpa nods, slow and serious, like we have just chosen our expedition gear. "Good choice," he says. "Every dead end is a clue, if you know how to listen to it." We put our pencil back at the start and we go. The line runs forward, turns, and stops. Dead end. But this time, we mark it with a small X. "Good," we say out loud. "Now I know." We try another way. The line wiggles left, wiggles right, and stops again. Another X. "Good. Now I know." It feels a little like losing, at first. Every X is a tiny defeat. But then we look at the paper and we see it. The X's are not just marks. They are talking. They are telling us which way not to go. The maze is not a trap anymore. It is a conversation. We are not stuck. We are solving. We look at Grandpa. He is watching us, his eyes twinkling. "See?" he says. "The maze is telling you its secrets." We look at the paper. The X's are everywhere, but they are pointing the way. We just have to follow them. But will we have enough X's to find the treasure?

s2b.text: "A hint," we say. "Tell us the sneaky trick." Grandpa leans in close, like a fellow explorer sharing secret treasure map knowledge. He lowers his voice. "The trick," he whispers, "is to start at the finish." We blink. "But that is backwards!" Grandpa grins. "Exactly! The start of a maze has many choices. It is designed to confuse you. But the finish? The finish usually has only one path leading away from it. It is much easier to find your way out of a room with only one door." He taps the middle of the maze. "So, you flip your pencil. You start at the treasure, and you walk the maze backwards." We look at the paper. It feels like cheating, but it also feels like genius. We put our pencil on the finish, right where {surprise_at_finish} is waiting. We start to draw. The line goes backwards, out of the middle, and into the passages. And it is amazing. The maze seems to open up like a zipper. The dead ends we found before are not even on this path. The way is clear. It is a straight shot, right back to the start. We did it. We solved the maze by walking it backwards. We look at Grandpa, our mouths open. He just winks. "The sneakiest tricks," he says, "are the ones that are hiding in plain sight."

s3.text: Grandpa taps the middle of the maze. "So what did you find?" We tell him, and his eyes go crinkly at the corners. "Then you know the secret," he says. "Turn the paper around. Start at the treasure. Walk backwards." We spin the page. We put our pencil right on the finish, and we begin to draw the other way. Backwards, the whole maze changes. Passages that looked sneaky now look plain. And here is the funny thing: the worst dead ends, the ones that giggled at us, are all huddled near the treasure, like the maze was guarding it on purpose. From this side, we spot them before they spot us. Around the last corner, the pencil line stops, turns, and lands on the start. "Solved," Grandpa says, and he reaches into his pocket and sets {surprise_at_finish} on the table like a tiny treasure chest. It tastes like victory. "Now," he says, pulling out a fresh sheet of paper, "do you want to draw a maze of your own, with your own sneaky dead ends? Or shall we try a different kind of puzzle altogether?"

s4a.text: "Our turn," we say, and Grandpa slides the fresh paper over like a map to somewhere. We draw a start. We draw a finish. Then we do the sneaky thing first: we put our pencil on the finish and draw backwards, so we know the path really connects. The line stops, turns, wiggles home. Almost. One corner dead-ends where it shouldn't. "A wall where a door should be," Grandpa murmurs. We erase one little line, and the path opens like a yawn. Now we pile on the dead ends, fat ones, giggly ones, all huddled near the treasure where they do the most guarding. Grandpa takes the pencil. He frowns. He groans. "Impossible," he declares, and solves it in about four seconds. "Hey!" we shout. He laughs so hard his chair creaks. "A fair stump," he says, "is a gift. You made me feel clever and slow at the same time." We put the maze in our pocket, to take home.

s4b.text: "The code," we say. Grandpa's eyes go crinkly, and from his shirt pocket he pulls a folded note. Inside is a row of numbers: 8, 5, 12, 12, 15. "Numbers standing where letters should be," he says. "Very rude of them." We stare. Nothing. Then we remember the maze, and we try it backwards: what if 1 is A, all the way at the start of the alphabet? We count on our fingers. 8 is H. 5 is E. 12 is L. And 12 again. "A pattern that repeats," Grandpa says softly, "like a path you walk twice." 15 is O. The word sits there on the table, plain as toast. HELLO. "Hello back," we say to the note, and Grandpa laughs. "A code is just a maze made of symbols," he says. "Once you find the way in, it can't wait to be solved." We fold the note small and put it in our pocket, next to the pencil. All the way home, the world looks full of secret paths, waiting.

c1.question: "Do you want to hunt for clues by marking every dead end, or shall I give you a hint about a sneaky trick?"

options.label: Mark every dead end with an X to gather information
Ask Grandpa for the backwards trick

c2.question: "Now that you know the secret, do you want to draw your own maze for me to solve, or try cracking a code I wrote just for you?"

options.label: Make your own maze and test it backwards
Solve a number code by finding the repeating pattern

maze_name.role: What Grandpa calls the maze he drew for us

surprise_at_finish.role: The tiny treasure Grandpa hid at the finish

stories.title: The Balloon That Sailed the Stripes

s1.text:
This book is older than me, and older than my grandma, and maybe older than the hills. Feel the cover. Soft as a dog's ear, isn't it? Every page is a drawing of the same place, added by somebody in our family. And this page at the back is blank. It's waiting.

Let me tell you about the night it nearly got its drawing.

I was about your age, and Grandma Sef finally said I was old enough to sail the whole route with her. Her balloon was called the Stripe, and it floated at the thin, fuzzy edge of space, right above Jupiter.

Jupiter is a gas giant, {child_name}. That means it's all clouds, top to bottom. No ground anywhere. Nothing to stand on, ever. Just cloud bands, stripes of cream and rust and gold, sliding past each other slow as honey.

Nix was there too, counting moons in his tally notebook. "Seventy-nine! Eighty!" he kept saying. And Stir the robot was cooking something that smelled like tomato soup.

Grandma Sef patted the sketchbook. "One full route," she said, "and the page is yours."

s2a.text: "Up we go!" Grandma Sef said, and the Stripe lifted to the very top of the highest cloud band. We sailed the stripes like a train on tracks. "Cream station!" Grandma Sef called. "Tan station! Rust station!" Nix pressed his nose to the glass. "What comes after rust? I want to guess right." "Guess," said Grandma Sef. Nix squeezed his eyes shut. "Blue?" "Pale blue-grey," Grandma Sef announced, "next station!" Nix whooped. "I nearly said grey!" Grandma Sef pointed at the stripes sliding past each other. "The light ones blow one way, the dark ones blow back, side by side, like two rivers running opposite ways." Stir dinged a little bell. "Soup! Stripe-swirled soup!" It was swirled cream and rust, just like the clouds. "Jupiter's whole day is only ten hours," said Grandma Sef. "So it's breakfast again already." Nix counted on his fingers. "Again?" We drank our soup while the stripes hurried past, faster and faster. "Wait," said Nix, leaning forward. "What's after rust? I forgot already!"

s2b.text: "Down we go," Grandma Sef said softly, and the Stripe sank toward the deep orange mist. We hovered above it. The fog turned slowly, thick as tomato soup, as porridge, as the jam at the bottom of the jar. Grandma Sef pressed her hand flat to the bubble window. "Feel, {child_name}. No floor out there. Just fog turning to soup, all the way down." Nix leaned so far out his nose nearly touched the glass. "But if there's no ground anywhere, what's holding us up?" Stir handed us cocoa, warm in our hands. "The balloon floats on Jupiter's breath," Stir said, "the way a leaf floats on a pond." Nix looked at his cocoa, then at the mist. "So we're a leaf?" "A very cozy leaf," said Grandma Sef. I watched the fog curl far below, slow and orange, and wondered what it would feel like to dip a finger in. "Would it feel like bathwater?" I asked. "Warm," said Grandma Sef, "and thick, and it would hold you like soup holds a spoon."

s3.text:
Back on the route, something is growing over the curve of the world. A dot. A coin. A dinner plate. Until it fills the whole round window, edge to edge.

"There she is," says Grandma Sef. "The Great Red Spot."

It isn't red, really. It's orange, deep and warm, turning slow as syrup. A swirl bigger than the whole Earth, just turning and turning in the clouds.

Grandma Sef opens the sketchbook, soft as a dog's ear, to a page near the front. "My great-grandmother drew this. The very same swirl. It's been turning for hundreds of years, {child_name}. Since long before anyone we know was born."

"Hundreds?" says Nix, looking up from his tally notebook. "That's more than all my moons."

We drift along the rim, where the orange clouds curl like the top of tomato soup. Stir says the soup is ready, and nobody answers, because nobody wants to look away.

"Watch," Grandma Sef whispers. "It moves. But only if you're patient."

So we watch. And the Spot turns, slow and sure, like it has all the time in the world.

Then Nix sits up straight. "Dots! Bright dots, ahead!" His pencil is already moving. "Moons, {child_name}. Big ones. Waiting to be counted."

s4a.text:
The Stripe bumps, soft as a kiss, against the moon-hopper station. "Out we hop," says Grandma Sef.

We step onto the big moon, and the ground is real and still and dusty under our boots. And there, filling half the black sky, hangs Jupiter. Striped. Enormous. Close enough to touch, almost.

"Moons!" shouts Nix, notebook already open. "Count with me, {child_name}. Io, with its orange volcano fountains, fizzing like a pot that boils over. Europa, white and cracked as old ice on a pond. Ganymede. Callisto. Four!" He presses a sticker into my hand. "For your tally."

"Europa looks like a skating pond," I say.

"Under the ice?" Nix grins. "A whole secret ocean. Hiding."

The radio operator waves us past her window. "Before you go — look." She points. On her fingertip, a tiny blue dot. "Earth. That's home, that is."

Home. That little.

Back aboard, Grandma Sef opens the sketchbook, soft as a dog's ear, to the blank page at the back. "Yours," she says.

So I draw. {spot_drawing}. Nix sticks my sticker in the corner. Stir brings soup.

And that, my love, is the end of the remembering. Because this book on your lap — this very one, soft as a dog's ear — is that book. And this page, still warm from my hand, is the page I drew that night, when I was about your age.

s4b.text:
"Stay aboard it is," says Grandma Sef, and the Stripe turns its nose toward the dark.

The map room is at the back, where the windows go black as bedtime. Nix flips a switch. And the whole room blooms — seventy-nine tiny lights, one for every moon, glowing like fireflies in a jar.

"Seventy-nine," Nix breathes. "All of them. But which line is the way home?"

Then a golden dotted line draws itself through the lights, curving between the moons, slow and sure. "That one," says Grandma Sef. "It always knows."

"Breakfast!" calls Stir. "Timed to the minute. Jupiter spins so fast, a whole day there is ten hours. Eat slow, and the sunrise comes back around before you've finished."

So we eat tomato soup, and watch the light creep over the cloud bands, gold on cream on rust. A whole sunrise, before the bowls are empty. Nix licks his spoon. "Best timed breakfast ever," he says.

We lay our souvenirs in a row on the table. A jar of cloud-banded light. My drawing of the Spot. Nix's moon stickers. The whole trip, in a row.

Then Grandma Sef opens the sketchbook, soft as a dog's ear, to the blank page at the back. "Yours," she says.

So I draw. {spot_drawing}.

And that, my love, is the end of the remembering. Because this book on your lap is that book. And the page you're looking at right now — that's the page I drew, when I was about your age.

c1.question: "Well, {child_name}, the stripes are calling from up top, but the deep orange mist is humming down below. Do we ride the cloud bands like a train, or sink down and peek into the fog?"

options.label: Sail along the colored cloud bands and count them like train stations
Drop lower to hover above the deep mist where there is no ground at all

c2.question: "Last stop before home, {child_name}. We can hop out onto the big moon and stand under all those stripes, or stay cozy aboard and watch the whole moon-map light our way back. Which sounds like yours?"

options.label: Dock at the moon station, collect the last stickers, and see Earth on a fingertip

sets_slots.spot_drawing: the Great Red Spot with four bright moon buttons beside it

options.label: Sail to the map room, watch 79 moons glow, and catch one last ten-hour sunrise

sets_slots.spot_drawing: the striped balloon sailing a golden dotted line through tiny glowing moons

child_name.role: What Grandma Sef and Nix call the child listening, inside the memory

spot_drawing.role: What the child draws on their sketchbook page at the end
spot_drawing.default: the Great Red Spot with a tiny smiling balloon beside it

s1.text:
The computer lab after school smells like warm dust and the lemon wipes Ms. Okafor uses on the keyboards. Theo is the last one here, and he has a job to do.

On the big monitor glows the class picture: {photo_subject}. It is so bright it almost hums. Theo holds up his phone, because his sister Nadia is never going to believe how good it looks on this screen. She loves this stuff. She once spent a whole dinner explaining why the microwave clock is green.

Click.

Theo looks at the photo. Then he looks at the screen. Then back at the photo.

"No way," he says out loud.

Because there, slanting across the photo like a fat gray stripe, is a dark band. It covers half the banana. But when he looks up at the real monitor, the picture is smooth. Perfect. No band at all.

He takes another picture. Click. The band is back, in a slightly different place.

"That is not there," Theo tells the screen. The screen does not argue. It just glows.

He leans in close. He waves his hand in front of the monitor. Smooth. He takes a third photo, holding his breath this time, as if that could help. Click. Band.

"Theo?" Ms. Okafor is stacking chairs in the corner, and she has that smile teachers get when they already know the answer to something. "Find something interesting?"

"My photo has a stripe in it," Theo says. "But the screen doesn't. I checked like five times."

"Hmm," says Ms. Okafor, which is not an answer at all. She sets down the last chair. "Well. The lab is yours until five, if you want to poke at it."

Theo is already reaching for his phone to call Nadia. Because a band that shows up in a photo but not in real life? That is not a glitch. That is a clue.

s2a.text:
Nadia arrives in nine minutes flat, still wearing her swim bag, and Theo holds up the phone without a word. She looks at the photo. She looks at the screen. Her eyes go huge.

"Oh, we are so doing this," she says.

Ms. Okafor keeps a magnifying glass in the supply drawer, the heavy kind with a metal rim, and she slides it across the desk like she's passing them something valuable. "Careful with my treasure," she says.

Theo presses it gently against the monitor, right on the banana's yellow curve.

The smooth picture falls apart.

"Whoa," he breathes. Up close, the banana isn't a banana at all. It's rows and rows of tiny glowing tiles, packed together like the mosaic on the community center wall. Except each tile is glowing from inside.

"Look closer," Nadia says. She's practically lying on the desk. "Each tile. Tell me what you see."

Theo tilts the glass. Each little tile is really three even tinier lights, standing side by side. One red. One green. One blue. On the yellow part of the banana, the red and green ones are blazing and the blue is dim. On the blue background, it's the opposite — blue burning bright, the other two barely awake.

"They're mixing," Theo says. "Like paint. But with light."

"They're called pixels," Nadia says, and she says it like she's handing him a present. "Picture elements. Every picture on every screen is a mosaic of them. Red, green, blue, over and over, millions of them, and your eye just... mixes it all together."

Theo pulls the glass away. Banana. Puts it back. Tiles. Away. Banana.

"Okay, but wait." He picks up his phone again. "If it's all just little lights glowing away — then why does my camera see a stripe?"

Nadia's grin gets wider. "That," she says, "is the good part."

s2b.text:
Nadia arrives in nine minutes flat, still wearing her swim bag, and Theo holds up the phone without a word. She looks at the photo. She looks at the screen. Her eyes go huge.

"Okay," she says. "We need to catch it in the act."

"Catch what? Nothing's moving."

"That's what it wants you to think." She taps his phone. "Does this thing do slow motion?"

It does. Theo props the phone against a stack of keyboards, aims it at the banana, and hits record. They let it run for ten seconds. Nadia is gripping the back of his chair hard enough to wobble it.

"Play it," she says. "Slow."

They watch. And there it is — something Theo's eyes have never once caught in his whole life. In the slowed-down video, the picture isn't just sitting there. A bright wave sweeps down the screen, top to bottom, drawing the picture as it goes. Then it jumps back to the top and does it again. And again. And again.

"It's repainting itself," Theo whispers. "The whole screen. Over and over."

"Sixty times a second, probably," Nadia says. "It's called the refresh. And no —" she holds up a finger, because she knows him, "— not like refreshing a drink, not like refreshing a webpage. Like a painter repainting the same wall, top to bottom, so fast you never catch the brush moving."

Theo stares at the monitor. Perfect, smooth, still. Lying to his face, sixty times a second.

"So my camera..."

"Your camera snapped its picture in the middle of a repaint. Half the wall was fresh, half was still waiting. That's your band." Nadia spins the chair around to face her. "The screen was never showing the whole picture at once, Theo. Not ever. It's a mosaic of light that gets rebuilt faster than your eyes can see."

Theo looks at the banana. The banana, somehow, looks smug.

s3.text:
Nadia arrives in seven minutes flat, still wearing her swim team jacket, and Theo watches her eyes go wide the second he shows her what he found.

"Okay," she breathes, like someone just handed her a present. "Okay, okay, okay."

She goes straight to the whiteboard and starts drawing. Tiny squares, rows and rows of them, like a mosaic made of light. "Every pixel," she says, "is three tiny lamps. Red, green, blue. That's it. That's the whole trick." She dots three little circles inside each square. "And the graphics chip? It reads numbers in memory — like two-five-five, two hundred, zero — and tells each lamp exactly how bright to glow. Red all the way up, green most of the way, blue off. Gold."

Theo stares at the mosaic. "So the banana is just... numbers?"

"Numbers becoming light," Nadia says, and her voice goes soft and reverent, the way it does. "And here's the part that's going to break your brain. The screen doesn't paint the picture once. It paints it, wipes it, and paints it again. Sixty times a second. That's the frame rate. Sixty whole paintings, every single second, and your eyes never catch a single one."

The lab hums. The monitor glows.

"But my camera," Theo says slowly, "takes its pictures at a different speed."

Nadia stops. She turns. She is grinning like crazy, but she waits.

"So sometimes," Theo says, "my camera catches the screen... halfway. Half the old painting, half the new one. And the seam where they meet—"

"—is the band," Nadia finishes, barely a whisper. "Theo. The band was never on the screen. It was the instant between two paintings."

Theo looks at the monitor. Sixty paintings a second. Happening right now. Happening the whole time.

"Nadia," he says. "I want to see it."

s4a.text:
"Feel it," says Ms. Okafor, and she vanishes into the supply closet. She comes back holding something small and square and worn soft at the corners. "From the animation shelf," she says. "Sixty pages. One second."

It's a flipbook. A fat little pad of paper, and on the first page, a cat crouches.

"Hold it with your thumb," Nadia says, practically vibrating. "Flip slow first. Just look."

Theo flips slow. Page by page, the cat creeps upward — a whisker here, a paw there. Sixty separate drawings. Sixty still, quiet cats.

"Now fast," Nadia whispers.

Theo bends his thumb and lets the pages run. Riffle. And the cat jumps — smooth as water, one clean leap, up and over and gone. Sixty frozen cats melt into one living one, right there in his hands.

"Whoa," Theo says.

"That's the frame rate," Nadia says. "That's what the graphics chip is doing right now, sixty times a second, so fast your eyes give up and just say cat." She flips it again herself, greedy for it. "Video games do the exact same thing. And Theo — the science museum downtown has a whole wall, thousands of tiny lights you can touch. Red, green, blue. You can stand inside a pixel."

"Before you go," Ms. Okafor says, and the lab printer hums awake. Out slides a strip of paper: the banana photo, magnified until the mosaic shows — rows and rows of tiny glowing tiles, red, green, blue, red, green, blue.

At home, Theo tapes the strip into his notebook, right on the first page. He looks at it for a long time. A picture made of numbers. Numbers made of light.

"Sixty paintings a second," he tells the quiet room, "and I caught the seam."

s4b.text:
"One more time," Theo says, lifting his phone. "But now I know what I'm hunting."

Nadia pulls a chair up close, her shoulder warm against his. "The band is the seam between two paintings. Sixty chances a second. So we don't get lucky — we get patient."

They take pictures. Click. Clean. Click. Clean. Theo's thumb starts to ache. Click. Clean.

"It's weirdly hard to catch a thing on purpose," he mutters, "when you caught it three times by accident."

"Science," Nadia says solemnly, and they both crack up.

Click.

Theo looks down. There it is — the fat gray band, slanting across the banana like it owns the place. Caught mid-refresh, half old painting, half new. "Got you," he whispers.

"Print them," says Ms. Okafor, and she means both. Out of the lab printer they come, side by side: the banded photo and a clean one. Proof. The invisible repaint, pinned to paper.

Ms. Okafor carries the pair across the lab and tacks them onto a corkboard labeled in her neat handwriting: QUESTIONS WE LOVE. "First entry of the year," she says.

"You should see the science museum downtown," Nadia says, bumping Theo's shoulder. "There's a wall made of thousands of tiny lights. You can stand inside a pixel mosaic. We're going. I'm not asking."

Then Ms. Okafor presses one more print into Theo's hand — a small square, the banana magnified until the mosaic shows: tiny tiles, red, green, blue, red, green, blue.

It rides home in his pocket, a pocket-sized piece of the trick. That night he holds it up to the lamp and the little tiles glow.

"Sixty paintings a second," Theo says, "and here's the proof. Right here."

c1.question: "Two ways to sneak up on this, Theo — do we press the magnifying glass right up against the glass and see what the picture is made of, or do we film the screen in slow motion and catch it in the act?"

options.label: Look at the screen up close with the magnifying glass
Record the screen in slow motion to catch what eyes miss

c2.question: "So now you know the secret — sixty brand-new paintings every second. Do you want to feel how separate drawings turn into smooth motion, or hunt that sneaky band one more time now that you know exactly what it is?"

options.label: Try the sixty-page flipbook from the animation shelf
Photograph the screen again to catch the mid-refresh band on purpose

photo_subject.role: The picture displayed on the lab screen that Theo photographs
photo_subject.default: a golden banana on a bright blue background

s1.text: I remember a morning on the sandy riverbank, where the mud was soft and the ferns waved tall. Grandpa Ankylosaurus thumped his tail club. Boom. Boom. "Today," he said, "we build the BIGGEST stomp-print ever! A stomp you can keep! So big {child_name} can sit inside it!" So we gathered. Stegosaurus carried pebbles on her plates. Plop, plop. A little feathered dinosaur fluttered down with fluff in her beak. "Oooh," she said, "what does THAT do?" We patted the mud flat, flat, flat. Soft as porridge. But nobody knew how to make the three toes yet — and the toes are the whole footprint.

s2a.text: "Stomp it is!" says Baby Triceratops. Up, up she rears — and STOMP! STOMP! STOMP! Three big toes! Mud goes splash! "Again! Again!" we shout, and she giggles so hard her horns wobble. But then — bloop. One toe wall slides down, slow as honey. The little feathered dinosaur flutters close and peeks in. "Oooh," she says, "why did it fall?" Grandpa's eyes go twinkly. "A wobble is a teacher!" he booms. And we look at the slumpy toe, and we start to think.

s2b.text: "Slow and gentle," says Stegosaurus, and she tips her sunny plates. Plop, plop, plop — three smooth pebbles for three toes. We pat-pat-pat, one little push at a time. So neat! So tidy! But the little feathered dinosaur tilts her head. "Oooh," she says, "is that a toe for a mouse?" We look. The middle toe is teeny-tiny — more a dimple than a toe. Grandpa's eyes go twinkly. "A wobble is a teacher!" he booms. And we look at the little toe, and we start to think.

s3.text: Grandpa Ankylosaurus nodded at the mud. "First we pat. Flat, flat, flat." Boom, boom, boom went his tail club. We patted too, with our hands and our feet. Then we pressed the three toes in, slow and careful. Baby Triceratops bumped the wall with her frill. Bump! It stayed! Stegosaurus plopped pebbles on for toenails. Plop, plop. The little feathered dinosaur tucked fluff into the cracks. "Oooh," she said, "what did YOU find?" We stepped back. A stomp-print as long as a bathtub! Big enough to sit in! Grandpa lifted his head. "Now — how do we CELEBRATE a footprint this fine?"

s4a.text: "We ROAR!" said Grandpa. So we lined up all around the print. "One, two — ROOOAR!" we shouted. ROOOAR went the dinosaurs. Roar! went {child_name}. One roar is fun. Everyone roaring is a whole song! Then one stomp each. Stomp! Stomp! STOMP! Up burst the birds from the ferns — flutter, flutter, like confetti in the sky! The little feathered dinosaur spun in a circle. "Oooh! It tickles my FEATHERS!" Grandpa pressed one smooth pebble into my hand, warm from the sun. A pebble toenail, just for me. And that pebble sits on my shelf still.

s4b.text: "We SIT!" said Grandpa. So I climbed down, down, into the stomp-print. Squish went the mud. I sat right inside it, small as an egg in a nest. "It is SO big," I said. "It is SO you-sized," said Grandpa. The little feathered dinosaur fluttered down and tucked one soft feather behind my ear. "Oooh," she said, "what does THAT do?" A small bird landed on the edge. Tweet-tweet! it sang. And she sang back — tweet-tweet! — almost the same. Then home we went, squish, squash, squish. And that feather is in my pocket still, soft as the day it was given.

c1.question: "The mud is ready, little stompers! Now — do we make the toes with a big brave STOMP, or pat them in slow and gentle with pebbles?"

options.label: Stomp the toes in big and splashy
Press the toes in slowly with smooth pebbles

c2.question: "A footprint this fine needs a finish! Do we ROAR together so the whole riverbank hears it — or climb in and SIT inside it, to feel how big it truly is?"

options.label: Everyone roars and stomps a song together
Sit inside the giant print like an egg in a nest

child_name.role: the child listening, who in the memory was there helping

stories.title: The Blue Marble at the End of the Road

s1.text:
Do you remember the smell of cut grass at dusk? I do. It was the summer I turned eight, and Grandpa set up his old brass telescope in the backyard.

Click. Whirr. The telescope moved like it was waking up.

"Take a look," Grandpa said. "Tell me what you see."

I pressed my eye to the eyepiece. At first, just darkness. Then — there. A tiny blue marble at the very end of a long, dark road of space.

"I see it!" I said. "It's so blue."

Grandpa leaned close. "That's Neptune. The farthest planet from the Sun."

I looked again. The blue was deep, like the bottom of a swimming pool. And something else — a thin white ribbon stretched across it. A cloud.

"But Grandpa," I said, pulling back from the telescope. "If it's so far away, why does it look so bright?"

He smiled. "That's the mystery, isn't it?"

Click. Whirr. The telescope shifted, keeping the blue marble in view.

I looked through again. The ribbon of cloud seemed to move, just a little. Like something was pushing it along.

"What pushes a cloud that far away?" I whispered.

Grandpa tapped the brass tube. "Let's find out."

s2a.text:
"Look again," Grandpa said. "Tell me if that blue reminds you of anything."

I pressed my eye to the eyepiece. Click. Whirr. The brass tube settled.

"It's like the deep ocean," I said slowly. "The part where the sunlight gives up."

Grandpa nodded. "Down there, fish make their own light. Little lanterns swimming in the dark."

I pictured them — tiny glowing fish, drifting where the blue goes black. Then something else caught my eye. A thin, faint ring around the planet. Like the ghost of a hula hoop.

"Grandpa! It has a ring!"

"Does it now?"

"Barely. Like it's shy." I pulled back, blinking. "So the blue isn't just a trick of being far away."

"No," Grandpa said. "It's something else. Something the planet is doing all by itself."

I looked again. The white ribbon of cloud stretched across that deep blue, and the faint ring held it all like a secret.

"What makes a planet glow like that?" I whispered.

Grandpa tapped the telescope. "That's what detectives are for."

s2b.text:
"Grandpa," I said, "how far away is it? Really?"

He leaned against the fence. "So far that sunlight takes more than four hours to get there."

"Four hours?" I pulled back from the eyepiece. "That's longer than a car ride to Grandma's."

"Much longer." He pointed up. "The Sun is way behind us, like a warm lamp on a porch. By the time its light reaches Neptune, it's tired and thin."

I looked through again. Click. Whirr. The telescope held steady.

The blue marble hung there, glowing. The white ribbon of cloud drifted across it, slow and sure.

"But Grandpa — if the Sun is that far away, the blue can't be borrowed light. Not bright like that."

"No," he said. "It can't."

"So where does it come from?"

He smiled. "The planet must be making its own color somehow. Mixing it deep inside, where we can't see."

I pressed my eye close again. The blue seemed to pulse, just a little. Like it knew something.

"What kind of planet makes its own blue?" I whispered.

"Let's find out."

s3.text:
Grandpa unfolded a big piece of paper on the grass. It was covered in dots and lines, like a map of the sky.

"Look here," he said, pointing to a drawing of the Sun. "Sunlight looks white, but it's really made of all the colors mixed together. Red, orange, yellow, green, blue."

I nodded. "Like a rainbow."

"Exactly. Now, Neptune is wrapped in a gas called methane." Grandpa tapped the paper. "Methane acts like a sieve."

"A sieve? Like for flour?"

"Just like that. When the sunlight hits Neptune, the methane catches the red light. It holds onto it. But the blue light?" Grandpa wiggled his fingers. "The blue light bounces right back off. It travels all the way across that long, dark distance, through the cold, and right into our telescope."

I looked through the eyepiece again. Click. Whirr. The blue marble was still there, glowing.

"So the blue is the light that escaped," I said.

"That's it. The methane let the blue go free."

I smiled. It was a good trick. But then I noticed the white ribbon again. It wasn't just floating. It was stretched into a long, thin line. And below it, I saw another one. And another. They were all combed into stripes, all pointing the same way.

"Grandpa," I said. "The clouds. They're all lined up. Like something is combing them."

Grandpa leaned in. "Something is pushing them. Something fast."

"What is it?" I asked.

s4a.text:
"What pushes them?" Grandpa said. "Wind. The fastest wind in the whole solar system." He held up one finger. "Over a thousand miles an hour. Faster than anything on Earth."

I blinked. "A thousand?"

"That wind hurries the clouds along," Grandpa said. "It stretches them into ribbons, all combed the same way. Like the stripes you see."

I looked through the eyepiece again. Click. Whirr. The white ribbon raced across the blue, thin and fast.

"It's like someone combed the whole sky," I whispered.

Grandpa nodded. "The wind does the combing. Every day. Every night. It never gets tired."

I pulled out my notebook and wrote it down. Neptune. Fastest wind. Clouds in ribbons. My pencil scratched quick across the page.

When I looked up, Grandpa was holding something small and round. A blue marble, deep as Neptune itself.

"For you," he said. "A little piece of the faraway world."

I held it up to the sky. The marble glowed, just like the planet. I slipped it into my pocket, where it sat cool and smooth against my leg.

"Thank you," I said.

Grandpa smiled. "Keep it close. The farthest things aren't so far when you carry them home."

s4b.text:
"But Grandpa," I said, still watching the clouds. "Does the wind ever stop?"

He shook his head. "No. Neptune makes its own weather, deep inside. It doesn't need much sunlight. The wind just keeps going."

"Always?"

"Always. Like a engine that never runs out."

I thought about that. A wind that never rests, hurrying clouds across a world so far away.

"Let's draw it," Grandpa said. He pulled out crayons from his pocket. Blue, white, a little gray.

We sat on the grass and drew together. I made the deep blue circle. Grandpa added the white ribbons, streaky and fast. We drew line after line, all pointing the same way, all racing.

"There," Grandpa said. "A map of the wind."

I held up the drawing. The clouds looked like they were moving, even on paper.

"Can I take it home?"

"Of course. Tape it to the refrigerator. Every time you see it, you'll remember. The wind is still blowing out there. Right now."

I folded the drawing careful and held it tight. The farthest planet, with its racing clouds, was coming home with me.

"Thanks, Grandpa," I said.

He winked. "The wind never stops. Neither does a good mystery."

c1.question: "Do you want to look at the color first, or shall we measure how far away it is?"

options.label: Look at the deep blue color
Measure the long road of light

c2.question: "Do you want to know what pushes those clouds, or do you want to know if the wind ever stops?"

options.label: Find out what pushes the clouds
Ask if the wind ever stops

s1.text: Morning. Just barely. {hero_name} stands on the platform, and the whole sky is the color of warm toast. Right in front of us, a long green train hums softly — and look. Look at the steam. It curls up from the roof, thick as soup, as porridge, as the warm breath of someone still sleeping. A whistle goes. Toot-toot! Then — clang! — a woman in a bright red cap swings down from the front car. "You're here! You're here!" she says. "I'm Conductor Zara, and this is the Breakfast Express. We ride all around the world, tasting how kids start their day." She holds out her hand. "Somewhere right now, a kid is eating warm rice for breakfast. Somewhere else, it's flatbread with honey. Want to come see?" We look at the steam. We look at her big smile. We climb aboard.

s2a.text: The train slows. Whoo-ooosh. "Japan!" calls Zara. We step off into a small warm kitchen. Steam curls up from a bowl of rice, thick as soup, as porridge, as breath on a cold morning. A grandmother smiles. "For breakfast," she says, "we crack an egg on top. Like this." Tap. Crack. Plop. The yolk sits on the rice, golden as a tiny sun. She stirs with chopsticks, and the sun melts into the grains. "Now you," she says, and hands us a pair. {hero_name} pinches them tight. The rice slips. It slides. It will not stay. "Slow," she says gently. "Like picking up a little bird." We breathe out. We try again.

s2b.text: The train slows. Whoo-ooosh. "Ethiopia!" calls Zara. We step off into a kitchen that smells like warm bread and spice. On the table lies a big round injera, soft and spongy, with steam still curling off it. A father tears a piece with one hand. "Like this," he says. "Then scoop." He folds it around a spoonful of red lentils and pops it in his mouth. "Now you." {hero_name} grabs the edge and pulls. Rrrrip! The piece is huge, bigger than our whole hand. Everyone laughs, kind and warm, and we laugh too. "A little smaller," he says, smiling. "Try again."

s3.text: Back on the train, the whistle goes. Toot-toot! The Breakfast Express hums and rolls. Conductor Zara leans close. "What did you find out there?" she asks. We tell her, and her eyes go wide and bright. "Steam rising," she says softly. "Warm food. Kids eating breakfast in all kinds of ways." Outside the window, the world slides by — green hills, then rooftops, then streets waking up. The train rocks us gently, side to side, like bathwater. Zara stands up tall. "Next stop," she says, "a busy street corner in Vietnam. Somewhere right now, a kid is slurping noodles for breakfast." Slurping! We look at the steam curling from the roof. We look at her big smile. The whistle sings again, and the train hurries on, deeper into morning.

s4a.text: The train stops. Steam everywhere! It curls from a big pot on the street corner, thick as soup. A cook smiles at us. "Pho for breakfast," she says. With long chopsticks, she lifts slippery noodles from the bubbling pot. Swish! Into a bowl they go. "Somewhere right now, a kid is slurping these," Zara whispers. The cook hands {hero_name} small chopsticks. "Try!" We pinch. We lift. A noodle wiggles... and plop! Back it splashes. Everyone smiles, and we try again. This time — slurp! Warm broth, soft noodles. Our whole belly goes cozy. The cook wraps up chopsticks for {hero_name} to keep. "For home," she says. We climb aboard, holding them tight, tasting that warm soup all the way back.

s4b.text: The train stops. Steam curls from a little bakery door, sweet and warm. Inside, a baker with flour on her nose smiles. "For breakfast," she says, "we dip." She hands {hero_name} a piece of baguette, still warm, and a bowl of hot chocolate. "Somewhere right now, a kid is dipping bread just like this," Zara whispers. We dip. We lift. Drip, drip! Sweet chocolate drops on the table. The baker laughs softly and slides us a napkin. "It means the chocolate is good," she says. We bite. Crunch, then soft, then warm chocolate. Our whole mouth is happy. The baker wraps a small baguette for {hero_name} to carry home. "For later," she says. We climb aboard, holding it close, the taste of dipping still on our lips.

c1.question: "First stop, adventurer! Would you like to visit a kitchen where rice is steaming, or a home where bread is torn with fingers?"

options.label: Visit Japan for rice with egg
Visit Ethiopia for injera and lentils

c2.question: "Our last stop! Shall we visit a street corner where noodles swim in hot soup, or a bakery where bread dips into chocolate?"

options.label: Visit Vietnam for pho
Visit France for baguette and hot chocolate

stories.title: The Cake That Couldn't Go Back

s1.text:
Saturday morning, and Grandma's kitchen smells like {cake_flavor}. Sunlight pours through the window, and the flour dust hangs in it like slow, tiny snow.

We are helping our cousin bake Grandpa's birthday cake. Our little sibling Pip is helping too, in Pip's own way.

"Fffzzz!" says Pip, as the baking soda hits the bowl. "Fffzzz! The bubbles are waking up!"

We measure. We stir. The recipe says three eggs, and the shells go crack, crack, crack. Butter slides into the sugar and melts into yellow swirls. Every ingredient goes in, and the spoon goes round and round, and the batter turns thick and glossy, like a blanket you could pour.

"Into the pan," says our cousin. "Into the oven. Now we wait."

So we wait. And the kitchen gets warmer. And the smell gets bigger and bigger, until it fills the whole house like a hug.

Then the timer rings. Ding!

Our cousin opens the oven, and there it is. Golden. Puffed up. Standing tall all by itself.

Our cousin slides a toothpick into the middle and pulls it out. Clean. Not one drip.

Pip stares at it. Pip's eyes go wide.

"Wait," says Pip. "Wait. An hour ago it was soup. Soup! You could pour it!"

Pip pokes the top gently, and it springs back.

"Why is it a house now?"

s2a.text:
"The list," we say. "Interrogate the list."

Our cousin spreads the recipe card on the counter like a treasure map, and we lean over it, three detectives in a row. Pip climbs onto a stool to see.

"Milk," our cousin reads. "Went in pourable." We cross it off.

"Eggs. Went in runny." Crossed off.

"Flour. Soft as dust." Crossed off.

"Butter." Pip giggles. "Butter went in like a sleepy stick."

And that reminds us. This morning, the butter sat on the counter waiting its turn, and by the time we reached for it, it had gone slump-shouldered and shiny, sliding sideways all by itself. No oven. Just a warm kitchen.

"So warmth was already changing things," our cousin says, tapping the card. "Before the oven even got a turn."

Then Pip does something brilliant. Pip takes the practice egg, the extra one, and cracks it into the little pan. Crack. We watch the clear part slowly, slowly turn snowy white, like frost spreading across a window.

"It's not runny anymore," Pip whispers. "And it can't go back."

We stare at each other. Every single ingredient started soft, or pourable, or runny. But something in that oven built a house out of soup.

"The oven did it," we say. "But how?"

s2b.text:
"The window," we say. "Stake out the window."

Our cousin grins and sets the timer. "Detectives, take your positions."

So we kneel down in front of the oven, three in a row, with Pip squished in the middle. The oven light glows like a little sunrise, and through the glass we can see the pan, and the batter, pale and shiny and perfectly still.

"It's not doing anything," says Pip.

"Wait for it," our cousin says.

And then we see it. The batter is climbing. Slowly, so slowly, up the sides of the pan, like dough waking up and stretching after a long nap. The middle rises in a soft, round hill.

"It's growing!" Pip shouts. "It's growing right now!"

"Fffzzz," Pip whispers, remembering. "The bubbles. The bubbles are doing something in there."

We watch and watch. The timer ticks. Our tummies rumble, but the timer decides, not our hunger, so we wait. And slowly, slowly, the pale top turns golden, like toast, like sunshine, like the crust of warm bread.

"It's changing right in front of us," we breathe.

But the glass keeps the secret. We can see the cake rising and turning gold, but we cannot see how. What is happening inside that golden hill? What are the bubbles building in there?

"We have to get inside that cake," says Pip.

s3.text:
Ding! The timer rings, and the whole kitchen seems to lean in. Our cousin opens the oven and out it comes, golden and tall, and Grandpa arrives at that exact moment, the way grandpas do when cake is close. He leans over the pan. He looks a long time. "Well," he says. "Look at that."

We crowd around. "What did you find?" our cousin asks, and we tell it, and Pip tells it too, louder, with extra fffzzz. Whatever we each saw, the clues click together like two puzzle pieces. The toothpick came out clean, so no soup is left hiding in the middle. And along the top edge, where the crust meets the pan, we can see them: tiny holes. Tiny rooms.

"The bubbles!" shouts Pip. "They got stuck! The Bubble Mayor lives here now!"

Our cousin nods, slow and sure. "That's the answer. Heat built a million little walls around a million little bubbles. It turned a puddle into a sponge."

Grandpa taps the golden top, and it springs back under his finger. "So nobody can un-bake it," he says. "Not ever. Just like nobody can un-white an egg."

"You can't un-cake a cake," says Pip, very seriously.

But the cake is still whole. The proof is hiding inside, in the crumb, in all those bubble rooms waiting to be found. Our cousin picks up the knife, and looks at us, and smiles.

s4a.text:
“Cut it,” says Pip. “I have to see the Bubble Mayor.”

Our cousin slides the knife through, slow and careful, and the cake opens like a book. We lean in close. The inside is soft and pale gold, and it is full of holes. Tiny ones, smaller than peas. Big ones, fat as marbles. Each one is a little room where a bubble stood, right up until the heat froze the walls around it.

“That one,” says Pip, pointing at the biggest hole. “That is {bubble_name}. That is the whole house.”

Grandpa bends down and looks through his glasses. “Well, would you look at that,” he says. “You made me a sponge.”

We laugh, and then the doorbell rings. The neighbor is here, right on time, and our cousin cuts the first slice and puts it on a plate, and Grandpa holds it like it is treasure. Because it is.

Pip leans over and whispers to the cake. “You can’t go back,” Pip says. “You’re a cake now, forever.”

And we know it is true. Some changes are one-way doors. That is exactly what makes a cake a cake.

s4b.text:
“Wait,” we say. “Let’s keep it whole.”

So our cousin puts the knife down, and we swirl the frosting on top, thick and smooth, hiding every secret underneath. The cake sits on the plate like a treasure chest, and nobody walking by would ever guess what is locked inside.

We carry it to the table, very slowly, the way you carry something that matters. Grandpa follows us, and Pip walks backward in front of the cake, watching it the whole time, like it might get away.

Then the doorbell rings. The neighbor is here, right on time. We light the candle, and the flame wiggles, and Grandpa closes his eyes and blows. Everyone claps. And then, only then, our cousin picks up the knife and cuts the first slice.

The cake opens, and there they are. All the tiny holes. All the little rooms. The neighbor gasps, and Grandpa leans in close.

“That one,” Pip announces to the whole room, pointing at the biggest hole, “is {bubble_name}.”

We already knew. We were the only ones who knew, and now everyone does. Heat built something that can never go back, and we built it for someone we love.

c1.question: Our cousin taps the recipe card and says, 'Detectives, we can interrogate the ingredient list, or we can stake out the oven window and catch the cake in the act. Which is it?'

options.label: read the recipe card and question every ingredient
kneel at the oven window and watch the cake change

c2.question: Grandpa rubs his hands together and asks, 'Do we cut it open right now and show everyone the bubble rooms, or keep it whole and let the secret wait until the candle is lit?'

options.label: slice it open now and reveal the tiny holes
carry it whole to the table and save the reveal

cake_flavor.role: the flavor of Grandpa's birthday cake

bubble_name.role: the name Pip gives to the biggest bubble hole in the cut cake

stories.title: The Cape That Chose Its Own Star

s1.text: Grandma Nella's spare room smells like sunshine and peppermint tea. In the corner, her pedal sewing machine sits like a sleepy pet, waiting for its feet to move. "We want to make a dress-up cape," we say. "One that feels like us today." Grandma Nella opens the button drawer. It is sorted by colour, like a box of sweets. "Every great cape starts with a plan," she says. So we draw one with crayons. A cape with a big star on the back. But the star comes out wobbly. It looks like a blob. We giggle. "Blobs are better," we decide. Grandma Nella nods. "Then let's find some fabric." Whirr-whirr-WHIRR goes the machine, like a tiny train.

s2a.text: "The shelf," says Grandma Nella. We follow her to a tower of folded cloth. She pulls out three pieces. "Feel first," she says. The first is soft and stripy, like a kitten in a ladder of colours. The second is smooth and sparkly. The third is bumpy, like toast. We touch the stripy one. Then the bumpy one. Then back to the stripy. "This one?" we ask. Then the sparkly one slides cool under our fingers. "No, this one!" Grandma Nella laughs. She swipes her hand across it. The sequins flip from silver to blue, like fish scales changing in the sun. We swipe back. Blue to silver. "Fabric starts as one big flat sheet," she says. "We cut the shapes out, like cookies from dough." Whirr-whirr-WHIRR goes the tiny train.

s2b.text: "The button tin," says Grandma Nella. She tips it out, and buttons spill everywhere. We make pattern games. Big ones here, little ones there. Then red ones, blue ones, green ones. Then we count the holes. Two holes. Four holes. "A pattern is something that repeats," says Grandma Nella. "Again and again. Like red stripe, blue stripe on a sock." We go to the fabric shelf and touch the soft, stripy one. Its stripes are a pattern we can follow with our eyes. "This one," we say. "The stripes will help us cut straight," says Grandma Nella. "Fabric starts as one big flat sheet. We cut the shapes out, like cookies from dough." Whirr-whirr-WHIRR goes the tiny train.

s3.text: "What did you find?" Grandma Nella asks, and her eyes go crinkly. We show her, and she spreads our fabric on the table like a picnic blanket. "Every great cape starts with lines," she says, and draws them in chalk. The big scissors go crunch-crunch. But our line goes wiggly! We trim it. Wiggly again! Trim it again. "Wiggly lines are just design changes," says Grandma Nella. Then the needle keeps un-threading itself. Again and again! Grandma licks the thread, squashes it flat, and it slides through like a bunny through a tunnel. Whirr-whirr-WHIRR goes the little train. Seam by seam, the cape becomes real. We try it on. It is lopsided. One armhole is tight. But on the back, our blob-star catches the light and throws tiny dots dancing across the ceiling. We twirl. The dots twirl too.

s4a.text: The door bangs open. "I need the long scarf!" Pip shouts, grabbing it from the dressing-up corner. "Watch this!" Pip spins, and the scarf floats out like a ribbon. We spin too. Our lopsided cape swishes around our shoulders, and every time we turn, the blob-star throws tiny lights across the walls. "It's a dance!" we shout. "A spinning, flashing dance!" Grandma Nella's feet start to pedal. Whirr-whirr-WHIRR. The little train is our music. We spin slow. We spin fast. The sparkles flash every single turn, like they know the steps too. At last we flop down, dizzy and giggling. "This cape needs a name," says Grandma Nella. We think hard. We name it together: {cape_name}. On the walk home, wrapped up warm, it still catches the streetlights. Then it hangs on our door hook, throwing one last tiny light. "Goodnight, {cape_name}," we whisper.

s4b.text: Pip arrives dragging a cardboard box. "This is my stage!" Pip announces, flipping it over. "And we are doing a show." We wrap the cape around our shoulders and climb up. "I am a star," we say, "who has forgotten all their lines!" "So make up new ones!" Pip calls. So we do. We say silly things. We say grand things. The cape's lopsided hem swishes at exactly the wrong moments, which makes the star even funnier, and the blob-star on our back sparkles every time we bow. Grandma Nella is the whole audience. She claps like thunder. "Encore! Encore!" When the show is over, one sequin flips blue and drops into our hand. "Your ticket stub," says Grandma Nella. We name the cape together: {cape_name}. We carry it home folded over our arm, soft and warm like a sleeping cat. The blue sequin goes on our windowsill, where it catches the morning sun.

c1.question: "Now, my love, a cape can begin two ways. Do you want to go hunting through my fabric shelf for the cloth that feels like you today, or shall we tip out my button tin and play pattern games first to warm up our choosing eyes?"

options.label: Go straight to the fabric shelf and choose the cloth by feel
Tip out the button tin and play sorting pattern games first

c2.question: "The cape is DONE!" Pip shouts, spinning once on the spot. "So what does a brand-new cape do first, swirl through a made-up dance until the sparkles flash, or star in a pretend-show on my box stage?"

options.label: Invent a spinning dance where the sparkly bits flash
Star in a pretend-show on Pip's cardboard box stage

cape_name.role: What we name the finished cape in the warm landing

stories.title: The Case of the Cosmic Leftovers

s1.text:
The meteorite is heavier than it looks. {hero_name} holds out both hands, and {guide_name} drops it in—chunk. Dark as a burnt biscuit, speckled with tiny silver flakes, cold from its long trip through space. "Four and a half billion years old," {guide_name} says, like that's a normal thing to say on a Tuesday. "Older than Earth. Make of that what you will."

"What I will," {hero_name} says, turning it over, "is that this feels like a clue."

The teacher is handing out notebooks, the cheap kind with stiff covers. "Detective notebooks," she announces. "Because today, we are investigating a mystery." She points at the big glowing model of the solar system hanging from the ceiling. "Between Mars and Jupiter," she says, "there is a ring of rubble. Millions of rocks, all shapes and sizes, going round and round the sun like a construction site nobody ever cleaned up. The question is—why is it there?"

{hero_name} stares up at it. It does look wrong. The planets are all neat and round, and then there's this... mess. Like somebody started building something and gave up.

That's when {hero_name} feels the wiggle. Small, green, and extremely pleased with itself, Detective Zorp climbs out of {hero_name}'s jacket pocket wearing a fake mustache he definitely did not have yesterday. He pulls out a magnifying glass the size of a button and presses it against the meteorite.

"State your name," Zorp says to the rock.

The rock says nothing.

"Hmm," says Zorp. "Suspiciously lumpy. And silent. Classic guilty behavior." He looks up at {hero_name}, mustache twitching. "Partner, I think these rocks know something. And I intend to find out what."

s2a.text:
"The heavy clues," says {hero_name}.

"Excellent choice." {guide_name} leads us to a glass case and pulls on white gloves. "Two kinds of evidence today."

The first rock is dark and flecked with metal, like someone spilled iron filings into chocolate batter. "This one froze fast," says {guide_name}. "Molten metal, locked in place before it could sink."

The second is full of tiny glassy beads, round as fish eggs, pressed into gray stone. "And this one froze slow. These little spheres were liquid drops, floating, before they hardened."

"Different moments," {hero_name} says, writing it down. "From the formation."

"From before there was an Earth to stand on."

Detective Zorp has been circling the metal rock, mustache twitching. "Partner, I must interrogate this one personally." He climbs onto the case, wedges himself underneath, and tries to balance it on his head.

It does not balance. It is much heavier than it looks. Zorp wobbles. Zorp tips. Zorp goes over sideways with a small squeak, arms pinned, mustache crooked.

"The suspect," he says from the floor, "is resisting arrest."

{hero_name} hauls him up, and he straightens his mustache with great dignity. "Write this down, partner."

So {hero_name} writes, in big letters: THESE ROCKS ARE OLDER THAN EARTH.

Zorp taps the notebook. "Older than Earth. Which means they were already here when the planets were still being made. Witnesses, partner. Every single one of them."

{hero_name} looks at the dark rock, at the silver flakes frozen mid-sink, and something tingles at the back of the neck. Witnesses to what, exactly?

s2b.text:
"The crime scene," says {hero_name}. "I want to walk it."

"Then follow me." {guide_name} leads us into a long dark hall, carrying two lamps. She sets one at our feet, then walks and walks and walks, until she's a speck, and sets the second lamp down far away. A tiny glow, like a night-light left on in another neighborhood.

"Those two lamps," she calls, her voice thin with distance, "are two asteroids. Everything between them is what the belt is really made of."

"Which is?"

"Nothing. Walk it, Detective."

So {hero_name} walks. And walks. The far lamp doesn't seem to get any closer. The floor stretches on, dark and empty, and it's like being the only kid in a playground the size of a country. {hero_name} writes in the notebook: THE BELT IS MOSTLY NOT THERE.

Somewhere in the dark, a small voice wails. "Partner? Partner! I have been walking for hours! There is nothing here! No rocks, no clues, not even a bench!"

{guide_name} sweeps her flashlight across the floor and finds him, a tiny green speck halfway between the lamps, sitting down with his mustache drooping. She carries him back in her cupped hands.

"Space," Zorp announces, climbing onto {hero_name}'s shoulder, "is too spacious. I do not recommend it."

"So," says {guide_name}, clicking off one lamp. "Millions of rocks, spread thinner than flour dusted across a whole kitchen. Does that look like a planet that exploded?"

{hero_name} stares into the enormous dark between the lamps. No. It doesn't. An explosion would leave a pile. This is more like... ingredients that never got mixed.

"Then what," {hero_name} says slowly, "stopped the recipe?"

Zorp's mustache lifts. "Now that, partner, is the question."

s3.text:
"Detectives!" the teacher calls, tapping the glowing model. "Gather round. I have a second clue, and it changes everything." She makes the planets spin. "Watch closely. Every planet orbits the Sun in the same direction. And they all travel on the same flat level—like this." She holds her hand out flat and slides it through the ring of planets. "One direction. One flat plane. Like pizza dough, all spun from the same ball."

Zorp climbs onto {hero_name}'s shoulder for a better look, mustache bristling. "So what did you find back there, partner? Anything the rocks confessed?" He twirls the end of his mustache. "Because I have a theory. Food fight. The planets had a food fight, and nobody cleaned up."

{hero_name} watches the model turn. Round and round, all one way, all one flat spinning disk. Then the eyes go to the rubble between Mars and Jupiter. The pieces are small. Really small. And spread out so far that if you stood on one, the next would be a dot in the black.

"Wait," {hero_name} says slowly. "If everything formed from one spinning ball of dough... then the belt isn't a planet that crashed. The pieces are too little. Too far apart. They never got to join up in the first place."

Zorp gasps. "Not broken?"

"Never built," {hero_name} says, and writes it in the notebook in big letters: NOT BROKEN. NEVER BUILT.

Zorp leans over the page, squinting through his button-sized magnifying glass. "Hmm. So the rocks aren't guilty of anything." He strokes his mustache. "They're... leftovers. Ingredients that never made it into the pizza."

"Exactly," {hero_name} says. "But that means something stopped them. Something kept those pieces from joining up." The pen taps the notebook. Tap. Tap. "And if they never became a planet... what does that make them? Failures? Or something else entirely?"

Zorp's eyes gleam under the fake mustache. "Partner," he whispers, "I think our suspects just became witnesses."

s4a.text:
"The cold trail," {hero_name} says. "Let's follow the ice."

{guide_name} grins and flicks off the lights. The room goes dark, and then—whoosh—a long, glowing streak appears on the ceiling. A comet. It has a fuzzy head and a tail that stretches across the whole room like a scarf caught in the wind.

"Comets," {guide_name} says, "are the other leftovers. The icy kind." She holds up a lumpy white ball. "This model is made of ice and pepper. Dirty snowball, basically. That's what a comet is—ice, dust, and rock, all mixed together and frozen solid."

Zorp scrambles up {hero_name}'s arm, mustache quivering. "Frozen? Frozen means evidence preserved!" He leans toward the model, magnifying glass ready. "I must taste it. For science."

"Zorp, maybe don't—"

Too late. Zorp licks the model. His whole face scrunches up. "Brain freeze!" he squeaks, clutching his head. "But... deliciously solved!"

{guide_name} laughs. "He's not wrong. Comets are like messages in a bottle, thrown to the edge of the solar system billions of years ago. The ice inside them matches the cold chemistry of the young solar system—before planets, before fish, before trees. Each comet is a frozen piece of the beginning."

{hero_name} stares at the glowing streak on the ceiling. Ice older than anything alive. A message from before there was anyone to read it. The pen moves almost by itself: COMETS = FROZEN MEMORIES.

"So the asteroids are rocky leftovers," {hero_name} says slowly, "and the comets are icy ones. Both are... memories of how it all started?"

"Both are witnesses," {guide_name} says. "They remember the formation."

Zorp, still rubbing his forehead, nods solemnly. "The case deepens. But how do the ice witnesses connect to the rock witnesses? That's the real mystery."

{hero_name} taps the notebook. Tap. Tap. Two kinds of leftovers. One story. But how do they fit together?

s4b.text:
"The gravity twist," {hero_name} says. "I want to see how Jupiter stirred the pot."

{guide_name} pulls out a spinning stool—the kind office chairs have, but smaller—and sets a rubber ball on the seat. "Watch," she says, and gives the stool a slow spin. The ball rolls in a wobbly circle, never settling, never smooth. "That ball is trying to orbit. But something keeps knocking it off course."

She taps the stool with her finger. Tap. The ball wobbles harder.

"That's Jupiter," {guide_name} says. "Jupiter is enormous—more than twice as heavy as all the other planets combined. Its gravity is so strong that it kept stirring the asteroid belt, over and over, like a giant hand knocking the pieces apart every time they tried to clump together."

{hero_name} watches the ball lurch and wobble. It never finds a rhythm. Never settles into a clean orbit. "So the pieces wanted to join up," {hero_name} says, "but Jupiter wouldn't let them?"

"Exactly. The belt is a construction site where the foreman kept knocking the bricks apart."

Zorp's eyes go wide. He scrambles down from {hero_name}'s shoulder and marches straight to the stool. "I must experience this gravity for myself. For the case." He climbs onto the seat, grips the edges with his tiny green hands, and looks up. "Spin me, partner. Gently."

{hero_name} gives the stool a slow push. Zorp goes round and round, mustache flapping. "Oh," he says. "Oh no. Oh—" The stool stops. Zorp wobbles off, legs wiggly, and sits down hard on the floor. "Gravity," he declares, pointing a shaky finger upward, "is very rude."

{guide_name} grins. "But it's the reason the belt exists. Jupiter's gravity kept those pieces from ever forming a planet. They stayed small. Stayed scattered. Stayed... unused."

{hero_name} writes it down: JUPITER = THE TROUBLEMAKER. Then, underneath: THE BRICKS NEVER GOT USED.

Zorp, still dizzy, leans against {hero_name}'s shoe. "Unused bricks," he mumbles. "But unused for what? That's the question, partner. What were they supposed to build?"

c1.question: Dr. Stone holds up two evidence bags and says, 'Detective, we can examine the heavy clues up close in the gallery, or we can walk the crime scene and see how empty this belt really is. Which calls to you?'

options.label: Study the meteorites in the lab
Pace the distance between the lamps

c2.question: The teacher spins the stool slowly and asks, 'We know the pieces never joined. Do you want to follow the cold trail to the comets, or stay here and see how Jupiter's gravity stirred the pot?'

options.label: Chase the comets to the deep freeze
Watch the gravity demonstration

stories.title: The Case of the Scooting Spoons

s1.text:
"Three spoons," says Grandma. "One each. Middle of the counter."
We are at Grandma's, laying the table for lunch, and her counter is so high we have to go up on our toes. We put the three shiny spoons in a row. Then we go for the napkins.
Scrape. Scrape.
We turn round. All three spoons have slid away down the counter into the same corner, by the big drawer, and they are lying there nose to nose.
We carry them back to the middle. Down go our chins on the cold counter to watch them.
Slowly, slowly, the spoons scoot back to the corner.
"Grandma," we say. "Your spoons are going somewhere."
Grandma says spoons do not go anywhere, and goes on stirring the soup.
So we wind up our little tin robot {robot_name} and stand him on the counter. Click, clack, click, clack. Then his boots reach that corner and stop dead. He waves both arms about. He cannot lift a foot.
"Bzzt," says {robot_name}.
Something in that corner is pulling.

s2a.text:
"Spoons first," we say.
We go round the kitchen and collect every spoon there is. The shiny metal one goes down in the middle of the counter. Scoot, scoot, scoot. Off it goes to the corner and lands with a tiny click.
"Wooden one next," we say, and down goes Grandma's big spoon, the one she stirs the soup with. We wait. We wait a bit longer. It lies there like a dropped sock.
Then we stand the bendy plastic spoon from our picnic box in the same spot. Nothing. Not one wobble.
"It is picky," we say.
{robot_name} taps his own tin head, which is what he does instead of thinking.
One more test. We hold one finger out over the corner and keep it there, right where every spoon stops.
No tug. No tickle. Nothing at all.
"It does not want fingers," we say. "It wants shiny metal, and it wants it hard."
We cannot see it. But now we know what it likes.

s2b.text:
"Boots," we say. "Follow the boots."
We wind {robot_name} up and stand him at the far end of the counter. Click, clack, click, clack. Off he goes, happy as anything.
Then he comes near the corner and his boots swerve. He did not turn. His feet turned for him. He does a wobbly dance on the spot and sticks fast.
"Bzzt," says {robot_name}, which means come and get me.
We pick him up and start him again from the other side. Near the corner, grabbed. Far away, nothing.
So we lay him flat in our hand and slide him slowly across, like a little sled, and this time we feel it ourselves. A soft strong tug, right through our fingers. It is the tug the fridge door gives when it takes the last bit shut all by itself.
We look at the counter. Bare wood. Nothing on it at all.
"It is not up here," we say. "It is underneath."
Something under there is reaching up through the wood.

s3.text:
The corner. The big drawer under it.
"Go on, then," says Grandma, kneeling down beside us. "Hold the handle and pull straight. Then it comes out slowly and nothing tips over."
So we pull straight, and the drawer slides open. Rubber bands. Birthday candles. A ball of string. And stuck to the shiny metal rail along the inside, holding on with both of its ends, a big red horseshoe magnet.
"That!" says Grandma. "That has been lost since Easter."
She puts it into our hands. It is heavier than it looks. We bring one spoon slowly towards it, and the last little bit the spoon does by itself. Tug! It clacks on.
"A magnet attracts anything with iron in it," says Grandma. "Spoons, yes. Robot boots, oh yes. Not wood, though, and not plastic, and not one single finger."
Shut in that drawer, it was pulling straight up through the counter, the way the smell of toast comes up through a whole house.
That is why the spoons scooted. That is why the boots stuck.

s4a.text:
Grandma ties the ball of string onto the magnet. We take the big wooden spoon for a rod, because the magnet will never once grab that.
The three metal spoons go out on the kitchen rug. Those are the fish.
We swing the magnet down low over them. Lower. Lower.
Tug! A spoon comes up off the rug and clacks on.
"One," says Grandma.
We catch the second. We catch the third. Then {robot_name} waddles over and stands right underneath the magnet with both arms up.
"Bzzt," he says, which means me next.
Up he swings, boots first, buzzing his giggly buzz. We lower him gently back onto the rug, and he comes round and asks again.
Grandma brings the cookies over and sits down on the rug with us, and we hold the magnet above one cookie, just to be sure. Cookies have no iron in them. Cookies stay put.
"Three spoons and a robot," says Grandma. "Nobody has ever fished this kitchen better."
We leave the string tied on. Tomorrow the rug will be full of fish again.

s4b.text:
"A pull that strong needs a job," we say.
We carry the magnet across the kitchen, and before we even get there it jumps out of our hand and lands on the fridge door. Thunk. Under all that white paint, the fridge is metal too.
{robot_name} salutes it with one tin arm.
Grandma digs out our drawing from yesterday, the one with the purple dinosaur. We slide the paper under the magnet and let go. The magnet holds it flat against the door, like a thumb that never gets tired. It is pulling straight through the paper, the way it pulled straight up through the counter.
The shopping list goes up next. Then the photo of us in our rain boots.
"That is my whole kitchen sorted," says Grandma.
Before dinner we go back to the corner where it all started. We put a spoon down, get our chins on the counter, and watch.
It does not move. Not one scrape.
Our magnet has better things to do now. It is holding a purple dinosaur, and it will still be holding it in the morning.

c1.question: "Two clues, then," says Grandma, wiping her hands. "You can put things down on that counter and see which ones run away. Or you can send that robot in again and follow his boots. Spoons, or boots?"

options.label: Put things down and see which ones run away
Send the robot in again and follow his boots

c2.question: "Well, it is yours until dinner," says Grandma. "You could tie it on that string and go fishing on the rug. Or you could give it a proper job on the fridge door. Fishing, or helper?"

options.label: Tie the magnet on the string and fish the rug
Give the magnet a job on the fridge door

robot_name.role: the little wind-up tin robot companion the child names

stories.title: The Case of the Too-Easy First Level

s1.text:
I want to tell you about a detective I knew.

Not the kind with a magnifying glass and a raincoat. Well — all right, there was a magnifying glass. But it belonged to Detective Dee, and Detective Dee was a sock puppet with button eyes and a voice like a kazoo with opinions.

It was a rainy Saturday, the kind that makes the living room feel like a cave in the best way. Big screen glowing. Blanket fort sagging. And {detective_name} was three levels into {game_world} — you know the one, with the hero who leaps and the coins that go *plink* when you grab them.

Level one? A breeze. A stroll. A gentle hop over a pit so small it might as well have apologized.

But level three kept bonking them. Boing. Off the moving log. Boing. Into the mud. Again.

"One more try," {detective_name} muttered.

That is when Detective Dee slid off the sofa arm, held the magnifying glass up to the glowing screen — the pixels went big and blocky and beautiful, like a mosaic made of sugar cubes — and declared, in that kazoo voice:

"Something about level one was suspiciously polite."

{detective_name} paused the game. "Polite?"

"Too easy. Too friendly. A level that never pushes back?" Dee tapped the glass. "That is not a level. That is a butler holding a door. And butlers, my friend, always know something."

Rain ticked the window. The frozen hero hung mid-jump on the screen, one coin still spinning, waiting.

"So what do we do?" {detective_name} asked.

Dee's button eyes gleamed. "We go back to level one. And this time — we read it."

s2a.text:
Back to level one. Detective Dee rode {detective_name}'s hand like a captain on a mast, magnifying glass sweeping the screen.

"Begin the heist," Dee whispered. "Walk. Do not jump. I want to see the crime happen."

So {detective_name} walked. The hero strolled left to right, whistling a little tune — and stopped. Right at the edge of the first pit. One jump wide. Not two. Not a scary gap. Exactly one.

"Freeze!" Dee squawked. "There. You see it? That pit is placed so walking fails. The game is not being nice, partner. It is teaching your thumb where the jump button lives."

{detective_name} blinked. "The pit is a lesson?"

"A lesson with a moustache and a fake name," said Dee. "Now hop it."

They hopped. And there, dead center in the path, sat the first coin. Waiting. Shining. The hero's toe brushed it and — plink! — the score ticked up, bright and instant.

Dee gasped so hard the sock nearly came off. "The coin! It chimes the second you touch it! That is not decoration, that is a reward loop — the game saying, good job, do it again, here is a shiny thing!"

"So the whole level..."

"Is a tutorial in disguise!" Dee held the glass to the screen, and the pixels went big and blocky, like clues under a lamp. "The pit teaches jumping. The coin teaches grabbing. And nobody ever told us. That, partner, is the politest trick in gaming."

{detective_name} grinned. "What else is it hiding?"

Dee's button eyes narrowed. "Only one way to find out. Squeeze."

And they squeezed.

s2b.text:
"We need a witness," {detective_name} said, reaching for the phone. "Somebody who built one of these things."

Dee gasped. "Your cousin. Mara. The game-maker. Oh, she is SO a suspect."

Mara answered on the second ring, and {detective_name} put her on speaker so Dee could interrogate properly.

"Mara," {detective_name} said. "Why are first levels always so easy?"

A pause. Then Mara laughed — the kind of laugh that knows something. "Easy? Or easy on purpose?"

Dee leaned so close to the phone his button eyes nearly touched it. "Answer the question, suspect!"

"Hi, Dee," Mara said, completely unsurprised. "Okay, one hint. But then you have to come over Saturday and watch my old school project, glitches and all. Deal?"

"Deal," said {detective_name}.

"When I made my game," Mara said, "I spent a whole week deciding where to put my very first obstacle. One little pit. Want to know where it went?"

"Where?"

"Right where the player couldn't avoid it. Smack in the path. Because if they could walk around it, half of them would never learn to jump — and then level two would eat them alive."

Dee made a noise like a kazoo falling down stairs. "She ADMITS it! The pit was a trap! A helpful trap!"

"A tutorial," Mara said. "The best ones never say 'press this button.' They just put a pit exactly one jump wide and let you figure it out. And the first coin? Dead center, so nobody misses it."

{detective_name} looked at the frozen screen, where the hero hung mid-jump over one small, polite pit.

"Saturday," Mara said. "Bring the sock."

Dee straightened. "Tell her the sock brings YOU."

"He heard that," said Mara, and hung up laughing.

s3.text:
Dee lowered the magnifying glass, slow and solemn, like a detective pocketing a diamond. "Whatever you just found," the kazoo voice whispered, "it has an address. And I know where it lives."

An hour later we were squished onto Mara's couch. Mara made games — well, one game, an old school project, glowing on her laptop. Above the screen she'd pinned her level sketches to the wall, pencil lines and arrows and little stick heroes, like a tiny design studio had exploded in an orderly fashion.

"Show me level one," Dee commanded.
