Mara loaded it. The hero trotted out. And there — the first enemy, shuffling along slower than a queue at the post office. It couldn't even bonk you, not if you were the tiniest bit careful.

"Watch," said Mara. "My friends playtested this. When someone missed a jump — boing, into the mud — I moved the platform closer. And I dropped a coin right where they should land. Like a signpost. A shiny, plinking signpost."

Dee went very still. A sock going still is a dramatic thing.

"The pit," Dee breathed. "It was never there to stop anybody. It was there to teach the jump. The enemy teaches the dodge. The coin teaches the landing." The magnifying glass rose, trembling. "This whole level is a tutorial — wearing a mustache!"

Mara grinned. "A tutorial in disguise. Nobody reads instructions, so level one teaches by need. You need to jump, here's a pit. You need to dodge, here's a slow shuffler. And every time you get it right — plink — a coin, a chime, a little burst of yes. Goal, action, reward. Then again. Goal, action, reward. That loop runs the whole game. That's the engine under everything."

"A reward loop," Dee whispered, like naming buried treasure. "Case closed."

Then the button eyes narrowed.

"Mara. Why is that wall... a slightly different shade?"

Mara's grin went mysterious. "Play it," she said, handing over the controller. "With your new eyes."

s4a.text:
{detective_name} steered the hero back through level one, past the polite little pit, past the slow shuffler, all the way to that wall. Up close, through Dee's magnifying glass, the pixels really were a different shade. Off. Like one wrong Lego in a wall of red.

"Do it," Dee whispered. "Boop the wall."

"You can't boop a wall."

"Detectives boop."

So {detective_name} walked the hero straight into it. And the wall slid open.

No key. No button. Just a hidden room, glowing gold, treasure chests stacked like pancakes, and right in the middle — a tiny sprite of Mara, waving. A little speech bubble popped up: *You found me!*

"Mara!" {detective_name} spun around. "You're IN the game?"

Mara shrugged, but she was grinning. "Makers hide themselves sometimes. And here's the thing — nobody told you that room existed. The wall told you. One off-color patch, that's the whole clue. Games leave secrets like footprints. Once you learn to read them..." she tapped the screen, "...you start seeing them everywhere."

"Footprints," Dee breathed. "Made of pixels. The perfect crime."

Later, when the rain had softened to a patter and Mara had gone to make cocoa, {detective_name} opened their notebook to a fresh page. At the top they wrote: *Clues Games Leave.* Underneath: *1. A wall that doesn't match is a door that hasn't admitted it yet.*

Detective Dee got tucked back onto the sofa arm, case closed, magnifying glass under one fuzzy arm. Beside him, in the notebook margin, {detective_name} drew a tiny detective badge.

"Same time next Saturday?" {detective_name} asked.

The sock said nothing. But the button eyes gleamed.

s4b.text:
{detective_name} looked at the odd-colored wall. Then at Mara. Then back at the wall.

"Later," they said. "First — teach me to build one. A level. A tiny one."

Dee gasped so hard a button eye rattled. "The detective becomes... the criminal mastermind."

"The *designer*," Mara laughed, and pulled up a blank screen. Empty. Just a grid, waiting. "Okay. One pit. One coin. One enemy. That's your whole budget. Where does the pit go?"

{detective_name} thought about it. "Near the start. So the player has to jump right away."

"Why?"

"Because... if they jump early and nothing bad happens, they learn the jump is safe. Then when it matters later, they already know how."

Mara's eyebrows went up. "That's level design. You just did level design."

They placed the pit. They dropped the coin right over the landing spot — a shiny little signpost. Then the enemy: one slow shuffler, waddling along. "Slow," {detective_name} said, "so nobody gets bonked while they're still learning."

"A tutorial in disguise," Mara said. "Your mustache, detective."

Then she opened her animation folder, and {detective_name} leaned in close. There was the squirrel hero — or rather, twelve of him, frame by frame, tail up, tail down, mid-wiggle. "I draw every hop," Mara said. "Twelve drawings for one second of wiggle."

"Twelve!" Dee fainted backward off the couch arm.

That night, {detective_name} opened their notebook to a fresh page and wrote at the top: *My First Tutorial.* Underneath: a pit, a coin, and one extremely slow shuffler, drawn with great care.

Dee climbed back up, adjusted his magnifying glass, and cleared his tiny kazoo throat.

"The case," he announced, "is closed. And the detective..." a dramatic pause, "...is officially brilliant."

"We both are," said {detective_name}.

"Correct," said the sock.

c1.question: Detective Dee swivels on your hand and booms, 'Every great detective chooses a door, partner! Do we replay level one and squeeze it for clues, or do we shake down my prime suspect, your cousin who BUILT one of these things?'

options.label: Replay level one and hunt for clues inside the game
Call Cousin Mara and ask the game maker directly

c2.question: Mara leans back and grins. 'So, detective. You've cracked the tutorial. Now what, do you go poke that suspicious wall, or do you sit down and build a sneaky first level of your own?'

options.label: Push on the odd-colored wall and chase the hidden secret
Stay with Mara and design a tiny tutorial level yourself

detective_name.role: The kid detective's name, used by Mara and the storyteller

game_world.role: The made-up game the kid plays, with a hero, a first pit, and a shiny first coin
game_world.default: a squirrel pirate hopping through Treetop Lagoon

stories.title: The Case of the Vanishing Bones

s1.text: The museum after closing time is a different place. The lights are low, the floors shine, and everything is very, very quiet. Dr. Amara, the paleontologist, walks with soft shoes and a softer voice, as if the whole building is asleep and she does not want to wake it. Beside her walks Riley, the detective she called in for a very strange case. "This way," Dr. Amara whispers. They stop in front of a glass case taller than a door. Above it hangs the dark silhouette of an enormous shark, long as a bus, painted on the wall. Inside the case, on a bed of blue velvet, lie rows of teeth. Small ones. Big ones. All dark, all triangular, all shining under a single spotlight. "Ancient shark teeth," says Dr. Amara. "Older than the dinosaurs. Older than the mountains." Riley leans close. The glass fogs a little. "So where is the rest of it?" Dr. Amara smiles the way people smile when the mystery is about to begin. "That," she says, "is the case. Dinosaurs left bones everywhere. Legs like tree trunks. Skulls like bathtubs. But sharks?" She taps the glass gently. "Teeth. Only teeth. The whole skeleton... vanished." Riley looks at the painted shadow on the wall, then at the little dark teeth in the case. A body that big, gone. A smile left behind. "Tell me everything," says the detective.

s2a.text: "The teeth, please," Riley says. "A good detective always checks the evidence first." Dr. Amara nods, her eyes twinkling like a kid sharing a secret. She pulls a small drawer from the cabinet. It slides open with a soft wooden sound. Inside, on a bed of dark velvet, sits a single tooth. It is small, dark, and triangular, with edges sharp enough to slice through time itself. "This one," Dr. Amara whispers, "is older than the mountain outside." She places it in Riley's palm. It is cool and hard, like a stone that has been sleeping for a million years. "But here is the problem," Dr. Amara says. She reaches up and touches the tip of her own nose. "Press here. Gently." Riley presses. The nose bends. It is soft. It is bendy. "That," says Dr. Amara, "is cartilage. The stuff that made up the ancient shark's whole body." Riley looks at the tooth, then at her own nose. The tooth is stone. The nose is soft. "So the sharks didn't vanish," Riley says slowly. "They just... left only their hardest parts behind." Dr. Amara smiles. "Exactly. The ocean patrol has been swimming for four hundred million years. They simply don't bother with bones."

s2b.text: "The timeline," Riley says. "I want to see when." Dr. Amara's eyes light up. She reaches under the counter and pulls out a long, rolled scroll of thick paper. It is heavier than it looks. Together they carry it to the open floor, where the moonlight falls in silver squares through the tall windows. "Now," Dr. Amara whispers, "we unroll the past." The paper unfurls across the floor, longer than the rug, longer than the hallway. At the far left, almost at the edge of the world, are the first sharks. Then, much later, the dinosaurs appear, stomping through the middle. And way, way at the end, so close to the edge it makes you dizzy, are the humans. "Look," says Dr. Amara. She places the small dark tooth right beside a dinosaur bone. The tooth is small, dark, and triangular, and it sits there like a stone that remembers the deep. Riley stares. The tooth is older. Much older. "They were here first," Riley says. "The sharks were swimming on their ocean patrol long before the dinosaurs even learned to walk." Dr. Amara nods. "Ancient survivors," she says softly. "They watched the mountains grow."

s3.text:
"What did you find?" asks Dr. Amara, leaning in.

Riley holds it out, and her eyes go wide. "Oh," she whispers. "This changes things. We need to see a living one. We need to see how a shark actually behaves."

Which is why, just before sunrise, they are standing on the deck of a small research boat, the sky turning the color of a pale peach. The sea is flat and gray-green, and the only sounds are the soft slap of water and the gulls arguing overhead.

Beside them stands Dr. Reyes, a marine biologist with a thermos in one hand and a laptop in the other. "We call this the ocean patrol," she says. "We follow the sharks we've tagged and see where they go."

"There," says Dr. Reyes, pointing. "Fin."

A dark triangle slips through the water, smooth and unhurried. It passes the boat without a glance. The shark does not turn. It does not circle. It simply keeps going, as if they are not there at all.

"It's ignoring us," says Riley.

"It always does," says Dr. Reyes. "That's the thing nobody tells you. Sharks are busy. They have somewhere to be."

She turns the laptop around. On the screen, a small dot moves along a glowing line, steady as a heartbeat. "This shark has been swimming for three days without stopping. It doesn't sleep the way we do. It just keeps cruising."

Riley watches the dot glide across the map, slow and sure, as if the ocean were a road and the shark knew every turn.

"Ancient," says Dr. Amara softly. "That's how they've always been. Swimming. Patrolling. Not interested in us at all."

Riley looks from the screen to the water, where the fin has already vanished into the gray-green distance.

"So the bones vanished," says Riley, "but the shark didn't. It just kept going."

s4a.text:
Riley taps the laptop screen. "How does it work? The skin. The nose. Everything."

Dr. Reyes smiles and reaches into a bucket by her feet. "I thought you'd ask." She pulls out a small square of grey leather, dried and stiff. "Sharkskin. Preserved. Go on."

Riley takes it. One way, it slides smooth, like the worn arm of a favourite sofa. The other way...

"Whoa."

"Sandpaper," says Dr. Reyes. "Rub your hand the wrong way on a shark and you'd know about it."

Riley turns the square over. "Why would a shark need to be sandpaper?"

"It doesn't," says Dr. Reyes. "That's just what happens when you're covered in tiny teeth instead of scales."

"Tiny teeth?"

"Everywhere. Even on its eyeballs."

Riley stares at the little grey square. Even its skin is made of teeth. Even its skin is a weapon.

Dr. Reyes pulls out a folded diagram, a shark drawn in careful pencil, its snout dotted with small dark freckles. "And these," she says, tapping the freckles, "these are how it hears dinner from a mile away."

"Freckles?"

"Sensing freckles. They feel the tiniest heartbeat in the water. A flounder hiding under sand. A fish with a limp."

Riley looks from the diagram to the empty grey-green sea. The fin is long gone. But suddenly the water feels different. Fuller. Watched.

"So that's the answer," says Riley slowly. "They never changed because they never had to. They were already perfect."

Dr. Amara nods, once, her eyes bright. "Case closed," she whispers.

Riley slips the sharkskin into a pocket. Small. Rough. Older than mountains.

"Ancient," says Riley. "And still on patrol."

s4b.text:
Riley points at the moving dot. "Where is it going?"

Dr. Reyes leans over the laptop and zooms in. The coastline appears, a pale curve, and along it, small blue shapes. Swimmers. Dozens of them, speckled along the beach like sprinkles on a cake.

"It's heading right for them," says Riley.

"Watch," says Dr. Reyes.

The dot glides closer. Closer. It passes the first blue shape. It does not stop. It passes the second. It does not turn. It slides along the whole dotted line of swimmers, steady as a tram on rails, and keeps going.

"It didn't even look," says Riley.

"It never does," says Dr. Reyes. "Three days of tracking. It has passed swimmers, surfers, a very unfortunate beach ball, and one dog that fell off a paddleboard. It ignored all of them."

"What does it care about?"

Dr. Reyes taps the screen. A smaller dot, orange, flickers far ahead. "That. A school of mackerel, two miles north. It smelled them an hour ago."

Riley watches the dark dot cruise on, unhurried, unbothered, the swimmers shrinking behind it. The shark has somewhere to be. The shark has always had somewhere to be.

"It swam past dinosaurs," says Dr. Amara softly. "It swam past everything. It just keeps swimming."

Riley thinks of the little dark tooth in the museum case, sitting on blue velvet under its spotlight. A smile with no body. A mystery with a very simple answer.

"The bones vanished," says Riley, "because sharks don't stop long enough to leave any."

Dr. Reyes laughs. Dr. Amara closes the laptop gently, like a book at bedtime.

"Case closed," says Riley, and puts both hands on the rail, watching the water where the shark is still, somewhere, swimming.

c1.question: "We have two ways to solve this mystery," Dr. Amara says, holding up a dark fossil tooth. "We could examine these ancient teeth closely to learn what they're made of, or we could unroll the great timeline and see exactly when sharks first appeared. Which evidence calls to you?"

options.label: Study the fossil teeth in the drawer
Look at the timeline on the floor

c2.question: "The screen shows where our shark is swimming," the biologist says, looking up from the tracker. "We could focus on how its body works, its sandpaper skin and sensing freckles, or we could follow its path to see what it actually cares about. What should we investigate?"

options.label: Learn about the shark's special skin and senses
Follow where the shark is swimming

s1.text:
Pickles is yowling again. Yowling and yowling, because robotics club ran late and her dinner is late and she does not care about gear ratios at all. We are in Grandpa's garden shed, which smells like grass clippings and old wood, and every shelf is stacked with things that might be useful someday. Jars of screws. A bicycle wheel. Three umbrellas with no handles.

"She has a point," Grandpa says. He is sitting on the upturned bucket that is his thinking seat, and he unscrews the top of his thermos very slowly, the way he always does before a big decision. He calls that thermos the Professor. Nobody knows why. He takes a sip. He waits. "Hmm," he says. "The Professor thinks we have ourselves an invention problem."

Pickles yowls. It is the loudest sound a small cat can make.

"A machine," we say, "that feeds her on time. Every time. Even when we're late."

Grandpa stands up and pulls a dusty box off the highest shelf, and inside are the strangest things we have ever seen. A mousetrap attached to a doorbell. A wooden spoon with a motor glued to it. "My prototypes," he says, like he's introducing old friends. "That one was supposed to stir my tea. That one was supposed to find my glasses. Neither one worked even a little bit."

He taps the side of the box. "Every inventor starts exactly here. One small, annoying problem, and one idea that probably won't work. That's how the steam engine happened, and the telephone too. Somebody annoyed, somebody tinkering."

Pickles headbutts Grandpa's shin, hard.

"The Professor thinks," Grandpa says, pouring the last sip into his cup, "that we'd better start drawing."

s2a.text: Grandpa pats the Professor and grins. "The library it is." So we grab our bikes and pedal into town, the evening air cool on our faces, while Pickles watches from the window with her tail flicking like a metronome. The library's invention corner smells like paper and glue, and we spread out books about James Watt, who took Newcomen's clunky steam engine and remixed it into something that actually worked, and Alexander Graham Bell, who mashed a telegraph wire together with a vibrating diaphragm and called it a telephone. We take apart a broken radio from the donation bin, and the inside is a city of wires and tiny screws. Grandpa shows up with the Professor and settles into a chair. "See this?" he says, tapping a diagram of Watt's engine. "A patent. It's a paper that says, 'This is my idea, and you can't steal it.' But here's the clever part. It also tells everyone exactly how it works, so the next inventor can stand on your shoulders and build something even better." We sketch our first messy diagram on the back of a receipt, drawing gears and levers and a little door for the food. It looks like spaghetti had a fight with a clock. But it's ours.

s2b.text: "The shed," we say, and Grandpa nods slowly. "The Professor approves." We raid the pegboard for hooks and pulleys, dig through jars of screws, and pull apart the disassembled radio on its mat, revealing a jungle of wires and a motor that might still work. Maya bikes over with her electronics kit, and she spreads it out on the workbench like a treasure map. "You need a timer," she says, holding up a little circuit board. "Something that ticks until it's dinner o'clock, then bam, it triggers the motor. That's how the internet started, you know. ARPANET took computers that already existed and phone lines that already existed and just... remixed them so universities could share stuff." We sketch our first diagram on the back of a seed packet, labeling it 'Prototype 1' in big letters and taping the corners down with duct tape. Grandpa consults the Professor, sipping slowly. "Hmm," he says. "The Professor thinks you're onto something. Or possibly onto the floor. Hard to tell with prototypes." The diagram is already smudged with fingerprints and crossed-out lines, but it's a start.

s3.text:
Back in the shed, Grandpa unrolls the diagram on the workbench. It already has one coffee ring on it, from before. "What did you find out there?" he asks, and we tell him everything, and he nods and adds three more squiggly lines to the drawing with his pencil. Now it looks like a map of a place that does not exist.

"Prototype 1," Grandpa announces. "The Professor expects great things."

We build the hopper out of a cardboard box, because cardboard is the best building material ever invented and nobody can prove otherwise. The kibble goes in the top. Underneath, Grandpa rigs a little gate with string and a pulley off an old clothesline, and we hold the whole thing together with duct tape and hope. Mostly hope.

"Test run," Grandpa says. He pours in a scoop of kibble. We pull the string.

The gear slips. The string tangles. The gate opens sideways, then not at all, and then the whole hopper folds itself up with a sad little crunch, like a cardboard box sitting down because it is tired. Kibble goes everywhere. Pickles strolls in and starts eating it off the floor, which is not the point at all.

"Hmm," Grandpa says. He unscrews the Professor. He sips. He waits so long we think he has fallen asleep with his eyes open. "The Professor thinks of Bell and Watson."

"The telephone guys?"

"Those very guys. Do you know how many different diaphragms they tried before one carried a clear voice? Dozens. Dozens and dozens. Little discs of this, little discs of that. Every single one that failed told them something." He taps the collapsed hopper with one finger. "A Prototype 1 that falls down is not a defeat. It is a clue with a crunch."

We look at the wreckage. The string is wrapped around the gear like spaghetti. And that is when we see it: we yanked. The gate never had a chance. It does not need a yank. It needs a slow, steady push, the kind that does not hurry.

Grandpa is already reaching for the pencil, and the diagram gets its first piece of tape.

"Wait," Theo says, slowly, the way he talks when an idea is still warming up. "Why don't we use something that pushes slow? Like... like my bike pump?"

s4a.text: "A bike pump," Grandpa says, and he is already rummaging. "Air. Slow, steady air." He comes up holding the pump in one hand and a plastic water bottle in the other, and he holds them up like two puzzle pieces that have been waiting to meet. "James Watt did exactly this, you know. The old steam engines wasted half their puff, so Watt bolted on a separate part, a condenser, and suddenly the whole thing worked twice as well. He didn't invent a new engine. He remixed an old one." We tape the bottle to the pump, hose it to the gate, and the diagram gets two more pieces of tape and a big arrow that says AIR GOES HERE. "Prototype 2," Grandpa announces. "The Professor is watching." We press the pump. The piston sighs. The gate slides open, slow as sunrise, and kibble pours into the bowl in a perfect little waterfall. Pickles eats her dinner on time, and we cheer so loudly the shed door rattles in its frame. Later, Grandpa stamps the diagram with his old ink stamp: PROTOTYPE 2, IT WORKS. "We could file a patent," he says, sipping. "But the real prize is this drawing. The next inventor reads it, and builds something even better." The diagram comes home with us, taped and ringed and beautiful. Pickles purrs against it all evening.

s4b.text: "Wires and a motor," Maya says, and she is already elbow-deep in the bin of old radio parts. "The internet worked like this, you know. Nobody invented new wires. They took phone lines that already existed, and computers that already existed, and taught them to talk to each other. Remix." She holds up a little motor and a coil of speaker wire, and her grin says these two are about to become best friends. We wire the timer to the motor, tape a cardboard scoop to its spinning bit, and the diagram gets two more pieces of tape and a cloud of squiggly lines that Grandpa labels THE BRAIN. "Prototype 2," he announces. "The Professor is listening." The timer ticks. Beep. The motor hums, the scoop turns, and kibble tips into the bowl in one neat little avalanche, right on time. Theo dances. Pickles eats. Maya looks at the whole humming, beeping thing and says, "You realise this is basically a robot." Grandpa raises the Professor in a toast. "Every inventor," he says, "stands on someone's shoulders." The little scoop motor comes home with us, beeping softly in our pocket. Pickles follows it around like a new friend.

c1.question: "Well now," Grandpa says, patting the Professor, "do we go hunt for ideas in the library's invention books, or do we stay right here and see what the shed wants to give us?"

options.label: Go research how old inventors remixed ideas
Stay and tinker with parts and Maya's electronics

c2.question: "The gate needs a slow, steady push," Maya says, tapping her chin. "Do we build it with air and bottles, or with wires and a motor?"

options.label: Remix a bicycle pump and water bottle into a slow piston
Remix a timer circuit and old radio parts into a motor scoop

s1.text: The garden club meets after school, between the raised beds, where the sundial points its long shadow across the path. Granny Rosa is waiting for us, holding a cardboard box lined with foil. "This, cariños, is a little sun-trap," she says. "A solar oven." Pip leans in so close his nose nearly touches it. "Does it work?" "Sunlight is energy," says Granny Rosa. "It travels eight whole minutes to reach us. Aim it right, and it warms land and sea, feeds every plant in this garden — and melts chocolate." She says the party is Friday. A melty-snack party, if we can make the oven work. Nobody in our club has ever made one work. Pip licks the spoon anyway, before we've even started. "Just checking," he says. Miso the cat is already asleep in the brightest patch of path, purring like a tiny engine. Granny Rosa sets the box on the sundial's stone. "One sunbeam," she says. "That's all we need to catch." We look at the box. We look at the sky. Friday is very soon.

s2a.text:
"Feel first," we say. "Where is the warmth hiding?"

Granny Rosa presses her palm flat on the sundial stone. "Here," she says. We press ours down beside hers. The stone is warm as toast. "The sunbeam left its energy right here."

We try the sunny path. Warm. We try the soil under the big shady leaves. Cool as bathwater gone cold. "The sunny spots keep the rays," says Pip, hopping from one to the other. "The shady ones never got them."

And Miso the cat? She has moved. She was asleep by the gate this morning. Now she is stretched out on the warm stone, purring like a tiny engine, right where the sunbeam landed. "She follows it," we whisper. "All afternoon, she follows it."

Then we peek inside the oven. The chocolate is still hard as a coin.

Pip groans. "Impossible."

But wait. We look closer at the foil. It is dull. Pale. Not shiny at all. "Granny Rosa," we say slowly. "The foil is backwards. The dull side is out."

She taps it with one finger. "The sunbeam knocked, cariños," she says. "But we did not let it in."

s2b.text:
"A race," we say. "Make the sunbeam prove it."

Granny Rosa brings two squares of paper — one black, one white — and lays them side by side on the sunny path. On each one, she sets an ice cube. "Same sun," she says. "Same rays. Now we watch."

We crouch down. We wait.

The black paper's cube slumps first. It goes soft, then flat, then it is a puddle soaking into the paper. The white paper's cube just sits there, barely sweating, like it has all day.

"The black one drank the rays!" Pip shouts. "The white one bounced them away!"

"Dark things hold the energy," says Granny Rosa. "Pale shiny things send it back."

And that is when we see it. We look at our oven. We look at the foil. It is dull. Pale. Not shiny at all. "Granny Rosa," we say slowly. "The foil is backwards. We glued it dull side out."

She taps it with one finger. "This side says go away," she says. "The shiny side says come in."

Pip stares at the oven. Then at the puddle. Then at the oven again. "So the sunbeam came," he says, "and we told it to leave?"

s3.text: Pip is still turning his discovery over in his hands when Granny Rosa claps once. "So," she says. "Tell me what you found." We tell her, both of us talking at once, and she listens the way she listens to seedlings — all the way to the end. "Then we know the rule," she says. "A ray carries energy. We must catch it, not bounce it." We peel the foil off, flip it shiny side out, and smooth it down with our thumbs. Granny Rosa props the lid open with a stick. "Now we wait." We wait. Miso waits too, curled in his bright patch, purring. When we lift the lid, the chocolate is soft only at the very edges. The middle sits there, hard as a button. Pip sags. "We fixed it," he says. "Why isn't it fixed?" Then I see it. The sunbeam isn't in the box at all. It's lying on the path, bright as spilled honey, a whole step to the left. "The lid's tilted wrong," I say. "We aimed it and the light walked away." Pip groans. But Granny Rosa just points at Miso, who has moved three times this afternoon, each time into the sun. "The cat does not give up when the light walks," she says. "He walks with it." We look at the seedlings, all leaning the same way. We turn the oven like a face toward the light.

s4a.text: "We out-wait it," we say. "Like the cat." So we wedge the stick lower, and the foil lid tilts until the sunbeam slides off the path and lands inside the box, right on the chocolate. "There," whispers Pip. "We invited it in." Granny Rosa sets a stone where the oven's shadow falls. "The Sun walks," she says. "Every twenty minutes, we walk the box after it." And we do. All afternoon we turn our little sun-trap like a sunflower turning its face. Then Pip shouts. "It's moving! The chocolate is moving!" It bubbles. It shines. The whole garden smells like a candy shop. At Friday's party, Granny Rosa raises her cup. "To the sunbeam we finally invited in." We each take home a seedling pot for our own sunny sills. That night, Pip watches moonlight lie on his windowsill, pale and cold, with no energy in it at all. He opens his garden journal and writes: the Sun is a stove.

s4b.text: "We out-smart the sky," we say. Because the forecast has turned. Grey clouds are coming, and Friday looks doomed. But Granny Rosa taps the sundial. "The Sun keeps banker's hours, cariño. My mother taught me. Catch it early, and save it." So all week we watch the clouds and chase the bright mornings. On Thursday, the sky opens wide and blue. We aim the sun-trap, and the sunbeam lands square on a whole tray of chocolate. It bubbles. It shines. We fill a dark coiled hose with water, and the Sun warms it through, just like Granny's old baths. Friday dawns grey as dishwater. But our saved solar snacks are ready, and the whole class eats sun-cooked chocolate under a cloudy sky. "We caught the sunshine before the grey even got here," says Pip, grinning. We take home a chart of clouds-versus-sun, and Pip titles it: We Outsmarted the Weather. One seedling pot each, too — for the first sunny windowsill we can find.

c1.question: "The chocolate is still hard as a coin, and Pip wants to quit. So — do we go feel where the sun's warmth is hiding in this garden, or do we make the sunbeam prove itself with a little race?"

options.label: Walk the garden pressing palms to stone, soil, and path to feel where the Sun's energy lands — and follow Miso the cat
Set up the black-paper vs white-paper ice cube race to see which one soaks up more solar energy

c2.question: "Two ways to catch this sunbeam, cariño. Do we out-wait it — aim the oven like a sunflower and follow the light all afternoon? Or do we out-smart the sky — watch the clouds and harvest the sunshine before the grey days come?"

options.label: Angle the flap just right and keep re-aiming the oven as the Sun moves, melting the chocolate the patient way
Track clouds against the sundial, catch one bright morning, and pre-cook the party snacks with stored solar energy

s1.text: The water under the boat was making a noise like a thousand tiny crackers snapping at once. Crackle. Pop. {hero_name} pressed both hands flat against the glass bottom of {boat_name} and felt it, a fizzing little tickle, right up through the floor. "Hear that?" said Marina. She ran the snorkel tours, and she talked about the reef the way other people talk about their own street. She did not say the fish. She said the neighbours. "That's the city waking up," she said. "The workers are already out." {hero_name} looked down. Below the glass, the morning sun fell through the water in long, wobbling nets of gold, and far beneath them lay pale sand and dark shapes that might have been towers, or might have been rocks. "It's called a coral reef," Marina said, "but really, it's a city. It has cleaners, and guards, and builders, and all of them live off tiny drifting specks called plankton that float past like delivery carts." She grinned. "And everybody here has a deal with everybody else. You clean my teeth, I don't eat you. That's symbiosis." She handed {hero_name} a mask. "The quiet tide won't last. Once the big engines start, the shy ones hide. So. Do you want to hear about the city, or do you want to meet it?"

s2a.text: The water slid shut over their heads, cool and quiet, and the crackling came from everywhere at once. Marina pointed down, and they followed her into the canyon. Two tall walls rose on either side, and the space between them was full of fish, streaming along in both directions like traffic on a busy street. A school of silver ones parted around them, quick as a blink. Marina pressed her finger flat against the wall and waited until they did the same. The wall was warm. Bumpy. Alive. This whole tower, she told them, had been built by coral polyps, animals smaller than a fingernail, stacked on top of their grandmothers and great-great-grandmothers. Inside each polyp, tiny golden algae were catching the sunlight right now, turning it into food, like little solar panels that fed the whole city. Then they heard it. Crunch. Crunch. Something big and slow came around the bend, a parrotfish with a beak like a garden gate, biting chunks out of the coral. Old Bumper. He cruised past without a glance, and out of his tail end poured a soft white cloud of fresh sand, settling down through the water like snow. Marina's eyes went wide and delighted, and she pointed after him. He was heading deeper in, toward a wall nobody had bitten yet. They kicked off the canyon floor and followed the falling snow.

s2b.text: The turtle was waiting above the reef top, moving its flippers the way slow swimmers do in a pool, barely trying, going somewhere anyway. Marina waved, and the turtle did not wave back, because it was a turtle, but it did wait for them to catch up. They swam alongside, looking down. From up here the city made sense. Towers here. Streets there. A flat rooftop where fish drifted in a loose crowd, the way pigeons gather on a church. Marina pointed down at a boulder of coral and told them to look closer. The whole surface was fuzzy, and the fuzz was mouths. Coral polyps, each one the size of a grain of rice, and inside every single one, a million golden algae were drinking the sunlight and turning it into food, enough to feed the whole reef. Solar panels, Marina called them, with her eyebrows up. The turtle dipped its head, slow and certain, toward a flat coral head a little way off. Big fish were gathering there already, lining up in a neat row, one behind the other, like customers waiting outside a shop before it opens. Nobody was pushing. Everybody seemed to know exactly where to stand. The turtle was going to join the line, and it was not going to slow down for them. They kicked hard to keep up.

s3.text: The trail ended at a wide, flat coral head, pale as a dinner plate, and Marina pulled up short. "Well," she whispered. "The car wash." Big fish hovered over it in a patient line, one behind the other, waiting their turn like cars on a Saturday. At the front, a grouper the size of a door hung perfectly still with its mouth wide open. "What did you just find?" Marina murmured. "Hold on to it. This is where it fits." Then {hero_name} saw the cleaner. A tiny striped fish, no longer than a finger, darted straight into the grouper's open mouth. In. Around. Out through the gills. "That's Pip," Marina said. "He eats the itchy bits right off their teeth. Nobody eats Pip. That's the deal." The grouper didn't flinch. It was holding still on purpose, the way you hold still for a haircut. "Symbiosis," Marina said. "Pip gets lunch. The grouper gets clean. Neither could do the other's job." {hero_name} drifted closer, slow as sinking snow — and something small and orange shot out of the anemone below and bumped the mask with its nose. A clownfish, no bigger than a thumb, guarding its whole house. It glared. It charged again. Then it dove back into the tentacles, safe where any other fish would be stung. Nearby, a striped damselfish fanned its tail over a patch of purple eggs while hungry shapes circled and circled. "Easy," Marina whispered. "This whole place runs on trust. One splash, and the line scatters." {hero_name} held very, very still, and the line held too.

s4a.text: "The edge," said {hero_name}. "I want to see the deep." Marina kicked slow, one hand resting light on the mooring buoy line, so {boat_name} stayed exactly where the bottom fell away. "My grandfather taught me this spot," she said. "The city ends here. After this, no streets." {hero_name} looked down. The coral towers stopped all at once, like a town at the edge of a map, and below them the water went blue, then bluer, then a blue so deep it drank the light. No bottom. None. "The day shift doesn't go down there," Marina said. "Different neighbours do." Something moved far below. A long grey shape, unhurried, sliding through the dark like a door closing slowly. "Shark," Marina whispered. "Doing the night patrol." Then a jellyfish drifted up past the drop-off, glowing faintly at the edges, pulsing like a slow heartbeat, and behind it, smaller lights blinked on and off, on and off, fish that carry their own lamps because the sun's never reached them. {hero_name} held very still and watched one light travel a long way through the dark. "Will we ever go down?" {hero_name} asked. "Not today," Marina said. "Some doors stay closed for another trip. That's all right. It means the city's bigger than one visit." Back on the boat, the light going gold and thin, Marina pressed something into {hero_name}'s hand. A handful of beach sand, soft as flour. "Most of that," she said, "is parrotfish poop. They crunch coral all day, and out comes sand. Half this beach came through a fish." {hero_name} laughed and didn't let go of it. Below, along the reef, little lights were coming on, one by one, all down the streets. The night shift, clocking in.

s4b.text: "We'll stay," said {hero_name}. "I want to watch the shift change." "Good," said Marina. "Then pick one spot. One patch of coral. Don't look anywhere else." {hero_name} chose a round coral head below the boat, bumpy as a loaf of bread, and waited. Nothing happened. The water went from gold to copper to a deep, soft purple. Still nothing. "Is it broken?" {hero_name} whispered. "Patience," Marina said. "The night shift doesn't hurry." And then, on the one patch {hero_name} was watching, something moved. A tiny tentacle, thin as an eyelash, reached out of a hole that had been shut all day. Then another. Then the whole coral head was waving, hundreds of feathery arms unfolding like slow fingers, all reaching into the dark water. "The polyps," Marina breathed. "They build the towers by day and catch plankton by night. Same workers. Double shift." {boat_name}'s lights came on, and the street filled with shapes that had been hiding since morning. A long skinny fish slid out of a crack and hung upside down, hunting. Something with too many legs picked its way along a ledge. And there, on the same coral head, the damselfish that had fanned its eggs all day was still there, still fanning, working the night shift too. "She never stopped," {hero_name} said. "Some jobs don't end," said Marina. "Two cities, {hero_name}. Same walls, same street. One sleeps, one wakes." She handed up a handful of beach sand, soft as flour. "Souvenir. Most of it's parrotfish poop, if you can believe it." {hero_name} could. Below, every wall was waving now, all down the street, like the whole city saying goodnight and good morning at the very same time.

c1.question: "First stop on the tour, and you get to pick it. Do you want to drop down into the canyon where the builders work, or ride along with my old turtle friend and see the whole city from above?"

options.label: Drop into the coral canyon to meet the builders
Glide with the sea turtle above the reef

c2.question: "The sun's dropping, so we can only do one more thing. Do you want to swim out to the edge and look down into the deep, or stay right here and watch this street wake up for the night shift?"

options.label: Swim to the reef edge and peer into the deep blue
Stay and watch the reef change to its night shift

boat_name.role: The glass-bottom boat's name, used playfully by Marina

stories.title: The Click That Opened the Clubhouse

s1.text:
The clubhouse door banged open for the third time that morning. Bang. Bang. Bang.

Nina caught it on the fourth swing and held it shut with her shoulder. "Grandpa, this door will not stay closed. The wind just laughs at it."

Grandpa sat on his stool in the garage, surrounded by jars of screws and coils of rope and one very dusty bicycle. He took a slow sip from his thermos. Cinnamon tea. He always drank it slowly, like the tea had all day.

"What you need," he said, "is a latch that holds tight but opens when you say so. No key. Just a button."

Nina's eyes went wide. "A button? Like a doorbell?"

"Better." Grandpa set the thermos down on the workbench with a soft clink. He reached behind him and pulled out a jar of nails and a roll of copper wire, shiny and orange like a penny's insides. "We're going to build an electromagnet. A magnet you can switch on and off."

Nina let go of the door. It banged open again. She didn't even flinch.

"A magnet that sleeps?" she said.

"Exactly. When the current flows through the coil, it wakes up and grabs. When the current stops, it lets go." He tapped the wire. "Patience, sparky. We'll make it behave."

Nina grinned. "Let's build it."

s2a.text:
"Quick first," said Nina. "I want to see it move."

She wrapped the wire around the nail the way you wrap a scarf when you're late for the bus — round and round, twenty loops, loose and springy, ends sticking out like two tails. Grandpa watched, sipping. He did not say a word.

Nina clipped the wire ends to the battery. "Wake up, coil," she whispered.

The nail gave a tiny hum. Nina dangled a paperclip underneath it — and the paperclip jumped. It stuck. It wobbled. It hung on for one whole second, trembling like a leaf, and then — plip. It dropped onto the workbench and lay there, ordinary as anything.

"It grabbed!" Nina shouted. "Did you see? It grabbed and then it just — gave up."

Grandpa chuckled into his thermos. Cinnamon steam curled up around his eyebrows. "The current is flowing, sparky. But your coil is sleeping on the job."

"Sleeping? It was awake for a whole second."

"A loose coil is a lazy coil." He set the thermos down with its soft clink. "All those gaps between the loops? The current wanders through them like a kid dawdling to school. It gets there, but it's too tired to hold anything."

Nina picked up the paperclip and held it to the nail again. Nothing. Not even a shiver.

"So how do we wake it up for real?" she asked. "The latch plate is a lot heavier than one paperclip."

Grandpa smiled into his tea. "Patience, sparky."

s2b.text:
"Slow and careful," said Nina. "If we're building the latch for {clubhouse_name}, we're building it right."

She wrapped the wire around the nail one turn at a time, each loop snug against the last, neat as thread on a spool. Twenty turns. Thirty. Her tongue stuck out the corner of her mouth. Grandpa sipped and watched, and the garage went quiet except for the tiny squeak of wire on nail.

"There." Nina sat back. "Forty turns. Tight as a hug."

She clipped the wire ends to the battery and held a paperclip underneath, ready for the jump.

Nothing happened.

Not a twitch. Not a hum. The paperclip just dangled from her fingers, bored.

"Wake up," Nina said. She shook the battery. "Wake up, coil. I did everything right."

Grandpa leaned over and peered at the wire ends. Then he tapped one with a single finger. "Ah. There's your trouble, sparky. See the shine?"

Nina looked. The copper at the very tip gleamed, smooth and glossy.

"That shine is a coat," said Grandpa. "An invisible jacket called enamel. Every bit of this wire is wearing one, so the turns don't short against each other. Very useful." He took a slow sip. "But it also keeps the current out. Your battery is knocking on the door, and the jacket won't let it in."

"So my perfect coil can't even hear it?"

"Not one knock." He handed her a small square of sandpaper. "Rub the ends bare, sparky. Let the copper say hello."

s3.text:
Grandpa unscrewed the thermos and took a slow sip. "So," he said. "What did you find?"

Nina told him, and he nodded the whole way through, like he was filing every word in a drawer.

"Good. Now we fix it properly." He held up the wire. "See these ends? Dull. A current is shy, sparky. It won't jump through grime." He handed her a square of sandpaper, rough as a cat's tongue. "Rub until it shines like a new penny."

Nina rubbed. Poppy rubbed too, mostly her own thumb, and Maya turned the nail so the light caught it. Bright. Brighter.

"Now the coil." Grandpa's fingers moved slow and sure, wrapping the copper around the nail in tight, tidy loops, each one snuggled against the last like cinnamon rolls in a pan. "Loose loops make a lazy magnet. Tight loops make a strong one."

Nina wrapped the next ten herself. One slipped sideways and she started it over without being asked.

"Patience, sparky," Grandpa said, and winked, because she'd beaten him to it.

"How do we know it's really working?" Maya asked, pencil ready.

Grandpa pressed two fingers gently to the coil. "Feel. When the current flows, the wire gets warm. Just a little. Like a pocket where a hamster's been sleeping."

Nina touched the coil. Warm. Truly warm.

"It's awake," she whispered.

The nail hummed — a tiny, furry sound — and the whole pile of paperclips leapt. Clack. They hung off the nail in a fat silver bunch, wiggling.

Poppy squealed so loudly the screw jars rattled on the shelf. "IT'S ALIVE!"

"It's an electromagnet," Maya said, but she was grinning too, already sketching: nail, coil, battery, every part labelled in her neatest letters. "So we can build it again. On the door."

Nina looked at the clubhouse door, hanging open, waiting. The magnet on the bench was strong. But a door was a bigger, heavier job.

She squeezed the coil. Still warm.

"Let's make it stronger."

s4a.text: They bolted the magnet to the clubhouse door and pressed the button. Click. The magnet woke up and grabbed the metal plate. It grabbed so hard that the door would not budge. Nina pulled. Poppy pulled. Maya pushed from the side. Nothing. The door was stuck shut, and they were all outside. "It's too strong," Nina said. Grandpa sipped his tea. "Patience, sparky." Nina stared at the door. Then she ran to the recycling bin and came back with a piece of cardboard. She slid it between the magnet and the plate. The pull softened. She pressed the button again. Click. The latch popped open. "Yes!" Poppy shouted. Grandpa pointed across the valley. "See that crane at the junkyard? It drops cars with the same kind of switch." Nina smiled and slipped the little sanded coil from the first wobble into her pocket. It was still warm. "Let's go inside," she said. "The {clubhouse_name} is open for business." {button_press}

s4b.text: Before they bolted anything to the door, Nina held the humming electromagnet near Maya's compass. The needle twitched. It swung. It pointed right at the magnet. "Whoa," Maya whispered. "It's pulling the needle." Nina grinned. "Let's find every magnetic thing in the yard." They tested the mailbox, the swing set, a old tin can, and Grandpa's toolbox. Maya drew a treasure map, marking every spot where the needle danced. By dusk, the latch was ready. Poppy pressed the button. Click. The door swung open. They cheered and tumbled inside. Maya taped the map to the wall, right next to the coil that started it all. Grandpa leaned in the doorway, sipping his tea. "A magnet that sleeps and wakes," he said, "can even steer you home." Nina looked at the map, then at the coil in her hand. "We built that," she said softly. {button_press}

c1.question: "Now, sparky, do we wrap this coil quick and see what happens, or do we go slow and careful from the very first turn?"

options.label: Wrap it fast and test it right away
Wrap it slowly and neatly, turn by turn

c2.question: "The magnet works, little builder. Do we bolt it straight onto the door, or do we play with it first and see what else it can show us?"

options.label: Mount it on the clubhouse door right now
Test it on the compass and hunt for magnetic surprises

clubhouse_name.role: The name of Nina's clubhouse, painted on the door

button_press.role: The final button press that releases the latch, played out with sound
button_press.default: Poppy presses the big red button and everyone counts down from three

stories.title: The Clock That Drank the Light

s1.text:
"Look at that," says Maya, pressing her nose to the observation glass. "It's eating the stars."

You stand between her and Zix in the classroom of the ship Steady, watching the live feed. Gargantua-9 hangs there — a hole in space where the light bends wrong, stretched into a ring of fire around nothing at all.

"That's the event horizon," Zix breathes. "The edge of the world."

Nobody moves. Behind you, Alex waves from the pilot's seat, but you can't look away from the screen. Your wristwatch ticks. Steady. Normal. Tick, tick, tick.

Then something bumps your knee — a clank of metal against your shin.

"Hello, hello!" Pip the probe looks up at you with brass fittings gleaming, his metal arms spread wide to show off the dents. "Three dips I've taken! Three! And each time, the gravity pulls me like taffy — stretched me thin as spaghetti!"

He clicks, delighted, and spins in a circle.

"You're really going down there?" you ask.

"We all are!" Pip's gears whir with joy. "To see the singularity! To feel spacetime stretch! To watch the light slow down and stop and—"

"Easy, Pip," Alex calls back. "We haven't launched yet."

Maya is already gripping your hand. "You ready?" she asks.

Outside, the black hole waits, drinking the light. Your watch keeps ticking — for now.

s2a.text:
"Jupiter it is!" Maya shouts, her eyes bright.

Alex leans forward in the pilot's seat. "Hold on to your hats, everyone. We're going to borrow some speed."

The ship Steady tilts, and suddenly the viewscreen fills with swirling orange and cream stripes. Jupiter! It looks close enough to touch, a giant ball of storms bigger than a thousand Earths.

"Feel that?" Zix whispers.

You do. It's like a gentle hand reaching out from the planet, wrapping around the ship, and pulling you forward. Not scary — just strong. Like when someone bigger holds your hand on a crowded street.

"Even Jupiter bends spacetime," Pip clicks, spinning in a circle. "Watch. Watch."

He rolls a marble across a piece of stretchy fabric. The marble curves, spiraling down toward a heavy ball in the middle.

"Mass bends space," Pip says. "Like a trampoline with a bowling ball in the middle. The black hole? That's a bowling ball the size of a million suns."

You glance at your wristwatch. Still keeping its ordinary time.

Behind you, the Sun shrinks to a bright dot, then to a spark, then to almost nothing. Ahead, the darkness grows. The ship curves, faster now, flung forward by Jupiter's pull.

"There," Alex says quietly.

The black hole fills half the viewscreen. The ring of fire around it glows brighter than ever, and the center is so dark it hurts to look at. You watch it anyway. Nobody moves. The only sound is your watch, small and steady, ticking against your wrist.

Then Maya's hand finds yours. "We can hover here at the safe edge," she says, "or we can climb into The Firefly and go down on the tether. What do you think, {hero_name}?"

s2b.text:
"Straight across," you say. "Let's see the light bend."

Zix gasps.

"What?" you ask.

"Look. Look at the stars."

You press your face to the glass. The stars ahead are multiplying — one star becomes two, then four, then a dozen, all smearing into a glowing hoop of gold around the black hole.

"Einstein ring," Maya breathes. "That's one star, {hero_name}. Just one. But the black hole bends its light so much that we see it everywhere at once."

"Look at it go," Pip whirs, his brass fittings gleaming. "The light stretches and stretches, warm and golden, all the way around the dark."

You watch the ring shimmer. It's beautiful and strange, like looking through a curved window at the whole universe. You don't say anything. Neither does Maya. The ring turns, slow and golden, and for a moment you just stand there, the two of you, looking.

Your wristwatch ticks on, steady. For now.

The ship glides closer, and the ring grows wider, brighter. The darkness in the middle yawns open like a mouth, swallowing the light whole. Drinking the light.

"We're almost there," Alex says from the pilot's seat.

Maya turns to you, her hand on your shoulder. "We can hover here at the safe edge, or we can climb into The Firefly and go down on the tether. Which one, {hero_name}?"

s3.text:
"What did you find?" Maya asks, leaning close. "Tell me everything."

But before you can answer, the ship Steady shudders — gently, like a cat settling — and the view outside swells. Gargantua-9 fills half the sky now. Not a hole. A whirlpool. Spacetime itself dragging around it, slow and thick as honey pouring off a spoon.

"We're here," Alex calls from the pilot's seat. "Safe orbit. The good ledge."

Pip clicks at your elbow. "Look, look! Your watch!"

You lift your wrist. Steady as your own heartbeat.

Then Zix points at the screen. "And the beacon. The one we left behind, back where it's safe."

Far out there, well clear of the dark, the numbers spin — whirling, blurring, hours tumbling past in seconds. Your breath catches. Same moment. Two speeds. Time itself stretching like taffy near the edge.

"Now watch," Maya whispers. "This is the part that matters."

Pip releases a probe — small, brave, blinking red. It drifts toward the swirling dark. Closer. Closer. The signal light flickers on the screen, slowing, reddening, stretching into a long thin thread of color.

Then it stops.

Frozen. Red as the last coal in a fire. Hanging there at the edge of everything.

Nobody speaks. The ring turns, slow and golden, around the dark. The dark drinks. Maya's hand rests on the glass, perfectly still. Even Pip's gears go quiet.

"Event horizon," Zix breathes at last. "It can't come back. Not the probe. Not the light. Not even the signal."

The red dot fades. Goes black.

Your watch ticks on, steady and warm against your pulse, and the black hole turns and turns, drinking the light, and nobody says anything at all for a long, long moment.

s4a.text:
"Down we go," Maya says, and the Firefly drops.

You stand at the center of the glass dome, feet together, just like she showed you. Gravity pulls at your shoes. Then your knees. Then your hair — not hard, but different. Your feet feel heavier than your head.

"Feel that?" Maya asks. "That's the stretch. Spacetime pulling on us, hard."

You look down. The event horizon waits below — not black, but empty, a place where light goes in and doesn't come out. You check your wristwatch. Steady as your own heartbeat, exactly as it was in the classroom. It always will be. A clock never feels strange to the wrist that wears it.

"Look up," Maya whispers.

Through the dome, the stars behind you are speeding up. Whirling. Hours passing in heartbeats. Alex's voice crackles over the radio, fast and chipmunk-high: "You're—almost—too—close—"

"We're fine," Maya says, but she's already pulling the lever. "Hold on."

The Firefly strains. The tether groans. For a moment you hang there between the dark below and the racing universe above, and your watch keeps its calm, ordinary tick while the whole sky hurries.

Then — snap — you're rising. The stars slow. Alex's voice drops back to Alex's voice. Your watch has not changed at all.

Back at the Steady, Alex hugs you hard. "You were gone for hours!"

"Minutes," you say, catching your breath. "We were only gone minutes."

You are both right. That is the strangest part. Your watch says minutes. The ship's clock says hours. And when you look at the photo Maya took — your reflection stretched long and thin in the warped light, smiling — you hold it a moment longer. You don't say anything. The you in the picture is still smiling back.

s4b.text:
"Pip's ready," Zix says, and the little probe drops.

You watch from the Steady's observation deck, hands pressed to the glass. Pip's tether unspools — down, down, toward the swirling dark. His camera feed fills the screen.

"See?" Maya points. "His clock."

On Pip's brass chest, a tiny dial ticks. Slow. Slower. Tick... ... ...tick... Almost stopping.

"And ours?" you ask.

Zix grins. "Hold yours up next to the screen."

You do. Tick, tick, tick. Steady, ordinary, exactly as it has been all day — a clock never runs strangely for the person holding it. But beside Pip's dial the difference is enormous. Three of your ticks for one of his. Then five. Then ten.

"Time dilation," Maya breathes. "He's falling slow. And from down there, we're the ones racing."

Pip's signal light glows red. Redder. Stretched thin as a thread. His voice crackles through, delighted and stretched long: "Friend. I see. The singularity."

The data streams across the screen. Mass crushed to a point. Smaller than an atom.

"Reel him back," Alex calls. "Now."

Zix pulls the winch. The tether hums. Pip rises — slowly, slowly — and his dial ticks faster, and faster, until it keeps pace with yours again, and the universe settles back into one speed.

When Pip clanks onto the deck, he's different. Stretched. One brass rivet pulled long and thin as wire. His little dial says a quarter past two. The clock on the wall behind him says ten to six.

"For you," Pip clicks, handing the rivet over. "Souvenir."

You hold it tight. Behind you, Alex laughs. "My hair grew a whole centimetre waiting for him!"

You don't answer right away. The rivet is warm in your fist. Below, the black hole turns and turns, drinking the light.

"Worth it," you say.

c1.question: "We can take the long way 'round and steal some speed from Jupiter's pull, or cut straight across the dark to see the starlight bend. Which feels right to you?"

options.label: Slingshot past Jupiter
Direct route to the ring

c2.question: "I can take us down in the glass bubble to feel the stretch ourselves, or we can send Pip to the edge while we watch from here. What should we do?"

options.label: Go down in the shuttle
Send the probe and watch

hero_name.role: The child hero traveling to the black hole

s1.text:
It is a summer afternoon, and we are at the library. Me, Dad, and my big sister, squeezed around one little table.

Dad is reading the newspaper upside down. He does not know it is upside down.

My sister is flipping through a big space book. Suddenly she stops. "Whoa," she says. "Look at this."

It is a comet. A lumpy, dirty snowball of ice and dust, zooming through space. The book says its real name is something long and boring, so we give it a better one. We call it {comet_name}.

"Here is the weird part," my sister says. She holds up two pages, side by side. "Look."

In the first picture, {comet_name} wears a long, glowing tail. It streams out behind it like a scarf in the wind. Beautiful.

In the second picture, there is no tail at all. Just the same lumpy snowball, dark and plain, like a dirty sock someone left in space.

"Same comet," my sister says. She taps one page, then the other. "Two coats."

Dad looks up from his upside-down newspaper. "Maybe it got cold," he says, "and took the fancy one off."

My sister rolls her eyes. But she is smiling. "Seriously, though," she says. "Why does it have a tail sometimes, and not other times?"

Nobody at the table knows. Not even Dad.

s2a.text:
"Test one," my sister says. "Us. Right now."

So we raid the kitchen. Ice from the freezer, dirt from Dad's plant, cracker crumbs from the bottom of the box. We pack it all into one lumpy snowball. It looks exactly like {comet_name}. If {comet_name} were dinner.

"To the porch," my sister says. "The lamp can be the Sun."

Dad carries it on a plate like a fancy dessert. "I shall miss him," he says.

We set our comet under the porch lamp and we wait.

Then — wisps. Little curls of steam, lifting off the ice. The ice shrinks first. The dirt just sits there, exactly where we packed it.

"The tail," my sister breathes. "It's the ice! Warmed up, turning to gas. That's the glowing coat."

"And the crumbs stay behind," I say. "Like somebody snacking on the walk home."

Dad nods solemnly. "I knew it. I always snack on the walk home."

But my sister has gone quiet. She is looking at the library book again, at that one strange drawing. The one where the tail streams out ahead of the comet. In front of it.

"Our steam went up," she says slowly. "It didn't go backwards. And it definitely didn't go frontwards."

She taps the page. "So why does {comet_name}'s tail sometimes point the wrong way?"

Nobody knows. Not even Dad.

s2b.text:
"Planetarium," my sister says. "They have a pretend comet. We can watch the whole trip."

The planetarium is dark and round and smells like old carpet. In the middle, on a long metal track, hangs a lump of dry ice. Above it, a lamp.

"That lamp," the planetarium lady says, "is the Sun. Watch close."

The comet starts to move. Slow. It loops way out to the far end of the track, into the cold dark corner. Nothing happens. No tail. Just a plain lumpy snowball, like a dirty sock someone left in space.

"Years," the lady says. "It spends years out there."

Then the comet swings back. Closer to the lamp. Closer. And — steam. A long glowing tail blooms off the ice, right on cue.

"There!" my sister grabs my arm. "That's the coat! It only grows near the Sun!"

"Ice, warming up," I say. "Leaving crumbs behind."

Dad is squinting at the ceiling. "I wish on that one," he whispers, pointing at a painted star, "for {wish_thing}."

"Dad. That's paint."

"A moth once," he says sadly.

But my sister is frowning at the model. The comet is heading home now, back toward the dark — and its tail is leaning away from the lamp. Still pointing away. Even on the return trip.

"Wait," she says. "If the tail is just melted ice, it should drag behind. But it doesn't. It points away from the Sun. Both ways."

She looks at me. "Why?"

Nobody knows. Not even the planetarium lady. Well — she knows. But she is smiling, and not telling.

s3.text:
That night we drive to a hilltop field. Me, Dad, and my sister, with a blanket and a thermos of cocoa. The ranger shows us where to spread out, away from the path. "Lie back," she says. "Eyes up."

"What did you find?" my sister whispers. I tell her about it. She nods, like she is filing it away.

Then the ranger tells us the secret. "Sunlight pushes," she says. "Like wind. So a comet's tail always streams away from the Sun." She holds up her hand, fingers spread. "When the comet is heading home, it chases its own tail."

Dad gasps. "Like a dog!"

"A very cold dog," my sister says.

"And the tail itself?" the ranger says. "Ice. Sun-warmed ice, turning to gas, blowing outward. The comet only grows its tail on the near part of the orbit. Close to the Sun." She smiles. "Two coats. One for near, one for far."

It clicks. Both mysteries, solved at once.

Then my sister opens her notebook. She goes quiet. "Look," she says. Her tally marks from last year. Circled. This exact week. "How did the sky know?"

s4a.text:
We lie flat on the blanket. The grass pokes my back. I don't care.

"Shh," the ranger says. "Let your eyes learn the dark."

So we wait. We count slow minutes. One cocoa. Two cocoa. Three cocoa.

Then, little by little, the sky fills in. Stars I couldn't see before just pop into place, like somebody turning up a lamp.

"There!" Dad whispers. A streak. Quick as spilled salt.

"I wish," he says, very solemn, "for {wish_thing}."

The ranger chuckles. "You just wished on a grain of comet dust."

Dad sits up. "A crumb?"

"A crumb," she says. "{comet_name} drops them, circling the Sun, visit after visit. And Earth plows right through the trail. Same dusty road. Same week. Every year."

My sister grabs her notebook. "That's why my dates match!"

We count eleven streaks before the cocoa runs out. Eleven crumbs, falling home.

At the car, my sister circles next August in the notebook. I fold the blanket. It smells like grass. And in my pocket, wrapped in a tissue, is one little crumb of dirt from our test comet.

"For luck," Dad says.

Like we need it.

s4b.text:
"Walk with me," the ranger says. So we do.

The field is dark and bumpy. Crickets everywhere. Dad keeps pointing. "There! No, there!"

"Watch where they start," the ranger says. "Not where they go."

We trace the streaks backward, with our fingers, like following string. And here's the strange thing. They all spray out of one spot. One patch of sky, between two stars.

"That's the radiant," the ranger says. "The crumbs all come from there."

"Crumbs?" Dad says.

"{comet_name} sheds dust on every trip around the Sun. A whole ribbon of it, floating in space. Earth's orbit crosses that ribbon in the same place, every single year." She taps my sister's notebook. "That's how your dates knew."

Dad stops walking. He spreads his arms. "Then I wish," he says, "for {wish_thing}!"

He trips over absolutely nothing. He wishes anyway, from the ground.

Back at the blanket, we split the last of the cocoa, three sips each. The ranger folds her star chart into my sister's hands. The shower's week is circled in red.

"Keep it," she says. "For next year."

Dad brushes grass off his knees. "Best wish I ever fell for."

c1.question: Our sibling taps the two drawings and says, "We could test a comet ourselves, or go watch one pretend to be a comet. Which do we do first?"

options.label: Make a dirty-snowball comet at home and warm it by the porch lamp
Visit the planetarium's steaming model comet under its pretend Sun

c2.question: The ranger clicks off her red flashlight and asks, "Do you want to lie back and let the show come to you, or walk with me and chase where these streaks are coming from?"

options.label: Stay on the blanket, wait for our eyes to adjust, and let the meteors surprise us
Walk the field with the ranger and trace the streaks back to their constellation

comet_name.role: The comet in the library book, which we nickname and track all story

wish_thing.role: The small silly thing Dad keeps wishing for on meteors

stories.title: The Compass That Points to Wonder

s1.text:
The compass ticks in my pocket before we even see the scientist.

She is waiting for us at the trailhead, kneeling beside a long line painted on the ground. It runs the whole length of the clearing, disappears into the trees, and comes out the other side. "That's the Mesozoic," she says. "The whole age of dinosaurs, start to finish. We're going to walk it."

We walk. The painted ground is warm under our shoes. We pass a Stegosaurus, painted small, its plates like a row of kite shields. We keep walking. We walk past ferns and horsetails and a painted dragonfly as big as a seagull. We walk and we walk and we walk, and still the scientist says, "Not yet. Tyrannosaurus is way up at the far end. The Mesozoic is enormous. It goes on for millions and millions of years."

My legs are tired. That is the point, I think.

Then the compass in my pocket goes wild. It ticks, it whirs, it spins around and around, and then it stops dead. CLUNK. The needle is pointing off the painted line, toward a place in the air that looks like heat rising off a road, or mist that has forgotten to be anywhere.

"Ah," says the scientist. "It's found the way in."

She stands up and brushes the dust off her knees. "Before we go through, I'll teach you the trick. When we get to the other side, don't run around looking for dinosaurs. Stand still. Listen. The sound always comes first — a footprint filling with water, a groove dragged in the dust, eggshells cracking. The ecosystem comes to you if you let it."

We step through the mist.

On the other side it is dawn, and the light is the colour of weak tea. Horsetails crowd the path, thin and green and jointed like bamboo. Something small darts across our feet — a little early dinosaur, no bigger than a chicken, gone before we can see it properly. Another one follows. Then another.

The scientist holds a finger to her lips. We stand still. We listen.

And the Triassic comes to us.

s2a.text:
The boom comes first. Boom. Boom. The ground hums under our shoes, and then the treetops part and a neck rises through them like a periscope, higher and higher, until a head the size of a horse looks down at us from the clouds. "Brachiosaurus," the scientist whispers. "Eating the leaves nobody else can reach." Scraps of green rain down through the branches, and below, a crowd of little dinosaurs darts about catching them, like children under a piñata.

Then we hear it. A long, low note, sad as a foghorn. Off the trail, half hidden in the ferns, stands a calf — small for a Brachiosaurus, which means only the size of a bus. It calls again. The note rolls out across the miles. Nothing answers.

"Lost its herd," says the scientist. "The herd will call back. They always do. We just have to help it listen."

The calf looks at us with an eye like a dinner plate, and then it follows us, boom, boom, boom, like an enormous lost puppy. Its breath comes down warm on my hair.

In my pocket the compass ticks and whirs and spins. CLUNK. The needle points toward the river. "The herd may have crossed there," the scientist says. "Come on, little one."

The calf calls once more. We all hold still and listen.

s2b.text:
The rustle comes first. Then the thump. Thump. Thump. The ferns shiver, and out of them ambles something low and wide, plated like a knight, dragging a groove in the dust behind it with a club on the end of its tail.

"Ankylosaurus," the scientist breathes. "Our lucky day."

It walks beside us like it has decided to. Its armor is studded and ridged, like the bottom of a boot, and its eye, small and calm, watches us the way a dog watches from a doorstep. Where its tail drags, it writes a long line in the dust, and little lizards come to sun themselves in the groove.

Then the light changes. A shadow slides across the open ground — wide-winged, silent, gone as fast as it came. The Ankylosaurus stops. It plants its feet. And it thumps its tail, once, so hard the thump goes through the ground and up into my ribs. Thump. The shadow does not come back.

"See that?" the scientist whispers. "Armor is just another way of belonging. Everything here fits into everything else. That's the ecosystem."

The Ankylosaurus walks on, and we walk in its shadow, which is the safest place in the whole Jurassic noon.

In my pocket the compass ticks, whirs, spins. CLUNK. The needle points ahead, to the river crossing. The Ankylosaurus stops at the edge of the ferns. It will not come further. It thumps its tail once more, gently, like a door closing, like goodbye.

s3.text:
The compass ticks again, and we follow it down to a wide river, brown and slow. The scientist kneels at the muddy edge. Three-toed footprints, each one bigger than a dinner plate, and every one of them filling slowly with water. Plip. Plip. "Whatever made these," she says, "is very close."

Then the bushes part, and she is there. A Triceratops, old and grey, one horn chipped short, standing right in our path. She studies us for a long moment. We stand very still. Then she snorts, turns, and walks on — and somehow we understand we are meant to follow.

She leads us through her whole herd at dawn, and the sunrise comes up behind a row of huge frills and lights them like stained-glass windows, every one patterned differently. "Each frill tells the others who she is," the scientist whispers. "A whole family, watching out for each other."

We splash across into the Cretaceous evening — and something small and feathered darts in, snatches {shiny_thing} right out of my pocket, and runs. "Hey!" we shout, and chase it, the compass spinning madly, over a rise and onto a warm volcanic plain.

We stop. Eggs. Arranged in careful circles, as far as we can see. The little thief is gone somewhere among them, and the compass spins faster than it ever has, unable to pick just one wonder among thousands.

s4a.text:
"Shh," the scientist whispers. "This one."

One circle of eggs, close enough to touch. We stand the way she taught us at the very start — still, listening. My legs want to fidget. I don't let them.

An egg rocks. Stops. Rocks again.

"Hatching takes patience," she breathes. "We're good at patience. We practiced."

So we wait. The plain is quiet except for wind in the ferns, and somewhere far off a herd calling, low and slow. The egg rocks. Stops. My heart thumps so hard I'm sure the egg can hear it.

Then — a crack. A hole. A tiny beak, peeping. A damp little head pushes through, covered in fluff, and the chick tumbles out onto the dust, no bigger than my two hands. Peep. Peep.

After all the giants, the biggest moment of the whole day is the smallest thing in it.

A shadow falls over us, gentle as a curtain. A Maiasaura — enormous, duck-billed, careful. She bends her huge head down and nudges her chick toward the soft ferns, and the chick peeps and wobbles and goes.

Something tickles my shoe. The little feathered thief is back. It drops {shiny_thing} at my feet — then picks up a curved piece of broken eggshell instead, and is gone. A trade. Fair enough.

The scientist smiles and opens the misty door, and we step through into our own time, where a fossil hunter is brushing dust from a stone. "Look," she says. "A fossil eggshell, from a nest just like that one. Here — you can keep a small piece."

So {fossil_keepsake} comes home in my pocket, next to the compass.

The compass ticks. Whirs. Spins once, slowly — and CLUNK.

For the first time all day, it is pointing home.

s4b.text:
"Quick," the scientist says, "before it lands."

The shadow glides ahead of us down the cliff path, wide as a classroom, never hurrying. We hurry. Down, down, around a bend of warm rock — and out onto a beach where the wind smells of salt and fish.

The sky is full of them. Pterosaurs, wheeling over the waves, long crests catching the light. And here comes our shadow, sinking lower, lower — and the biggest one of all folds its leathery wings like an umbrella closing, and lands on four feet, light as a kite set down.

"Not dinosaurs," the scientist whispers. "Their cousins. They share the Mesozoic skies."

Out past the waves, dark shapes slide under the water — long necks, slow flippers. The whole ecosystem, above and below, all at once.

Something taps my shoe. The little feathered thief followed us all the way to the sea. It drops {shiny_thing} at my feet, snatches up a shining fish scale from the sand instead, and is gone. A trade. Fair enough.

The scientist opens the misty door, and we step through into our own time, where a fossil hunter is brushing dust from a stone. "Look," she says. "A real fossil feather."

Then she points at the fence. A sparrow sits there, bright-eyed, feet gripping the wood. Scaly feet. A hunter's feet.

"Birds," the scientist says, "are living dinosaurs. The Mesozoic never really ended."

So {fossil_keepsake} comes home in my pocket, next to the compass.

The compass ticks. Whirs. Spins once, slowly — and CLUNK.

For the first time all day, it is pointing home.

c1.question: "Two trails into the Jurassic noon, friends. The compass likes them both. Do we follow the boom — the big footsteps up into the conifer forest? Or the thump — something low and armored out on the fern prairie?"

options.label: Follow the giant footsteps into the conifer forest to meet Brachiosaurus and the lost calf
Follow the low ground-shaking thump onto the fern prairie to walk beside Ankylosaurus

c2.question: "The compass has gone quite silly — it can't choose. So you must. Do we stay right here, very still, beside this one circle of eggs... or do we follow that enormous shadow down to the sea?"

options.label: Stay quietly beside the nest and wait for one egg to hatch
Follow the huge gliding shadow down to the rocky coast to meet the pterosaurs

shiny_thing.role: The small shiny object from our pocket that the troodontid steals

fossil_keepsake.role: The small thing the scientist lets us carry home at the end

s1.text:
It is night, and the market is wide awake. Paper lanterns glow above us like little moons, and everywhere — everywhere — steam is rising from a hundred stalls, curling up past our noses.

"Smell that?" says {guide_name}, the Traveling Chef, walking beside us with a wooden box tucked under one arm. "Noodles. Dumplings. Something with spice in it — ooh, that one's making my nose tingle."

Ours too. It tingles in a nice way.

{guide_name} stops and opens the box. Inside, on a folded cloth, lie three things: a fork, a spoon, and a pair of chopsticks, smooth and dark.

"My magic wands," {guide_name} says. "Every place in the world eats with something clever. Hands, forks, chopsticks — all of them right, all of them smart. The trick is knowing which one the food is asking for."

"The food asks?" we say.

"Oh yes. You just have to know how to listen."

And that is when we see it. Above the nearest stall, a wisp of steam rises — but it does not drift away like the others. It curls. It bends. We hold our breath and watch. Slowly, slowly, it shapes itself into two long, thin lines, side by side, pointing down into the market like an arrow.

For a moment, nobody says anything. The steam waits.

{guide_name} leans close, eyes bright. "Well, well," the Chef whispers. "The steam has chosen. Follow it!"

s2a.text:
The steam curls into two long lines and drifts through the market, and we follow it, slow-slow, watching it bend and curl above the stalls, until we duck under a curtain into a noodle house. Low table. Floor cushions. A Street Vendor stands behind a sizzling pan, holding two metal chopsticks longer than our arms.

"Watch," the Vendor says. Click-click-click! The chopsticks flip little round takoyaki balls so fast our eyes cannot follow. "Now you."

We sit. Our own chopsticks feel like two slippery sticks. We pinch a shiny noodle. It wiggles. It drops. Plop. We try a pea — ping! It shoots across the table and the Vendor catches it in a bowl without looking.

"Chopsticks are not for stabbing," the Vendor says, grinning. "They are for pinching. Like a heron's beak. Gentle."

We try again. Gentle. The noodle lifts! It dangles. We slurp it up — slurp! — loud as we can, because here, slurping cools the noodles and tells the cook the meal is good. The Vendor slurps back, louder. It is a compliment, in noodle language.

The Vendor grins. Above us, the steam waits, curling slow.

s2b.text:
The steam curls into a soft round shape and leads us down a quiet street to a kitchen window glowing yellow. Inside, a grandmother is pressing dough between her hands. Pat-pat-pat. Pat-pat-pat.

"Come in, come in," she says, not stopping. Her hands rock back and forth, and the dough turns — a little flatter, a little rounder, every pat. "The tortilla tells you when it is ready. Listen."

We listen. Pat-pat-pat. Like a slow heartbeat.

She puts a small ball of dough in our palms. It is warm, like a potato just out of its jacket. We pat. Back and forth, hand to hand. Ours goes lumpy. It goes lopsided. It looks more like a map than a moon.

"Again," she says, and her thumb smooths our edges. "Soft hands. The dough likes soft hands."
