We pat. Softer. Rounder. And there it is — a real tortilla, thin and pale gold. She lays it on the hot pan and it puffs up like it is taking a deep breath.

"Now the clever part," she says. She spoons beans into the middle. "Fold it around them, like a little blanket. Then your fingers stay clean — and the food carries itself."

We fold. We bite. Warm beans, warm corn, warm everything.

s3.text:
The steam curls around us like a soft ribbon, and the market spins away. When it lets go, we are standing in a warm dining room where the air smells like toasted cumin, and a long table is crowded with people passing dishes and laughing.

"What did you find back there?" {guide_name} asks, eyes bright. But before we can answer, an old grandmother at the table pats the seat beside her. "Sit, sit!" she says. "You are just in time."

In the middle of the table waits a huge platter of rice, golden and steaming, with sauce pooled in the middle like a little lake. We look around for our tools. No forks. No chopsticks. No spoons.

"Ah," says {guide_name}, rubbing hands together. "This food asks for something different."

The grandmother holds up her right hand and wiggles her fingers. "Your hands," she says. "The best tools of all. Here, we eat with our fingertips. You can feel if the rice is too hot. You can feel if the sauce is thick enough. Your fingers know before your tongue does."

We stare at our hands. After using tools, touching the food feels strange — like wearing shoes after going barefoot all summer.

"Try," she says gently. "Mix a little ball. Rice and sauce together. Your fingers will learn."

We reach out. The rice is warm, the sauce smooth. It squishes between our fingers in a way that makes us laugh. The table goes quiet, watching us kindly. The warmth seeps into our palms.

"There," says {guide_name}. "You are listening now."

s4a.text:
The steam lifts us up and spins us around, and when it lets go, we are standing in a sunny courtyard where blue and green tiles cover the walls like a puzzle. In the middle of a low table sits a big clay pot with a pointy lid, and steam is curling out from under it, smelling like cinnamon and something smoky.

"A tagine," says {guide_name}, bowing to a woman with a kind smile and brass tins in her hands. "Morocco. We eat together here, from the same dish."

The woman opens a tin. "Smell," she says. We lean in. Sweet, like cookies. She opens another. This one is deep and red and makes our noses tingle.

"Cinnamon," says {guide_name}. "And paprika. The tagine knows both."

We sit in a circle. There are no forks, no spoons — only baskets of crusty bread. The woman tears off a piece and dips it into the stew in front of her. "Eat from what is before you," she says. "The bread is your spoon."

We tear. We dip. The bread soaks up the sauce, warm and soft, and the spices dance on our tongues. {guide_name} grins. "You are listening with your hands now."

Before we go, the woman presses a small scroll into our palms. It is a curl of cinnamon bark, brown and fragrant. "For your journey," she says.

The woman waves from the courtyard. The steam curls around us one last time, and the cinnamon smell fades as it carries us home.

s4b.text:
The steam lifts us up and spins us around, and when it lets go, we are standing in a crowded dining room where the air smells like earth and pepper. A huge tray sits in the middle of the table, covered with a flat, spongy bread that looks like a pancake but feels like a cushion.

"Injera," says {guide_name}, nodding to a girl about our age who is already tearing a piece off the edge. "Ethiopia. The bread is the plate, and the spoon, and everything."

The girl holds up her right hand. "Use this one," she says. "The clean hand. Tear like this — quick, like turning a page."

We try. The injera is soft and stretchy, and it sticks to our fingers at first. The girl laughs, not mean, but like she has done this a hundred times. "Again," she says. "Pinch and pull."

We pinch. We pull. The bread tears clean, and we scoop up a pile of spicy stew. It is warm and a little sour, and the injera soaks it up like a sponge. {guide_name} watches, eyebrows raised. "You see? The food told you what it needed."

We eat until our fingers are tired and our bellies are full. Before we go, the girl tears off a small piece of injera and folds it into our hands. "To remember," she says.

The girl's laugh follows us out. The steam curls around us one last time, and we eat the warm bread on the way home.

c1.question: "The steam is splitting, little travelers! Shall we chase the clicking chopsticks to the noodle house, or follow the warm pat-pat-pat to the tortilla press?"

options.label: Chase the clicking chopsticks to the noodle house
Follow the warm pat-pat-pat to the tortilla press

c2.question: "The steam is calling us to our final feast! Do we follow the scent of cinnamon to the tagine, or chase the smell of earthy spice to the injera?"

options.label: Follow the scent of cinnamon to the tagine
Chase the smell of earthy spice to the injera

stories.title: The Cranky Freezer and the Dancing Pearls

s1.text: Grandpa's backyard is hot enough to make the picnic table sticky under our elbows. The dog flops in the one patch of shade, watching us like we might drop something good. In the middle of the table sits the old ice cream machine, a wooden bucket with a crank on top, and Grandpa pats it like an old friend. "This one's cranky," he says. "But it makes the creamiest ice cream in the world. If we do our jobs right." He pours ice into the bucket, then reaches for the big bag of chunky salt. "Now here's a curious thing," Grandpa says. "Why would we put salt on ice?" We don't know. "Because salt makes ice colder," he says, sprinkling it in. "So cold it drips and sizzles and turns to slush. And that slush is what freezes our cream." The dog's ears go up. The ice pops and crackles in the bucket, and Grandpa grins. "Listen to that," he says. "It sounds like it's working already." We lean in close. The wooden bucket is sweating, and the dog is licking his lips, and we haven't even started cranking yet.

s2a.text: "Right now!" we shout. Grandpa laughs and pours the cream into the metal canister. "Then we stir," he says. "That's the secret. Stirring keeps the ice crystals tiny. Tiny crystals make creamy ice cream." He sets the canister deep in the salty slush. Sizzle. Drip. The bucket is already working. But {dog_name} grabs the rope toy, and {cousin_name} shouts, "Tag, you're it!" and we run. We run and run, and the crank sits still. Nobody stirs. When we come back, panting, Grandpa lifts the lid. "Uh oh," he says. Inside is one frozen brick. {cousin_name} presses the spoon into it, and the spoon bends like it's made of rubber. "The crystals grew big," Grandpa says. "Big crystals make ice, not ice cream." The bucket sizzles and drips, and our spoon is bent, and the brick does not care.

s2b.text: "The night market!" we say, and Grandpa pockets some coins. The market is all lanterns and noise, and {dog_name} pulls us straight to the bubble tea shop, where steam fogs the windows. The owner waves us close. "Want to see the pearls?" she asks. She lifts the pot lid, and a hundred dark pearls tumble and dance in the boiling water. "They're tapioca," Grandpa says. "A stretchy root, cooked till it's chewy." "Why do they wiggle?" {cousin_name} asks. "The heat makes them dance," says the owner. They bounce and bob, and they look so squishy that we cannot help it. We poke one with a fork. Then another. Then we squash down, and the pearls burst and stick, flattening into one shiny blob at the bottom of the pot. "Oh," we say. The owner peers in. "That," she says, "is not bubble tea."

s3.text: Back at the picnic table, our cousin {cousin_name} is waiting, and {dog_name} is dancing around her feet. "So," she says, wiping her hands on her shorts. "What did you find?" We tell her, and she listens all the way through, nodding slowly. "I know what went wrong," she says. "And I know how to fix it." She taps the wooden bucket, where the salty slush is still sizzling and dripping down the sides. "Ice cream is fussy," {cousin_name} says. "If cream freezes without moving, it grows big, crunchy ice crystals. Like a frozen brick. But if we keep stirring while it freezes, the crystals stay tiny. Too tiny to feel. That's what makes it creamy instead of icy." Grandpa leans on the crank. "So the cranking isn't just for fun?" "The cranking is everything," she says. Then she grins. "And the pearls? They need to dance. If the water isn't swirling, they stick together in one big blob. Keep them moving, and they stay separate and chewy." {dog_name} barks once, like he agrees. "So we stir, and we swirl," Grandpa says. "Shall we?"

s4a.text: "I'll crank first," Grandpa says, gripping the handle. "Then you two." He turns it, slow and steady, and the wooden bucket sizzles and drips, sizzles and drips, like it's cheering us on. My turn next. The handle is harder than it looks. It pulls my arms down, and the salty slush sloshes against the sides. "Why does it fight so much?" I ask. "Because the cream is freezing," {cousin_name} says. "It's getting thick. That's the crystals staying tiny." {dog_name} watches the drips hit the grass. His tail thumps. My arms ache, but I keep going, round and round, until Grandpa says, "Now." We pull out the paddle. The cream is smooth and pale, soft as a cloud. No crunch. No ice. Just creamy. We eat it at the picnic table, and {dog_name} gets his own tiny scoop in his bowl. The bucket drips quiet now, like it's resting too.

s4b.text: "Fresh water," {cousin_name} says, and Grandpa fills the pot. We wait for the bubbles, then she tips the pearls in. "Now stir. Fast. In a circle." I take the spoon and swirl. The pearls tumble and spin, brown little balls dancing in the water. "Why do they stick if we stop?" Grandpa asks, leaning in. "Because they're made from tapioca," {cousin_name} says. "A stretchy root. It gets sticky when it cooks. Keep them moving, and they stay separate." I stir faster. My wrist aches, but the pearls keep dancing, turning clear at the edges, bouncy and dark. "Done," she says. We scoop them into cold milk tea. The pearls sink, then rise, chewy and soft. Grandpa takes a sip. "In Japan," he says, "they make mochi, chewy rice cakes. In Mexico, paletas, frozen fruit bars." {dog_name} licks a drop from the table. The pearls bounce in my cup, and I chew, and chew, and smile.

c1.question: "Should we start cranking this ice cream right now, or walk to the night market to get those chewy pearls first?"

options.label: Make the ice cream right away
Visit the night market for pearls

c2.question: "Now that we know the secret, do you want to churn the ice cream until it's smooth, or boil a fresh pot of pearls until they bounce?"

options.label: Fix the ice cream by stirring while it freezes
Fix the pearls by swirling the water

s1.text: I remember a little princess named {princess_name}. She wore a blanket cape, much too big, and a crown of {crown_style}. Her bedroom was her palace. The lamp glowed like a throne-room fire. Grandmother stood guard by the door. "The moon will rise soon," she said. "Set your crown on the windowsill, and the moon might light it up." So the little princess hurried past the cardboard castle, where a paper knight stood on the wall. "Good night, Sir Knight!" she called. Then she climbed up by the window to wait. Waiting is hard for small royals.

s2a.text: "While we wait," said Grandmother, "shall we twirl the time away?" Yes! The little princess twirled. Her cape went whoosh. She twirled again, slow, slow, and her cape bloomed like a big bell. Then Grandmother asked, "What crown does a moon deserve to see? The cardboard crown, colored bright? Or the daisy crown, smelling sweet?" The little princess chose. She carried it carefully, carefully, past Sir Knight, and set it on the windowsill. "Now the moon can find it," she whispered. Waiting felt important now.

s2b.text: "While we wait," said Grandmother, "shall we say good evening to the whole court?" Yes! The little princess waved her slow royal wave, side to side, side to side, like a flag in a breeze. She waved to the royal cat on his cushion-throne, and gave him one soft pat. Then Grandmother asked, "What crown does a moon deserve to see? The cardboard crown, colored bright? Or the daisy crown, smelling sweet?" The little princess chose. She carried it carefully, carefully, and set it on the windowsill. "Now the moon can find it," she whispered.

s3.text: Then a pale glow crept along the edge of the roof. Up climbed the moon, round as a coin. Its light found the crown on the glass, and tiny golden dots began to dance — across the ceiling, over the walls, onto the sleeping cat's back. "Why does the moon shine all by itself?" whispered the little princess. "My crown only shines when light finds it." Grandmother bowed from her post by the door. "Some things carry light," she said, "and some things share it. Both are grand." She smiled. "And how does a royal say good night to a moon?"

s4a.text: "A wave," said the little princess. "A slow, royal wave." She lifted her hand high and waved it side to side. Side to side. The moonlight twinkled on her crown, as if the moon were waving back. Then off came the crown. Clink. It was the loudest sound in the hushed room. Cape, crown, and slippers waited on the chair, glowing softly. One golden dot stayed above her pillow. Even grand princesses take off their crowns at night. And I remember, she slept like royalty.

s4b.text: "A bow," said the little princess. "A deep, deep bow." She bent down slowly, so slowly that her crown slid forward. She caught it with both hands. Grandmother bowed back from her post by the door. Then off came the crown. Clink. It was the loudest sound in the hushed room. Cape, crown, and slippers waited on the chair, glowing softly. One golden dot stayed above her pillow. Even grand princesses take off their crowns at night. And I remember, she slept like royalty.

c1.question: "While we wait for the moon, my little royal — shall we twirl the time away, or shall we go and say good evening to the whole court?"

options.label: twirl slowly and watch the cape bloom open like a bell
give the royal cat and the whole room a slow parade wave

c2.question: "The moon is shining right on your crown, little royal. How shall we say good night to it — with a slow royal wave, or with a deep, deep bow?"

options.label: a slow parade wave, side to side like a flag in a breeze, and the moon twinkles back
a bow so deep the crown slides forward and has to be caught with both hands

crown_style.role: what the crown is made of — crayon-colored cardboard or a chain of daisies

stories.title: The Day the Sky Played Copycat

s1.text:
We are lying on our backs on the big blanket in the yard, you and me, with the grass prickling at our elbows where they hang off the edge. Two cups of lemonade stand in the grass beside us, going warm.
Above us the sky is not doing much. Blue, and some clouds.
So we play cloud shapes.
"Sock," we say, and then "Pancake," and then "Hairbrush, upside down."
Then a cloud comes over that is almost a rabbit. Nose, tail, one ear. Almost.
"It needs one more ear," we say, out loud, the way you do.
And the cloud stretches, and pops out a second ear.
We sit up fast and look at each other. Then we look back up at the sky.
"Longer tail," we say, carefully.
The rabbit grows a tail so long and so fluffy that it drags along behind him across the blue.
The sky heard us. The sky is playing, and the rabbit hops slowly on over the fence, waiting to hear what we say next.

s2a.text:
"Dragon!" we shout, both of us, hands cupped round our mouths.
Three clouds slide together. One end pulls out into a long swishy tail. Two lumps flatten into wings. The front grows a snout with a curl on the end of it, like the handle of a jug.
Our dragon has one problem. It is made of cloud, so it cannot do fire.
It tries anyway. It huffs, and out comes one small white ring, which floats off and bothers nobody.
"Again!" we shout.
It huffs harder. Two rings.
Then it fills its whole chest, which takes a while, because its chest is the size of our school. It holds the air in. It lets go with everything it has.
And it sneezes.
Achoo. A cool sprinkle of drizzle comes down over the yard and lands on our faces and in our open shouting mouths. We put our tongues out and catch some.
We laugh until we have to lie down again.
High up over the oak tree, our dragon huffs one more little ring and looks extremely pleased with itself.

s2b.text:
"Whale!" we shout, both of us, hands cupped round our mouths.
One long cloud comes rolling round and fat, like a pillow with more pillows stuffed inside it. A wide flat tail puffs out of one end. Near the other end a small dark dent opens and closes, and that is her eye, and it is looking straight down at us.
She swims. Slow flips of that big tail carry her right across the middle of the blue.
Then, fwoosh. She spouts. A tall white fountain goes up off the top of her head, curls over, and breaks apart into six little clouds.
"Do it again," we say.
Fwoosh. Another six.
Fwoosh. Twelve more this time.
The little ones come along behind her, biggest at the front and smallest at the back, and every one has a small flat tail of its own.
"Six," we count out loud. "Twelve. Eighteen. Twenty." Then we lose count.
The sky is full of whales. There are far too many whales in the sky now, and we do not want a single one of them to go.

s3.text:
Then the game gets out of hand, which is where all the best games go.
Our {cloud_shape} cloud stops doing what we say and starts doing what we do.
We lift one hand and wave. It waves back with a fat white arm.
We hop on the blanket. It bounces.
We do our silliest dance, wiggle, wiggle, spin, and the whole sky turns and spins with us.
"Try this," we say, and we lie down flat as two pancakes. All across the sky the clouds come down flat as wide grey pancakes. We jump up. They leap. We fall over laughing, and forty clouds fall over too, and the sky is packed fence to fence with copies of us.
Which is when the yard goes dim.
That is the trouble with a skyful of clouds. There is no room left for the sun to get through, and a drizzle starts up, tick, tick, into our lemonade.
"That was us," we say.
We carry the blanket under the porch roof, cups and all, where it stays dry and we can still see everything.
Up there, the clouds jiggle. They are waiting for our next move.

s4a.text:
"Wind!" we shout, and then we do the thing that makes one. We fill our cheeks up fat and blow straight upwards, as hard as two people can.
And the sky copies us.
The sky blows.
It comes over the fence first, through the grass, up our sleeves, lifting our hair off our foreheads and flapping the corner of the blanket like a flag. Then it gets in among the clouds and starts pushing.
That is what wind is for. Wind is the thing that moves clouds about. It shoves them along the sky the way we shove a boat across the bath, and it never asks them where they want to go.
The grey pancakes stretch out into long white ribbons. The copies come apart. Our {cloud_shape} cloud is the last one left, and on its way out it waves one arm at us, off to be somebody else's cloud over somebody else's yard.
Then the sun is back on the grass. The drizzle stops. There is nothing left up there but three small puffs, hurrying.
We carry the cups out into the warm and drink the lemonade.
"It tastes of rain," we say.

s4b.text:
We do not say anything at all. We stand up slowly, and lift one hand, and wave as slowly as we can.
A thousand cloud arms wave back.
"Goodnight, clouds," we say. "Thank you for playing."
And then, because copying is the only thing they know how to do, they copy the quiet as well. The bouncing stops. The jiggling stops. They stretch themselves out flat and thin, the way a sheet gets smoothed over a bed, until the whole sky is one soft grey layer with the light coming through it.
The drizzle gives one last tick into the grass and stops.
Our {cloud_shape} cloud comes down low over the porch to say goodbye. It stretches, and stretches, and yawns itself out into a white wisp no thicker than a thread.
Then the sun finds the gap underneath, low and gold. We drag the blanket back out of the porch into it and sit down.
We pour out what is left of the lemonade and clink the two cups up at the sky.
"Same time tomorrow," we say. "Bring new clouds."

c1.question: "It only works if we say it out loud," we whisper. "So say it big. A dragon, or a whale?"

options.label: A huffing, puffing cloud dragon
A spouting cloud whale, and all the little clouds she makes

c2.question: "Our game," we say, "so it needs our ending." Up above, all those copies jiggle and wait. "We can blow, and let the wind take them off somewhere else. Or we can go quiet, and see whether they copy that too. Wind, or goodnight?"

options.label: Blow, and let the wind carry the clouds away
Wave the clouds goodnight and let them copy our quiet

cloud_shape.role: the cloud shape we ask the sky to make, chosen at the first choice

stories.title: The Detective and the Crumbs of Everything

s1.text:
It was a cold, clear night, and Detective Marisol Vega was on a stakeout.

"The backyard is quiet," whispered a tiny voice from her jacket pocket. "TOO quiet. The galaxy holds its breath!"

That was Zorp. Zorp was a small plush alien, and he narrated everything like a space epic, even breakfast.

Marisol's brother Theo stood beside her, breathing on his hands to warm them. Above them the sky was black and deep and sprinkled with stars, and somewhere up there was a comet nobody in their family had spotted yet. Marisol intended to be the first.

"Binoculars up," she said.

"Binoculars UP!" squeaked Zorp. "The brave detective raises her mighty—"

"Zorp."

"Sorry. Quiet. Too quiet. Got it."

Marisol swept the binoculars slowly across the sky. Roof. Chimney. Stars. Stars. And then—

"There!" She grabbed Theo's sleeve. "There it is! I found it!"

The comet hung in the dark like a fuzzy crumb on a bakery counter, with a long glowing tail streaming off to one side.

Marisol lowered the binoculars. Then she raised them again. Then she lowered them again.

"Theo," she said slowly. "Comet tails point away from the sun. That's the rule. The sun is down there, behind the hills. So the tail should point up."

"And?"

"The tail points sideways."

Theo squinted. "Maybe it's... a relaxed comet?"

"Comets don't relax."

From her pocket came a gasp. "A MYSTERY! In the cold depths of space, a clue appears—"

Marisol pulled out her detective notebook and clicked her pen. "Case number one," she said. "The comet with the sideways tail. I'm calling it {comet_name}."

She wrote the name at the top of a fresh page, then stamped the cover with her favorite word: {detective_badge_word}.

"The Case of the Cosmic Crumbs," she said, "is officially open."

s2a.text:
The next morning, Marisol and Theo pedaled to the space museum, Zorp bouncing in her pocket like a very dramatic popcorn kernel.

"The heroes approach the Temple of Ancient Stones!" he squeaked.

Inside, the guide smiled at Marisol's notebook. "You want the meteorite case. End of the hall."

And there it was. A dark little rock under glass, no bigger than a bar of soap, with a bumpy crust like the edge of burnt toast.

"That," said the guide, "is a piece of an asteroid. It fell out of the sky and landed in a farmer's field. And here's the wild part — it's older than any rock on Earth. Older than the mountains. Older than the oceans."

Marisol pressed both hands to the glass. "Older than everything?"

"Older than everything here."

"A MESSAGE IN A BOTTLE!" Zorp declared, popping up. "Flung across the endless void from the dawn of TIME ITSELF!"

"Zorp, it's a rock."

"It's a rock that REMEMBERS."

Marisol flipped her notebook open to the sketch of {comet_name} and held it beside the case. Crumb on a bakery counter. Crumb under glass. Both leftovers. Both from the very beginning, when the planets were still forming.

"Theo," she whispered. "This rock was there. At the formation of the whole solar system. It's a clue that fell out of the sky on purpose."

"Rocks don't do things on purpose."

"Then it's a clue that fell out of the sky by accident, and I don't care, because look at it."

Theo leaned in close. "So if the comet's a crumb and this is a crumb..."

"Then somebody," Marisol said, "left crumbs all over the solar system. And I want to know why."

"DUN DUN DUN," said Zorp.

s2b.text:
That evening, Marisol and Theo climbed the hill to the observatory, where Dr. Okafor had the big telescope aimed at a faint, slow-moving dot.

"An asteroid," she said, stepping aside so Marisol could look. "There it goes. One of millions."

"MILLIONS!" squeaked Zorp. "A mighty swarm, packed shoulder to shoulder in the cold dark—"

"Actually," said Dr. Okafor, "that's the funny part." She pulled out a chart of the solar system and tapped the ring between Mars and Jupiter. "This is the asteroid belt. In pictures it looks like a crowded rock field. Ships dodging, rocks bonking into each other. But that's not true. The belt is almost entirely empty space."

Marisol looked up. "Empty?"

"If you stood on one asteroid, you probably couldn't even see the next one. They're spread out over millions and millions of kilometers. All the asteroids together weigh less than the Moon."

There was a small thump. Zorp had fainted backward into Marisol's pocket.

"The pictures LIE," he moaned. "The epic space chase through the deadly rock field... a fantasy!"

"But wait." Marisol pulled out her notebook, flipping to the sketch of {comet_name}. "If they're leftovers from the formation of the solar system — crumbs from when the planets got baked — why are they spread out? Crumbs don't spread themselves. Somebody sweeps them."

Dr. Okafor raised one eyebrow. "Somebody... or something. Something big enough to stir a whole belt."

Theo looked at the chart. Then at the telescope. Then at Marisol. "Something big," he repeated. "Like, planet big?"

"Jupiter big," said Dr. Okafor.

Marisol clicked her pen and wrote one word on the page, in capital letters: SUSPECT.

"The Case of the Cosmic Crumbs," she said, "just got a lot bigger."

"DUN DUN DUN," said a muffled voice from her pocket.

s3.text:
Back inside, Marisol spread her notebook open on the kitchen table and clicked her pen twice, which was her thinking sound. "Okay," she said. "Tell me everything. What did you find out there?"

Theo talked. Zorp added trumpets. Marisol wrote it all down, and when they were done she tapped the page. "So now we have this, plus the sideways tail. The Sun pushes a comet's tail around like wind pushing smoke. That's clue one."

"Clue one!" Zorp squeaked from her pocket. "The detective's mighty brain awakens!"

Marisol pulled out the model they'd built last week, the one with little balls for planets. She pointed at the space between Mars and Jupiter, where they'd scattered a whole handful of crumbs and pebbles. "The asteroid belt. Millions of chunks, all circling, and they never got together into a planet. You know why? Jupiter. It's so big its gravity kept stirring them, like a spoon in a pot that never stops. The pieces kept bumping and flying apart. They never got to build."

Theo frowned. "So the planets formed all neat and tidy, but—"

"But why are so many pieces still wandering?" Marisol finished. She wrote the question in big letters. Then she stared at it. Then she gasped so hard Zorp nearly fell out of her pocket.

"Leftovers," she whispered. "Theo. The asteroids, the comets — they're leftovers. From the formation of the whole solar system. When everything formed, most of the dust and rock baked into planets. But these bits never got used. They're the crumbs that never became cake."

"Crumbs," Theo breathed.

"And because they never got baked, they never changed. They still remember the beginning. Every comet, every asteroid — it's a piece of day one, still floating around."

Zorp made a strange sound. Marisol looked down. The little alien was weeping, tiny plush tears on his tiny plush cheeks. "The crumbs," he whispered, "are the TREASURE MAP. The greatest case in the galaxy, solved by—"

"Not solved yet," said Marisol, standing up. Because a real detective with an answer this big had to do something about it. But what?

s4a.text:
Family night at the museum was loud. Kids everywhere, sticky fingers, a dinosaur skeleton towering over the lobby. Marisol stood beside the meteorite case, notebook in hand, Zorp riding shotgun in her pocket.

"Citizens of Earth!" Zorp squeaked. "The detective prepares to reveal the greatest secret in the—"

"Zorp."

"Right. Quiet."

Dr. Okafor tapped the microphone. "Everyone, this is Marisol. She has something to tell you about that little dark rock."

Marisol stepped up. The rock sat behind the glass, small and gray and ordinary. Nobody ever looked at it twice.

"This rock is a crumb," she said. "From the bakery of the beginning. When the solar system formed, most of the dust and rock baked into planets. But some pieces never got used. They never changed. They still remember day one."

She pointed at the asteroid belt poster. "The asteroid belt is full of crumbs. Comets too. They're leftovers, and they're the oldest things you can touch."

A little kid in the front row gasped. "That rock remembers the beginning?"

"That rock IS the beginning," said Marisol.

Dr. Okafor smiled and peeled a sticker off a sheet. It said JUNIOR DETECTIVE in silver letters. She pressed it onto Marisol's notebook, right next to the name {comet_name}.

"Case closed," said Dr. Okafor.

"Case CLOSED!" Zorp shouted. "The galaxy rejoices!"

On the way out, Marisol stopped at the gift table. She picked up a postcard of Ceres, the quiet round world hiding among the crumbs, and tucked it into her notebook.

"You coming?" Theo asked.

"Yeah," said Marisol, patting her pocket. "We're coming."

s4b.text:
The backyard was cold again, but Marisol didn't mind. The comet was leaving, and she had to see it off.

"There," said Dr. Okafor, pointing through the telescope. "Still got that sideways tail."

Marisol looked. The comet hung in the dark, fuzzy and glowing, its tail streaming off at that strange angle. The Sun's invisible fan, pushing the tail around like wind pushing smoke.

"It's a dirty snowball from the beginning," Marisol said. "A crumb that never got baked. And it's been carrying that memory for billions of years."

"Billions," Theo breathed.

Zorp sniffled from her pocket. "The brave crumb sails into the void, alone but unforgotten—"

"Zorp."

"Sorry."

Marisol pulled out her notebook and clicked her pen. She wrote the final entry: "Comet {comet_name}. Dirty snowball. Tail blown sideways by the Sun's fan. Leftover from the formation of everything. Case closed."

She underlined the name twice.

"You're really naming it {comet_name}?" Theo asked.

"I already did," said Marisol. "It's official. It's in the notebook."

Dr. Okafor handed her something small and heavy. A meteorite replica from the observatory gift table, dark and pocked and cool to the touch.

"A crumb that remembers," said Dr. Okafor.

Marisol held it up to the sky. The comet was already fading, already sailing away into the deep black. It would be gone for years.

"Goodbye, {comet_name}," she whispered.

She tucked the meteorite into her pocket, next to Zorp, and patted it once.

"Come on," she said. "Let's go inside. I'm keeping this on my windowsill."

c1.question: Theo squints at the notebook and says, "Okay, detective, the tail is weird. Do we go touch an actual space rock at the museum, or do we go spy on the asteroid hideout through the big telescope?"

options.label: Visit the meteorite under glass at the space museum
Visit the observatory to see the asteroid belt

c2.question: Dr. Okafor taps the solved notebook and asks, "The case is cracked, Marisol. Will you announce it to the whole museum on family night, or shall we watch your comet sail off and close the file under the stars?"

options.label: Present the solved case at museum family night
Watch the comet's farewell from the backyard

comet_name.role: The name Marisol gives the comet she spots

detective_badge_word.role: The silly word Marisol stamps on her detective notebook cover

s1.text:
The rain came sideways that afternoon, drumming the library windows like fingers on a table. Nico sat in the maker corner, drawing lightning bolts in the margins of a comic, and tried to explain the feeling to Ms. Okafor.

"You know when you're almost caught?" Nico said. "Not caught. Almost. Like the storm is right behind you, breathing on your heels, and one bad turn means it gets you. I want a game that feels like that."

Ms. Okafor did not say that's nice, dear. She said, "Ah. Tension." Then she wheeled over the maker-kit cart, which rattled like a toolbox, and slapped a laminated chart on the table. It said VERSION 1 in fat marker letters. "Rule one of game design," she said. "The first version is allowed to be ugly. It is supposed to be ugly. Ugly is how you find the fun."

So Nico built ugly. Twenty minutes, tops. A shoebox lid for the board. Grid paper squares drawn in wobbly pencil. Buttons for runners, dice for the storm, and a spinner cut from a cereal box that said TOASTY O'S across the middle. Nico wrote one rule on an index card: Roll. Run. Don't get caught.

It was not a game yet. It was a pile of stuff with a wish inside it.

Then a chair scraped across the carpet. Pip, Nico's little sister, dragged it over backwards and climbed on like it was a throne. She was six. She treated every game like a championship final.

"Player one," Pip announced. Then, in the sports-commentator whisper she used for important moments: "And here comes Pip now, stepping up to the board, the crowd going wild—"

"There is no crowd," Nico said.

"The crowd is in my head," Pip said, and snatched the dice.

s2a.text:
"Walking storm," Nico said. "Where everyone can see it coming."

Ms. Okafor raised one eyebrow. "Bold. Version one is supposed to be ugly, not terrifying."

Nico found a black button and set it on the last square of the grid. "New rule. Every round, the storm creeps one space forward. It walks. We run." Nico wrote it on the index card, right under Don't get caught. The shoebox lid rattled when the table bumped, buttons and dice and cardboard storm all jumping together, a whole game shaking in a box.

Pip leaned in so close her chin nearly touched the board. "The crowd holds its breath," she whispered.

They played. Pip rolled, moved her blue button three squares, and grinned. Then the storm moved. One space. Closer.

"Fine," Pip said. "Pip is not worried. Pip has legs."

Round two. Pip rolled a one. The storm moved one space. It was right behind her button now, close enough to breathe on its heels.

"The crowd is worried," Pip whispered.

Round three. Pip rolled a two and ran. The storm moved one space and landed on her square.

"Eaten," Nico said.

Pip sat back in her backwards chair and crossed her arms. Then, in the full commentator whisper: "Ladies and gentlemen, the storm is unbeatable and frankly rude. The crowd is going home. The crowd is getting a snack."

Nico looked at the board. Three turns. The game loop had spun exactly once, goal and choice and consequence, and then it was over. Nobody got to try again, because there was nothing to try. A chase nobody can survive isn't a chase.

"Okay," Nico said slowly, and picked up the black button. "Ugly found the problem. The storm walks too fast."

The shoebox rattled. Something in there was about to get swapped out.

s2b.text:
"Hiding storm," Nico said. "In a deck of cards. Nobody knows what's next."

"Sneaky," Ms. Okafor said. "I like it. Remember, ugly is allowed."

Nico cut index cards in half and drew a storm cloud on every single one. Trouble, trouble, trouble. Forty cards, shuffled into a fat stack. "New rule. Every turn, we flip a card. Storm card means the storm jumps us. When the deck runs out, we've outrun it. We win."

Pip cracked her knuckles like a tiny athlete. "The crowd is ready."

They played. Flip a card, move a button, wait. Flip, move, wait. The storm jumped them on turn four, and Pip gasped so hard she nearly fell off her chair, which was the best moment of the whole game. Then it was turn nine. Turn fifteen. The deck was still fat. The shoebox lid sat there with its wobbly pencil squares, and nothing rattled, because nothing was happening.

Turn twenty-two, Nico looked up. Pip had stopped moving her button. She had lined up all the spare buttons in rows, red ones and yellow ones, and was quietly building a farm.

"The crowd has left the stadium," Pip murmured, placing a cow. "The crowd is raising chickens now."

Nico flipped another card. Trouble. Nobody gasped. The consequence was taking so long to arrive that when it finally did, nobody cared. The game loop was still spinning, but so slowly, so lazily, that the itch to try again had fallen asleep.

"Okay," Nico said, and pushed the fat deck away. "Ugly found the problem. The storm hides too well."

Pip looked up from her farm. "Can the chickens stay?"

"The chickens can stay."

The shoebox rattled. Something in there was about to get swapped out.

s3.text:
By the next afternoon, version two of Storm Sprint was ready. Nico had swapped the wobbly pencil lines for tape, and the shoebox lid no longer rattled with quite so many wrong pieces. "It's getting lighter," Pip said, shaking it. "Like it's shedding its baby teeth."

They played. And this time, the game loop spun. You wanted to reach the lighthouse. You chose a path — the fast rocks or the long sand. Then the dice rolled, the storm answered, and you either whooped or groaned and reached to go again. Pip lost twice and didn't care at all. "Again," she kept saying. "The crowd demands a rematch."

Then Ada arrived. Ada, who always found the secret door in everything. She watched one round, chin in her hands, then picked up her button.

She moved slowly. Not unluckily — deliberately. One square at a time, along the safe sand path, every single turn. The storm never once came close.

"And Ada takes the lead," Pip whispered, leaning in. "She's playing it safe. Very safe. Suspiciously safe."

Ada won. They played again. Ada won. A third time, Ada won, with the same slow, steady, joyless march.

Pip's shoulders slumped. "The crowd," she said quietly, "has gone home."

Ms. Okafor had been watching from the cart. Now she rolled her chair over and looked at Nico. "So," she said. "Right now — is this game decided by luck, by skill, or by one boring trick?"

Nico stared at the board. The sand path sat there, plain as day, winning without any fun at all.

"A trick," Nico admitted. "One boring trick."

"Then the game isn't finished," Ms. Okafor said. "It's just told you where it's broken. What did you two find out there, while you were playing?"

"That slow wins," Pip said gloomily.

"Then let's make slow interesting," said Nico.

s4a.text: One change only. Nico stared at Ms. Okafor's chart, then pulled out a fresh index card and wrote in careful letters: STORM SURGE. Once per game, when this card is drawn, the leaders slide back two spaces and the stragglers jump forward two. "That's it?" Pip said. "One card?" "One card," said Nico. "One splash of luck." They played version three. The storm surge hit on the second turn, and Ada went flying backward off the sand path with a yelp that made Pip snort juice out her nose. It was funny. It was also broken, because Ada's slow march still won, just slower. Version four shuffled harder. Still broken. Version five moved the surge to mid-game, and suddenly Ada's strategy was merely good instead of guaranteed. She frowned. She recalculated. Version seven, and the table went quiet — the good kind of quiet, where everyone was thinking so hard you could hear it. Pip was behind by three spaces. The surge card flipped. She rocketed forward, and the whole table gasped. "And Pip closes the gap," she whispered, gripping her button. "The crowd is on its feet." She rolled. She ran. She lost by one space. Pip slapped the table, not hard, just enough to make the dice jump. "Can we go again?" Nico wrote it word for word on the shoebox lid. Then Nico tucked the crossed-out rules inside — version three, version four, every wrong turn — a paper trail of everything the game had taught its maker. The box rattled lighter on the walk home. "It's shedding its ugly," Pip said, hugging it. "Soon it'll be nothing but fun."

s4b.text: One change only. Nico stared at Ms. Okafor's chart, then picked up a marker and crossed out a single line on the rules card: the safe path now costs one token per turn. "So slow play bleeds your supplies," Nico said. "And the risky path pays out." Ada raised one eyebrow. "You're pricing my strategy." "I'm balancing it," said Nico. They played version four. Ada tried her slow march and watched her tokens drain away, turn by turn, until she had to abandon the sand path entirely and invent something new on the spot — a weird, darting route through the middle that nobody had tried. She lost. She grinned. "Again," she said. Version five tweaked the token cost. Version six found the sweet spot, and the table went quiet — the good kind of quiet, where everyone was thinking so hard you could hear it. Pip was ahead by two spaces, but her tokens were gone, and the risky path was the only way home. "And Pip commits to the rocks," she whispered, rolling. "No safety net. No plan B. The crowd cannot look." The dice tumbled. The storm missed by one square. Pip won by one space, and before Nico could even finish recording the result, she slammed both palms on the table. "Can we go again?" Nico wrote it word for word on the shoebox lid. Then Nico folded the version chart — every iteration, every crossed-out number — and tucked it inside the box like a map of everywhere the game had been. The box rattled lighter on the walk home. "What's next?" Pip asked. Nico shook the box and listened to the pieces settle. "I don't know yet," Nico said. "But I already want to play it."

c1.question: "Every chase needs a clock, love. Do you want your storm to walk across the board where everyone can watch it coming, or hide inside a deck of cards so nobody knows what's next?"

options.label: the storm marker creeps forward one space each round, visible to everyone
the storm hides in a deck of trouble cards that runs out

c2.question: "One change only, that's the rule of the chart. Will you tip the luck dial with a storm-surge card that mixes everyone up, or tip the skill dial and make that safe path cost something every single turn?"

options.label: add one storm-surge card that shuffles leaders and stragglers, giving losers hope
make the safe path cost a token per turn so slow play starves itself

s1.text:
Sunlight pours through the tall museum windows and lands on the biggest skeleton we have ever seen. Sue. Forty feet of bone, with teeth as thick as bananas, grinning down at the marble floor.

"She does that to everyone," says a voice beside us.

It's Dr. Maya Chen, a real paleontologist, with a golden magnifying glass hanging on a cord around her neck. She looks up at Sue the way you look at an old friend.

"Here's a mystery," she says. "Nobody ever saw a living T. rex. Not one person, ever. The last one died sixty-six million years before the first human stood up. So how do we know Sue was a teenager when she died? How do we know she gained kilos a day, like a growing kid? How do we know her cousins had feathers?"

We stare at her. "How?"

Dr. Chen lifts the golden magnifying glass over her head and holds it out to us. "The bones know," she whispers. "Every secret is written right into them. You just have to learn to read."

She presses the glass into our hand. The warmth of her pocket spreads into our palm. The cord settles, soft and heavy, against our wrist. For a moment nobody speaks. The whole museum seems to hold its breath.

"Detectives," she says, "your first case is waiting." She points up, up, up, to a dark line running through Sue's enormous leg bone. "What do you see?"

s2a.text:
"The dig site," we say.

Dr. Chen's eyes light up. "Montana," she whispers. "Wonder."

She leads us down a hallway and through a door, and suddenly the air smells like dust and sunshine. The floor is covered in red-brown rock and sand. A sign reads: Hell Creek Formation, Montana. Just like the real place where Sue was found.

"Sixty-six million years ago," Dr. Chen says, kneeling down, "a T. rex died here. Mud covered her bones. More mud piled on top, year after year, until the weight pressed everything flat. Slowly, the bone turned to stone. That's a fossil."

She points to something sticking out of the rock. A bone, dark and heavy-looking, half-buried.

"Go on," she says. "Touch it."

We kneel beside her. The bone is cool and rough under our fingers, like old tree bark. We don't move. Gritty sand presses into our knees. The room is so still we can hear the air conditioning hum. Under our fingertips, the bone's roughness is not smooth like a river stone but pitted, like a sponge made of rock.

"Now," Dr. Chen says, lifting the golden magnifying glass. "Look closer."

We press the glass to the bone. The surface swells into view, and suddenly we see them: tiny lines, like the rings inside a tree trunk, stacked one on top of another.

"Growth rings," Dr. Chen breathes. "Every year, this dinosaur added a new ring. Count them."

We count. Seven. Eight. Nine.

"Nine years old," Dr. Chen says. "Just a kid. A teenager, really. Still growing."

We look up at her. "How do you know?"

She taps the glass. "The rings are far apart. That means fast growth. This T. rex was gaining kilos every single day. Like you, after a growth spurt."

We stare at the bone. Nine years old. Still growing. Still hungry.

"But how did it live?" we ask. "What did it do all day?"

Dr. Chen smiles. "That's the next clue."

s2b.text:
"The workshop," we say.

Dr. Chen grins. "Trix," she whispers. "Wonder."

She leads us down a hallway and through a door marked Preparation Lab. Inside, the room is bright and quiet. Long tables stretch across the floor, covered in soft blue padding. And on the tables, bones. Dozens of them, each one wrapped in white cloth like a birthday present.

"This is Trix," Dr. Chen says. "She came all the way from Montana in crates. Every bone was wrapped by hand and carried here like treasure."

A woman in a white coat looks up from the nearest table. She's holding a bone the size of a baseball bat, unwrapping it slowly, carefully, like it might break.

"This is Dr. Patel," Dr. Chen says. "She's a preparator. She puts dinosaurs back together."

Dr. Patel smiles at us. "Want to see?"

We nod. She lays the bone on the table and picks up another one. She turns them both in her hands, then fits them together with a soft click.

"Like a puzzle," we say.

"The world's biggest jigsaw," Dr. Patel says. "And we don't have the picture on the box."

Dr. Chen lifts the golden magnifying glass. "Look at this one," she says, pointing to a huge jawbone lying nearby.

We press the glass to it. The teeth swell into view, thick and curved, each one as big as a banana.

"Whoa," we breathe.

"Those teeth could crush bone," Dr. Chen says softly. "But here's the mystery. Was she a hunter? A scavenger? Both?"

We look up. "How do we find out?"

Dr. Chen taps the glass. "We keep reading."

s3.text:
"Well?" Dr. Chen's eyes are shining. "What did you find?"

We tell her, and she listens with her whole face, the way grown-ups almost never do.

"That," she whispers, "is a clue worth keeping." She taps the golden magnifying glass in our hand. "Come on. The bones have more to say."

We follow her past Sue's great grinning skull, down a hallway, through a door that says STAFF ONLY. Her laboratory is small and quiet and smells like dust and coffee. A microscope waits on the counter like a silver robot.

"Sit." Dr. Chen pats a tall stool. "You're going to read a bone."

She slides something under the microscope — a slice of T. rex bone, thin as a potato chip, glowing amber in the light.

"Look."

We press our eye to the lens. For a moment, there is only light, a warm golden glow that fills our whole eye. Then, the rings appear. Dozens of pale rings, curving through the bone like the rings inside a tree trunk. The world inside the lens is so small, and so complete.

"Growth rings," says Dr. Chen. "One for every year of this dinosaur's life. Count them."

We count. Out loud. Slowly. "Fourteen... fifteen... sixteen."

"Sixteen," Dr. Chen repeats. "This T. rex was a teenager. And look how wide the rings are." Her finger traces the glass. "Wide rings mean fast growing. This dinosaur gained two kilograms every single day. Like gaining a big bag of flour, every day, for years."

We pull back from the microscope and stare at her. "Every day?"

"Every day," she says. "Young, healthy, and growing like a weed. The rings never lie."

She lifts the magnifying glass and turns it slowly in the light.

"But bones can tell us more than age," she whispers. "Much more."

s4a.text:
Dr. Chen leads us back through the museum, past Sue's grinning skull, to a side room with a glass case. Inside, something small and feathered hops from perch to perch.

"A chicken?" we ask.

"A living relative," says Dr. Chen. She opens the case and gently lifts the bird out. It settles on her arm, warm and light, its tiny heart beating fast against her sleeve. We can feel the bird's warmth from where we stand, a little furnace of life. Its feathers are so soft they look like they might come apart if we breathed on them too hard. "Watch its feet."

The chicken steps down onto the table. Three toes forward, one back. Scales on its legs. A funny little strut.

Dr. Chen holds up a photograph of a T. rex foot bone. "Same shape," she whispers. "Same number of toes. Same way of walking."

We look from the chicken to the photograph, then back to the chicken. "So T. rex was like a giant chicken?"

Dr. Chen laughs, delighted. "Not quite. But birds are the closest living relatives of T. rex. And some of its cousins had feathers." She strokes the chicken's soft head. "We know this because the bones match. The wishbone. The legs. The way the hips are built."

The chicken pecks at a button on her coat. We reach out and feel its feathers, soft as dandelion fluff.

"No human ever saw a living T. rex," Dr. Chen says. "But the clues are everywhere. In the fossils. In the growth rings. In this little bird."

She lifts the golden magnifying glass and holds it over the chicken's foot. "Detectives," she whispers, "the mystery is solved. The bones were telling the truth all along."

We smile. The chicken clucks, as if it agrees.

s4b.text:
Dr. Chen leads us back through the museum, past Sue's grinning skull, to a tall glass case. Inside, an enormous skull rests on a velvet cushion. Not Sue's — another T. rex, with a snout longer than our arm.

"Look at these spaces," says Dr. Chen, tapping the glass. Two huge openings in the skull, right where the nose would be. "Room for smelling organs. T. rex had one of the most powerful noses of any animal ever."

We press our hands to the glass. It's cool under our palms, and we can smell the faint, musty scent of old velvet. The shadow of the huge skull looms over us, dark and still. "How powerful?"

"It could smell a dead dinosaur from miles away," she says. "Like you smelling cookies baking, but from the other side of town."

She moves her finger down to the teeth. Thick as bananas, curved like steak knives. "And these. Scientists measured the bite force by studying the skull shape and the tooth marks on fossil bones. T. rex could bite through bone like you bite through a carrot."

We stare at the teeth. "Without ever seeing it happen?"

"Without ever seeing it happen," Dr. Chen confirms. She lifts the golden magnifying glass and holds it over the skull. "The bones tell us. The size of the nose holes. The shape of the jaw. The wear on the teeth. Every clue is written right there."

She turns to us, her eyes bright. "No human ever saw a living T. rex. But we know it was a teenager. We know it grew fast. We know it smelled everything."

She presses the magnifying glass into our hand. "Detectives," she whispers, "the mystery is solved. The bones were telling the truth all along."

We look up at the skull and grin back.

c1.question: "Would you like to see where we find these ancient bones, or would you prefer to see how we put them together once they're found?"

options.label: Visit the dusty dig site where fossils are found
See the museum workshop where skeletons are assembled

c2.question: "Now that we know it was a fast-growing teenager, would you like to meet its living relative, or would you rather discover its super-powered senses?"

options.label: Meet the live chicken and learn about bird connections
Discover the amazing nose and powerful teeth

stories.title: The Door in the Tide Pool

s1.text:
The tide has gone out and left the black rocks shining. We are at the very edge of the sea, you and me, shoes in one hand.
Tick. Tick. Tick.
Something is tapping, down in a pool no bigger than a washing-up bowl.
We kneel on the dry grey ledge, not the green slippy part, because that is the good place to kneel. Then we look in.
At the bottom a little crab is knocking on a round door made of shell.
The door swings open. In he goes.
"Wait for us," we say, and push our hands through after him.
Warm water folds round us like bathwater. Down we drift in silver bubbles that let us breathe and talk.
Something wide and brown comes rowing up.
"Well," hums an old sea turtle, slow as a yawn. "Somebody found our door."
Her shell is patched like a quilt. She is {companion_name}, and she has swum here a hundred years.
"Climb on." She pats her wide back with one flipper. "Everybody down here has a door. Wait till you see the rest."

s2a.text:
We slide off the shell and paddle after the crab.
He does not go forwards. He goes sideways, tick tick tick across the sand, quick as a wind-up mouse.
"Legs bend out," he says, without stopping. "Sideways is just how the legs go."
So we turn sideways and kick sideways too. We are terrible at it. We laugh until our bubbles wobble.
He leads us in among the kelp, brown ribbons taller than a door. Then he stops and taps a rock. Tap tap.
Out come four hermit crabs, each carrying a curled shell on his back like a rucksack.
"House swap," says our crab.
The big one is squeezed in like a foot in last year's boot, so a friend shoves a roomier shell over, and he hops out, hops in, and turns round twice.
"Better," he says.
So that is their door, and they take it with them.
Our crab points a claw along the sand, to where the water is turning gold.

s2b.text:
{companion_name} tips us off beside the ray.
There is no kick in her at all. Her fins go up, and down, and up, like somebody shaking out a bedsheet, and that is the whole of her swimming.
"Try it," hums {companion_name}.
We stretch our arms wide and ripple them. We wobble. The ray tips one wing tip, which we decide means not bad.
Off over a meadow of pale sand we go, past garden eels that stand up like little question marks and duck back down.
Then the ray stops. She settles flat and shivers, and the sand drifts over her back until there is nothing left of her but two small eyes.
"Where has she gone?" we ask, loudly, so she can hear.
The sand puffs. She is laughing.
Her door is just the floor, and she pulls it over herself.
Then up she bursts, and we follow her wing tips to where the water is turning gold.

s3.text:
The gold is the reef, and the reef is going to bed.
"Tuck in close, little bubbles," hums {companion_name}.
Clown fish are wriggling down into an anemone's soft waving arms, the way you wriggle down under a blanket. A striped fish yawns and fans his fins. We yawn back.
Then five squid come whooshing over our heads, each one squirting a jet of water to shove itself along. Whoosh.
A starfish is crossing a rock on hundreds of sticky feet. It will take him all night. He does not mind.
Low in the reef wall is a hole with a tidy heap of pebbles outside it, and in the hole sits an octopus. Eight arms. He waves them at us one at a time, and his skin goes pink, then spotty, then pink again.
"That is him talking," whispers {companion_name}. "Pink means hello."
We say hello back with our whole arm.
"One more wonder," she hums, "and then home through your own door."

s4a.text:
We settle down in front of the octopus's hole, quiet as two bubbles.
His front garden is pebbles and shells, laid out just so. He nudges one along with an arm tip, and then he is happy with it.
Then he starts putting his colours away.
Pink first, rippling down all eight arms at once. Hello, friends.
Then spots, hurrying across his head, which is what giggling looks like on an octopus.
Then a deep slow purple, the colour of the jam at the bottom of the jar, and it stays.
One arm curls in. Then the next. Then the next, like lamps going out along a hallway.
Before the last one tucks away, he reaches into his garden and holds out one small spiral shell, shiny as a coat button.
We take it in both hands. He pulls a flat white stone across his doorway.
{companion_name} carries us up and out through the little shell door, onto the warm sand.
"Now you know," she hums. "Some friends say goodnight in colours."

s4b.text:
"Hold on to the front of my shell," hums {companion_name}. "Squid, if you please."
The squid line up round us and squirt. Whoosh. Up we all go, {companion_name} rowing steady, the squid looping about her like ribbon coming off a spool.
The blue above us goes lighter. Lighter. Then silver.
And there is the moon, lying on the ceiling of the sea, wobbling about like a coin at the bottom of a glass of water.
Moonlight comes down in long soft beams. A fish swims into a beam and lights up, then swims out and goes dark again.
Far below, the whole reef is glimmering, tucked in.
"Every door down here opens somewhere," says {companion_name}. "That one opens onto the sky."
The squid do one loop each, wave a tentacle each, and off they go.
Then she rows us home to the little shell door and presses something into our hands. A small white shell, round as the moon.
"So you remember," she hums. "The sea keeps a moon of its own."
"Goodnight, {companion_name}."

c1.question: "There goes your crab," says {companion_name}. "And there goes a ray, sliding along on her own. Crab, or ray? You pick."

options.label: Follow the sideways-walking crab
Glide along with the ray

c2.question: "Now then," hums {companion_name}. "Stay and watch him put his colours away? Or hold on tight and go up with the squid, right up to the moon? Octopus, or moon?"

options.label: Watch the octopus put his colours away
Ride up with the squid to see the moon

s1.text:
The argument lasted an entire rainy afternoon at the library chess club. Should a dragon cost five coins or six? Voices got louder. Someone knocked over a bishop. And that was when {designer_name} stood up on a chair and shouted the words that changed everything: we could just MAKE one.

That night, at the kitchen table, {designer_name} cut a cereal box flat and borrowed dice from three other games. The idea felt enormous in their head, a whole treasure island, players racing across it, coins to spend, a dragon at the far end. But when they picked up the pencil to write the first rule, the island turned to fog. The pencil hovered. Nothing came.

The doorbell rang. It was {friend_name}, rain on their hood, holding something small and battered between two fingers.

Sir Bouncesalot. The d20. The luckiest die in the world, if you asked {friend_name}, which nobody ever did.

They placed it on the table with great ceremony, like a knight laying down a sword, and looked at the blank cardboard.

A dragon to be slain, they said.

{designer_name} laughed, and something loosened. Okay, they said. Okay. What do we actually need?

{friend_name} rolled Sir Bouncesalot across the cereal box, because of course they did. Twenty. A good omen, obviously.

So they started with what they knew. Players need something to want. The treasure. Write it down. Players need a choice, a real one, not a fake one. Spend coins to move fast, or save them for the dragon, or buy a little luck. Write it down. And every choice needs a consequence, or nobody cares about anything. Write it down.

Goal, choice, consequence. Around and around.

They did not know it yet, but they had just built the thing that lives inside every game ever made. The loop. The engine.

{designer_name} drew a small star in the corner of the cardboard. It came out lopsided.

Version one, they said.

{friend_name} picked up Sir Bouncesalot and held it high. Then let the quest begin.

s2a.text:
Play it, said {designer_name}. Obviously. We have to know.

{friend_name} grinned and grabbed the phone. Twenty minutes later Zara from chess club was sitting at the kitchen table, turning a cardboard coin over in her fingers, looking at the hand-drawn island the way a dragon looks at a sheep.

I'll go first, she said.

Zara did not move toward the treasure. Zara did not buy luck. Zara bought the dragon card. Every single round, she bought the dragon card, and every single round it stomped across the board and ate whatever the rest of them had built. On turn six, {friend_name} rolled Sir Bouncesalot with full ceremony, both hands, eyes closed, a small hum of destiny. Three. Zara's dragon ate their last coin anyway.

Eleven minutes after it started, it was over.

Zara pushed back her chair, and she said it kindly, which somehow made it worse. This part is boring. And also, I won without trying.

The kitchen went very quiet. Sir Bouncesalot sat on the table showing his three like a small bad moon.

{friend_name} picked him up and rolled him again, gently, as if apologizing. Six. Also bad.

Okay, said {designer_name}. Their ears were hot. Okay. Let's think.

They stared at the board. The treasure path. The luck cards. The dragon, sitting there at the far end, fat and smug, the best thing on the island by a mile.

Wait, said {designer_name} slowly. The problem isn't that the dragon is strong.

{friend_name} looked up.

The problem is that nothing else gives you a reason not to take it. Moving fast is worse. Luck is worse. Saving is worse. It's not a choice at all. It's just a door with one handle.

Zara leaned back in. Huh, she said. That's true. I never even read the other cards.

{designer_name} flipped the cereal box over and picked up the pencil. The first star, the lopsided one, was on the other side now, hidden against the table. They drew a new one in the fresh corner. It came out a little straighter.

Version two, they said.

{friend_name} lifted Sir Bouncesalot high. The quest continues.

s2b.text:
Ask around, said {designer_name}. If we're wrong, I want to know before Zara does.

So the next morning, before anyone rolled anything, {designer_name} tucked the notebook under one arm and biked to the library, {friend_name} rattling alongside with Sir Bouncesalot in a jacket pocket like a tiny knight in a carriage.

The librarian listened to the whole thing. The island, the coins, the dragon. She did not fix anything. She just asked one question.

What do you want players to feel, right here? And she tapped the page where the dragon card was drawn.

{designer_name} opened their mouth and nothing came out. Nobody had asked that. They had argued about five coins or six for an entire afternoon and nobody had once asked that.

The librarian pulled a book off the shelf and found a picture of a seesaw. A game is balanced like this, she said. A beginner should beat an expert sometimes. Not always. Sometimes. If the expert always wins, the beginner quits. If it's pure luck, the expert quits. You're building the middle.

Then she told them about a man named Reiner Knizia, who has made hundreds of games, more than almost anyone alive, and who still builds every single one out of cardboard first. Ugly first versions, she said. On purpose. Cardboard is where games go to tell the truth.

{friend_name} leaned over the book. Hundreds, they whispered. And he still tests them. Like quests.

They biked home fast. The notebook felt heavier than before, in a good way, like a tool instead of a diary.

That afternoon they played version one anyway, just the two of them, because now they wanted to see it break. And it broke. {friend_name} played the Zara strategy, dragon card every round, and the game folded in eleven minutes flat. Sir Bouncesalot rolled twenty twice and it changed nothing, which {friend_name} took as a personal insult.

But this time {designer_name} was watching the seesaw. Every round, the dragon side just sat on the ground. Nothing weighed anything against it.

There, said {designer_name}. That's the wobble. It's not that the dragon is strong. It's that nothing else is a reason.

{friend_name} nodded slowly, then flipped the cereal box over. New corner. Fresh cardboard.

{designer_name} drew the star again. Straighter this time. You could tell what it was now.

Version two, they said.

{friend_name} raised Sir Bouncesalot like a banner. The quest continues.

s3.text:
Back at the kitchen table, {designer_name} stared at the lopsided star in the corner of the cardboard. Version one had wobbled. It had creaked. And somewhere in the middle of all that wobbling, a strange idea had landed: maybe it was supposed to.

"You know what?" {designer_name} said slowly. "I think version one was meant to be terrible. That's not failure. That's the job."

{friend_name} looked up from Sir Bouncesalot. "Say that again."

"Designers call it iteration. You build a version, you watch it break, you fix the thing that broke, and you build it again. Great games go through hundreds of versions. Hundreds."

{friend_name} was quiet for a moment. Then they picked up the pencil and pressed it into {designer_name}'s hand.

"Then stop talking," they said, "and iterate."

So they did. They crossed out the dragon's price and wrote something new: the dragon costs more every time someone buys it. First player pays five. Second pays seven. Third pays nine. Suddenly the dragon was not a shopping trip. It was a decision.

"And this," {designer_name} said, drawing a new card with a flourish, "is the lucky map. If you're losing, really losing, you can spend your last coins on a shortcut through the jungle. Might work. Might not."

{friend_name} grinned. "Skill for the expert. A real chance for the beginner."

"Balance," {designer_name} said, and the word felt like a key turning.

They redrew the star. Still a little wobbly. But better. Definitely better.

Version two.

{friend_name} lifted Sir Bouncesalot high, closed their eyes, and rolled with the ceremony of a knight anointing a battlefield. The die clattered across the cardboard.

They played. The loop turned. Goal, choice, consequence, around and around, and this time the game had a heartbeat. It was not perfect. Something still snagged near the end, something {designer_name} could not quite name yet.

But when the last coin was spent and the dragon finally fell, {friend_name} looked up with wide eyes and said the only word that matters in game design.

"Again."

s4a.text:
"Luck," {designer_name} said. "We tip it toward luck."

{friend_name} stood up so fast their chair wobbled. "At last," they said, lifting Sir Bouncesalot to the light like a chalice. "The die has been waiting for this moment."

So version three grew chances the way a garden grows weeds. The lucky-map deck got fatter — shortcuts, rainstorms, a monkey who steals coins and sometimes gives them back wearing a tiny hat. {designer_name} added a weather die. Roll it at the start of each round: sun means everyone moves fast, wind means the boats drift, and rain means the dragon stays home and naps.

"Rain," {friend_name} breathed, reading the new card. "The dragon naps. That's beautiful."

Then came the playtest that nobody saw coming. {friend_name}'s mum wandered in for a cup of tea, got handed the dragon piece, and stayed. She had never played a board game in her life. She asked what the coins were for twice. She moved her boat the wrong way and apologised to it.

And she won.

Not by accident — by weather. Rain, rain, rain, three rounds running, and while Zara's brilliant plans drowned in puddles, Mum's little boat drifted straight into the harbour on a lucky map she'd drawn by pure fluke.

Zara put her face in her hands. "I have been defeated," she said, "by a nap."

But here is the thing {designer_name} noticed, scribbling in the notebook: Mum never once asked what the rules meant. The weather die explained itself. The lucky map explained itself. The game made sense to someone who had never played anything — and she still had to earn it, coin by coin, roll by roll.

"One more," Zara said.

They played three rounds. Nobody stopped saying it. One more. One more.

Late that night, {designer_name} redrew the star in the corner of the rules card. Straighter. Brighter. Almost perfect.

Version four, they wrote.

The storyteller still has that card. And tucked inside the notebook, drawn better every single time, is the star — proof that the best games are the ones where anyone at the table can win, on any given night, if the rain falls just right.

s4b.text:
"Skill," {designer_name} said. "We tip it toward skill."

{friend_name} looked down at Sir Bouncesalot, cradled in their palm. "You hear that?" they whispered to the die. "She thinks she doesn't need you." They rolled it anyway, for luck, because some habits are sacred.

So version three sharpened its teeth. Coins could be saved across rounds now — hoard them, spend them later, feel clever. And the dragon? The dragon could be baited. Leave a trail of coins leading away from the treasure, and the greedy old thing would follow it, sniffing, while you slipped in the back way.

Zara's eyes went very bright.

It took her four turns. Four. She saved coins in rounds one and two, bought nothing, let everyone think she was floundering. Then in round three she laid a coin trail like breadcrumbs, sent the dragon waddling off toward the far beach, and strolled into the hoard with her pockets empty and her smile enormous.

"Three-turn trap," she said, leaning back. "I planned it before you finished shuffling."

{designer_name} stared at the board. Then at the rules. Then at Zara.

"That's brilliant," they said. "That's — wait. If you can do that, a new player will never win. Ever."

Zara's smile faded. She looked at the coin trail, at the dragon, at the hoard. "Oh," she said. "Oh no. I broke my own favourite game."

They fixed it together. One small rule: the first time you play, the dragon likes you. It starts one step closer to your boat. A soft landing. A welcome.

The final playtest ran long past dinner. Nobody noticed. Every choice mattered now — every coin, every turn, every risk — and even the players who were losing leaned forward, elbows on the table, watching the board like it might tell them a secret.

The storyteller still has the notebook. On the last page, under RULES, version four, someone has written in hopeful pencil: version five ideas.

The star in the corner is drawn better than ever. But there is room, still, for it to grow.

c1.question: "Right," says {friend_name}, slamming Sir Bouncesalot onto the table like a gauntlet. "The rules exist. Do we play this beautiful disaster right now and watch it burn, or do we sneak it past someone who actually knows games first?"

options.label: Test version one immediately and let it fall apart
Take the rules to the game librarian before anyone plays

c2.question: "Okay, version three needs a soul," {designer_name} says, tapping the pencil. "Zara wins every time she thinks, and your mum wins every time she's lucky. Which way do we tip the seesaw — more luck, so anyone can win? Or more skill, so outsmarting someone feels amazing?"

options.label: Grow the lucky-map deck and let dice shake the island
Add saving, baiting, and long plans for clever players

designer_name.role: The kid designer, the child in the story

friend_name.role: The skeptical best friend and keeper of Sir Bouncesalot

s1.text:
We are asteroid mappers, you and I, on the bridge of our small ship. Out the window, the asteroid belt drifts past — a slow river of stones, tumbling between Mars and Jupiter. Every rock has its place, and our job is to write those places down, so every ship that comes after us knows the safe way through.

Pip, our little robot probe, buzzes at his launch pad. "Can I go? Can I go? My camera eye is polished. I'm ready."

"Soon," we tell him. "One more stretch to chart."

Our dog, Biscuit, is curled asleep by the window, and the ship hums under our feet like a cat in a sunny spot. The map on our screen is nearly finished — a dotted line winding between a hundred grey boulders, each one circling the sun in its own slow orbit.

Then Biscuit lifts his head.

A low growl, soft and rumbling, rolls out of him. His ears point straight at the window.

"What is it, boy?" we ask.

Pip's camera eye swivels. "Looking," he whirs. "Looking... oh. Oh! One of the rocks is drifting. It's not where the map says it should be."

We press our noses to the glass. There it is — a stone the size of a house, sliding slowly, quietly, sideways. Right toward the shipping lane.

s2a.text:
"We can push it," we say. "Easy."

We bring {ship_name} around, slow and careful, until our nose touches Wanderer's cold grey side. Biscuit stands at the window, tail low, watching.

"Pushing," we say. "Now."

The engines whine. The whole ship shudders, and the floor hums hard under our boots. Wanderer does not move. Not even a pebble's width.

"Push harder!" Pip calls from his pad. "I'm bracing! I'm bracing!"

We push harder. The engines whine higher, a thin sound like a kettle about to whistle. Still nothing. Wanderer just sits there, big as a house, in no hurry at all.

"Stop, stop," Pip says. His camera eye has gone very still. "Look at it. Really look."

We look. The rock hangs there, quiet and slow.

"It's falling," Pip says softly. "Toward the Sun. It's always falling. But it's moving sideways so fast it keeps missing. That's what an orbit is."

"So it's not stuck," we say.

"No. It's... busy." Pip's eye swivels to the map, where the freighter's dotted line grows closer. "And it's very, very heavy."

s2b.text:
"The tow cable," we say. "We'll pull it out."

Pip launches with a happy buzz, the cable spooling out behind him, thin and silver. He loops it around Wanderer's middle, once, twice, and clicks it fast. "Got it! Got it! Pull away!"

We ease {ship_name} forward. The cable goes tight. The engines grumble, the deck trembles, and Biscuit gets up to watch, ears high.

For one whole second, it works.

Then — ping! A sharp little sound, like a plucked string. The cable snaps, and its loose end whips away into the dark. Biscuit barks — one short, surprised woof — and Wanderer tumbles slowly onward, still in the lane.

"Oh," says Pip, very small, drifting back to us with the broken end.

"It's all right," we tell him. "You tied a good knot."

His camera eye lifts to the rock. And stays there. "Wait," he whirs. "Wait. Look at it. Really look."

We look. The stone hangs in the black, turning over and over, slow as a minute hand.

"It's falling," Pip says softly. "Toward the Sun. Always falling — but moving sideways so fast it keeps missing. That's what an orbit is."

"So it isn't stuck," we say.

"No. It's busy." His eye swivels to the map. The freighter's dotted line is getting close.

s3.text:
Pip's camera eye is shining brighter than ever. "What did you find?" he whirs. "Tell me, tell me!"

We tell him. And everything changes.

"So Wanderer isn't lost," Pip says slowly. "It's orbiting. Just like all the others. Around and around the Sun, like a ball on a string."

He unrolls our star chart across the floor, and we kneel beside it, Biscuit's chin warm on our knee. Pip's little light draws a circle on the map. "The Sun pulls every rock inward," he says. "Always inward. But the rocks keep whirling forward, so they never fall in. They just... swing. Forever."

We watch the dotted lines curve around and around. A hundred stones, all swinging.

"So we don't need to push Wanderer away," we breathe. "We only need to bend its path."

"A nudge," Pip whispers. "A tiny, gentle, sideways nudge, at exactly the right moment. Then its orbit curves all by itself, and it slides out of the lane like a marble rolling off a table edge."

Our ship's radio crackles. The freighter's voice, far away but closer now: "Asteroid mappers, we are approaching the lane. Is the way clear?"

Biscuit's ears go up. We look at the drifting stone, then at each other.

We know what to do. Now we have to do it gently.

s4a.text:
"I'll go," Pip says. "I'm small. I'm quick. My thruster is ready."

We open the hatch, and out he zips — a spark of silver in the dark. Biscuit presses his nose to the glass. We hold our breath.

Pip flies to Wanderer's side, slow and careful, and plants his little thruster against the stone. "Mapper," he calls over the radio, "tell me when."

We watch the dotted line on our screen. Wanderer swings onward. Closer. Closer.

"Now!" we shout.

Pip's thruster fires — one bright blink. The great stone shivers. Then, slow as a yawn, it slides sideways, tipping out of the shipping lane like a stone stepping over a stream.

"It worked!" Pip cheers. "It worked, it worked!"

The freighter sails through, safe and sound, its lights blinking thank you.

Pip comes home buzzing, and tucked in his memory bank is a treasure — a close-up photograph of Ceres, the round dwarf planet, all pocked and pale and ancient. "I saw it," he whispers, "while I was out there."

We pin his picture above the map, where everyone can see.

s4b.text:
"We'll do it together," we say. "The whole ship. Softly."

Biscuit stays asleep as we ease in beside Wanderer. Slow. Slower. We match its speed exactly, until stone and ship drift side by side, like two leaves on the same pond.

Our hull touches its flank — the gentlest kiss of metal on rock. The ship hums. The stone hums back.

"Now," Pip whispers from the window.

We give the smallest push. So small Biscuit doesn't even stir. So small we barely feel it ourselves. But Wanderer feels it. Its orbit bends, just a whisper of a curve, and the great stone drifts clear of the lane, slow and graceful, turning in the starlight.

The freighter sails through, safe and sound.

Then — clink. Something tiny bounces off our window. A chip of asteroid rock, no bigger than a button, broken free by our gentle push. We scoop it in with the net.

It sits in our palm, grey and ordinary-looking. But Pip's eye goes wide. "That stone," he breathes, "is older than the Earth."

We keep it in a little box by the window, where the sun can find it.

c1.question: "Wanderer is in the lane and the freighter is coming. Do we push it with the ship, or pull it with the tow cable?"

options.label: Push the asteroid with the ship's engines
Pull the asteroid with a tow cable

c2.question: "We know the secret now—a small nudge at the right moment. Do we send Pip out to do it alone, or do we take the whole ship in close and do it together?"

options.label: Send the robot probe to nudge the asteroid
Take the ship in close and nudge it ourselves

s1.text:
"Quick," says Pip. "They're waking up."

We are standing at the mouth of a limestone cave, and the dusk is coming down soft and grey around us.
