It was covered in dark rock, and a red-hot volcano was grumbling on its side. Ploom! It puffed out a cloud of smoke and glowing lava. {child_name}'s jaw dropped. One moon was a giant ice cube with a water-sprayer, and the other was a fiery rock with a volcano. How could they both be moons? The mystery was getting bigger.

s3.text: Zorp's eyes went wide as dinner plates. "Show me! Show me what you found!" he cried, nearly dropping his contraption. {child_name} held it out, and Zorp bounced on his toes. "Yes! YES! Now we can solve the whole moon mix-up!" He grabbed a rubber ball tied to a string from his pocket. "Watch closely, {child_name}!" Zorp swung the ball around his head. Round and round it went. "The string pulls the ball in, just like gravity pulls a moon! The moon wants to fly away, but gravity says, 'No, no, stay with me!' So the moon goes around and around. That is an orbit!" {child_name} laughed. "So the planet is like... holding strings on all its moons?" "Exactly!" Zorp cheered. "And each moon is different! Some are icy cold, some have rumbling volcanoes, all because of how they were made long ago. But they all dance the same circle dance!" {child_name} looked out at the moons again. They weren't just floating anymore. They were a family, swinging around their planet like balls on invisible strings. "We did it," {child_name} whispered. "We solved it."

s4a.text: "The icy moon!" cried {child_name}. "Let's go!" Zorp zipped them down in his wobbly shuttle. "Now, {child_name}, the ice is strong here, but we stay on the marked path," Zorp said, patting a rope tied to a flag. "Safety first!" They stepped out onto the frozen ground. It sparkled like a million tiny stars. Crunch. Crunch. Their boots made the only sound. Above them, the black sky stretched forever, and the giant planet hung overhead like a lantern. Suddenly, the ground rumbled. Rumble. Rumble. "Look!" Zorp pointed. A geyser burst from the ice, shooting glittering water high into the black sky. It sparkled like fireworks made of diamonds. "It's beautiful," {child_name} breathed. When it was time to go, Zorp chipped off a small piece of ice. It glowed in {child_name}'s glove. "For you," Zorp said with a grin. "A piece of the moon to take home." And so, {child_name} brought home a piece of sparkling ice, and it glowed softly in their glove all the way back.

s4b.text: "The volcanic moon!" shouted {child_name}. "I want to see the lava!" Zorp whooped and steered them toward the moon with the grumbling volcano. He parked the shuttle behind a big, warm rock. "We stay here, {child_name}," Zorp said wisely. "The rock keeps us safe from sparks." They climbed up and peeked over the top. The volcano rumbled. Grumble. Grumble. Then—whoosh! Bright orange lava bubbled up and flowed down the side like thick, glowing soup. It cooled and hardened right before their eyes. They watched the glow fade to dark rock. "It's making new land!" {child_name} gasped. "The moon is growing!" Zorp nodded, his eyes twinkling. Later, Zorp picked up a small, dark rock from the cooled lava. "Fresh from the moon," he said, placing it in {child_name}'s hand. It was still warm. And so, {child_name} brought home a small rock from the new land, and it stayed warm in their pocket all the way back.

c1.question: Robo-Guide says, 'Should we start with a model to see how gravity works, or zoom to a moon to see the differences up close?'

options.label: Start with a gravity model
Zoom to a moon to see differences

c2.question: Zorp exclaims, 'Now that we know the secret, shall we visit the icy moon with its sparkling geysers, or the volcanic moon with its fiery eruptions?'

options.label: Visit the icy moon
Visit the volcanic moon

child_name.role: The name of the child astronaut in the story

s1.text:
Grandpa's garage smells like sawdust and old rain boots. We have newspaper spread everywhere. On the floor. On the table. Even on the cat.

"Today," we say, "we paint a giant orange sunset banner for the porch!"

Grandpa claps. "Splendid!" He squeezes out two fat blobs of paint. One red, one yellow. They sit on the palette like two little hills.

Mixmaster Max watches from the workbench. He is Grandpa's old garden gnome, with a pointy hat covered in dried paint drips. He holds the palette with his stiff plaster hands. He is very good at supervising.

"Now," says Grandpa. "Where is the orange?"

We look. No orange. Only red. Only yellow.

"Hmm," we say. "We need orange."

Max's hat wiggles. Just a tiny bit.

s2a.text:
"Careful scientists," we say. "One drop at a time."

Grandpa nods. "Very wise." He squeezes fresh red onto a clean corner of the palette. Then yellow. Two little islands, not touching.

We dip the brush in red. Then yellow. Swirl, swirl, slow.

"Look," we whisper. The red is turning peachy at the edges.

Mixmaster Max leans in. His hat nearly touches the paint. "Steady," says Grandpa.

Swirl. Swirl. The yellow melts into the red like butter into toast.

"Is it orange yet?" we ask.

Max's hat wiggles. Not quite. But something is happening in the middle of the palette, something warm and glowing, like a tiny sun waking up.

s2b.text:
"Crazy inventors!" we shout. "Great big swoosh!"

Grandpa grins. "My favorite kind." He hands us the big brush, the one as wide as a spoon.

We plunge it into the red blob. Then the yellow. Swoosh!

Paint flies. A red dot lands on Mixmaster Max's nose. He does not blink. He is very professional.

"Again!" says Grandpa.

Swoosh, swoosh! The colors crash together like waves. Red streaks through yellow. Yellow streaks through red. It looks like a storm on the palette.

"Whoa," we breathe. The middle is glowing. But the edges are wild, all swirly and streaky.

Max's hat tilts. Is it supposed to look like that?

s3.text:
Grandpa leans over the palette. "What did you find?" he asks.

We show him. He nods slowly, the way he does when the tomato soup needs stirring.

"Ah," he says. "A wobble. Every good mix has one."

He holds our brush under the tap. The water runs pink, then clear. "Clean tools," he says, "make true colors."

We dip the brush. We add yellow, bit by bit. The red softens. Tangerine. Then glowing sunset orange.

"Look!" we shout, because we cannot help it.

Mixmaster Max's hat wiggles. The orange swirls on the palette like a tiny sun, right there in Grandpa's garage.

"Now," says Grandpa, "the banner."

s4a.text: We paint the sun with our perfect orange. Big, round strokes. While it dries, a real bee lands on the windowsill. Its legs are dusted yellow, just like our paint. "Look," we whisper. "It carried the yellow here." Grandpa nods. "Then let's give it somewhere to land." We mix a tiny drop of red into white. Pink. Soft as a kitten's ear. We dab a flower in the corner. The bee hums. We hang the banner on the porch. The real sunset matches ours. The bee visits our painted blossom. "Hello Sunshine," we say. Max's hat wiggles.

s4b.text: We paint the sun with our perfect orange. Then we look under the workbench. The shadow there is gray, not orange. "Why?" we ask. Grandpa scratches his chin. "Let's find out." We add one tiny drop of black to our orange. It turns brown, like mud. We paint a cool shadow beneath our sun. "Shadows aren't gray," Grandpa says. "They're where the light hides." We hang the banner on the porch. The real sun sets. Our painted shadow grows long. "Hello Sunshine," we say. Max's hat wiggles.

c1.question: "Do we mix like careful scientists, one drop at a time, or like crazy inventors with a great big swoosh?"

options.label: Mix slowly and watch each swirl
Mix with a big dramatic swirl

c2.question: "Shall we paint a flower for the bees we saw, or a shadow for the mysteries under the table?"

options.label: Paint a pink flower that bees would visit
Paint a dark shade shadow under the sun

s1.text: Rain on Nana's windows again. The whole house smells like toast and cat. Biscuit is sitting on the piano stool, staring up at the old upright like it swallowed a mouse. Her whiskers twitch. 'What is it, Biscuit?' we whisper. Biscuit pats the keys with one soft paw. Plink. Plink. The piano is covered in family photos and a dusty lace cloth, but underneath, it's all wood and wires and secrets. Nana calls it {piano_name}, which is a funny name for a piano, but it's true — when you press a key, it goes clank. Today the piano tuner is coming. Mr. Figg. He has a mustache like a walrus and a bag full of tiny tools. 'There's a sticky key,' Nana says. 'Middle C. It sticks.' Mr. Figg lifts the top of the piano and props it with the wooden stick. We lean in. Inside, there are rows and rows of little felt hammers, all wearing fuzzy gray sweaters, waiting to jump up and tap the strings. 'Look,' we breathe. 'They're all asleep.' Our little sister, who is three and very loud, bangs a key with her whole hand. 'That one smells like purple!' she shouts. Mr. Figg doesn't even blink. 'Ah,' he says. 'A synesthete.'

s2a.text:
"First," says Mr. Figg, "you must see the hammers work." He presses a key, and inside, a little felt hammer in its fuzzy gray sweater jumps up—boing—and taps a string. "Now," he says, "the Soft-Off. Who can play the quietest note?"

I go first. I press so gently the hammer barely tiptoes up. Ting.

"Too loud," says my sister. She breathes on a key like it's a dandelion. The hammer just sighs against the string. Nothing.

Biscuit watches with her wide eyes. She lifts one soft paw and pats, so light, like a snowflake landing. Plink.

"I win," we whisper.

Then we try together. We hover our fingers. We breathe. We giggle because nobody can hear anything at all, and Biscuit is purring louder than the piano.

s2b.text:
"Watch," says Mr. Figg. He plays a run, and inside, the hammers leap like tiny acrobats in fuzzy gray sweaters, bouncing up to tap the strings.

"Now the Animal Game," he says. "Every key is an animal."

I press a low note. "Hippo," I say. It goes deep and grumbly.

My sister bangs a high one. "Baby chick!" It goes peep peep peep.

Biscuit pats the middle. "That's a frog," we decide.

Then we all play at once. The low notes stomp like elephants. The high notes scatter like mice. My sister shouts, "That one smells like purple!" and Mr. Figg just nods, playing faster, and the whole zoo escapes into Nana's living room, loud and wonderful and completely out of control.

s3.text: Mr. Figg opens the top of the piano wide. "Now we find the frog's sore throat," he says. He lifts out the action — that's the row of hammers, all in their gray sweaters — and peers in with a little light. "Well, well." Under Middle C, wedged tight against the key, is a toy mouse. Biscuit's toy mouse. "So that's where it went," we whisper. Mr. Figg takes a long, thin tool from his bag. "Key spoon," he says. He slides it under the key, gentle as anything, and eases. The mouse does not budge. He tries again, from the side. Wiggle, wiggle. Pop! Out it comes, dusty and gray. Biscuit's ears go flat. Her eyes go wide. She leaps onto the keys. Her soft paws patter across the white and black. Run, run, run. The piano makes a wild, scrambled song. Up and down. Loud and soft. Biscuit is composing. 'She's playing!' we shout. Mr. Figg laughs so hard his mustache wiggles. Biscuit runs faster. The hammers inside jump and tap. The strings hum. 'How do we stop it?' we ask. Mr. Figg wipes his eyes. 'We don't,' he says. 'We let it finish.'

s4a.text: The song slows. Biscuit stops. She looks at us, then at Mr. Figg, then at the keys. 'Well, that was a ruckus!' says Mr. Figg, holding Biscuit who is still twitching her tail. 'Now, do you want to play the softest duet ever, or shall we listen to the piano purr?' We look at our sister. She is already sitting at the bench, her hands hovering. 'I want to play my purple note,' she whispers. 'Soft. Like a secret.' Mr. Figg nods. 'Then let us begin.' He lifts the lid. Inside, the little felt hammers are still wearing their fuzzy gray sweaters, but now they are awake. Watching. Waiting. We press a key. A tiny, tiptoeing bass note. Our sister presses her purple note. It is so soft it is almost not there. A whisper. A breath. Biscuit sits between us, purring. Mr. Figg shows us the damper. It falls like a little pillow, tucking the string in. 'There,' he says. 'The quietest sound is the bravest.' We take home a felt hammer-shaped cookie from Nana. It is sweet and soft and gone in one bite.

s4b.text: The song slows. Biscuit stops. She looks at us, then at Mr. Figg, then at the keys. 'Well, that was a ruckus!' says Mr. Figg, holding Biscuit who is still twitching her tail. 'Now, do you want to play the softest duet ever, or shall we listen to the piano purr?' We press our ears against the wood. Mr. Figg plays one last loud note. The hum buzzes through the whole piano. It feels like a purring cat. A giant, wooden cat. We lift our fingers. We listen. The sound gets smaller. And smaller. Like it is walking away down a long hallway. A hallway with no end. Biscuit's ears twitch. She hears it too. Mr. Figg smiles. 'The piano is saying goodbye,' he says. 'In its own way.' He opens his toolbox. Inside, there is a tiny tuning wrench. A toy one. He gives it to us. 'For next time,' he says. We take it home. We hold it tight. We remember the piano's secret purr. It is still buzzing in our ears.

c1.question: "Alright, you two," says Mr. Figg, wiping his hands on a rag. "Do you want to see how these little hammers work, or shall we just start making some noise?"

options.label: Watch the hammers dance
Start the animal game

c2.question: "Well, that was a ruckus!" says Mr. Figg, holding Biscuit who is still twitching her tail. "Now, do you want to play the softest duet ever, or shall we listen to the piano purr?"

options.label: Play a quiet duet with my sister
Feel the hum and hear the sound fade

piano_name.role: The old upright piano in Nana's living room

s1.text:
The rain has stopped. We are out on the path in our boots, you and me, and the whole garden smells of wet stone.
Down by our left boot an ant goes past. Then another. Then a whole line of them, marching along a crack in the paving, every one carrying something. A crumb. A seed. A piece of petal three times her size.
"They have a road," we say. "Look. Every one of them goes exactly the same way."
Then the road runs straight into the puddle.
To us it is a splash of silver. To an ant it is a lake with no far side. The front of the line stops dead. Ants hurry up and down the edge, bumping into each other, turning back, trying again.
Their road is gone.
A ladybug lands beside our knee, red with tiny black dots. It is {ladybug_name}, who inspects everything we build, and she taps her feet and waits.
"All right," we say. "We are building them a bridge."

s2a.text:
A leaf. The fig tree has one as wide as our two hands, and we carry it back flat in front of us like a tray.
Down it goes. One end on the near shore, one end on the far shore.
It reaches.
Then it slides. The wet stone lets go, and one end drops in with a plop.
"Take two," we say.
We fish it out and shake it off. This time we hold the near end down under a flat pebble and press another onto the far end. We push the leaf with one finger. It stays exactly where we put it.
{ladybug_name} climbs on. Out she walks to the middle on her tiny feet, without a sound. She turns round once. She walks back.
The bridge held her.
And our leaf is so wide that six ants could cross it side by side.

s2b.text:
Twigs. Two of them lie by the flowerpot, and we pick the two that match.
We lay the first one across the puddle like a rail. We lay the second right beside it, close as two fingers.
Then they roll. Both twigs turn over at once and clatter down into the water.
"Take two," we say.
We pull them out and wipe off the mud. This time we press each end deep into the soft ground until it grips. We wiggle them. They hold.
Now there is a tiny railway over the lake.
{ladybug_name} climbs up and walks out along one twig, all the way to the middle. She stops. She taps twice with her feet. She comes back.
The bridge held her.
And here is the clever part. Between our two twigs runs a narrow gap, just wide enough for an ant to walk down inside, out of the wind.

s3.text:
Our {bridge_deck} bridge goes right across the water and does not wobble one bit.
Now the ants will cross.
We watch. We wait. The first ant reaches the bridge, touches it with her antennae, and turns straight round. The next one does the same.
"Why not?" we say. "It is right there in front of you."
An ant does not follow a road with her eyes. She follows a smell. Every ant who walked that crack left a little smell behind, and following that smell road is like following toast up the stairs to the kitchen.
Our bridge does not smell of anything at all.
Then one small ant does a brave thing. She steps on. Two steps, stop. Three more steps. Now she is out in the middle, all on her own above the water.
Our fingers itch to help. We press them flat on the stones instead, because a finger the size of her street is no help to anybody.
She reaches the far side, and now her smell is on the bridge.

s4a.text:
A wall of grass. We pull the tall blades from the edge of the lawn and stand them in the soft ground all along the windy side. Now there is a green fence as high as our hand.
The wind pushes. The grass leans right over and springs back up. The {bridge_deck} bridge does not shiver at all now.
Behind that little wall, the crossing is as still as a hallway.
"Come on," we whisper. "Come on."
And the line starts. One ant, then two, then a whole marching row, antennae tapping the smell road the brave one left behind. One carries a crumb bigger than her own head and does not slow down for a second.
{ladybug_name} sits at the end of the bridge like an inspector at a gate, watching every ant go by.
The sun comes out and turns the puddle gold. We lie on our elbows and watch the road cross the water, and cross, and cross.
"We built that," we say. "Plops and pebbles and wobbles and all."
Well done, us. Well done, ants.

s4b.text:
Ramps. We scoop dry sand from under the flowerpot, pour a slope at the near end, and pat it smooth. Then another slope at the far end.
Now the bridge starts gently, like the ramp up to the library door.
The next ant walks straight up it without stopping once.
And here they come. The whole line pours up the sand and onto the {bridge_deck} bridge, tap tap tap, over the water and away.
Then the most surprising thing of the whole morning. At a gap in the stones, three ants take hold of one another's legs, and a fourth one walks over the top of them.
"They are doing it too," we say. "They are building a bridge out of ants."
{ladybug_name} spreads her wings and flies one slow circle above the crossing, like an inspector saying yes.
"We built that," we say. "Plops and sand and wobbles and all."
Well done, us. Well done, ants.

c1.question: We look round for something long enough to reach the whole way over. "It has to touch both shores," we say. "One big flat leaf off the fig tree, or two straight twigs laid down like rails. Leaf, or twigs?"

options.label: Lay one big flat leaf across
Lay two twigs down like rails

c2.question: The wind keeps shivering the water, and both ends of the bridge stand up like little cliffs. "One more thing and the whole line can come," we say. "A wall of grass along the side to stop the wind, or two sandy ramps so they can walk straight on. Grass, or sand?"

options.label: A wall of grass to stop the wind
Two sandy ramps up onto the bridge

ladybug_name.role: the ladybug who inspects everything we build

bridge_deck.role: what we laid across the water

stories.title: The Great Reef Repair & The All-Night Cafe

s1.text:
"Perfect," says Kit, spitting out the snorkel mouthpiece. "Absolutely perfect."

The lagoon is flat and blue and full of promise. It smells like salt and sunscreen. Kit has a bucket, a toy hammer, and absolutely no idea how to build underwater. But today is the day. Today, Kit builds something magnificent.

A noise comes from the water. Bloop. Bloop.

Then, zoom. A bright green face pops out of the lagoon. It has big yellow eyes and a beak like a parrot.

"You look like a builder," says the fish. "I am Pippin. And I have a problem."

Pippin is a parrotfish. His teeth go click-clack when he talks. Click-clack. Like a key turning in a lock.

"The storm broke it," says Pippin. "Come see."

Kit puts on the mask. The water is warm as bathwater. Underneath, the reef is a whole neighbourhood. Purple fans wave. Orange fish dart. And there, on the sandy bottom, lies a broken coral head. It looks like a smashed cake.

"The polyps need a home," says Pippin. "Tiny builders, like you. But they cannot start without a hard place to hold on to. A starter structure. Something that clicks together."

Kit looks at the broken pieces. They are heavy. They are covered in algae. They do not want to fit.

"We need a plan," says Pippin. He clicks his beak. "And we need a name. What shall we call your invention?"

Kit picks up a curved piece. It is rough and lumpy. It looks like a castle turret.

"The Click-Clack Castle," says Kit.

Pippin's eyes go wide. "Oh," he says. "That is a very good name. Now. How do we make it stay?"

s2a.text:
Pippin dives. His tail goes flip-flip-flip. "Follow me," he says. "We hunt for bones."

Underwater, the world turns blue and wavy. Kit swims down, down, to the sandy bottom. Pippin points with his beak. "Not that one. Too soft. Not that one. Too wobbly. We want the strong ones. The clicky ones."

Kit picks up a flat white piece. Tap tap tap. It goes thud. Like a sponge. Pippin shakes his head. "No good. That one is full of holes. The polyps would fall through."

They search. Flip flip. Dig dig. Kit finds a chunk of limestone. It is heavy and grey. Tap tap tap. Click. Like a key turning in a lock. Pippin's eyes go wide. "Oh. That is the one."

They pile the good pieces up. Click. Click. Click. Each one locks against the next. Kit's fingers are wrinkly. Kit's back is tired. But the pile grows. A floor. A wall. A turret. The Click-Clack Castle has a skeleton.

Pippin clicks his beak. "Strong bones," he says. "Now we need the glue."

s2b.text:
"Forget the bones," says Pippin. "We go straight to the good stuff."

He dives. His tail goes flip-flip-flip. Kit follows, down, down, to a rocky ledge. Pippin wiggles his eyebrows. "Behold," he says. "My secret stash."

He pulls out a sack. It is full of sand. White, fine, soft as flour. "I made this myself," says Pippin. "Parrotfish poop out sand. It is a gift."

Kit giggles. "You pooped that?"

"I did," says Pippin. "And it is perfect. But watch." He opens the sack. The current grabs the sand. Whoosh. It drifts away like smoke. "See? It will not stay. We need help."

A tiny fish zooms over. Blue and yellow, no bigger than Kit's thumb. "Cleaner wrasse," says Pippin. "She makes the sticky stuff. Watch."

The wrasse spits. A blob of algae glue lands on the sand. Pippin mixes it with his fin. Squish squish. It turns into paste. "Symbiosis," says Pippin. "I give her a cleaning. She gives me cement. Everybody wins."

Kit pokes the paste. It sticks. "Now," says Pippin, "we build."

s3.text:
Kit picks up the first big piece. It is heavy and lumpy. "Here goes," says Kit.

They set it on the sand. Kit stacks the next piece on top. Then another. The Click-Clack Castle grows taller. Taller. Kit grins. "Look at it go!"

Then the water pushes. A slow, strong surge, like someone rocking the whole lagoon. The tower wobbles. Wobbles. And down it comes, clatter-clatter, into the sand.

"Oh no," says Kit.

Pippin blows a stream of bubbles. "Hmm," he says. "Hmm, hmm."

Then, from a crack in the old reef, a tiny voice speaks. "Too tall. Too fast."

Out peeks a little creature, no bigger than Kit's thumb. She is soft and pink, with waving arms like tiny feathers. "I am Polyp-ella," she says. "I know about building. We polyps built this whole reef, you know. Bit by bit."

"What did we do wrong?" asks Kit.

"You built up," says Polyp-ella. "But the reef grows wide first. Low and snug. Like a hug." She waves her arms. "And those broken bits? They are not rubbish. A piece of coral can grow again, if you tuck it into a crack where it fits just right. Snug as a tooth in a gum. Then it holds on. Then it builds."

Kit looks at the broken pieces. Kit looks at the cracks in the old reef.

"So we start low," says Kit slowly. "And we click the pieces into the cracks."

"Click," says Polyp-ella, and her little arms snap together.

Pippin's eyes go round. "Kit," he whispers. "What did you just find out there? Because I think it changes everything."

s4a.text:
The sun is high. The water is warm and bright. Kit and Pippin work low and slow. They tuck the broken pieces into the cracks. Click. Click. The Click-Clack Castle grows wide, like a hug. 

Then, a shadow. A big, grumpy shadow. It is Grouper Grumps. He is huge and brown and frowning. He stops right next to them. He opens his mouth wide. 

"Do not mind him," whispers Pippin. "He is at the cleaning station."

Tiny cleaner wrasses dart out. They swim right into Grouper Grumps' mouth. They pick and clean. Grouper Grumps stays very still. His big body blocks the pushing water. It makes a calm, quiet pocket. 

"Quick," says Kit. "While he is still."

Kit pushes the last piece into the crack. Click. It fits perfectly. The castle is done. It is low and wide and strong. 

Then, something wonderful. Tiny pink arms peek out of the new cracks. The polyps! They wave their little tentacles in the sunlight. They look like tiny flowers opening. 

"They are moving in," says Pippin. His beak goes click-clack. "They like it."

Grouper Grumps closes his mouth. The cleaner wrasses swim away. He looks at the new castle. He gives a slow, grumpy nod. Then he swims off. 

Kit smiles. The reef feels right. The sun shines down. The polyps wave. The Click-Clack Castle is home.

s4b.text:
The sun goes down. The lagoon turns dark blue. Then black. Kit waits. Pippin floats nearby. The water is quiet. Too quiet. 

Then, the moon rises. It is round and white. It fits into the night sky like a coin in a slot. Click. 

The reef wakes up. Tiny lights glow. The coral polyps stretch out their arms. They reach for tiny bits of food floating by. They look like a garden of stars. 

"The night shift," whispers Pippin. 

Something moves. An octopus slides out of a crack. She is soft and grey. She changes color to match the sand. She wraps one arm around the castle. She holds it steady. 

"Thank you," whispers Kit. 

The octopus winks. 

Kit takes the last piece. It is smooth and heavy. Kit fits it into the top crack. Click. The sound echoes in the quiet dark. 

The polyps get to work. They wave their arms. They build. They are the real builders. 

Kit watches. The moon shines down. The octopus holds on. The Click-Clack Castle stands strong in the dark. 

"We did it," says Kit. 

"We did," says Pippin. "Now the reef can grow."

c1.question: "We've got a broken neighborhood and a lot of work to do, kid. Do we start by hunting for the strongest bones—the rocks and skeletons—or do we dive straight into my secret stash of reef cement?"

options.label: Hunt for foundation stones and coral bones
Gather the sand and biological glue

c2.question: "The wobble taught us to build low and slow. Now, do we finish this while the sun is high and the cleaning station is open for business, or do we wait for the moon when the real builders wake up?"

options.label: Build now in the daylight with the fish neighbors
Wait for the night shift and the hunting corals

s1.text:
I remember the evening Grandpa Zed spread yesterday's newspaper over the kitchen table, slapped it flat with both hands, and declared it an invention laboratory. "Tools out!" he announced, which meant one jam jar of buttons, a ball of string, three spoons, and the good scissors.

You were there because of the picture. Ms. Orbit had pinned a photograph of Saturn to the classroom wall, and you had stared at it through the school telescope night until your eye ached. The rings were not one solid band, like a plate around a ball. They were millions of pieces of ring ice, each one glittering, each one travelling its own orbit, side by side, never crashing. The photograph was stuck to our fridge with a banana magnet, and you looked at it every time you got the juice.

"I want to build that," you said. "The real way. Not a solid ring."

Grandpa Zed unclipped his Wobble-Whistle from his shirt pocket and gave it a test toot. It went wheeee-ooo-oop, a silly sliding note, like a kazoo falling downstairs. "The Wobble-Whistle only blows when something wobbles out of place," he said. "If it stays quiet, your machine is right." He set it on the newspaper like a tiny silver judge.

"Then let's begin," you said.

And that is when the trouble started, because nobody in the whole history of the kitchen table had ever made hundreds of tiny things stay side by side without sticking into one.

s2a.text:
"Dive!" you shout, and Grandpa Zed flings open the craft drawers so fast that a spool of thread bounces off the table.

Out come the silver sequins. Out come the tiny white beads. Out comes the glitter, which Grandpa Zed holds at arm's length like a jar of jam that might explode. "Ring ice," he says, "comes in sizes."

So you sort. Sequins into the bowl marked sand-size. Beads into pebble-size. And into the bowl marked house-size go the big sparkly buttons, because some pieces of Saturn's rings really are as big as houses. Your fingers go silvery. Grandpa Zed's eyebrows go silvery. Nobody knows how.

Then he unrolls a clear plastic sheet, measures it twice with a string, and cuts a great ring shape. Snip. Wheeee-ooo-oop goes the Wobble-Whistle. Snip. Wheeee-ooo-oop. "It toots at my scissors," Grandpa Zed says, offended. "My scissors have never wobbled in their lives."

Last, you paint the foam ball, swirling gold and yellow until the clouds roll like stirred whipped cream.

You both stand back. Hundreds of pieces, all sorted. "Now," says Grandpa Zed slowly, "how do we keep each one on its own orbit?"

The Wobble-Whistle is quiet. Too quiet.

s2b.text:
"Slow and steady," you say, and somebody knocks at the door. It's Pip, come to help, already wearing a painting shirt.

So the two of you mix. Yellow and gold, gold and yellow, and Pip brushes the foam ball while you turn it, round and round, until the clouds roll and tumble like stirred whipped cream. "Saturn's clouds really do that," you tell Pip. "They swirl in bands, all the way around."

Then Grandpa Zed clears his throat and reads Ms. Orbit's note aloud. "Each piece of ring ice follows its own orbit," he reads, "like runners in separate lanes. Side by side. Never crashing."

"Lanes," says Pip. "We need lanes."

So before anyone touches glue, you rehearse. Grandpa Zed unrolls the string, and together you lay it in circles on the newspaper, one lane, two lanes, three, each with its own gap between. The Wobble-Whistle hums along like a tiny engine, pleased.

Then Pip sneezes. The strings slide. The lanes tangle into one fat band.

"That," says Grandpa Zed, pointing, "is exactly what Saturn never does."

You all stare at the tangle. The rehearsal has shown you the whole problem, right there on the table.

s3.text:
Back at the newspaper laboratory, Grandpa Zed leaned over your shoulder. "Well?" he said. "What did you find?"

You told him, and his eyebrows climbed so high they nearly left his face. "Then we build!" he declared.

You tipped the beads onto the plastic. Hundreds of tiny ring-ice pieces, glittering like sugar on a counter. You pressed them in place, quick-quick, before the glue dried.

But beads are beads. They rolled. They slid. They bumped into each other and clumped into one thick solid band, exactly like the plate-around-a-ball you had promised not to make.

Wheeee-ooo-ooo-oooop. The Wobble-Whistle blew its longest, silliest note yet, a kazoo tumbling down three flights of stairs.

"The judge has spoken," said Grandpa Zed gravely.

You looked at the photograph on the fridge, held up by its banana magnet. The real rings were not one band. They were spread out, with a dark empty lane right through the middle, a gap where nothing travelled at all.

"Spread them out," you said. "Each bead gets its own lane. And we leave the gap empty."

So Grandpa Zed laid down thin string lanes, and you pressed each bead into its own dab of glue, on its own orbit, side by side. Slow work. Good work.

The Wobble-Whistle stayed quiet.

And slowly, the ring stopped being a band and became a crowd of glittering travellers, each one moving along beside the others, never crashing.

s4a.text:
“A shepherd,” you say. And because every shepherd needs a name, you give it one: {moon_name}.

You press the tiny moon at the edge of the gap, and Grandpa Zed leans in close. “Out on the real Saturn,” he says softly, “a little moon does exactly this. Its quiet pull keeps the wide dark lane swept clear, like a shepherd walking beside the flock.”

You hang the model from the lamp cord. Grandpa Zed gives it one gentle spin.

{ring_piece_sound}.

The ring ice glides, each piece on its own orbit, side by side, never crashing, and the dark gap runs clean through the middle with {moon_name} keeping watch. The Wobble-Whistle does not make a peep.

Outside the window, fireflies are blinking in the garden. “Look,” you whisper. “Ring ice.”

Grandpa Zed smiles and drops one silver sequin into your pocket, a small spare traveller to keep.

And that is why, even now, whenever something I build wobbles before it works, I still hear that Wobble-Whistle, sliding downstairs, telling me to spread things out and try again.

s4b.text:
“A geyser moon,” you say. “Like Enceladus.”

You paint the little moon white as bath snow, and Grandpa Zed holds the tiny brush steady while you dab three pale plumes at its south pole. “Real geysers,” he says, “spray water ice straight into space. Some of it may even feed a ring.”

“So the ring ice and the geyser ice could be cousins,” you say.

“Family,” says Grandpa Zed, and hangs the model from the lamp cord. One gentle spin.

{ring_piece_sound}.

The pieces shimmer side by side, each on its own orbit, never crashing, the gap running clear and dark. The Wobble-Whistle stays quiet a long moment, then toots one proud note, rising this time, ooo-oop-wheeee, a kazoo bounding up the stairs.

“The judge approves,” you say.

Pip dips the smallest brush and signs the golden clouds with one tiny swirl.

I kept one bead from that night. It sits on my windowsill still, and when the morning light comes through, it glitters like a small piece of Saturn that decided to stay.

c1.question: "Inventors!" Grandpa Zed booms, twirling the Wobble-Whistle. "Do we dive straight into the craft drawers and gather our ring ice, or do we paint and plan our orbits first, nice and slow?"

options.label: Raid the craft drawers and sort the ring ice pieces
Paint the golden clouds and rehearse the orbit lanes with string

c2.question: Pip lifts the tiny unpainted moon and grins. "Our model needs one last traveler. Should this little moon be a shepherd who guards the gap, or a geyser moon who sprays ice fountains into space?"

options.label: Make it a shepherd moon whose pull keeps the gap clear
Make it a geyser moon like Enceladus, spraying ice fountains

moon_name.role: The tiny shepherd moon added to the model

ring_piece_sound.role: The sound the model makes when it spins correctly

s1.text:
Our invention shed stands at the bottom of the garden, and the best thing in it is {robot_name}, who we built ourselves out of tins and springs.
{robot_name} has one job. Every morning his arm reaches down, takes a sock off the floor, and drops it in the basket. Plop. Plop. Plop.
That is the morning we like.
This morning: whir, clunk, fling!
A sock goes past our ear like popcorn out of a pan with the lid off. The next one lands on the ceiling fan and rides round and round up there like a stripy flag. The third one comes down on our jam sandwich.
"Sorry," says {robot_name}. "Sorry. Sorry."
He is not doing it on purpose. His arm flings when it should place.
Whir, clunk, fling!
Down come our goggles, because inventors do not stand about while socks are in the air. We drag the toolbox over and open the squeaky lid. Bolts. Springs. Rubber bands.
Two ideas turn up at once, and both of them are excellent.

s2a.text:
"Springs!" we say.
Out comes the biggest spring in the shed. We bolt it to an old umbrella and wire a colander on top, upside down, to hold whatever lands in it. Three wobbly legs. One winder.
Ta-da. The springy catcher, standing guard beside the sock basket.
We wind it up and step back. {robot_name} whirs.
Clunk, fling! Boing! The catcher jumps and grabs the sock right out of the air.
"Caught it!" we shout.
Then the spring boings again. The sock shoots straight back out, off the wall, off the lamp, and lands on {robot_name}'s head.
Boing. Boing. Sock ping-pong.
Our catcher catches everything and lets go of nothing.
We laugh so hard our goggles slide off.
Then we listen, because every single fling sounds exactly the same. Whir, clunk, fling. Whir, clunk, fling. The same clunk, the same wobble, the same too-high throw.
"That clunk," we say. "That clunk is in your elbow."
We write CLUNK on the shed wall in chalk letters as big as our hands.

s2b.text:
"Funnel!" we say.
Out comes the old paddling pool. We roll a cardboard tube as tall as we are, tape the pool on top, and lean it all over the sock basket. It stands there like an ice cream cone built for a giant.
We fold our arms and wait. {robot_name} whirs.
Clunk, fling! The sock sails up and straight over the top of our funnel. It lands on the shed roof.
Clunk, fling! Over the funnel, onto the roof, next to the first one.
By the time the basket should be full, the roof is growing socks.
So we climb into the pool ourselves and slide down the tube, because somebody ought to get some use out of it. Wheee.
Then we sit still and listen, because every single fling sounds exactly the same. Whir, clunk, fling. Whir, clunk, fling. The same clunk, the same wobble, the same too-high throw.
"That clunk," we say. "That clunk is in your elbow."
We write CLUNK on the shed wall in chalk letters as big as our hands.

s3.text:
Back to the workbench.
Our {first_gadget} did not fix the flinging, and we would build it again tomorrow, because it handed us the clue. A machine does everything the same way every time. That is why one clunk was enough.
{robot_name} comes over and lays his arm on the bench like somebody at the doctor.
"Switch first," he says, and clicks his own switch off, the way he always does before anybody opens a door in him. His fans wind down to nothing. Now the gears will hold still while we look.
We take the smallest screwdriver, open the little door on his elbow, and shine the flashlight in.
Two gears sit in there with their teeth laced together, like two hands with the fingers laced. And jammed between the teeth is one small metal bolt.
"Bolt," says {robot_name}. "In my elbow."
It must have rolled in on tidy-up day. Round come the gears, bump goes the bolt, clunk goes the elbow, and up flies the sock.
We jump up and do a victory wiggle.
Then we stop. That bolt is deep in there, and our smallest finger is far too fat.

s4a.text:
"Magnet," we say. "Metal wants metal, and a magnet has no fingers."
We tie the round red magnet from the shed fridge onto a string, and the string onto our bendy fishing rod. The bolt-fisher. Everything needs a name.
Switch off, fans quiet. {robot_name} holds stiller than he has ever held anything.
We hold the string and let the magnet down through the little elbow door. Down. Down.
Click.
The bolt jumps up onto the magnet like a letter finding the fridge door. We wind the string round our hand and lift it out slowly, and there it is, riding home on the end.
"Got you," we say.
We close the little door and click his switch back on. His gears turn. Whirrr. Not one clunk anywhere in him.
Now the big test. We put one sock on the floor. {robot_name} rolls over, reaches down, and puts it in the basket.
Whir. Plop.
We take ten more socks, and he plops all ten.
Then we put the bolt on his front, like a medal.
"Mine," says {robot_name}, who is extremely pleased with himself.

s4b.text:
"Wobble," we say. "Shake it out of him."
We stand our drum on the workbench and strap the eggbeater to it with three rubber bands. Turn the handle, and the drum shivers like jelly on a spoon. Perfect.
We lift {robot_name} up on top of the drum, switch off and fans quiet.
"Ready?" we ask.
"Ready," says {robot_name}.
Crank, crank, crank! The drum wobbles, and {robot_name} wobbles with it. The chalk hops off the shelf, and our own teeth wobble a bit as well.
We watch the little elbow door. Nothing yet. We crank a smidge faster.
Wobble, wibble, wobble. Tink!
Out hops the bolt, and it rolls off down the workbench, over the end, and lands in our two cupped hands.
"Caught it," we say.
We click his switch back on. The gears turn. Whirrr. Not one clunk anywhere in him.
Now the big test. We put one sock on the floor. {robot_name} rolls over, reaches down, and puts it in the basket.
Whir. Plop.
Ten more socks, and he plops all ten.
The bolt goes in our pocket. Tomorrow we are building something out of it.

c1.question: {robot_name} rolls to the toolbox and holds up the biggest spring in one hand and the old paddling pool in the other. "Springs," he says. "Or funnel. You pick."

options.label: Build a springy catcher
Build a giant funnel

c2.question: {robot_name} clicks his own switch on again for a moment. "I am full of metal," he says. "And I am extremely good at wobbling. Magnet, or wobble? You pick."

options.label: Fish the bolt out with a magnet on a string
Shake the bolt out with a great wobble machine

robot_name.role: the tidy-up robot we built and are fixing

first_gadget.role: the contraption we built for our first fix attempt

stories.title: The Great Space Station Sock Chase

s1.text:
We are the newest crew on the space station, and today we get our first real job. Yesterday we were still in the underwater training pool, where Coach Dex taught us to tighten bolts while floating upside down. "Slow hands," Coach Dex burbled through the water. "Space likes slow hands."

Now Commander Rosa floats beside us in the kitchen corner, with her boots hooked under a rail so she does not drift away. "Crew," she says, "unpack the kitchen. Make it ours."

We unzip the lunch pouch. We are careful. We are so careful.

But out pops a pea.

It does not fall. Down here, nothing falls. The pea just floats, slow and green and serious, right past Commander Rosa's ear.

"Oh," says Commander Rosa.

The pea bumps the window and turns, like a tiny green moon that forgot where moons go.

Then the speaker crackles. "Station, this is mission control." It is Flight Director Bea, and we can hear her smile. "You have a visitor up there."

Commander Rosa looks at us. We look at the pea. The pea looks at nobody, because it is a pea.

"Crew," says Commander Rosa, "what do we call him?"

s2a.text:
"Chase it!" we shout, because we cannot help it.

The pea bobs past the sleeping bags, which are stuck to the ceiling like bats in pyjamas. We push off after it.

Here is the secret nobody told us: there is no up and no down here. The ceiling is a floor if you want it to be. We bounce. We tumble. We bump the wall with our knees and laugh.

"Wait," says Commander Rosa, unhooking her boots. "New game. Catch General Pea without touching any wall."

We reach. The pea drifts. We stretch out one long arm, and the pea turns, slow and green and serious, just past our fingertips.

"He is winning," says Commander Rosa, bumping the ceiling with her head. "He has trained for this."

The speaker crackles. "Station, how is the visitor?" asks Flight Director Bea.

"Undefeated," says Commander Rosa. "Mission control, why does juice climb straws?"

"Ask Coach Dex," says Bea. "And crew? He says: slow hands."

Slow hands. We stop reaching. We wait. The pea floats closer, closer —

and bumps our open palm like it meant to all along.

"Gotcha," we whisper.

"Now," says Commander Rosa, grinning, "who wants to let him go again?"

s2b.text:
"Let him go," we say. "He has places to be."

General Pea drifts toward the window, slow and green and serious, like a tiny moon on important business.

The speaker crackles. "Station, this is mission control." It is Coach Dex this time, and we can hear the training pool in his voice. "If you want a real game, start bigger. One sock. Slow hands."

One sock. We toss it. It turns over and over like a sleepy fish, and Commander Rosa catches it against her chest.

"Too easy," she says. "Next."

A shoe. Then two socks. Then — somebody shouts it — the commander's lunchbox.

"My lunchbox," says Commander Rosa, delighted. "Fine. But if we lose it, we eat toothpaste for dinner."

The lunchbox sails. Three of us bounce off the walls to intercept it, and Commander Rosa hooks her boots under the rail and leans out like a goalkeeper.

"Mine!" we shout.

"Mine!" she shouts back.

The lunchbox spins past us all, heading for the kitchen wall — the Velcro wall, where everything sticks to everything and spoons go to be lost forever.

"Oh no," says Commander Rosa. "My pudding is in there."

s3.text:
Back in the kitchen corner, the pea is still floating, slow and green and serious. But now it has company. A wobbly ball of orange juice is drifting right beside it, and both of them are heading for the control panel.

"Oh no," says Commander Rosa. "My lunchbox!"

But it is too late. The lunchbox bumps a switch. The juice ball bumps another. And suddenly the whole station is playing music — loud, bouncy, terrible music.

"My playlist!" says Commander Rosa. "Isn't it wonderful?"

It is not wonderful. But Coach Dex's voice crackles over the speaker. "Crew, time for your two hours of space exercise!"

"Can we exercise to the music?" we ask.

"Slow hands," says Coach Dex, "but fast feet!"

So we dance. We bounce off the walls. We spin like slow tops. The pea bobs past us, and we could swear it is dancing too.

Then the Velcro chaos begins. The checklist sticks to the sock. The sock sticks to Commander Rosa. And Commander Rosa sticks to the wall.

"Crew," she says, wiggling one boot, "I appear to be stuck."

The music plays on. The pea floats by, looking very pleased with itself.

s4a.text:
"A chain!" says Commander Rosa. "Pass me down, one hand at a time."

So we build a chain of us. I grab the rail. You grab my ankle. The next hand grabs yours. We stretch down the module, wobbling like a slow banner, and the last hand grabs Commander Rosa's boot.

"Pull!" we shout.

We pass her along, hand over hand, and every small handhold matters. My job is just to hold on. But my holding holds you, and your holding holds her. Rip! The Velcro lets go, and the whole chain sproings into a giggling knot.

"Crew," says Commander Rosa, peeling a sock off her shoulder, "that is exactly how a crew works."

Then she goes quiet. "Look."

Outside the window, the Earth is sliding into its ninth sunrise of the day. And there hangs the Moon, close and bright and round.

"Some crews are training right now," she says softly, "to walk on that."

We press our noses to the glass. Behind us, the pea bumps gently against the window, turning slow and green and serious.

"He wants to be a moon too," we say.

So we tuck him into a pouch, safe and snug, our very own tiny green moon to take home.

"Slow hands," says Commander Rosa, smiling. "Good work, crew."

s4b.text:
"A race!" says Commander Rosa, wiggling her stuck boot. "Far end of the station. No touching anything. And the winner is whoever crashes the softest."

"You're stuck," we point out.

"Then you'd better crash into me very, very softly."

We push off. We float. No hands, no feet, just us drifting down the whole long module like slow dandelion fluff. The terrible music plays. The pea bobs alongside us, racing too, in its solemn pea way.

"Don't touch the walls!" calls Commander Rosa.

Too late. You bonk a rail. I spin like a top. We are not winning on style.

But ahead of us, the sleeping bags wait, fat and puffy and strapped to the wall right beside the commander. We aim for the softest one. We tuck. We land.

Floof.

It is the softest crash in the history of crashing. The whole wall of sleeping bags puffs out, and the Velcro lets go with a happy rip, and Commander Rosa tumbles into the pile with us, laughing so hard she can't talk.

The speaker crackles. "Station, this is mission control." Flight Director Bea is laughing too. "We've been watching. You are officially the silliest crew in orbit."

We unstrap a Moon dust sticker from the care package and press it on our sleeve. And past the window, slow and green and serious, General Pea sails on, orbiting his station, keeping an eye on his crew.

c1.question: "Do we chase that runaway pea right now, or do we start the game of catch with something bigger?"

options.label: Chase the pea through the station
Start with a sock and escalate

c2.question: "Do we build a human chain to pass me down, or do we race to see who can float the farthest without touching anything?"

options.label: Build a human chain to free the commander
Race to float without touching anything

s1.text: Maya is eating {breakfast_food} at the kitchen table, and I am sitting right beside her, because that is where I always sit when something smells this good. Sunlight is pouring through the window, all over the table, all over the plate. {stuffed_owl} the stuffed owl is on the windowsill, watching us with his big round eyes, the way he does every morning. "Morning, {stuffed_owl}," Maya says, with her mouth full. The tablet rings. Brrring! Brrring! It is {grandmother_name}, calling from Japan, and Maya answers fast, because talking to {grandmother_name} while eating {breakfast_food} is the best kind of breakfast. "Good morning!" we shout together. But on the screen, {grandmother_name} is not eating breakfast. She is in her pajamas. She is brushing her teeth. Behind her, the window is dark. "Good night," she says, with toothpaste foam on her lip. Maya stops chewing. I stop too. We look at our sunny window. We look at her dark one. "Wait," Maya says slowly. "How is it bedtime THERE when it is breakfast HERE?" {stuffed_owl} says nothing. He just stares, like he knows something we do not.

s2a.text: "The globe!" Maya shouts. She grabs it off the shelf and thumps it onto the table, right between the {breakfast_food} and the syrup. "And Dad's flashlight," I say, already pulling open the drawer. We click it on. The beam hits the globe, and half of it lights up bright as our window. The other half stays dark. "Look at that line," Maya whispers. We lean in close. There it is, right down the middle, where the bright stops and the dark begins. Not a straight line, but a soft, fuzzy edge. "Now spin it," I say. Maya turns the globe slowly, slowly. The line does not move. But the countries do. We watch Japan slide out of the light and into the shadow. We watch our own town come around into the sun. "One side is always lit," Maya breathes. "And one side is always dark. And the spin carries us from one to the other." {stuffed_owl} stares from the windowsill. He knew all along.

s2b.text: "The map," Maya says. "Dad, show us the time zone map." Dad pulls out his phone and taps the screen. The world appears, covered in stripes, twenty four of them, like the slices of an orange. "Each slice is one hour," Dad says. We find our slice, right where we live. Then we count over to Japan. Seven slices away. "So when the sun is here," Maya says, pointing at our stripe, "it is already night there?" "Watch," Dad says. He spins the map with his finger. The stripes slide past, west to east. We see our slice move into the light. We see Japan's slice move into the dark. "The Earth spins under the sun," Dad says. "Each time zone gets its turn in the light." Maya looks at the phone, then at the window. "So {grandmother_name} is just waiting for her turn?" "Exactly," Dad says. {stuffed_owl} blinks, slow and wise.

s3.text: Maya looks at me, and her eyes go wide, the way they do when a puzzle piece clicks into place. "So that is it," she says slowly. "The Earth is spinning. Like a giant top, but slower. One whole turn takes a whole day." "Rotation," I say, because it is a good word, round and rolling in my mouth. "And that is why the Sun looks like it is moving across the sky. It is not moving. We are." On the screen, {grandmother_name} nods, toothpaste foam still on her lip. "So right now," Maya says, "we are on the sunny side, and you are on the dark side." "Two hemispheres," {grandmother_name} says. "Half the world is having breakfast. The other half is brushing its teeth." Maya giggles. "And the line between them is always moving, isn't it? Creeping across the Earth, bringing morning to some people and bedtime to others." "Like a wave," I say, "but made of light." {stuffed_owl} stares at us from the windowsill, and I could swear he looks pleased. "But wait," Maya says, and her forehead wrinkles. "If the Earth is spinning that fast, why don't we feel it? Why don't we fall off?"

s4a.text: "Let's show her," Maya says, and she is already off her chair, pulling the globe from the shelf. It is heavy and round and cool in our hands. We hold it up to the tablet camera, and Maya gives it a slow spin. "See?" she says. "Here is Japan, turning toward the dark. And here we are, turning toward the light." {grandmother_name} leans close to her screen, her eyes wide. "I see it!" she says. "I am spinning right into bedtime!" We put {stuffed_owl} on the windowsill, right where the sun hits, so he can watch the night side for us. "He will keep an eye on the dark half," Maya says. {grandmother_name} laughs, a warm, sleepy sound. "Then I will dream of you," she says, "spinning toward tomorrow." We finish the last bites of {breakfast_food}, and the syrup is sweet, and the day is ours. The Earth will keep turning. It always does. And tonight, when it is our turn for dark, {stuffed_owl} will be awake, watching the light creep toward someone else's morning.

s4b.text: "Let's draw it," Maya says, and she grabs the big pad of paper and the fat markers. We draw the Earth, a great blue circle, and right down the middle we draw the line. On one side we write MORNING, and on the other side we write NIGHT. We hold it up to the camera. "This is us," Maya says, pointing. "And this is you." {grandmother_name} claps her hands. "That is exactly right!" she says. "You are in the light, and I am in the dark." "When the Sun comes up here tomorrow," Maya says, "we will wave at it for you." "And when the Moon comes out here tonight," {grandmother_name} says, "I will wave at it for you." We put {stuffed_owl} right on top of the globe, on the dark half, a tiny guardian of the night. He looks very serious. He looks very important. We are all spinning together, under the same sky, and somehow that makes the kitchen feel bigger, and cozier, and full of light.

c1.question: "Should we spin the globe to see the light move, or should we check the map on Dad's phone to see the time zones?"

options.label: Use the globe and flashlight to recreate day and night
Look at the time zone map on the phone

c2.question: "Should we show Grandmother how the Earth spins using our globe, or should we draw her a picture of the day and night line?"

options.label: Demonstrate with the globe and flashlight
Create a drawing to hold up to the camera

stuffed_owl.role: The cozy companion on the windowsill

breakfast_food.role: What Maya is eating when the mystery begins

s1.text:
Maya's boots squelched in the mud. Biscuit's nose was already down, sniffing the shallow pond behind Grandpa Joe's garden, his tail going thump-thump-thump against her leg.

"Biscuit, wait," Maya said, but Biscuit did not wait. Biscuit never waited.

Grandpa Joe pointed with his stick. "Look there. In that puddle."

Maya crouched low. Floating in the brown water was a cluster of clear jelly beads, like someone had spilled a jar of tiny glass marbles. Each bead had a black dot inside. And each dot was wiggling.

Wiggle. Wiggle.

"Grandpa," Maya whispered. "They're moving."

"They are," said Grandpa Joe.

Biscuit shoved his wet nose right up to the water's edge. Sniff. Sniff. He sneezed, and the beads bobbed.

Maya pulled out her notebook. "What are they?"

"That," said Grandpa Joe, "is a very good question."

The dots kept wiggling. Wiggle. Wiggle. Like they had somewhere to be.

s2a.text:
We waited. And we waited. Biscuit did not wait well. He flopped in the mud with a sigh that blew bubbles in the pond.

Then, one sunny morning, the jelly beads were gone. In their place swam a hundred tiny black tadpoles, wiggling like commas with somewhere to be. They darted and zipped, just like little fish.

"Grandpa Joe!" Maya shouted, because she could not help it. "They hatched!"

Grandpa Joe settled beside her, his knees going squelch in the mud. "Look at the sides of their heads," he said. "See those feathery bits?"

Maya leaned in close. Fluttering at the sides of each round head were tiny, frilly gills, soft as dandelion fluff.

"They breathe underwater," Grandpa Joe said, "just like fish do."

Biscuit could not stand it anymore. He lunged forward to lick the water. His tongue splashed. His nose went under. He snorted, shook his head, and sneezed so hard his ears flapped.

Achoo!

Ripples raced everywhere. The tadpoles scattered, then zipped right back, wiggling and fluttering.

"They still don't look like frogs," Maya said, writing in her notebook. "Not one bit."

"Not yet," said Grandpa Joe, and he stayed, watching them dart.

s2b.text:
Biscuit's nose hit the ground. His tail went thump-thump-thump. Then he took off into the damp woods behind the pond, crashing through the ferns.

"Biscuit, wait!" Maya called. But Biscuit never waited.

We followed him under the trees, where the ground was soft and dark and smelled like rain. Moss squished under our boots. Biscuit stopped beside a rotten log, barking at a puddle no bigger than a dinner plate.

"What is it, boy?" Maya asked.

Grandpa Joe caught up, puffing, and put a hand on Maya's shoulder. He looked into the puddle and smiled. "Well, look at that."

Swimming in the little puddle was a tadpole with two tiny legs sprouting near its tail. And the tail was much shorter than before.

"Where did its tail go?" Maya asked.

"The tail is shrinking away," said Grandpa Joe. "The body is using it up, like food, to grow those legs."

"It eats its own tail?" Maya said. "That's amazing. And a little bit yucky."

Biscuit barked at the log again, then turned around three times and nearly sat down right on the moss.

"Biscuit!" Maya laughed. "You'll squash it!"

The little tadpole kicked its new legs and hid under a leaf. Its tail kept shrinking. But how? And why?

s3.text: Biscuit froze. His ears shot straight up. Splash! Something small and green had landed right on a lily pad, wobbling like a bowl of jelly. It had legs, proper legs, but behind them hung a stubby little tail, wiggling like it hadn't got the message yet. "Grandpa," Maya breathed. "Is that a frog?" "Almost," said Grandpa Joe, his eyes crinkling. "That's a froglet. Right in the middle of metamorphosis. Its body is rebuilding itself, bit by bit." "Rebuilding?" Maya whispered. The froglet's skin gleamed, wet and shining, like it was wearing the pond itself. "It has to stay moist," Grandpa Joe said. "Frogs drink and breathe right through their skin." Biscuit leaned in for a sniff. The froglet leapt, a clumsy, splashing hop, and landed with a plop. Maya flipped open her notebook and drew a circle: egg, tadpole, froglet, frog, and back to eggs again. "So what happens next?" she asked. Grandpa Joe smiled. "Let's find out."

s4a.text:
Biscuit splashed straight into the sunny puddle, his tail going thump-thump-thump against the water. Maya crouched beside him, and there it was. Their frog. All grown up, no tail at all, sitting in the shallows with its green skin glistening like a wet sponge.

"It's not drinking," Maya whispered. "But it's sitting in water."

"Watch close," said Grandpa Joe.

The frog sat perfectly still. It did not sip. It did not gulp. It just soaked, right through its skin, like the puddle was seeping into its whole body.

"Frogs don't drink with their mouths," Grandpa Joe said. "They soak up water through their moist skin. They breathe through it too."

Maya's eyes went wide. "Through their skin?"

"Every bit of it," said Grandpa Joe.

Biscuit leaned in for one last sniff. The frog gave a small, satisfied blink. They watched it blink. It watched them back.

"We should name it," Maya said. "Something that fits."

Grandpa Joe smiled. "What do you think?"

Maya looked at the frog, sitting proud in its puddle, skin shining like it had swallowed the whole pond. "{guide_frog_name}," she said.

At the puddle's edge, something smooth caught her eye. {treasure_name}, cool and speckled, waiting to be picked up. Maya slipped it into her pocket, where it sat warm and small, like a secret.

Grandpa Joe's hand rested on her shoulder. Biscuit's tail went soft.

"Come on, Biscuit," she said. "Let's go home."

s4b.text:
Biscuit's nose went straight to the ground, sniffing hard, his tail going thump-thump-thump against Maya's leg. He stopped at a fallen log and barked once, sharp and sure.

Maya knelt down. Tucked into a cool, muddy crack beneath the log was their frog. Fully grown now, no tail at all, its skin shining wet even in the shade.

"Why is it hiding?" Maya whispered. "The sun is out. It could be hopping anywhere."

"Feel the air," said Grandpa Joe.

Maya held out her hand. The air was warm and dry. But under the log, the mud was cool and damp, like a wet flannel pressed to the earth.

"That frog has to stay moist," Grandpa Joe said. "It breathes and drinks right through its skin. If it dries out, it cannot breathe properly. So it finds the cool, wet places and waits."

"Like us finding shade on a hot day," Maya said.

"Exactly like that," said Grandpa Joe.

Biscuit wagged his tail so hard his whole back end wobbled. The frog blinked at them from its muddy crack, calm as anything. They watched it blink. It watched them back.

"We should name it," Maya said. She looked at the frog, tucked safe in its cool, dark pocket of earth. "{guide_frog_name}."

Beside the log, half-buried in the mud, something smooth and cool caught her fingers. {treasure_name}. Maya slipped it into her pocket, where it sat small and certain, like a promise kept.

Grandpa Joe's hand rested on her shoulder. Biscuit's tail went soft.

"Come on, Biscuit," she said. "Let's go home."

c1.question: "Should we wait by the pond to see what hatches, or follow Biscuit's nose into the damp woods to find a bigger clue?"

options.label: Stay by the pond to watch the jelly beads hatch
Follow Biscuit into the damp forest floor

c2.question: "Do we look for our froglet in the sunny puddle, or check the cool mud under the log?"

options.label: Search the sunny puddle where the frog sits out in the open
Peek under the log into the cool, muddy crack

guide_frog_name.role: the small green tree frog who appears at each stage

treasure_name.role: the small smooth stone or shell found at the pond's edge

s1.text:
When I was nine, I spent the last week of summer in Abuela Rosa's garden, and that is where this story begins, so that is where we will begin too. Imagine you are there with me, {child_name}, kneeling in the dirt beside the milkweed, with grass stains on your knees and the whole garden humming around you.

Abuela Rosa is on her knees too, because she says the best things in a garden happen down low. Her hat is too big. It slides over one eye every time she bends, and she bends a lot.

"Look," she whispers. "Under the leaf. Always under."

She turns a milkweed leaf over, gentle as turning a page, and there it is. A tiny egg, no bigger than the head of a pin, cream-colored, sitting all alone on the soft green underside.

"One egg," she says. "One butterfly. But not the one you think."

She taps the leaf with one brown finger. "The caterpillar inside this egg will hatch, and eat, and make a chrysalis like a little green lantern. And the butterfly that comes out will lay eggs of her own, far north of here. And those eggs will make butterflies, and those butterflies will make a butterfly who flies all the way to Mexico. A whole continent, {child_name}. Three generations to cross it."

"But you'll never see that one," I say.

"Never," says Abuela Rosa, and she smiles like that is the whole point. "I plant flowers for butterflies I will never meet. Somebody's great-grandchild has to eat on the road."

And she points to the wooden sign at the garden gate, painted by hand, a little crooked: Monarch Waystation.

s2a.text:
"We wait," you say, and Abuela Rosa grins like you have chosen the better treasure.

So we wait. Three days. Four. The chrysalis hangs under the leaf like a little green lantern, and every morning we kneel in the dirt and check it, and every morning it is just a lantern, until the fifth morning, when it is not.

The green has gone thin. Inside, something dark is moving.

"Now," whispers Abuela Rosa. "Watch now."

The case splits. A line of black appears, and then a leg, and then the whole butterfly comes sliding out, slow as honey off a spoon, and she is a mess. Her wings are crumpled, like a letter somebody forgot in a pocket and washed.

"Is she broken?" you ask.

"No," says Abuela Rosa. "She is new. Watch."

And the butterfly hangs there, and pumps. Her wings get bigger. Bigger. She is filling them up, like blowing up two orange balloons, and the crinkles smooth out as we watch.

"Inside that lantern," Abuela Rosa says, "the caterpillar turned to soup. Real soup. And the soup built this. Wings where legs used to be."

You look at the wet, trembling butterfly, and you think about soup, and you cannot quite believe it, except there she is.

But her wings are still soft. Still dripping. She hangs from her empty lantern and does not fly.

"Will she?" you whisper.

"She has to," says Abuela Rosa. "She has eggs to lay up north."

The butterfly hangs. The garden hums. We wait.

s2b.text:
"Follow her," you say, and Abuela Rosa nods like you have chosen the braver thing.

So when the butterfly drops off her leaf, we go. She does not soar. She wobbles, low over the grass, dipping like a paper plane that nobody folded quite right, and we follow on our knees at first, then crouching, then tiptoeing, and Abuela Rosa's hat slides over her eye and she does not even fix it.

"She has never flown before," Abuela Rosa whispers. "Imagine. Never once, and now this."

The butterfly bumps the air. She tilts. She catches herself, and lands on a zinnia, bright orange, the color of a pumpkin left in the sun.

"Watch her face," says Abuela Rosa.

The butterfly unrolls her tongue. It comes out long and thin and curled, like a garden hose uncoiling, and she dips it into the flower and drinks.

"Nectar," says Abuela Rosa. "Sugar water. That is her gasoline, {child_name}. Every flower is a gas station."

The butterfly drinks. Her wings open and close, open and close, slow, like she is practicing being a butterfly.

"This one will fly north," Abuela Rosa says. "Not far. Maybe to the next state. She will lay her eggs there, and her children will fly farther, and her grandchildren farther still, and her great-grandchildren will see Mexico."

You look at this wobbly, brand-new thing, tipping on a flower, and you try to picture her crossing a whole continent.

"She can't even fly straight," you say.

"Not yet," says Abuela Rosa. "But she knows the way. She was born knowing."

The butterfly lifts off. Wobbles. Goes.

s3.text:
Whatever you found there, hold on to it, because summer turned, the way it does, and the milkweed went gold at the edges. Our butterfly — strong now, bright as a lit window — lifted off Abuela Rosa's hat one morning and did not come back. But she did not fly alone. All across the sky, others were drifting south too, orange as marigolds, a whole river of wings going one way.

"Migration," said Abuela Rosa, shading her eyes. "Come on. I know where that river stops to drink."

It stopped at a rest stop in Kansas, of all places, where somebody had planted zinnias between the parking lot and the highway, and a crooked little sign said Monarch Waystation. The same promise. A thousand miles from her garden.

A woman with a clipboard knelt in the zinnias. "Tagger," Abuela Rosa whispered. "Watch."

The woman held a butterfly like it was made of breath. On its wing she pressed a sticker lighter than an eyelash. "This one is the supergeneration," she said. "Eight months alive. She'll fly where her great-grandparents flew, with a compass in her antennae that reads the sun. Want to hold her? One second. That's all."

One second. Wings tickling your palm like a tiny heartbeat. Then the woman nodded, and you opened your hands, and up she went — south, south, carrying your one second with her.

s4a.text:
"Up," you say, and up we go.

The butterfly finds the wind the way you find a warm spot in a swimming pool — by feel. It is called a thermal, an invisible elevator of rising air, and she steps into it like she has done it a hundred times, though she never has. Her great-grandmother did it. That is almost the same thing.

Round and round we spiral, and she does not flap once. She weighs less than a paperclip, {child_name}. The wind carries her like a dandelion seed with opinions.

And then the land unrolls below us like Abuela Rosa's map come alive. Farms in squares, green and gold. A silver river stitching through. Cities that glint and give off their own warmth, which the butterflies feel from a mile up. Highways with trucks crawling along them like beetles in no hurry.

We stay aloft the whole day. Fifty miles, and her wings barely move. She glides. She trusts the air she cannot see, and after a while, so do you.

"She never learned this," you say.

"No," says Abuela Rosa, far below and somehow beside us all the same. "Nobody taught her. The knowing came with the wings."

By evening the wind cools and lets us down gentle as an elevator reaching the ground floor, and there, ahead, blue against the sky: mountains. The last ridge before the forest. She rests on a thistle, sipping nectar, fueling up for morning.

You are lighter than you were this morning. Some of you is still up there, gliding.

s4b.text:
"The forest," you whisper, and we walk.

The last mile is uphill, into the oyamel forest, where the air turns cold and the mist hangs between the trees like breath. A guide named Elena meets us at the trailhead. She holds one finger to her lips.

"Listen first," she says. "Then look."

At first you hear nothing. Then — a sound like soft rain on a roof, except the sky is clear. Elena smiles. "Wings," she says. "Millions of them, opening at once to catch the sun."

And then you see. The branches are not branches. They are butterflies, clustered so thick the boughs bend under them, gray as bark with their wings closed. Then the sun touches them and the whole tree opens — orange, orange, orange — like someone struck a match inside the forest.

"Now," Elena says. "Your butterfly. The one with the tag. Among all of these."

Millions of wings. One sticker lighter than an eyelash.

You walk slow. You look the way Abuela Rosa taught you — under, always under. And there. On a low branch, third cluster from the trail, a fleck of white no bigger than a crumb.

"That's her," you breathe. "That's Zigzag."

Elena kneels beside you. "The great-grandchild," she says, "of a butterfly from a garden very far away."

You think of Abuela Rosa, kneeling in the milkweed, planting flowers for a butterfly she would never meet. You are meeting her now.

The forest rains softly around you. Wings. Just wings.

c1.question: "Do you want to wait and watch the chrysalis crack open, or follow her very first flight across the garden?"

options.label: Watch the chrysalis open
Follow the first flight

c2.question: "Do you want to soar with her on the wind, or walk quietly into the forest where she will land?"

options.label: Ride the thermals high above the land
Walk into the butterfly forest

s1.text: The summer I turned nine, the sky over Grandma Basil's village snowed grey. Not cold snow. Warm, soft, floaty snow that landed on your nose and tasted like nothing at all. Every grown-up in the village grumbled and swept their steps. But not Grandma Basil. I found her marching between her bean rows with her dented tin flask, the one she calls her expedition flask, like an explorer crossing a jungle. "Cocoa?" she said, and shoved a cup into my hands before I'd even said hello. And then I looked up. Properly up. The beans. Oh, the beans. They didn't grow like normal beans. They towered. They twisted up past the fence, past the apple tree, past the roof of her shed, thick as my arm and greener than green. Every garden in the village had beans. I'd seen them. They came up to your knee, maybe, on a good year. These came up to the sky. "Grandma," I said, slowly, "why is your garden so much taller than everybody else's?" Grandma Basil went very still. Then she crouched down beside me, scooped up a pinch of dark, crumbly earth, and held it up to the light like a jewel. "That," she whispered, "is exactly the right question." She tipped it into her pocket and clicked the flask shut like a detective closing a case. "Pip," she said, "this is now an official expedition. And that is evidence."

s2a.text:
"The evidence, Captain," I said. "We dig in."

"Excellent choice." Grandma Basil struck the flask against her knee like a gavel. "Interrogate the soil."

We knelt right down between the bean rows, and the earth smelled like rain and something darker. Something secret. I pushed my fingers in.

It was almost black. It crumbled soft as cake between my fingers, soft as the inside of a brownie, nothing like the pale dusty dirt at the schoolyard that poofs up and makes you sneeze. This stuff clung. This stuff held on like it had a job to do.

"Feel that," Grandma Basil said. "That is fertile ground. Richest dirt on the hillside. But why?" She tapped her chin. "Why here and not there?"

Then she marched me to the porch, where grey dust still sat on the railing in a thin line, like pepper nobody had swept. She dripped water on it from her flask cup. Tap. Tap. Tap.

The grey went dark. It slumped. It melted down into the crack between the boards like sugar melting into warm cocoa.

"Rain does that," she whispered. "Every shower. The grey falls, the rain taps it, and down it goes, into the ground, into the beans." She leaned so close her eyebrows nearly touched mine. "Something grey is disappearing into this earth, Pip. It falls. It vanishes. And the beans get taller."

I looked at my black-cake fingers. I looked at the railing. I wrote it in my notebook, in big letters: CLUE NUMBER ONE.

"Grandma," I said. "The garden is eating something."

She grinned like I'd just found buried treasure. "Now you're detecting."

s2b.text:
"Mr. Fen," I said. "The oldest witness on the hillside. We squeeze."

"Bold move, Captain." Grandma Basil saluted me with the flask. "Witnesses first. Evidence doesn't run away, but old men do take naps."

Old Mr. Fen sat on the next porch over, in a chair that creaked like a ship, and grey dust lay on his railings in soft drifts, like flour in a bakery nobody had tidied. He saw our notebooks and his eyes went bright.

"You're asking about the grey," he said. It wasn't a question.

"Please, Mr. Fen," I said. "Tell us everything."

He rocked. Creak. Creak. "I was about your size. Summer it was, middle of summer, and the sky snowed. Warm snow. Grey as porridge, soft as anything, falling and falling." He held his hands out, cupped, like he could still catch it. "And the sun, Pip, the sun hung up there at noon like a great glowing orange behind a bedsheet. All day. Weeks."

"Weeks," I breathed.

"Everybody swept their rooftops," he said. "Swept and grumbled, grumbled and swept. And the strangest thing." He leaned forward, and his voice dropped to a whisper, and Grandma Basil leaned in so far she nearly fell off the steps. "The next spring, everything grew like mad. The whole hillside. Green like you'd never seen."

I scribbled so fast my pencil squeaked. CLUE NUMBER ONE: the sky once snowed grey, warm, in summer, and it fell RIGHT HERE.

"Mr. Fen," I said slowly, "what was it?"

He smiled, gappy and mysterious. "That's for your expedition to find out."

Grandma Basil clicked her flask open and poured him cocoa, grave as a judge. "Witness rewarded," she said. But outside, the grey kept falling, and nobody had answered my question at all.

s3.text: "Well?" said Grandma Basil, scooping me up a fresh cocoa. "What did the expedition turn up?" I told her, and her eyes went round as dinner plates. "Then it's time," she said, "for the photograph." From her shed she pulled a frame wrapped in an old tea towel. Inside was her house, and behind it the mountain, wearing a huge grey plume on its head like a feather hat. Below it, the whole village sat dusted grey, every roof, every street, every hat. "It snowed grey here once before," she said. "Long before I was born. The grey came out of the mountain itself. And that funny orange sun you get on dusty days? That's the dust, scattering the light about." Before I could even whistle, somebody knocked. It was Dr. Loom, the soil scientist, with a backpack full of little jars that clinked when she walked. Grandma Basil nearly burst with pride. "Show her!" she said. I held out what I'd found, and Dr. Loom put one grey speck under her magnifying glass. "Look," she said. I looked. It wasn't a soft flake at all. It was a jagged little mountain of rock, sharp-edged and glittery, packed with minerals. "Mineral dust," said Dr. Loom, beaming. "Volcano dust. It lands, it breaks down over years and years, and it feeds the soil until the soil turns fertile. Rich enough to grow a forest." I looked at the dark earth under my shoes. I looked at the young woods behind the garden. I looked up at the beans, towering past the roof. "So the mountain," I said slowly, "fed your garden?" Grandma Basil clicked her flask shut like a detective closing a case. But she didn't smile. Not quite.

s4a.text: "The garden," I said. "Let's toast the garden." Grandma Basil's eyebrows shot up like two startled caterpillars. Then she did something I'd never seen her do. She sat down, right in the dirt, between the bean rows. "My own grandmother called it the ash year," she said quietly. "She swept that roof every single day, and she cried while she swept. All that grey, falling and falling, and nobody knew when it would stop." She twisted the lid off the expedition flask and poured three thimbles of cocoa, one for her, one for me, one for the earth. "But the next spring," she said, and her voice got big again, "she planted beans. And Pip. They were the best beans of her whole life. She said the mountain had paid its rent." I laughed, and then I looked up, way up, at the tallest bean of all, twisting past the shed roof like it was trying to tickle the sky. "That one needs a name," I said. "An explorer's name." Grandma Basil clapped dust off her hands. "Go on then." "Sir Climbsalot," I said. "Knight of the Ash Year." Grandma Basil toasted him with her thimble.
