Then Dr. Loom held out one of her little jars, and together we pressed in a pinch of the dark, crumbly soil, the secret slow kind, grey dust turned living. I screwed the lid on tight. That evening the sunset went blindingly bright, all orange and rose, because of the dust still floating high up. "Look there," said Grandma Basil, pointing at the first star. "Venus. She's wrapped in thick clouds too, but hers never rain ash." I walked home with the jar heavy in my pocket and grey dust on my boots, and every step felt like walking on a mountain's slow gift.

s4b.text: "The sky," I said. "Let's follow it off the planet." Dr. Loom made a noise like a kettle getting excited. That evening she spread her star chart across Grandma Basil's porch table and pinned down the corners with cocoa cups. "First stop," she said, and pulled out a photograph. It was a blotchy yellow ball with a great red spot on it. "Jupiter's moon. It's called Io. And right now, this very minute, it is erupting. Volcanoes shooting plumes straight up into space. Higher than anything on Earth." I stared at it. A whole moon, snowing grey onto itself, forever. "So our mountain," I said slowly, "is not the only one doing this?" "Doing what?" said Grandma Basil, eyes twinkling over her flask. "Feeding things," I said. "Dusting. Building. Planets do it. Moons do it." Dr. Loom tapped the chart. "Everywhere, Pip. Everywhere." Then Grandma Basil pointed up, past the porch roof, to where the sunset was blazing orange and rose. "And that sky up there? Same trick as the dusty days. Light getting scattered about." She pointed again, at the first bright star hanging in the glow. "That's Venus. She's wrapped in thick clouds of her own. But hers never rain ash." I looked at the orange sky, and the bright planet, and I thought about our grey summer, and it wasn't strange anymore. It was just something worlds do, the way gardens grow and beans climb. Before I left, Dr. Loom gave me a strip of tape, and I fixed one grey speck into my notebook, right on the first page. Underneath I wrote: tiny mountain, future garden. I carried it home under the bright scattered sky, and the whole way, the dust on my boots glittered.

c1.question: "Every expedition needs a first move, Captain. Do we dig into the evidence ourselves, or do we go squeeze a story out of old Mr. Fen?"

options.label: Examine the dark soil up close
Visit the neighbor who remembers

c2.question: "Mystery solved, but an explorer always picks the last trail. Do we stay and toast the garden that ate a volcano, or do we follow this thing clear off the planet?"

options.label: Celebrate in the garden and name the tallest bean
Look at the stars and other worlds with Dr. Loom

s1.text:
"Feel that," says Ranger Bea. She presses her flat palm to the boardwalk rail and waits.

Wren presses hers down too. The wood is warm. Not sun-warm, because the sun is barely up. Warm from underneath.

"Rock down there is still hot," Bea says. "Hot from deep inside the earth. Geothermal, we call it. The ground here sits right on top of it, like a pot on a stove that never quite turns off."

Wren looks out. Steam rises off every pool in the geyser basin, so the whole valley looks half-erased, like somebody took a soft eraser to the hills. Theo stands on his toes to see over the rail. Grandma Sela breathes in slow, the way she does at the bakery before the door even opens.

"Smells like boiled eggs," Theo says.

"That's the minerals talking," says Bea. "You'll get used to it."

They walk on, and the boardwalk ticks under their boots. Twenty years Bea has walked this path, and she still stops at every rail like it's the first time. Wren likes that about her.

"We're going to the little one," Grandma Sela says. "The one that blows when it feels like it. Nobody can tell you when. You just have to be there."

"Before the sun burns the steam off," Bea adds, "is when it's prettiest. So. No dawdling." She says it flat, without hurry, and somehow that makes Wren's feet go faster.

And low in Wren's belly, so quiet she doesn't notice it yet, something small begins to fizz. Like water at the bottom of a deep, twisty tube. Just starting to warm.

s2a.text:
"The warm patch," Wren says.

Bea leads them off the boardwalk, six steps, no more, to a bare circle of ground where the snow melted first. "Kneel if you like," she says. "Everybody does."

Wren kneels. The warmth comes up through her knees, through her palms, slow and steady, like bathwater that hasn't cooled yet. Steam curls around her ankles and wraps her shins, and for a second she is just a head and shoulders sitting in a cloud.

"Now," says Bea, unfolding a painted diagram from her jacket, "here's what's under you." Her finger traces a long crooked straw of cracks, down and down into dark rock. "Rain sinks in. Down there it sits on the hot stone and bubbles hotter and hotter, until it can't sit any longer. Then up it comes, all at once." She taps the bottom of the drawing. "A geyser is just water that got too warm to stay."

Wren traces the twisty tube with one finger. Down, around the bend, down again. The ground hums faintly under her shins, and something hums back, low in her belly. The fizz from this morning is climbing. It rises up her neck the way warmth rises through the planks, into her cheeks, hot as soup steam.

"Wren?" Theo holds out his notebook. "You said you'd write the times."

She looks at the page and the numbers swim. Her eyes sting, and she cannot say why.

"Give it a minute," says Grandma Sela, settling down beside her on the warm ground, close enough that their shoulders touch. "Some things come up on their own schedule."

Wren grips the edge of the notebook. The fizz is still rising.

s2b.text:
"The bench," Wren says. "I want to see the big one keep its promise."

They climb the boardwalk to where a crowd already waits, jackets zipped to chins, breath puffing white. Ranger Bea takes a stub of chalk and writes on a little board: next eruption, plus or minus ten minutes. She underlines it twice.

"Twenty years I've chalked that board," she says, "and it's been wrong maybe four times. That geyser keeps its word better than most people."

Grandma Sela finds them a spot on the bench. The slats are cold through Wren's jeans, a shock after the warm rail. Theo clicks his pen, ready. Everyone faces the pool, which sits quiet and round, steaming gently, like soup somebody set down to cool.

"Any minute," somebody whispers.

Wren waits. The pool gulps, once, a deep swallow from far underground, and settles back to quiet. And low in Wren's belly, the fizz from this morning swells. Her chest starts to rise and fall the way the pool does. In, out. In, out. Faster.

The pool gulps again. So does Wren.

She grips the bench slats with both hands. The chalk says ten minutes. Her own feeling has no chalkboard, no schedule, no twenty-year ranger to say when it will blow. It is coming anyway.

Grandma Sela says nothing at all. She just scoots closer along the bench, slow and quiet, until her shoulder is warm against Wren's arm, and stays there.

"Watch the water, love," she murmurs. "I'm right here."

The pool holds its breath. Wren holds hers too.

s3.text:
The round pool is quiet when they reach it. Quiet on top, anyway.

"This is {small_geyser_name}," says Ranger Bea. "It keeps its own schedule. What did you find out there?" She asks it like someone asking the weather, and Wren tells her, and Bea just nods, slow, like it all belongs to the same story.

Then the pool swells. The whole surface lifts, like something underneath taking a deep breath, and sloshes back down. Wren's chest heaves with it before she can stop it.

Grandma Sela notices first. She kneels down on the boardwalk, right there, and takes Wren's hand. "I stood here when I was nine," she says. "With a feeling exactly this size."

"Watch the water," Bea says quietly. "It breathes before it blows. Big pools, small pools — they all fill up, hold, and let go. You can breathe with it if you want. In. Out. It helps."

So they do. In, while the pool swells and gulps. Out, while it settles. In. Out. Theo breathes so loud his cheeks puff, and nobody minds.

The fizz low in Wren's belly rises, the way water rises in a deep, twisty tube, warming and warming until it has to come out.

The geyser bursts upward, taller than Bea, taller than the trees, a huge white cloud of steam that wraps warm around their legs and smells faintly of boiled eggs. And Wren's tears come out with the burst, all at once, exactly the same.

Afterward everything is soft and blurry and slow, the way a body feels after crying hard. Grandma Sela keeps hold of her hand. The steam drifts. The pool goes quiet again, settling, and somewhere below, the water begins, patiently, to warm once more.

s4a.text:
"Slow feet," says Wren, and Grandma Sela nods like that was the only answer.

They walk to where the terraces begin, and Wren stops. The ground here is made of steps. Wide, shallow, creamy-orange steps, each one holding a thin sheet of water that slides over its edge, slow as honey. 

"Mineral terraces," says Grandma Sela. "The water carries stone dissolved in it. When it cools, the stone stays. One crust at a time, over years and years."

Wren kneels and puts her fingers in the trickle. Warm. The edge of the step is rough under her thumb, like the rim of a pie crust.

Grandma Sela pulls a photo from her pocket, soft at the corners. A small girl stands on these same steps, squinting at the sun. "Me," she says. "Nine years old."

Wren looks from the photo to the stone. The steps in the picture are thinner. Lower. Since then, spill after spill, the water has built them up, slow and steady, into something new that was there all along.

"See?" says Grandma Sela. "It doesn't hurry. It just keeps coming up warm, and letting go, and what it leaves behind stays."

Wren's shoulders drop. She hadn't known they were up so high.

Grandma Sela presses something into her palm. A warm flat pebble, the color of the terrace steps. "It was warm from the water," she says. "Carry it home."

Wren closes her fingers around it. It fits exactly.

s4b.text:
"One more watch," says Wren, and Theo's notebook is already open.

They sit by {small_geyser_name} while the sky goes deep blue. The little geyser doesn't burst big again. It does smaller things. A gulp. A slosh. A sudden spit of steam, like it's clearing its throat.

"After-bursts," says Ranger Bea. "Write them down."

Theo writes the first one. Wren writes the second, in her own handwriting, pressing hard so the numbers stay. 6:14. 6:31. 6:49. She stares at the column. "There's a rhythm," she says slowly. "Not a clock rhythm. A breathing rhythm."

Bea sets up a small telescope on the boardwalk and aims it at a bright steady light. "Saturn," she says. "Rings and all. It has a frozen moon, and out of cracks in the ice, water shoots straight into space. A geyser basin, on another world."

Wren lies back on the warm planks. The heat from the ground comes up through the wood into her shoulder blades. She looks at the little ringed dot and thinks about ice holding water under pressure, somewhere out there, letting it go into the dark.

Even Saturn's moon fills up, holds, and lets go. Her feeling doesn't seem strange anymore. It seems like the size of things.

Grandma Sela kneels beside her and presses a warm flat pebble, the color of the terrace steps, into her palm. "From the warm ground," she says. "To take home."

Wren slips it into her pocket. Around her ankles, the last steam goes thin, and the fizz goes thin with it, and the night is wide and ordinary and good.

c1.question: "The basin's got two kinds of mornings, Wren. Do you want to stand on the warm patch where the snow melted first and feel what the ground's up to, or walk up to the bench and wait for the big one that keeps its promises?"

options.label: Stand on the warm ground and learn what the earth is doing underfoot
Go wait on the bench for the famous geyser that erupts on schedule

c2.question: "Now that the basin's had its say and you've had yours, what does this evening need? Slow feet and old stone with me at the terraces, or one more watch beside Little Gulp while the stars come out?"

options.label: Walk with Grandma Sela to the mineral terraces and see what slow water builds
Stay with Theo timing the small geyser until the telescope comes out

small_geyser_name.role: The small unpredictable geyser Wren's family waits beside

stories.title: The Howl That Pulled the Thread

s1.text:
"Listen," says Scout. "A wolf."

The radio receiver on her belt crackles, and a howl slides out of it — long, low, and silver, like someone pulling a thread of sound across the whole valley. Scout freezes with her hand on the volume knob, grinning the way she does when a muddy track turns out to be a treasure map.

"That's the Lamar pack," she says. "Fourteen of them, all told. Want to know what they did?"

We're standing in the ranger station at Yellowstone, and outside the window the Lamar Valley is doing what it does now — willow trees crowding the riverbanks, tall as houses, green as anything. Grandma June is beside us, holding a photograph so old the corners have gone soft.

"This is the same valley," she says. "Thirty years ago."

We look at the photo. Then out the window. Then back at the photo.

The valley in her picture is bald. The river is there, but the banks are bare dirt, chewed down to stubble, not a tree in sight. It looks like a place that had its hair cut too short and never grew it back.

"That's the same place?" we ask.

"Same bend in the river," says Grandma June. "Same mountains."

Scout taps the photo with one finger. "Same river, too. But it changed its mind about where to go."

We open {companion_name} — that's what we call our clue list, the notebook where we write down everything that doesn't add up. We write: *Grandma June's valley has no trees. Ours has thousands. Same place. Why?*

"Here's the thing," Scout says, and her voice drops like she's telling us a secret. "The wolves did it. Fourteen wolves, brought back in 1995. They changed the elk. The elk changed the willows. The willows changed the beavers. And the beavers changed the river."

We stare at her.

"That's a food web," she says. "Every living thing tugging on every other living thing. And the wolves? They're the keystone species — the one that holds the whole arch up. Pull them out, and everything falls. Put them back, and everything stands up again."

The howl comes again through the receiver. Closer this time.

"So," Scout says, picking up her binoculars. "Do you want to pull that thread with me? Because I know where it starts."

We look at Grandma June. She folds the photograph and puts it in our hands.

"Take it," she says. "You'll want to compare."

We tuck it into {companion_name}, right next to the question we can't stop thinking about.

How can fourteen wolves change the course of a river?

s2a.text:
"Tracks first," we say. "Let's pull."

Scout grins and shoulders her pack. "Good. Snow doesn't lie."

The Lamar Valley crunches under our boots. Grandma June waves us off from the station porch, and then it's just us and Scout and a white field stitched with elk tracks — hundreds of them, pressed thick as footprints on a city sidewalk, all hurrying the same direction.

"Look at this," Scout says, kneeling. "A crowd of elk came through here. But watch." She sweeps her arm along the riverbank. "Not one of them stopped to eat."

We look. The willows along the water are tall and shaggy, taller than Scout, taller than the station roof. But down at our feet, half-buried in snow, are stubs — old, chewed stumps no bigger than a knee.

"Before the wolves," Scout says, "elk lounged in this valley all day, every day. Safe, lazy, munching every green shoot before it could grow. Those stumps are willows that never got a chance." She taps the receiver on her belt, and it crackles — a howl, far off, threading through the cold air. "Then the wolves came home. And the valley stopped feeling safe."

"So the elk left?" we ask.

"Not left. Moved. Kept moving. Nervous elk don't stand around eating a riverbank bald." She points uphill, where the tracks climb toward the trees. "And the moment the elk stopped chewing — the willows stood up."

We crouch beside a stump and write in {companion_name}: *Elk ate the willows. Wolves scared the elk. Willows came back.*

It's a good clue. A real one. But we stare at it, and something tugs.

"Scout," we say slowly. "Willows are just trees. How do trees move a river?"

Scout's grin goes wide, like we've just found the X on her treasure map.

"Now you're asking the right question," she says. "And the answer has big flat tails."

s2b.text:
"Let's stay," we say. "We want the before."

Grandma June's whole face softens. "Then walk with me, thread-pullers."

The riverbank is ankle-deep in wildflowers, and the river talks the whole way — a low, busy mutter over the stones. Grandma June walks slow, one hand trailing through the grass like she's petting it.

"When I was eleven," she says, "this bend was silent. No willows for the wind to shush. No beavers slapping the water. And never, not once, a wolf howl. In seventy years, I never heard one." She stops and looks at the water. "The elk stood right there in the river all day, still as lawn ornaments. Nothing ever bothered them, so why would they move?"

"Lawn ornaments," we repeat, and write it in {companion_name}.

Back at the station, she pulls out Dr. Mara's photograph collection — a shoebox so full it won't close. We spread the pictures across the table, and we match them to the view out the window, one by one. Bare banks. Bare banks. Bare banks.

Then Grandma June turns the last bare one over.

"Look at the back," she says.

Pencil, faded: *1995.*

"That's the year the wolves came home," she says. "Fourteen of them, carried here in crates. After that, every picture in this box starts changing." She taps the photos into a line, like dominoes. "Wolves were endangered, you know. Gone from most of the country, nearly forever. Bringing them back was the hardest thing this park ever did."

We write it big across a fresh page: *1995. The year everything turned.*

But the thread tugs. We know when the river changed. We know who started it.

"Grandma June," we say. "A wolf is a meat-eater. A river is water. How does one reach the other?"

She smiles and closes the shoebox, gentle as a secret.

"That," she says, "is exactly what the beavers have been waiting to tell you."

s3.text:
Scout's truck rattles up the hillside track, and at the top, the whole valley opens below us like a map that somebody made real.

Dr. Mara is already there, kneeling on the grass with an actual map spread out and a rock holding each corner. "You found something," she says. It isn't a question. "What did you find?"

We tell her, and she listens the way grown-ups almost never do — all the way to the end, without once saying uh-huh. Then she taps the map. "Good. Because what you just found is one thread. I want to show you the whole rope."

She pulls out a notebook, older than {companion_name}, its pages soft as cloth. "Every year since 1995, I've counted beaver colonies in this valley." She opens it, and there they are: columns of years, columns of numbers. We run our finger down the page. One colony. Then two. Then five. Then nine. The numbers climb like stairs.

"The wolves came back in 1995," Dr. Mara says. "Watch what the beavers did after."

"They multiplied," we whisper.

"Now here's the part that bends people's brains." She picks up three flat stones and builds a little arch on the map, two standing, one across the top. Then she slides the top stone out. The whole thing collapses with a small, sad clatter.

"That top stone is the keystone. The wolves are a keystone species — pull them out, the arch falls. Put them back, everything stands." She rebuilds it. "The wolves chased the elk off the riverbanks. The willows grew back. And willows are beaver food, beaver houses, beaver everything. The wolves didn't just change the elk. They handed the valleys back to the willows, and the willows handed the rivers back to the beavers."

We look down at the living valley. From up here we can see it — the ponds strung along the river like beads on a string, each one still and dark, each one holding water back, slowing the river down, making it wander.

"The river changed its mind," we say, "because the beavers told it to."

"And the beavers could tell it," says Scout, "because the wolves told the elk." She grins. "That's a ripple effect. One splash, and the rings reach the far bank."

We write it all in {companion_name}, and the thread in our heads pulls tight: wolf, elk, willow, beaver, water. But down there, the ponds are shining. We haven't stood in one yet.

"Can we go down?" we ask.

Dr. Mara is already folding her map. "I thought you'd never ask."

s4a.text:
We wade down at dawn, and the mist is still curled on the water like a cat that isn't ready to move. Scout holds up one hand. We stop. We listen.

A frog plops. A duck mutters. Somewhere in the reeds, a muskrat is minding its own small business, and the whole pond is so still it seems to be holding its breath.

"Count," Scout whispers.

So we do. Frogs along the muddy edge, too many to finish. Ducks in the middle, folding themselves into the quiet. And under the willows, where the side-channel runs cool and dappled, trout hover in the shadow like silver thoughts. We peer past the dam at the sunny stretch beyond it. No trout there. Not one.

"Why do they hide under the willows?" we ask.

"Shade keeps the water cold," says Dr. Mara. "Cold water holds more air. The willows are doing that. The willows the elk stopped eating. Because of the wolves."

There it is. The whole thread, lying in the water in front of us.

Then the pond goes whap — a beaver's tail, slapped flat on the surface, and the beaver itself glides past with a willow branch in its mouth, dragging it home like a workman carrying a plank. It doesn't look at us. It has a river to slow down.

Grandma June laughs, very softly, into her sleeve.

We open {companion_name} and write the last line, the one the whole valley has been spelling for us: the wolves scared the elk, the trees grew, the beavers dammed, the water slowed — and the river healed. Underneath, because it still surprises us, we add {favorite_clue}.

Grandma June bends down and lifts a willow leaf off the water, wet and yellow as a little sun. She presses it flat between the pages.

"For the road home," she says.

The mist lifts. The pond answers with one more plop.

"Fourteen wolves," we whisper, closing the notebook. "And all of this."

s4b.text:
We climb back up to the lookout as the light goes gold, and Dr. Mara spreads the old map on the rock, weighting the corners with stones the way she did before. "Now," she says. "Look down. Then look at the map. Tell me what's wrong."

We look down. We look at the map. And the wrongness jumps out at us like a frog off a bank.

The map's river wanders all over the valley, looping and curling like a dropped piece of string. The living river below us runs steadier, held in place, its banks gripped by willow roots like fingers holding on.

"The map says it should wander more," we say slowly. "But it doesn't."

"The beaver ponds slow the water," says Dr. Mara. "Slow water drops its silt. The banks build up and hold. The willows grip them. The river settles." She taps the old loops on the map. "This river hadn't made up its mind. That one has."

And from up here, we can see the whole thing at once. The hills where the elk graze, warier now, keeping moving. The green willow crowd along the banks. The beaver ponds strung down the valley, each one catching the low sun and flashing it back at us, like the valley is signaling. One thread, pulled through the entire food web, and every knot in it visible from this one rock.

Scout's receiver crackles. We all go still.

A howl slides out of it — long, low, and silver — and this time another answers it, from the far side of the valley, and then a third, farther off, the sound threading back and forth across the dusk like someone stitching the whole valley shut for the night.

"That's them," Scout whispers. "The keystone species, saying goodnight."

We write the last line in {companion_name}: the wolves scared the elk, the trees grew, the beavers dammed, the water slowed — and the river changed its mind. Underneath, because it still surprises us, we add {favorite_clue}.

Then Scout opens her pack and takes out a rubber stamp from the ranger station — a wolf track, five toes and all — and presses it onto the page, firm and black.

"So you remember," she says, "who pulled the thread."

We close the notebook. The valley hums. And all the way down the hill, the howls keep stitching.

stories.title: The Humming Road to the Hive

s1.text:
When I was nine, my Grandma June kept bees in wooden hives at the edge of a wildflower meadow, and she knew every one of them by name.

"Now, {child_companion_name}," she said to me one early-summer morning, in her slow warm drawl. "You want to know where honey really begins? It doesn't begin in a jar. It begins right here."

She pointed one knobby finger at a single {favorite_flower}, bending in the breeze. The air around it was humming — not loud, just a low, contented hum, like the meadow was purring.

On the flower sat a bee. A fuzzy, stripey, busy little worker, and her whole back was dusted gold with pollen, as if she'd rolled in it on purpose.

"That one's Scout," said Grandma June. "She's been out since sunup. Watch her close, now."

I watched. Scout buried her head in the petals, and the gold dust puffed up, and some of it drifted down and settled on the flower like powdered sugar on a cake. That dust, Grandma said, is how a flower makes seeds — and Scout was carrying it from bloom to bloom all over the meadow. That's called pollinating, and bees do it for whole fields, whole orchards, without ever being asked.

"Here's the thing about Scout," Grandma June murmured, crouching down beside me so we were eye to eye with the bee. "She's headed home to the colony sooner or later. And if we're patient, and we're polite, and we don't go grabbing — she'll lead us the whole way. Flower to meadow to hive. The whole humming road."

Then Scout lifted off.

A bee is quick. Quicker than you'd think. She rose in a wobbly little spiral, gold dust trailing off her like a tiny comet, and hung in the air for one second — choosing.

"Easy," said Grandma June. "Watch where she lands."

s2a.text:
Scout dipped low, and we followed her into the meadow, where the clover grew thick as a carpet and the poppies nodded their red heads over it.

"Keep your feet soft," Grandma June murmured. "We're guests at her breakfast table."

We crouched beside a clover head, and Scout landed right on it. Then something wonderful happened. Out of her mouth came a long, thin tongue, like a tiny straw unrolling, and it reached down deep into the flower where the nectar hides. She drank, and drank, and while she drank, the yellow pollen stuck to her fuzzy body in thick golden dust.

Then she lifted, and the dust drifted, and some of it settled on the very next flower she touched.

"See that?" said Grandma June, her voice low and slow. "That's pollinating. Every flower Scout visits, she leaves a little gold behind. And that gold is how the flower makes seeds."

I looked at the trail of dust behind her, marking every stop like footprints. "How many flowers does she visit?"

"Hundreds," said Grandma June. "Every single day."

We followed. Clover, poppy, clover again. Scout worked them one by one, never hurrying, never skipping, and the gold trail grew longer behind her. The meadow widened around us, and the hum grew with it — not one bee now, but dozens, then hundreds, all working the same field, all dusted gold, all carrying the meadow's future on their backs.

"They're a team," I whispered.

"A colony," said Grandma June. "One family, one job."

Then Scout paused. Her pollen baskets — the little golden lumps on her back legs — were nearly full. She hung in the air, heavy with gold, and turned her head toward home.

s2b.text:
Scout rose, and we chased her up into the orchard, where the apple trees stood in long straight rows, every branch dressed in white and pink blossom.

The petals were falling. Slow, soft, drifting down like snow that had forgotten it was winter. One landed on my sleeve, and I held it carefully, like something precious.

"Listen," said Grandma June.

I listened. The whole orchard was humming — not one bee, but hundreds, working the blossoms from branch to branch. Standing in the middle of it, the trees seemed to hum like a struck tuning fork, a low steady music that you could feel in your chest.

Scout landed on a blossom near my shoulder, and Grandma June reached out one finger and lifted the branch gently, so we could see.

"Every apple you eat in autumn," she said, in her slow warm drawl, "begins right here. Right now. A bee like Scout carries pollen from flower to flower, and the flower swells, and the petals drop, and an apple grows where the blossom used to be."

I stared at the little white flower. "This becomes an apple?"

"This becomes an apple," said Grandma June. "No bees, no apples. No cherries. No strawberries. The bees feed the trees, and the trees feed us."

Scout buried her head in the blossom, and the gold dust puffed up, and some of it drifted down onto the petals like powdered sugar. She was dusted head to toe now, heavy with nectar, her pollen baskets fat and gold.

Then she lifted off, and flew straight — not wandering, not stopping — straight toward something we couldn't see.

Grandma June smiled. "She's headed home. And I know a shortcut."

s3.text:
Scout rose from where she'd been working, circled once overhead, and then flew a line so straight it looked drawn with a ruler. Home.

"Now we go see," said Grandma June, standing up slow, "what she tells the others." She'd already pulled on her white suit and veil, and she handed me a smaller one that smelled like sunshine and old cotton. "What did you find out there?" she asked, and I told her as we walked, and she nodded like it was the most important news she'd heard all week.

The hives stood in a row at the meadow's edge, white boxes humming like a whole city behind a wall. Grandma June lifted the lid off the nearest one, gentle as opening a picture book, and the world turned warm and dark and gold.

Comb. Everywhere. Walls of it, hanging in perfect rows, and on every wall — bees. Thousands and thousands of them, all sisters, all working. The sound rose up around us like a song with no words.

"Nearly every one of these is a girl," Grandma June murmured. "Each doing her own small job."

And then — a small striped shape tumbled in past my ear. Scout. She landed on the comb, and she began to dance.

Round and round in a figure eight, waggling her stripey behind with every step. The other bees crowded close, touching her with their feelers, reading her map.

"She's telling them," Grandma June whispered. "How far. Which way. Watch."

We watched. And one by one, then ten by ten, the sisters lifted off the comb and poured out into the sunlight, all flying the same dead-straight line Scout had flown. Out over the meadow. Exactly the way she'd come.

"Well, I'll be," said Grandma June, soft and proud. "They heard her."

s4a.text:
"Now then," said Grandma June, "let's see what the sisters have been saving."

She lifted out a frame, slow and careful, and it was heavy — heavy with honey. Row after row of little wax cells, each one sealed with a tiny flat white lid, like jars lined up on a pantry shelf.

"This is the comb where the honey sleeps," she said. "One bee brings home nectar in her honey tummy, and she passes it to a sister, and that sister passes it on, and every pass makes it thicker, until it's this."

She peeled back one little lid with her fingertip. Inside, the honey glowed dark gold. She touched it and held her finger out to me, and I tasted honey that had never once left the hive until that moment. It tasted like the whole meadow, warm and sweet and wild.

"Here's the humbling part, {child_companion_name}," Grandma June said. "One bee, in her whole life, makes about a twelfth of a teaspoon. That taste you just had? That's the life's work of many sisters, all together. So I only ever take the spare."

Walking home through the meadow, she told me a coral reef is the same kind of wonder under the sea — thousands of tiny animals building something bigger than any of them.

I carried home a little jar, and the smell of wax stayed on my fingers for days. And I still think of that one spoonful as a whole meadow, flying in formation.

s4b.text:
"Now then," said Grandma June, "let's see if we can find the mother of everyone."

She lifted out a deeper frame, slow and careful, and she pointed one knobby finger. And there — walking calm and unhurried through her daughters — was the queen.

Longer than any bee I'd seen. Slower, too, like she had all the time in the world. While we watched, she tucked an egg into a cell, and the workers hurried around her, feeding her, guarding her, smoothing her path.

"Every single bee in this humming city is her child," Grandma June whispered. "Tens of thousands of daughters. And here's the secret of it, {child_companion_name}: the colony works because no bee does the whole job alone. Some gather. Some build comb. Some fan their wings all day to keep the hive cool. And the queen mothers them all. One team."

I watched the queen walk on, patient as anything, and the whole frame seemed to breathe around her.

As we closed the hive, Grandma June pointed at the comb — all those perfect six-sided cells, fitted together without a gap. "Coral builds the same patient way," she said. "Tiny creatures, one small piece at a time."

She let me keep a chunk of empty comb, and I set it on my windowsill. It still smells faintly of summer. And of thousands of sisters.

s1.text:
Maya pressed her hand flat against the rock. It was warm, and it was black, and it was twisted into ropes and waves, as if the whole hillside had once been soup that someone forgot to stir.

"Basalt," said Kai, the volcano guide. "This was lava once. It ran right past where you're standing, a hundred years before you were born."

Maya looked up the mountain. Above them, the ground steamed in thin white ribbons. And there, glowing through the steam like a nightlight left on in a hallway, was a line of orange.

"Is that—"

Maya watched it. The orange line didn't move, and it did move, and the steam curled up around it and the whole mountain seemed to breathe. Nobody said anything for a moment. Pip's whirring went quiet.

"Slow as honey on a cold morning," Kai said at last. "But moving."

Pip shot up from her shoulder. His camera-eye blinked green. "Beep! I see it! I see it! It's making a pattern up there, like—beep—like the swirl on top of a cake!"

"It's going to build new land," Kai said. "Brand-new, never-before-stepped-on land, right where it meets the sea."

Maya felt her heart thump. New land. Ground that didn't exist yesterday.

"Can we watch it happen?" she asked.

"If we're quick," Kai said. "The lava won't wait, and the sun won't either." He pointed down the slope. Two paths wound through the black rock. One followed the glowing line closely, along a ridge of warm stone. The other dropped toward the beach, where they could hear the ocean hissing.

Pip hovered between them, whirring. "Beep. Which way, Maya?"

s2a.text:
"Underground," Maya said. "I want to see where the lava hides."

Kai grinned and led the way to a round black mouth in the hillside. "A lava tube," he said. "The lava's secret highway."

They ducked inside, and the world went quiet. The air turned cool as a cellar. Pip's light clicked on, and Maya gasped.

The walls were smooth and wavy, like the inside of a curl of melted chocolate. Long ago, a river of fire had poured through here, and it had left its fingerprints everywhere — drips on the ceiling, frozen mid-drip, like icicles that forgot how to melt.

"Beep!" Pip's light swept the floor. "Patterns! Look, look — the floor has ripples, like the sand at the beach. The lava flowed here in waves!"

Maya ran her hand along the wall. It was slick and cold now. Hard to believe it had once run like soup.

"Where does it come out?" she asked.

"That's what we're going to find out," said Kai.

They walked deeper. The tunnel curved, and curved again. Pip flew ahead, his light bouncing off the black glass walls. "Beep — Maya! The tube splits up here!"

Kai held up his lantern. Ahead, the passage forked. One way dipped down, narrow and dark, sloping into the earth. The other climbed up toward a round hole in the ceiling, where gray light spilled in like milk through a crack.

"A skylight," Kai said. "Where the roof fell in, long ago."

Maya looked down the dark slope. Then up at the light. Her hand went to her pocket, where the grain of black sand waited.

Pip hovered between the two ways, whirring softly. "Beep. Down deeper, or up to the light?"

s2b.text:
"The glowing river," Maya said. "I want to watch it move."

Kai nodded. "Then let's find the good ridge. I know a spot where we can see the whole flow."

They climbed over the black ropes of basalt, Pip buzzing ahead like an excited bee. At the top of the ridge, Maya stopped.

Below them, the lava crawled. It was orange and red and black all at once, with a crust that cracked and glowed and cracked again, like the top of a crème brûlée that kept healing itself.

"It's so slow," Maya whispered.

"Here, yes," said Kai. "Slower than a snail. But watch."

He pointed. Further down, the slope steepened, and the lava changed. It poured faster there, smooth and bright, like syrup sliding off a spoon.

"Beep!" Pip shot up, camera-eye blinking. "Maya! Maya! I can see the pattern! The lava goes slow where it's flat, fast where it's steep. Like you on your scooter!"

Maya laughed. It was true. The lava wasn't one river. It was a hundred rivers, some creeping, some racing, all of them turning the green forest below into black, steaming rock.

"It's eating the trees," she said softly.

Kai said nothing. He stood beside her, watching.

Maya watched a fern. The black crust touched its tip. The tip vanished. Then the fronds, one by one, sinking slow. In its place: rock. Brand-new rock, still glowing at the seams.

Pip whirred low beside her ear. "Beep. Look — the river splits up ahead. One arm goes toward the tube. The other goes toward the sea cliffs, where the ocean is hissing."

Maya's heart thumped. The sea. That was where the island would grow.

"Which one do we follow?" Pip asked.

s3.text:
They reached the coast where the world was being made.

The air smelled of salt and warm stone. In front of them, the glowing river of lava met the ocean. Where the orange touched the blue, great clouds of steam rose up, white and thick, like a giant's kettle boiling. Hiss. Pop. The sound of new land being born.

Maya stepped onto the beach. The sand was black as midnight, and it was warm. Not hot like a stove, but warm like bathwater that had been sitting in the sun. She wiggled her toes. This ground did not exist yesterday. It was the newest ground on Earth.

Pip hovered low, his camera-eye whirring as he looked at the wet sand. "Beep. Maya, look. The waves are making patterns in the black sand. Swirls and curls. Did you see anything like that back there?"

Maya smiled. "I found something," she said. She didn't say what. It was her secret, tucked safe in her pocket.

Kai stood beside her, watching the lava flow. "The island is growing," he said. "Every second, it gets a little bigger. A little taller."

Maya watched a wave roll in. It was warm, too. It washed over her feet, and when it pulled back, it left behind new black sand, smooth and shiny.

She looked at the steam rising. She listened to the hiss. She felt the warm wave pull back from her toes.

s4a.text:
"The columns," Maya said. "Let's climb."

Kai grinned. "Good choice. Follow me, and watch your step."

They walked up the slope, away from the hissing beach. The ground changed under Maya's feet. It became flat, smooth tiles, all fitted together like a puzzle. Each tile had six sides. Hexagons.

"Whoa," Maya breathed. "Did someone carve these?"

"Nope," Kai said. "When lava cools slowly, it cracks into these shapes. Perfect six-sided columns. The mountain built them all by itself."

Pip zipped ahead, his camera-eye whirring. "Beep! Maya, the pattern goes on and on! Like a honeycomb made of stone!"

Maya stepped carefully from one hexagon to the next. They were warm beneath her shoes. She crouched down and ran her fingers along the cracks between the tiles. Deep down, the rock still held the day's heat.

"How did the mountain build all this?" she asked.

"One layer at a time," Kai said. "Lava flows out. It cools. It hardens into basalt. Then more lava flows on top. Again and again, for thousands of years."

Maya looked down the slope. She could see the layers, stacked like pancakes, each one a different shade of black and gray.

Then something sparkled.

"Pip! Come here!"

The drone hovered down. "Beep. What is it?"

Maya reached into a crack between two hexagons. She pulled out a single grain of black sand, smooth and round and shiny as glass.

"It's perfect," she whispered.

"That," Kai said, "was liquid fire once. And now it's yours."

Maya tucked it into her pocket. The tide was coming in. It was time to go.

s4b.text:
"Let's wait," Maya said. "I want to watch."

Kai smiled. "Then we'll sit right here."

They settled onto a smooth rock, warm from the sun. Pip landed beside Maya, his camera-eye fixed on the glowing river. The sun was sinking low, turning the steam pink and gold.

"Watch the edge," Kai said quietly. "Where the lava meets the water."

Maya watched. The orange flow crept forward, slow as syrup. When it touched the ocean, the water hissed and bubbled. Steam rose up in great white clouds. And then, right at the edge, something new appeared.

Black sand. Fresh. Brand-new.

"Did you see that?" Maya whispered.

"Beep. I saw it," Pip said. "The island just got bigger. Right there. Right now."

Maya felt her heart thump. She was watching the exact moment the Earth made new land.

The lava kept coming, inch by inch. The steam rose and rose. The sun sank lower, and the sky turned purple and orange.

"How long will it keep growing?" Maya asked.

"As long as the lava flows," Kai said. "Maybe all night. Maybe all week. The mountain decides."

Maya sat very still. She didn't want to miss a single second.

Finally, Kai stood. "It's time. The flow is slowing. If you want to step onto the new ground, do it now, before it cools completely."

Maya stood, too. She walked to the edge of the black sand, where it was still warm and soft. She stepped onto it. Her footprints were the first ones ever made on this brand-new ground.

She bent down and picked up a single grain of sand. It was still warm.

"This was liquid fire this morning," she said.

"And now it's yours," Kai said.

Maya tucked it into her pocket. She could feel it there, warm against her leg. Behind her, the ocean hissed.

stories.title: The Island That Grew from Fire

s1.text:
Let me tell you about the morning {travel_buddy} and I climbed a sleeping mountain.

It began with a postcard from Pip the Volcanologist — three words and a drawing of a thermometer: "Come quickly. Warm." So we packed our boots and sailed to the Pacific, to a green island in the great ring of fire, where the sea meets mountains that once breathed flame.

The volcano rose out of the mist like a giant curled up under a grassy blanket. Dormant, Pip called it, bouncing on her heels at the trailhead. "Not extinct — never extinct. Just... dozing." She pressed her palm flat to the ground, and we did too. The earth was warm. Not warm like sunshine. Warm like a cat that's been sitting in your spot and just got up.

"Feel that?" Pip whispered. "That's geothermal — heat rising from deep below. The mountain's still awake down there."

A thin ribbon of steam curled from between the rocks, white against the green. Pip pulled out her brass thermometer, the one that rattles in its case, and held it over the vent. Her eyes went wide.

"Forty degrees! Oh, that's lovely. That's bathwater-warm."

The steam drifted up past our knees, and the whole hillside smelled faintly of minerals, like coins held in a hot hand. {travel_buddy} looked at me, and I looked at {travel_buddy}, and we both looked up the slope where more steam rose, thicker, waiting.

Pip grinned and tucked her thermometer away. "The crater rim is where it gets interesting. Shall we?"

s2a.text:
"Up we go," says Pip, and up we go, along a path that zigzags into the crater itself. The walls rise around us in stripes — rust-red, ash-grey, black as toast. Pip runs her hand along them. "Each stripe is an old eruption," she says. "This mountain has been building itself for thousands of years, one layer at a time."

We climb down into the bowl, and the air changes. It smells like rotten eggs — sharp and funny and impossible to ignore. {travel_buddy} pinches their nose. Pip laughs. "That's sulfur! That's the mountain breathing. A dead volcano — an extinct one — smells like nothing at all."

She kneels by a crack in the rock and slides the brass thermometer in. We crouch close. The needle trembles, climbs, stops. "Sixty degrees," Pip whispers, like she's telling a secret. "Hot enough to cook an egg, right under our boots."

Then she presses her palm to the crater floor, and we press ours beside hers. The rock hums with warmth, deep and slow, like something enormous turning over in its sleep. Pip picks up a small dark stone, pocked with holes, and drops it into my hand. It's still warm. "Volcanic rock," she says. "The mountain made that. Take it — a souvenir from a giant who's only dozing."

I close my fingers around it. Below us, somewhere far down, the heat keeps rising.

s2b.text:
"Follow the steam," says Pip, and we do — down a narrow path where white ribbons curl between the rocks, thicker and thicker, until the air itself feels like a warm washcloth on our faces.

Then the path turns, and there it is. A pool hidden in the stone, no bigger than a bathtub, bubbling at the edges like a pot that knows it has all day. Pip claps her hands. "A hot spring! The mountain's own bathtub."

We sit on the warm rocks and pull off our boots. The water is bathwater-warm — no, warmer — and tiny bubbles tickle our toes. {travel_buddy} wiggles them, and the bubbles wiggle back. Pip dips her brass thermometer in and holds it up to the light. "Forty-two degrees," she announces. "Oh, that's splendid."

"How does it get so warm?" we ask, and Pip taps the rock beneath her. "Rainwater sinks down, down, down through cracks in the earth — deeper than any well — until it meets rock heated by the sleeping volcano. The rock warms the water, and the water rises back up, bringing the heat with it. Geothermal," she says, rolling the word like a marble. "Earth-heat. In some places, people pipe this very warmth into their houses to heat their rooms and fill their baths."

We lean back on our elbows, toes in the warm water, steam rising all around us. Somewhere far below our feet, the mountain is quietly keeping the kettle on.

s3.text:
Pip tucked her thermometer away and pointed down the far slope, where a little white boat bobbed at a wooden pier. "That's Kai," she said. "He's been waiting for us."

Kai waved us aboard, and the boat hummed to life under our feet. We slipped along the coast, past green cliffs, past a round lake sunk into the mountain's top — water the color of turquoise, still as glass. "The old crater," Kai said over his shoulder. "The mountain sleeps up here. But out there?" He nodded toward the open sea. "Out there, it's still building."

"Building what?" {travel_buddy} asked.

"New land," Pip whispered. "Islands begin underwater, you know. A volcano erupts beneath the waves, lava meets cold sea, and hardens into rock. Layer after layer, year after year, until one day — the top breaks the surface."

Then we saw it. Ahead, the ocean was steaming. Great white clouds rose off the water, and the surface bubbled like a pot left on the stove. Pip snatched up her brass thermometer and dangled it over the side on a string.

"Ninety-two degrees!" she cried. "Ninety-two! The sea is practically soup!"

Kai cut the engine, and we drifted. The boat rocked gently. Bloop. Bloop. A bubble the size of a bathtub swelled up beside us and burst, sighing warm mist across our faces.

Pip gripped the rail, her eyes shining. "Somewhere under this boat, right now, lava is meeting the sea. We might be watching an island being born."

{travel_buddy} leaned close to me. "Do you think we'll see it happen?"

The water bubbled louder. Pip held her breath. So did we.

s4a.text:
"Hold tight," Kai says. He steers us close — close enough to feel the heat on our faces, but behind the big wave-breaker rocks where the water stays calm. "This is where the mountain meets the sea."

Then we see it. Orange lava, bright as the inside of a toaster, pours into the water. Sssssss. Steam explodes upward, white and roaring. The lava hits the cold sea and turns black instantly, hardening into jagged rock that tumbles and piles.

"Look!" Pip shouts over the hiss. "New rock! Brand new! The youngest rock on Earth!"

We watch the island grow. Inch by inch. A black ledge extends where there was only water a moment ago. Pip dangles her thermometer on its string. "One hundred degrees! Oh, it's cooking!"

The steam drifts apart, and Kai noses the boat toward a beach of sand black as licorice. We hop out. The ground is warm through our shoes.

Pip picks up a gray stone, light as a sponge. "Pumice," she says. "It floats." She tosses it into a pool. It bobs like a cork.

{travel_buddy} finds a smooth black pebble, still warm from the sun. We dig a small hole in the dark sand, rich as crumbled chocolate cake, and tuck a seed inside. "For the island," Pip says softly.

We climb back aboard, pockets heavy with stone. The new rock steams behind us, cooling into land that will be here long after we're gone.

"We saw it born," {travel_buddy} whispers.

Kai smiles. "And it'll keep growing. Come back in a hundred years — you won't recognize the place."

s4b.text:
Kai beaches the boat on sand black as pepper. "The geysers are just ahead," he says. "Stay on the wooden path. The ground's thin here — like the crust on a pie."

We follow him past pools that bubble like pots of oatmeal. The air smells of minerals, sharp and warm. Then we see the field: white cones of stone, and from the biggest one, a rumble.

"She's building," Kai whispers. "Count with me."

We crouch low. The pool in the cone's mouth swells, trembles. Pip grips her thermometer. "Ninety-eight... ninety-nine..."

"One," we say together. "Two. Three—"

Whoosh. A column of water shoots straight up, taller than a house, glittering in the sun. It rains down warm as bathwater, and we shriek with laughter, soaked and steaming.

"Every island in this chain," Kai says, wiping his face, "started like this. A volcano grows underwater, breaks the surface, then sleeps. That one there—" he points to a green hump across the bay, "—is dormant. The one beyond it? Extinct. Finished. But this field is still wide awake."

We explore the black sand, finding stones that glitter like dark glass — obsidian, Pip calls it, volcanic glass. And pumice, gray and holey, light as a cracker. {travel_buddy} drops one in a pool. It floats, bobbing like a toy boat.

We plant a seed in the dark soil, tucking it in deep. Pip presses her palm to the ground one last time. "Warm," she says happily. "Still rising."

We carry home a stone that floats, and the smell of the warm earth on our clothes.

c1.question: "The mountain is speaking to us through heat," Pip says, adjusting the brass thermometer. "Shall we climb into the crater to see the sleeping volcano's rocky layers, or follow the warm steam to find the hot springs hidden in the rocks?"

options.label: Explore the crater's rocky heart
Soak in the geothermal hot springs

c2.question: "The sea is building new land ahead," Kai says, gripping the boat's wheel. "Do we sail close to watch the underwater volcano create new rock right before our eyes, or explore the black sand beach where geysers shoot water high into the sky?"

options.label: Watch the island being born
Discover the geyser beach

travel_buddy.role: The child companion joining the expedition

stories.title: The Island That Took Its Time

s1.text:
The boat engine coughs, and stops. "Listen," says Captain Belen. "That's the Humboldt Current. She brought the first travellers here, millions of years ago."

We stand on a beach made of black glass. The rock is sharp enough to cut your eyes just looking, and nothing grows here but one green shoot, thin as a hair, sticking out of a crack.

"This is the youngest island," says Ranger Luz. She picks up a stone, turns it over. "The volcanoes built it from the sea floor. Everything alive had to arrive somehow. Swim, fly, or float."

Captain Belen laughs. It sounds exactly like a seal barking. "The currents are my old friends," she says. "That one, the Cromwell, she carries turtles sometimes."

Then the dark stones move.

Not stones. Iguanas. A heap of them, black as the rock, piled together for warmth. One lifts its head and sneezes — two jets of salt spray, like a tiny whale spouting.

"Marine iguanas," says Luz. "Endemic. That means they live here, and nowhere else on Earth."

We crouch down. The iguana looks at us with one golden eye. Its claws are long, made for gripping rock in rough water.

"But why here?" Luz asks. She looks at us, really asks. "Why did they become swimmers here, and nowhere else?"

The green shoot trembles in the wind. The island waits.

s2a.text:
"Up we go," says Ranger Luz. "Step where I step."

The lava trail is crunchy, like walking on burnt toast. Luz shows us the good rock — the flat, dull pieces that don't wobble. "The shiny ones are tricky," she says. "They look solid, but they're thin as eggshells."

We climb and climb. The wind gets bigger. And then — the rim.

The crater opens below us, huge and quiet. Thin wisps of steam curl up from cracks, like the volcano is dreaming about breakfast.

"It's sleeping," Luz says. "Not done. Just resting."

We look out. The whole island chain spreads below us — one, two, three dark humps in the blue sea, each one smaller and greener than the last.

"They're still growing," Luz says. "The youngest one is barely born. The oldest has had time to collect things."

She tells us about a tiny lizard, long ago, clinging to a drifting branch. "The branch floated for weeks. The lizard held on. When it washed up here, it was alone — so it changed. It became something new."

Something black moves on the rocks below. A bird — but what a bird. It spreads its wings, and they are stubby, useless little things, like a child's drawing of wings.

"Flightless cormorant," says Luz. "Its ancestors flew here. But there was nothing to escape from, and the fishing was good. So the wings shrank."

The cormorant waddles to the edge. Then — torpedo. It vanishes into the sea, faster than a thrown stone.

"It gave up the sky," Luz says softly, "for the water."

We stand very still. The steam curls. The islands wait, each one holding its own secret shapes.

s2b.text:
"Shoes off," says Captain Belen. "Feet on the wet rock. The crabs won't bite — much."

We wade. The water is cold and warm at the same time, cold where the waves splash, warm where the sun sits in the pools. Sally Lightfoot crabs scuttle sideways, red as stop signs, quick as dropped marbles.

"Watch," says Belen. She points at a heron, standing so still it might be made of wire. "He's waiting for the pool to forget he's there."

Then — a flash of black and white. A penguin. A penguin, here, where the sun is hot enough to fry an egg on the black rock. It squints at us, unimpressed, then folds itself into the water and is gone.

"Galapagos penguin," says Belen. "The Cromwell Current carried its great-great-grandparents here from the cold south. They liked the fish. They stayed."

"But it's hot," we say. "Penguins are supposed to be cold."

Belen laughs, that seal-bark laugh. "The current keeps the water cold enough. They live nowhere else on Earth. Endemic. Like the iguanas."

A blue-footed booby lands on a rock beside us. It looks at us. We look at it. Then it lifts one foot — electric blue, bright as a fresh marker — and sets it down. Lifts the other. Sets it down. A slow, silly dance.

"The bluer the feet," Belen says, "the healthier the bird. They're showing off."

The booby stares at us, one blue foot raised, waiting.

We hold our breath and stay.

s3.text:
The boat engine coughs, and stops. "Santa Cruz," says Captain Belen. "The island that took its time."

Ranger Luz is waiting on the dock, and beside her stands a woman with a tortoise shell badge on her shirt. "Dr. Amara," says Luz. "She raises the babies."

"Tell me," says Dr. Amara, kneeling so her eyes are level with ours. "What did you find out there?"

We tell her, all of it tumbling out, and she listens the way grown-ups rarely do — all the way to the end. Then she opens a wooden box.

Inside, on a bed of sand, sits a tortoise the size of your fist. Its shell is soft-looking, like a leather coin purse. It blinks at us. It is so small we hold our breath without meaning to.

"This one hatched last week," says Dr. Amara. She turns it gently, and there on its shell is a tiny tag. "This tells me which island it belongs to. When it is big enough, it goes home. Only home. Each island grows its own tortoises."

She sets down two old shells, empty and light. One is round as a helmet. One rises up in front, like a saddle.

"Touch them," she says.

We do. The dome is smooth all over. The saddle curves up like a wave about to break.

"On islands where the grass grows low, tortoises wear the dome. On islands where food grows high, they wear the saddle — it lets them stretch their necks up." She looks at us. "The island shapes the shell. Every single time."

Luz asks her question one more time, quietly. "So why here, and nowhere else?"

And now we know the answer ourselves. "Isolation," we say. "The islands are cut off. So each one made its own animals."

"Endemic," says Dr. Amara, smiling. "Here, and nowhere else in the universe."

The baby tortoise stretches its neck toward the sun. Somewhere on these islands are the giants it will become — tortoises as heavy as three grown-ups. We came all this way to meet one.

s4a.text:
"Up," says Ranger Luz, and we climb while the sky is still grey.

The salty shore falls away. Then comes the dry scrub, all cactus and dust, and then — just like that — mist. Cool, green mist that touches our faces. Three worlds, stacked like pancakes.

"Shhh," says Luz. "Look at the boulders."

We look. The boulders are dark and round, scattered through the grass. Then one of them lifts its head.

Not boulders. Tortoises. Giants, grazing in the mist, slow as clouds.

We stand very still. One is close — so close we can hear the grass tearing, slow and steady, between its jaws. Its shell rises up in front like a saddle. Its neck stretches out, wrinkly and long, like an old man reaching for his glasses.

"That's {tortoise_name}," whispers Luz. "A saddle-shell. Some of these giants were born before your great-grandparents. Before cars. Before airplanes."

A hundred years of slowness. We watch it chew. We watch it blink. Nothing about it hurries, and nothing needs to.

On the trail down, Luz stops and picks something up — a small curved piece of shell, shed from a growing tortoise, smooth as a skipped stone. "Here," she says, pressing it into our hand. "One island made this shape. Now it's yours."

On the boat, Captain Belen cuts the engine one last time. The sea lions bark. The misty hill fades behind us.

"Slow ones," says Belen, laughing her seal laugh. "They took their time. And look how far it got them."

We hold the piece of shell, and we understand.

s4b.text:
The afternoon is gold when we climb into the highlands, and someone is already there.

She sits on a folding stool beside a giant tortoise, a pencil in her hand. She has silver braids and boots older than we are.

"Abuela Pilar," says Ranger Luz, softly. "My grandmother."

"Shhh," says Abuela Pilar, not unkindly. "He is eating."

So we sit in the grass and watch. The tortoise tears the grass slowly, its saddle shell rising in front like a wave about to break. When it finally rests, Abuela Pilar opens an old notebook, fat and soft as bread.

"Look."

Page after page of drawings. The same tortoise. The same shell. 1965. 1975. 1985. Every decade, drawn again — a little bigger, a little more worn, always him.

"I was younger than you when I first saw him," she says. "I have watched him my whole life. And do you know why we watch?"

We shake our heads.

"Because he lives here and nowhere else. Not anywhere in the universe. If he is gone from here, he is gone forever. So someone must always be watching." She looks at us a long moment. Then she tears one page from her notebook — a drawing of him, saddle shell and all — and presses it into our hands. "Now you have watched him too."

On the sail home, Captain Belen cuts the engine. The sea lions bark across the gold water. We hold the page carefully, flat on our knees, so the wind cannot take it.

"Sixty years," says Belen, shaking her head in wonder.

"Sixty-one," we say.

c1.question: "Two ways to meet this island, shipmates," says Captain Belen, spinning the wheel. "Do we climb up to the volcano's rim and see how the islands were born — or do we poke around the tidepools and meet whoever the sea delivered?"

options.label: Hike the lava trail to the crater rim with Ranger Luz
Explore the tidepool shore with Captain Belen

c2.question: "The giants are up in the mist," says Ranger Luz, tapping two times on the map. "We can rise with the sun and watch the highlands wake — or go at golden hour and meet my grandmother, who has watched one tortoise for sixty years. Which visit shall it be?"

options.label: Climb at dawn to find the giant tortoises waking in the mist
Visit Abuela Pilar and the tortoise she has watched for sixty years

tortoise_name.role: The ancient saddle-shell tortoise we finally meet in the highlands

s1.text:
Our little round boat is out on the warm blue sea, just us, rocking. The water is as warm as a bath somebody ran an hour ago.
We lean over the side and watch the water.
Whoosh!
A spout of spray goes up beside us and comes down on our heads. Up he comes, smooth and gray like a wet stone. Our friend.
But today {whale_name} cannot keep still. He wiggles left. He wiggles right. He turns a slow squirmy circle, the way you squirm when a label in your shirt is scratching your neck.
The itch sits right in the middle of his back. His flippers are too far forward to get at it. His tail is too far back.
"Nobody can reach it," we say.
His pod tried all morning. His mama's flipper was too big, his cousin's too small.
So the itch stays where it is, itching.
We hold on to the boat and let him come to us, because he is the one who knows how close is close. He puts one eye out of the water and looks at us.
We know that look.

s2a.text:
"Seaweed," we say. "Soft is what an itch wants."
We reach down into the cool water for long ribbons of it, and braid them the way you braid three bits of string. Over and under. Over and under. Then we take our longest oar and tie the fat green braid onto the end.
One brush. Enormous.
{whale_name} floats up close and holds still. Almost still.
We lean out over the water and swish the brush along the middle of his back. Swish. Swish.
His whole body shivers. Then he giggles, a bubbly whale giggle, like the last of the bathwater going down.
"That is not a scratch," we say. "That is a tickle."
He rolls right over, and half the sea comes into the boat and into our socks.
We wring out our hats and take another look at our brush. Too floppy. Too swishy. Now too wet.
"It does not want swishing," we say. "It wants a proper rub."
"Not finished yet," we tell him.

s2b.text:
"Bubbles," we say. "Fizz it out of him."
Our boat keeps a bubble maker under the seat. We turn the little brass crank. Brrrr.
Up comes a silver stream of bubbles, right under {whale_name}, hundreds of them, shining as they climb.
They fizz along his tummy. They fizz up his sides. They pop all over his back. Pip, pip, pip.
{whale_name} shuts his eyes and hums, low and long, and the hum comes up through the floor of the boat into our feet.
Then we look again. He is still wiggling.
"Faster!" we say, and we crank until the whole sea round him is a silver cloud.
Pip, pip, pip. Every bubble touches the itchy spot, pops, and is gone, like the fizz on the top of lemonade.
{whale_name} blows a puff of spray out of his blowhole, which is how a whale sighs.
"It does not want fizzing," we say. "It wants a proper rub."
"Not finished yet," we tell him.

s3.text:
We sit down in the bottom of the boat and let it rock while we think.
Our {first_try} did not reach the itch, but it told us one thing.
"Not tickly," we say. "Not fizzy. A slow steady rub, from something exactly the right size and exactly the right rough."
We have nothing like that in the boat. So we shade our eyes and look at the sea instead, because the sea is full of things, if you know what you are looking at.
Out that way, a pod of dolphins is leaping. One, two, three, up and over and down. Their clicks and whistles come across the water like somebody tapping a spoon on a cup. A dolphin flipper is small and smooth, about the size of our two hands together.
And over the other way the water goes pale, where a sandbank lies under the shallows with the sun on it. Ripple, ripple, ripple, all the way across. It looks like the scratchiest blanket in the world.
{whale_name} swims one slow circle round the boat and waits. He is being very patient about it.

s4a.text:
We cup our hands round our mouths and call across the water.
The smallest dolphin comes first, quick as a stone skipping. Her face pops up beside the boat, smiling whether she means it or not.
We point at {whale_name}. We point at the middle of his back.
"Click, whistle, click," she says, which can only mean leave it to me.
She swims one circle round him. Then she lays her flipper flat on the itchy spot and rubs, round and round, small slow circles, the way somebody rubs your back when you cannot get to sleep.
{whale_name} stops wiggling. His long flippers droop. His eyes close. He goes soft and heavy in the water, floating like a boat with nobody in it.
Then, whoosh! Up goes the tallest, mistiest spout we have ever seen, and it comes down on all of us like warm rain.
The itch is gone.
The little dolphin leaps and flips twice, for no reason except that she can. Dolphins rub each other like that all day long, it turns out. His pod comes over, and soon the whole sea is splashing.
"Tomorrow," we tell {whale_name}. "Same spot. Bring your dolphin."

s4b.text:
We turn the boat for the pale water, and {whale_name} comes along beside us.
The water here is clear as glass. We look down and see the sand in long ripples, with deep water all round it and plenty of room over it for a whale to roll.
"Down you go," we say. "Have a proper scratch."
{whale_name} turns over and puts his back against the ripples. Then he wiggles. Wiggle, wiggle, wiggle.
The sand rubs him, slow and steady and exactly the right rough. He rolls one way. He rolls back the other. Little clouds of sand puff up round him like flour off a counter.
His rumble comes up through the floor of the boat, the way a cat's purr comes up through your knees.
One more long wiggle, and he stops.
No squirming. No twisting. Just a whale, holding still in the clear water, grinning at nobody.
Whoosh! Up goes a tall misty spout.
His pod comes over to see, and one by one every whale in it comes down onto the sand and wiggles too.
"The sea had a brush the whole time," we say. "It was just the size of a beach."

c1.question: "Hold on, friend," we say. "We could braid you a brush out of seaweed. Or we could crank up the bubble maker and fizz you all over. Seaweed, or bubbles?"

options.label: Braid a long seaweed brush
Fizz the itch with the bubble maker

c2.question: "Look at those two things," we say to {whale_name}. "A dolphin flipper is exactly the right size for your back. That sandbank is exactly the right rough. Dolphin, or sandbank?"

options.label: Call the dolphins over
Wiggle on the ripply sandbank

whale_name.role: the young whale with the itchy spot

first_try.role: the gadget we used for our first helping attempt

s1.text:
The back corner of the library smells like peppermint tea and old paper, which is our favourite smell in the world. Nana June lets us spread out on the carpet there, right under the window, and today we have something to show her.

It's a flipbook. Three weeks of work. Our jumper — {jumper_name} — crouches on page one, leaps across pages two through twenty-three, and lands on the other side of a puddle on page twenty-four. Twenty-four drawings. We counted twice. We were so proud of that number we told everyone at the bus stop.

"Watch this," we say.

Nana June puts down her knitting. The needles keep going anyway, soft little clicks, like they knit on their own when she's thinking.

We flip the pages.

And our hearts sink.

{jumper_name} goes up. And up. And hangs there, floating, slow as a bubble in bathwater. The puddle waits below, patient as a cat. By the time the landing finally comes, we've almost forgotten there was a jump at all.

"Hmm," says Nana June.

She says it the way she says everything — like she's turning it over, not closing it. She takes a sip of tea. Click, click go the needles.

"Twenty-four frames," we say. "We worked so hard."

"I can see that," she says. "Every drawing is beautiful. But you know what I noticed? The puddle seems to win."

She's right. That's exactly it. The puddle sits there, wide and calm, and {jumper_name} just drifts over it like a leaf on a slow river. No spring. No pop. No land.

We look at the flipbook. We look at each other. Three weeks of evenings, and the jump won't land.

"Why does it look so wrong?" we ask.

Nana June smiles into her tea. "Now that," she says, "is a very good question."

s2a.text:
"More," we say. "More frames. Twenty-four wasn't enough, so we'll do thirty-six. Forty. It'll be smoother, and smooth is good, right?"

Nana June picks up her knitting. Click, click. "Worth a try," she says.

So we draw. We draw until our pencils are little stubs, until the pencil sharpener is full of cedar smell, until our fingertips are grey with graphite. Thirty-six frames now. {jumper_name} crouches in six frames instead of three. The leap takes eighteen. The landing, twelve. Every single in-between is perfect. We line them up on the carpet like soldiers.

"Watch," we say.

We flip.

And it's worse. Somehow it's worse. {jumper_name} doesn't float now — {jumper_name} *drifts*, slow and dreamy, like an astronaut walking on the moon. The puddle below seems to stretch wider, lazy as a cat in a sunbeam. The jump takes forever. We could go make toast. We could knit a scarf.

Nana June pours the tea. Peppermint steam curls up between us. "May I ask you something?" she says. "What's the most important moment in this jump?"

We look at our thirty-six beautiful drawings.

We can't answer.

Every frame looks exactly as important as every other frame. Which means none of them are.

s2b.text:
"Cut it," we say. "It's too slow, so make it fast. Snappy. We'll erase every other drawing and it'll have *pop*."

Nana June picks up her knitting. Click, click. "Worth a try," she says.

So we erase. Twelve frames now. Gone, the careful in-betweens. Gone, the soft arc of the leap. Our eraser is worn to a nub and there are little grey crumbs all over the carpet, but the book is thin and quick. It feels dangerous. It feels like a race car.

"Watch," we say.

We flip.

And it's a disaster of a whole new flavour. {jumper_name} doesn't float — {jumper_name} *teleports*. One frame on the ground, one frame in the air, one frame across the puddle. Blink and you miss it. The jump looks like a magic trick gone wrong, all vanish and no wonder. And the puddle — we could swear the puddle is wider. Unimpressed. Almost bored.

Nana June pours the tea. Peppermint steam curls up between us. "May I ask you something?" she says. "What's the most important moment in this jump?"

We flip our twelve chopped-up pages.

We can't answer.

Whatever the most important moment was, we erased it.

s3.text:
The bell above the library door jingles, and a voice says, "Whoa. Eraser snowstorm."

It's Theo. He's in high school now, but last summer he took an animation workshop, and Nana June waves him over like she'd been expecting him all along.

"Show him," she says.

We hand over the flipbook. Theo flips it once. Twice. Then he grins — not mean, just like he's spotted something hiding in plain sight.

"Okay, first — twenty-four drawings is a lot of work, and the work is good. But the problem was never how many drawings you made." He taps the cover. "It's where the drawings are."

He pulls a scrap of paper from Nana June's bookmark pile and draws three quick figures: {jumper_name} squashed low, {jumper_name} stretched at the top of the leap, {jumper_name} stuck to the ground like a dart.

"These are keyframes. The important moments. Crouch, peak, landing." He dots lines between them. "Everything else is an in-between — just a bridge. Bridges don't get to decide anything. Keyframes do."

Then he draws a tiny ladder beside the crouch, little tick marks crowding together at the bottom, spreading wide at the top, bunching up again at the landing.

"This is a timing chart. It tells the in-betweens where to stand. Bunch them near the crouch and the landing, and the jump eases in slow, then snaps out fast. Spread them all even — like yours — and everything floats."

We stare at the ladder. So that's what went wrong. Our twenty-four drawings were standing in a perfectly even line, like kids waiting for the bus. Nobody was hurrying. Nobody was snapping.

"Here's the secret the pros know," Theo says. "They animate on twos. Twelve drawings a second, not twenty-four. Twelve, in the right places, beats twenty-four mushy ones every single time."

Click, click go the needles. Nana June pours Theo a cup of tea without asking, which means he's allowed to stay.

"So," he says, pulling our pencil toward him. "You know the secret now. You've got one afternoon and a puddle that keeps winning. How do you want to rebuild the jump?"

s4a.text:
We look at the flipbook — three weeks of it — and then at the fresh stack of blank paper Theo slides across the carpet.

"New drawings," we say. "Clean start."

"Good call," he says. "Now draw the jump before you draw the jump."

So we do. Three keyframes, big and bold, one per page: {jumper_name} squashed low like a coiled spring, {jumper_name} stretched thin at the very top of the leap, {jumper_name} planted on the far bank like a flag claiming the moon. We hold them up side by side and, honestly, the jump already works. Three drawings, and you can feel it.

Then the timing chart. We pencil a little ladder beside each keyframe — ticks crowded tight at the crouch, spreading wide through the soaring middle, bunching close again at the landing. "Slow in, snap out," we whisper, like a spell.

Nine in-betweens next. Only nine. Each one knows exactly where it stands, because the chart says so. Twelve drawings total. On twos, each gets two beats of the light.

It takes one hour. Not three weeks. One hour.

Nana June puts down her knitting. We flip.

{jumper_name} crouches — and waits there, gathering weight like a held breath — then springs, hangs at the top for one delicious beat, and comes down with a stomp we can feel through the carpet. Clear of the puddle. The puddle that is now wide as the whole library carpet, and it doesn't matter, not one bit, because the jump lands with room to spare.

Nana June claps. The needles click. Even the puddle seems impressed.

"Twelve drawings," Theo says. "Told you."

Before we leave, Nana June presses something into our pocket — the timing chart from our best keyframe, folded small. "A treasure map," she says.

We pat our pocket the whole walk home.

s4b.text:
We look at the flipbook, and we just can't throw it away. Three weeks of evenings live in those pages.

"Rescue," we say. "The good poses are in there somewhere."

"Then let's go fishing," says Theo.

We spread all twenty-four drawings across the carpet, and Nana June leans over her tea while we hunt. Some drawings are mush. But some — some make us gasp. We circle them with a red pencil: the crouch on page two, low and loaded like a cat about to pounce. The peak on page thirteen, stretched and weightless. The landing on page twenty-two, feet down, knees bent, solid as a fencepost.

"Those are your keyframes," Theo says. "They were good all along. They were just drowning."

Now the timing chart. We pencil a ladder beside each keyframe — ticks crowded at the crouch, spread wide at the peak, bunched tight at the landing. Then we redraw the in-betweens to match, nine of them, each one standing exactly where the chart tells it to. Twelve drawings. On twos. The other twelve pages we set aside gently, like guests who stayed a little too long.

We flip.

{jumper_name} crouches and holds it, gathering real weight — then springs, hangs at the top for one floating, golden beat, and stomps down hard on the far bank. Clear of the puddle. The puddle that is now wide as the whole library carpet, and it loses anyway.

Nana June claps, and her needles click like tiny applause of their own.

"Same jumper," Theo grins. "Same hands. Different where the drawings stand."

On the way out, we slide one page into our pocket — the rescued crouch, the drawing that was good all along and only needed friends in the right places.

"Keep it," says Nana June. "Some things are worth rescuing."

We already knew that. We rescued it.

c1.question: "Well, my dears," Nana June says, setting down her knitting, "when something won't work, you can pile more onto it — or you can trim it down. Which sounds like your fix?"

options.label: Add even more drawings — 36 frames must be smoother than 24
Erase every other frame to make the jump twice as fast

c2.question: "Okay, you've got the secret now," Theo says, tapping his timing chart. "So do we start fresh with brand-new keyframes, or do we dig through your old drawings and rescue the good poses hiding in there?"

options.label: Redraw the jump from scratch with three bold new keyframes and a timing chart
Keep the old drawings, find the keyframes hiding in them, and re-time the in-betweens

jumper_name.role: The character we are animating, who keeps failing to clear the puddle

s1.text:
The grass is stiff and white tonight, so we keep to the dry path, the way we always do.
The bowl we left by the back step has frozen over. We lift the lid of ice out whole. It cracks in our mittens into a hundred pieces, and every piece slides off the same way across the stone.
"Look at them go," we say.
Behind us the telescope begins to glow.
