So we climb through the little round door, out onto the soft dark of the sky, and there she is, rocking on the starlight. {boat_name}, with her sail of shimmer. We climb aboard.
Then the sky in front of us turns gold. Here comes Saturn, huge and creamy, wearing wide bright rings around its middle like a hat with no top.
From here the rings look painted on, smooth as a plate. We sail closer, and the smooth hoop breaks apart. The rings are ice. Millions of separate pieces, small as peas, big as houses, all sliding the same way.
Just like our step.
{boat_name} slows down to look.

s2a.text:
{boat_name} tips her sail and slides down into the lane.
On our left, a wall of tumbling ice. On our right, another one. Both walls are moving, turning over and over, and there is not one sound in the whole sky.
Ice crumbs the size of sugar tap along the sail. Tick. Tick. Tick.
We lie on our backs in the boat and watch Saturn’s golden stripes slide by above us.
Then something comes trundling along the top of the wall. A little round moon, no bigger than a hill, rolling along the edge of the ring and bumping stray chunks back into line.
"Pardon me," it says to a lumpy one. "Coming through. Whoops. So sorry."
It leans against the lumpy one and pushes, and the lump wobbles back where it belongs, going the same way as everything else again.
"That is my job," it says. "I keep this edge tidy."
We wave.
"Sorry," it says to us, and off it trundles, apologizing to every single thing it passes.

s2b.text:
{boat_name} settles on the flat top of the great slab, gentle as a leaf on a pond. We step out.
We are standing on an island, and the island is turning, slow and steady, so the stars swing by over our heads.
The ice is clear as a window. We kneel and look down and there are bubbles in there, tiny and round, held still for a very long time.
"Knock knock," we say, and we knock on it. Tock, tock. It is harder than any ice at home, and colder than the freezer, so our mittens stay on.
Up here we hardly weigh a thing. We hop, and up we go, and down we come slow, and land in a crunch of ice sand.
So we hop again.
Then we stand still and look out. The ring runs away from us in both directions, a bright road with no end, and thousands of ice islands roll along beside us, big and small, all going the same way we are.
Nobody bumps. Nobody stops.

s3.text:
We wave goodbye to {first_marvel}, and {boat_name} lifts up over the top of the rings.
Now we can see them whole. Flat bright circles, one inside the other, like ripples in a puddle that stopped halfway. Straight through them runs a dark gap wide enough to sail a whole town along.
Under the rings, Saturn turns. Stripes of cream and butterscotch and honey slide past each other, slower than we can watch.
There is no ground down there. Saturn is a great ball of cloud, with nowhere to put your feet, and that is fine, because we have a boat.
Then the little round moon comes trundling over the top of the ring, out of puff.
"Sorry," it says. "Sorry. But you have to see the moons. Saturn has dozens and dozens of moons."
It points one frosty bump at a small white moon, puffing snow up into the sky.
Then it points at a big orange one, wrapped up in a thick fuzzy blanket of air.

s4a.text:
{boat_name} sails out to the small white moon, the whitest thing we have ever seen, with long blue cracks near the bottom, like the split along the top of a loaf.
Out of those cracks come fountains.
Real fountains of ice crystals, going up higher than any mountain, and silent the whole way.
"In," we say. "Sail us right in."
So she does.
Snow drifts all around us, slow and sparkling. It does not come back down. It turns over and keeps going up.
We put our arms out and spin, and the snow settles on our sleeves, on the sail, in our hair.
And here is the best part. This snow never comes back to the little moon. It drifts out and out and joins the rings.
That small white moon has been snowing its own soft fluffy ring for a very long time.
We sail home with the fountain shining behind us, out through the round telescope door, onto the cold grass, and we shake real ring snow into the bowl on the step.
"Goodnight, snowy one," we say. "Keep puffing."

s4b.text:
{boat_name} turns toward the big orange moon, and it grows until it fills the sky like a giant apricot.
Its air is thick and fuzzy and we cannot see the ground at all. So down we go, through the haze, slow and gentle.
Then the world opens underneath us. Hills. Dark winding rivers. Flat still lakes. And over all of it a soft orange light, like the inside of a paper lantern.
It is raining here. Not fast rain. The drops are fat and they drift down as slowly as feathers, all the same slow way, so we can watch one drop the whole way from cloud to ground.
The air is heavy and thick, and we are light as paper. And that means something wonderful.
We hold our arms out. We flap.
And we fly. We really fly, in slow circles under an orange sky, over rivers on a moon.
"Flap," we say. "Keep flapping."
We flap until our arms are tired and happy. Then we climb back into {boat_name} and sail home, out through the round telescope door, onto the cold grass.
We are still flapping.

c1.question: "Two places," we say. "Down into the dark lane where the ice opens up, or out onto one of those great flat slabs? Lane, or island?"

options.label: Sail down the wide lane between the rings
Land on the floating island of ice

c2.question: "So," says the little round moon, wobbling on the ring edge. "Snow puffing out of the white one, or that big orange sky? Snow, or orange?"

options.label: Sail to the little moon that puffs snow into the sky
Sail to the big moon with the thick orange sky

first_marvel.role: the marvel we stopped at first

s1.text:
Pip hurried down the wooden pier at dusk, hugging a borrowed notebook, and the boards went creak, creak, creak under their shoes.

"Careful!" called {keeper_name}, the night-watch keeper, from the little hut at the end. "That last board has opinions."

Pip stepped over it. "I'm here to sketch the light," Pip said. "If it comes back."

"Oh, it comes back," said {keeper_name}. "The question is whether it lets you look."

The sea below was black as a cupboard with the door shut. Pip leaned over the rail, pencil ready.

Then it happened.

A small blue pulse bloomed in the dark water. A lantern switching on. Pip gasped and pressed the pencil to the page.

Gone.

"Did you see it?" Pip whispered.

"I always see it," said {keeper_name}. "I've just never seen what makes it."

Pip stared into the black. Nothing. Not a ripple.

Then the whole sea exploded.

SPLOOSH!

Something enormous burst up beside the pier, and the splash went up like a fountain and came down like rain. Pip got it full in the face.

"Sorry! Sorry!" said a whiskery voice. A young harbour seal hauled his chin onto the lowest board, beaming. "Barnacle," he said, by way of hello. His nose bumped the pier. The pier wobbled. Pip's pencil nearly went overboard.

And all around Barnacle, the water glittered. Thousands of tiny lights, scattered by the splash, drifted and swirled like sparks off a bonfire.

"Plankton," breathed Pip, sketching fast. "The plankton glows."

Barnacle looked down at the shining water around his whiskers. Then he looked back up at Pip, and his eyes went round.

"Pip," he said slowly. "The water is looking at you."

s2a.text:
"The deep end," said Pip. "Where the big water hides."

They crept to the pier's end, where the boards stopped and the sea dropped away into black. Barnacle flopped along beside them, trying to tiptoe. A seal cannot tiptoe. Every step went thump.

Pip leaned over the edge, notebook ready.

"There!" Pip whispered.

Below them, a jellyfish pulsed through the dark. Its bell squeezed and stretched, squeezed and stretched, pushing it along like an umbrella opening and closing. And it was see-through. Clear as a window. Clear as bathwater.

Pip squinted. Inside the jellyfish, right in the middle of its see-through tummy, a tiny green spark glowed.

"It's glowing!" Pip said. "But it's green, not blue. And it's inside."

"Maybe it ate a light bulb," said Barnacle.

"It ate plankton," said {keeper_name}, coming up behind them. "A glowing one. The jellyfish swallowed it whole, and it's still shining in there. Like a lantern swallowed by a window."

Pip sketched fast. The jellyfish drifted past, green spark blinking inside its clear belly, and its bell kept pulsing. One squeeze pushed it forward. One squeeze scooped up dinner. One squeeze breathed. Three jobs, one squeeze.

But it did not flash blue.

"That's not our light," Pip said slowly. "Something else made that blue flash. Something bigger."

The jellyfish pulsed away into the dark, carrying its little green lantern with it.

s2b.text:
"Under the pier," said Pip. "Where the shadows keep secrets."

They ducked down the wooden steps and crouched between the pylons. The water here was still and dark, and the air smelled like salt and old rope. Barnacle squeezed in beside them, which meant there was suddenly much less room.

"Sorry," he whispered. His whiskers tickled Pip's ear.

Then Pip saw them.

Jellyfish. Dozens. Hundreds. A whole jelly bloom, drifting past like slow snowfall. Moon jellies, pale and round, each one pulsing its bell in no hurry at all. They came in a silent parade, too many to count, tumbling gently over each other like bubbles in a bath.

"It's snowing jellyfish," Pip breathed.

Pip reached out one finger, slow as anything, toward the nearest one. The jellyfish felt the water move and pulsed away, quick and soft, like a soap bubble escaping.

No flash. No blue light. Nothing.

"Why won't they glow?" Pip whispered.

SPLOOSH.

Barnacle had fallen in.

He surfaced a moment later, snorting water out of his nose, looking extremely pleased with himself. "I'm fine!" he announced.

And then Pip saw it. Everywhere Barnacle had splashed, the jellyfish near him pulsed and flashed. A tiny blue blink. Then another. Then another.

"They glow when they're bumped!" Pip said, grabbing the notebook. "Not all the time. Only when something touches them!"

Barnacle looked at the jellies blinking around him. "I did that?"

"You did that," said Pip. "But you didn't make the big flash. Something else did."

The bloom drifted on, dark and silent, keeping its secret.

s3.text:
"What did you find?" Barnacle whispered, dripping on Pip's shoes.

Before Pip could answer, {keeper_name} clicked off the red torch. The dark came down like a lid. "Now we wait," she said. "Quiet as pebbles."

They sat. Pip hugged the notebook. Barnacle tried to sit quiet as a pebble, which for Barnacle meant wobbling like a jelly in a jar.

The black water gave nothing back. Not a ripple. Not a spark. Pip's eyes began to invent lights that were not there.

"I don't like waiting," Barnacle breathed, and his whiskers tickled Pip's ear. "Waiting is just standing still with your hopes up."

Then his stomach rumbled. Rumble. Rumble. Loud as a boat engine in the quiet.

"Sorry," he whispered. "All this thinking about plankton."

He slid off the pier, meaning to be silent, and made the smallest splash of his entire life. It was still an enormous splash.

Pip held their breath. The sea settled. Nothing.

Then, out in the black, Barnacle's nose bumped something soft and clear, something that had been drifting there all along, invisible as a held breath.

FWOOSH.

Blue fire bloomed under the water, silent and huge, a lantern switching on inside a cupboard the size of the sea. Barnacle yelped and spun, and every way he turned the dark lit up around him, ring after ring of cold blue flame.

"Pip!" he shouted. "The water found me back!"

And far below the light, something much larger turned, slow and curious, and looked up at them out of the deep.

s4a.text:
The great shape turned once, slow as a moon, and slid away into the dark it had come from. The rings of blue flame folded in after it, smaller and smaller, until the last one winked out like a candle pinched between fingers.

"Come up," Pip called softly. "Before you set it off again."

Barnacle hauled himself onto the pier, streaming, and flumped down beside the notebook. "I didn't touch it," he said. "Much."

Pip opened the notebook flat on the boards. {keeper_name} clicked the red torch on, just a whisper of light, and held it over the page. Pip's pencil moved fast. A bell like a clear umbrella. Trailing arms. A bloom of blue in the middle.

"Label it properly," said {keeper_name}, leaning in. "A discovery nobody can read is only half a discovery."

So Pip wrote, tongue between teeth. Bioluminescence — light made by a living thing. Plankton — the tiny drifters that sparkled when Barnacle splashed. And along the bottom, in Pip's best writing: a jelly bloom, when the jellies gather like lanterns at a window.

"There," Pip said. "Pinned down. It can't be forgotten now."

{keeper_name} took the pencil and, in the corner, drew a small round seal with enormous splashes and very surprised eyes. Barnacle inspected it, whiskers twitching.

"That's me," he said, pleased. "I look brave."

"You look surprised," said Pip.

"Bravely surprised."

They walked home along the pier, boards going creak, creak, creak, the notebook tucked safe under Pip's arm. Out in the black water, one small blue pulse bloomed, far off, saying goodnight. Pip didn't need to sketch it. The page was warm in Pip's mind, a {lantern_word} small enough to fit in a pocket, and keep.

s4b.text:
The great shape turned once, slow as a moon, and slid away into the dark it had come from. Barnacle watched it go with his chin on the boards.

"It has cousins," Pip said suddenly, closing the notebook. "{keeper_name}, doesn't it? Things that carry light the same way."

"So they say," said {keeper_name}, eyes crinkling. "Along the shore path, this time of year."

That was enough for Pip. "Come on."

They left the pier, boards going creak, creak, creak behind them, and took the shore path where the grass grew tall and salty. Barnacle galumphed along the waterline beside them, because paths, he explained, were for creatures with no flair.

Then Pip stopped.

Above the grass, a tiny green light blinked on. Off. On again. Then another. Then a dozen, drifting and winking over the dark field like slow sparks that had learned patience.

"Fireflies," Pip breathed.

One floated close, and Pip held still as a pebble while it pulsed, right beside Pip's ear. On. Off. A little lamp carried through the night, same as the jellyfish below — one in the black water, one in the black air, each making its own light out of nothing but being alive.

"You're doing it too," Pip whispered to it. "Bioluminescence."

The firefly blinked, unimpressed, and wandered off.

Down at the waterline, Barnacle reared up for a farewell. "Tell it I said—" he began, and overbalanced, and his goodbye splash went up like a fountain and came down like rain. The fireflies scattered, laughing in light, if light can laugh.

Pip laughed too, and wiped the drops off the notebook, and looked back once — at the sea, at the grass, at all those small lamps going on and off in the dark.

"Goodnight, {lantern_word}," Pip said, and carried the glow of it all the way home.

c1.question: "Do we peer into the deep end where the big water hides, or duck under the pier where the shadows keep secrets?"

options.label: The deep water past the pier's end
The shadowed pylons underneath the pier

c2.question: "Shall we pin this night down in your notebook, or chase its cousins along the shore?"

options.label: Sketch and label the discovery in the notebook
Walk the shore to look for fireflies

lantern_word.role: What Pip calls the jellyfish's light (used in the final line)

s1.text:
Come close, {listener_name}, and I will tell you something true. When I was young, I worked on a ship that sent robots down to visit the deepest, coldest, darkest neighbourhood on Earth. The deep sea trench. A place with no streetlights, no moon, no sun at all.

That night, young Dr. Okafor sat in the control room, warm cocoa in hand, eyes on the screen. Outside, the submersible {submersible_name} sank slowly down, down, down, past the very last reach of sunlight. Its robot arm, Pico, waved gently at the passing water. Pico waved at everything. It could not help itself.

The water turned black as the inside of a pocket.

Then — flash.

One tiny blue light blinked on the screen, far below. Then it was gone.

Dr. Okafor leaned in. "Did you see that?"

"See what?" said the pilot.

"A light. Down there. Where no light should be."

They rewound the camera. There it was again. Flash. One small spark of blue in all that dark, like a firefly at the bottom of the world. And then nothing.

Nobody on the ship could say what made it.

Dr. Okafor checked the clock. The {submersible_name} could only stay down so long before its batteries called it home. If they wanted to find that light, they had to look now.

"Take us down," said Dr. Okafor. "Slowly."

And down they went, into the dark, looking for the little light that had already vanished.

s2a.text:
"After it," said the pilot. "Hold on."

The {submersible_name} tipped its nose down, and down went the light trail with it. The seafloor broke open beneath them — a deep sea trench, a canyon in the dark, dropping away to nowhere.

"Look at the depth counter," whispered Dr. Okafor.

The numbers climbed and climbed. Past the tallest mountains on land. Past the deepest valleys. And still the trench went down.

"And the temperature?"

"Sinking toward freezing," said the pilot. "Colder than anywhere on Earth up top. And that little flash is down here somewhere."

Outside, Pico the robot arm waved into the black. Slowly. Gently. Hello out there, it seemed to say. Pico waved at everything. It could not help itself.

The water pressed black as the inside of a pocket.

Then — blink.

Two tiny lights, far down in the trench. Not one. Two.

"Did it just—" the pilot started.

"It answered," breathed Dr. Okafor. "It saw Pico wave. And it waved back."

The two lights hung there in the dark, small and steady, watching them. Whatever made that flash was alive. And it knew they were here.

s2b.text:
"Wait," said Dr. Okafor. "Kill the headlights. Let's see what the dark does on its own."

The pilot hesitated. "All of them?"

"All of them. Just for a minute."

Click. The {submersible_name} went dark. Outside, the black pressed in close as a held breath.

At first, nothing. Then — faint glimmers. Here and there, along the trench wall, tiny white lights began to show. Dozens of them. Hundreds. A whole hidden world clinging to the rock in the deepest place on Earth.

"Look at them all," whispered the pilot.

"An ecosystem," said Dr. Okafor softly. "Down here. Where nothing should grow."

Pico the robot arm held very still. Even Pico knew not to wave now.

And then — one light moved.

Not white. Blue. It did not cling to the rock like the others. It swam. Slow and sure, it drifted away from the wall, out into the open dark, heading their way.

"It's an animal," breathed Dr. Okafor. "It's alive. And it's coming closer."

The blue glow grew. Bigger now. Brighter. Right toward the window.

Nobody moved. Nobody spoke. The little light came on.

s3.text:
Down and down went {submersible_name}, with Pico waving at the cold black water. Then Dr. Okafor pointed at the screen. "There. What did you just find?"

A small fish drifted into the lights. It carried its own glowing blue lantern, right there on its body. Flash. Flash.

"It makes its own light," whispered Dr. Okafor. "Special chemicals inside it. That is called bioluminescence."

Beside it floated a stranger thing. A barreleye fish, with a head you could see clean through. Its eyes swivelled up inside its own clear skull, watching for food above.

"Look at that," said the pilot. "Nobody expected a window for a head."

Dr. Okafor smiled into the cocoa. "So that is the answer. Fish live where there is no sunlight because their bodies are built for it. They carry their own light. They bear the near-freezing water. They wear strange shapes that help them find food where almost nothing grows."

An adaptation, {listener_name}. A body built for the dark.

Pico reached out, slow and gentle, and waved at the little lantern fish. The fish flashed back, once, as if to say hello.

Then the clock chimed. Soft but sure.

"Batteries," said the pilot. "Time to rise."

Dr. Okafor looked at the screen, at the small blue light bobbing in the biggest, darkest neighbourhood on Earth. "We came for a mystery. We found it. Now — what proof do we carry home?"

s4a.text:
"The picture," said Dr. Okafor. "One good picture."

But the lantern fish was busy. It darted left. It darted right. Flash. Flash. It did not know it was supposed to hold still.

"Easy, Pico," whispered Dr. Okafor. "Slow."

Pico moved out, gentle as falling snow. The robot arm hovered near the little fish, not grabbing, not chasing. Just waiting. The fish turned. Its blue lantern glowed bright against the black water.

Click.

One perfect photograph. The fish's light caught mid-flash, a tiny blue star in the deepest dark.

"Got it," said the pilot.

Up they rose, up and up, until the stars came out and the deck rocked gentle beneath their feet. Dr. Okafor held the printed photograph in both hands. It was the first light she ever brought back from the deep.

And here is the true part, {listener_name}. That photograph still hangs by my bed. The little lantern fish glows blue against the black, right beside my night-light. Two small lights, keeping each other company.

We have explored only five percent of the ocean. Five percent. That means more lights are waiting down there, in the biggest, darkest neighbourhood on Earth. More little lanterns, blinking in the cold.

Maybe one night, you will go down and find one.

"Goodnight, little fish," I say to the photograph. And sometimes, I think it flashes back.

s4b.text:
"The water," said Dr. Okafor. "Bring me a bottle of the deep."

Pico reached out, slow and careful, toward the trench wall where the white creatures clung. The robot arm dipped a small glass vial into the cold black water. It filled up, dark and plain, looking like nothing at all.

"Just water?" said the pilot.

"Wait," said Dr. Okafor. "Wait and see."

Up they rose, up and up, until the ship rocked gentle beneath them and the laboratory lights glowed warm. Dr. Okafor carried the vial to the microscope. She added one drop of a special chemical. She turned off the lights.

And there it was. Faint, but true. A tiny blue glow, right there in the water. The same light-chemical the fish carried in their bodies. The whole neighbourhood glowed, even the water itself, so faint that eyes could not see it. But the machine could.

"The dark is not empty," whispered Dr. Okafor. "It is full of light we cannot see."

And here is the true part, {listener_name}. That little glass vial sits on my shelf to this day. It looks like plain dark water. But I know what hides inside. The ocean is mostly unexplored, which is exciting, because it means there is always more to find. More lights waiting in the cold, more secrets in the deep.

"Goodnight, little vial," I say. And sometimes, I think it glows back.

c1.question: "That flash is down there somewhere, friends. Do we chase it into the trench, or do we sit quiet in the dark and let it come to us?"

options.label: Follow the flash down toward the deep sea trench
Turn off the headlights and watch what the darkness does

c2.question: "We can only bring one thing home from this dive. A picture of our glowing friend — or a bottle of the deep water itself?"

options.label: Have Pico take a close-up photograph of the lantern fish
Have Pico collect a sample of the deep trench water

listener_name.role: The child being told the story, whom the storyteller addresses in the frame

submersible_name.role: The name of the submersible robot, painted on its side

stories.title: The Leg That Drew Itself Back

s1.text:
“Wake up, water-babies!”

That is {axolotl_name}, our hero, swimming upside down under a lily pad. “Breakfast time! Follow me!”

We are water-babies too, you and me. We live in the green canals of Xochimilco, where we never grow up. We keep our feathery gills forever. We keep our smiles forever. And we spend every day gliding between the brown root-curtains of the floating gardens.

{axolotl_name} swishes ahead with Shade, a speckled sibling who hides in the shadows. “Watch this!” our hero calls. Slurp! A water bug vanishes into that wide, smiling mouth. “The vacuum-gulp! Family trick!”

Shade wiggles its gills. They wave like pink underwater flowers. “And these,” Shade says proudly, “are our breathing-plumes.”

A wooden boat poles past. It is Professor Puddlejump in the Question Mark, asking the water questions out loud. “Good morning, feathery ones!”

Up on her floating garden, Doña Marisol waves a trowel. “Careful near the tall reeds, little ones. The heron likes to fish there today.”

But {axolotl_name} is already chasing a bug. “I am too fast for—”

A shadow crosses the water. A snatch! A twist! A splash!

We tumble into the reeds. {axolotl_name} pops up, grinning that built-in grin.

But one front leg is gone.

s2a.text:
“Easy,” says Shade. “Legs pop back by morning. Like a whale spout — up it comes!”

So we tuck deep into the reeds, where the roots hang down like brown spaghetti. Shade shows us the softest mud. “Best hiding spot in the canal. Nothing finds us here.”

We wait. The water goes dark, then silver, then pink.

“Morning!” {axolotl_name} wakes us with a tail-wiggle. “Watch this!”

We look. We lean closer. We look again.

Where the leg was, there is only a smooth pink nub. No toes. No bones. Just a soft little bump, like the eraser end of a pencil.

“But — it was supposed to pop!” says Shade. “Whale spout! By morning!”

A shadow slides over the reeds. It is Professor Puddlejump, peering down through a glass-bottomed bucket. Her eye fills the whole circle, huge and blinking.

“Ah!” she says. “The leg is drawing itself back in! Slowly, slowly — like a pencil line sketching toes. That takes weeks, little ones. Not one night.”

Weeks. The reeds suddenly feel very open. A heron could look straight down here.

“A slow-growing leg,” says the Professor, “needs a slow, safe, well-fed wait.” She taps the bucket. “And this, I am afraid, is not it.”

s2b.text:
“Who needs four legs?” Shade flicks its speckled tail. “I declare a one-legged hunting contest! Fastest slurper wins!”

The water bugs line up on a lily stem. They look very small and very quick.

“Go!”

{axolotl_name} lunges. The bug zips left. Our hero spins in a wobbly circle — three legs paddle, one side pushes, round and round like a leaf in a drain.

“Round one to the bug!” says Shade.

Round two: zip, gone. Round three: the bug actually waves goodbye.

“One more!” {axolotl_name} cries. “The fish-leap!”

Our hero coils, springs — and tumbles in a silly somersault, mouth wide, catching nothing but a long green ribbon of weed. It hangs from that smiling face like a moustache.

We cannot help it. We laugh. Even Shade laughs.

“All right,” Shade admits, wiping a tear from its gills. “That contest was a stinker of an idea.”

Professor Puddlejump poles past in the Question Mark, watching through her bucket. “Axolotls are not fast hunters, little ones. They are still hunters. Hold perfectly quiet — then slurp at exactly the right moment.”

Still. Our hero looks at the wobbly water, at the three paddling legs, at the empty stomach we can all feel.

“But I cannot hold still,” {axolotl_name} says quietly. “Not without somewhere steady to perch.”

s3.text:
"What did you find out there?" Shade asks, wiggling close.

Before we can answer, a voice floats down from above. "Little ones!" It is Doña Marisol, leaning over the edge of her floating garden. "I know the perfect spot. Look — under my chinampa, where the roots hang down like brown curtains. Safe and shady, with bugs drifting through all day long."

A hideout! Just what a growing axolotl needs.

We swim for the garden. But the way in is a narrow reed tunnel, and {axolotl_name} squeezes — wiggles — and stops.

Stuck. Properly stuck.

"My gills are squashed!" our hero gasps.

Shade grabs hold of that wiggly tail and pulls. Pop! Out comes {axolotl_name}, tumbling into the root-tangle. "No more tunnels for me," our hero says. "A stuck axolotl cannot hunt!"

Inside, the curtains sway. Bugs drift past, slow and dreamy. Slurp. Slurp. {axolotl_name} learns the rhythm: hold still, wait, gulp.

Every day, Professor Puddlejump poles over in the Question Mark with her bucket. "Look here!" she whispers. "A pale little bud!" Then, days later: "Bumps! Those are bones, sketching themselves in!" Then: "Toes! Tiny toes, drawing themselves back!"

The heron's shadow glides overhead once more.

This time, {axolotl_name} simply vanishes into the curtains. Smiling.

s4a.text:
"While we wait," says Professor Puddlejump, tapping her waterproof notebook, "we become students of this little castle."

And we do. We name it the {hideout_name}, because the roots hang down like brown theatre curtains. We learn that breakfast-bugs drift through at sunrise, and sleepy beetles at noon. Shade, who knows every shadow, declares one corner "the thinking spot."

Every day, the Professor sketches. "Look," she whispers. "The leg is drawing itself back in. First the pale bud, then the bones, then — see? — tiny toes, one by one."

We watch the pencil line grow. It is slow, and it is perfect.

When the last toe finishes, {axolotl_name} hosts a graduation gulp. One perfect still-slurp, right in the middle of the {hideout_name}. Shade claps its gills. "Even handsomer than the old one," Shade says.

We glide home under the flower rafts. In our hero's pocket of root-curtain, tucked safe, is the Professor's sketch: the leg, half-drawn, becoming whole.

s4b.text:
"While we wait," says Professor Puddlejump, "we could open the doors."

So we do. Shade, won over completely, brings other young axolotls to the {hideout_name}. They come wiggling through the reeds, nervous and quick. "Watch," Shade tells them. "The still-slurp works."

And who teaches them? Our hero, who was once the wobbliest hunter in the canal. {axolotl_name} floats, patient as a stone, while little ones practice holding still. "Feel the water," our hero says. "Let the bugs come to you."

Professor Puddlejump sketches it all in her notebook. "A school of stillness," she chuckles.

When the last toe finishes drawing itself in, the hero leads the first class in a synchronized graduation gulp. Six little mouths, one perfect slurp. Shade brings a gift: a fallen scarlet gill-frond feather, pressed into the roots. It reads, in axolotl, "safe water here."

We glide home under the flower rafts, carrying that feather in our pocket of root-curtain.

c1.question: Shade flicks his speckled tail and says, "A leg's a leg, little one — do we tuck into the reeds and wait for it to pop back, or do we show this canal that three legs are plenty?"

options.label: Hide in the reeds and wait for the leg to come back
Hold a one-legged hunting contest to show nothing is wrong

c2.question: Professor Puddlejump taps his notebook and asks, "The leg knows its job now — but what will you do with the waiting? Study this little castle of yours, or open its doors?"

options.label: Become students of the hideout and watch the leg finish itself
Turn the hideout into a school for other young axolotls

hideout_name.role: the root-tangle hideout under the floating garden

s1.text:
Let me tell you about the autumn my young friend {maker_name} built something out of nothing, at a kitchen table, with a pencil and a stack of graph paper.

It started on a Tuesday. {maker_name} had just finished the first level of a favorite game — the kind with a little hero, {hero_sprite}, who hops across platforms collecting {collectible}. Nothing unusual there. But this time, {maker_name} put the controller down and sat very still.

"Grandma Rhea," {maker_name} said. "That level never told me anything. Not one word of instructions. And somehow I knew exactly what to do."

Grandma Rhea looked up from her tea. She does not play games. She has never held a controller in her life. But she pulled her chair closer, the way she does when something interesting is about to happen.

"Show me," she said.

So {maker_name} started the level again. And there it was — a low wall, just high enough that you had to jump. No sign. No arrow. Just a wall you could not walk past, so your fingers figured it out on their own. And right past the wall, a coin floated in the air, placed exactly where your jump would land. You did not read about jumping. You jumped, and the game caught you, and the coin said: yes, like that.

"The whole level is a tutorial," {maker_name} said, "but it never says so. It just... teaches you by letting you play."

Grandma Rhea sipped her tea. "Why did that sparkle?" she asked, pointing at the screen.

{maker_name} grinned. "That's the reward. The game gives you something small and good every time you get it right, so your hands want to try the next thing."

{maker_name} pulled out the graph paper. Blank squares, hundreds of them, waiting.

"I want to make one," {maker_name} said. "A level that teaches like that. No instructions at all."

Grandma Rhea poured more tea. "Then we had better get comfortable."

s2a.text:
"How it moves," said {maker_name}. "Before it looks like anything, it has to feel like something."

Maya nodded, like that was the right answer. "Then you get to do what every big studio does first. You build the ugliest version of the game on purpose."

So {maker_name} opened a blank project and made one small grey square on a plain dark screen. No hero. No scarf. Just a square that could run left, run right, and jump when you pressed the button.

"That's the whole game?" Grandma Rhea asked, setting down two cups of tea.

"That's the whole game," Maya said. "For now. It's called a grey-box. If a plain square is fun to move, everything you build on top will be fun too."

{maker_name} pressed jump. The square rose, hung in the air a moment too long, and drifted down like a leaf. It worked. It was not fun.

"It feels floaty," {maker_name} said.

"Then change one number," Maya said, pointing at the screen. "Jump height. That's it. One number."

{maker_name} typed a smaller number. The square hopped — quick, low, a neat little pop. Then a bigger number, and it sailed nearly off the screen. They tried numbers back and forth until the jump rose fast and came down faster, with a soft thud you could almost feel in your thumbs.

"There," Maya said. "That's the mechanic. One thing done well is worth ten things done badly."

Grandma Rhea leaned closer, wrapping her hands around her cup. "Why did that one feel nice? The hop. Why is a hop nice?"

{maker_name} opened their mouth to answer, and stopped. The square sat on the screen, waiting. The jump felt good now — {maker_name}'s thumbs knew it. But nobody in the kitchen could say why.

s2b.text:
"How it looks," said {maker_name}. "If I'm going to spend weeks on this, I want to love looking at it."

"Fair," Maya said. "Then you're doing what the old pixel artists did. One square at a time."

{maker_name} opened a grid on the screen — tiny boxes, like the graph paper, only these could hold color. Zoomed all the way in, the hero was nothing but a scatter of squares. One dark square for an eye. Two pointed ones for ears. A row of warm orange down the back, and a single red line underneath that, zoomed out, became a scarf in the wind.

"It's a mosaic," {maker_name} said. "Every pixel placed on purpose."

"Why is the scarf red?" Grandma Rhea asked, settling in with her tea.

"So your eye finds it," {maker_name} said. "Even when the hero is tiny, the scarf tells you which way you're moving."

Dev from the club leaned in the doorway, home from school. "What does the fox collect?"

"{collectible}," {maker_name} said, and Dev grinned like that was exactly right.

Then came the paper. {maker_name} drew level one in pencil, one square at a time. A flat start, so your fingers could learn to walk. Then a gap — exactly one jump wide, no wider. And past the gap, the first of the {collectible}, drawn floating precisely where a jump would carry you. You would not read about jumping. You would jump, and the game would catch you, and the jar would say: yes, like that.

"The level is the tutorial," {maker_name} said. "It just never says so."

Grandma Rhea studied the maze of penciled squares for a long moment.

"It looks lovely, dear. But tell me — why would anyone play it twice?"

The pencil stopped. The kitchen went very quiet, because nobody had an answer.

s3.text:
That Saturday, the game club met in the school library, and the level was ready. A whole first level, playable, built from everything the week had taught. {maker_name} slid the laptop across the table. "Dev, you try first."

Dev cracked his knuckles like a professional. {hero_sprite} hopped onto the screen, and off they went — over the low wall, past the first ledge, collecting {collectible} as they went. Then came the gap over the pit. Dev jumped. Down went {hero_sprite}. Dev jumped again. Down again. The third time, Dev laughed — but it was a thin laugh, and he pushed the laptop back. "I'm just bad at this," he said. "You play."

The room went quiet. Grandma Rhea, who had brought her tea in a thermos because she refused to miss the big day, poured a cup and set it beside {maker_name}.

"He jumped wrong," {maker_name} said. But the words came out slow, like feet testing ice.

Grandma Rhea blew on her tea. "Three times wrong? At the very same spot?" She tilted her head. "That's not a boy problem, love. That's a wall problem. Show me what you just found."

So {maker_name} looked at the level the way its maker should. The landing platform sat one square too far. Nobody had told Dev where to leap from. {maker_name} dragged the platform closer, and right at the edge of the pit, placed one of the {collectible} — floating exactly where a good jump begins. A signpost that says, without words: from here.

"Dev. One more go."

Dev sighed, sat down, ran at the gap — and sailed clean across. First try.

"See?" said Grandma Rhea, raising her cup. "The level learned to teach."

s4a.text:
That night, {maker_name} opened the sound box. A voice, Grandma Rhea had said. What if every {collectible} had one? At the library maker space, headphones on, {maker_name} gave each jar a note, one step higher than the last. Bloop. Bloop. Bloop. Five in a row, and the jars played a tiny melody — a song of your own success, and you never knew you were making it.

Then the sparkle. A soft golden puff when a jar was caught, and a little counter in the corner, ticking up. Goal, jump, chime, sparkle, count. New goal. The loop clicked shut, warm as a locket.

"Again," said Grandma Rhea, and she hummed the little tune back, wrong but happy.

At the club, a younger kid wandered over. Never seen the game. No instructions. They watched the wall, and jumped. They followed the jar, and leapt. They heard the notes climb and chased the next one, grinning at the music they didn't know they were making. The level taught them everything.

Ms. Okafor printed the level map and pinned it on the club wall. Grandma Rhea listened to the chimes, and said softly, "That's why you go back."

And that is how {maker_name} went home with a creased graph-paper map in one pocket and a song in the other, knowing they had not just made a game. They had designed fun itself — the kind that says well done without a single word.

s4b.text:
That night, {maker_name} tore up level two. A ladder, Grandma Rhea had said. So the level became a staircase — not a cliff. The first step taught one small hop. The second asked for the same hop, a little higher. The third put a jar over a gap, and the jump you already knew carried you across. Every new skill shook hands with an old one.

Then, the answering back. Every {collectible} got a small sparkle when it was caught, and a counter in the corner, ticking up. One, two, three. The game saying, in its own quiet way: I saw that.

At the club showcase, Dev played the whole thing, start to finish, without one word of help. Nobody told him anything. The level told him everything.

A visiting kid watched, mouth open. "How did the game know what to teach me next?"

{maker_name} looked at the staircase on the screen and felt something settle into place, like a key turning. The level itself was the teacher they had set out to build. It had been the teacher all along.

Ms. Okafor pinned the map on the club wall. Grandma Rhea asked for a printout of {hero_sprite}, mid-leap, and framed it for the kitchen wall, right beside the kettle. "So I can see the little champion," she said, "while the tea brews."

And that is how {maker_name} came home with a pixel portrait for the fridge and eyes that had changed for good — eyes that now read every game the way its makers do, finding the gentle teacher hiding inside level one.

c1.question: Maya spins her chair around and grins: "Every game starts as a question — 'is this fun?' So what do you want to build first: how it moves, or how it looks?"

options.label: Build the plain prototype first — a square that runs and jumps, to find the fun before the art
Design the pixel hero and sketch level one on graph paper first, like an architect's plan

c2.question: Grandma Rhea sets down her tea, watches Dev collect three things in total silence, and asks: "The game works, dear — so why does it feel like nobody's saying well done? What will you give it: a voice, or a ladder?"

options.label: Build the reward loop through sound — a rising note for every collectible, so success plays a melody
Build the reward loop through structure — a staircase of levels where each new skill shakes hands with the old ones

maker_name.role: The 12-year-old maker at the center of the story

hero_sprite.role: The little character in the game being built
hero_sprite.default: a fox with a red scarf

collectible.role: The thing the hero collects in the game

s1.text:
The tide is coming in, and Dr. Okafor is kneeling at the edge of it, shining a small red light into a rock pool. "Look," she whispers. "The anemones open when the Moon pulls the water high. The crabs know it too. The whole beach keeps the Moon's time."

We crouch beside her. The water creeps up the sand in a scalloped line, like the hem of a dress being lifted, and the full Moon hangs over the sea, enormous and yellow.

"Beautiful, isn't it," says a voice behind us. "I still can't get over it."

It's Commander Ruth. Retired astronaut. She has been to that Moon, and she sits down in the sand with us like it's her favourite chair.

"How far away is it?" we ask.

"Watch." She tips a bag of marbles into her palm. "If the Earth were this big," she says, holding up one blue marble, "the Moon would be this big." A small grey one. "And the distance between them would be..." She lays the blue marble down, then paces along the beach, setting marbles in the sand one by one. Thirty of them, in a long gleaming line. "Thirty Earths away. That's how far I flew."

We stare down the line of marbles. Thirty Earths.

"Here's the thing," Ruth says, and her voice drops to a half-whisper, like she's telling us a secret she still half doesn't believe. "My rocket is fueled. She's waiting at the pad, right now, tonight. Nobody goes anymore. But I could. We could." She looks at us, eyes wide. "The tide turns in an hour. If we're going, we go before it does."

The Moon shines down on the long line of marbles, and waits.

s2a.text:
Ruth leads us up the beach to where the rocket waits, tall and silver in the moonlight. "What do we call her?" she asks. We tell her. "{rocket_name}," she repeats, grinning. "Perfect. Climb in."

We strap into seats that smell of metal and old leather. Ruth counts down, her voice steady. "Three. Two. One."

The rocket shakes awake beneath us. It is not loud. It is deep, a rumble that starts in our toes and climbs up our spines. Then, suddenly, silence. Earth falls away.

For three days we float. Ruth shows us how to drink from bubbles that wobble in the air, how to sleep strapped to the wall. We watch our planet shrink. First it is a blue marble, then a thumbprint, then a bright coin behind us. Ahead, the Moon grows. It fills the window until we can see the grey seas, dark and smooth.

"That one," Ruth whispers, pointing. "The Sea of Tranquility. That's where we're going."

She touches the glass. "I still can't believe we did this. Thirty Earths away, and we just... went."

The Moon waits, enormous and grey and close enough to touch.

s2b.text:
Ruth shakes her head. "Not yet. First, you need to hear how it really sounded."

She drives us to Houston, to a room full of glowing buttons and a screen as big as a house. A man named Gene meets us there. He has kind eyes and a vest covered in pins.

"This is where we sat," he says, "when Eagle landed. Listen."

He plays a tape. It crackles. A voice counts down fuel. "Sixty seconds." An alarm blares. "Thirty seconds." The voice is calm, but we hear the tightness underneath. "Contact light. Okay, engine stop."

Then, crackling across thirty Earths: "Houston, Tranquility Base here. The Eagle has landed."

Gene wipes his eyes. "We almost ran out of fuel. Almost had to call it off. But we didn't."

We board the rocket with those voices in our ears. Launch shakes us loose from Earth, and for three days we coast. Gene's steady voice comes over the radio sometimes, checking in. We watch Earth shrink to a blue marble, then a thumbprint. The Moon grows until it fills the window, grey seas spreading out below us.

"Now you're ready," Ruth whispers. "Now you know what it took."

The Sea of Tranquility waits below, dark and smooth and real.

s3.text:
"Whatever you just found," Ruth whispers, "hold onto it. Because where we're going, nothing changes. Ever."

The lunar module detaches with a soft, mechanical clunk. We are falling toward the grey. Suddenly, yellow lights flash across the console. Alarms beep, sharp and fast. 

"Program alarm," a voice crackles in our headsets. It is Gene, from mission control, on the old tape. "Fuel at sixty seconds."

Ruth's eyes go wide. Her hands fly over the switches. "Just like my first time," she breathes. She grips the joystick. The computer stops flying. Ruth flies.

Grey dust swirls beneath the triangular windows, kicked up by our engine. It billows like flour spilled across a dark counter. 

"Thirty seconds," Gene counts.

The dust settles. We touch down with a gentle, bouncing thump. 

Silence. Total, absolute silence.

Ruth unbuckles her straps. Her hands are shaking, but she is grinning. "Welcome to the Sea of Tranquility."

We open the hatch. We climb down the ladder and step out. The ground is soft, a deep grey powder. We do not walk here. We bounce. Slow, floating kangaroo hops. 

Ruth points to a patch of undisturbed dust. "Look."

Bootprints. Crisp, sharp, and perfect. 

"Apollo," Ruth whispers. "Those prints will last a million years. There is no wind to blow them away. No rain to wash them flat."

We look at our own feet. We have left prints too, right beside theirs. 

Ruth turns to us, her helmet reflecting the blue Earth. "We have time for one moonwalk. What should we do with it?"

s4a.text:
"The laser," we say. "Let's measure it."

Ruth grins, wide and bright. "Good choice."

We bounce across the grey dust to a small, portable station. Ruth unfolds a tripod and aims a thin tube toward the Apollo mirrors, left behind years ago. "The mirrors are still there," she whispers. "Waiting."

She presses a button. A green beam shoots out, thin as a thread. We watch it race across the black sky, strike the Moon, and bounce back. A timer on the console blinks: 2.5 seconds.

"There and home again," Ruth says, her voice full of wonder. "The Moon is drifting away from us, crew. A few centimeters every year. But tonight, we measured it. We caught it in the act."

We fly home. The Pacific Ocean rises to meet us, moonlit and silver. We splash down with a great, soft whoosh, and the waves rock us gently.

Later, on a hilltop, Dr. Okafor meets us. She hands us a small card. It shows the time our laser took: 2.5 seconds.

"Proof," she says, smiling. "You measured the Moon's slow goodbye."

We hold the card tight. The Moon is leaving, centimeter by centimeter. But tonight, we reached it.

s4b.text:
"The bootprint," we say. "And a stone."

Ruth nods, her eyes shining. "Then let's make it count."

We bounce over to the Apollo prints, crisp and perfect in the dust. Carefully, we lift our boot and press it down beside theirs. One new print, sharp and clear, next to the old ones.

Then we kneel and pick up one small, smooth grey pebble. It fits in our palm, cool and heavy.

"A piece of the Moon," Ruth whispers. "To carry home."

We fly back. The Earth grows big and blue in the window. We splash down in the Pacific, and the waves rock us gently.

Weeks later, we are in a backyard, wrapped in blankets. The full Moon hangs overhead. Slowly, Earth's shadow creeps across it, turning it a deep, coppery red.

"An eclipse," Ruth breathes.

We hold up our grey pebble. In the red moonlight, it glows almost the same color.

"You brought the Moon home," Ruth says softly.

We sip our {eclipse_snack}, warm and sweet, and watch the red Moon shine. The journey is over. But the Moon is still with us.

c1.question: "Here's the thing, crew — a rocket ride is only half the story. Do you want to climb straight aboard and feel her wake up under you, or stop at mission control first and hear how the landing really sounded, alarms and all?"

options.label: Climb straight aboard the rocket and launch immediately
Visit mission control first to hear the real landing tapes and meet the ground crew

c2.question: "One moonwalk, crew, and then we go home. We can aim the laser at the mirrors Apollo left behind and measure the Moon itself — or we can add one bootprint next to theirs and pick one small stone to carry back. Which is it?"

options.label: Fire the laser at the Apollo mirrors and measure the Moon's slow drift
Leave one bootprint beside the Apollo prints and bring one grey pebble home to an eclipse night

rocket_name.role: The name of the rocket that carries us

eclipse_snack.role: The treat shared on blankets during the lunar eclipse ending

stories.title: The Long Way Round the Sun

s1.text:
The tide is going out when we reach the beach, and the whole shore is shining. Puddles everywhere — long ones, round ones, one shaped almost exactly like a whale.

"Quick," says the kite surfer, and her name is Wren, which is a good name for someone who spends her life in the wind. "Before the sun gets higher. Look."

We kneel beside the whale-shaped pool. And there it is — faint little wisps, rising off the water. Steam. From a puddle.

"Is it hot?" we ask.

"Feel," says Wren.

We dip our fingers in. Warm as bathwater. Warm as the cat's spot on the sofa.

"The sun did that already," Wren says. "And here's the part I love. The light warming this pool left the sun eight minutes ago. Eight whole minutes, flying through space, and then — plop — it lands here, in this puddle, on this beach, and gets straight to work."

"What work?" we ask.

"Lifting." She points at the wisps. "Solar energy, turning water into air. That's the water cycle starting, right under our noses. That steam will be a cloud by lunchtime."

We watch the little wisps rise and vanish. Rise and vanish.

Then Wren's brass watch — battered, enormous, older than all of us put together — gives a tick so loud we both jump.

"Sea breeze," she says, grinning. "Right on time. The sun heats the land, the land heats the air, and the air starts to move. That's my ride." She looks out at her little sailboat, {our_vessel}, bobbing at the end of the jetty. "Want to see where the warmth goes next?"

Yes. Yes, we do.

s2a.text:
Wren pulls the sail tight, and {our_vessel} leans into the wind. We are flying across the bay, the water glittering so bright it makes us blink.

"Feel that?" Wren shouts over the rushing air. "That's the sun, pushing!"

We laugh, because it sounds like a joke. But then we look at the sail — curved tight as a drum — and we feel the boat leap forward. The wind is invisible, but it is strong enough to carry us.

"The sun heated the land," Wren explains, her hands busy with the ropes. "Warm air rose. Cool air rushed in to take its place. That's all wind is — the atmosphere moving, because the sun told it to."

We watch the steam from the pools drift up and become clouds. We watch the clouds cast shadows that race across the water. And we feel the same sun that warmed the puddles now filling our sail, pushing us toward the farmland shimmering on the horizon.

Wren's watch ticks, loud and important. She grins. "Right on time," she says. "The sun is never late."

We are small, and the bay is wide, and the wind is doing exactly what the sun wants. We hold on tight, and we let it carry us.

s2b.text:
We kick off our shoes and wade into the warm shallows. The water is bathwater-warm, and the sand squishes between our toes.

"Watch," says Wren, and she runs back to her kite.

We stand at the tide line, the water lapping at our ankles, and we watch her go. The kite pulls her across the bay, fast and bright, a wedge of color against the blue. She is riding the very wind the sun has been stirring all morning.

From here, we can see the whole thing at once. The steaming pools behind us. The moving air in front of us. Wren's sail, a bright triangle, catching the sun-built breeze.

"The sun heated the land," we say, remembering. "The land heated the air. The air started to move."

And there it is — the connection. The steam rises from the pools, becomes clouds, becomes wind. The wind pushes Wren's kite. The sun is doing all of it, all at once, all around us.

We walk up the coast path toward the farmland, the warm sand giving way to warm earth. Wren's watch ticks, loud and important, from her pocket. We don't need to look. We know the sun is right on time.

s3.text:
The farm sits in a wide green valley, and the farmer is waiting at the gate as if she knew we were coming. Maybe she did. Wren's watch has been ticking importantly for the last half mile.

"You made it," the farmer says. Her name is Lark, and her hands are rough as toast. "Quick, before the light changes. Hold out your hands."

We hold them out. She drops one small wheat grain into our palms.

"Crush it," she says. "Go on."

We press it between our thumbs and it cracks open, and the smell rises up — warm and golden, like bread just thinking about becoming bread.

"That," says Lark, "is bottled sunshine. Green plants catch solar energy and turn it into food. Every stalk in this field is doing it right now, all day, all summer." She waves at the horizon, where the wheat glows and glows. "The climate gives us the season. The sun does the rest."

We look at the little crushed grain. Warm. Small. Ordinary.

"But how?" we ask. "How can this be the same thing that steamed the sea and filled a sail?"

Lark grins. "That's the question, isn't it? The light goes higher from here, and stranger. Up through the pass, toward the top of the world." She points. "Two ways up. The slow path through the meadow, or the steep one along the ridge. Which do you fancy?"

s4a.text:
The path climbs and climbs, and the air turns cold and thin, but the sun on our faces is hot as a held hand. At the pass, the weather scientist is waiting, wrapped in a red scarf. "Quick," she says. "Before the evening chill. Look at this rock."

We look. One side is bare and warm. The other wears a dusting of snow.

"Same rock," she says. "Two different weathers. The sun hits one side straight on, and the other at a slant, and the angle changes everything." She presses a small dark panel into our hands — a solar panel, cool and smooth — and tips it toward the light. The dial leaps. We shout, because we cannot help it.

Inside her little station, wrapped in blankets, we study her graph: a whole year of temperature, climbing and falling like a slow wave. "The Earth is tilted," she says. "So one half gets its summer while the other gets winter. Same sun. Different lean."

Her watch — no, Wren's watch, ticking in Wren's pocket all this time — gives its most important tick yet. Outside, on the ridge, a tiny beacon blinks, powered by nothing but daylight.

"It'll blink all winter," she says. "On saved sunshine."

Before we go, she presses a stone into our hands, flat and grey and warm from the sun-side of a rock. We carry it down the mountain, and it holds its heat the whole way, like it doesn't want to let the day go either.

s4b.text:
We ride north and north, until the snow starts, and the glaciologist meets us where the marker flags begin. The sun here never climbs. It hangs low all day, golden and tired, and our shadows stretch long and blue across the ice.

"Endless sunshine," she says, "and the ice never melts. Feel it." We press our palms to the snow. Cold as the inside of a freezer, even at noon.

"The light arrives at such a slant up here," she says, "that it spreads out thin, like butter scraped over too much bread. Same sun as your valley. Hardly any warmth per patch. That's why climates differ — the tilt of the whole planet, deciding who gets the straight light and who gets the slant."

We walk the flag line and back before dark, and the low sun skims the ice at its goldenest, and for a moment the whole white field glows like the top of a lantern.

On the dark sail home, Wren points at the moon, silvering the waves. "That's the sun too," she says. "Bounced off the moon, following us into the night."

We think about that. Wind, warmth, bread, snow — one sun, working on one atmosphere, all along. In our pocket, the wheat grain rides home, wrapped in its twist of paper. Sunshine, caught and kept.

c1.question: "The breeze is waking up, right on time. Do you want to feel it from my boat, or watch it work from the warm sand?"

options.label: Ride out on the sailboat to feel the sun-built wind fill the sail
Walk the tide line and watch the kite and sail show the wind's shape from land

c2.question: "This grain's sunshine, caught and kept. But the light goes stranger from here — up into the thin cold air, or all the way to where it never sets. Which would you see?"

options.label: Go up to the mountain pass to see how the angle of sunlight splits the world
Travel to the far north to see sunlight too slanted to melt the ice

our_vessel.role: The small sailboat the kite surfer takes us out on

s1.text:
The Deep-Space Messenger pressed a finger to the map, and a tiny light blinked back, far out past everything. "That's Voyager 2," she said. "A probe. A robot ship we sent to visit the planets, and it did, every one, and now it's been alone out there for twelve years. Its instruments are going quiet. Before they do, someone ought to say hello." She looked at you. "Happy birthday, actually. Will you take it?"

You would.

The ship waited with a glass dome over the top like a bubble, and it was called {ship_name}. You climbed in, the Messenger tucked the message in beside you — {probe_gift} — and the whole station let go with a soft, deep hum.

Up you went.

Earth shrank. First it was the whole sky, then a blue marble you could hide behind your thumb, then just a bright star like all the others, except it wasn't like the others at all.

"Well, hello out there," said a voice, warm and crackly, like a radio left on in the next room. "Probe Pilot speaking. I'll be flying this bus. Old Voyager's got a head start, but we've got the faster ship and the better snacks." A pause, full of static. "First entry in your notebook, kid. That blue star back there? One moon. Write it down. One's where everybody starts."

s2a.text: Jupiter fills the whole dome, striped like a jawbreaker, and the Cloud Cartographer climbs aboard with her pencils tucked behind one ear. She smells like graphite and peppermint. "Look at that," she says, pointing at the Great Red Spot. "A storm bigger than your whole world. It's been spinning since before your grandmother's grandmother was born." You press your hand to the glass. The crimson clouds swirl slow and thick, like tomato soup when you stir it, and you can see smaller storms inside it, tumbling like berries in the mix. "How do you map something that never stops moving?" you ask. She grins and opens her notebook. "Carefully. And fast." Her pencil scratches. "Fourteen moons so far, kiddo," crackles the Probe Pilot. "Write 'em down." The Cartographer looks up. "We can dive closer to the storm's edge, feel the wind in our teeth, or swing out to Saturn and walk the rings. Which way?"

s2b.text: Saturn hangs there like a toy, yellow and quiet, and the Ring Shepherd meets you at the edge with boots that grip the ice. The rings aren't solid at all. They're chunks of ice, some as big as houses, tumbling past in a slow parade that catches the light. "Watch this," the Shepherd says, and points. A tiny moon zips through the gap, sweeping the path clean like a snowplow on a winter street. "That's how the rings stay neat." You reach out and touch a passing berg. It's cold and rough, like the inside of a freezer, and it hums against your palm. "Sixty-two moons," crackles the Probe Pilot. "Write it down." The Shepherd stamps her boots. "We can walk the ice bridge into the ring plane, right into the thick of it, or keep pushing out to the blue giant. What do you say?"

s3.text:
"So," the Probe Pilot crackled, warm as ever. "What did you find back there?"

Whatever it was, it went into the notebook, and the ship hummed on, out past the place where the sun still looked like a sun.

"Next stop, the red one," said the Pilot. "Mars. Whole planet the color of an old penny."

Mars rolled up under the dome, rusty and round, and on it sat a volcano so wide it would take all day to walk around the bottom of it. "Olympus Mons," the Pilot said. "Biggest mountain anybody knows about. And look there—two little moons. Phobos and Deimos. Lumpy as potatoes, both of them. Write it down, kid. Two more for the collection."

Two more. The count in the notebook was growing.

Then Venus, shining like a lantern, wrapped in thick gold clouds. "Pretty, isn't it? But that one's backwards. Spins the wrong way, slow as you like. A day there lasts longer than a year." A static chuckle. "No moons. Not one. Venus travels alone."

And last, little Mercury, gray as the ash in a fireplace, close enough to the sun that one side sizzles while the other side freezes. "No moons there either. Too close to the sun to hang on to anything."

The ship turned its nose outward, and the sun shrank behind them, smaller and smaller, until it was just the brightest star in the window.

"That's the inner worlds," the Pilot said softly. "Rock and fire and empty. And your blue marble, back there with its one moon. Funny, isn't it. The only one with oceans. The only one with anybody waving goodbye."

The notebook felt heavier already. Out ahead, the dark was waiting, and it was full of moons.

s4a.text:
"Neptune," the Probe Pilot whispered, static soft as snow. "Last stop. Hang on to your hat."

The planet filled the dome, blue as a gas flame, and clouds of white streaked across it faster than anything on Earth. "Fastest winds in the whole family," the Pilot said. "Fourteen moons, kid. Fourteen. Write 'em down."

Your pencil moved. The count in the notebook had never been so big.

Then you saw it. A tiny silver thing, tumbling slow, with a dish antenna big as a dinner table. Voyager 2.

"She's listening," the Pilot said. "Send it."

You pressed the button, and the recording of Earth ocean waves went out into the dark. For a long moment, nothing. Then a beep. Then another. Then a picture came back across the years, Neptune's white streaks seen from up close, one last look.

"She says thank you," the Pilot said, and the static sounded like a smile. "She'll carry that song forever now."

You wrote fourteen in the notebook, and under it, one more line: Voyager 2, still traveling.

The ship turned for home. In your pocket, the recording of the wind played soft, a new sound for your collection, and the Probe Pilot hummed an old astronaut song all the way back.

"Not bad for a birthday," you said.

"Not bad at all," said the Pilot. "Happy birthday, kid."

s4b.text:
"Neptune," the Probe Pilot said, and for once there was no crackle in the voice. "End of the line."

The planet was blue and huge and streaked with white, and the winds there could outrun a jet plane. "Fourteen moons," the Pilot said. "Count 'em if you can."

You counted. Fourteen. The notebook was full of numbers now, and every number was a world.

Then the Deep-Space Messenger leaned forward. In her hand was a small glass vial, and inside it, ocean water from home. "Voyager's been carrying a message from Earth all these years," she said. "Time we gave her the thing itself."

You watched the vial go, a tiny sparkle across the dark, into the probe's sample collector. Voyager 2 beeped once, and sent back a picture.

It was Earth. From that far out, it was just a pale blue dot, small as the period at the end of a sentence.

"That's everybody," the Pilot said quietly. "Everybody you ever knew, right there on that dot."

You looked a long time. Then you wrote fourteen in the notebook, and under it: one home.

The ship turned around. In your pocket was a photograph, the whole solar system family portrait, and the Probe Pilot was humming, warm and crackly, all the way back.

"She's not alone anymore," you said.

"Never was," said the Messenger. "She had us."

c1.question: "We've got fuel for one good look, kiddo—do we chase the biggest storm in the solar system at Jupiter, or do we skate out to walk on Saturn's icy rings?"

options.label: Dive into Jupiter's Great Red Spot
Walk the bridge through Saturn's ring system

c2.question: "Voyager's listening, but she's tired. Do we send her the song of Earth oceans to carry forever, or do we give her the water itself to hold?"

options.label: Play the recording of Earth waves

sets_slots.probe_gift: a recording of Earth ocean waves

options.label: Pour the vial of Earth ocean into the collector

probe_gift.role: The specific message or object carried to Voyager 2
probe_gift.default: a recording of Earth ocean waves

s1.text:
The coding club room smells like pencil shavings and hamster. In the corner, Hammy runs on his wheel. Squeak. Squeak. Squeak. Around and around he goes, and he never gets anywhere, and he never seems to mind.

We are trying to get somewhere. On our screen, a little robot sprite stands in front of a treasure door, and floating beside the door is a golden key. It shines. It waits. It does not move, because neither does Zap.

"Pick up the key," we tell the computer. We even say please.

Zap stands there.

"Pick up the key!" we say, louder, the way you'd say it to a dog who is pretending not to hear.

Zap stands there some more. His little pixel face does not even blink.

"Why won't he DO anything?" we ask.

Ms. Bit, who runs coding club and wears sneakers with lightning bolts on them, leans over our shoulder. "Because a computer can't guess," she says. "It only does exactly what you type. Not almost what you type. Exactly."

"So we have to tell him everything?"

"Everything," she says. "In his language. That's what code is — commands a machine can follow."

We look at Zap. Zap looks at the key. Somewhere in his little robot head, we are pretty sure, he is waiting for us to get it right.

s2a.text:
"Every step," we say. "We can do that."

We start typing. "Pick up the key." Zap's arm moves. "Pick up the key," we type again. His other arm moves. "Pick up the key." His fingers wiggle. "Pick up the key." His left foot slides forward.

"How many was that?" we ask.

Hammy squeaks. Squeak. Squeak. We lose count.

"Pick up the key," we type again, and then, because our fingers are getting tired, "drop the key."

Zap drops it. The key clatters to the floor, spins once, and stops.

"No, wait, pick it up again," we type, but Zap is already walking. He walks right past the key, right past the door, and bumps into the wall. Bump. Bump. Bump.

"He can't stop," Ms. Bit says, "because you haven't told him to."

We look at the screen. Zap is still bumping. The key is still on the floor. And we have typed so many commands we can't remember which ones worked.

s2b.text:
"A loop," we say. "Let's use a loop."

Ms. Bit shows us the command. "Repeat," we type, "pick up the key."

Zap picks up the key. Then he picks it up again. Then he picks it up again. Then he starts spinning in circles, holding the key out like a trophy, faster and faster.

"Stop," we type. Zap keeps spinning.

"STOP," we type, louder. Zap spins faster. The key is a golden blur.

In the corner, Hammy starts running in his wheel. Squeak. Squeak. Squeak. Faster and faster, like he's trying to keep up.

"Why won't he stop?" we ask.

"Because a loop repeats forever," Ms. Bit says, "unless you tell it when to stop. And you didn't."

Zap spins. Hammy runs. The key flashes. We are all going in circles, and none of us knows how to make it end.

s3.text:
Ms. Bit pulls up a chair. It rolls. It always rolls. "Okay," she says. "Show me what you actually told him. Not what you meant to tell him. What you told him."

We lean in close. Our older sibling leans in too, and reads the code out loud, slowly, like a recipe.

"Loop," they say. "Do the thing. Check for the key."

"And?" says Ms. Bit.

"And... keep going."

Hammy squeaks in the corner. Around and around.

We stare at the screen. We read it again, out loud this time, because hearing it is different than seeing it. "Keep going... keep going..."

Wait.

"There's no stop," we whisper. "We never told him when to stop."

"There's an 'if' missing," says our sibling. "Or it's upside down."

Ms. Bit grins, and her lightning-bolt sneakers tap the floor. Tap tap. "Now you're hearing it," she says. "A loop without the right 'if' is a hamster wheel. It runs forever, and it never once checks for the key."

We look at Zap. Zap looks at the key. The key shines.

"So what did you find?" Ms. Bit asks. "Tell me."

s4a.text:
"The 'if' is backwards," we say. "It checks if Zap is holding the key before it tells him to pick it up."

"So flip it," says Ms. Bit.

We type the fix. Loop. Do the thing. If you see the key, grab it. Then stop.

Zap moves. He walks. He bends. He picks up the golden key, and it fits the lock like it was always meant to. Click. The door swings open.

Behind it is not treasure. It is a screen full of buttons and sliders, and one says JUMP HEIGHT. We drag it up. Zap leaps so high he bonks the top of the screen and giggles. Actually giggles.

"You just designed a game level," says Ms. Bit. She hands us a sticker shaped like a moth. "Bug of the Week. Because a bug is just a discovery wearing a disguise."

We stick it on our sleeve. We are never taking it off.

s4b.text:
"The 'if' is backwards," we say. "It checks if Zap is holding the key before he picks it up."

"So flip it," says Ms. Bit.

We type the fix. Loop. Do the thing. If you see the key, grab it. Then stop.

Zap moves. He walks. He bends. He picks up the golden key, and it turns in the lock like it was always meant to. Click. The door swings open.

Behind it is not treasure. It is a message box, blinking. A note from our friend across town pops onto the screen. "Did you fix it?" it says.

"We did," we type back. "Zap finally listened."

Ms. Bit prints our fixed code and hands it to us like a certificate. "Show your family," she says. "Tell them you found the bug, and the bug found you back."

We fold the paper carefully. It goes in the front pocket, where the important things live.

c1.question: "You could type out every single step for Zap, one command at a time, or you could try using a loop to repeat the action. Which way feels right to you?"

options.label: Write every command one by one without a loop
Use a loop command to repeat the action

c2.question: "The door is open! Do you want to see how Zap can jump higher and design your own game level, or shall we use this code to send a message to a friend's computer?"

options.label: Explore game design by changing Zap's jump height
Use the fixed program to send a message to a friend

stories.title: The Meadow Behind Grandpa Milo's House

s1.text:
Grandpa Milo sits down on the back step with his cup of warm milk. We sit down beside him, you and me, and the garden has gone soft and blue.
"Smell that," he says. "Warm grass and wet leaves. That is a firefly smell if ever there was one."
"When I was small there was a whole meadow behind our house. Every night that June I asked: are they here yet? And every night the same answer. Not yet. Soon.
Then one evening the air went still and sweet, and I was out through the gate with my shoes half on.
The meadow was grey green, and not one light in it. Not one. But it felt ready, the way a room feels ready before the cake comes in.
So I stopped in the gateway and looked round, because out there you get everything by sitting still and nothing by running about. The only question was where a boy ought to sit."

s2a.text:
"The wall, then. An old stone wall ran along the top of the meadow, and those stones had been drinking sun all day.
I climbed up and sat down, and the warmth came through my trousers like sitting where the cat has just been.
From up there I could look down the whole meadow to the black line of the woods.
So I waited.
A moth came at my face and I let it go by. The sky went from blue to grey to almost nothing at all.
Nothing yet.
And then, far off by the woods, one small green light came on.
Only one.
I leaned forward. It floated up, went out, and came on again a little higher, as if it had climbed two stairs I could not see.
Then one came on just below the wall, close enough to touch, and I kept my hands flat on the stone and let it drift past my knee."

s2b.text:
"The grass, then. I waded down into the middle, where the grass came up past my chest and closed over behind me and made a little green room with nobody in it but me.
I lay back and let the grass hold me up like a hand.
Down at that level I could look at a snail asleep on a stem, a beetle climbing another one, and the smell of warm hay right against my face.
Nothing lit up. Not yet. I waited.
Then something switched on beside my cheek.
A small green light, so close that I could see the little dark body holding on to the grass stem with its feet. It came on smooth, like a lamp, and went off again.
I put one finger up near it, slowly, the way you go near anything that small. The light was cool, with not one bit of heat in it.
So I stayed as still as a stone, and watched the little lantern climb higher up the stem."

s3.text:
"From the {waiting_spot} I watched the whole meadow come on.
One, then three, then twenty, then more than anybody could count, the way the streetlights come on down a road while you look somewhere else.
Green lights drifting low over the grass and climbing high round the pear tree. Some blinked quick and busy. Some drew one long slow line and went dark.
My grandmother said they were all talking to one another. Hello. Hello. Here I am.
Well, one of them was a terrible talker."
Grandpa Milo holds up one finger and waits, then puts it down again.
"Like that. There was a firefly who was always late. The whole meadow would blink together, and then, long after everybody had gone dark, up would come one small light on its own. I called that one {firefly_name}.
Not yet, not yet, and then, {firefly_name}, blinking after the lot of them. I laughed out loud in the dark.
Then, away up the hill, I heard our kitchen door open."

s4a.text:
"I held my hand out flat and still, like a little landing field.
My arm got tired. A mosquito went past my ear and I let it go, because a hand that swats is a hand nothing lands on.
And then, late as always, {firefly_name} came along. Something as light as a crumb touched down on my finger.
I did not breathe.
And then the little lantern came on. My whole palm went green. I could look at the lines in my own skin, lit up from underneath. Cool light. It did not burn one bit.
Three blinks, and {firefly_name} lifted off my finger and went away over the grass, blinking late as ever.
All June the answer had been not yet. Now it was standing on my finger.
I never took one home in a jar. My mother said their light belongs to the meadow, and after I had held one on my hand I knew what she meant."
Grandpa Milo looks into his cup and smiles. "That is the whole story. Nothing happened at all, and I have remembered it my whole life."

s4b.text:
"I started home slowly. Up the hill through the long grass, walking the way you walk when you do not want an evening to finish.
The lights came with me. One drifted along by my shoulder for a while. One blinked in the hedge, went out, and blinked again further along, like a lamp somebody was carrying.
Halfway up I turned round and looked at the whole thing one more time. On and off and on, all the way down to the woods. Somewhere in the middle of it, {firefly_name} was still blinking late.
My mother was standing in the doorway with the kitchen light warm behind her. She did not tell me to hurry up.
She just said, they came, then.
And I said, they came.
And we stood in that doorway together and watched until the milk on the stove wanted her."
Grandpa Milo looks out at the dark garden for a while. "That meadow is still there," he says. "It blinks every June. Some things wait for you your whole life."

c1.question: Grandpa Milo taps the step. "You pick it for me," he says. "Up on the warm stone wall, where I could see the whole meadow at once? Or down inside the tall grass, where it grows over your head? Wall, or grass?"

options.label: Wait up on the warm stone wall
Wade down into the tall grass

c2.question: Grandpa Milo turns his cup round in his hands. "Here is the part I still think about," he says. "Do I hold out my hand and stay where I am? Or do I start up the path for home while the whole meadow is still going? Hand, or path?"

options.label: Hold out a hand and wait for the late one
Walk home slowly with the lights coming along

firefly_name.role: the one firefly who always blinked late

waiting_spot.role: where Grandpa Milo waited for the lights

s1.text:
We are the new crew at the animation studio, and our first job is to stand very still in a very long corridor. The walls are covered in pencil drawings, floor to ceiling, hundreds of them, each one pinned up beside its neighbour. Each drawing shows the same tiny wire puppet. In the first, he is crouched down low. In the next, he is crouched down low, but his foot is a whisker further forward. In the next, the whisker is two whiskers.

"They're the same drawing," we say. "Over and over."

"Count them," says a voice. A woman with a pencil behind her ear is watching us from the floor, where she sits with a stack of paper. "I'm the in-betweener. I draw the ones in between."

So we count as we walk. Ten. Fifty. A hundred. And slowly we see it: the crouch becomes a spring, the spring becomes a stretch, and drawing by drawing, whisker by whisker, the little puppet is climbing into the air. Nobody moves him. He just moves.

At the very end of the corridor, the last drawing shows him mid-leap, arms flung wide, frozen at the top of the world.
