And there, sitting on the doorframe beside it, is the puppet himself. Real. Wire and all. Posed exactly like the drawing, mid-leap, as if he has hopped clean out of the paper and is waiting for us to notice.

"That's {puppet_name}," says the in-betweener, gathering up her pages. "He's always one step ahead. He knows the way in."

She pushes the door open, and cool air smells of clay and dust and old wood.

"Coming?"

{puppet_name} tips forward off the frame, lands on the floor beyond without a sound, and we follow.

s2a.text:
"Sit," says the in-betweener, and she pulls out a second stool for {puppet_name}, though he is already posed on the corner of her desk, one wire foot pointing at the lightbox like he has been waiting all morning.

Her desk glows. Under the glass is a bright white light, and on top, two drawings lie side by side. In the first, a cat is crouched low, belly nearly touching the ground. In the second, that same cat is mid-leap, paws out, tail flying. Between them: nothing. Empty paper.

"Two poses," she says. "The crouch and the leap. The leap needs to get from here to there. Watch."

She slides a thin stack of drawings onto the lightbox and flips them with her thumb. The pages ripple. And there it is: a wave travels across the paper, the cat stretching up, up, up from crouch to leap in a dozen tiny steps.

"Those are the in-betweens," she says. "The stepping-stone frames. Nobody cheers for them, but they do the heavy lifting."

Then she puts the stack in our hands. "Your turn. Slow first."

We flip slowly, and the cat stutters — crouch, hover, hover, leap — like a film tripping over its own feet.

"Now fast."

We flip fast, and the cat flows. One smooth spring, crouch to sky, right there under our thumbs.

"Feel that?" she says. "That's frame rate. Twenty-four frames every second, and your thumb just decided how many the cat got. Fast moments want a brand-new drawing each frame. Slow ones can hold one drawing for two."

{puppet_name} taps the desk, once, impatient.

"He's right," she says, standing. "The drawings are only half of it. Come see the other half."

s2b.text:
{puppet_name} is already through the side door, and we chase him into a room the size of a warehouse — except it is not a room. It is a film strip, stretched out wide, and each frame along it is big enough to walk into. A whole corridor of frozen instants, waiting.

We step into the first frame. Inside, a clay ball hangs in the air, stretched long like a teardrop, mid-fall. We walk all the way around it. It does not move. It cannot. This is one frame, one instant, and the ball is stuck being exactly this shape forever.

The next frame over, the ball is flat. A pancake. Squashed against the ground for exactly one frame.

"Why is it a pancake?" we ask.

"One frame of squash," says the in-betweener, catching up behind us, "makes the bounce feel heavy. You'd never see it on screen — but you'd feel it was missing."

Then we come to a whole shelf of frames that are exactly the same. The same rabbit, mid-crouch, in room after room after room. Five of them. Identical.

"The pause before the leap," she says. "The rabbit holds still so the jump, when it comes, means something. Slow moments hold one drawing for two frames, sometimes more. Fast moments get a brand-new drawing every single frame."

And in the last room, {puppet_name} is waiting. Posed mid-spring, wire arms flung wide, one step ahead of us as always — but frozen, like the rabbit, like the ball, one millimetre of movement at a time.

"He's not ahead of us," we say slowly. "He's just been posed that way."

"Now you're getting it," she says. "Nothing here moves. Things are moved. Somebody has to decide how far, and how often. Somebody like you."

s3.text:
The door lets us out into a room that is mostly table. On the table sits a whole village, small enough to hold in your arms. Houses with crooked chimneys. Lampposts the size of crayons. And over it all hang real studio lamps, big as dinner plates, pouring down daylight.

A woman with paint on her sleeves is bent over the tiny street, and beside her, on the corner of a cobbled lane, stands {puppet_name}. One step ahead of us. Again.

"You found something," she says, without looking up. "Good. Keep hold of it." She straightens. "Want to see inside him?"

She flicks a switch and a panel on the wall lights up white. On it, dark and delicate, is {puppet_name}'s skeleton: not bones, but a metal armature, all little ball-and-socket joints, like tiny bicycle chains strung into a person. Every joint turns. Every joint holds a pose.

"That's how he can stand on one toe and wait," she says. "He's been crossing this street since morning." She holds up her finger. "He's come about that far."

"Since morning?" we say.

"The whole walk takes a week. Every second of him is twenty-four photographs. Twenty-four little nudges." She taps the table beside his foot. "That's the frame rate. It's not a walk at all, really. It's a stop motion. Hundreds of frozen moments, one after another, and the screen does the moving."

We look at the lampposts. We look at the long, long lane. A week of whiskers.

"So," she says, and her hand hovers over him, open and steady. "One of you gets to move him. Once. And it has to be less than a millimetre."

The lamps hum. The village waits.

"What did you find, back there?" she asks softly. "Because whatever it was — bring it with you. He'll need it."

s4a.text:
"Now," we say. "Move him now."

The animator grins and steps back. "He's all yours. Remember — less than a millimetre."

We lean over the village until our noses nearly touch the lampposts. {puppet_name} stands on the cobbles, mid-step, patient as a comma. We take his little wire arm between finger and thumb, and we give him {nudge_direction}. It is barely anything. It is almost nothing at all.

"Perfect," she whispers. "Hold your breath."

Click. The camera blinks. One photograph, one frozen instant, and our millimetre is inside it forever.

"Can we see?" we ask. "Can we see it move?"

She carries the camera's card to a screen, and the day's few seconds play. There — the lampposts, the lane, and {puppet_name}, walking. And right there, in the middle, his arm lifts. Small. Smooth. Alive. Ours. He is waving at us from inside the film.

We shout, because we cannot help it.

"Come on," she says. "One more thing."

The screening room is dark and smells of warm dust. The projectionist, an old man with rolled sleeves, threads the film. "Normal speed, your eyes glue the pictures together," he says. "So we'll go slow."

The projector clatters, then slows. Clack. Clack. Clack. And now we see it: between each bright picture, a blink of dark. A gap. Our eyes have been erasing that gap our whole lives, stitching stillness into motion without ever telling us.

"Twenty-four of those every second," he says. "Twenty-four little darknesses you never noticed."

Before we leave, he snips one frame from the reel and presses it into our hand. One tiny printed picture of a wire puppet, arm raised, mid-wave.

"That one's yours," he says. "You made it move."

All the way home, we hold it up to the light. It does not move. It never will again. But we saw it move, and we know the secret now: motion is just stillness that believes in the next frame.

"One millimetre," we whisper, "and he waved."

s4b.text:
"The whole route first," we say. "We want to know every step."

"Good choice," says the animator, and she lifts the lamp so the light falls along the lane. "Walk it with your eyes. He starts here."

We tiptoe our gaze down the cobbled street, past the crayon lampposts, each one no taller than our little finger. Past a bakery with a door that really opens. Over a bridge the size of a shoebox, where a painted river waits, silver and still.

"Here," she says, and her finger stops at a tiny fountain, "he pauses. Two whole frames. The pause before the leap — that's what makes the leap feel like a leap. Stillness is part of the motion."

We picture it: {puppet_name} gathering himself, springing, clearing the fountain by a whisker, landing on the far side of the village a week from now.

"How many photographs?" we ask.

"Hundreds. Thousands, maybe. One nudge at a time." She hands us the pointer. "Go on. Give him his first."

We take his little wire arm between finger and thumb, and we give him {nudge_direction}. Click. The camera blinks. Frame one of a very long walk.

"Now come and see what you're part of," she says.

The screening room is dark and smells of warm dust. The projectionist, an old man with rolled sleeves, threads a reel of finished film. "Normal speed, your eyes glue the pictures together," he says. "So we'll go slow."

The projector clatters, then slows. Clack. Clack. Clack. And there it is: between each bright picture, a blink of dark. A gap our eyes have been erasing all our lives, stitching stillness into motion and never telling us.

"Your frame will have one of those gaps on each side," he says. "Hundreds of frames, hundreds of little darknesses — and the walk will look like one smooth thing."

Before we go, the animator unrolls a tiny map of the village, the route drawn in pencil, small numbers marked along it. Frame one. Frame two. All the way to the fountain, and beyond.

"Take it," she says. "So you know where he's going."

We carry it home like a treasure. Somewhere in that studio, {puppet_name} is standing very still, one millimetre into his journey, and every day somebody will move him one millimetre more.

"Walk well," we whisper. "We know the way."

c1.question: "He's already slipped ahead of us, that puppet. Do you want to sit at my desk and learn how the drawings between the poses do the moving, or would you rather chase him through the door where the frames are big enough to stand inside?"

options.label: Stay at the lightbox desk and learn how in-betweens work
Chase the puppet into the walk-in film strip

c2.question: "One nudge is all a frame gets. Do you want to move him right now and watch your millimetre turn into motion, or walk his whole route across the village first so you know every step his week will take?"

options.label: Nudge the puppet now and see the playback

sets_slots.nudge_direction: a wave of his arm, the width of a pencil line

options.label: Tiptoe the puppet's week-long route through the village first

sets_slots.nudge_direction: his first step off the mark, toward the fountain

nudge_direction.role: The tiny movement we give the puppet on the stop-motion set, which we later watch become motion on screen

s1.text:
New-comics day at Page and Panel smells like fresh paper and the pretzels from the cart outside, and the bell over the door goes ting when our best friend bursts in, waving something over their head. Not a comic. A flipbook. 

"You have to see this," they say. "I drew it all week. It's called {flipbook_name}."

We squeeze onto the window bench together, Pip the shop cat hopping up beside us, because Pip has opinions about everything. The pages are thick as toast. On the first one, way out at sea, there's a little bump of a wave, just a squiggle of blue pencil. Our friend holds the corner of the book. "Ready?"

We nod. Pip puts one paw on the edge like he's ready too.

Thumb down, and the pages start to flip. Flip flip flip. The bump grows a shoulder. Flip flip flip. The wave stands up. Flip flip flip flip. It curls over itself, taller and taller, and the little surfer on her board looks up at it, and our friend flips faster, and the wave leans, and leans, and

Blank.

The last page is torn out. There's just a ragged paper fringe where it used to be, and the flipbook shuts with a soft thwap. The wave is still up there, leaning. It never comes down.

"Wait. Flip it again," we say.

They flip it again. Flip flip flip. Bump, shoulder, curl, lean — thwap. Blank. Pip pats the ragged edge with his paw, pat pat, like he's checking under it.

"It was there last night," our friend says, and their voice goes small. "I watched it crash a hundred times. It was the best part. It was the whole point."

We look at the torn fringe. We look at Pip, who is sniffing it very seriously, whiskers twitching. A wave that never crashes. A last page, gone. Somebody took it — or something did.

"Okay," we say, and we can feel the mystery settling onto the bench beside us, warm as a cat. "Let's find that crash."

s2a.text:
The library is three blocks of Pip trotting ahead of us, tail up like a flag. Ms. Okafor is stamping returns when we slide the flipbook onto her desk, and she stops mid-thump. "A wave with no crash," she says. "That is a crime against pacing."

She pulls a comic from the shelf behind her, one of the old mysteries, and lays it flat. "Look at this page." Five skinny panels in a row, a detective sprinting, each one a blur of legs. "Small panels go fast. Your eye hops. Hop hop hop." Then she turns the page, and the whole next page is one enormous panel — the detective's face, gasping, in front of an open door. "Big panel," she says, "makes you stop. Holds you there. The page turn is the drumbeat before the reveal."

"That's what my last page was," our friend whispers. "The whole crash. One big panel."

"Someone knew that," Ms. Okafor says. "They took the drumbeat."

Pip hops onto the desk and sniffs the flipbook's torn corner, then sniffs the ruler Ms. Okafor uses to tear checkout slips. He looks at us. We look too. Both edges carry the same gray pencil smudge, soft as a thumbprint.

"Someone traced it," we say. "On this ruler. Recently."

Ms. Okafor raises one eyebrow. "Then your page didn't run away. It was borrowed."

s2b.text:
My sister is at the kitchen table with her tongue in the corner of her mouth, drawing. Pip hops onto the chair beside her and watches like an art critic. "Don't bump the table," she says. "I'm on panel three."

Her strip is called {sister_strip}, and today's one is about her dog. In the first three panels — small ones, squeezed together — the dog is a streak of mud and paws, door to hallway to stairs. She drew him three times in one panel once, to show sprinting, but today it's three little panels, hop hop hop, fast as a heartbeat.

Then, at the bottom, one huge panel: the dog flopped on his bed, asleep, one ear up. The whole row slows down just looking at it.

"Small panels speed time up," she says, not looking up. "Big ones slow it down. That's the whole trick."

Our friend goes very still. "The flipbook," they say. "The little pages flip fast. But the last page — the crash — that was the slow one. The big moment."

We look at the muddy paws in her strip, hurrying inside. Somebody hurried with the flipbook too. Grabbed it, traced the crash, put it back — quick panels, not slow ones. They didn't steal it to keep it. They borrowed it in a rush.

"Sis," we say slowly. "Who used your desk last night?"

She finally looks up. "Why do you think I'm drawing muddy paws?"

s3.text:
Back at the kitchen table, we spread everything out. On one side, the sister's comic strip, {sister_strip}, all four panels of it. On the other, the flipbook, still open to that ragged edge. Pip sits right in the middle, tail curled over his paws, looking from one to the other like he's reading both at once.

"Okay," our friend says. "Tell me what you found."

We tell them. All of it. And as we talk, their eyes get wider and wider, and they start flipping the corner of the flipbook without even meaning to, flip flip flip, that little wave rising and rising and never coming down.

"Wait," they say suddenly. "Let's test something."

They pull {sister_strip} closer. "Read it with me. Out loud. And every time we turn a page or hit the end of a row, we clap. Once. Like a drumbeat."

So we do. We read the first panel, and clap. The second, and clap. The rhythm of it is steady, like a heart beating. Pip's ear twitches at every clap.

"Now the flipbook," our friend says.

We flip. Flip flip flip. Clap. Flip flip flip flip. Clap. The wave grows, the wave curls, the wave leans —

Thwap. Blank. No clap. The drumbeat just stops, right where the crash should be, and the silence where it belongs is so loud it almost rings.

"That's it," our friend breathes. "That's the whole problem. The pacing is broken. The reveal is gone." They look at the smudges on the table, at the strip, at the flipbook. "Somebody needed that wave. Somebody who was making something."

Pip stands up, stretches, and puts one paw flat on {sister_strip}. He looks at us.

"We know how they did it," we say slowly. "But we don't know where the page is now."

Pip's tail flicks. Once. Like a drumbeat.

s4a.text:
Pip's paw comes down on the birthday card, right on the envelope flap, and his tail flicks. Once. Like a drumbeat.

"The card," our friend breathes. "It's tomorrow. I never even opened it."

We slide it out of the envelope, slow, because some part of us already knows. The front says Happy Birthday in blue pencil — the same blue pencil as a certain wave. Pip stands on his hind legs, front paws on the table edge, watching like it's the best show in town.

"Ready?" we ask.

"Ready," our friend whispers.

We open the card.

The wave stands up.

It's a pop-up. Somebody traced the missing last page onto stiff paper, folded it flat, and glued it in — so when the card opens, the wave rises, curls, and comes crashing down in one smooth paper swoop, right over a tiny pop-up surfer who rides it all the way to the bottom. Flip, flip, flip — crash. The drumbeat lands. The pacing is perfect. The reveal is enormous.

"The flipbook was missing its crash," our friend says, laughing now, "because the crash was busy being a birthday present."

There's writing inside, small and neat: You draw the best waves. I wanted yours to move forever. Happy birthday.

We read it twice. Pip sniffs the pop-up wave very seriously, then boops it with his nose, and it wobbles, and we all laugh.

There is cake, because of course there is cake — chocolate, with one blue squiggle of icing on top that looks suspiciously like a wave. And while we eat, our friend takes a pencil and adds one more name to the flipbook's cover, right under theirs. The tracer's name. "They made the crash matter," they say. "They get a credit."

Before we leave, our friend presses something small and sticky into our palm. A sticker. A tiny traced wave, mid-crash, no bigger than a thumbnail.

"So you remember," they say, "that every wave comes down somewhere."

We stick it on our sleeve. Pip purrs. And all the way home, we can still hear it — flip flip flip, and then, at last, the crash.

s4b.text:
"We could find the page," our friend says slowly. "Or..." They look at the flipbook, at the ragged fringe, at Pip. "Or we could draw a new one. A better one. A crash so big it was worth waiting for."

Pip's tail flicks. Once. Like a drumbeat saying yes.

So we clear the table and get to work. Our friend sketches; we steady the pages. And because we have learned something today, we do not rush. We make the crash slow.

"Big panels," our friend says, drawing one huge box across the page. "Big panels stretch time out. The wave hangs there. Nobody breathes."

"And small ones?" we ask.

"Small ones for the crash itself. Lots of them. Quick quick quick." They grin. "That's pacing."

So the new last page gets a layout of its own: one tall panel where the wave leans and leans, then a row of tiny ones — the curl tipping, the first white splash, the surfer's eyes going wide — and then, at the very bottom, one enormous panel for the crash itself, all spray and foam and a surfer riding it out with her arms up like she planned the whole thing.

We tape it in, careful, right against the ragged fringe. The flipbook is whole again. Thicker, even.

"Read it with me," our friend says. "Out loud. Clap on the page turn, like before."

We flip. Flip flip flip. Clap. The bump, the shoulder, the curl. Flip flip flip flip. Clap. The wave leans — and this time the page turns, and the clap lands, and the crash fills the whole bottom panel, enormous, and we shout, because we cannot help it.

Pip pats the new page with his paw, pat pat, approving.

"It's better than the one I lost," our friend admits. "Because we made it together."

Before we go, they run a photocopy of our last page and fold it into our hands. "The original stays in the book," they say. "But the crash belongs to both of us."

We carry it home flat in our pocket, warm as a secret. And sometimes, before bed, we unfold it and flip the whole story through our thumbs one more time — flip flip flip, lean, clap — and the wave comes down, every single time, exactly when it should.

c1.question: Do we want to visit the librarian to see how a real mystery comic handles its missing page, or go straight to my sister who is drawing her dog strip right now?

options.label: Visit the school librarian
Visit the older sister

c2.question: Do we flip the birthday card open right now to see if the wave crashes, or draw a brand-new last page together to make the crash even bigger?

options.label: Open the birthday card to see the reveal
Draw a new last page together

flipbook_name.role: The title of the flipbook with the missing last page

sister_strip.role: The name of the sister's comic strip about the dog

stories.title: The Moat That Waited for a Wave

s1.text: The sand was warm before we even saw it. "Off we go, {hero_name}," said Granny, and her bucket went swing, swing, swing. Up the wooden path we climbed, up over the dunes, and the grass heads nodded at us. Whisper, whisper. Then — the whole beach! Gold as far as we could look. And there, down below, went a curly line of things the sea had left behind. Shells. Seaweed. Foam bubbles, winking in the sun. Granny stopped. She put her hands in her pockets, where her found shells rattled. "Now who," she said, "left a trail like that? And where does it go?"

s2a.text: "Toes in!" you shout, and off the path you hop. The sand is hot on top — hot, hot, hot! "Quick," says Granny, "push your toes down." Down you push, and — oh! Underneath, the sand is cool, like a secret waiting. "Well, would you look at that," says Granny. You wiggle-walk along the trail, past a white feather, soft as a whisper. Granny scoops up two handfuls of sand. One is dry — it slips away like sugar, fssst, through her fingers. One is damp — it holds its shape, like a little hill. "Now why," she says, turning her hands over, "does one run away and one stay put?" Ahead, the shells glint. Wink, wink. The trail curls on, down to the wet sand, and your toes are already going.

s2b.text: "Up high!" you shout, and up you climb, up among the nodding grass. Whisper, whisper. Granny pats the sandy hill. "The wind built this," she says. "And the grass holds it still, like fingers holding tight." You stand on top and — oh! You can see the whole trail at once, like a seagull would. A white feather. A round dark hole, where a crab lives. A spiral seashell, pink as a sunset. All in a row, pointing down, down, down to the wet sand. "There it is!" you shout. "The whole trail!" Granny's shells rattle in her pocket. "Now where," she says, "does it end?" Down you scramble, legs tickled by spiky grass, down to where the line goes on.

s3.text: Down we went, onto the smooth wet sand. It was cool and firm under our toes. "The sea's doorstep," said Granny. "Best place to stand." Then we saw it. A round dark hole. And tiny footprints all around it, like a star. Out popped a little crab, the colour of sand. It ran sideways. It stopped. It looked at us. Then — zip! Back in its hole. "Oh!" we laughed. Granny rattled her pocket shells. "What did you find back there?" she asked. "Tell me on the way." Because look — the line of foam bubbles ended right here. And there stood the biggest sandcastle we had ever seen. A big kid waved a spare spade. "Want to help?" they called. "We need one more thing!"

s4a.text: "I'll drizzle!" said {hero_name}. The spade was heavy and good. Wet sand slid off it in lumpy ribbons. Plop. Plop. And the ribbons held their shape, right on top of the big castle. "My tower," said {hero_name}. The big kid dug the moat, round and round, deep and curly. Then we all sat back. And waited. One wave stopped far away. The next came closer. The next, closer still. "Here it comes," whispered Granny. And one foamy edge swirled right into the moat. Fizz! Bubbles everywhere! The castle stood dry inside. {hero_name} planted the spiral seashell on top, for a flag. On the way home, Granny held out a smooth little periwinkle. "That one's safe to take," she said. So we did.

s4b.text: "I'll dig!" said {hero_name}. The spade bit into the wet sand. Scrape. Scrape. Round and round the big castle went the moat, deep and curly, and {hero_name} patted the walls smooth. The big kid drizzled the towers. Plop. Plop. Then we all sat back at the sea's doorstep. And waited. One wave stopped far away. The next came closer. The next, closer still. "Here it comes," whispered Granny. And one wave slid all the way up and filled the moat. Fizz! Bubbles everywhere! The castle stood dry inside. {hero_name} planted the spiral seashell on top, for a flag. On the way home, Granny picked up a fan-ridged shell from the tideline. "That was once an animal's house," she said. "You may keep it." So we did.

c1.question: "Two ways down to that shiny line, my love — do you want your toes in the hot sand right now, or shall we climb up high first and spy the whole trail like seagulls?"

options.label: Hop off the path onto the hot dry sand and find the cool layer underneath
Climb to the dune top and read the whole trail of tide-gifts from above

c2.question: "There's one job left and one job going spare," says the older kid, holding out the spade. "Will you drizzle a tower on top, or dig the moat that the sea's going to fill?"

options.label: Build a small drizzled tower on top of the big castle
Dig the deep curly moat that waits for the wave

hero_name.role: The hero's name, used by Granny and the narrator

s1.text:
{hero_name} had a pocket full of falling things.

A chestnut. A feather. A strip of birch bark that curled like a question mark. Every evening, up on the orchard hill, {hero_name} dropped one and wrote down what it did. And every single one did the same thing.

Down.

Tonight it was {falling_thing}. {hero_name} held it out over the grass, let go, and watched. Down it went, straight as a plumb line, and tucked itself into the clover like it had done it a hundred times. Which, in a way, it had.

"Sixty-three," {hero_name} wrote in the notebook. "Falls down. Like everything."

And that was when {hero_name} looked up — and there it was. The Moon. Just risen, huge and gold, hanging over the orchard like it had been hung on a nail.

Not falling.

{hero_name} stared at it. Sixty-three things in the notebook. Sixty-three things, and every one of them came down. Apples came down — this whole hill was proof of that. Rain came down. Stars didn't, but stars were far and small and nobody expected them to. The Moon was enormous. The Moon was close. The Moon was, when you thought about it, the biggest falling thing there had ever been, and it had never once landed.

"Hey, Mr. Abernathy," {hero_name} called, because Mr. Abernathy was out fixing his fence again, the way he was most evenings, and the fence ran right along the good dropping spot. "How come the Moon doesn't fall?"

Mr. Abernathy leaned on the post and looked up at it, the way you look at an old friend who has just done something surprising.

"Funny thing," he said. "It does."

"It does not," said {hero_name}. "It's up there."

"It falls," said Mr. Abernathy, hammering in a nail like that settled it. "It falls all the time. It just keeps missing."

Above the orchard, the Moon hung gold and patient, as if it were listening. As if it had all night to explain itself, and intended to take all night to do it.

s2a.text:
"Trampoline it is," said Mr. Abernathy, and he vanished into his garage and came back rolling something across the grass. A bowling ball. Old, black, heavy as a bag of apples. He heaved it up onto the trampoline in the corner of his yard, and it sat down in the middle with a slow, satisfied creak, and the whole black skin of the trampoline dipped around it like soup settling in a bowl.

"Now," he said, and he pressed something small and cool into {hero_name}'s hand. {marble_color}. "Roll it straight across. Try."

{hero_name} knelt at the edge and rolled it, hard and true, straight for the far side. And the marble did not go straight. It slid down into the dip, swung around the bowling ball in a long smooth curve, climbed a little, curled back, and went circling, circling, around and around the heavy ball like it was tied to it by a string.

There was no string. {hero_name} checked. {hero_name} picked the marble up and rolled it again, and again it curved, and again it circled, and nothing touched it at all.

"It's not pulling it," {hero_name} said slowly. "Nothing's pulling it. It's just... following the dip."

"Mm," said Mr. Abernathy, leaning on the fence. "Heavy thing makes a dip. Little thing follows the curve. Funny place to find that out, a backyard."

{hero_name} looked at the bowling ball, heavy and still in its hollow. Then up at the Moon, enormous over the orchard, circling and circling and never landing.

"Earth is the bowling ball," {hero_name} whispered.

Above them, the Moon kept falling around the curve of the world, and missing, and missing, on purpose, forever.

s2b.text:
"The picture, then," said Mr. Abernathy, and he went inside and came back with a stack of old astronomy magazines tied up in string, smelling of dust and somebody's attic. He flipped through them on the fence post until he found the page, and then he held it out without a word.

{hero_name} looked. And looked again.

It was a photograph of deep space, black as the bottom of a well, and scattered with galaxies like seeds on dark soil. But in the middle of it, something was wrong. There was a smear of blue light, bent into an arc, stretched like taffy, a whole galaxy pulled into a glowing curve around a patch of nothing.

"What is that?" {hero_name} asked.

"A galaxy," said Mr. Abernathy. "Very far away. Its light has been traveling toward us for longer than there have been people to see it. And on the way, it passed something heavy. Something so heavy it bent the path of the light itself, the way a magnifying glass bends sunbeams. That's why the galaxy looks smeared into an arc. We're seeing it around the curve."

{hero_name} stared at the blue streak. "But light doesn't weigh anything. You can't pull on light. There's nothing to grab."

"No," said Mr. Abernathy, pleased. "There isn't. So it isn't being pulled, is it? It's following something. The heavy thing made a dent in... well. In the way there is to go. And the light just went the only way it could. Around the bend."

{hero_name} looked from the photograph up to the sky, where the Moon hung gold over the orchard, going around and around its own bend.

Nothing was pulling it either. {hero_name} was suddenly sure of that. The Moon was following a curve, the way the light followed a curve, and the curve was made by the heavy Earth sitting in the middle of it.

"It's not falling toward us," {hero_name} said. "It's falling around us."

The Moon said nothing. It had been keeping the secret a long time, and it could keep it a little longer.

s3.text:
By suppertime the idea had followed {hero_name} home, the way a song follows you in from outside. It sat at the table. It leaned over the soup. It would not go away.

Then the screen door banged, and there was Junie, home from the space museum trip, smelling of bus seats and gift-shop fudge.

"You won't believe what I saw," Junie said, dropping into a chair. "Astronauts. Floating around inside the station like dandelion fluff. And get this — the man said there's gravity up there. Almost as much as down here."

{hero_name} put down the spoon. "That's wrong. If there's gravity, they'd fall."

"That's what I said!" Junie waved a breadstick. "But he swore it. Gravity, and floating, both at once."

They looked at each other. Outside the window, the yard lay dark and familiar, and the trampoline sat in the middle of it like a held breath.

"Come on," said {hero_name}.

The night air was cool and smelled of cut grass. {hero_name} climbed onto the trampoline and set {marble_color} on the stretched black fabric, right at the edge. It sat there a moment. Then it rolled — slowly, then faster — spiraling down into the dip their weight made, round and round and round.

"Watch," {hero_name} said softly. "It falls the whole time. It just keeps going sideways."

"So it never lands," Junie breathed. "It's always falling in, and always missing."

"Like the astronauts. Falling around the Earth, together with their station." {hero_name} felt the pieces slide into place, smooth as the marble circling. "The apple falls straight down the dip. The Moon falls sideways around it. Same fall. Same dip. Different speed."

They looked up. The Moon had risen over the orchard, gold and enormous, watching them the way it had watched all along — patient, round, and quietly, endlessly, missing the ground.

"It knew," whispered {hero_name}. "All this time, it knew."

s4a.text:
"Make one," said {hero_name}. "Before bed. I want to make one."

The Moon climbed a little higher, as if to get a better view.

They took turns. Junie went first, flicking the marble across the fabric. It shot straight into the dip and stopped. Plop.

"Too slow," said {hero_name}.

Junie tried again, harder. The marble zipped clean across the trampoline and off the far edge into the grass.

"Too fast," said {hero_name}. "It has to be exactly sideways. Fast enough to miss, slow enough to stay."

Then it was {hero_name}'s turn. A breath. A flick. The marble curved, caught the slope of the dip, and began to circle. Once around. Twice around. Junie grabbed {hero_name}'s sleeve. Three times around — three whole circles, falling the entire time, missing the entire time — before it spiraled gently down into the middle and lay still.

For a moment neither of them said anything.

"That," whispered Junie, "is what the Moon is doing. Right now. Over our heads."

"Falling," said {hero_name}. "Just too sideways to land."

Up in the bedroom, by the light of one lamp, {hero_name} opened the notebook to a fresh page and wrote slowly, pressing hard: "Sixty-four. The Moon is falling. It's just too sideways to land. An orbit is a fall that never stops missing."

Then {hero_name} picked up {marble_color} — still warm from the night air, smooth as a drop of water — and slipped it into the pocket with the chestnut and the feather and the curl of birch bark. A pocket full of falling things, and now one that had learned to miss.

Outside the window, over the dark orchard, the Moon rolled on around its invisible dip, gold and patient, falling and falling and never once landing. It had been keeping the trick longer than anyone. It did not mind sharing it.

"Goodnight, you," said {hero_name}, and went to sleep with the curtain open, so the Moon could keep an eye on things. It always did.

s4b.text:
"The hill," said {hero_name}. "I want to say goodnight properly."

So they climbed, the two of them, up through the orchard rows where the grass grew long and the apples hung dark against the sky. The Moon climbed with them, the way it always does — you walk, and it comes along, quiet as a dog.

At the very top, {hero_name} stopped. From here the whole hill fell away, and the sky opened up enormous, and there was the Moon, gold and round, rolling along overhead.

"Watch," said {hero_name}.

{hero_name} took out {falling_thing} — the same one from the very start, from drop number sixty-three — and held it out over the edge of the hill, and let go.

Down it went. Straight down the invisible dip, into the dark grass. Gone.

And overhead, at exactly the same time, the Moon went sailing on around the very same dip — the same fall, the same curve, only sideways, only too fast to ever arrive. Two falling things. One little and quick and done in a heartbeat. One huge and patient and sixty-three drops in the making. Same motion. Different speed.

"I see it," breathed {hero_name}. "I actually see it. The apple and the Moon. The same thing."

"Newton saw it first," said Junie. "But you saw it too."

Before they left, {hero_name} did one more thing. From the low branch by the fence, they picked one perfect apple — the roundest one, the one that shone — and set it on the fence post, right where Mr. Abernathy would find it in the morning.

"For Newton," said {hero_name}. "He started it."

They walked home down the hill in the dark, and the Moon came with them the whole way, over the orchard, over the rooftops, over the yard where the trampoline sat holding its quiet dip. It was not floating up there. It had never been floating. It was falling — beautifully, endlessly falling — and somehow that made it feel less like a stranger in the sky and more like an old friend who had been doing the same lovely trick all along, waiting for somebody to notice.

"Goodnight," said {hero_name} at the door. "Keep missing."

And it did.

c1.question: "Your Moon's been keeping that secret a long time. We could chase it right here in the yard with my old trampoline, or we could chase it through a picture my magazines have been saving — which calls to you?"

options.label: Try the trampoline experiment with the bowling ball and marble
Look at the magazine photograph of the galaxy bent into an arc

c2.question: "So now you know the Moon's oldest trick. Do you want to make an orbit with your own hands before bed — or climb the hill and say goodnight to the one that's been doing it all along?"

options.label: Go back to the trampoline and throw the marble at the perfect sideways speed
Climb the orchard hill and watch the apple and the Moon do the same thing

hero_name.role: The curious kid who collects falling things

falling_thing.role: The small object the hero drops at the very start and again at the warm landing

marble_color.role: The marble the hero rolls around the trampoline dip, which comes home in their pocket at the end

s1.text:
Tom volleys the ball into the dusk. Up it goes, hanging for one held breath against the purple sky — and down it comes. Down. Every single time.

"Again," says Grandpa Ivo from the deck chair.

Tom kicks. Up. Down. He catches it on his instep and points with his chin. "Then how come that doesn't?"

The Moon is rising over the rooftops, fat and yellow, just sitting there. Not falling. Not even wobbling.

"Ah," says Grandpa. "You've noticed the Moon's little trick."

He disappears into the shed and comes back wheeling something that should have been thrown out years ago. The Moon-O-Matic: brass, dents, clock parts sticking out at odd angles, one small puff of steam where steam should not be. It hiccups. It clanks. Out of a slot at the front pops an index card.

Grandpa reads it aloud. "THE MOON IS FALLING RIGHT NOW. IT JUST KEEPS MISSING." He taps the card. "Useless machine. Except for this."

One dial on the whole contraption still works. It is labeled SIDEWAYS, and when Grandpa turns it, the needle swings up and points at the Moon.

"Sideways," Tom says slowly. "The Moon is falling... sideways?"

"Falling and missing," says Grandpa. "Forever. That's the whole trick, and nobody believes a machine that also says the Moon is not made of cheese, probably."

Tom looks at his football. Down every time. He looks at the Moon. Never down, not once in four billion years.

"I'm going to build it," he says. "A real working model. The falling that never lands. For the science fair on Friday."

Grandpa's eyebrows go up. Then he reaches into his coat and pulls out an old tin that rattles.

"Then you'll need a Moon," he says, and opens the lid.

Marbles. Dozens of them, glinting in the last of the light.

"Pick a good one," says Grandpa. "It's got a lot of missing to do."

s2a.text:
Tom's finger hovers over the tin. "The green one. The cat's-eye. It looks like it's already watching something."

"A Moon with eyes," says Grandpa approvingly. "Excellent."

In the garden, Tom sets the football on the grass. Earth. He places the green marble a hand's width away and flicks it gently past. Then he bends down with a drinking straw and puffs it sideways as it rolls.

The marble curves. It actually curves — a lovely bend around the football, and Tom's heart leaps.

"It's working! It's—"

His puff runs out. The marble straightens and plinks dead into the football. Plink.

The Moon-O-Matic hiccups. A card drops out. Grandpa reads it by torchlight. "SIDEWAYS SPEED MUST NOT RUN OUT." He hands it over. "First useful thing it's said all year."

Tom tries again. Puff. Curve. Plink. Again. Puff, curve, plink. His cheeks ache. The marble doesn't care about his cheeks.

"It curves while I'm blowing," he says, flopping onto the grass. "The second I stop, it stops being a Moon and goes back to being a marble."

"So sideways is right," says Grandpa, "but breath runs out."

Tom pulls out his notebook and writes: sideways matters — but you can't puff forever. Something else has to keep it going.

He holds the green cat's-eye up to the real Moon. "You don't have a straw up there. What have you got?"

The Moon says nothing. The machine hiccups. Somewhere in its brass belly, a dial twitches toward SIDEWAYS and stays there.

s2b.text:
Tom digs past the green ones and pulls out the midnight-blue marble, flecked with silver. "This one. It's got stars in it already."

"A Moon with its own weather," says Grandpa approvingly.

In the garden, Tom sets the football on the grass. Earth. Then he ties a length of string to the blue marble — Grandpa holds one end — and swings it around the football in a wide, smooth circle.

It orbits. Perfectly. Round and round, silver flecks flashing in the dusk.

Grandpa slow-claps. "Ladies and gentlemen, the Moon."

Tom grins so hard his face hurts. "Done. Science fair, here I—"

Clank. The Moon-O-Matic shudders, and a card shoots out onto the grass. Grandpa picks it up and reads: "WHERE IS THE STRING IN SPACE?"

Tom's grin slides off. He looks at the string in his hand. He looks up at the real Moon, hanging over the rooftops with no string, no hand, nothing holding it at all.

"It's a cheat," he says quietly. "The string's doing everything. The marble's not falling and missing — it's just... tied on."

"A pull isn't a bend," says Grandpa, winding the string back in. "Real gravity has no string. The Moon is falling toward Earth every second — and something about its sideways speed means it never arrives."

Tom writes in his notebook: orbit works, but it's a cheat. Gravity isn't a rope. So what bends the path?

He pockets the blue marble. "You're still my Moon," he tells it. "We just haven't earned you yet."

s3.text:
Friday night. The school hall smells of crisps and poster paint, and Ms. Okafor waves Tom over to the wobbliest stall in the room.

"Tom! Just the person." Her stall is a trampoline with a bowling ball sunk in the middle, and coins spiral slowly down the dip and vanish with a clink. "Show me what you've got."

Tom sets up attempt three: clingfilm stretched tight over a mixing bowl. He rolls {moon_marble}. It skids straight off the edge and under a chair.

"Too shallow," says Ms. Okafor. She presses the bowling ball deeper, and the whole trampoline sighs. "The Sun makes a deep hollow. Earth makes a smaller one. You make a dent so tiny you'd need a microscope. Mass bends the space it sits in. The more mass, the deeper the bend."

"So I need a deeper dip," Tom says.

"A deeper dip, and—" 

She never finishes. Little Pip from Year Two reaches across the stall for a juice carton, misses, and pokes the trampoline with one finger.

Two marbles are already rolling. The slow one spirals glumly down, down, and clunks into the bowling ball. But the fast one — the fast one whips around the wall of the dip, round and round, like a skateboarder in an empty pool, and it does not fall in. It just keeps missing.

The hall noise fades right out of Tom's ears.

"Did you see?" he whispers. "Nobody pushed it. Nobody pulled it. The dip did everything. It just needed to be going fast enough — sideways."

Ms. Okafor is grinning. "There it is. That's the whole secret. The Moon isn't held up by anything. It's falling around the Earth, forever, because it has just the right sideways speed for the curve it's falling through."

Tom pulls the Moon-O-Matic's last index card from his pocket, the one he has been carrying all week. He looks at {moon_marble} in his palm. Sideways speed. No string. A deep, smooth curve. Three pieces, and one chance left.

"Ms. Okafor," he says. "Can I borrow the trampoline?"

From somewhere under the stall, the Moon-O-Matic dings — once — like a tiny brass bell.

s4a.text:
Tom doesn't say a word. He just takes the clingfilm off the mixing bowl, balls it up, and drops it in the bin. Ms. Okafor watches. The whole stall watches.

"Right," Tom says. "Properly this time."

He stretches a real sheet over the washing-up basin from the caretaker's cupboard, pulls it drum-tight, and sinks the football in the middle. The dip goes deep and smooth, walls curved like the inside of a teacup. He weighs {moon_marble} in his hand.

Little Pip has stopped drinking his juice. "Is it going to work?"

"It has to," Tom says. "Three times round. Falling and missing. That's an orbit."

He places the marble at the rim. He thinks about his right boot, laces through the ball, the way Grandpa taught him. Sideways. Not at the middle. Never at the middle.

He flicks.

The marble flies along the wall, fast, low, hugging the curve. Once around. Twice around. The hall has gone very quiet. Three times around — always falling, always missing — before it slows, spirals down, and rests against the football.

The stall erupts. Pip shouts, "It missed! It missed!" Ms. Okafor hangs a gold star on the stall front, and under the table the Moon-O-Matic clanks and spits out one last card.

Grandpa reads it. "TOLD YOU SO. PROBABLY."

Walking home under the real Moon, fat and yellow over the rooftops, Tom keeps the marble warm in his fist. "You're falling right now," he tells it. "You just keep missing."

The Moon says nothing. It is busy.

s4b.text:
"Pack it up," Tom says. "My Moon should fly where the real one is."

So they load Grandpa's car with the trampoline sheet, the football, the binoculars, and a blanket that smells of the shed, and drive up through the dark lanes to the hilltop meadow. The grass is cold. The first stars are out. And there, climbing over the town lights below, is the Moon — the actual Moon, the one that has been missing the Earth for four billion years.

Grandpa spreads the sheet between four fence posts. Tom sinks the football in the middle. The dip isn't perfect — the ground is lumpy and one corner keeps slipping — but it's deep, and it's smooth enough.

"Ready?" says Grandpa, binoculars ready.

Tom sets {moon_marble} at the rim. He thinks of laces through the ball, of sideways, of the fast marble in the hall that just kept missing. He flicks.

The marble whips around the wall of the dip. Once. Twice. Three whole times, circling the football Earth while the real Moon climbs higher, and Tom's chest does something funny, because they are both up here now, his marble and that Moon, doing the very same thing.

Grandpa lowers the binoculars. "The apple and the Moon," he says quietly. "Same thing. Both falling along the bend. Only the apple has no sideways speed, so it meets the ground. And this blanket is the only reason we're not sliding along the curve ourselves."

"The ground catches us," Tom says.

"The ground catches us," Grandpa agrees. "The Moon is still falling. It just keeps missing."

Tom watches his marble settle against the football. He picks it up, warm from his pocket, and holds it so the real Moon shines on it.

On the ride home he falls asleep with it in his fist, and dreams in circles.

c1.question: "Pick your Moon, lad," says Grandpa, rattling the marble tin. "Green cat's-eye, or the blue one with the silver flecks?"

options.label: the green cat's-eye marble
the midnight-blue marble with silver flecks

c2.question: "You've got the sideways flick and the deep bend," says Ms. Okafor, arms folded. "So — rebuild it here, tonight, in front of everyone? Or pack it up and fly your Moon under the real one?"

options.label: rebuild the model right now at the fair
take the model up the hill under the real Moon

moon_marble.role: the marble chosen to play the Moon — picked by the child at c1 and carried through every attempt and both endings

s1.text:
It is ten o'clock at night, and the volcano looks completely, totally, boringly normal. Pip knows this because Pip is looking right at it, through the big round window at the top of the observatory, and it is just sitting there being a mountain. Same dark shape. Same little curl of steam. Same everything. So why, WHY, did Dr. Voss just walk over to the big alert poster on the wall and move the pin from green to yellow?

"Excuse me," says Pip. "The mountain looks exactly the same as yesterday."

"Does it?" says Dr. Voss, and she taps the poster twice, like that's an answer.

Meanwhile, Bramble the goat is climbing the coat rack. He has already conquered the bookshelf this morning, and after lunch he summited the filing cabinet, and now he is standing on the very top of the coat rack wearing his tiny yellow hard hat, looking extremely proud of himself, as well he should. Everyone at the observatory treats Bramble like a fellow mountaineer, because honestly, he has summited more things in this building than most actual mountaineers.

Pip pulls out {notebook_name} and opens it to the very first page, which is completely blank, which is a tragedy. Something made Dr. Voss change that poster. Something is going on under that mountain. And Pip is going to figure out what it is and write it down, clue by clue, starting tonight.

"Okay," Pip says. "How do you know? How can you possibly tell something's different when it looks exactly the same?"

Dr. Voss grins. She points across the room at a machine that looks like a metal barrel with a needle on top, and the needle is scratching back and forth across a long strip of paper, wiggle, wiggle, wiggle.

"That's a seismometer," she says. "It listens to the mountain's hiccups. And Bramble's stomach. They sound surprisingly similar."

Bramble bleats, offended.

"The mountain has been hiccupping all week," Dr. Voss says. "Little tiny earthquakes, too small for us to feel. But the seismometer feels every single one. And that's not the only sign we've got."

She turns to Pip. "So. Where do you want to start? We could go look at the tilt meters on the side of the mountain, where the ground is swelling up like a great big bubble. Or we could check the gas sensors in the crater, which have been sniffing something new in the steam. Which one?"

Bramble hops down off the coat rack and trots over, ready for adventure. He does not care which one. He is ready for both.

s2a.text:
"The drum," says Pip. "I want to hear the hiccups."

"Then follow me," says Dr. Voss, and she leads Pip down into the basement, where the seismometer lives, because it needs somewhere quiet to listen. Bramble comes too, clip-clopping down the stairs behind them. His hard hat keeps slipping over his eyes.

The drum is tall as Pip and covered in paper, and the needle is dancing across it like it has had far too much sugar. Zig, zag, zig, zag. Hundreds of tiny wiggles, one after another, all day long.

"Every one of those zigs is a little earthquake," says Dr. Voss. "Too small for us to feel. But the mountain feels them. That's rock cracking, deep down, as magma squeezes its way up toward the surface."

"Hiccups," says Pip, writing it down in {notebook_name}. "The mountain has hiccups."

"Hundreds a day," says Dr. Voss. "And lately they've been climbing. Getting shallower. The magma is on the move."

Then the needle goes WILD. It scrawls a huge spike right across the paper, so big it nearly jumps off the drum.

"Whoa!" says Pip. "Was that a big one?"

Dr. Voss leans in and squints at the spike. Then she snorts. "Nope. That's a truck."

"A truck?"

"Delivery lorry on the road outside. The seismometer hears everything, so we check every signal twice."

Bramble bleats, which probably means he knew that already.

Pip grins and writes it down, clue number one: the hiccups are real, and they are climbing toward the surface. The mountain is stirring. But Pip is watching it now, and Pip is not going to miss a single wiggle.

s2b.text:
"The slope," says Pip. "I want to see the ground move."

"Then we hike," says Dr. Voss, and she grabs her rucksack. Bramble practically leaps off the floor. He loves a hike. He is already at the door, hard hat on, ready to lead the expedition.

Up the mountain they go, Bramble marching in front like a tiny furry general. Every time they pass a bump, he stops and plants his hoof on top of it, claiming it for the team. By the time they reach the GPS station, Bramble has summited seven bumps, two rocks, and one very surprised sheep.

The GPS station is a tripod with a metal box on top, blinking quietly at the sky.

"This little gadget talks to satellites," says Dr. Voss. "It measures exactly where the ground is. And look." She shows Pip the screen. "Four centimeters. The ground here has risen four centimeters in just one month."

"Four centimeters?" says Pip. "That's... not very much."

"Not to you and me," says Dr. Voss. "But to a mountain? That's enormous. It means the whole side of the volcano is puffing up, like bread dough rising in a tin. Something underneath is pushing it up from below."

Pip stares at the ground. It looks completely still. Completely normal. But the numbers say it moved. The satellites saw it from space.

"So the mountain is swelling," Pip says slowly, writing it down in {notebook_name}. "Like it's taking a great big breath."

"Exactly," says Dr. Voss. "And we want to know what's making it breathe."

Bramble bleats and plants his hoof on the tripod. Claimed. Pip laughs and writes clue number one: the mountain is swelling, and something deep down is doing the pushing.

s3.text: Back at the ranger station, Dr. Voss spreads the big paper map across the table and weighs down the corners with a mug, a flashlight, and Bramble's food bowl, because Bramble is already standing on the map. "What did you find?" she asks, and Pip tells her, and she pins it right onto the mountain where it belongs. Then she adds two more pins herself. "Gas readings doubled overnight," she says. "And the hot spring by the trail has gone milky, steaming harder than anyone remembers." Pip stares at the map. The pins are not scattered. They are stacking, like the mountain is clearing its throat and hiccupping at the same time. "One clue is a maybe," Dr. Voss says. "Three clues are a pattern. And the pattern says something is rising from the magma chamber, a few kilometers down." "How can you possibly know that?" Pip asks. "The hiccups told us," says Dr. Voss. "Quake-waves bend when they pass through the magma chamber, the way a bat's squeaks bounce around a cave and tell it the shape of the dark. The waves come back bent, and bent means molten, and molten means the mountain is waking up." Pip writes it all down in {notebook_name}, pressing so hard the pencil nearly snaps. Bramble bleats and stamps one hoof on the map, right on the summit of {volcano_name}, like he is claiming the climb. Dr. Voss taps the pins. "So, team. The clues agree. But agreeing on clues is not the same as knowing what to do. What do we do with a pattern?"

s4a.text:
"We speak," says Pip. "A pattern nobody hears is just a secret." Dr. Voss nods slowly, then grins. "Then let's go say it out loud." Bramble hops off the map and trots to the door first, hard hat on, like he has been waiting for someone to say that all night.

The mayor's office smells like coffee and old paper. Dr. Voss lays the map on the desk, and Pip opens {notebook_name} and reads the clues one by one, voice wobbling at first, then steady. The mayor listens. She asks two questions. Then she picks up the phone and says, "Raise the forecast. An eruption is likely within weeks. We start the plan tomorrow."

And the plan is surprisingly not scary. It is radios checked, bags packed, posters updated. It is a drill the whole town already knows, like a fire drill, only with better snacks. Pip stands on a chair at the community hall and shows everyone the pins. "One clue is a maybe," Pip says. "Three clues are a pattern. The mountain has been talking for weeks. We just listened."

Weeks later, on a bright cold morning, {volcano_name} huffs out a great grey plume of ash, slow and grumbly, like an old dog getting up. And here is the thing: nobody runs. Everybody is already on the viewing hill with thermoses and binoculars, watching the mountain do the thing it said it would do.

That night Pip writes the last page of {notebook_name}: "We knew because we listened." Then Dr. Voss hangs a little brass medal around Bramble's neck, for services to mountaineering. Bramble tries to eat it. Obviously.

s4b.text:
"Not yet," says Pip. "Soon, but not yet. If we speak too early, people stop listening. I want to watch until the clues say now." Dr. Voss looks at Pip for a long moment, then nods. "Then we watch," she says. "All of us. Round the clock." Bramble stamps one hoof on the summit of {volcano_name}, which everyone understands to mean he volunteers for the night shift.

So the observatory becomes a ship, and the mountain is the weather. Pip reads the seismometer drum at midnight, the needle scratching its little hiccups across the paper, wiggle, wiggle, wiggle. At dawn, Dr. Voss sniffs the gas sensors and writes the numbers down. Bramble stands sentinel on the porch roof in his hard hat, staring at the mountain like it owes him money. Days pass. The hiccups stay small. The swelling stays slow. "Still not yet," Pip whispers every night, and it is a strange, patient kind of brave.

Then, on the ninth night, everything changes at once. The drum goes wild, hiccups tumbling over each other. The gas readings jump. The ground swells like the mountain is taking one enormous breath. Pip's pencil flies across the page. "Now," Pip breathes. "NOW."

The forecast goes out with time to spare, and the town does its calm, well-practiced dance: radios, bags, posters, the viewing hill. When {volcano_name} finally huffs its great grey plume into the morning sky, the whole town is already watching, safe and ready, and it is the most magnificent hiccup anyone has ever seen.

Pip closes {notebook_name} on its last page: "The mountain talked for weeks. We just had to keep listening." Bramble gets a medal. He tries to eat that too.

c1.question: "The mountain is telling us something, Pip. Where should a detective listen first — down at the drum that hears every hiccup, or up on the slope where the ground itself is stretching?"

options.label: Visit the seismometer station and read the wiggly lines
Hike up to the GPS station and measure the swelling ground

c2.question: "Three clues, one pattern. So, detective — do we take this to the mayor and speak the forecast out loud today, or do we keep every eye on the mountain until the signs say 'now'?"

options.label: Help deliver the forecast to the mayor so the town prepares now
Join the round-the-clock watch until the clues spike together

volcano_name.role: The name of the volcano being watched

notebook_name.role: What Pip calls the clue notebook

stories.title: The Mountain That Holds a Piece of Sky

s1.text:
"Look at that mountain," says Grandmother Ora. "It is holding a piece of sky."

Wren looks up. The mountain is big and green, and the top is cut off flat, like a giant took a bite out of it.

"It is a volcano," Ora says, "but it is fast asleep. We are going to climb the outside, walk along the top edge, and go right down inside it." She points to a wooden sign with four pictures on it: the climb up, the walk along the rim, the way down inside, and a bright blue lake at the bottom.

"Is that real?" Wren asks. "That blue?"

"It is real," says Ora, "and it is hiding. You cannot see it from here. The rim of the mountain is in the way."

Then Ora kneels down on the path. "Look at this first." Right beside the path is a round hole in the ground, no bigger than a bathtub. Rainwater sits in the bottom of it.

"That is a crater," Ora says. "A little one. A bowl. This mountain is full of bowls, Wren, and every bowl is holding something different. That one is holding rain. What do you think the big one is holding?"

"The blue lake," Wren says.

"Maybe," says Ora. "Maybe more."

A ranger comes to the gate. Her name is Sable, and she carries a battered brass notebook that belonged to her own grandmother. She flips it open to a clean page.

"I draw every bowl I find," Sable says. "Today you will add one drawing of your own. What do you say?"

Wren says yes before Sable has finished asking.

s2a.text:
"Up," says Wren.

So they climb. The path is steep and the stones are sharp and dark, and Sable goes first, steady as a goat. "These rocks were thrown," she says over her shoulder. "When this mountain blew its top, it flung rock out in every direction, and the rock piled up all around the hole. That pile is what you are standing on. The rim is the mountain's own mess, frozen."

Then Wren is at the top, and the whole world opens.

On one side, the land runs away flat and green, all the way to the far-off shine of the sea. On the other side, the ground falls away into an enormous bowl, and at the bottom of it sits the lake, so blue it does not look like water at all. It looks like the piece of sky Ora promised, tucked into the mountain's hands.

"Whoa," Wren says, because she cannot help it.

Sable stands beside her on the backbone of the rim. "Now look at the edges. See how some are sharp and jagged? Those are young. And see how some are round and soft, with grass on them? Those are old. A crater keeps its own record, Wren. You just have to learn to read it."

Wren reads it. The whole shape at once: the ring, the bowl, the blue.

Sable opens the brass notebook. "Your first drawing."

Wren draws the rim as a ring, a dark circle with the blue eye of the lake inside it. Sable nods slowly. "My grandmother would have liked that one."

Far below, the lake glints. The way down is steep, and thin white steam curls up from the inside wall like the mountain is thinking about something.

s2b.text:
"Down," says Wren. "I want to feel it breathe."

So they take the zigzag path, down and down the inside wall, into the bowl itself. The air changes. It grows warm and damp, and white steam curls up from cracks between the stones, slow and quiet, like the mountain is sighing in its sleep.

Wren holds out her hand. The steam is warm on her palm, and it smells like matches just after they go out.

"Those are fumaroles," says Sable. "Steam vents. Hot rock is still hiding down below, even now, long after the volcano stopped rumbling. The mountain is asleep, little one, but it is not cold."

Wren crouches beside a vent. The warmth comes up through the ground and into her knees. "So it is pretending?"

"It is resting," says Sable. "There is a difference." She spreads her arms wide, at the whole enormous valley around them. "And this, all of this, is a caldera. Once, the top of the mountain was hollow underneath, and the roof caved in, and left this. A bowl inside a bowl."

Ora points. Right up to the warm ground, where nothing should want to grow, small yellow flowers are blooming, bright as buttons. "Look at that," she says softly. "The brave ones always come first."

Sable opens the brass notebook. "Your drawing."

Wren draws the steam rising in loops, and at the bottom of the loops she draws three yellow flowers, bigger than they really are. Sable smiles at that and says nothing at all.

The trail keeps dropping. Somewhere below them, past the warm stones, Wren can smell cold water.

s3.text:
The path ends at a shore of dark pebbles, and there it is. The lake. It lies so still that the whole rim floats upside down in it, a second mountain hanging under the first.

"Two bowls," Sable breathes, flipping open the brass notebook. "One holding water. One holding sky."

A man waits beside a wooden boat, coiling a long rope with a stone tied to the end. "Captain Ivo," Ora says. "He knows this lake better than anyone."

"Better than anyone alive," Ivo agrees. He helps us in, and the boat slides out without a ripple. "Here is the strange thing, {hero_name}. No river runs into this lake, and none runs out. Only rain falls in, and snow melts down from the rim. Nothing stirs it. That is why it stays so clear."

Wren leans over the side. Far, far below, a sunken log hangs in the blue, not on the bottom, just hanging, as if the water were air and the log had never learned to fall.

"How deep does it go?" she asks.

"That," says Ivo, patting the coil of rope at his feet, "is the question."

Ora points back at the shore. From out here you can see it plainly: a ring of green trees hugging the rim all the way round. "The rim holds the snow," she says. "The snow feeds the soil. The plants came first, close to the water, and the rest followed. A scar that turned into a home."

Sable's pencil is already moving. "Draw what you see, {hero_name}. Whatever this bowl is holding, it goes in the book."

Wren looks down into the blue eye of the lake, and the blue looks back.

Ivo stops the boat in the middle and takes up the weighted rope. "So," he says. "How shall we take this mountain's measure? Drop the line straight down and see if it touches bottom, or row to the far side and measure from the deep middle?"

s4a.text:
"Drop it," says Wren. "I want to know the number."

Ivo grins and lets the rope go. It slides over the side, fast, then faster, pulling the coil off the floor of the boat. The stone sinks, and the rope follows it down, and down, and down. Ivo feeds it through his hands. The coil shrinks. And still the rope keeps going.

"How much is left?" Wren asks.

"Almost none," says Ivo. The last of the line slips over the side and vanishes into the blue. He holds up his empty hands. "Four hundred metres of rope, shipmate. And it never touched the bottom."

Wren stares down where the rope went. No number. Just blue, going on.

"This bowl has been filling since the mountain fell in on itself," Ora says quietly. "All that rain. All that snow. Some bowls hold water. This one holds time."

Ivo takes a small glass bottle from his pocket, dips it full of lake water, and presses it into Wren's hand. The water is so clear it looks like nothing at all. "Then take some of the time home," he says.

That night, at the trailhead, an astronomer lets Wren look through her telescope. The Moon swims up huge and white, and it is covered in round bowls, dozens of them, every one sharp as the day it was made.

"No rain up there," the astronomer says. "Nothing ever fills them in."

Wren opens Sable's brass notebook and draws a Moon-crater, small and sharp, beside the blue eye of the lake. Two bowls. One holding time. One holding stillness.

The bottle rides home in her pocket, cool against her leg, with four hundred metres of nothing at all inside it.

s4b.text:
"Row," says Wren. "I want to stand in the green ring."

Ivo pulls the oars, and the boat slides across the still water toward the far shore. The far wall of the caldera fades to blue with distance, as if the mountain were forgetting its own edges. The boat noses into the shallows, and Wren steps out into a meadow that rings the whole bottom of the bowl, green and humming with bees.

Ora walks beside her, touching the plants as they pass. "The fireweed came first, after the mountain blew. Then the pines. Then everything else. Each ring you see is a year the mountain spent healing."

Wren crouches at the water's edge. A pale stone lies among the dark pebbles, light as a sponge and full of tiny holes. She picks it up and drops it in the shallows. It floats.

"Pumice," says Ora. "The mountain made that, in the middle of the explosion. The bubbles are the blast, frozen. You are holding a piece of the worst day this mountain ever had."

Wren turns it over in her hand. It weighs almost nothing. She puts it in her pocket.

That night, at the trailhead, an astronomer swings her telescope from the Moon's sharp white craters to a tiny bright dot. "Mercury," she says. "A whole world of bowls. No rain, no air, nothing to soften a single one."

Wren opens Sable's brass notebook and draws the pumice stone, small and pocked, beside a Moon-crater. Two bowls. One holding green life. One holding only its scars.

All the way home, the stone rides in her pocket, light as the mountain's own breath.

c1.question: "Two ways in, little one. We can climb straight up and stand on the rim's backbone, or we can slip down the inside trail where the mountain breathes. Which calls you?"

options.label: Take the steep outer trail to stand on the high rim and see the whole crater at once
Take the zigzag path down the inside wall to the warm steam vents

c2.question: "Here's the choice, shipmate. I can drop the rope and we'll learn this lake's deep secret, or we can row to the far meadow where your grandmother's flowers keep the mountain's first story. What's it to be?"

options.label: Stay at the rail and let the depth rope pay out toward the bottom of the lake
Row to the far meadow and walk the ring of first plants with Grandmother Ora

hero_name.role: The hero's name, spoken by Ora, Sable, and Ivo

s1.text:
"Do you hear that?"
We are sitting on the warm grass at the foot of the tallest mountain, you and me. The ground hums underneath us. It feels like a cat purring, if a cat were as big as a hill.
In the rock there is a little round door. We touch it. It is warm, the way the oven door goes warm when bread is baking inside.
We push. The door swings open.
"You came! You came!"
A small orange lizard is hopping about in front of our feet, grey ash dusted along her back like flour on a counter.
"I am {companion_name}," she says. "The mountain is awake today. It is singing."
We stand very still and listen. Rumble. Rumble.
"Do you want to find out where the song comes from?"
We do.

s2a.text:
We take the path beside the hot river.
It is lava. Melted rock, come all the way up from deep under the ground, moving slower than honey slides off a spoon.
"Watch this," says {companion_name}. She flattens herself onto a floating black stone and rides past us like a little boat.
The river runs thick and orange down the middle and gold along both edges. Bubbles push up and pop. Bloop. Bloop. Every pop throws one spark into the air.
We hold our hands out. The sparks drift close, then wink away before they ever reach us.
"Come nearer," she says. "The black stone is the good path. It went cold a long time ago."
So we walk where she walks.
Around the bend the light grows rounder and bigger, the rumble climbs up through our shoes, and the tunnel opens out into a room so bright that we have to blink.

s2b.text:
We take the stairs. Up and up they twist, and every step hums a little under our shoes.
"Listen," says {companion_name}. "Listen, listen."
We press our ears flat against the warm wall. She puts her ear against it too, right beside ours.
Rumble. Rumble.
"Do you know what that is?" she whispers. "Hot rock. Down deeper than the deepest well, rolling over slowly, the way you roll over in bed before you wake up."
That is the mountain, singing.
We climb until the air turns golden and the steps go warm under our feet. Then the stairs stop.
Below us the floor opens into a room so bright that we have to blink.

s3.text:
This is the heart of the mountain.
In the middle lies a wide pool of lava, round as a dinner plate made for a giant. It is thick and slow and orange, like tomato soup on the stove just before it starts to bubble.
And it does bubble. Slowly. Bloop. Bloop.
{companion_name} sits down on the warm floor and folds her front feet, like somebody waiting for a show to begin.
Then, suddenly, a huge bubble swells up in the middle of the pool, like dough puffing up in a warm kitchen.
The song is getting louder.
"Soon it sings out loud," says {companion_name}. "Not a frightening loud. The kind where the mountain throws sparks out of the top, like a firework party."
"When?" we ask.
"Soon."
We can hardly stand still.

s4a.text:
A warm wind comes rushing up a tall stone chimney and lifts us like two leaves.
{companion_name} rides on our shoulder, holding tight with all four feet.
We come out at the very top of the mountain, under a whole skyful of stars.
"Here," she says. "Behind this big rock. This is the good place to stand."
So we stand where she says, and we wait. And the mountain sings.
Sparks fountain up into the dark, a thousand of them, orange and gold and gone. Soft ash drifts down and settles in our hair. Far away down the other side, a thin ribbon of lava writes slow gold squiggles on the black.
We shout. The mountain rumbles. Nobody can hear anybody at all, and it does not matter one bit.
When the last spark winks out, we find a little pebble by our boot. Cooled lava. Still warm as toast.
It goes in our pocket.
"Goodnight, mountain," we say. "Thank you for the song."

s4b.text:
We climb back to the little round door and sit down in the doorway, feet in the warm dark, faces in the cool night.
"Watch the top," says {companion_name}.
The mountain sings. Out of the top comes one soft grey puff, and then another, and the ash comes drifting down over the hills like somebody shaking flour across the whole world.
"Now watch what it does," she whispers.
Everywhere the ash lands, the ground turns soft and rich. Ash is full of the good things that hungry soil likes to eat. By morning, she says, the grass will be standing taller, and the sunflowers on the far hill will lean over as if they are saying hello.
That is what all the puffing is for. The mountain is feeding its own garden.
{companion_name} digs in the ash beside her feet and holds something up to us. One sunflower seed.
"Plant it at home," she says. "Then the mountain grows in your garden too."
We hold it carefully all the way back.
"Goodnight, mountain. Grow well."

c1.question: "Two ways," says {companion_name}. "Down beside the hot river, or up the stairs into the rumble. Which one?"

options.label: Down beside the hot river
Up the stairs into the rumble

c2.question: "So," says {companion_name}. "Up at the top when it sings? Or down here, to see what the ash is for? Top, or ash?"

options.label: Up at the top when it sings
Down here, to see what the ash is for

s1.text:
Thursday afternoon, in the basement of the community center, where the radiator clanks and the whole room smells faintly of pencil shavings and hot computers. Sam and I are on the floor with the laptop between us, and tomorrow is the showcase.

"Okay," Sam says. "Run it again."

Our maze game is almost done. Almost. The little explorer on the screen turns left, grabs the golden key, and then, for no reason any of us can see, walks straight through a wall.

"It's not supposed to do that," Sam says.

"It's never supposed to do that," I say. "It keeps doing it anyway."

Priya pulls her chair over, the wheels squeaking on the floor. Priya is in high school, and she volunteers here on Thursdays, and she has this way of leaning toward a bug like it's a wrapped present.

"Tell me," she says. "What did you expect it to do? And what did it actually do?"

"Expected: wall stops him," Sam says. "Actual: wall is apparently a rumor."

Priya grins and scrolls up. And up. And up. Our game isn't one screen of code anymore. It's one long scroll, hundreds of lines, all in one piece, like a pot of spaghetti where you can't find the end of a single noodle.

"Who wrote this part?" she asks.

We both look at Marcus. Marcus wrote the core of it three weeks ago, in one heroic Saturday. He comes over and squints at his own code like it's written in a language he used to speak.

"What does this variable do?" Priya asks. "This one called... x2?"

Long pause. "Something important," Marcus says. "Probably."

Priya doesn't laugh. She does something better. She points at the top of the screen, where our game starts, and then down at the very bottom, where it ends, way out of sight.

"You've built a whole kitchen in here," she says. "But nobody labeled the jars."

s2a.text:
"Delete it," Sam says. "It looks weird. Just delete it."

The line sits there, glowing on the screen: a variable called d, doing something to the score. Nobody remembers writing it. Marcus squints. Priya leans in, elbows on her knees.

"What do you expect will happen if we delete it?" she asks.

"Score stops doubling," I say.

"And what will it actually do?"

"Same thing, hopefully."

We delete it. We run the game. The explorer grabs the key, and the score does not double. It does not do anything. It sits at zero like a stone. We collect three coins, five coins, ten coins. Zero. Zero. Zero.

"Oh no," Sam says.

"The line was doing two things," Priya says, and she is not even slightly upset. She looks delighted. "It was adding the points and doubling them. You threw out the whole recipe because it had one weird ingredient."

We put the line back. The score works again. And then, at eleven, it doubles.

"So the bug is in there," Marcus says slowly, "inside d. But d doesn't tell us anything. It's like a jar labeled... I don't know. 'Stuff.'"

Priya taps the screen. "Exactly. Somewhere inside this d, two jobs are hiding in one coat. We can't fix it until we can read it."

"How do you fix something you can't read?" I ask.

Priya smiles. "You open the jar," she says. "And you smell what's inside."

s2b.text:
"Copy it," I say. "Just for now. Paste the scoring part somewhere safe, poke at the copy, and leave the real one alone."

Sam drags the chunk of code into a new spot at the bottom of the scroll. Now there are two: the original, with that unreadable variable called d, and our copy, which we rename test_score because we are geniuses.

We run the game. The explorer grabs the key. Score climbs. At eleven, it doubles. But now we can poke the copy without fear. Marcus finds a line, changes a number, and the copy stops doubling.

"Fixed!" he says.

We run the full game. The explorer grabs the key. Score climbs. At eleven, it doubles.

"Wait," Sam says. "We fixed it. I watched you fix it."

"You fixed the copy," Priya says. "The game is still running the original."

So we fix the original too. We run it again. The score climbs past eleven, past twelve, and stops doubling. We cheer. Then Sam collects a bonus coin, and the score goes backwards.

"What," Marcus says.

"You fixed one copy one way and the other copy another way," Priya says, and her eyes are shining. "Now the game has two versions of the truth. Which one runs depends on which path the explorer takes."

"It's like having a twin," Sam says, "who never got the memo."

"Copies are traps," Priya says. "They look like safety, but they drift apart. And underneath both of them is still that variable called d that nobody can read."

She taps the screen. "One jar. One label. That's the fix."

s3.text:
So we tried the classic move. We sprinkled print commands everywhere, like salting soup. Run it. The screen filled up with messages, scrolling and scrolling, faster than anyone could read.

"It's saying everything," Marcus said, "and telling us nothing."
