Priya reached over and stopped the program. "Okay. What did you expect it to do? And what did it actually do?"

"Expected: one message when he hits a wall," I said. "Actual: nine hundred messages about everything he's ever done."

"Then let's not interrogate the computer," Priya said. "Let's just read it. Out loud. Like a story."

So Sam read. "When the explorer moves... check if... d is less than..."

"What's d?" Marcus asked.

"You wrote d," Sam said.

"That was three weeks ago," Marcus said. "I've lived a whole life since then."

We all leaned in. Somewhere in that scroll, the score was doubling, and the wall was turning into a rumor, and none of us could see where, because every line was wearing a disguise.

Priya tapped the screen. "New plan. We take the scoring part out and give it its own name. A function. Something we can test all by itself, with pretend numbers, like shaking one jar instead of sniffing the whole kitchen."

So we did. We lifted the scoring code out of the scroll and named it update_score, which is a boring name but an honest one. Then we fed it pretend points: ten, then ten more.

"Twenty," Sam said.

"Forty," the computer said.

We all made the same face. There it was. Not hiding in nine hundred messages. Just sitting in one small named box, doubling everything we handed it.

"Found you," Marcus whispered.

"Now the wall," Priya said. "Rename d. Call it what it actually is."

Sam typed: distance_to_wall. And the moment the words were on the screen, two more bugs just... stood up and waved. Lines that had looked fine said things like if distance_to_wall is less than zero, which is nonsense, and we could finally see it was nonsense, because the words were telling the truth now.

"Three bugs," I said. "They were there the whole time."

"They were wearing name tags," Priya said. "The name tags said x2 and d."

s4a.text:
So we fixed the doubling line. One tiny change, where the score was adding itself twice. Then we looked at the rest of it, the same stretch of instructions written out three separate times, in three separate places, like the same recipe copied onto three sticky notes.

"We could make that its own function too," Sam said. "One jar. One label."

So we did. Priya calls that a refactor, which sounds like something a pit crew does, but really it just means: same soup, better kitchen. We ran the game. The explorer turned left, grabbed the key, and bonked politely into the wall, which was finally, gloriously, a wall.

"Run it again," Marcus said.

We ran it again. And again. It just worked, every time, which is maybe the most boring and most beautiful thing a program can do.

Saturday, the basement filled up with parents and little kids and folding chairs. Our laptop sat on the table with a paper sign: MAZE GAME, MADE BY US. A man in a puffy coat played it, and his explorer bonked into a wall, and he laughed and said, "Ha! Got me."

"How'd you make the walls work?" he asked.

And here is the part I did not see coming. Marcus, who wrote the scroll, who named a variable x2 and forgot it, leaned in and explained the whole thing. The function. The pretend numbers. The names that tell the truth. He explained it to a stranger, out loud, and every word was right.

Priya was by the whiteboard, pretending not to listen. Somebody had drawn two jars up there. One said Paprika. The other one used to say Stuff, and somebody had crossed it out and written Cumin, in careful letters, so the next cook would know.

"Next Thursday?" Sam said, packing up the laptop.

"Next Thursday," I said. "We're going to read the robot club's code. Like a story."

Marcus shouldered his bag. "Their variables are all called things like q."

We walked up the stairs together, into the cold, and the radiator clanked goodbye behind us.

s4b.text:
So we fixed the doubling line. One tiny change, where the score was adding itself twice. We ran it. The score counted up properly, ten, twenty, thirty, like a person who has learned to count.

"Done," Marcus said, and reached for the lid of the laptop.

But I was still reading. That is the thing about code with honest names: you keep reading it, the way you keep walking down a street when the houses get interesting. And there, in the part about moving, something looked off.

"Wait," I said. "What happens if he goes diagonal?"

Sam tried it. Up and sideways at once. The explorer slid clean through the corner of a wall, smooth as butter off a knife.

"A fourth bug," Priya said, and she said it the way you say "more cake." "You never would have seen that in the scroll. It was hiding under the tangle. You cleared the tangle, and there it was."

We fixed that one too. Then we broke the whole game into small named parts, one job each, the way a recipe says preheat the oven and means it. Functions all the way down, every jar labeled.

Saturday, the basement filled up with parents and folding chairs. A kid, maybe seven, stood at our table watching the explorer bonk into walls.

"How does it know?" the kid asked.

Sam did not answer. Sam did something better. He turned the laptop around and read the code out loud, the actual words. "If distance to wall is zero... stop."

The kid's eyes went wide. "Oh," he said. "I get it!"

Nobody had ever said that about the scroll.

Priya was by the whiteboard, smiling at nothing. Somebody had drawn two jars up there. One said Paprika. The other used to say Stuff, and somebody had crossed it out and written Cumin, in careful letters, so the next cook would know.

"Think that kid will come Thursday?" Marcus asked.

"He'll come," Priya said. "They always come. Somebody reads them the code like a story, and then they have to know how it ends."

We packed up slow, nobody in a hurry, the radiator clanking like it was keeping time for us.

c1.question: "Okay, so the score's doubling and I have no idea why. Do we just delete the line that looks weird, or do we copy it somewhere else so we can poke at it without breaking the whole thing?"

options.label: Delete the suspicious line and see what happens
Copy the code to a safe place and test it there

c2.question: "We found the bug and fixed it, but now that the code is actually readable, I keep noticing other stuff. Do we call it done and demo what we have, or do we keep reading and see what else is hiding in there?"

options.label: Call it done, demo the working game, and explain the fix to visitors
Keep reading the now-clear code to see what else might be hiding

stories.title: The Mystery of the Enormous Footprint

s1.text:
{hero_name} walked into the Green Valley with a yellow backpack, a magnifying glass, and a notebook that was only for mysteries.
The path was wet from last night's rain, and ferns leaned in over it, taller than doors.
Then the ground went boom, and {hero_name} felt it come up through both boots.
"Something big," said {hero_name}. "Something very big."
Boom.
And there in the path, where the mud was softest, lay a footprint. It was wider than the bath at home, with four huge round toes, and the rain had filled it to the brim. It looked just like the fossil prints in {hero_name}'s dinosaur book, only fresh.
{hero_name} crouched at the edge and looked down into the water.
"Who made you?" whispered {hero_name}.
{hero_name} opened the notebook. Mystery number one, whose footprint is this?
Up on the hill, the tallest treetops looked nibbled flat across the top. Down here beside the print, a long swishy line curved away through the mud.
Then, down by the lake, something enormous put one more foot down.

s2a.text:
Up the hill, then.
{hero_name} climbed until the tall trees stood close enough to touch, and looked up.
Every one of them had a flat top. Above a certain line the leaves were gone. Below the line they hung on thick and green, without one bite out of them.
"Neat," said {hero_name}. "Neat as the crusts cut off a sandwich."
The magnifying glass was no use up here, so {hero_name} put it away and thought instead.
Nothing had touched the low leaves. So whatever ate up here could not reach down there, and did not need to.
{hero_name} leaned on the notebook and wrote it down. Clue one. Taller than a house. Maybe taller than two houses. Eats leaves.
Boom.
{hero_name} turned round and looked down through the ferns. The booms were coming from the lake, slow, with a long wait in between, the way somebody walks when nothing is hurrying them.
"Right," said {hero_name}, and pulled the backpack straps tight.

s2b.text:
Down on hands and knees, then.
The swishy line curved off through the mud like a spoon dragged through porridge, and {hero_name} crouched low and went along beside it with one hand flat on the ground.
"A tail," said {hero_name}. "A tail as long as a slide."
Then footprints turned up on both sides of the line, and they were not all the same size. Some enormous, like the one back on the path. Some middle sized. Some small and round, no bigger than a dinner plate, wandering off the trail and back.
{hero_name} pointed at each one in turn and counted. Big prints, middle prints, little prints, all walking the same way.
"A herd," said {hero_name}. "A whole family out together, with one tail dragging down the middle."
Something pale lay in the mud. {hero_name} lifted it out: a fern leaf, snipped off flat across the top.
"Leaves," said {hero_name}. "They stopped here to eat leaves."
Boom.
Every toe on the trail pointed the same way, down towards the lake.

s3.text:
{hero_name} crouched behind a fern as wide as an umbrella and watched the lake.
The booms were close now, and every one shook the puddles into rings, and {hero_name}'s heart went along with them, boom boom, only faster.
Then the treetops opened and up came a neck.
Up, and up, and up. {hero_name} leaned back to look at the top of it.
"Oh," said {hero_name}. "Oh, hello."
She was enormous, grey green and slow, with sleepy eyes the colour of wet stone. She reached her neck out sideways, took hold of the very top of a tree, and stripped the leaves off flat across. Just like the treetops up on the hill. And behind her, sliding through the mud, came one long swishy line. Her tail.
{hero_name} stayed put. The ground behind the fern was firm to stand on, and big animals like plenty of room. From back here you could see the whole of her at once.
{hero_name} jumped up and down without a sound.
"It is you," whispered {hero_name}. "I am almost sure it is you."

s4a.text:
Down by the mama's legs stood a baby long neck, no taller than a pony.
It lifted one foot and stamped it into the mud, then the other. Stomp, stomp, stomp, and behind it a line of little round prints, the size of dinner plates.
"Little feet, little prints," said {hero_name}.
Then the mama took one step.
Boom.
Her foot went down into the soft mud and lifted away again. Four huge round toes.
{hero_name} put the notebook flat on the ground beside it and drew round the inside of one toe. One toe filled the whole page.
"Case closed," said {hero_name}. "It was you all along."
The baby lifted its head and let out a small happy honk, like a party horn.
Then the mama's neck came down, all the way down, until her nose touched the yellow backpack. Her breath smelled of fern leaves.
Over at the water's edge, a Triceratops walked in to drink beside the herd. {hero_name} wrote three horns in the notebook, for tomorrow.
"See you tomorrow," said {hero_name}.

s4b.text:
Back at the enormous footprint, {hero_name} crouched in the ferns and waited.
Boom.
The herd was coming to drink. Out of the trees leaned the mama's long neck, and her front foot came down in the mud, right next to the old print.
When she lifted it away, there was a brand new footprint. The same size, and the same four round toes.
"Case closed," whispered {hero_name}. "It was you."
The old print had one more thing in it. Three tiny frogs looked up at {hero_name} out of the water. A small bird landed on the rim, put its beak in, and drank the way you test the bathwater with one finger.
Somebody's step had turned into a swimming pool for frogs.
{hero_name} put the notebook on one knee and drew the whole thing, frogs and bird and all.
The mama rumbled, like a lorry a long way off.
So {hero_name} stepped into the soft mud and pressed one small footprint next to hers.
"There," said {hero_name}. "Now there are two of us."

c1.question: {hero_name} tapped the pencil on the page. "Two clues," said {hero_name}. "Flat treetops up the hill, or the swishy line down in the mud. Treetops, or mud?"

options.label: The nibbled treetops on the hill
The swishy line in the mud

c2.question: {hero_name} counted on two fingers. "One," said {hero_name}. "There is a little one down by her feet, making little prints. Two. My enormous print is back along the trail, waiting. Baby, or puddle?"

options.label: The little dinosaur by the mama's legs
Back at the footprint puddle

hero_name.role: the child explorer solving the footprint mystery

s1.text: We are tucked in bed, you and I, under the glow of the nightlight, when the ceiling begins to change. It ripples like dark water. For a moment, that is all — we lie very still, listening to the quiet. Then the ceiling opens, slowly, into a map of stars, and they settle into place one by one, as if someone were lighting them. A low hum arrives, soft and far away, before anything else does. Outside the window, a train pulls up, glowing soft as moonlight. Its name shines in silver letters: {train_name}. The door slides open, and a figure in a long coat steps out. "All aboard," says the Sleep Conductor, tipping a cap that sparkles like the sky. We climb aboard. The carriage hums beneath our feet, a gentle rhythm, like a heartbeat. The Conductor smiles. "First stop, the spiral staircase. Every full turn is one sleep cycle. Ready?" The train begins to move.

s2a.text: "Observation deck," we say together. The Conductor grins and pulls a brass lever. The train tilts, climbing the spiral staircase inside your head. One full turn, one sleep cycle. We step out onto the deck just as the train slides into Light Sleep Station. The lanterns along the track dim to a warm amber, soft as the glow of toast in the oven. The world outside the windows slows down. It feels like drifting on a gentle river, the kind that rocks you without trying. "Look," whispers Pippa the bushbaby, pointing with one tiny paw. "Your eyelids." And there they are, reflected in the glass, fluttering like moth wings. We hold very still and watch them. Nobody says anything for a moment. The Conductor leans on the rail beside us, quiet, and tips their cap. The train hums under our feet, slower now. Pippa curls up on my shoulder, her heartbeat a tiny drum against my ear. Ahead, the track splits. One line rolls on toward Deep Sleep Station. The other curves away toward a glass dome gleaming in the dark. "Brain Observatory," says the Conductor. "But we can only visit one before the deepest sleep comes."

s2b.text: "The Observatory," we say. The Conductor nods and flips a silver switch. The train hums, then slips onto a side track that curves away from the main line. We climb a narrow stair and step into a glass-domed car filled with soft blue light. Screens cover the walls, each one showing a different line. Some are quick and jittery, like ants racing across the glass. Others roll slow and smooth, like waves on a calm sea. "Those are your brain waves," says a voice. A figure in a long scarf steps forward, holding a glowing pen. "I'm the Wave-Maker. Watch." She draws in the air, and the lines appear, hanging like ribbons. We reach out and trace them with our fingers. The quick ones tickle. The slow ones feel like stroking a cat. We stand there a while, tracing, and she lets us. The train rocks gently. Pippa yawns, her tiny mouth opening wide. Outside the dome, the main line glows in the distance. "Time to go back," says the Wave-Maker. "The deepest sleep is coming."

s3.text: The train slows. "Deep Sleep Station," the Conductor says, soft as a finger to lips. We step out into air that is cool and blue, and the whole world feels tucked under a heavy blanket. Even our footsteps are quiet here. The Conductor points to a signpost carved with one word: Cycle 1. "Listen," they say, and nothing more. We listen. Far off, something vast breathes in and out, in and out, and the floor rises and settles beneath us, gentle as a rocking chair. We stand there a long while. No one speaks. The Conductor watches the blue dark, hands folded, and lets the breathing be the only sound. Behind us, the train hums, ready to climb. The staircase spirals up through the blue dark, and somewhere at the top, eyes are beginning to flicker under closed lids. "Next stop, REM," says the Conductor. "How shall we go up?"

s4a.text: "The Control Room," we say together. The Conductor grins and pulls a brass lever. The staircase spirals up, and we step off into a round room full of soft lights. In the centre, a screen glows like a window. We lean close. It is our own face, asleep in bed. Our eyes dart left, then right, under closed lids. We watch. Nobody says anything. Back and forth, back and forth, quick as minnows under the skin. A figure with gentle hands waves from a desk covered in zigzag lines. "I am the Wave-Maker," they say. "See these busy brain waves? Sharp and quick, like city lights. Your body lies still as a statue, but your mind is dancing." We keep watching our own sleeping face. The Conductor touches our shoulder. "The train is finishing its first full cycle," they say. "Every turn of the staircase is one sleep cycle. And they all connect, like links in a chain. Shall we see where they meet?" We nod, and the room begins to hum.

s4b.text: "The Dream Library," we say. The Conductor smiles and opens a door stitched with stars. Inside, shelves stretch high, filled with glowing books. A figure with kind eyes and ink-stained fingers turns to us. "Welcome," says the Brain Librarian. "This is where your day gets sorted during REM." She pulls a book from the shelf. Its pages shimmer. We see bits of our own day inside: a joke we laughed at, a game we played, something new we learned. She points to a reading mirror. We look in. Our own eyes flicker under closed lids, left and right, quick as minnows. We watch them for a moment, and she lets us, saying nothing at all. We touch the glowing page, and it feels warm, like toast. The Conductor appears beside us. "The train is finishing its first full cycle," they say. "Every turn of the staircase is one sleep cycle. And they all connect, like beads on a string. Shall we see where they meet?" We nod, and the books hum softly.

c1.question: "We can ride the observation deck and watch the world drift by as we fall into light sleep, or we can slip into the Brain Observatory to see the waves your mind is making right now. Which calls to you?"

options.label: Ride the observation deck to experience light sleep
Visit the Brain Observatory to see the brain waves

c2.question: "We're approaching REM—the busy dreaming time. Would you rather step into the Control Room to see your own eyes flicker and watch your brain light up like a city, or visit the Dream Library to discover what all that dreaming is for?"

options.label: Enter the Control Room to observe REM from outside
Enter the Dream Library to understand the purpose of REM

train_name.role: The name of the sleep train

stories.title: The Night We Shrunk the Whale

s1.text: Down in the basement, past the laundry baskets, our cousin {cousin_name} fixes phones at a workbench. It is nearly bedtime, and the whole room is dark except for one thing: an old monitor with a cracked corner, glowing with a single white square. Just one. It hangs there like a tiny window with the light left on. "Come look at this," {cousin_name} says, "before it goes to recycling tomorrow." She hands us a jeweler's loupe — a little glass eye on a handle. We lean in close. Closer. The square fills our whole eye, soft and warm and humming. "That," she whispers, "is a pixel. The smallest thing a screen can say." The smallest thing. We look at her. She is grinning. "And tonight," she says, "we're going to follow it all the way to the biggest. Want to?" We nod so hard the loupe nearly falls off our nose. She lifts the monitor's lid like the top of a treasure chest. The little pixel twinkles, as if it heard its name. And then — it winks.

s2a.text: "First," says {cousin_name}, "we look inside." She clicks the loupe into a stand and twists a knob on her bench lamp. The light gets brighter, and brighter, and — whoa. The white square splits. Right down the middle. It is not one light at all. It is three skinny bars, standing shoulder to shoulder: one red, one green, one blue. Like a tiny striped scarf, glowing. "Every pixel is really three little lights," {cousin_name} says. "Red, green, blue. Watch." She twists the knob the other way, and the three bars glow brighter and brighter until they smear together — and the square is white again. Just like that. Three colors, holding hands so tight you cannot see the fingers. Something wiggles in our pocket. Pip pops out, puffed up with pride. "That's me!" he squeaks. "Three little lights! I've been carrying them the whole time!" He glows red. Then green. Then blue. Then a wobbly, show-off white. We laugh. But {cousin_name} is looking at the screen, thoughtful. "So if one square hides three lights," she says slowly, "what do you suppose a whole picture is hiding?"

s2b.text: "Or," says {cousin_name}, "we find out where a square comes from." She pulls out her phone. "I took this on the ferry this morning." It is {whale_photo}. Water everywhere. It is the best photo we have ever seen. "The camera didn't draw this," she says. "It chopped it. The second that whale jumped, the camera sliced the whole splash into millions of tiny numbered squares. Millions. Each one a pixel, each one with a number that says exactly what color to glow." She pinches the screen and zooms. In. In. The whale's smile stretches into giant soft blocks — gray ones, white ones, one surprising pink one where the splash catches the sun. In our pocket, Pip groans. "Ooooh," he says, stretching wide as a pancake. "I feel it every time. Zooming is very stretchy work." {cousin_name} zooms back out, and the blocks melt into a whale again, just like that. "Cameras and screens speak the same language," she says. "One catches the squares. One shows them." She taps the phone, and her eyes go bright. "So what happens when we send these numbers somewhere enormous?"

s3.text: Back upstairs, {cousin_name} is already holding our coats. "What did you find?" she asks. We tell her, all in a tumble, and she listens like it's the best news all week. "Then there's one place left," she says. "Buckle up." We drive through the dark, and Pip rides in our pocket, glowing softly, like a night-light that got to come along. The museum is closed, but a side door opens, and a guide with a silver remote smiles at us like she's been waiting all night. "Your whale came," she says. "It's loaded." She leads us into a room so dark it feels like being underwater. And there, on the wall, glows a screen bigger than a real whale — and on it, our whale, frozen mid-splash, enormous and still. Pip trembles in our pocket. He can feel it: millions of his cousins, all glowing at once. The guide holds out the remote. "How close should the whale get?" she says. "You decide."

s4a.text: "Dive closer," we say. "Zoom in." The guide presses the button. The whale shivers — and falls apart. The whole room gasps. Where one enormous animal hung a second ago, now there are a million glowing tiles, like a kitchen floor made of light. We walk right up, close enough to feel the warmth of the screen on our cheeks. Up close, every tile has three tiny stripes inside it: one red, one green, one blue. "Every pixel is really three little lamps," the guide says, "holding hands." In our pocket, Pip stretches wide with a happy squeak, suddenly as big as a sandwich. "Find the nose," we whisper. So we hunt along the glowing wall until — there. One tile, brighter than the rest, right where the whale's nose-tip used to be. We press one finger to its warm light. "Hello, you," we say. On our way out we peek through an open door, where an artist nudges single pixels with a pen, making a cartoon eyebrow twitch. At home, {cousin_name} gives us the loupe to keep. We press it to our own TV and whisper hello. We know their secret now. And Pip glows in our pocket all the way home.

s4b.text: "Drift back," we say. "Zoom out." The guide presses the button. The tiles shiver — and melt. Millions of little squares let go of their edges, all at once, like sugar dissolving in warm milk. And then the room goes very quiet. Because there, turning slowly in the dark, is one whole whale. Enormous. Mid-splash. So real we hold our breath without deciding to. "That's their favorite trick," the guide says softly. "Disappearing together, to become something bigger than any of them." In our pocket, Pip squeezes down small again, sighing a tiny, contented glow. On our way out, we pass a lobby screen where a video game is paused — a whole world of castles and clouds, and now we know: it's all the same tiny squares, agreeing. The guide tucks a postcard of the whale into our hand. "So you remember," she says. At home, we prop it beside the TV. Every picture we ever see will have a secret in it now, and we carry that secret home. Pip settles into our pocket, small and warm, and the whale goes on leaping, quietly, forever.

c1.question: "Two ways in, explorers. Do you want to look INSIDE the square — or see where a square comes from?"

options.label: peer through the loupe into the pixel's three hidden lights
see how the camera chopped a real whale into numbered squares

c2.question: "The remote is yours now. So — do we dive closer, until the whale falls apart into light? Or drift back, and watch a million little lights become one whale?"

options.label: zoom closer until the whale becomes a mosaic of glowing squares
zoom out and watch the squares melt into one enormous whale

cousin_name.role: the older cousin who repairs phones

whale_photo.role: the single photo that travels from the cousin's phone to the giant museum screen
whale_photo.default: a whale leaping out of the ocean, frozen mid-splash

stories.title: The Night the Bay Turned Into a Lamp

s1.text:
Old Nell keeps her diving mask on a nail by her door. It is scratched and salty and older than you are.
On warm evenings she sits at the end of the dock with her feet over the water, and if you sit beside her she tells you about the sea.
Tonight she reaches up and taps the mask twice. That means a good one is coming.
"There was a night," she says, "when this whole bay turned into a lamp."
She points out past the moorings with one bare foot.
"I had a little wooden boat then. {boat_name}, with one oar that squeaked. No wind that night, and the water lay flat and black, like a floor somebody had just washed."
"So out I rowed. Squeak. Squeak."
"And then I stopped rowing." Nell holds up a hand and keeps it there. "Because something under my boat was pale."
"Not the moon. The moon was still behind the hill."
"A soft round glow, deep down. Then another one beside it. Then another."
Nell turns and looks at us.
"Jellyfish. Hundreds of them, drifting in on the tide."

s2a.text:
"I held my lantern right down at the water," said Nell, "and up they came to it. The little ones."
"Small as plums. Small as buttons."
"And see-through, every one of them, so I could look straight through a jellyfish and watch my own lantern shining out the other side."
She holds her fingers apart to show how small.
"Mostly water, you know. Almost all water, in a thin round coat."
"And the way they swim." Her hand opens and shuts. "Squeeze, and glide. Squeeze, and glide. Like a little umbrella in the rain. Every squeeze pushes it up a bit, then it rests and sinks back down again, all night long, going nowhere in particular."
"One of them wobbled along beside my oar and did not mind me one bit."
Nell pats the boards of the dock.
"I kept my fingers in the boat, mind. We look at jellyfish. We do not touch them. It is a friendly rule. It lets you sit as close as you please."

s2b.text:
"I blew my lantern out," said Nell. "Puff."
"And then I could not see a thing, and the dark came up to my chin. So I sat still and counted slow. One. Two. Three."
She counts on her fingers.
"And bit by bit my eyes learned the dark. And then the bay came on."
"Not one glow. Thousands." Nell opens both arms wide. "Pale green and pale blue, all the way out to the black cliffs. Some deep down and blurry. Some hanging just under the top, bright as dropped coins."
"A little wave rolled through, and every light rolled with it, and the whole bay wobbled and shone."
"So I put one oar in. Slow as I could."
"And the water lit up round it in a ring."
She draws the ring in the air.
"Then I did it again. Ring after ring after ring, off into the dark. And I laughed out loud, all on my own in the middle of the water, with nobody to hear me but {boat_name} and that squeaky oar."

s3.text:
"I still remember {first_sight}," said Nell. "But that is not the part I tell people."
She leans in.
"Here is that part. Something big came up beside my boat. Slow. So slow."
"A pale white bell, as wide across as a dinner plate, turning over and over as it rose, until it hung just under the top of the water, close enough to lean out and put my hand on."
"I did not." Nell lays both hands flat on her knees and leaves them there. "Like this. We look, and we do not touch, and that way the sea and I stay friends."
"It floated along beside {boat_name}, opening and closing, opening and closing. Like something breathing in its sleep."
"And it had no face to look back at me with. It did not need one."
"It only drifted. The way its kind have drifted since long before there were boats, or oars, or people to be amazed at them."
Nell is quiet for a moment.
"And the tide was getting ready to turn."

s4a.text:
"I let the oars rest," said Nell, "and I went wherever she went. Nothing about that night was in a hurry."
"Past the old post with the mussels on it."
"And then the tide turned. You can feel a tide turn, if you are sitting still enough. The water sighs and starts off the other way."
Nell tips her hand slowly over.
"Down she went. Turning as she sank, going dimmer and rounder and smaller, until she was one little coin of light. Then a smudge. Then nothing."
"And all round her the thousands of small ones were sinking too, back to the deep water where they spend the day."
"The bay went dark and ordinary again. So I rowed home. Squeak. Squeak."
"I tied {boat_name} up and stood about on this dock with wet feet for a long while."
Nell reaches up and taps her old mask twice.
"Some nights the sea puts its lamps on," she says. "You do not have to do a single thing about it. You only have to be out there, looking."

s4b.text:
"I rowed in," said Nell, "and tied {boat_name} up with glowing fingers. Truly. The shine faded off my hands while I climbed the headland path in the dark, and my feet know every root of that path, so I took it slow."
"And I sat down on the flat rock at the top, and there it was. The whole bay at once, below me, like a bowl of milk with a light left on inside it."
"Out at the mouth, three fishing boats were coming home, each with a small yellow lamp at the front. People made those lamps, so people could find their way home."
"And underneath those boats the whole sea was shining pale green, and nobody made that at all. It has been at it far longer than there have been people to watch."
"The little lamps came in one by one and went out. The big one stayed on till the tide turned."
Nell looks out at the dark water.
"That is why I sit here every evening," she says. "Not waiting for anything. Keeping the sea company."

c1.question: Nell taps the mask again. "Two things I could have done," she says. "Hold my lantern right down at the water, or blow it out and let my eyes learn the dark. Which would you have done? Lantern, or dark?"

options.label: Hold the lantern down close to the water

sets_slots.first_sight: the little ones opening and shutting like tiny umbrellas

options.label: Blow the lantern out and let her eyes learn the dark

sets_slots.first_sight: the whole bay glowing at once, all the way out to the cliffs

c2.question: Nell holds up two fingers. "I could drift along beside her and see where she went," she says. "Or row in and climb the headland and look down at the whole lot of it. Drift, or climb?"

options.label: Drift along beside the big jellyfish
Climb the headland and look down at the whole bay

boat_name.role: the night diver's little wooden boat

first_sight.role: what the diver looked at first when the bay lit up
first_sight.default: the little ones opening and shutting like tiny umbrellas

stories.title: The Night the Eyes Came Back

s1.text:
The first thing you need to know about Shep is that he once carried a live black-footed ferret home to the porch, gentle as a ferry, and set it down like a delivery. That was three years ago, back when everybody thought the ferrets were gone from this ranch for good. Gone. Extinct, maybe, the way a word can sound like a door closing.

Tonight we are standing in that same Wyoming dusk with Nico and Dr. Wren, and the sky is the color of plum jam. Shep trots beside us, his tail thumping a jaunty drumbeat against our legs. Thump. Thump. He knows this job.

"Clipboards," says Dr. Wren, pressing one into our hands. "And the spotlight. You sweep the beam low over the prairie dog town, slow, like you're painting a fence. What you're looking for is eyeshine. Two little green sparks. Emerald, like someone lit tiny lanterns in the dark."

"Every pair of eyes is one ferret," Nico says. "We count them all. That's the whole job."

"The count matters," Dr. Wren says, "because a population is just a fancy word for how many are left. Last year we counted nine. Nine is not a lot. This year, the first hour of looking has found zero."

Zero. The word sits down in the grass and does not move.

"Zero doesn't mean gone," Dr. Wren says quickly. "It means we haven't looked in the right places yet. That's why I need counters who are thorough. Counters who are honest. Midnight is our deadline. We count every ferret on this ranch before then, or we don't know what we're working with."

Shep sits down in the grass and looks out at the prairie dog town, ears up, like he is listening for something we cannot hear yet.

We lift the spotlight. The beam lands on the first mound, pale and round as a dinner plate.

Nothing.

We move it to the next one. Slow. Like painting a fence.

"They're out there," Nico says. "Shep found one before."

Thump. Thump. Goes the tail.

s2a.text:
"On foot," we say, and Dr. Wren nods like she hoped we would. "The old way."

So we walk. Shep out front, nose down, tail going thump, thump against the dark. We sweep the spotlight low, slow, like painting a fence. Burrow after burrow. Mound after mound.

Nothing.

"Eyes," Nico whispers. "Come on. Two little green lanterns."

But the prairie dog town is empty as a cupboard before breakfast. An hour of walking, and the only eyes we find belong to one sleepy owl, who blinks at us like we woke him up for nothing.

"Zero," Dr. Wren says, and writes it down honest. "The ferrets hunt at night, and they hunt far. A black-footed ferret can travel miles before sunrise. Our little line of walkers can't cover it."

Then Shep stops. Freezes. His whole body goes still as a fence post.

"What, boy?"

He trots to the far fence, the one at the very edge of the ranch, and points his nose at the wire. There, trembling in the wind, is a single strand of fur. Pale gold, with a black tip.

Dr. Wren lifts it free, gentle as a secret. "Ferret," she says. "Fresh. It crossed here tonight, heading out past the fence."

We look out past the wire, into all that dark.

"They're not gone," Nico says. "They're scattered. Wider than anybody can walk."

Somewhere out there, tiny green lanterns are moving, and our boots cannot reach them. Shep leans his warm shoulder against our leg, and the wind carries the strand of fur smell past his nose one more time. Thump, goes his tail. One beat. A promise.

s2b.text:
"The lab," we say, and Dr. Okafor's whole face lights up like a porch lamp. "Good. The ferrets leave us letters everywhere. We just have to read them."

Her field lab is a trailer that smells like coffee and warm dust, and it is crowded with little paper bags. "Hair and scat from the burrow mouths," she says, handing us tweezers. "Every sample tells me who walked by. Collect them like treasure."

So we do. Shep supervises, nose working, tail thumping the trailer steps. Thump. Thump. By midnight the table is covered in bags, and Dr. Okafor feeds the samples into a humming machine that reads DNA — the tiny instruction book inside every hair.

"First letter," she announces, peering at the screen. Then she laughs. "Weasel."

"Second?"

"Cat. The ranch's own cat, I'd bet my boots."

Half our treasure belongs to the wrong animals entirely. Nico groans. "We're counting everybody except ferrets."

But then the machine hums again, and Dr. Okafor goes very quiet. "Ferret," she says. "Real ferret. And another. And one more." She spins the screen around so we can see. "They're out there, friends. That's the good news. The strange news is — they're nearly all related. Cousins. Brothers and sisters."

"Is that bad?" we ask.

"It's the start of something called an extinction vortex," she says. "When a population gets small enough, everyone left is family, and the number shrinks faster and faster — like leaves circling a drain. The ferrets aren't just few. The few is pulling them down."

The words sit down in the trailer and get heavy.

"So counting them isn't enough anymore," Nico says slowly.

Dr. Okafor shakes her head. "No. The number itself is the emergency now." Shep pushes his warm head under our hand, and outside, somewhere in the dark, two green lanterns we haven't found yet are burning.

s3.text:
The ranch kitchen at midnight smells like coffee and old boots, and the table is covered in maps. Shep pushes his head under our arm while Dr. Wren clears a space between the mugs. "All right," she says. "Tell me what you found out there." We tell her, every bit of it, and she listens with her pencil pressed flat against the table, nodding slowly, the way you nod when a puzzle piece finally turns the right way around.

"That confirms it," she says at last. "The population is real. But it is dangerously small, and now we know why our first fixes failed." She holds up one finger. "We tried vaccinating ferrets by hand. We could not find enough of them to catch." A second finger. "We tried vaccine bait for the prairie dogs the ferrets depend on. It melted in the summer heat. Both times, we were reaching for one animal at a time."

Nico unrolls a hand-drawn map of the prairie dog town, weighted at the corners with a flashlight and a spoon. Dr. Okafor leans over it and marks the healthy zones from her samples, small green circles blooming across the paper. And there it is, the whole problem at once, spread out between the jam jar and the salt.

"So we stop reaching for one ferret," Nico says slowly, "and reach the whole prairie."

"Drones," says Dr. Wren. "Dropping vaccine pellets over the entire town." 
"{pellet_flavor} flavored," Nico says. "Obviously."
"And at Marisol's breeding center," Dr. Okafor adds, "new ferrets. Unrelated ones, to freshen the family tree. A recovery needs both."

Thump. Thump. Shep's tail, under the table.

"It launches at dawn," Dr. Wren says. "Two missions. We can only join one."

s4a.text:
The drone sounds like a helpful bee. We stand with Dr. Wren on the safe side of the fence, Shep's ears tilted at the hum, and watch it drift over the prairie dog town in slow straight rows. The pellets patter down like slow rain. Plip. Plip. Plip. Dr. Wren reads the map and nods at every green circle. "Good coverage," she says. "Now the prairie waits for dark."

Dark comes, and we sweep the spotlight low over the mounds, slow, like painting a fence.

Nothing.

Then — two green sparks. Emerald, like tiny lanterns.

"One," Nico whispers.

The beam slides on. Two more sparks, close together. Then a small tumbling shape, all elbows, chasing its mother through the grass.

"A kit," Dr. Wren breathes. "That's not just a population. That's a family."

We count fourteen before midnight. The last pair of eyes is small and steady and does not blink, and Nico grins at us. "That one's yours. Name it."

"{ferret_name}," we say, and the name fits like a collar.

Before we leave, Dr. Wren holds out her phone toward Shep and presses record. Jingle. Jingle. Goes his tagged collar. "There," she says. "The sound of this ranch working." She hands us a labeled envelope, and inside it is the bit of fur from the fence, proof that one hair can restart a whole population.

We ride home with the envelope in our pocket and the jingle in the phone, and somewhere behind us in the dark, {ferret_name} is still out there, glowing.

s4b.text:
Marisol's breeding center smells like clean straw. The ferret kits here are raised with barely any human contact, so they stay wild. We watch the oldest one through the window of her pen, a small masked face with bright dark eyes, and we keep our hands folded and our voices low. Wild is the whole point.

"She doesn't know our names," Marisol says. "That's how you know we did it right."

We help her ready the crate: fresh straw, water, one glove slipped under the door like a gift. Then we drive to the ranch at dusk, the crate riding quiet between us, Shep's tail thumping a slow drumbeat against our legs. Thump. Thump.

On the prairie dog town, Marisol sets the crate down facing the grass. She opens the door and steps back, and we step back too, because this part belongs to the ferret.

For a moment, nothing. Then she pours out of the crate like spilled water, low and quick and gone into the grass, and the grass closes over her like it was keeping her a place.

An hour later the spotlight finds her: two green sparks, emerald, tiny lanterns in the dark. Home.

"You did the hard part," Dr. Wren says. "Name her."

"{ferret_name}," we say, and the night seems to hold it gently.

Back at the kitchen table, Marisol gives us a paper map of the ranch, one green dot for every known ferret. Thirteen dots, where last year there were nine. "And far away in Brazil," she says, "people are planting bridges of trees so isolated monkeys can find each other too."

We pin the map up at home, and Shep sleeps under it, and somewhere out there {ferret_name} is glowing in the grass, and the map is only just beginning.

c1.question: "The ferrets are hiding from my spotlight, friends. So which crew are you — do we walk the burrows on foot and search the old way, or do we let Dr. Okafor read the clues they left behind in the lab?"

options.label: Walk the prairie dog town with the spotlight crew and search burrow by burrow
Help Dr. Okafor count ferrets from hair and scat DNA in the field lab

c2.question: "Dawn's coming and the plan has two halves. Who's coming with me to fly the vaccine drones over the prairie — and who's going with Marisol to help a brand-new ferret come home?"

options.label: Join the drone crew dropping vaccine pellets across the whole prairie at dawn
Go to the breeding center and help return a hand-raised kit to the wild

ferret_name.role: the name we give the very last ferret we find, the one whose eyeshine proves the population is still alive

pellet_flavor.role: the silly flavor Nico suggests for the drone-dropped vaccine pellets, repeated in the landing

stories.title: The Night the Sand Went Soft

s1.text:
Sabina puts out her last lamp before she begins.
"There," she says. "Now we can see properly."
We are sitting on her back step, you and me, with the warm dark all around us and the sea making its slow sound at the bottom of the garden. Sabina has been watching this beach since she was smaller than you are.
"Forty years," she says, "and I still get out of bed for it."
She points with her chin, down the sand, at a low ring of stones.
"A nest. Ninety days it has been down there, quiet as a loaf rising under a cloth. Tonight it is ready. I can tell, because the top of the sand has gone soft."
We walk down and sit where the sand is cool, well back from the stones. Sabina clicks off her torch and puts it in her pocket.
"No lights now," she says. "When they come up, the water must be the brightest thing they can see."
And the water is bright. A long pale road of it, running from the sand all the way out to the sky.
We wait.

s2a.text:
We lie back and look up.
There are so many stars that the sky looks spilled, like sugar knocked off a table.
"Keep half an eye on the stones," Sabina whispers, "and half an eye up there."
The pale road on the water is still the brightest thing on the whole beach. Brighter than the houses. Brighter than the stars.
"That is how they know," she says. "They come up out of the dark sand and they run at the brightest place they can find. Which is the sea. It has worked for a very long time."
A little wind comes off the water and goes across our faces, cool on top and warm underneath.
Sabina does not move at all. Only her eyes move, back to the ring of stones.
We keep half an eye up and half an eye down, exactly as she said.

s2b.text:
We lay one hand flat on the sand.
It is warm. Warmer than the air, the way a bath stays warm after you have let some of it out.
"That warmth is doing the work," Sabina whispers. "Ninety days of sun, cooking them slowly, down where nothing can reach them."
We keep our hand still.
And then, under our palm, something goes tick.
Very small. Once, and then twice, and then a soft busy scratching, like somebody turning over under a heavy blanket.
"Ah," says Sabina, and she says nothing else for a long moment.
The scratching comes again, closer to the top.
We take our hand away, gently, and sit back on our heels, and neither of us says a word.

s3.text:
We forget all about {first_watch}.
The sand inside the ring of stones is moving.
First it only shivers. Then the middle sinks down into a little dish, the way porridge sinks when you press it with a spoon.
A flipper comes up. Then a head, no bigger than a bottle cap, black and wet and shining.
"Here they come," breathes Sabina. "Watch now. Watch."
And out they pour. Ten, then twenty, then more turtles than we can count, tumbling over each other and sorting themselves out and setting off down the sand, all of them pointed the same way, at the pale road on the water.
Their flippers make a sound like rain starting on a roof.
One is slower than the rest. It comes up last, at the back of everybody, and stops to have a think.
"That one," says Sabina softly. "There is always one."
We call that one {turtle_name}.

s4a.text:
We walk down beside them, slowly, keeping well out of their way.
Nobody carries anybody. Nobody helps. That is the rule, and Sabina says the crawl is good for them anyway, like a stretch first thing in the morning.
The sand is a river of small dark backs, all going one way.
At the edge, the first wave comes up to meet them and takes about thirty of them at once, lifting them off their feet, and suddenly they are not clumsy any more. They are swimmers. They were swimmers all along and nobody told them.
{turtle_name} arrives last, thinks about it, and goes in on the second wave.
Then the beach is empty and quiet and the pale road is just a road again.
Sabina lets out a breath she has been holding for a while.
"Off they go," she says. "Some of them will come back to this exact beach one day and do the whole thing again."
We walk home very slowly.
"Goodnight, small ones," says Sabina, at the top of the steps. "Swim well."

s4b.text:
We stay where we are and keep our eyes on {turtle_name}.
Everybody else has gone. It is only this one now, at the top of the sand, working away.
One flipper. Then the other flipper. Then a rest.
"No hurrying," Sabina says, to us or to the turtle, we are not sure which.
It goes crooked for a bit and then finds the bright water again and straightens itself out. It climbs over a shell twice its own size. It stops once more, right at the wet part, as if the cold has surprised it.
Then a wave comes in and lifts {turtle_name} up as easily as picking up a leaf, and turns it around, and takes it away.
The sea does the rest.
Sabina puts her hands on her knees and gets up.
"Slow ones get there too," she says. "That is the whole thing, really."
We walk back up to the house without our torch, because our eyes have got good at the dark by now.
"Goodnight, small one. Swim well."

c1.question: Sabina keeps her eyes on the stones. "While we wait," she whispers, "you can look up at the sky, or you can put your hand flat on the sand. Sky, or sand?"

options.label: Look up at the stars while we wait
Put a hand flat on the warm sand

sets_slots.first_watch: the warm sand under our hand

c2.question: "Now," says Sabina, getting slowly to her feet. "You can walk down beside them to the water. Or you can stay up here with {turtle_name}. Walk, or stay?"

options.label: Walk down beside them to the water
Stay up here with the slow one

turtle_name.role: the one hatchling slower than all the others

first_watch.role: what we were watching while we waited

s1.text:
It is late, and we are allowed to be outside.
We sit on the cool grass, you and me, with our jar of marbles between us. Red ones here. Swirly ones there.
The telescope stands on the flat paving stones, where its three thin legs never wobble.
Then a light slides across our hands.
"Look," we say.
The telescope’s round glass eye is glowing. We lean in close, and the glass opens like a little round door.
We climb through, one, two, and step out onto the soft dark of the sky.
Stars hang everywhere. A little silver boat rocks on the starlight, waiting for us, her sail a patch of shimmer, and her name is {boat_name}.
We climb aboard, and off she slides down a river of light.
Then she slows. The sky path splits in two. One way glows warm and red, with a small dusty world turning at the end.
"Mars," we say. "That one is Mars."
The other way shimmers, where a giant world wears wide bright rings, like a hat with no top.
Both are planets. Other worlds. Right here in the sky.

s2a.text:
{boat_name} lands soft on the red ground, and the dust puffs up over our boots like flour off a counter.
We hop out. And oh, we keep going up. High as a swing, then down slow, and we land without a sound.
"Again," we say.
So we hop again. Boing. Boing.
Everything here is rusty red. The rocks, the hills, the little stones by our boots. Even the sky is a soft butterscotch color.
Two tiny moons cross over us, one quick and one slow, playing chase.
A whirl of dust comes twirling past, spins twice, and goes.
We crouch down and draw a big smiling face in the dust with one finger. Wide eyes. Wide smile.
"For whoever comes next," we say.
Then {boat_name} rings her bell. Ding. Time to sail.
We climb aboard with red dust still on our sleeves, and Mars shrinks below us to a red marble rolling through the dark.

s2b.text:
{boat_name} sails toward the rings, and they widen and widen until they fill the whole sky.
"No marble in our jar wears a hat like that," we say.
From far away they looked painted on, one smooth silver hoop. Up close we can see the secret.
Pieces. Millions of separate pieces of ice, tumbling side by side, all going the same way. Small as peas. Big as snowballs. A few as big as a house, and every single one catches the sun and winks at us.
We lean over the side and hold a hand out flat above them. They pour past underneath, turning over and over, and there is no sound at all.
One tiny bead of ring ice hops up into the boat. We hold it up. Round, cold, clear as a windowpane.
"Back you go," we say, and we put it over the side, and off it goes with the parade.
Behind us the ringed planet turns, slow and golden. Then the sail fills with starlight. We ride on.

s3.text:
We wave goodbye to {first_world} and follow the river of light onward.
Then something enormous comes up out of the dark in front of us.
Jupiter. The biggest planet there is. Every other planet could fit inside it with room left over.
"That is the big marble," we say. "The one nobody ever trades away."
Jupiter is striped all over, cream and orange and toffee brown. Down in the stripes one huge orange swirl turns round and round, and it has been turning in that same spot for hundreds of years.
{boat_name} is a ladybug sailing past a beach ball.
Little moons zip everywhere around us, dozens of them.
"Nine," we count. "Ten. Eleven. Twelve." Then we run out of numbers and start giggling instead.
Far off at the edge of the dark, two more lights wait for us. One is small and blue and icy, the farthest of them all. The other is a blue and white marble, and looking at it makes us go quiet, because we are almost sure we know it.

s4a.text:
{boat_name} sails on, out past the last of the firefly moons. The dark gets deeper. The quiet gets bigger.
And there it is. The farthest world, blue as the deep end of the swimming pool, with long white wisps of cloud combed sideways by the wind.
"That is the marble that rolls under the sofa," we whisper.
We look back for the sun, and it is only one more bright star. There is not much light out here, so the little blue world keeps what it gets and shines with it.
We tuck our hands under the warm shimmer sail and watch until our eyes are full.
Then {boat_name} swings around and takes us home. Past the striped giant. Past the rings. Past red Mars.
Out through the round telescope door, onto the cool grass, where the jar is still open.
We dig out our darkest blue marble and put it down on the paving stone, a long way from all the others.
"That one is yours," we say to the sky. "Goodnight, farthest world. Keep shining."

s4b.text:
{boat_name} turns toward the blue and white marble, and it grows until it fills the whole sky.
White clouds curl across it like cream stirred into blueberry milk. Under them lie wide blue seas, and green land, and brown land.
Then we both gasp, because we know it.
"That is ours," we say. "That is home."
Earth is a planet too. A world in the sky, sailing along with Mars and Jupiter and all the rest. Down under those clouds is our garden, our telescope, our own bed with the covers pulled back.
{boat_name} glides down through the soft clouds, slow as a leaf, and slips through the round telescope door.
We hop out onto the grass. It is cool. The night is quiet.
We dig in the jar for the blue and white swirly one, the one we never trade, and hold it up against the sky.
"We live on one of you," we whisper to the planets. "We live on this one."
Then we carry the best secret in the world off to bed.

c1.question: {boat_name} holds still between the two ways, her sail gone loose. "Red dust, or bright rings?" we say. "Mars, or rings?"

options.label: Land on the red dusty world
Sail out over the shining rings

c2.question: {boat_name} turns her sail one way, then the other, and waits for us. "Out to the icy one, or over to the swirly one?" we say. "Ice, or marble?"

options.label: Sail out to the farthest icy world
Turn toward the blue and white marble

stories.title: The Number That Always Comes Home

s1.text:
Grandpa's kitchen table is covered in the usual things. A chessboard with the squares worn soft. A jar of rice, fat and dusty. And his chipped blue teacup, the one with the crack running down the side like a tiny river.

We are sitting across from him, me and {friend_name}, and {friend_name} has their arms crossed. "Number tricks are just showing off," {friend_name} says. "There's always a catch."

Grandpa doesn't argue. He just taps his teacup twice. Tap. Tap. That means something is about to matter.

"Pick a number," he says. "Any number. Don't tell me."

{friend_name} picks one. I pick one too. Grandpa tells us to double it. Then add ten. Then halve it. Then take away the number we started with.

We do it in our heads. It takes a second. Then Grandpa looks at {friend_name} and says, "Five."

{friend_name}'s mouth drops open. "How did you—"

"And you," Grandpa says, turning to me. "Five."

He's right. We both got five. We started with different numbers, secret numbers, and we both landed on five.

"That's not possible," {friend_name} says.

Grandpa taps the teacup again. Tap. Tap. "It's not magic," he says. "It's a pattern. And patterns don't care what number you pick."

He leans back. "The question isn't how I knew. The question is why it works." He waits. "So. Do you want me to tell you the secret, or do you want to figure it out?"

s2a.text:
"The fair," {friend_name} says, before I can even breathe. "If this trick is so tough, let's break it in public."

So we take the chessboard, the rice jar, and Grandpa's chipped blue teacup to the school fair, and Grandpa sets up a little booth with a hand-painted sign: {trick_name}. Kids line up. Grandpa taps the teacup twice. Tap. Tap. "Pick a number," he tells a girl with pigtails. "Double it. Add ten. Halve it. Take away your number." She gasps. "Five!"

Then {friend_name} cracks their knuckles. "My turn." They lean in and whisper their number, but I hear it. It's huge. It's a number with a lot of zeros in it. The crowd goes quiet. Grandpa just smiles. "Double it," he says. {friend_name} does, slowly. "Add ten. Halve it. Take away your number." {friend_name}'s eyes go wide. "Five," they say, very quietly. "It's still five."

The whole line cheers. {friend_name} flops down next to me. "We fed it a monster," they say, "and it still came home." Grandpa taps the teacup. Tap. Tap. "Patterns don't care how big you go," he says. "But I think you're starting to see why."

s2b.text:
"We'll stay," I say, and {friend_name} nods. "Rice turning into trouble sounds better than telling."

Grandpa grins. He opens the jar, takes out one grain of rice, and sets it on the first square of the chessboard. "One," he says. Then two grains on the next square. "Doubling." Then four. Then eight. {friend_name} yawns. "This is the trouble? It's just rice."

Grandpa keeps going. Sixteen. Thirty-two. Sixty-four. The pile is still small enough to hold in your hand. "See?" {friend_name} says. "Doubling is slow."

Then the pile jumps. A hundred and twenty-eight. Two hundred and fifty-six. Grandpa has to scoop rice out by the cupful now, and the jar is getting light. "Five hundred and twelve," he says, and the heap slides off the square and onto the table. {friend_name} yelps and jumps back. "Where did it all come from? It was nothing a second ago!"

Grandpa taps the teacup twice. Tap. Tap. "That's the secret," he says. "Doubling stays quiet for a long, long time. Then it runs away so fast it could fill this whole kitchen. And it started with one grain." He pours the rice back into the jar. "Same as the trick. Small steps. Big landing."

s3.text:
Back at the table, Grandpa pushes a piece of paper toward us. "Show me what you found," he says.

We tell him. Both of us. The words tumble out, and {friend_name} waves their hands around, and Grandpa just listens, nodding, tapping his teacup twice when we get to the good part. Tap. Tap.

"So the trick always lands on the same number," he says. "No matter what you pick." He picks up a pencil. "Let me show you why."

He draws a little box on the paper. Just a square. "This is your secret number. We don't know what it is, so we draw it as a box." Then he draws another box next to it. "Double it. Two boxes." He writes a ten beside them. "Add ten." Then he crosses out one box and half the ten. "Halve it." Then he crosses out the last box. "Take away your number."

We stare at the paper. The boxes are gone. All that's left is five.

"The boxes cancel out," I whisper.

"Every time," Grandpa says. "The number you pick disappears. That's the secret. The trick doesn't care what you started with. It eats the boxes and leaves the five."

{friend_name} leans back in their chair. "So it's not magic at all."

"It's better than magic," Grandpa says. "It's a pattern. And patterns work for everyone."

He taps the teacup one more time. Tap. Tap. "Now," he says. "What do we do with it?"

s4a.text:
"Teach it," {friend_name} says, before I can even open my mouth. "Somebody else has to feel that."

So we carry the trick out to the fair, where Grandpa sets up a little booth with a hand-painted sign: {trick_name}. A younger kid wanders over, scuffing one shoe in the grass.

"Pick a number," {friend_name} says, leaning in just like Grandpa did. "Any number. Don't tell me."

The kid picks. We walk them through it, step by step. Double it. Add ten. Halve it. Take away your number. The kid's forehead wrinkles up.

"Five," {friend_name} and I say together.

The kid's mouth drops open. "How did you—"

And there it is. The same baffled face we made. It works even better when you're the one saying it.

Back home, Grandpa taps the teacup twice. Tap. Tap. Then he tips the rice jar, and one single grain rolls across the table. "For your pocket," he says. "One grain, doubled and doubled, makes a mountain."

I keep it there all the way home. Small as anything. Hiding a mountain.

s4b.text:
"Peek," I say. "I want to see what else a secret can hide."

Grandpa's eyes crinkle. He pulls a fat old notebook off the shelf and blows the dust off. "The trick hid a number," he says. "But secret steps can hide a message, too."

He opens to a page covered in numbers. "Each number stands for a letter. One is A, two is B. Simple. But unless you know the steps, it just looks like a list of groceries."

{friend_name} grabs the pencil. "So we could write notes nobody else can read?"

"Try it," Grandpa says.

We scratch away, tongues out, turning letters into numbers. When we slide the paper across, Grandpa reads it slow, then laughs. "'Grandpa is a noodle.' Charming."

He taps the teacup twice. Tap. Tap. Then he tears out a small square of paper, covered in his own tiny numbers, and folds it into my hand. "For later. Solve it when you're home."

Then he tips the rice jar, and one grain rolls out. "For luck," he says. "One grain, doubled and doubled, makes a mountain."

The note stays folded in my pocket, warm as a secret, all the way home.

c1.question: "Do you want to test this trick in front of the whole fair, or stay right here and watch rice turn into trouble?"

options.label: Take the trick to the school fair and test it on lots of kids
Stay at the table and explore the doubling rice clue

c2.question: "Now that you know the secret, do you want to teach the trick to someone new, or peek at how secret steps can hide a message?"

options.label: Share the trick with a younger kid and pass on the wonder
Follow the secret-step idea into codes and hidden messages

friend_name.role: The skeptical best friend who helps test the trick

trick_name.role: The name Grandpa gives his number trick at the fair booth

s1.text: When I was small, my Grandpa took me to see the biggest water there is. We stood at the top of a wooden boardwalk, little {child_name} and Grandpa, and the wind was full of salt. Far away, past the dunes, there was a thin blue line. And there was a sound. A roaring whisper, soft and huge at the same time. "Do you hear that?" Grandpa said. "That's the ocean. It's calling us." I listened. The whisper tickled my ears. It sounded like a giant breathing in and out, in and out. Grandpa tucked my collar against the wind and took my hand. "Come on," he said. So we stepped onto the boardwalk, and the whisper got a little louder.

s2a.text: "The waves!" I said. Grandpa laughed and we ran straight down to the water's edge. The roaring whisper was loud now. Whoosh. A wave came sliding in, and its foamy fingers tickled my toes. "Jump!" said Grandpa. We jumped, hand in hand, and the wave ran away. Then it came back. And it ran away again. Splash! A drop landed right on my lips. I licked them. "Salty!" I said, and I laughed and laughed. Up above, a seagull went round and round. He landed close by and tipped his head, as if he had never, ever seen anyone laugh at the ocean before.

s2b.text: "The quiet sand," I whispered. So we tiptoed along where the tide had just slipped out. The sand was damp and cool under my bare feet. "Look close," Grandpa said. "This sand is made of tiny pieces of shell and rock. Every piece is different." I squatted down. It was true! And the tide had left treasures. A smooth grey stone. A spiral shell. A little pool that held the whole sky. I stood very still and looked. The sky lay there, quiet, in the sand. Then I put the shell in my pocket. Hop, hop, hop. A seagull landed behind me and pecked at my stone before I could grab it. "Mine," he said. "I saw it second." Grandpa winked at me. "Fair's fair," he told the bird. "The ocean is breathing out now," he said. "Soon it will breathe back in."

s3.text: "What did you find?" Grandpa asks. But before I can tell him, the path ends at the rocks. The water hides here in cracks and crannies. I step in. Ankle deep. The sand fizzes under my toes. It wobbles me. I giggle and squeeze Grandpa's hand. "Look," Grandpa whispers. A little crab scuttles sideways. Scuttle, scuttle. We dig soft in the wet sand. A clam squirts a tiny fountain. Plop. Pip leans so far over the pool he nearly tumbles in. "Careful, Pip," I say. Above us, pale and round in the daytime sky, hangs the moon. "She is pulling the tide," Grandpa says. "Like the ocean breathing." The water creeps back in around the rocks. The pools will soon belong to the sea again.

s4a.text: Along the wrack line, where the tide leaves its treasures, a beachcomber with a bucket waves us over. "Looking for a shell?" she says. She lifts out a spiral one, smooth and pink inside. "A sea creature once lived here," she says. "Now it's an empty house. Hold it to your ear." I press it close. Whoosh. The ocean's voice, right there in my hand! "It's the sea," I whisper. "It came home with me." Grandpa smiles. "Then give it a name, little one." And that is the shell I still keep on my shelf. {shell_name}, I called it. Hold it to your ear, just like this. Do you hear it? The ocean is still inside, saying goodnight.

s4b.text: Grandpa and I climb back up the beach, slow and sandy, and turn for one last look. The water touches the sky in every direction. Big and blue and breathing. Side by side, we wave. "Goodbye, ocean!" I shout. And the biggest, splashiest wave comes running up the shore. It claps soft against the sand. Whoosh. As if the ocean is waving back. Pip circles once and cries, "It heard you! It heard you!" Grandpa squeezes my hand. "It will remember us," he says. I picked up one smooth stone from the tide line that day. It lives in my pocket still. And every time I see the sea, I wave. Because the ocean always, always waves back.

c1.question: Grandpa squeezes my hand and says, "Well now, the ocean has two front doors. Do we go straight down and let the waves chase our toes — or do we tiptoe along the quiet sand and see what the tide left behind for us?"

options.label: Run down to the water and play the wave-chasing game
Walk the quiet damp sand and hunt for what the tide left behind

c2.question: Grandpa shades his eyes and says, "The tide's turning, little one. Shall we find a shell to carry the ocean's voice home in — or climb up high and give the big water one last wave goodbye?"

options.label: Find a seashell that holds the ocean's sound and carry it home
Climb up and wave one last goodbye to the whole ocean

child_name.role: The child in the storyteller's memory — the little version of the teller, named so the listening child can step into the story

shell_name.role: The name the child gives the seashell they carry home, which the storyteller still keeps on a shelf

stories.title: The Painting That Changed Its Mind

s1.text:
Aunt Bea's garage smells like rain and toast. It is a drizzly Saturday, the door is half open, and the river at the end of her street is doing the thing that started all of this.

Last night, at sunset, we saw it. The Tomato, sitting on the water, glowing a red so red that Pip actually grabbed my arm. "That," Pip said. "That exact red."

So here we are, with a canvas propped on two paint cans, and five little dabs of paint on a board. Five. The grumpy clerk at the art shop talked us out of twenty colors and into these.

"Mixing," he'd growled, like it was a secret. "That's where the real colors live."

"He's probably right," Aunt Bea says, tying on her apron. "But I still don't like him."

We squeeze out the dabs. Red, yellow, blue, white, and a brown the color of a paper bag. Aunt Bea hands us sticks of charcoal, soft as burnt toast, and we sketch the Tomato — the fat little hull, the crooked mast, the stripe Pip insists on even though the real boat doesn't have one.

"It's our painting," Pip says. "The boat can have a stripe if it wants."

Then comes the part Aunt Bea calls the underpainting. We mix brown and a little red, thin it out, and wash the whole canvas with it, until our boat and our water and our sky all look like they are made of toast.

"Gravy," Pip says, squinting. "It looks like gravy."

It does. It really, really does.

"Every painting starts ugly," Aunt Bea says. "That's how you know you're doing it right."

I look at our five little dabs, then at the window, where the drizzle has smudged the world grey. And I wonder — quietly, so Pip won't hear — if that sunset red is even hiding in there. Five colors. That's all we get.

"Right," says Aunt Bea, picking up a brush. "Let's find out."

s2a.text:
"Charge," Pip says, which is not a real plan, but it sounds like one.

So we charge. I scoop red and yellow into one big puddle, and Pip dumps in blue, and then, because more feels like the answer, we swipe in white and brown too, and stir the whole thing with the handle of a brush like we're making soup for a giant.

"Sunset soup," Pip says. "Dinner is served."

For one second, it's beautiful. Swirls of gold and pink chase each other around the puddle, and I think, we did it, we found it.

Then the swirls slow down. And slump. And the whole puddle settles into the exact color of wet cardboard.

"No," Pip says. "Un-serve it."

We paint it on anyway, because maybe the canvas will fix it. It does not fix it. The sky goes on lumpy and grey-brown, and where I scrubbed too hard, a thin blue line peeks out from under the new paint, like the canvas is raising one eyebrow at us.

"It's glaring," I whisper. "The painting is actually glaring."

"It has a right," says Aunt Bea, leaning over our shoulders. "You asked every color to shout at once. Red bounces light back at you — that's why it glows. But blue and brown soak light up like sponges. Mix them all together and the sponges win. Nobody's bouncing anything."

"So the red was in there," Pip says, "and we drowned it."

"Little bit," says Aunt Bea. "Good news is, paint dries. This painting is about to become the bottom layer of a better one."

I look at our cardboard sky and our boat the color of tomato soup, and I swear the thin blue line wiggles, just slightly, like it's laughing at us.

"Stop laughing," Pip tells it. "We're revising."

s2b.text:
"Slow," I say. "We sneak up on it."

Aunt Bea shows us the trick: hold the brush way out at the far end of the handle, like a wizard's wand, so your hand can't boss the bristles around. We mix the thinnest pink, thin as skim milk, and lay it over the gravy sky. It dries. We lay another. The wiggly brush paints the river grass almost by itself, little green flicks standing up along the bank, and Pip gasps like we've grown a lawn.

"Layer," Pip whispers, like it's a magic word. "Another layer."

So we layer. And layer. And here's the thing nobody warns you about: careful has a trap in it too. The water starts out shimmery, and I think, one more pass will make it shimmerier. It does not. The next pass dulls it. The pass after that kills it dead. Our river sits there flat and grey and overworked, like bread dough somebody kneaded for an hour out of spite.

"I was being so gentle," I say. "How did gentle break it?"

The painting says nothing. It sulks. You can feel it sulking. And under my dull grey water, that thin blue line peeks out, smug as anything, like it knew this would happen.

"You can argue with a painting too politely," Aunt Bea says. "You fussed the water until it gave up. A painting wants a little pushback. Bold strokes, then leave it alone."

"And the red?" Pip asks, because the Tomato is still the color of tomato soup, and sunset is not getting any closer.

"Still hiding," Aunt Bea admits. "But your layers are honest ones. A dull river can be woken up. Scrape a little, splash a little. Paintings forgive."

"Hear that?" Pip tells the canvas. "You have to forgive us. Aunt Bea said."

The blue line keeps peeking. I choose to believe it's thinking it over.

s3.text:
Whichever way we went looking, the wall sent us back to the same place. The middle of the painting. And it is ugly.

Not gravy-ugly. Worse. Our sky has gone the color of old dishwater, and the red we chased all morning is buried somewhere under it, sulking.

"It got worse," Pip says. "We made it worse."

"Good," says Aunt Bea.

We both stare at her.

"Now there's something to argue with." She presses the palette knife into my hand. It is small and flat and cool, like a spreader for toast. "The wall taught me this part. A painting is never one painting. It's a stack of them, and sometimes the top one has to go."

"Scrape it?" I say. "Off?"

"Off," she says, and her eyes are doing the thing they do when the river is about to flood and she loves it.

The knife feels like a lie in my fingers. We worked all morning on that sky. But the painting is already arguing with us — it has been arguing all day — and right now it is saying, in its grumpiest voice, go on then.

So I press the blade in, low on the canvas, and pull.

The dishwater sky comes off in a thick curl, like frosting off a cake, like mud off a boot. It is horrible. It is wonderful. Pip makes a sound like a kettle.

"Again," Pip whispers.

We scrape. Curl after curl. And then I stop, because there, in the groove the knife just made, something is glowing. A thin pink line. Yesterday's sunset, still alive under all that grey, waiting.

"It was hiding," Pip breathes. "The whole time, it was just hiding."

"That's the secret of layers," Aunt Bea says. "Nothing is gone. It's underneath."

We step back to see it better. All the way back, bumping into the stool, knocking a paint can with my heel, until we are squinting from the doorway like people at a museum.

And from there, finally, the painting starts telling us the truth.

s4a.text:
"It wants to keep the ghost," Pip says.

The painting says nothing, which is how it says yes.

So we leave the groove alone. The pink line stays, thin and stubborn, like a scar that turned out to be a smile. Around it, we build the new sky in layers — a wash of blue, then a thinner blue, then a blue so pale it is almost the color of the rain outside. Each layer dries a little darker than the last, and the groove glows up through all of them, warm as a window at night.

"It's not arguing anymore," I say.

"It's purring," Pip says.

Then Pip reaches for the yellow, and the brush slips, and a blob — a whole blob — lands on the wet canvas, right where the far shore is supposed to be.

"No," Pip whispers.

But the painting doesn't flinch. The blob sits there, round and bright, and Aunt Bea tilts her head.

"Look at that," she says. "The porch light."

And it is. The exact warm spot the picture was missing, the one we didn't know it needed until it arrived by accident. Pip dabs it once, gently, with the corner of a rag, and the porch light softens into the shore like it was always there.

We step back. All the way back, past the stool, past the paint can, to the doorway where the drizzle is still going. From here, nothing is wrong. Nothing at all.

At the very edge of the canvas, one thin blue line of the old muddy sky peeks out from under the new one. We look at it. The painting looks back.

"Leave it," Pip says.

"Leave it," Aunt Bea agrees.

Because a finished painting is not one painting. It is every painting it ever was, stacked up and still glowing through.

s4b.text:
"Bury it," Pip says. "Bury the whole thing."

The painting growls, but it is the kind of growl that means go on, I dare you.

So we do. We load the brush with blue — not dishwater blue, but the blue of the river just before the sun hits it — and we lay it over the groove, over the ghost, over every grey mistake, in strokes so bold Aunt Bea actually claps once, like a seal.

"More," she says.

We layer. Blue over blue, then a thin white dragged across the top like fog lifting. The sky stops sulking. It starts shining.

And then — the red. We don't mix it. We build it. A dab of red, a touch of yellow, a breath of brown, tiny strokes side by side until the Tomato's hull glows the way it did last night, the way that made Pip grab my arm. Five colors. That was all we ever needed.

"It arrived," Pip whispers. "The red arrived."

Then the brush slips. A blob of yellow lands on the wet sky, fat and ridiculous, right above the mast.

Pip freezes. Aunt Bea freezes. The painting waits.

"It's the sun," I say.

And it is. Low and silly and exactly where the sun should be, like the painting knew all along and was just waiting for us to catch up. Pip adds one thin line of white underneath it, and the whole sky warms.

We sign the corner. All three of us, our names small and crooked, stacked like the layers themselves.

From across the garage, the painting looks right. Not perfect — right. Like it finally stopped arguing and started agreeing.

At the edge, one thin blue line of the first failed sky still peeks out. We leave it there.

"Proof," Aunt Bea says, "that it was always becoming this."

c1.question: "Five colors is all you've got, so how do you want to hunt that red? Charge in and mix the whole puddle, or sneak up on it layer by layer?"

options.label: Mix every color together and hunt the red head-on
Build the red slowly, one thin layer at a time

c2.question: "That scrape left a ghost of the old sky in the groove. Do we keep the ghost and paint around it, or bury it under a brand-new sky?"

options.label: Leave the ghostly groove showing and build the new sky around it
Layer a bold new sky right over the old one

s1.text:
The sand is still cool from the night, and it squeaks under our shoes as we stand at the bottom of the biggest thing we have ever seen. A pyramid, tall as a mountain, with sides so flat and smooth they look poured.

"Good morning," says the architect, unrolling a long papyrus across a flat stone. "You came. Good. Look here." On the papyrus, drawn in black ink, is a square. Just a square. "Before it was a mountain," the architect says, "it was this. One flat face. Then four more, leaning in to meet at the top. Five faces, and every one of them flat."

Something skitters over our toes. A little sand-coloured lizard, quick as a dropped pin. "Sef," says the architect, "our inspector."

Sef dashes up the first stone block, stops, and taps the corner with one foot. "One," he says. Then another foot, another corner. "Two. Three. Four." He looks back at us, delighted. "Square base. Four corners. Counted them myself."

The architect rolls the papyrus tight. "Here is the thing. At the top of this pyramid is a door. It has been shut a very long time.
