Its lock is waiting for three flat shapes — three tiles — and the path up has three stops, one tile at each." A pause. "Nobody remembers which three shapes the door wants. So we collect all three, and we find out."

Sef is already three blocks up, feet pattering on the stone. "Coming?" he calls.

The sun lifts over the sand. The pyramid's flat face turns gold, all at once, like someone switched it on.

"Coming," we say.

s2a.text:
"The bees," we say, and the architect nods. "This way, then."

Round the corner of the pyramid, the air goes warm and humming. Rows of wooden boxes sit in the sun, and bees drift over them like slow golden sparks. The beekeeper waves us closer and lifts out a wooden frame. "Look," she says. "The bees build their own rooms."

The comb is packed with little cells, wall to wall. Sef scampers along the frame's edge, tapping. "One, two, three, four, five, six!" he says. "Six sides on every single one."

"Six flat walls," says the beekeeper, "fitting together with no gaps. Clever bees."

We run a finger along one cell's edge. Smooth as toast crust. The bees hum on, busy with their own warm work, and for a moment we just listen.

"And the box they live in?" the architect asks.

The beekeeper pats the long wooden hive. "Two matching ends, straight sides all the way along. A prism, same as your tiles." She reaches into her pocket and presses a flat rectangle tile into our hand. "For your door."

Sef is already darting back toward the main path. "The mason's waiting!" he calls. "And the sun's getting higher!"

We tuck the tile safe and hurry after him.

s2b.text:
"The crystals," we say, and the architect smiles. "This way, then."

Round the corner of the pyramid stands a long hall with a glass roof, and inside, enormous crystals hang from the ceiling like fireworks that froze mid-burst. The light comes through them in slow gold squiggles. Nobody says anything for a moment. Even Sef holds still.

A museum guard meets us at the door. "Quickly, before the crowds," she says, and presses something cool into our hands. A real quartz prism, small enough to hold. "Turn it slowly. Count."

We turn it. Six long flat faces, smooth as window glass, running straight from end to end. Then two pointy ends, one at each side. Sef skitters up our sleeve and taps each face with one quick foot. "One, two, three, four, five, six!" he says. "Six long ones. Two pointy ones. Counted them myself."

"Two matching ends," says the guard, "and straight sides all the way along. That's what makes it a prism."

The prism catches the sun and throws a tiny rainbow onto our sleeve. Sef leans close. He doesn't tap it. He doesn't count it. He just watches it tremble there, small and bright, until the guard takes back the quartz and hands us a flat rectangle tile instead. "For your door," she says.

Sef is already at the hall's far door, dancing from foot to foot. We tuck the tile safe and climb after him, up toward the sun.

s3.text: Back on the winding stone path, the architect's mason friend is waiting, a fresh-cut block on his palms. "Look," he says. "Six square faces, every one the same size. A cube." He turns it over and over, slow as a pot on a wheel. Then he lifts a flat cardboard model and folds it up, fold, fold, fold, until a cross of six squares becomes a box in his hands. Sef skitters around it once, twice, then stops. "Six!" he cries. "Six faces. I counted." The mason laughs and presses a small square tile into our pocket, beside the one we already carry. Two tiles now. "And the third?" we ask. The architect points up, where the pyramid's four triangle faces lean together to one bright point. "At the top," he says. "Where the last tile waits." As we climb, Sef fishes a little stone die from the mason's pouch and rolls it. "Guess the bottom," he says. We guess. "Seven's partner," Sef says, grinning. "Always." We pocket that small magic and climb on, ready for the door.

s4a.text:
"Up," says the architect. "While the light is gold."

So we climb, out into the bright air, block by block, until the whole pyramid falls away below us. Sef darts ahead, his quick feet tracing every edge. "Left wall," he calls. Then, scampering across, "Right wall. They match! Like folded wings."

They do. The four great triangle faces lean in from every side, and here at the very top they meet at one sharp point, touching the sky. Left and right rise like mirror images of each other.

The architect kneels by a small stone door set into the point. "Three hollows," they say. "Square. Rectangle. Triangle. And only one careful try before the sun is high."

We reach into our pocket. Two tiles already wait there, warm from the climb. The architect presses the third into our hand — the triangle, smooth and sharp-cornered. "You do it," they say.

Square. Click. Rectangle. Click. Triangle.

Click.

The door swings open, and the sunrise pours in. Below us the whole pyramid spreads out like the papyrus plan come alive — square base, four flat faces, every line exactly where it was drawn.

"Counted them all myself," says Sef, puffing out his little chest.

We tuck {keepsake_tile} into our pocket, warm from the sun, and carry it home.

s4b.text:
"Inside," says the architect. "The heart knows the way."

We slip through the old doorway, and the bright air folds away behind us. A narrow passage. Then a room. Then another. Cube-shaped rooms, each one with six flat faces, opening into more and more.

"A maze," we whisper.

Sef's tail flicks. He dashes left, stops, dashes right. "This one!" he cries. "Look — left wall, right wall. They match. Like folded wings."

He's right. The rooms where left and right mirror each other lead onward. The lopsided ones loop us back. So we follow the matching rooms, fold by fold, deeper into the pyramid's heart.

The heart chamber is small and still. The architect lifts a lamp, and there on the far wall is the door. "Three hollows," they say softly. "Square. Rectangle. Triangle."

Two tiles wait in our pocket already. The architect presses the third into our hand — the triangle, smooth and sharp-cornered. "You do it," they say.

Square. Click. Rectangle. Click. Triangle.

Click.

The walls glow, warm and golden, as the shapes click home. Sef pats the door with one quick foot. "Six faces in the rooms. Three in the lock. Counted every one."

We tuck {keepsake_tile} into our pocket, smooth from our careful hands, and carry it home.

c1.question: "Two little paths wind round the base, friends," says the architect, tapping the papyrus. "One hums with bees and their six-sided rooms — one glitters with crystals grown into perfect prisms. Which shall we walk first?"

options.label: Visit the beekeeper's garden and count the hexagon cells
Step into the glass hall and hold a real quartz prism

c2.question: "Here the path forks for the last time," the architect whispers, Sef's tail flicking between the stones. "We can climb on, out into the bright air, all the way to the point where the four triangle faces touch the sky — or slip through this old doorway and find the heart of the pyramid from inside. Where do our feet belong?"

options.label: Climb the open-air path to the pyramid's point at sunrise
Slip inside and solve the maze of cube-shaped rooms

keepsake_tile.role: Which single tile we tuck into our pocket to carry home at the end

s1.text: I remember a warm evening street, and a little stand with cups lined up like towers. You were there, {child_name}, watching the worker drop a fresh pot of pearls into their sweet syrup bath. "They need a little more time," the worker said, "to turn dark and chewy." So we waited. Pip the shop cat sat by the door, sniffing the steam. Sniff. Sniff. Then—achoo! One great dignified sneeze. Pip blinked slowly at every cup, as if personally approving each pearl. You leaned on your elbows. I leaned on mine. The pearls took their bath, and the street smelled like sugar and rain.

s2a.text: "Let's watch," you say. The worker lifts the lid just a crack. Steam curls up, warm and sweet. Inside, the pearls tumble slow, slow, slow — like marbles in honey. "They started out hard and white," she says. "Only a long warm bath makes them soft and chewy. Some things cannot be hurried." Pip stands on his hind legs, front paws on the counter, peeking in. The worker shows you the little mat. "Stand here, back from the warm pot. You can still see the steam dance." You stand. You watch. The pearls turn darker, shinier, rounder. Little moons in a pot. Pip blinks, slow. Are they ready yet? Not yet. But soon.

s2b.text: "Let's say hello," you say. At the next table, a grandmother eats sweet pearl soup. She lifts one warm pearl on her spoon and holds it to the lantern light. It glows — a little moon on a spoon. "It began as a root called cassava," she says, "growing in the ground far away." Pip follows, sitting at her feet, hoping. Unashamedly hoping. She smiles and gives him one pearl. He licks it once, twice, then gulps. You lean close. The pearl on her spoon glows warm and brown. But your own pearls — are they still in their bath? Are they ready yet? The grandmother winks. "Good things take time."

s3.text: "The pearls are done," the worker calls softly. She pours the cold tea over ice, spoons in the dark warm pearls, and slides in the very big straw. You take the first slow sip, {child_name}. And something small and wonderful happens. The cold arrives on your tongue first. The sweet follows a blink later, like a flower opening after a shiver. You try it again, slowly, just to feel the two arrive one after the other. Cold. Then sweet. Cold. Then sweet. Pip blinks slowly at your cup, as if he can taste the evening too. "What did you find?" the worker asks, smiling. But you are busy sipping, feeling the little moons wait at the bottom.

s4a.text: The cup feels light. Almost gone. But the worker tilts it, just a little, and points. "Look," she whispers. There, hiding in the corner, is one last pearl. One dark little moon, waiting all along. You aim the big straw, {child_name}. Slowly, slowly, it travels up — like a slow little elevator, rising just for you. You chew it softly. It is the smallest bite. Somehow, it is the biggest. Pip blinks once, slow and sure. And that is why, whenever I see little moons at the bottom of a cup, I remember that the best sweet things take their time.

s4b.text: You set the cup on the step, {child_name}, and sit beside Pip. Little rings of water bloom on the wood. The street turns soft and gold. You sip slowly. Cold. Then sweet. Cold. Then sweet. The last pearl waits at the bottom, in no hurry at all. Neither are you. Pip's tail curls around your ankle, warm as a scarf. Then — there it comes, up the straw, in its own good time. Pip gives one slow approving blink. And whenever the evening is warm and unhurried, I remember that some joys cannot be rushed — they arrive in their own good time, like pearls.

c1.question: "While the pearls take their bath, little one — would you like to watch them tumble in the pot, or go say hello to the grandmother with the glowing spoon?"

options.label: Stay and watch the pearls tumble and darken in the pot
Visit the grandmother and see a pearl glow like a little moon

c2.question: "The cup is nearly empty, little one. Shall we tilt it and hunt for the last pearl hiding at the bottom — or sit on the step with Pip and let the evening finish slowly?"

options.label: Tilt the cup and hunt for the last hidden pearl with the big straw
Sit on the step with Pip and sip slowly until the last pearl comes on its own

child_name.role: the child in the memory, whom the storyteller addresses as 'you'

s1.text:
The wind up here smells like salt and pennies. We stand on the edge of a cliff that is slowly, slowly falling into the sea. Dr. Petra taps the rock with her hammer. Clink. Clink. "Listen," she says. "The mountain is talking."

Below us, waves chew at the cliff's ankles. Gulp. Gulp. A chunk of gray rock lets go. It tumbles down, knocks into other rocks, and lands on the beach with a rattle like teeth in a jar.

"That," says Dr. Petra, "is erosion. The sea is eating the mountain, one bite at a time."

She picks up a pebble from the pile. It is sharp-edged and gray, still rough from its fall. "This one just broke off," she says. "Feel those corners. It hasn't been anywhere yet." She drops it into our hands. It is heavier than it looks, and cold from the shadow of the cliff.

"You think it's finished," she says. "A pebble. Done. But this is just the beginning. Every rock is on its way to becoming another kind of rock. That is the rock cycle. This little one is about to take a very long trip."

We look at the pebble. It looks ordinary. It looks like nothing. But Dr. Petra is smiling like she knows a secret.

"What should we call it?" we ask.

"You name it," she says. "You're carrying it."

We turn the pebble over. It has a white stripe through the middle, like a road. "Scout," we say. "We'll call it Scout."

Dr. Petra nods. "Good name for a traveler. Now hold tight. The first part of the journey is the wildest."

s2a.text:
Captain Zed is waiting at the river mouth with his boat, which is painted blue and has a dent in the side shaped like Australia. "Full speed to yesterday!" he shouts, and we climb aboard. The engine goes chug-chug-chug, and the river turns from slow brown to quick white.

We are going upstream, against the current, toward the young river. The boat shakes. Our teeth shake. Scout is safe in our pocket, but we can feel the pebble bouncing.

"Feel that?" Captain Zed shouts over the noise. "The river is young here. It has not learned to be calm."

The water is the color of milk mixed with chalk. It is full of sand and tiny bits of mountain. We look over the side and see cobbles rolling along the bottom, knocking into each other, getting scraped smooth. The river is carrying them downhill, toward the sea, toward the beach where we found Scout.

"Erosion," we say.

"Fast erosion," says Captain Zed. "The water is sandpaper. It is smoothing those stones right now."

The boat hits a rapid. We bounce. Spray hits our faces, cold and tasting like stone. Captain Zed laughs and shouts, "Toot-toot!" and we shout it too, because the river is loud and we are small and it is wonderful.

But the water is moving so fast. We cannot imagine it will ever slow down enough to drop these stones. We hold the rail and watch the white water rush past, carrying its load of mountains toward somewhere else.

s2b.text:
Dr. Petra leads us away from the cliff, down a path that switches back and forth like a zipper. The air changes. It stops smelling like salt and starts smelling like dust and old bread.

We are going down into the canyon. The walls rise up on both sides, striped red and brown and yellow, stacked like pancakes.

"Limestone," says Dr. Petra, tapping a gray layer. "Siltstone. Shale. Each one is a different time, pressed flat."

We walk deeper. The path gets narrow. The sun disappears, and the air gets warm. Not hot like summer, but warm like a cat sleeping in a patch of sun.

"Feel that?" Dr. Petra puts her hand on the rock wall. We put ours next to hers. The stone is warm. It is not supposed to be warm, but it is.

"We are close to where the mountain is cooking," she says. "Heat and pressure. Deep down, the limestone is changing. It is becoming marble. It happens slowly, over millions of years, but it is happening right now."

We look at the rock. It looks solid. It looks still. But Dr. Petra says it is twisting, changing, turning into something new.

"Scout could become this," she says. "If the pebble gets buried deep enough, cooked enough, it could become marble. Or something else. The rock cycle does not stop."

We touch the warm stone again. Somewhere below us, the mountain is working. We cannot see it, but we can feel the heat, and we know the rocks are moving, even though they look like they are standing still.

s3.text:
By sunset we reach the delta, where the river gives up and spreads into the sea. The water turns the color of hot chocolate, and it fans out in slow brown swirls, wider and wider, like someone spilled it on purpose.

Captain Zed stands at the wheel with his hat on sideways. "Full speed to yesterday!" he shouts, and the boat chugs forward. Toot-toot!

"Look there." He points with his chin. "That sandbar wasn't here last spring. The river dropped it. Every bit of mud and sand and pebble the water carries, it puts down right here. That's called a deposit." He grins. "The river is building, even when it looks like it's just wandering off."

He lets us take the wheel. It is warm from his hands and it hums through our palms. We steer around the sandbar, slow and careful, and the bottom of the boat slides past it with a soft shhhh.

"What did you find back there?" Captain Zed asks, nodding at our pockets. We tell him, and he whistles. "Good. Hold onto it. And hold onto Scout."

We look down at the pebble in our hand. The white stripe is smoother now. Rounder. It has been somewhere.

"This looks like the end," we say. "The river's done."

Captain Zed laughs, but kindly. "Done? Down under all that mud, the real work is just starting. Layer on layer, pressing down, squeezing tight. Give it a few million years and all that muck turns into proper rock. Sedimentary rock."

He pats the rail. "The journey's not over. It's just gone underground."

s4a.text:
Captain Zed points the boat toward the fire mountain. Steam curls from cracks in its side, white and slow, like the mountain is thinking. The ground feels warm through our boots. Warmer with every step.

"Easy now," he says. He knows the good ledge, flat and wide, where the heat cannot reach the boat's paint. We stand behind a hump of old black rock, and we watch.

The top of the mountain opens. Lava pours out, thick as tomato soup, as porridge, as the jam at the bottom of the jar. It glows orange. It moves like it has all day.

"Is it angry?" we ask.

"Angry?" Captain Zed laughs. "No. It's just doing its work. Old rock melts down there, deep where it's hot. Then it comes up here and cools off. New rock. Igneous rock. The mountain is making it right in front of you."

We watch the lava slow down. It stops glowing. It turns black and ropey, coiled like a sleeping snake. Crack. A sharp sound splits the air. The new rock breaks into tall columns, straight as pencils in a box.

"Basalt," says Captain Zed. "Hard stuff. Good stuff."

We reach out our hand. The air above the new rock shimmers. It is too hot to touch. We pull back.

"Not yet," says Captain Zed. "It has to finish becoming."

We look at Scout in our palm. Smooth now. Patient. We put it back in our pocket.

"Come on," says Captain Zed. "Yesterday is waiting."

Toot-toot!

s4b.text:
Captain Zed ties up the boat and leads us into the stone cave. It is quiet in here. Drip. Drip. Water falls from the ceiling, one drop at a time, slow as honey.

The walls glitter. Thin curtains of stone hang down, pale and rippled, like frosting on a cake that nobody cut. "Calcite," Captain Zed whispers. He is different in here. Softer. Like the cave asked him to be.

He shines his light on a spike of stone hanging from the ceiling. "That one," he says. "I came here when I was a boy. It has grown a whole centimeter since then."

"A centimeter?" we say. "That's all?"

"A centimeter is a lot," he says, "when you're a mountain."

He shows us how it works. One drop of water slides down. It leaves behind a tiny bit of stone, smaller than a grain of sand. Then the next drop. Then the next. Ten thousand years of drops, and you get a stalactite.

"The water is hollowing out the mountain," he says. "Making space. And in that space, new rock grows."

We touch the wall. It is cold and wet and very, very patient.

We take Scout out of our pocket. The white stripe glows faintly in Captain Zed's light. We hold it up to the stone curtain.

"Someday," we say, "this could be part of a cave."

Captain Zed nods. "Someday," he says. "It could be part of anything."

Drip. Drip.

We put Scout back. We walk out into the light.

c1.question: "Do we chase the pebbles down the fast water, or do we duck into the deep earth to see what the mountain is cooking?"

options.label: Chase the pebbles down the fast water
Duck into the deep earth to see the mountain cooking

c2.question: "Do we sail to the fire mountain to watch new rock being born, or do we walk into the stone cave to see the mountain being hollowed out?"

options.label: Sail to the fire mountain to watch new rock being born
Walk into the stone cave to see the mountain being hollowed out

stories.title: The Planet That Never Forgets Its Bumps

s1.text: {hero_name} is staring at the photo again. It is taped above the sink in Dr. Okafor's science room, big as a window, and it shows Mercury — a whole planet of bare rock, grey as dust on a shelf, and covered in dents. Not one or two dents. Hundreds. Thousands. Big dents with little dents inside them. "It looks like the baking sheet at my house," {hero_name} says, "after the muffins fought back." Dr. Okafor laughs — a big, warm laugh that fills the whole room. "Those dents are called craters," she says. "And now I have an idea." She pulls out a wide tray, fills it with flour, and sets down a bowl of marbles. Plop. One marble drops in. {hero_name} leans close. The dent sits there in the flour, sharp and perfect, not smoothing over, not fading — just staying. "Dr. Okafor," {hero_name} asks, "why does Mercury have so many craters? And why don't they ever go away?" Dr. Okafor taps the photo, right on the biggest dent of all. "That," she says, "is a very good question. And I know a robot who can help us answer it."

s2a.text:
“The flour tray!” {hero_name} says. “Detectives test things.”

Dr. Okafor grins and pushes the tray over. “Then test away.”

{hero_name} picks up a marble. It is cool and smooth and heavy for its size, like a tiny planet that fits in one hand. “Ready?”

“Ready,” says Dr. Okafor.

Plop.

The marble drops, and the flour jumps. A dent splashes out — round and deep, with a puffy rim all around it, and long pale rays shooting out like spokes on a bicycle wheel.

“Whoa,” {hero_name} whispers. “It made rays. Like sunbeams, but flour.”

“Craters do that,” says Dr. Okafor. “Rims and rays. The real ones on Mercury too.”

{hero_name} leans in close, close enough to smell the flour, and pokes the dent with one finger. Poke. The dent just sits there. Poke poke. Still there. Sharp as the moment it happened.

“It’s not filling back in,” {hero_name} says. “It’s not smoothing over. It’s just... staying.”

“It will stay,” says Dr. Okafor, “until somebody shakes the tray.”

They both look at the tray. The dent looks back, perfectly kept.

“But Dr. Okafor,” {hero_name} says slowly, “nobody shakes Mercury.”

Dr. Okafor’s eyes go wide and shiny. “Nobody,” she says, “shakes Mercury. And that, detective, is our very first clue.”

s2b.text:
“The photo!” {hero_name} says. “The clues are already up there.”

{hero_name} drags a chair to the sink, climbs up, and peers at Mercury, nose almost touching the biggest dent of all.

“Look,” {hero_name} says. “This crater has a littler crater inside it. And that one has an even littler one inside that. They’re on top of each other.”

“Layered,” says Dr. Okafor. “Like what?”

{hero_name} thinks. “Like footprints. On a path that nobody ever sweeps. New footprints squish the old ones, but they don’t rub them out.”

“Exactly,” says Dr. Okafor. “The new craters sit on the old ones, and the old ones are still there, still holding their shape, after... oh, a very long time.”

Then the computer screen on the counter lights up all by itself. Beep! Beep-beep!

“Did somebody say MYSTERY?” booms a bright, buzzy voice. “{robot_name} the robot lander, reporting for expedition duty! I have beeped on four planets and napped on one, and THIS is the greatest mystery I have ever beeped at!”

“Hello, {robot_name},” {hero_name} giggles.

“Greetings, detective! Now — a question from a robot who has rolled on that very rock. Those dents never fade. Never ever. So tell me...” The screen leans closer, the way a screen can. “What sweeps footprints away on Earth? And why doesn’t Mercury have any?”

{hero_name} stares at the layered craters. The answer is hiding somewhere in that grey, dented rock.

s3.text: Back in the science room, a screen blinks on. Beep-boop-BEEP! "Greetings, explorers!" says {robot_name}, rolling in circles. "I am {robot_name}, the greatest crater-climber in the whole solar system!" Dr. Okafor grins. "Show us your landing pictures, {robot_name}." The screen fills with grey dust. And there — footprints. Sharp little robot footprints, pressed into the ground years and years ago. "They look brand new!" {hero_name} says. "But wait — what did you just find out there? Tell me everything!" {hero_name} tells it, and {robot_name}'s lights blink fast. "Correct! Correct!" he chirps. "And look at my flag!" Sure enough, a tiny flag sticks up from the dust — frozen mid-flap, like it is still waving hello after all this time. "On Earth," Dr. Okafor says, "wind would blow those footprints away. Rain would wash them flat. But Mercury is bare rock, with almost no air at all." "Airless!" {robot_name} announces, striking a heroic pose. "No wind. No rain. No weather. Nothing ever comes along to smooth anything away." {hero_name} looks at the footprints. Then at the tray of flour, where the marble's dent still sits, sharp and perfect. "So the craters..." {hero_name} begins slowly.

s4a.text:
"...stay forever!" {hero_name} bursts out. "Mercury is bare rock with no air. So no wind ever blows. No rain ever falls. Nothing smooths the dents away — every crash from long ago is still written on its face!"

Beep-boop-BEEP! "The detective has solved it!" {robot_name} cheers, spinning in a circle. "Case closed!"

"One more thing," says Dr. Okafor. "Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun. It zooms around faster than any other world — one whole trip in just eighty-eight days."

"The speediest planet!" {robot_name} declares. "Race you around the Sun! Ready — set —" He rolls one quick lap around the science room and bumps gently into {hero_name}'s shoe. "You win," he beeps. "Rematch in eighty-eight days."

{hero_name} laughs. Then Dr. Okafor lifts one marble from the flour tray and dusts it off — just a little — so a faint white smudge still clings to it. "For the detective," she says.

{hero_name} holds it up to the light. A tiny dent of flour sits on its side, sharp and perfect.

"The planet that never forgets its bumps," {hero_name} says, and puts it in their pocket, "now has a detective who never forgets it back."

s4b.text:
"...stay forever!" {hero_name} bursts out. "Mercury is bare rock with no air. So no wind ever blows. No rain ever falls. Nothing smooths the dents away — every crash from long ago is still written on its face!"

Beep-boop-BEEP! "Correct, detective!" {robot_name} chirps. Then his lights blink twice, sly and slow. "But look closer. Between the craters."

The screen zooms in. And there, stretched flat between the dents, lie great dark patches — smooth as a tabletop, smooth as spilled chocolate that cooled on the counter.

"No bumps at all!" {hero_name} says. "What happened there?"

"Long, long ago," says Dr. Okafor, "hot melted rock bubbled up from inside Mercury. It flowed out, filled the low places, and hardened into flat plains."

"Mercury had a fiery youth!" {robot_name} announces, striking his most heroic pose. "Like a volcano! A whole planet of one!"

"A bumpy old face," {hero_name} says, "with smooth young patches hiding in between."

Dr. Okafor smiles and lifts one marble from the flour tray, dusting it off — just a little. "For the detective," she says.

{hero_name} rolls it in their palm, feeling the faint smudge of flour. "Some dents stay," {hero_name} says softly. "And some stories hide underneath."

c1.question: "Where shall we hunt for our first clue, detective—in the flour tray, or in the photo itself?"

options.label: Drop a marble in the flour tray to make a pretend crater
Look closely at the photo to spot overlapping craters

c2.question: "The case is solved, detective! Shall we race around the Sun with speedy Mercury, or peek at the dark smooth patches where old melted rock once flowed?"

options.label: Hear how Mercury, closest to the Sun, zooms fastest around it
Glimpse the smooth volcanic plains hiding between the craters

s1.text:
I remember the evening I walked the boardwalks of the hot spring valley with a child named {child_name} and their older sister. The light was going soft and gold, the way it does just before supper, and steam rose off the pools in slow ribbons. It curled around our knees. It made the whole valley look like it was wearing curtains.

Ranger Bea walked ahead of us, her boots knowing every board. She had been a ranger there for twenty years, and her voice sounded like the valley itself, low and unhurried, with a little sulfur in it. "Rotten eggs," {child_name} whispered, wrinkling their nose. "That's the springs breathing," said Ranger Bea. "Wait till you see the one I call the painter."

We crossed a little bridge over a stream that steamed. The boards thrummed under our feet. And then the path opened, and there it was.

The biggest pool I have ever seen lay stretched out in front of us like a dropped paint palette, still shining. Around its edges ran rings of color. Orange first, thick as the rim of a pumpkin. Then green, bright as the skin of a lime. Then a band of blue so clear it looked like the sky had slipped down for a drink. The whole thing steamed gently, as if it had just finished and was still warm.

Ranger Bea stopped at the rail. "We stay on the boards here," she said. "The ground looks solid, but it's thin as a pie crust in places. This is the best spot anyway."

But {child_name} had already gone quiet. They were leaning forward over the rail, staring hard at the orange ring, and the ground hummed faintly through the soles of our shoes.

s2a.text:
"Who painted it?" {child_name} asked, loud enough to scare a bird off a post. "Who painted the edges orange and green?"

Their sister snorted. "Nobody. It's just dirt. Or old paint flaking off the rocks."

Ranger Bea did not answer right away. She knelt down at the rail, slow as a setting sun, and waved us closer. "Look again," she said. "Tell me what you see."

We looked. The orange ring went all the way around the pool, every inch of it, and inside it sat the green ring, and inside that, the blue. Not a smear anywhere. Not one drip out of place.

"They're in rings," {child_name} said. "Perfect rings."

"And always in the same order," said Ranger Bea. "Blue in the middle, where it's hottest. Then green. Then yellow. Then orange on the outside, where the water cools. Every pool in this valley wears the same pattern, like someone arranged it on purpose."

Their sister leaned over the rail despite herself. "Dirt doesn't do that," she admitted.

"Dirt does not," said Ranger Bea. "And paint doesn't grow. But these rings do. A little farther out every year, slow as a fingernail."

{child_name} pressed their palms flat on the warm rail. Something was down there, working in the heat, painting in perfect order. Something that had never once been seen.

"So who is it?" they whispered. "Who's painting?"

s2b.text:
"Who painted it?" {child_name} asked, loud enough to scare a bird off a post. "Who painted the edges orange and green?"

Ranger Bea did not answer. She sniffed the air instead, like a bear catching supper on the wind. "Let's take the long way round," she said. "Up the terraces. I want you to meet the smell properly."

We climbed the steps beside the pool, and the ground changed under the boards. White rock rose on both sides of us in lumpy ledges, each one spilling into the next like a waterfall that had frozen mid-pour. "Mineral rock," said Ranger Bea, running her hand along a ledge. "The water builds it, drop by drop, the way dripping wax builds a candle."

{child_name} touched it. Warm. Slick. Alive-feeling, somehow.

Then the wind turned, and the smell rolled up the steps thick as soup steam. "Rotten eggs!" {child_name} gasped, pinching their nose.

"Sulphur," said Ranger Bea, breathing it in like fresh bread. "The deeper the water comes from, the stronger it carries. Down where this water started, it's hot enough to cook an egg, and it hauls sulphur up the whole way."

{child_name} looked back down at the pool, at the orange ring steaming far below. Then at the white rock. Then they wrinkled their nose again, on purpose this time.

"Bea," they said slowly. "Does the smell make the colors?"

s3.text:
Ranger Bea was waiting at the main pool, and she held up her thermometer like a wand. "Well," she said, in that slow sulfur voice. "What did you find?" {child_name} told her, and Bea listened all the way through, nodding, the way you do when a friend is telling you something good. "Then it's time you saw what I see," she said. "This pool has a secret, and it lives in the rings."

She knelt on the boards and dipped the thermometer into the orange edge. We waited. "Warm as a bath," she said, and showed us the little line of silver. Then she moved it to the green ring. "Cooler." Then the blue, right at the center, where the steam rose thickest. "Hot as tea fresh off the stove."

"So each color likes its own temperature?" {child_name} asked.

"Each color," said Bea, "is its own neighborhood. And here comes the person who can show you who lives there."

Footsteps on the boardwalk. A woman with a backpack and a grin that went ear to ear came toward us, carrying a case she held very carefully, the way you carry a birthday cake. "Dr. Moss," said Bea, "meet my favorite detectives."

"Detectives!" said Dr. Moss. "Then you need to see this." She set the case down on a flat rock, opened it, and there was a microscope, black and shining. With a tiny glass tube, she scooped up one drop of orange water and slipped it under the lens. "Look."

{child_name} looked. And gasped.

"It's wiggling!"

"The orange," said Dr. Moss softly, "is not paint. It's alive. Millions of tiny microbes, so small a thousand could stand on a freckle. They live only in hot water, and each kind has its own favorite warmth. That's why they line up in rings."

"They're painting the pool," {child_name} whispered.

"They ARE the pool," said Dr. Moss. "And they're painting it right now."

s4a.text:
The light slid lower, and the rings of the pool deepened, the orange glowing like embers settling down for the night. "So the pool really does paint itself," {child_name} said. "With painters too small to see."

"Every hour of every day," said Dr. Moss, closing her case as gently as she had opened it. "Long before us. Long after."

Ranger Bea touched the rail. "Stay a moment," she said. "Someone else comes to the warm water at dusk."

So we stayed, quiet as we could, and the ground hummed its low note through our shoes. Then came a soft padding from the rocks. A snow monkey picked its way down to a smaller pool nearby, fur silver in the last light, and lowered itself in slow, the way you slide into a bath that's almost too hot. It settled to its shoulders. Its eyes half closed. Its face went grumpy and blissful at once, like a grandpa who has claimed the best chair and means it.

{child_name} pressed a hand over their mouth, shaking. Even Ranger Bea smiled her slow smile.

"The microbes keep it warm for him," Bea murmured. "He'll never know. Good neighbors are like that."

On the walk back, {child_name} opened their notebook on the bridge rail and drew {notebook_doodle}, small and careful, in the corner of a page. I still have the memory of that page. The valley keeps the rest — the steam, the rings, the warm water waiting.

s4b.text:
The light slid lower, and the rings of the pool deepened, the orange glowing like embers settling down for the night. "So the pool really does paint itself," {child_name} said. "With painters too small to see."

"Every hour of every day," said Dr. Moss, closing her case as gently as she had opened it. "Long before us. Long after."

Ranger Bea looked out along the terraces. "Walk back with me," she said. "The night singers are starting."

So we said goodbye to the painter. {child_name} stepped back from the rail slow and careful, the way you leave a sleeping cat, and the boards thrummed under our feet as we went. The terraces steamed on both sides of us, quiet as sleeping animals. And then we heard it. First one cricket, trying its small violin. Then another. Then a whole orchestra tuning up in the grass beyond the boards, where the ground was cool and dark and theirs.

"They like the warm nights too," said Bea. "Everybody in this valley lives by the heat. The microbes in the water. The crickets beside it."

"And us?" {child_name} asked.

"You visit it," said Bea, "and you come back. That's a way of living by something."

At the bridge, {child_name} opened their notebook and drew {notebook_doodle}, small and careful, in the corner of a page. "So I remember the painters," they said.

"The painters will be here," said Ranger Bea. "Same time tomorrow. Same rings. Bring the notebook."

c1.question: "We could look close at the colors right now, or we could follow that smell and see where it leads. Which way do you want to go?"

options.label: Examine the colored rings immediately
Explore the terraces and sulphur scent

c2.question: "The mystery is solved, but the evening is ours. Shall we stay and see who else comes to the warm water, or walk back through the terraces and listen for the night singers?"

options.label: Wait by the pool for animal visitors
Return through the terraces as crickets sing

notebook_doodle.role: A small drawing the child makes in their notebook at the end
notebook_doodle.default: a tiny microbe wearing a scarf

stories.title: The Puddle That Kept a Secret

s1.text:
The grass in this valley is stiff with frost and crunches under our boots.
Steam comes up out of the ground all around us, in thin white threads. One thread drifts across our faces, warm, smelling of wet stone. The whole valley feels like a kitchen with a kettle on somewhere out of sight.
"Over here! Over here!"
{companion_name} is standing on a flat rock with her tail straight up. Our lava-lizard, from inside the mountain.
"I saved something for you," she says. "Come and look."
What she has saved is a puddle.
It is round as a dinner plate, sitting in a ring of pale crusty stone, doing nothing at all.
"Watch," says {companion_name}.
So we watch. The puddle burps up one bubble, and then two more. Then the water starts to wobble.
Whoosh.
Up shoots a spout of hot water, higher than a house, roaring, with steam peeling off the top. Then down it comes, and the puddle lies flat and quiet again.
We turn round to {companion_name}.
"Why does it do that?" we ask.
"Nobody has told me yet," she says.

s2a.text:
We kneel down on the pale crust. It is warm under our knees, the way a bed stays warm where somebody has just got out of it.
"Ear down," says {companion_name}. "All the way down."
We press one ear flat to the ground, and she flattens herself beside us and puts her ear down too.
Nothing.
Then, far under us, glug, glug: water, a lot of water, sliding along through cracks that nobody has ever seen.
Then a long slow hiss, exactly the sound a kettle makes just before it is ready.
Then one low knock, like somebody tapping on a pipe under the floor.
"Soup," says {companion_name}. "The ground is full of soup."
"Water," we whisper back.
"Soup would be better."
We keep our ear down there a long while, and we come up knowing two things. There is water under our knees. And something in the dark down there is making it hot.

s2b.text:
We go up the hill after the little stream, and {companion_name} runs ahead with her tail up like a flag.
The water in the stream is so cold it turns our fingers pink.
"Snow," she says. "Off the top of the mountain. It melts all day and it comes down here all night."
Then the stream does something strange. It gets to a crack in the pale rock, and it does not go round it. It goes in.
We pull a yellow leaf out of the grass and drop it on the water. The leaf spins once, slides into the crack, and is gone.
We wait. It does not come out anywhere.
So we lie down and hold our palms flat over the crack, and warm damp air puffs up into them.
"Cold water goes down," says {companion_name}. "Warm air comes up. Somebody under there is filling a kettle."
Where is all that water going?

s3.text:
Back at the puddle, {companion_name} sits down on the cool ground, a good way back from the ring.
"Here." She pats the stone beside her. "The ring belongs to the water while it is up. When it goes down, it is ours again."
So we sit with her and we count.
Nothing happens.
We count out loud together, but {companion_name} counts one, two, three, seven, banana, and we have to start over twice.
Then the puddle changes.
First it steams more.
Then the water swells the way water swells in a pan before it goes over, and small bubbles hurry up and pop.
Whoosh.
Up it goes, higher than the trees, white and roaring, and warm rain comes sprinkling down on our faces.
Then flat again. Then quiet.
{companion_name} turns round with enormous eyes.
"That was almost the same number," she says. "Almost exactly the same wait as last time."
So the puddle is not whooshing whenever it likes: it is whooshing on a timetable.

s4a.text:
{companion_name} fetches a flat grey stone from the shady side of a boulder. It is cold. Properly cold, like a spoon out of the drawer.
We stand where the ground is dry and hold the stone out into the drifting steam.
Whoosh.
White steam rolls over us, warm as breath on a cold morning, and when we bring the stone down it is covered in tiny shining beads. We touch one with a fingertip.
It is water. Only water, warm on our finger.
"Never smoke," says {companion_name}. "Only water, flying."
And now the whole thing clicks shut like a lid.
Rain and melting snow trickle down through the cracks. Far below, the rock stays warm, because the mountain is asleep down there. The trapped water gets hotter and hotter and hotter, until it cannot hold still one second longer.
Then up it all comes at once.
Whoosh.
Then the crack quietly fills with new water, and the kettle is on again.
We tip the beads off the stone and put it in our pocket.
"Goodbye, whooshing puddle," we say. "Thank you for the question."

s4b.text:
{companion_name} sweeps a patch of grey ash flat with her tail and starts to draw.
"Sky," she says, and scratches a line along the top. "Rain. Snow. All the cold water there is."
She draws it going down, down and down, a long crooked road through the rock.
"Now here." She taps the bottom. "Deep down the mountain is asleep, and the rock stays warm all night, the way a hot water bottle does."
She draws water gathering there.
"It gets hotter. And hotter. And it wants to jump straight up and be steam. But look." She scribbles in all the water lying on top of it, heavy as a pile of blankets. "It has to wait its turn."
"How long?" we ask.
"Until one bubble goes first," she says. "After that first bubble, nothing on earth can make it wait one second more."
Her tail draws an enormous arrow shooting up.
"Whoosh," says {companion_name}.
And right then, behind us, the real puddle whooshes. Exactly on time.
We laugh so hard we sit down in the frosty grass.
"Goodbye, clever puddle. We know your secret now."

c1.question: "Two ways to find out," says {companion_name}. "We put an ear on the ground and listen underneath. Or we go up and find out where that cold little stream is going. Listen, or stream?"

options.label: Put an ear on the ground and listen underneath
Go up and find out where the cold stream is going

c2.question: "Two ways to finish it," says {companion_name}. "I fetch you a cold stone and we catch some of that steam on it. Or I draw you the whole road the water takes, down and up, right here in the ash. Steam, or draw?"

options.label: Catch the steam on a cold stone
Watch the lizard draw the water's whole road in the ash

s1.text:
Rain on the shed roof. Drip, drip, plop, into the bucket by the door. It is Saturday, and Grandma's shed smells of sawdust and tea, and we have a plan.

"We are going to build a boat," we tell her. "A steam-boat. A tiny one that chugs across the big puddle by the gate all by itself. Puffing."

Grandma wipes her hands on her apron. "Big talk," she says, "for a rainy morning." She fills the kettle and sets it on the hotplate, because no invention in this family begins without tea.

We raid the shelves while it heats. A broken toy train, the good kind, heavy as a stone. An old radio with dials that click. And from the scrap tin, a coil of copper tube, bent into a squiggle like a piece of elbow macaroni. We straighten it out. It shines like a penny in a pocket.

Then the kettle whistles. One long note, then a huff, then a rumble deep in its belly, like a tiny train trying to leave the station.

We stare at it. It stares back, steaming.

"Did you hear that?" we whisper. "It sounds like a dare."

"Kettles do that," says Grandma, pouring. "Now. Your grand plan. What does it remind you of?"

Remind us of? It is brand new. Nobody has ever built a boat like ours.

"Humour me," says Grandma.

So we take apart the toy train, and there inside is a little wheel with scoops, made to catch a push. We unscrew the radio, and there is a coiled wire, made to carry a message. And the copper tube, we bend it again, one bend, so it can hold steam the way the kettle does.

Three old things. Three old ideas, sitting in our hands, waiting to be snapped together.

Grandma raises her mug. "Every invention is a remix, my loves. Somebody else's good idea, wearing your hat."

The kettle huffs, in company.

"Our boat needs a name," we say. "What should we call her?" — {boat_name}

"Excellent," says Grandma. "Now. How do we make steam push?"

s2a.text:
"Slap it together!" we shout, because we cannot help it.

Grandma grins into her mug. "Then slap, inventors."

We slap. The copper coil goes over a tea-light, one bend, two bends, no measuring, who has time. We jam a cork in the jar lid. We flip a margarine tub upside down and that is the hull, because it floats and it is free. Our best friend pokes the coil with a pencil. "Is it supposed to wobble like that?"

"Probably," we say, which is not an answer.

The water in the coil gets hot. We hear it tick. Then it hisses, like the kettle's little cousin, and a fat bubble of steam shoves out the back. The boat shoots forward, spins in a circle, and sinks with a glug.

Glug.

We stare at the bubbles. Our friend nods, very serious. "Magnificent."

"Truly," says Grandma. "Now. Tea." She pours, and over the steam she tells us about Mr. Watt, who did not invent the steam engine at all. Somebody else's engine kept wasting its puff, and Watt bolted on a separate cold bit, a condenser, so the steam stopped leaking away. One borrowed trick. That was the whole genius.

We look at our coil. It is wet. It is smug.

"The puff leaked," we say slowly. "It all went out the back and none of it stayed to push."

So we bend the tube again, one more bend, and wrap a strip of cold wet cloth around the middle of it, a little jacket, so the steam keeps its strength on the way through. The coil sits in our hands like it knows something now.

Grandma raises her mug to the kettle. The kettle huffs back, in company.

"Version two," she says. "Tomorrow. And this time, inventors, she floats."

s2b.text:
"Measure twice," we say. "We want to hear what it tells us."

"Good ears," says Grandma, and clears a space on the bench.

We sketch first. The boat on paper looks like a bathtub with ideas. Our best friend holds the ruler. We bend the copper tube slowly, one bend, then stop, then one more, checking the drawing each time like it might change its mind.

While we work, Grandma lifts down something heavy from the high shelf. An old telephone, black as a boot, with a round dial that goes whir-click when you spin it.

"Mr. Bell was not trying to invent the telephone," she says. "He was trying to stack telegraph messages on one wire, lots of little dots at once. Then one day a springy reed twanged by accident, and the wire carried the twang. A sound! He heard it and thought: oh. OH."

"So the telephone was a mistake?" our friend asks.

"The telephone was somebody listening to a mistake," says Grandma. "Different thing entirely."

She taps the phone's round earpiece. "Inside here, a thin skin that shakes when sound hits it. A diaphragm. Borrow it."

So we borrow it. We stretch a balloon skin over a tin can and press it against our coil, and now the boat has a heartbeat you can hear. Our friend taps the copper. The skin flutters, fast-fast-slow.

We carry version one to the puddle and light the tea-light. The diaphragm starts to flutter. Puff. Puff. The boat wobbles sideways, and the flutter goes fast-fast-slow, fast-fast — stop.

Silence. Drip, drip, plop, from the roof.

"It died," our friend whispers.

"But we heard it die," we say. "The puff was uneven. Fast, fast, slow. Something inside is not keeping the beat."

Grandma consults the kettle, pouring slow. The kettle huffs, steady as a clock.

"Then tomorrow," she says, "we find out why."

s3.text:
Back at the workbench, we spread out what we know. The kettle whistles, one long note, and Grandma pours without being asked.

"So," she says. "What did you find?"

We tell her, and it all comes down to one thing. Our steam arrives in a single big whoosh. One giant push, and then nothing. A boat cannot chug on a whoosh.

"Chug, chug, chug," says Grandma, tapping the table. "Little pushes. Even ones."

The shed door creaks. It is Priya, from our class, holding her bike helmet, dripping. "Steam-boats were invented ages ago," she says. "Like, two hundred years."

"True," says Grandma, unbothered. "And the man who patented the first good one got a piece of paper saying the idea was his, for a while. That is all a patent is. But paper never pushed a boat. He still had to build a prototype that worked, and he built it out of older ideas, like stepping stones across a river."

Priya comes in out of the rain. "So their boat is allowed?"

"Their boat is tradition," says Grandma.

The kettle huffs, in company. We consult it, the way we always do before a rebuild. It rumbles back, deep in its belly. Not in answer. In company.

Priya peers at the copper coil on the bench. "Your problem is the bends. They're all different sizes. Steam rushes through the big ones. I'm good at measuring," she says. "The best in our class, actually."

So we hand her the ruler. Together we mark the coil into even sections, one thumb-width each, and bend it slow, one bend, one borrowed idea at a time.

The rain patters on. The puddle is waiting.

"Version two," says Priya, and grins.

s4a.text:
Priya bounces on her toes. "The puddle. Now. Before the rain stops."

We wrap version two in a tea towel and run. The big puddle by the gate is brown and busy, raindrops pocking it like fingers tapping a table. Grandma follows with the kettle, because ceremony is ceremony.

We kneel at the edge. Priya lights the little burner, and we hold our breath so hard our cheeks puff out.

The copper coil trembles. Steam fills it, bend by bend, and then — chug. Chug. Chug. The boat scoots forward, puffing, our name for her painted on the side.

Three seconds. Then she stops. Dead in the water, one boat-length out.

"No!" we wail.

"YES!" shouts Priya, and we spin around. "Listen. The very first message ever sent on the internet? The computer crashed after two letters. L, O. They were trying to type LOGIN and it died. And it still counted! Two letters changed the world!"

We look at our boat, stalled and steaming. "So our boat just sent its first message," we say slowly. "Two chugs. What is she saying?" — {code_word}

"Then let's get the rest of the word out," says Priya. She reaches in, careful, and turns the coil one half-turn, so the last bend sits even with the others. "Even pushes. Like Grandma said."

The burner hisses. Chug. Chug. Chug-chug-chug, all the way across, the whole width of the puddle, puffing our code word into the rain.

We shout, because we cannot help it. Grandma applauds with her mug.

Back in the shed, she hangs the bent copper coil on the pegboard, on a hook all by itself. Below it she tapes a label in her spidery writing: Patent Pending, Puddle Division.

"Every patent starts as a puddle," she says.

The kettle huffs. In company.

s4b.text:
"Almost isn't enough," we say. "Not yet."

So the afternoon becomes a parade of almosts. We set version two in Grandma's old baking tray, filled at the sink. Chug, chug, chug — three seconds — dead. We unbend the coil, smooth one kink, try again. Seven seconds. Dead. Priya frowns at the ruler and moves one bend a thumb-width over. Eleven seconds.

Each time, Grandma tops up the teapot and tells another piece of the story.

"There was a man named Tim Berners-Lee," she says, "who invented the World Wide Web. But he didn't invent the pieces. Computers already existed. The internet already existed, carrying messages. He just snapped two old ideas together — like your train wheel and your kettle."

Chug-chug-chug. Dead at the far end of the tray. Twelve seconds.

"And here is the part I love," says Grandma. "He could have patented it. Gotten a piece of paper saying it was his, and charged the whole world to use it. Instead he gave it away. Free. So anyone could build on it. Remix it."

"He gave away his invention?" we say. "On purpose?"

"That's why you have a computer at school," says Priya, not looking up from the coil. "Okay. One more."

The light outside goes gold, then grey. The kettle whistles, consulted one last time, and rumbles back in company. Priya sets the boat in the tray.

Chug. Chug. Chug-chug-chug. Around the whole rim of the tray, one full lap, steady as a heartbeat.

We carry her out into the drizzle, and she crosses the real puddle without stopping once.

"Enough," we whisper. "It's enough."

Before bed, we tape the very first paper sketch to the shed wall — damp at the corners, signed by all three of us — so the next kid who raids this scrap tin can see exactly how we did it.

"Free to remix," says Grandma, turning off the light.

The kettle huffs. Goodnight.

c1.question: Grandma taps the kettle and asks: 'So, inventors — do we slap it together and see what breaks, or do we measure twice and listen to what it's telling us?'

options.label: Slap the prototype together fast and test it to destruction
Sketch carefully and give the boat a 'heartbeat' we can listen to

c2.question: Our best friend bounces on their toes: 'Version two is READY. Do we march it straight to the puddle for the big launch, or keep tinkering till it's perfect-perfect?'

options.label: Carry it to the puddle right now for the full-send crossing
Stay at the bench and polish the almost-there version until dusk

boat_name.role: The name we give our little steam-boat prototype

code_word.role: The two-letter message our boat 'sends' when it finally works, echoing the internet's first 'LO'

s1.text:
It is midnight, and the playground belongs to us. Just us, two swings, and a sky full of stars.

We pump our legs. Higher. Higher. The chains creak, the wind pushes our hair back, and then, right at the very top, it happens. That little float. For one whole second, nothing pulls us. We hang there, light as dandelion fluff.

Then gravity tugs us back down. It always does.

"Again!" we shout, and we pump harder, chasing that floaty moment. But the swing always pulls us home.

"You felt it," says a voice. "That little hang at the top."

A woman stands by the slide, silver-haired, wearing a flight jacket covered in patches. Behind her sits a bus with painted planets on the side. And at her feet, a small dog in a red bandana is bouncing on his hind legs, yipping at a firefly like it owes him something.

"I'm Reyes," she says. "Retired astronaut. And that menace is {dog_name}."

{dog_name} barks twice, spins in a circle, and stares at us like we are the most exciting thing that has ever happened.

"Here's the thing," Reyes says, leaning in. "That floaty second at the top of the swing? Up there, it lasts." She points at the stars. "Everything pulls on everything. That's gravity. The bigger something is, the stronger it pulls. Earth is big, so it pulls you back down. But somewhere smaller..."

She grins. {dog_name} grins too, somehow.

"Want to feel it stretch?"

s2a.text:
"The elevator," we say, and {dog_name} yips like we chose steak.

Inside, it's all glass. The operator, a woman with silver stars on her collar, points to a big red button. "Press it."

We press. The floor pushes up against our feet, and suddenly we feel heavy, like we're wearing a backpack full of rocks. Then lighter. Lighter. Our stomachs float up into our chests.

"That's gravity changing," the operator says. "The higher we go, the less Earth pulls."

Outside, blue sky turns purple, then black. Stars pop out in the middle of the day. We step onto the station's glass floor and look down. Earth swirls below us, blue and white, small enough to cover with our thumb.

"Our house," we whisper. It's a postage stamp. It's a dot.

Then {dog_name} barks. His red ball is floating away, drifting toward the ceiling, and he's paddling the air with his paws, swimming after it, but he can't reach. He looks at us, eyes wide, floating in place.

"Help," his face says. "Help, help, help."

s2b.text:
"The rocket bus," we say, and Reyes grins. "Good choice. {dog_name} loves the juice."

Inside, there are no seats, just handholds. Reyes squeezes a pouch, and a perfect orange blob floats out, wobbling like jelly. {dog_name} launches himself, mouth open, but the blob drifts left. He twists in the air, paws grabbing nothing.

"We're falling," Reyes says, steering with one hand. "Falling around Earth so fast we keep missing it. That's an orbit."

We look out. The Moon fills the window, close enough to see shadows inside the craters, gray and deep.

"Everything pulls," Reyes says. "The Moon pulls on us. We pull on the Moon. But Earth's pull is stronger because Earth has more mass."

We squeeze our own juice. It floats, a perfect sphere. {dog_name} barks, spinning, but the blob drifts just past his nose. He snaps at air. Again. Again.

"He'll get it," Reyes says, laughing. "Or he won't. Either way, he's happy."

s3.text:
The bus hums down to a stop, and the stars outside turn into grey rock. An asteroid, hollow as a pumpkin, with a doorway waiting for us.

Inside, the floor barely holds us. Reyes steps off the bus and floats up, slow as a bubble. {dog_name} pushes off with all four paws and tumbles, bandana flapping, chasing a blob of juice from his open pack. He snaps. He misses. He barks at it like it cheated.

"Small rock, small pull," Reyes says. "Watch this."

We bend our knees and jump, and we fly. Across the whole cavern. We land on the far wall with our feet and bounce back, laughing, because we cannot help it. For one long breath at the top of the arc, we hang there. The swing moment, stretched like taffy.

{dog_name} has found a bone somewhere. He digs at the grey dust with his front paws, but the dust just sighs up around him, and the bone floats out of the hole and bumps his nose. He sneezes. The dust goes everywhere.

"Even here," Reyes says, catching him gently, "everything still pulls on everything. This rock pulls on you. You pull on it. Even {dog_name} pulls, a tiny bit. It is just that Earth is so much bigger, its pull wins."

Ahead, the cavern splits into two tunnels, and the dog's ears go up.

"So," Reyes says, turning to us. "What did you find back there? And which way now?"

s4a.text: We take the tunnel with the soft blue light, and it opens into a round room where a scientist in grey coveralls is dropping things. Two balls, one big, one small, and they fall together, slow as snow, and bump the floor at the exact same time. "Ha!" she says, like she has won a bet. "Same pull, same fall. Watch." She holds out a stone the size of a plum and a grey feather. "Here. Feel." The stone sits heavy in our palm, pulling down like it wants the floor. The feather just lies there, tickling. "Mass," she says. "The stone has more of it, so it pulls harder on your hand. And your hand pulls back." We weigh them, stone, feather, stone again, while {dog_name} floats past upside down, still hunting that juice blob. The feather drifts off and lands on his nose, and he goes cross-eyed trying to bark at it. Time to go. Reyes tucks a small smooth stone from the asteroid's core into our pocket. "So you remember what light feels like." Then the bus, and the growing pull, and Earth rising up to meet us, and our legs settling heavy and safe onto the playground grass. Home. We stand in our own two shoes, and the stone is in our pocket, and the whole Earth is holding us gently in place.

s4b.text: We take the tunnel with the warm orange light, and it ends at a cavern with a window. Not glass. Crystal, grown right out of the rock, clear as ice, and through it hangs Earth, blue and white and enormous. "Oh," we say, because we cannot help it. {dog_name} plants his front paws on the window ledge and stares, ears up, tail going. Then something moves between us and the planet. A bird. A real bird, out here, wings beating, beating, beating, working against the pull with every stroke. It soars past the window so close we see its eye, bright and busy, and then it is gone, falling and flying and falling and flying toward home. "She is fighting the same force that holds us," Reyes says quietly. "Everything pulls on everything. She just pushes back." We watch until the bird is a speck, and the speck is nothing, and there is only Earth, pulling us gently even from here. On the way back, {dog_name} trots up with something in his mouth. His red bandana, the one he buried in the dust. It is grey now with asteroid grit, and he drops it in our lap like a present. We tie it around our neck on the bus ride home, and when Earth rises up to meet us, and our legs turn heavy and safe, the grit is still there, a tiny bit of somewhere else, holding on.

options.label: Ride the glass elevator straight up
Board the rocket bus that falls around Earth

c2.question: "Which tunnel calls to you—the one glowing soft blue like deep water, or the one shining warm orange like sunset?"

options.label: Enter the tunnel with soft blue light
Enter the tunnel with warm orange light

stories.title: The Puzzle That Took a Century

s1.text:
The wind on this beach in Brazil has a mind of its own. It flips {kid_name}'s hair. It rattles the little tin in Nana Pip's pocket, the one full of real jigsaw pieces, the one that goes everywhere she goes.

"Listen to that," says Nana Pip. "The tin wants to tell a story."

They walk the way they always walk, slow, with cocoa waiting back home in the chipped mugs. The sea hisses up the sand and slides away again. Nana Pip holds up her phone, and on it is a map of the whole wide Atlantic, blue as bathwater, with Brazil on one side and Africa on the other.

And {kid_name} stares at it, and stares, and then it just bursts out:

"Nana. The edge of Brazil looks like it could plug right into Africa. Like a puzzle piece."

Nana Pip stops walking. She smiles the smile she saves for very good moves in very hard puzzles. Out of the tin comes one green piece, shaped a little like Brazil itself, and she presses it into {kid_name}'s hand. It is warm from her pocket.

"A keeper for the tin," she says. "Because, my love, you have just asked the question that took a hundred years to answer. Grown scientists argued about it. Shouted about it. One man staked his whole life on it, and nobody believed him."

The wind tugs at her scarf. The sea goes hiss, and hush.

"But," says Nana Pip, tapping the map, "a coastline that fits is only the first clue. And a first clue might be real evidence, or it might be a pretty coincidence. Detectives have to decide which."

She raises one eyebrow. "So. Which is it?"

s2a.text:
The museum's back room smells of old paper and cold stone, and it is full of drawers. Hundreds of drawers, tall as Nana Pip, each one labeled with the name of a continent.

"South America," reads the curator, a woman with a magnifying glass on a string around her neck and the pleased look of someone who has been waiting all morning for exactly this visit. "And Africa. I keep them across the room from each other. Seems wrong, somehow."

She slides two drawers open, one with a rumble, one with a squeak. Inside, on beds of blue velvet, lie two flat stones. And in each stone, pressed like a leaf in a book, is the same little animal. Long thin body. Long thin tail. A little lizardy thing, no bigger than a banana.

"Mesosaurus," says the curator. "Say it with me, it's a good one. Meso-saurus."

"Meso-saurus," says {kid_name}, and it tastes like a word worth keeping.

"Now here is the puzzle," the curator says. "This little fellow lived in lakes and rivers. Fresh water only. It could no more swim the salty Atlantic than I could flap my arms and fly to the moon. And yet—" she taps one drawer, then the other, "—one of him turned up in South America, and his twin turned up in Africa."

Nana Pip leans close. Her tin rattles. "Go on, detective. Do the honours."

So {kid_name} lifts the two stones, one careful hand under each, and lays them side by side on the table. The two little lizards lie nose to nose, tail to tail, like a reflection, like twins separated at birth and meeting at last.

"Shapes can be coincidence," the curator says, and her eyes are shining. "One coastline hugging another — maybe. But twins? Twins are harder to wave away."

"A keeper for the tin," whispers Nana Pip, and out comes the tin, and in goes the moment.

But as they walk back into the daylight, Nana Pip's face goes thoughtful. "Two little lizards, my love. Against a whole ocean." She shakes her head slowly. "Who on earth would believe them?"

s2b.text:
The geologist's study is at the top of a narrow staircase that creaks like it is telling secrets, and the room itself looks like the inside of a very busy brain. Rocks on the desk. Rocks on the floor. Photographs of glaciers pinned to every wall, slightly crooked, held up with tape.

"Mind the teetering one," says the geologist, an old man with eyebrows like two grey caterpillars, as {kid_name} steps around a stack of stone samples. "It's been teetering since 1962. Hasn't fallen yet."

He lifts one dark rock with both hands and sets it in front of them like a cake. "Now. Put your finger here."

The rock has scratches. Long ones, deep ones, running side by side like the claw marks of something enormous, all dragging one way.

"Glaciers did that," the geologist says. "Ice, heavy as a mountain, sliding across the land, scraping its fingernails along the rock. And here is the part that keeps me up at night." He pulls out photograph after photograph and slaps them down in a row. "South America. Africa. India. Australia. The same scratches. The same claw marks. All pointing the same way."

{kid_name} runs a finger along the grooves. They are rough and cold and they all run one way, like hair combed flat, like sled tracks in snow.

"One giant ice sheet," the geologist says, "sliding across one giant joined-up land. Otherwise the marks wouldn't line up. They'd point every which way, like a dropped box of matches."

"Like a dropped box of matches," Nana Pip repeats with respect, and writes it down.

"And that's not all." The geologist whisks a cloth off a tray, and there lie pressed ferns, five of them, five continents' worth, and every frond the same shape, like five copies of one fingerprint. "Same plant. Five oceans apart. Ferns cannot fly, my friend. Somebody carried them — or the ground did."

Nana Pip's tin is out and open before she even speaks. "Keeper," she says firmly. "Keeper, keeper, keeper."

But on the stairs going down, she stops, and the creaks go quiet under them. "Scratches and ferns across five continents, my love. That can't be coincidence." She frowns. "So why won't anyone believe it? Where's the proof the whole world will accept?"

s3.text:
Nana Pip taps the phone, and the beach folds away like a map being closed, and suddenly we are standing at the back of a tall lecture hall in 1912, where the air smells of chalk dust and wet coats and the radiators clank like somebody stirring a very big pot.

"What did you find?" Nana Pip whispers. "Hold on to it. You are about to meet the man who needed it."

At the front, a man with round glasses is pinning up a map so enormous it needs two chairs and a stepladder. Alfred Wegener. He has chalk on his sleeve, chalk on his ear, and eyes like somebody who has been awake all night finishing a puzzle and does not regret it.

"Look," he tells the room, and his pointer taps one coastline, then another. Tap. Tap. "These edges fit. And that is not all." He pins up pictures of fossils, little curled ferns, twin creatures from opposite sides of an ocean. "The same plants. The same animals. The same scratches in the rock, as if the continents were once one great land that broke apart and drifted. I call it continental drift."

The room goes very quiet. It is the quiet of a hundred grown-ups all thinking at once.

Then an old geologist stands up, slow, and his voice is not unkind. "Mr. Wegener. Your clues are... interesting. But answer me this. What force could possibly move a continent?"

Wegener opens his mouth. Closes it. The chalk dust floats. He has every piece except one, and it is the one the whole puzzle hangs on.

"I... do not know yet," he says. "But the evidence is real."

Heads shake. Chairs scrape. The room files out into the cold.

Nana Pip's voice comes soft beside us. "He kept collecting clues anyway, my love. All the way to a lonely ice sheet in Greenland. Because a missing piece is not the end of a puzzle." The tin rattles. "It is an invitation."

s4a.text:
Nana Pip taps the phone, and the hall folds away, and we are standing on the deck of a night ship in the cold black Atlantic, where the sea slaps the hull and the stars are spilled salt. A young technician with headphones around her neck is bent over a long roll of paper, and the paper is growing, line by line, as the ship's sonar listens down into the dark.

"Shh," she says, grinning. "The ocean is drawing us a picture."

We watch the lines rise into a giant rumpled ridge right down the middle of the seafloor, like the earth has a backbone. And on either side of it, stripes. Dark, light, dark, light. Zebra stripes of magnetized rock, and here is the thing that makes the technician hold her breath: the stripes on the left mirror the stripes on the right. Perfectly.

"The rock at the ridge is brand new," she whispers. "It cools, it records the earth's magnetism like a tape recorder, and then it spreads away on both sides. The seafloor is being born at the plate boundaries. Right now. Under us. That is what moves the continents. That is the how."

The ship hums. The paper keeps growing. And every old clue clicks at once in our heads, tap, tap, tap, like Wegener's pointer.

The beach folds back around us. The wind is still showing off. Nana Pip takes the green piece from {kid_name}'s hand and snaps it into a blue one, shaped a little like Africa, and the click is the most satisfying sound in the world.

"A keeper for the tin," she says. But she does not put it in the tin. She puts it in your pocket. "Some pieces you keep on you."

We walk home slow, and the cocoa is waiting in the chipped mugs, and the piece is warm in your pocket where the answer used to be missing.

s4b.text:
Nana Pip taps the phone, and the hall folds away, and we are home at her kitchen table, where the cocoa steams in the chipped mugs and the tin sits open like a little treasure chest.

"Now," she says, pushing a sheet of paper toward you. "You are going to make the evidence with your own hands. Because an answer you build yourself is an answer you keep."

On the paper she has drawn a line down the middle. "The ridge," she says. "The plate boundary, where new seafloor is born." She hands you a shaker of iron filings, and you sprinkle them over the paper like pepper on soup. Then she slides a magnet under the table, slow, and you hold your breath.

The filings shiver. They stand up. They curve into stripes, dark and light, dark and light, marching away from the ridge on both sides. And the stripes on the left mirror the stripes on the right. Perfectly.

"Look at that," Nana Pip breathes. "Zebra stripes. The real ocean floor has them, my love. When rock cools at the ridge, it records the earth's magnetism like a tape recorder, and then it spreads. That is the proof Wegener never lived to see. The seafloor itself wrote down the answer, and it was spreading the continents apart the whole time."

You run the magnet again, and the stripes form again, and it does not get less wonderful.

Nana Pip pours the cocoa. Then she takes the green piece, the one shaped a little like Brazil, and slides it into a blue one shaped a little like Africa. Click. The best sound in the world.

"A keeper for the tin," she says. But she does not put it in the tin. She puts it in your pocket. "Some pieces you keep on you."

The cocoa is warm. The stripes are still on the paper. And the answer is yours, because your hands made it.

c1.question: "One clue is a maybe, detective. Two clues is a pattern. So — do we go open the museum's fossil drawers, or climb up to the old geologist's study and look at the rocks?"

options.label: Visit the museum back room to see the twin fossils
Climb to the geologist's study to see the glacier scratches and ferns

c2.question: "The answer came at last, out on the dark ocean. Do you want to stand on that night ship and watch the map grow — or shall we make the stripes appear ourselves, right here at my table?"

options.label: Sail on the 1950s research ship and watch the sonar reveal the ridge
Make magnetic stripes appear with iron filings at Nana Pip's table

s1.text: I remember a morning, little one, when you and I sat on a big warm rock. The sun had baked it cozy, like toast. Below us lay {pool_name}, still and clear as bathwater. We wiggled our toes. We waited. The sun spilled a golden ripple across the water. Shiver-shine. Shiver-shine. "Is anyone home?" you whispered. I listened. You listened. The pool went blub. Just one little blub. Somebody was waking up down there.

s2a.text: Then the sand goes puff. Up rises the octopus, slow and wiggly. One arm lifts. Then another. Curl. Uncurl. Each arm waves all by itself, like eight little hellos. You wiggle your fingers back. The golden ripple grows brighter. Shiver-shine. Shiver-shine. "Hello, wiggly one," you say. The octopus waves. We wave. But where is the little fish? We listen. We wait.

s2b.text: Then a silver fish darts in. Quick, quick, quick. It swims in small circles, round and round. Then it stops. It opens its mouth. Blub. Blub. Tiny bubbles float up, up, up. Pop at the top. "Blub blub," you say. The fish blows more bubbles. The golden ripple grows brighter. Shiver-shine. Shiver-shine. We watch the bubbles dance. But where is the wiggly octopus? We look. We wait.

s3.text: "What did you find?" I whisper. You wiggle your fingers. "Come and see!" And here they are, both friends together in {pool_name}. The octopus waves one arm, slow and sleepy. Hello. Hello. The little fish blows bubbles that float up, up, past its wiggly arms. Blub. Blub. Then, from under a pink coral branch, a tiny pink crab peeks out. It waves one little claw sideways. Hello to you too! Far away, a big whale hums a low, rumbly song. The water shivers gently. The golden ripple grows brighter on the sandy bottom. Shiver-shine. Shiver-shine. But the light is shifting now. Our quiet splash is beginning to pass.

s4a.text: You wiggle your fingers at the little fish. Wiggle, wiggle. It blows one last big bubble. Pop! The octopus waves one arm, slow and sleepy. Bye-bye. Bye-bye. We sit on our warm rock a little longer. The sun-baked stone feels cozy under us. The golden ripple fades, soft and low. Shiver-shine. Shiver-shine. "Do you hear it?" I whisper. Blub. Blub. The sound stays in your ears. We carry it home with us, all the way back. Eight arms waving. One little fish saying blub. You wiggle your fingers again, just to remember.

s4b.text: You blow a gentle kiss toward the water. Mwah. The octopus curls one arm into a soft spiral, like a hug. The little fish swims one last slow circle. Round and round. We sit on our warm rock a little longer. The sun-baked stone feels cozy under us. The golden ripple fades, soft and low. Shiver-shine. Shiver-shine. "Do you see it?" I whisper. The light shimmers on the sandy bottom. We carry the picture home with us, all the way back. One curled arm. One slow circle. You blow another kiss, just to remember.

c1.question: "Shall we watch for the wiggly arms, or listen for the blub blub bubbles?"

options.label: Watch the octopus wake up
Listen for the little fish

c2.question: "How shall we say goodbye to our friends?"

options.label: Wiggle your fingers like the octopus
Blow a soft kiss to the water

s1.text:
"Look at your thumbs," says Grandma Nessa. So we do. Mine bends back like a little hook. {cousin_name}'s sticks straight up, no bend at all. "Same family," Nessa says, "different cards."

We are at her kitchen table, the one with the blue checkered cloth, and cocoa warming on the stove. {cousin_name} rolls their tongue into a hot dog. I try. Mine just folds in half and lies there, like a slug napping.

"How come?" I ask. "We have the same grandma."

Nessa taps the old recipe book on the table. It is fat and worn, soft as a teddy bear's ear, with notes scribbled in the margins by her mother, and her mother's mother. "This is a copy," she says. "The real one is somewhere much, much smaller."

"Smaller than the book?" says {cousin_name}.

"Smaller than a crumb," says Nessa. "Every cell in your body has one. A whole recipe book, copied out, for making you."

She opens her coat pocket and takes out a thermos. She pours three cups, even though the cocoa on the stove is right there. "A marvel," she says, "deserves a warm sip and a slow look."

We sip. The kitchen goes very quiet.

Then the sugar bowl glints.

A pinprick of light, right in the middle of the sugar, like one grain has woken up. It grows. It hums, low and friendly, like the fridge at night. The kitchen seems to tilt, just a little, the way it does when you stand up too fast.

"Nessa," I whisper. "The sugar bowl is glowing."

"So it is," she says, and she does not sound surprised at all. She sounds like someone whose train has come in. "Drink up, you two. Nuclea wants to show us the original book. And she won't wait all night."

s2a.text:
We step through the pinprick, and the kitchen folds away behind us like a napkin.

Now we are standing inside something round and warm and humming. "A cell," says Nuclea, hugging her ledger. "One of trillions. And there—" she points, "is the book."

It is a staircase. A spiral staircase, turning up and up, and every step is made of glowing beads. Only four kinds. Nuclea says their names like old friends: A, T, G, C. "Four letters," she says. "That's the whole alphabet. And it spells you."

"Four letters spell all of me?" says {cousin_name}.

"Three billion steps," says Nuclea. "It spells everything."

Nessa pours cocoa from her thermos, right there on the third step. "A marvel," she says, "deserves a warm sip and a slow look."
