Then Nuclea does something wonderful. She takes hold of one tiny speck of bead, and she pulls. A silver thread comes out of it, thin as spider silk, and it stretches. Across the room. Down a long hall. Around a corner. Six feet of thread, Nuclea says, out of one speck too small to see. Then, quick as a yawn, it folds itself back into a dot.

"The thread won't hold long," she says. "Before it folds away again, read me one gene. One recipe, off the staircase. Any one."

We climb. The beads glow under our fingers, warm as toast. I find a run of steps that keeps repeating, and I read the letters out loud, slow, the way Nessa reads recipes. T. G. A. C.

"That one," says Nuclea softly, writing in her ledger, "has a say in the bend of your thumb. Only a say, mind. A thumb like yours is argued over by a whole committee of these, and they do not always agree."

I look at my thumb. The little hook. Written here, in beads, in every cell I have.

"So the whole book about us," whispers {cousin_name}, "fits inside something we can't even see?"

Nuclea smiles. "Every copy of it. In every cell. All night long."

s2b.text:
We step through the pinprick, and the kitchen folds away behind us like a napkin.

Nuclea leads us down a corridor that smells of paper and cocoa, into the coziest little office I have ever seen. A green lamp. A wooden table. Two dealers in waistcoats, shuffling cards.

"The shuffling station," Nuclea whispers. "Mind your elbows. Tonight's deal is nearly done."

The cards are not ordinary cards. Each one has a picture: a hooked thumb, a straight thumb, a rolled tongue, a flat one. "Trait tickets," says Nuclea. "One deck from your mother. One from your father."

The dealers slide the cards across the table, quick and gentle, half and half, exactly half and half. "Fifty percent from each," says Nuclea. "Always. But which fifty—" she taps her ledger, "that is the shuffle."

Two envelopes land on the table with a soft plap. One has my name on it. One has {cousin_name}'s.

Nessa pours cocoa all round, even for the dealers, who sip without stopping their hands. "A marvel," she says, "deserves a warm sip and a slow look."

We open my envelope. Hooked thumb. Flat tongue. A curl of dark hair. Then {cousin_name} opens theirs, and we both lean in, because the tickets inside are plainly, cheerfully different. Straight thumb. Rolled tongue. Freckles across the nose like spilled cinnamon.

"Same grandma," I say slowly. "Different cards."

"Now you see it," says Nuclea.

A train whistle sounds, far off and friendly. The dealers stamp both envelopes, thump, thump, and slide them across to us.

"Keep yours," says Nuclea. "The deal is done. But I wonder—" she looks at us over her ledger, "which tickets did you get, and which went to your cousin instead? Look closely, travelers. The answer is sitting at the kitchen table, right beside you."

s3.text:
The light folds us small, smaller than a crumb, and sets us down on a platform beside a long, low train. Its cars are the color of cocoa. The engine hums, low and friendly, like the fridge at night.

"Tickets," says a voice.

The conductor is tall and thin as a pencil, with a cap too big for him and a puncher in his fist. "Alder," he says. "Conductor Alder. End of the line, family tree, last stop. Lantern's already lit, and it won't wait all night." He looks at our hands. "Tickets, please."

I look down. There is a ticket in my fist. {cousin_name} has one too. Alder punches mine, then theirs, and squints at the holes like they say something he likes.

"What did you find back there?" {cousin_name} whispers to me.

Before I can answer, the whistle goes. Not loud. Warm, like a kettle just starting to think about it.

We climb aboard. The seats are soft as a teddy bear's ear, and the window runs the whole length of the car. Outside, the track stretches ahead, two long rails twisted together like a rope of licorice, and along it, little platforms with signs.

"First stop," Alder calls, "eye color."

We do not stop. We slow, and the sign slides past, and I see {cousin_name}'s eyes in the window glass, and mine beside them, same family, different cards.

"Blood type," Alder calls. "Earwax. Whether coriander tastes like soap to you."

{cousin_name} rolls theirs at me through the glass. I make my slug face. We laugh, because we cannot help it.

Then the train slows for real, and there on the next platform, cocoa thermos in hand, is someone I almost know. Young. Bright-eyed. Waving like the train is hers.

"Nessa?" I say.

She climbs aboard, pours three cups from the thermos, and holds up a ticket of her own. "One of mine never showed," she says, "not once, my whole life. Until it met a match." She sits down beside us and wraps her hands around her cup. "Drink up. The last stop is the family tree, and something has been riding hidden in it a long, long time."

s4a.text:
The train slows to a stop so soft I feel it in my teeth. Outside the window, a tree rises bigger than any tree has a right to be, its trunk wide as a house, its branches lit by a single lantern hanging from the lowest limb.

"Last stop," says Alder. "Family tree."

We climb down onto moss that squishes like cake. Young Nessa leads, thermos in one hand, and we climb — branch to branch, easy as stairs — up past leaves that are not leaves at all. They are portraits. Hundreds of them, swaying gently, each one framed in bark. A woman with my chin. A man with Nessa's bright eyes.

"Higher," Nessa says. "The newest leaves grow at the top."

And there, on a twig still green and growing, is a portrait half-finished. Me. My hook thumb, my fold-flat tongue, my freckles coming in one by one like someone is dotting them with a fine brush, right now, as we watch.

"That's me," I whisper. "It's still painting me."

"Always is," says Nessa. "Your whole life long."

Then {cousin_name} laughs out loud. On the twig beside mine, another portrait is finishing itself — and its hair is red. Bright, bright red, like nobody's in the whole family.

"There she is," Nessa says softly. "My mother's red hair. My ticket that never showed. It rode hidden in the book for three generations, waiting for a match. And tonight it finally climbed into the front seat."

She presses a plain ticket into my palm. It is warm, like it has been in a pocket a long time.

We sit on the branch, the three of us, and Nessa pours the last of the cocoa. Below us the lantern swings. I sip, and look at my leaf, and try to trace my freckles back — but the trail tangles, the way recipes do when everybody adds a note.

"Some you can trace," Nessa says, reading my face. "Some stay a mystery. Half from your mother, half from your father, shuffled like cards. The book gets copied either way."

The light folds us big again, back at the blue checkered cloth. The sugar bowl is just a sugar bowl. But in my pocket there is a small card, and on it, in Nessa's mother's handwriting: one new page, half from each, shuffled, ours alone.

"Mine's the freckles," I say. "I think."

"Worth a warm sip," says Nessa, "and a slow look."

s4b.text:
The train slows to a stop so soft I feel it in my teeth. Outside the window, a tree rises bigger than any tree has a right to be, its trunk wide as a house, its branches lit by a single lantern swinging from the lowest limb.

"Last stop," says Alder. "Family tree."

We climb down onto moss that squishes like cake. Young Nessa leads, thermos in hand, and we climb — branch to branch, easy as stairs — up past leaves that are not leaves at all. They are portraits, swaying gently, each one framed in bark. A woman with my chin. A man with {cousin_name}'s straight thumb.

"Higher," says Nessa. "The newest leaves grow at the top."

And there, on two twigs side by side, hang two portraits still wet with paint. Mine: hook thumb, fold-flat tongue, freckles. Theirs: straight thumb, tongue like a hot dog, and hair coming in red. Bright, bright red, like nobody's in the whole family.

"Two hands," Nessa says, "dealt from the same deck."

We sit on the branch between our leaves, and Nessa pours the cocoa, and we look. Really look.

"Your hair," I say to {cousin_name}. "It's like the tree saved up all its red just for you."

"Your freckles," {cousin_name} says back. "They're like... connect-the-dots that nobody finished. In a good way."

We laugh, because we cannot help it.

Nessa tucks a red ticket into {cousin_name}'s pocket and a blue one into mine. "Neither hand is better," she says. "There is no better. There is only yours, and yours, and the deck that keeps on shuffling."

"Same grandma," {cousin_name} says, like they're hearing it new.

"Different cards," I say.

The light folds us big again, back at the blue checkered cloth. The sugar bowl is just a sugar bowl. But in my pocket there is a small card, and on it, in Nessa's mother's handwriting: one new page, half from each, shuffled, ours alone.

{cousin_name} holds up their blue ticket against my red one, and grins.

"Good hand," they say.

"Good hand," I say back.

c1.question: "Two doors, travelers," Nuclea whispers, hugging her ledger. "Shall we climb the spiral staircase and read the letters ourselves, or visit the shuffling station and watch the cards being dealt?"

options.label: Climb the DNA staircase and read the four-letter code
Visit the shuffling station and watch the trait cards dealt

c2.question: "Last climb of the night," says young Nessa, pouring the cocoa. "Do we look for your own leaf and trace one trait home, or sit with your cousin's leaf and see how the same deck dealt two different hands?"

options.label: Find our own leaf and trace one inherited trait to its source
Sit with our cousin's leaf and compare the two different hands

cousin_name.role: The cousin who journeys beside us and gets a different envelope of traits

s1.text:
Listen. The moon is up, the sand is cool, and something big is coming out of the sea. Wave after wave it comes — a turtle, an old, old grandmother turtle, as wide as your kitchen table, with silver barnacles winking on her shell. And riding on her back, flat as a pancake, is a little fish. That is Pip. Pip is a remora, which means Pip sticks on tight and never, ever stops talking.

"Did you see that? Did you see those eggs?" Pip squeaks. "One hundred eggs, buried in the warm sand! And now — now! — she is swimming home. Across the WHOLE ocean. Weeks and weeks of nothing but water. Want to come?"

Of course we want to come.

The turtle slides back into the waves, and we ride close beside her, where the water is calm. Her name — well, her name is {hero_name}. And here is the wonder Pip keeps whispering about: somewhere out there, past the horizon, past the next horizon, is a meadow of green seagrass where {hero_name} feeds. She has no map. She has no road. But Pip swears there is an invisible ribbon stretched across the whole ocean, tied at both ends to one small patch of sand — and {hero_name} can feel it humming, the way you feel a cat purring.

"How does she KNOW?" Pip blurts. "It's all just water!"

{hero_name} says nothing. She lifts one great flipper, slow as a falling leaf, and the ocean current takes her.

The ribbon pulls. We follow.

s2a.text:
"Fast river it is!" Pip shouts. "Hold on to your hats! If you have hats!"

We swing wide — and there it is. A river inside the sea. Deeper blue than the water around it, running swift and sure, like a long blue road somebody poured into the ocean and forgot to take home.

{hero_name} doesn't hesitate. She spreads her flippers wide, like wings, and slides into the current — and stops paddling. Just stops. The river takes her.

"She's not swimming!" Pip gasps. "She's RIDING! Like an escalator! Like a moving sidewalk! Why doesn't every fish know about this?!"

Seaweed streams past us like flags in a parade. The water hums under our knees. And far off, on the edge of everything, rises the green cone of a volcanic island.

"Green Top," says {hero_name} — the first words we've heard her say out at sea. "That's my first landmark. Like a bus stop. I never miss it."

"But HOW?" Pip begs. "There's nothing out here! No signs! How do you know where to turn?"

{hero_name} is quiet a long moment. Then: "I have a map, little fish. But it's not made of paper. It's printed inside my head — glowing lines only I can feel. The whole Earth hums, and the humming tells me where I am. I just follow the lines."

Pip goes very still. Then, in a whisper: "A map... in her HEAD."

The current carries us on, swift and dark and blue. But ahead, where the river-in-the-sea ends, the open ocean waits — wide, and wide, and wide.

s2b.text:
"The golden island!" Pip shouts. "Trust me. Trust me. You're going to want to see this."

We turn away from the fast water, and there it is — a floating raft of golden sargassum, drifting far from any land. A whole island made of seaweed, bobbing and shining, thick as the jam at the bottom of the jar.

And it is full of life. Tiny crabs no bigger than your fingernail. Seahorses curled like question marks. And tucked under a golden leaf — a baby turtle. A baby turtle no bigger than a walnut.

"That's Kelp," Pip breathes. "He just got here. Just hatched. Just made his first scramble down the sand and into the waves — ALL BY HIMSELF."

Kelp looks up at {hero_name}, and his flippers are so small they look like flower petals. "Is it true?" he asks, in a voice like a squeak in a shell. "Am I really supposed to cross all of... this?"

"You are," says {hero_name}, gentle as low tide. "But not today. Today you only need to find the current. Feel for it — the water that moves faster, that pulls a little. That's your road. Ride it, and it will carry you to the feeding grounds."

"But how will I know the way?"

"The same way I do," says {hero_name}. "The beach where you hatched already holds your name. It will call you back when you're grown. It always does."

Kelp blinks his small dark eyes. Then he paddles out from under the leaf, braver already.

"Every turtle starts this small," Pip whispers. "Every single one. Even HER. Even the grandmother. The whole commute... begins with a walnut."

s3.text:
"What did you find back there?" Pip asks, for the tenth time. But the question floats away behind us, because now there is nothing. Nothing but water. Water below, water beside, water piled on water all the way to the sky. Weeks of it.

"How can she stand it?" Pip whispers. "It's all just BLUE!"

But {hero_name} swims on, steady as a heartbeat. She does not need to see the way. She feels it. Deep inside her head sits a map made of the earth's own pulling, and the stars wheel overhead like slow compass needles, and sometimes — Pip swears this is true — she lifts her head and smells the water, tasting for home.

High above, a frigatebird wheels. Ferra, she calls herself, all sharp wings and gossip. "You're still swimming?" she shouts down. "I've flown over three islands since breakfast!"

"Tell us!" Pip begs. "Tell us everything!"

But {hero_name} just swims. The ribbon hums.

Then, one dusk, the water below us turns dark as ink. Down, down, down goes a shadow — a leatherback turtle, huge as a grand piano, sinking toward a cold canyon where jellyfish glow like slow lanterns. We watch her go, our mouths open.

"She's going DOWN there?" Pip squeaks. "On PURPOSE?"

The ocean is deeper than we dreamed. And {hero_name} wears her home on her back, but she cannot hide inside it, not really. So she does the only thing there is to do.

She keeps swimming.

The ribbon pulls. We follow.

s4a.text:
And then, one bright morning, the blue runs out. The water turns green — green as grass, green as the inside of a lime, striped all over with ribbons of sunlight. Pip is the first to see it.

"Look! LOOK! The ribbon ends HERE!"

Below us, swaying slow as dancers, lies the meadow. Seagrass, miles and miles of it, waving in the current. And {hero_name} — old, steady {hero_name}, who swam a whole ocean without one wrong turn — puts her head down and eats. Munch. Munch. Like a great slow cow with flippers, after the longest walk to lunch in the world.

"So THAT'S the secret," Pip says at last, very quiet, which for Pip is nearly shouting. "The ribbon isn't tied to one place. It's tied to TWO. The nesting beach on one end, the meadow on the other — and she swims it. Again and again. Her whole life long."

We watch her graze, and the green light rocks us, and our bellies feel full just looking.

Before we go, {hero_name} noses down into the meadow sand and pushes up something small and smooth. A shell, white as the moon. She holds it out on one flipper.

"For you," Pip whispers. "So you remember the way."

We tuck it close. The ribbon hums behind us, already pulling her home. And someday, when the water turns green and the light comes down in stripes, we will know exactly where she is.

s4b.text:
But the meadow can wait. Because the ribbon pulls the other way too — and one night, when the seasons have turned and the stars have wheeled all the way around, {hero_name} lifts her head and smells the water.

"She's going BACK," Pip breathes. "Back, back, back — to the very same beach!"

The shore rises out of the dark, and the sand is cool, and the moon is up, and the beach — Pip swears it — the beach remembers her. It whispers welcome in a voice like small waves, because this is the patch of sand where {hero_name} hatched, long, long ago.

High above, Ferra circles down. "Stay behind me," she says, sharp wings folding. "Well above the tide line. That's where watchers stand."

So we stand where the sand is dry, and we watch. {hero_name} digs with her back flippers, slow and sure, scooping a nest shaped like a flask — narrow at the top, round at the bottom. And into it go the eggs. Pale. Round. Like the eggs the dinosaurs laid, long, long ago, on beaches not so different from this one.

"One hundred," Pip whispers. "One hundred little commuters, dreaming of the sea."

Before we leave, the beach gives us a gift: a warm handful of sand, cupped in our hands, still holding the day's sun.

"Take it," says Pip. "Both ends of the ribbon, tied to this one small place."

We carry it home. And under the sand behind us, the next crossing has already begun.

c1.question: "First leg of the commute, friends! Do we catch the fast river-in-the-sea and ride it like an escalator — or do we swing by the floating golden island first? I hear the tiniest turtle in the whole ocean is hiding there!"

options.label: Catch the great ocean current and ride the river inside the sea
Detour to the floating sargassum island to meet a brand-new hatchling

c2.question: "Here's the thing about the longest commute — it has TWO ends! Do we finish this leg and flop down in the green seagrass meadow for the biggest snack of our lives... or do we follow the ribbon the whole way back, back, back to the beach where Maris was born?"

options.label: Arrive at the sunny seagrass feeding grounds and rest after the crossing
Follow the ribbon all the way back to the nesting beach where Maris hatched

s1.text:
The dock smells of salt and tar and fish, and every ship in the harbor is getting ready to go somewhere. Ropes creak. Gulls argue overhead. We stand at the very end of the longest pier, where a small white boat bobs like it cannot wait one more minute.

"All aboard the water highway!" The voice arrives before the captain does — a great booming voice that makes the gulls stop arguing. Captain Marina sweeps off her hat and bows so low the hat nearly touches the dock. "You must be my crew. Today's current waits for no one."

"What current?" we ask. The sea looks like the sea. Blue, wavy, ordinary.

"Ah," says a quiet voice. Dr. Salma is kneeling on the deck, unrolling a map across her knees. On it, the ocean is dark and cold — and winding through it, painted in glowing blue, is a ribbon. A river. Inside the sea. We lean in close. "The Gulf Stream," she says. "Warm water, traveling. Stronger than every river on land poured together."

Something splashes beside the boat. A baby sea turtle, no bigger than a dinner plate, paddling in circles.

"He's waiting for his ride," says Dr. Salma. "The current carries turtles thousands of miles. It's a conveyor belt, and the whole planet rides it — heat, salt, travelers."

Captain Marina plants her boots wide and points out to sea with one sweeping arm. "The ribbon is out there right now, moving. We just have to find it."

"How do you find a river you can't see?" we ask.

"That," says Captain Marina, grinning, "is why I need a crew."

s2a.text:
"Follow the turtle!" we shout. "All aboard!" Captain Marina spins the wheel, and we chase a dinner plate with flippers. Pip paddles like he has somewhere to be. He does not look back once. "He knows," says Dr. Salma. "Watch."

We pass the mouth of a river, where the water swirls in two colors that will not mix. "Hold still," says Dr. Salma, and she dips a cup over the side. "Taste." One sip from the river side: cool, plain. One sip from the sea side: salt that makes our lips pucker. "Salinity," she says. "How much salt the water carries. The river has almost none. The ocean is loaded. The current knows the difference."

The water turns from green-blue to deep, bright blue, like someone pulled a curtain. The boat lifts. We are moving faster, and the engine is off. "We're on it!" Captain Marina booms. "The Gulf Stream! The little navigator found it!"

Pip stops paddling. He spreads his flippers and floats, and the current carries him like a moving walkway at the airport, except the walkway is warm and made of water and goes on for a thousand miles. We sail beside him, and the boat hums under our feet.

s2b.text:
"The color line!" we shout. Captain Marina's eyes go bright. "Full sail, shipmates!" She pulls a rope and the sail snaps tight, and the boat leans forward like a dog on a leash.

Dr. Salma stands at the bow, one hand shading her eyes. "There," she says. "Do you see it?" We squint. Far out, the water changes. On this side, green-blue, the color of shallow bathtubs. On the far side, deep sapphire, dark as a marble. A faint seam runs between them, wobbling like a line drawn in chalk.

"Warm water is clearer than cold water," says Dr. Salma. "The Gulf Stream carries almost no mud, no sand. Just heat and salt. That is why it looks so blue."

The seam gets closer. Closer. And then the boat gives a small lurch, like stepping onto an escalator, and suddenly we are gliding faster than the wind alone could push us. The water around us turns bright and clear, so clear we can see our own shadow on the surface, wobbling.

Two dolphins burst up beside the bow. They leap, splash down, leap again, riding the front of the boat like they have done this a hundred times. "They know the highway too!" Captain Marina laughs, and her laugh is louder than the wind.

s3.text:
"All aboard the water highway!" Captain Marina roars, and the little boat leaps forward.

The sea changes under us. One moment we are bouncing over ordinary waves — the next, the water turns smooth and swift, and the whole ocean seems to hurry beneath the hull. The glowing ribbon. We are riding it.

"Feel this," says Dr. Salma. She lowers a thermometer over the side on a long string, waits, then holds it up, dripping. "Bath-warm. This water left the Gulf of Mexico weeks ago, and it is carrying its warmth all the way to Europe. Like a conveyor belt that never stops."

We trail our fingers in the current. Warm. Truly warm, while the wind off the cold sea around us nips our ears.

"Sailors have ridden this river for hundreds of years," Captain Marina says, sweeping one arm along the horizon. "No sails needed. The sea does the work."

Something bobs alongside. {turtle_name}, paddling hard, then resting, letting the current carry him. His shell gleams. He looks at us as if to say — keep up.

"The loop he is on goes all the way around the ocean," says Dr. Salma. "A drop of water might travel a hundred years before it comes home."

A hundred years. We sit with that, rocking.

Then the air cools. The water darkens from blue to deep, deep slate. And ahead of us, rising off the sea like a wall, stands a great silver mist — the place where our warm ribbon meets the cold.

"There," whispers Dr. Salma. "What you found got us here. Now we see what's inside."

s4a.text:
"Into the mist," we say. Nobody shouts it. Even Captain Marina only nods, one slow nod, and turns the wheel.

The fog swallows the boat. The world goes soft and white and quiet — so quiet we can hear the water moving under us, swirling, whispering. Cool mist settles on our cheeks like tiny wet kisses.

Nobody says anything for a long moment. We just listen.

"This fog is born right here," whispers Dr. Salma at last, "where warm water kisses cold. The meeting makes the mist."

Then we see them. Beneath the boat, fish flash silver — hundreds, thousands, turning like one enormous coin spinning in the dark. We watch them turn. We do not say a word.

"The meeting stirs up food," Dr. Salma breathes. "The whole ocean comes to dinner."

We lean over the side and plunge one hand in. Warm. Cold. Warm again — swirls of both at once, curling round our fingers like the sea is stirring itself with a giant spoon.

Something bumps our knuckles. {turtle_name}! He pops up through the mist, riding the swirl, blinking at us as if to say — you came in! You came in!

Slowly the fog thins. Silver light breaks through, and Captain Marina swings the wheel. "The current points home, crew. All aboard!"

At the harbor, the Moon is rising, huge and orange. Dr. Salma points up at it. "That old Moon helps pull the tides," she says, "and the tides stir the very currents we rode today."

Then she presses something small and cool into our palm. A tiny glass float. "It measured the current for me for years. Now it is yours."

We hold it and say nothing. All the way home it stays warm in our pocket — like it remembers the ribbon.

s4b.text:
"Hold us here," we say, and Captain Marina plants her boots wide. "Edge of the mist it is. Best seats in the house!"

From the border, we can see everything. Fog rises off the water in slow curls, like the sea is breathing. Birds pour out of the white and dive, dive, dive. And at the surface, fish boil silver — thousands of them, churning the water where the currents stir up food.

"Now watch," says Dr. Salma. She lowers a clear tube into the sea, pulls it up, and holds it to the light. Inside, two waters swirl — and slowly, the heavier one sinks, sliding down through the lighter one like syrup through water in a glass.

"Salt," she says. "Salty water is heavier. It sinks — and that sinking helps push the deep currents along. The word for the saltiness is salinity. You cannot see it. But it moves the whole ocean."

We stare at the tube. Invisible salt, driving a river inside the sea.

A flipper waves at the edge of the mist. {turtle_name}, floating past, riding the ribbon out toward the open ocean — off on his hundred-year ride. We wave back. We wave and we wave, until the white takes him.

For a while nobody moves. The water laps at the hull, soft, and the mist goes on breathing without him.

Then Captain Marina turns the boat for home.

On the sail back we stop at a quiet beach, where the tide carries sand in and out, in and out. We float on our backs in the warm shallows, and the ocean holds us up like a hand.

Before we climb out, Dr. Salma presses something small into our palm. A tiny glass float. "It measured the current for me for years," she says. "Now it is yours."

We carry it home, still smelling of salt, and the float clicks softly in our pocket — like the sea saying goodbye.

c1.question: "The current's out there, shipmates, but it's invisible! So how do we find it — do we follow that little turtle, who looks like he knows the way, or do we chase the color line on the horizon, where the water changes from green to deep blue?"

options.label: Follow the baby turtle out to sea
Chase the color line on the horizon

c2.question: "Here it comes, crew — the meeting place, where warm water kisses cold! Do we drift right into the mist and feel it for ourselves, or hold at the edge where we can watch the whole swirling show?"

options.label: Drift into the mist and feel the meeting
Watch the swirling meeting from the calm edge

turtle_name.role: The name of the baby sea turtle who rides the current with us

stories.title: The River That Changed Its Mind

s1.text:
Ranger Ada hands us the binoculars before she even says good morning. "Look closer," she says. "The land is telling you something."

We are standing on a snowy hillside above the Lamar Valley, the three of us, our breath puffing out in little clouds. Below us the river curls through the valley in a lazy ribbon, bending this way and that, like it is in no hurry to get anywhere at all.

"Beautiful," we say.

"Mm," says Ada. She pulls a dented tin out of her coat pocket and pries it open. Inside are old photographs, soft at the corners. She holds one up against the real valley, right in front of our eyes.

And here is the strange thing. It is the same hillside. The same river. But in the photograph, the river runs almost straight, like somebody drew it with a ruler. The banks are bare. No willows, no trees leaning over the water, none of the shaggy green crowds of them that line the bends below us right now.

"That was taken here," Ada says. "Same spot. About seventy years ago."

We look at the photograph. We look at the valley. Straight river, bare banks. Curvy river, banks thick with willows.

"But rivers don't just... change," we say.

Ada smiles into her collar. She taps the photograph with one gloved finger. "This one did. It changed its mind. And nobody dug it a new path. Nobody asked it to move. The river did it all by itself."

Somewhere below, a raven croaks once, like it knows the answer and isn't telling.

"So here's the mystery," Ada says, tucking the tin away. "What makes a river change its mind?"

The wind comes up the valley, cold and clean, and the river bends and bends below us, keeping its secret.

s2a.text:
"Follow the wolves," we say, and Ada grins. "Then you'll want Dr. Moss. She reads snow the way you read a book."

Dr. Moss is waiting at the trailhead, already crouched over a line of tracks pressed into the white. "Wolf," she says, before we even ask. "Front paw, hind paw, front paw, hind paw. Look closer. See how the line stays straight? A wolf walks like it has somewhere to be."

We follow the tracks down into the valley, our boots crunching, the raven {raven_name} hopping along a fencepost beside us like he wants to see how this ends.

"There," Dr. Moss whispers, and points.

Across the snow, a wolf stands watching a herd of elk. Just watching. The elk are watching back. Nobody is running. Nobody is chasing. But the elk are bunched up tight near the trees, their ears swiveling, their whole bodies saying we are not staying here long.

"People think wolves change a valley by eating elk," Dr. Moss says. "But look closer. That wolf isn't eating anyone. She's just... there. And that's enough. The elk can't relax anymore. They can't stand in one spot by the river for weeks, munching every green thing down to the dirt. They keep moving. They stay near the forest, where they can duck away."

"So the wolves didn't eat the valley back," we say slowly. "They just made the elk nervous."

"Nervous enough to move," says Dr. Moss. "The elk changed first. Before a single tree grew back, before anything else — the elk changed how they walked through the world."

The wolf turns and trots away, and the whole herd shifts like one big animal, drifting toward the trees.

"But wait," we say. "If the elk just moved around... how did that make the river bend?"

Dr. Moss smiles. "Ask the trees."

s2b.text:
"The aspen grove," we say, and Ada nods like we picked the right door. "Up we go."

We climb above the valley floor, our breath coming faster, {raven_name} the raven gliding overhead from snag to snag. At the top of the slope, Ada stops. "Look closer," she says, and opens the dented tin again.

The photograph shows this exact hillside — bare. Just stubble and dirt and a few chewed-down sticks.

But the hillside in front of us is crowded with young aspen trees, taller than we are, their leaves trembling gold in the wind even though there is barely any wind at all. Aspens shiver like that. They tremble at almost nothing.

"Same spot," Ada says. "Fifty years between. So what happened?"

We look at the photograph. We look at the trees. "The elk stopped eating them?"

"Half right," Ada says. "The elk stopped *lingering*. Before the wolves came back, elk would stand down by that river all winter long, nibbling every willow shoot, every baby aspen, down to nothing. A tree never had a chance. But once the wolves returned, the elk got careful. They kept moving. They stayed near the forest edges. And the little trees by the river —" she sweeps her arm across the grove — "got to grow up."

"So the wolves changed the elk, and the elk changed the trees," we say. "Like a ripple in a pond."

"A ripple effect," Ada says, pleased. "That's exactly the word for it."

We touch one of the aspens, its bark smooth and pale under our fingers, and the leaves shiver above us like quiet applause.

"But Ada," we say. "Trees don't make rivers curve. So what happened next?"

Ada tucks the tin away. "Now," she says, "you need to meet the engineers."

s3.text:
The raven circles once more, then drops low over the water, and we follow it downstream to where the banks grow soft and green. Ada crouches in the mud and points. Sticks. Dozens of them, piled in a messy heap, each one chewed to a point at both ends, like pencils sharpened by someone with very strong teeth.

"Beavers," Ada says. "Look closer."

We look closer. The sticks are fresh, the wood still pale and wet. And just past the pile, the water slows. It spreads out wide and calm, pooling behind a dam of mud and branches, and the whole stream seems to take a deep breath and settle.

"What did you find back there?" Ada asks, tapping her tin. "Whatever it was, it led you here. Same as it led us." She doesn't wait for an answer. She never does. "The beavers came back because the willows came back. The willows gave them food and building sticks. And the beavers built dams, and the dams slowed the water, and the slowed water let the river bend."

We stare at the dam. A beaver is out there somewhere, probably adding one more stick right now, doing its small work, changing everything.

"So the river didn't change its mind on its own," we say slowly.

"No," Ada says. "Something changed it for them. Something that started the whole chain."

The raven lands on a bare branch above the dam and croaks, once, like it has been waiting for us to catch up.

Ada stands and brushes the mud off her knees. "One more piece," she says. "The first piece. The one that started the ripple." She looks at us, and her eyes are bright. "Are you ready to see it?"

s4a.text:
The raven doesn't wait. It lifts off the branch and flies up the valley, and we follow, scrambling over the snowy bank, our boots crunching in the cold.

It leads us to a rise above the river, where the snow is trampled and red. A wolf kill. An elk, half-eaten, lying in the willows. And there, perched right on the ribcage, is a golden eagle, huge and unbothered, tearing at the meat with its hooked beak.

We freeze. Ada puts a hand on our shoulder. "Look closer," she whispers.

We look closer. The eagle isn't alone. Three ravens hop in the snow nearby, impatient, waiting their turn. One of them is our raven. It croaks, once, like it's saying hello.

"The wolves did this," Ada says. "They hunted. They ate. And now they're feeding everyone else."

We watch. The eagle eats. The ravens wait. A magpie lands, bold as anything, and snatches a scrap. Further off, a coyote sits in the trees, patient, knowing its turn will come.

"One hunt," Ada says, "feeds dozens. The eagles, the ravens, the magpies, the coyotes, the foxes, even the beetles under the snow. That's the food web. And the wolves—" she taps her tin, "—the wolves are the keystone species. The one that holds the whole arch up."

We stare at her. "The arch?"

She kneels in the snow and builds it with her hands: a little curve of stones, one at the top. "Pull the keystone out," she says, and she does, and the stones tumble. "Put it back," and she does, and the arch holds. "That's the wolves. Take them away, and everything falls. Bring them back, and everything holds."

The raven croaks again, and this time it sounds like laughter.

s4b.text:
We follow Ada back to the ranger station, our legs tired, our heads full. The raven comes too, gliding above us all the way, like it wants to see how the story ends.

The station is small and warm, with a woodstove in the corner and photographs pinned all over one wall. Ada goes straight to the wall and points. "Look closer," she says, one more time.

It's the same river. The same bends we saw from the hillside. But this photograph is new, taken from the air, and the river doesn't just bend — it loops, it curls, it wanders like a lazy ribbon dropped on the floor. And all along the bends, little ponds glint in the sun. Beaver ponds. Dozens of them.

"Even the scientists were surprised," Ada says. "They knew the wolves would change the elk. They didn't know the elk would change the willows, the willows would change the beavers, and the beavers would change the river itself. That's the ripple effect. One change, touching everything."

We look at the old photograph, the straight river, the bare banks. We look at the new one, the curves, the ponds, the green. Same river. Different mind.

"The wolves are the keystone species," Ada says. "The one that holds the arch. Take them out, and it all tumbles. Put them back, and it all holds."

Before we leave, Ada walks us down to the stream behind the station. She crouches at the bank and picks up a small smooth stone, grey and round, worn soft by the water. She presses it into our hand.

"For your pocket," she says. "So you remember. One small thing can change everything."

We close our fingers around the stone. It's still warm from her hand.

The raven croaks once from the roof, and we look up, and it's gone.

c1.question: "The elk changed first — but do you want to follow the wolves to see how they did it, or climb to the aspen grove to see what grew back when the elk moved on?"

options.label: Follow the wolf tracks with Dr. Moss
Climb to the aspen grove with Ranger Ada

c2.question: "The river bends because of the beavers, the beavers build because of the willows, the willows grow because the elk moved, and the elk move because of the wolves. One last choice: do you want to see where the raven is leading us, or return to the ranger station to see the whole picture?"

options.label: Follow the raven to the wolf kill site
Return to the ranger station for the full picture

raven_name.role: What we call the raven who keeps appearing at the edges of the story

stories.title: The Robot Who Learned to Say I'm Not Sure

s1.text:
I was there the day a robot named {robot_name} learned to say it wasn't sure. And I promise you, nobody clapped harder than my grandpa, who does not trust robot cars one little bit.

The school gym didn't look like a gym anymore. Tape lines on the floor. Cardboard boxes everywhere, like a maze for a very confused mouse. And that hot, sharp smell of solder — Grandpa says it smells like burnt toast, and he's not wrong.

{coder_name} — that's me — was down on my knees, watching {robot_name} roll through the practice course all by itself. No remote. No help. Autonomous, which is a big word that just means: the robot decides.

Left at the chair. Around the bucket. Stop at the stuffed bear.

Perfect. Every time.

"Hm," said Grandpa Osei, behind me.

Grandpa's "hm" is never just a hm. It's a whole sentence wearing a small hat.

"What?" I said. "It's doing great."

"It is doing great," he agreed, in his warm, rumbly voice, "at doing the same thing over and over." He folded his arms. "But tell me this. When your robot is confused — when its eyes see one thing and its ears hear another — what does it do then?"

I opened my mouth. Nothing came out.

Because here's the thing about a robot: it only knows what you told it. If this, then that. And I had never told {robot_name} what to do when this and that didn't match.

"One hour to the regional final," Grandpa said, checking his watch. "Plenty of time."

On top of {robot_name}, a little yellow light blinked. The one I'd taped over because it looked silly. The one that meant: I NEED HELP.

I looked at it. It blinked back.

Maybe it wasn't silly after all.

s2a.text:
"Better eye," I said. "Fastest fix. The camera's the one that lied."

So we trusted it. I cleaned the lens. I bumped the confidence setting way up, so the camera had to be *really* sure before {robot_name} moved. Priya raised an eyebrow, but the clock said twenty minutes, and the camera was all we had time for.

First heat. The gym went quiet in that buzzing way, like a fridge full of whispers.

{robot_name} rolled out. Left at the chair. Around the bucket. Smooth as butter on warm toast.

Then it met the trash bag.

Somebody had dropped a big black garbage bag right in the middle of the course — an edge case, the judges called it, which means a surprise the rules forgot to mention. And here is the thing about cameras: they see light. Black plastic drinks light. It swallows it whole. So the camera looked at that bag and saw... nothing. Empty floor. A clear road.

{robot_name} drove straight into it. Not fast. Confidently. Like it was greeting an old friend.

*Bonk.*

The bag fell over. {robot_name} kept driving, wheels spinning, pushing the bag across the floor like a very slow bulldozer with a very dark secret.

The gym laughed — not mean. The way you laugh when a dog wears a hat.

Grandpa Osei leaned down. "Your robot's eyes did not lie," he said. "They told the truth about light. You just asked them the wrong question."

I stared at the little yellow light on top of {robot_name}, blinking away under its tape.

A sensor doesn't see the world. It sees one kind of thing. And every kind of thing has a different way of being wrong.

"Okay," I said, pulling out my laptop. "New plan."

s2b.text:
"The camera can't be trusted alone," I said. "So we swap. Ultrasonic."

Priya nodded. "Ears instead of eyes."

The ultrasonic sensor works like a bat. It shouts a sound too high for us to hear, then listens for the echo. Close thing, quick echo. Far thing, slow echo. No light needed. No black-bag trick.

I rewrote the code in twelve minutes flat. If echo comes back fast, then stop. Simple. Clean. Done.

Second heat. {robot_name} rolled out.

Left at the chair. Around the bucket. Past the spot where the trash bag had been —

*SCREECH.*

{robot_name} slammed its brakes so hard it rocked on its wheels like a nervous shopping cart.

Nothing there. Nothing in the way. Just a paper banner hanging from the ceiling, three feet above the course, saying GO ROBOTS GO in glittery letters.

The banner swayed. The echo bounced. The sensor heard: SOMETHING. And my code said: if something, then stop. Forever. There was no "then" for a banner that wasn't in the way.

{robot_name} sat there. Beeping. Stuck.

Beep. Beep. Beep.

The gym giggled. My face went hot as a soldering iron.

Grandpa Osei crouched beside me, his knees cracking like bubble wrap. "So," he said. "First it saw nothing where something was. Now it sees something where nothing is." He tapped the robot's shell. "You didn't fix the problem. You traded it."

He was right. One sensor, one blindness. Swap the sensor, swap the blindness.

The yellow light blinked under its tape. I NEED HELP.

One heat left. And neither eye nor ear alone could do it.

s3.text:
So we tried it. New code in, breath held, {robot_name} back at the start line.

Left at the chair. Around the bucket. And then —

Beep. Beep. Beeeep.

{robot_name} stopped dead in the middle of the course, little yellow light blinking like crazy, and would not move again. Not for anything.

"Both eyes said go," I groaned, flopping down at the repair table. "Both of them. Together. How can two answers agree and still be wrong?"

Grandpa Osei pulled up a chair. "Two wrong answers can shake hands," he said. "Happens all the time."

"But the battery's dead too," I said, prying it loose. "Ten minutes before the final. Perfect."

"Dead battery, live brain," Grandpa said. "Use the one you brought."

A girl from the next table leaned over. Priya, from the rival team, all elbows and safety goggles. "You're the obstacle-detection team, right? What did you two just find out there?"

I told her — well, I told her the shape of it. That we'd fixed one thing and found a worse thing hiding behind it.

She grinned like I'd handed her a present. "I invent edge cases for fun," she said. "That's the stuff nobody imagines until it happens. My team keeps a list. We call it the Doom List."

"A list," I said. "You can't list everything."

"Nope," she agreed happily. "That's the fun part."

Grandpa Osei had been quiet through all of this, turning the dead battery over in his big hands. Now he looked up, and asked the question he'd clearly been saving.

"So. When the thing doesn't know — when its eyes and its ears and its whole list all fail at once — what does it do?"

Priya opened her mouth. Closed it.

I opened mine. Closed it.

Nobody had an answer.

And sitting there, with the gym buzzing and the clock ticking, I realized that was the answer.

Nobody had ever told {robot_name} what to do when it didn't know.

The yellow light blinked on top of the robot. Patient. Waiting.

I looked at Grandpa. Grandpa looked at me.

"We have ten minutes," he said, "and I think you finally know what to build."

s4a.text:
I flipped open the laptop. My fingers knew what to type before my brain did.

If the eyes disagree — if they disagree by too much — then slow down. Slow to a crawl. Light the lamp. Wait for a human.

"A fail-safe," I said. "When it doesn't know, it stops pretending."

Grandpa read it over my shoulder. "Hm," he said. But this hm sounded proud.

Priya was watching from her table. "Your robot's going to be slow," she said. Not mean. Just true.

"I know," I said.

The whistle blew. Final heat. {robot_name} rolled to the line, yellow light bare for everyone to see. No tape this time.

Left at the chair. Around the bucket. Then — the mirrored tile, the one that had fooled every robot all day.

{robot_name} stopped. The light went on. Blink. Blink.

The whole gym went quiet. Somebody laughed — one short laugh, then swallowed it.

And then {robot_name} began to creep. Slow as syrup. Slow as a turtle in no hurry at all. Past the tile. Around the bear. Across the line.

Last place. By a mile.

The head judge walked over, and she was smiling. "Fastest robot didn't finish," she said. "Yours did — because it knew what to do when it didn't know." She held up the design prize. "This is the one we'd trust on a real road."

The gym erupted. Grandpa Osei clapped loudest of all, big hands like thunder.

"I trust this robot," he announced to anyone who would listen, "because it says so when it's confused!"

Later, we taped the little yellow light onto the trophy. Not over it. Onto it. Right on top, where everyone could see.

It blinked all the way home in Grandpa's car. The one he drives himself. For now.

s4b.text:
I looked at Priya. Priya looked at me.

"Twenty minutes," I said. "Doom List plus fail-safe?"

"Obviously," she said, already dragging her chair over.

We typed like the clock was personally insulting us. Her edge cases — the mirrored tile, the wobbly bridge, the chair that isn't quite where the map says — poured into my code like soup into a bowl. My rule wrapped around the whole thing: when the answers disagree by too much, slow to a crawl, light the lamp, flag a human.

"This shouldn't work," Priya said happily, slamming the battery in. "Two teams, one robot, no time."

"Autonomous," Grandpa said, "means the robot decides. You two finally decided something first."

The whistle blew. {robot_name} rolled out wearing both schools' colors — Priya had stuck her team's sticker on its side, crooked, and neither of us fixed it.

Left at the chair. Around the bucket. Then the mirrored tile, gleaming like a lie.

{robot_name} slowed. Stopped. The yellow light came on. Blink. Blink.

The gym held its breath.

Then the little robot crept forward — slow as honey, sure as sunrise — past the tile, over the bridge, around the bear, across the line.

Not the fastest. The only one that finished clean.

The noise in that gym. Priya screamed and hugged me and then pretended she hadn't. Grandpa Osei was on his feet, clapping like thunder, shouting, "It said so! It said so when it was lost!"

The judges gave us the design prize — both teams, one trophy, first time ever.

That evening, Grandpa leaned on the doorframe. "Well," he said. "Can I get a ride home in the car that admits when it's lost?"

"It's a toy rover, Grandpa."

"A man can practice," he said.

Priya's dead battery sits on our shelf now, both schools' initials Sharpied on the side. Useless. Priceless. The thing that reminded us: nobody knows everything. That's what friends are for.

c1.question: Priya leans over the pit table and says, "Your camera just told you a lie and your robot believed it. So which do you fix first — give it a better eye, or teach it what to do when its eyes argue?"

options.label: Swap in the ultrasonic distance sensor and trust it instead
Keep the camera — clean the lens and make it be really sure before it moves

c2.question: Grandpa Osei taps the laptop and says, "You've got twenty minutes. Do you make this robot careful all by itself — or do you and that girl stop pretending you're rivals and build the careful thing together?"

options.label: Write the fail-safe rule alone so the team's own work stands on its own
Merge code with Priya — her edge cases, their fail-safe — and enter as allies

coder_name.role: The kid protagonist who wrote the obstacle-detection code

s1.text:
On my windowsill there is a row of stones, and every one of them is a story. There is a flat grey skipping stone, a pebble with a stripe clean around its middle, and at the end, in its own egg-carton box, a pale rock so light it feels like a trick. That one is called {rock_name}. Here is how it got its name.

I was nine that summer, and I spent it on a black-sand beach with Nina, who collected rocks the way other people collect stickers, and her dog Biscuit, who collected sticks the way other people collect absolutely everything. Biscuit charged driftwood. Biscuit charged seaweed. Biscuit charged his own shadow once, and won.

The sand was black because the whole beach was old volcano, Nina told me, crushed up fine as pepper.

We were squatting at a rock pool, dropping pebbles in. Plip. Plip. Every single one went straight to the bottom, the way rocks do. Then Biscuit came galloping up with a pale stone in his mouth, dropped it at my feet, and nose-bopped it into the pool. Bonk.

It bobbed.

It sat on top of the water like a cork in a bath, and Biscuit barked at it, and it bobbed some more.

"No," said Nina, in the voice she saved for excellent things. "Rocks sink. Everybody knows rocks sink. {child_name}, why is that rock floating?"

s2a.text:
"Closely," I said. "Really, really closely."

Nina marched us down the beach to the family with the windbreak and the big umbrella, the ones who always had everything. She came back holding a magnifying glass the size of a dinner plate.

"Borrowed," she said, and flopped down on the sand. "Look."

I held the glass over the pale stone. And we both went very quiet.

It was covered in holes. Hundreds of them. Tiny pinprick holes, so small you could not fit a crumb in one, squashed up against each other until the whole rock looked like a sponge that had turned to stone.

"Bubbles," Nina breathed. "Somebody put bubbles in a rock."

I rubbed it with my thumb. It was scratchy, like a stiff dry sponge, the kind that scrapes the porridge pot. Scratch, scratch.

Biscuit wanted a look too. He shoved his nose right up against the holes, sniffed hard, and sneezed so violently he blew the rock clean off my knee. Then he sneezed again. Then he sneezed at his own sneeze, and we laughed so much we had to lie down on the peppery sand.

When we sat up, Nina opened her notebook and wrote, in big letters: CLUE ONE. HOLES.

"A rock full of holes would be light," she said slowly. "Like a sponge. Like bread." She tapped her pencil. "But {child_name}. Holes mean bubbles. And bubbles mean air. How does air get inside a hot melted rock?"

Biscuit sneezed at the rock again, as if to say, exactly.

s2b.text:
"Weigh it," I said. "Properly. With numbers."

Nina's eyes went round with delight, because Nina brings a kitchen scale everywhere. To the beach. To birthdays. Once, famously, to the dentist. She dug it out of the picnic basket from under the sandwiches and set it on a flat rock like a scientist in a film.

"First, a normal rock," she said.

She picked up a black pebble, the same size as our floater, and plopped it on the scale. The numbers spun and settled.

"Now the mystery."

She lifted the pebble off and put the pale stone on. We leaned in. The numbers wobbled, thought about it, and stopped.

"Half," Nina whispered. "{child_name}, it's barely half the weight. A rock this big should feel like a potato, and it feels like a bread roll."

Biscuit decided this was his moment to help. He put one paw firmly on the scale, and the numbers shot up and went wild, and he looked at us as if to say, you're welcome.

"Biscuit. Off."

Off he got, extremely pleased with himself.

Nina opened her notebook and wrote, in big letters: CLUE ONE. LIGHT. Suspiciously light.

She underlined suspiciously three times.

"So it's true," she said. "It's not a trick. It's really, properly light." She tapped her pencil, frowning. "But that doesn't tell us why. Rocks don't go on diets. Something made this one light, and I want to know what."

s3.text:
Biscuit, who had been watching all this with his head on one side, decided that science was taking far too long. He trotted to a bare patch of sand and began to dig. Sand flew. Sand fountained. Biscuit dug like a tiny furry excavator with somewhere important to be, and Nina and I leaned in, because when Biscuit dug, he usually found something, even if it was only a bigger hole.

"Woof," said Biscuit, in the voice he saved for excellent things.

There, at the bottom of the hole, sat a second stone. Nina lifted it out and whistled. It was black as the inside of a pocket, glassy and cold, without a single hole in it, and so shiny I could see my own face in it, all smudged and wobbly, like a reflection in a spoon.

"No holes," Nina said. "Not one. Feel how heavy."

She was right. It sat in my hand like it meant it. Nina took the pale rock in her other hand and held both arms out like a balance scale. Up went one side, down went the other. Up, down. Up, down.

"Same beach," she said slowly. "Total opposites. One floats and fizzes with holes. One's a lump of black glass."

"What did you two find over there?" called a voice. Ranger Jo, who led the lava-flow walk, came crunching across the sand in her big boots. She crouched, turned the black stone over, tapped the pale one with a fingernail, and grinned the way grown-ups grin when they know something delicious.

"Well, well," she said. "Obsidian and pumice. Here's the funny part, rock hunters. These two came from the very same eruption. Same volcano. Same blast of lava."

Nina's mouth fell open. Mine too. Biscuit barked at both rocks, just to be thorough.

"But they disagree about everything," Nina said. "How can one eruption make two rocks that don't even act like cousins?"

s4a.text:
"Up," said Nina. "Definitely up. I want to stand where it happened."

Ranger Jo led us up the cinder path, which crunched under our boots like breakfast cereal. Biscuit charged every switchback. "Firm trail here," said Ranger Jo, tapping it with her boot. "Step where I step."

At the top, she stopped. "Now then. You two just found something on this beach. This is where it started." She pointed at a pale, frothy cap of rock along the rim. "Lava fizzes, like a shaken fizzy drink. All that gas got trapped as bubbles, and then the lava cooled and froze the fizz mid-pop. That's pumice. The holes are the bubbles."

Nina held {rock_name} up beside it. Same froth. Same pinprick holes, like the bubbles at the top of a glass of lemonade, only stone.

"And your obsidian?" Ranger Jo pointed to the flow's edge, where the lava had met air and sea. "Cooled so fast it turned to glass. No time for bubbles. No time for anything."

"So the rock tells you," I said slowly, "how the lava behaved."

"The holes, the colour, the weight," said Ranger Jo. "That's the lava's handwriting."

Biscuit barked at the whole volcano, just to be thorough.

Back home, Nina wrote the label for the egg-carton box: {rock_name} — the rock that floats. And it sits on my windowsill still, pale and holey and full of frozen fizz, next to a stone so light it feels like a trick. Because it is one. The lava's best one.

s4b.text:
"The museum," said Nina. "I want to test them properly."

The museum room was small and cool and smelled of old wood. A volunteer named Fern brought out a tank of water, and her eyes twinkled. "Drop it in, then."

Nina lowered {rock_name} into the water. It floated. It bobbed gloriously on the surface like the tiniest boat, and Biscuit barked at it so hard his ears flapped.

"Now this," said Fern, and she brought out a piece of obsidian in two careful hands. "Glass, this one. Hold it flat in your palm, like me." She showed us, and we did, and the black stone lay in Nina's hand, heavy as a secret, shining like a dark mirror.

Then Fern slid a big magnifier over the pumice, and we leaned in. The holes swam up huge — hundreds of tiny bubbles, frozen mid-fizz, like the top of a fizzy drink stopped in time. "The lava fizzed," said Fern, "and the gas got trapped as bubbles before it could pop. Light, holey pumice. But lava that cools in a flash has no time for bubbles at all. Heavy, shiny obsidian."

Nina wrote in her notebook, her tongue between her teeth: "The texture, the colour, the weight — that's the lava's own handwriting."

Fern set one more stone beside them with a wink. "This one fell from the sky. Do you think it tells its story the same way?"

But that is another story. On my windowsill, {rock_name} still floats in its egg-carton box, keeping its secrets politely.

c1.question: "Every good mystery needs a first clue," Nina says, flipping her notebook open. "Do we look at this rock really, really closely — or do we measure how heavy it actually is?"

options.label: Inspect the stone with a magnifying glass
Test it on Nina's trusty kitchen scale

c2.question: Ranger Jo taps the two stones in Nina's palms. "The answer to this is written in two places. Shall we climb up to where the lava actually did it — or would you rather test these two properly at the museum table?"

options.label: Walk the old lava flow with Ranger Jo
Head to the museum's geology table

child_name.role: The storyteller's childhood self in the tale — the name Nina calls across the beach

rock_name.role: The nickname Nina gives the floating pumice, used playfully through the story and written on its egg-carton label at the end

s1.text:
Rain on the window. Nowhere to go. So I did what any genius does on a Saturday: I made a movie.

I sprawled on the bed, propped the phone against a lamp, and hit record. My little sister Jun was already laughing, because the plan was stupid. The plan was this: film the tablet in slow motion while it played her favourite cartoon, then watch it back and laugh at how the characters moved like sleepy snails.

"Action!" I shouted.

Jun made the tablet dance. The cartoon bounced. We cracked up.

Then we watched the video.

"Wait," Jun said. "Go back."

I rewound. We watched again.

There. Rolling across the screen, slow and dark, like waves made of shadow. Bands. Big ones. Moving from top to bottom, steady as a heartbeat.

"Is that on the tablet?" I asked.

Jun looked at the real screen. "No. It's just the cartoon."

She was right. The tablet looked totally normal. Bright, smooth, no bands anywhere.

But in the video? Bands. Clear as anything.

"Film it again," Jun said.

I did. Same thing. Dark stripes rolling through the picture, like the screen was hiding something and the camera caught it.

"Try my phone," Jun said.

I filmed her phone. Bands.

I filmed the laptop. Bands.

Every screen in the room had them. But only on camera. Not in real life. Not when we just looked.

Jun sat up very straight. "Okay," she said. "Why can the camera see something we can't?"

I stared at her.

She stared at me.

I grabbed the phone and shoved it in my pocket. "Come on," I said. "We're going to see Bex."

Because when something weird happens, and nobody has an answer, there's only one person who treats it like a case. Cousin Bex. Repair shop. Detective of broken things.

And this? This was definitely a case.

s2a.text:
The repair shop smelled like warm plastic and bubble gum. Bex was already waiting, feet up on the counter, chewing like a detective in an old movie.

"{hero_name}," they said, twirling a screwdriver. "You look like you found a ghost in your sandwich."

"Worse," I said. "Bands. On every screen. But only on camera."

Bex's boots hit the floor. Thunk. "Jun, get the evidence bag. {hero_name}, you're officially on the case. This is now {case_number}. The Rolling Bands."

They stamped it on a sticky note. THWACK. Then they swung the big magnifying lamp over a cracked-open monitor, the kind with its guts hanging out. The lens was round as a dinner plate.

"You want to know what a screen is made of?" Bex said. "Look."

I leaned in. Jun squished beside me. Under the glass, a plain white patch of screen was not white at all. It was stripes. Tiny stripes, crammed shoulder to shoulder. Red. Green. Blue. Red. Green. Blue. Like a million miniature Popsicles lined up in the world's tidiest freezer.

"Whoa," Jun whispered.

"Three little lights," Bex said. "That's the whole trick. Your eye mushes them together from far away, so you see white. But up close?" They tapped the glass. "A tiny light parade."

They grabbed a dial on the lamp's control box and turned it. The red stripes dimmed. The green and blue got brighter. The white patch turned purple. Then orange. Then a green so bright it looked like alien grass.

"Millions of colors," Bex said, "from three tiny flashlights. That's graphics for you. It's not paint. It's not ink. It's light, pretending."

Jun's eyes went huge. "So the bands... they're made of light too?"

Bex froze. Slowly, they tapped the sticky note. "Clue one, detective. Screens are tiny lights. But your bands are moving. And lights don't move unless something tells them to."

They handed me the magnifying glass. It was heavier than it looked.

"So," Bex said. "What's telling them?"

s2b.text:
Monday morning, I cornered Ms. Okafor in the computer lab before the bell even rang. She was wiping fingerprint smudges off a monitor with a cloth that looked older than me.

"Ms. Okafor," I said, "can a camera see something your eyes can't?"

She didn't even blink. "Finally," she said, "a good question."

She dug through a drawer full of tangled cables and dried-out markers, then pulled out two things: a little flipbook with a corner chewed by time, and a round plastic drum with slits cut in the side.

"Watch," she said.

She flipped the book slow. A stick figure lifted one arm. Page. Page. Page. Obviously just drawings. Boring.

Then she flipped it fast.

The stick figure waved at me. Smooth as anything. Like it was alive and glad to see me.

"Whoa," I said.

"Your eyes and your brain," Ms. Okafor said, "are lazy. In a good way. Show them still pictures fast enough, and they mush everything together into motion. They can't help it. They fill in the gaps."

She spun the drum. It was a zoetrope, she said. Inside, tiny horses galloped in a circle, legs blurring into a smooth run, over and over, forever.

"So the bands," I said slowly, "maybe they're not on the screen at all. Maybe they're a speed thing."

Ms. Okafor pointed at me like I'd just won a prize. "Now you're thinking. Your eyes blend fast things. A camera doesn't blend the same way. It catches slices. Freezes them. So if the screen is doing something fast enough to trick your eyes..."

"...the camera might catch it in the act," I finished.

She grinned and spun the zoetrope again. The little horses ran and ran.

"Clue one," I said, mostly to myself. "The bands aren't a thing. They're a speed."

Ms. Okafor flipped the book one more time. The stick figure waved goodbye.

"Go find out what your screen is doing," she said, "when it thinks nobody's watching."

s3.text:
The repair shop smelled like hot solder and lemon wipes. Bex had the lab table cleared, magnifying glass on a string, the works. Ms. Abernathy from school was there too, because Bex had phoned her and said, quote, bring the kid who pays attention.

"{case_number}," Bex announced, tapping a clipboard. "Status update. Tell me what you found."

So we told her. All of it. Jun waved the magnifying glass while I talked, and Ms. Abernathy nodded like she'd been waiting for this exact Saturday her whole life.

"Good," Bex said. "So we've got two facts. Fact one." She held up one finger. "Every screen is a grid. Millions of tiny squares, and each square is three even tinier lights. Red, green, blue. Mix those three, you get every color there is."

She passed the magnifying glass to Ms. Abernathy, who held it over her own phone. "Fact two," the teacher said. "A screen isn't one steady picture. It's still pictures, flipped fast. Sixty complete redraws every second. That's the frame rate. Your eye mashes them together and calls it motion."

"The camera catches the in-between," Bex said. "We don't. That's the whole trick."

I felt the answer getting close, the way you feel a sneeze coming.

Then Jun, who had been quietly poking the magnifying glass at a paused cartoon on the counter tablet, looked up.

"Okay but," she said. "How does each little light know what color to be?"

Nobody answered.

Bex froze. Ms. Abernathy froze. The shop's ancient clock ticked.

"Millions of lights," Jun went on, "sixty times a second, and they all just... know?"

Bex slowly set down the clipboard. "{hero_name}," she said, very serious, "the case is half-solved. We know what the screens are doing. We do not know who's giving the orders."

"There's one witness left," Ms. Abernathy said. "Someone who makes screens draw things for a living."

Bex was already grabbing her coat. "A graphics programmer. And I know exactly which one."

s4a.text:
The graphics programmer lived above a bakery, and her name was Paz. Bex knocked twice, then once more, like a code.

"{case_number}," Paz said, opening the door. "Bex texted me. I've been waiting all afternoon to show off."

Her living room was one enormous desk. On it: a racing game, frozen mid-turn. A red car hung in the air over a jump, perfectly still.

"One frame," Paz said. "Caught like a bug in amber. Look closer."

She handed me the magnifying glass. I pressed it to the monitor. There they were. Three tiny lights, red, green, blue, hiding inside every shadow, every tire, every speck of dust the car was kicking up. The whole world of the game, made of the same three lights.

"Now the fun part." Paz tapped a key. Numbers filled a side window, long columns, scrolling. "Every pixel has numbers in memory. Red, how much. Green, how much. Blue, how much. The graphics system reads them, sets the lights, done. One frame."

She tapped again. The car moved. Barely. A nudge forward.

"New numbers. New frame." Tap. Nudge. Tap. Nudge. "Sixty of these every second. Your eyes can't catch the swap, so your brain shouts motion."

"Sixty?" Jun whispered. "That's not fast. That's showing off."

"And my camera?" I asked.

"Your camera has its own grid of light-catchers, and it snitched. It caught the screen mid-repaint, top to bottom. That's your rolling bands. Case closed, Bex."

Bex clicked her pen like a gavel. "{case_number}: closed." She pressed something small into my hand. A pin. One salvaged pixel tile, three dead lights under a coat of glue. "For the witness who asked the right question."

That night, Jun filmed the TV in slow motion on purpose, just to watch the secret bands roll by. "Wave," she told the screen. "We see you."

s4b.text:
"Back to the shop," Bex said. "We're doing this the fun way."

Saturday night, lights low, rain on the windows. Bex pulled a salvaged screen from a crate, hooked it to a test board with a fat silver dial, and set the magnifying glass on the table like a surgeon's tool.

"{case_number}, final experiment. This dial controls the refresh. How fast the screen repaints itself. Watch."

The screen glowed with a cartoon sunset, smooth and ordinary. Bex turned the dial one click.

Nothing.

Another click.

"There," Jun breathed.

A line of light crawled down the glass. Slow. Visible. The top of the sunset lit first, then the next row, then the next, each line of pixels waking up in order, red, green, blue, over and over. The bands. Our bands. Rolling down the screen in real life, no camera needed, because Bex had made the screen too slow to lie.

"Numbers come in from the board," Bex said, tapping it. "The screen reads them, sets each little light, row by row. At full speed it does the whole glass sixty times a second. Faster than your eyes. Faster than anyone's eyes."

"But not faster than my camera," I said.

"Your camera snitched," Bex said. "That's the whole case. The bands were never on the cartoon. They were the screen, caught red-handed, repainting."

She spun in her chair, pulled out a rubber stamp, and slammed it on the clipboard. "{case_number}: closed." Then she took one dead pixel tile from the salvaged screen, dabbed it with glue, and stuck it on a pin. "Wear it. You earned it."

We walked home through the rain, and every glowing window on the street looked different now. A million tiny lights, keeping one enormous secret, sixty times a second.

Jun held the magnifying glass up to a shop window and grinned. "We see you," she said.

c1.question: "Two doors, detective. We can go look at what a screen is made of, up close under my lamp, or we can go find out whether your own eyes are the ones playing the trick. Which thread do we pull first?"

options.label: Go to Bex's repair shop and put a broken screen under the magnifying lamp
Go to the school lab and test the flipbook and zoetrope with the media teacher

c2.question: "Okay, but there's one thingy left. Do you want to see a game freeze like a statue so you can catch it being painted, or do you want Bex to slow a whole screen down until it can't hide anymore?"

options.label: Visit the game-designer parent and catch a single frozen frame, then watch sixty frames a second run
Stay at the shop while Bex slows a salvaged screen's refresh until the repaint is visible

hero_name.role: The kid narrator's first name, used by Bex, the sibling, and the teacher throughout

case_number.role: The dramatic case number Bex assigns the mystery, recurring as a running joke

stories.title: The Rumble in the Back Row

s1.text:
"Stand here with me," says the percussionist. "The orchestra is waking up."

We are backstage at the concert hall, right in the middle of the warm-up, and it is the best kind of noise. A violin slides up and down like somebody stretching. A trumpet goes braap, then giggles and tries again. Somewhere a flute is running up and down the stairs of its notes, fast as a squirrel.

The percussionist lays out her instruments on a long table, smallest to biggest, like setting the table for dinner. Triangle. Tambourine. Two wooden sticks that go clack.

Then we feel it.

Rumble. Rumble.

A low sound rolls through the floor and up into our shoes. It is round and soft and enormous, like thunder that has learned to whisper.

"What is that?" we ask.

The percussionist stops. She listens. "Not mine," she says. "Not yet, anyway."

Rumble. Rumble.

We look around. Nobody is playing it. The trumpet player is laughing. The flute is still doing its stairs.

"It sounds like a Grumble-Boom," we say. Because it does. It sounds exactly like a {mystery_sound_name}.

From her pocket, the percussionist pulls out Pip, a small soft mallet with a fuzzy head, and pats him once. "A mystery," she says. "Good. I have ten minutes before the conductor's signal. Let's find your Grumble-Boom."

s2a.text:
"The strings first," says the percussionist. "Feel what a vibration really is. Then we will know if your Grumble-Boom is one."

The violinist smiles and holds out her violin. "Gentle fingertips," she says. "Right here, on the strings."

We rest our fingers on the thin strings, soft as whiskers. The bow slides. The strings buzz under our skin, fast and tickly, like a tiny bee trapped in honey.

"Now the wood," she says. We touch the round wooden body. It hums against our fingertips, warm and alive. "The strings make the buzz. The wood turns it into song."

Rumble. Rumble.

The floor shakes under our shoes. The tremble rolls up our legs and into our chests, slow and deep and enormous.

We pull our fingers back. "That is not a string," we say. "Strings buzz fast. This is slow. It is too big for a string."

The percussionist pats Pip's fuzzy head. "Good ears," she says. "Not strings. So your Grumble-Boom is hiding in a family we have not checked yet."

She looks toward the back of the stage, where the floor is still trembling. "Let's keep listening."

s2b.text:
"Up we go," says the percussionist. "The brass is loudest. If your Grumble-Boom is hiding there, we will hear it clear."

We climb the steps to the brass section. The trumpet player grins at us. "Want to hear how a trumpet really works?" he asks.

He puts his lips together and blows a raspberry. Pbbbt! We laugh. "That is the buzz," he says. "My lips do that, and the trumpet turns it into this."

He lifts the trumpet and plays a note so bright and golden it makes us jump. It rings off the ceiling like sunshine breaking through a window.

Rumble. Rumble.

The floor trembles under our feet. But the sound is not coming from the trumpet. It is coming from behind the brass, low and slow, rolling like a big soft wave.

"That is not you," we say.

The trumpet player shakes his head. "Nope. I buzz. That thing does not buzz. It just... booms."

The percussionist pats Pip's fuzzy head. "Not brass," she says. "So your Grumble-Boom is hiding behind the loudest family in the orchestra. Clever thing."

She points past the trumpets, toward the back row. "Let's go deeper."

s3.text:
Back at the long table, the percussionist is waiting for us. She pats Pip's fuzzy head once, because a clue has landed.

"Tell me what you found," she says.

We tell her. She listens all the way through, nodding slowly, and then she holds up one finger.

"Then here is the clue that changes it. Whoever makes your {mystery_sound_name} is sitting down. The instrument is taller than they are. And it has a round skin stretched across the top."

We think about that. No strings. No mouthpiece. Nobody blows.

"But there is a mallet," she says, and pats Pip again.

A skin. A mallet. Taller than a person.

Before we can guess, the conductor steps onto the podium. The warm-up noise melts away. The baton rises, and it points straight at the back row, behind the trumpets and trombones.

Boom.

The floor trembles. Our shoes tremble. And there it is, hiding in plain sight all along: two enormous copper bowls, each with a great round skin stretched across the top, and the skins are trembling exactly the way the floor did.

"The timpani," whispers the percussionist. "The biggest drums in the orchestra."

Pip gets a pat. A big one.

s4a.text:
"We'll stay," we say. "Right here."

The percussionist grins and pulls up a stool for us, small and low, right beside the great copper bowls. "Best seats in the house," she whispers. "The floor does half the listening for you."

The conductor's baton falls, and the music begins. Strings first, soft as rain on a window. Then the woodwinds, curling through like ribbons. The brass waits, shining and patient.

And then we feel it coming. Through the floor, through the stool, up into our knees. The timpani is about to speak.

Boom.

It arrives in our bodies before our ears catch it. The percussionist leans close. "Feel that? The drums don't just make noise. They wait. They listen. And when the moment is right, they answer."

Another boom. This one is quieter, tucked underneath the trumpets like a heartbeat under a song.

"That one answered," she whispers. "The one before led. Can you feel the difference?"

We can. One pushes the music forward. The other holds it up from below, like hands under something heavy and precious.

The piece rolls on, and the {mystery_sound_name} rolls with it, and we sit in the back row feeling every single one arrive through the floor like a message meant just for us.

When the last note fades, the percussionist presses Pip into our hands. His fuzzy head is warm from all the patting.

"Keep him," she says. "You know the sound now. You'll always know it."

We slip out past the empty seats, Pip tucked safe in our keeping, and the rumble follows us home. Not a mystery anymore. A friend.

s4b.text:
"The box," we say. "We want the box."

The conductor's eyes light up. She steps down and holds out her hand, and we climb onto the small wooden podium. The whole orchestra spreads out before us, every face turned our way. It is very quiet and very high.

"Two signals," the conductor murmurs. "That's all you need. Hand low and slow means soft. Hand high and big means loud. The rest is just listening."

We raise our hand slowly, palm down, low. The strings begin, barely breathing. The flutes join, thin as thread. We keep our hand low, and the whole orchestra stays small, a hundred musicians holding their music like a candle in the dark.

Then we lift. Higher. Bigger. The brass opens up, golden and bold. The woodwinds climb. Our hand goes higher still, and the sound rises with it, filling the hall like bread rising in a warm kitchen.

At the very top, the percussionist catches our eye. She raises her mallet. We nod.

The great skin of the timpani trembles under one enormous stroke, and the boom rolls through the podium, through our shoes, through everything.

Then we bring our hand down, slow, slow, and the whole orchestra follows us into silence. A real silence, the kind that rings.

The conductor takes both our hands. "The loudest moment in this hall," she says, "started with the smallest flick of your wrist."

As we go, the percussionist presses Pip into our palm. "For the keeper of the {mystery_sound_name}," she says.

We walk out past the empty seats, and the rumble follows us, low and warm, like a friend saying goodbye.

c1.question: "We could hunt this rumble two ways, you and I — do we put our fingertips on the strings and feel what a vibration really is, or do we climb up and listen where the brass is loudest?"

options.label: Visit the violinist and touch the strings to feel them vibrate
Head up toward the brass section to listen from close by
