c2.question: "The mystery's solved, friends — so how do we finish? Do we stay back here and ride out the whole first piece beside the big drum, or does someone want to stand on my box and wave the orchestra loud and soft?" — asked by the percussionist, with the conductor smiling nearby

options.label: Stay beside the timpani and feel the whole first piece through the floor
Stand on the conductor's box and lead one loud-and-soft moment

mystery_sound_name.role: The child's private name for the strange rumble, spoken whenever the sound appears

s1.text:
"Look what just came in," says Dr. Maya. She turns her screen toward you, and there it is — a brand-new picture from Mars.

The whole planet glows red. Not gray like the Moon. Not blue like Neptune. Red, like the last ember in a campfire.

"Every night, the other planets send pictures too," Dr. Maya says. "Gray rocks. Blue ice. But Mars?" She taps the screen. "Mars is red all over. The ground, the hills, even the sky is pinkish. And nobody has ever taken a picture that shows us why."

Far away on that red world, a little rover is waking up. His name is Rusty. He has six wheels, one long neck, and two camera eyes that swivel like an owl's.

Rusty looks left. Red dust. He looks right. Red rocks. He looks down at his own wheels — red! He is coated in the stuff, and it never washes off, because it never rains on Mars.

"Trundle, trundle," go his wheels across the rusty plain, and a speck of red dust lifts off the ground and rides the wind beside him.

Today, Dr. Maya has a job for Rusty. "Take a picture," she says, "that tells us the rusty secret of Mars."

Rusty's camera eyes blink. Where does a little rover even begin?

s2a.text:
"The tracks," you say. Dr. Maya grins. "Tracks it is."

Trundle, trundle. Rusty rolls to the rim of Thumbprint Crater, and there they are — wheel tracks, pressed into the red dust long, long ago.

"Another rover made these," Dr. Maya says softly. "It stopped working before you were built."

Rusty follows the tracks down, down, down, and the speck of red dust rides the wind after him. At the bottom sits the old rover, still and dusty, its camera eyes closed.

But its last pictures are still inside. Rusty plugs in a cable — click — and the pictures fly home to Earth.

Dr. Maya looks at the first one. Then the next. Her eyes go wide.

"These pictures are years and years old," she says. "Before the big dust storm. Before everything." She turns the screen toward you. "And look — the ground is red in every single one."

You lean in close. Red ground. Red rocks. Red, red, red.

"So the dust storm didn't make Mars red," you say.

"No," says Dr. Maya. "Mars was already red. The rusty secret is older than we thought."

The little speck of dust settles on the old rover's back, and stays.

s2b.text:
"The volcano," you say. Dr. Maya whistles. "Olympus Mons. The biggest volcano anybody knows."

Trundle, trundle. Rusty climbs the long, gentle slope — so gentle it takes all morning — and the speck of red dust rides the wind beside him, up and up.

At last, Rusty's camera eyes blink at something new. Dark rock, ropy and swirled, like thick porridge poured out and frozen mid-plop.

"Lava," Dr. Maya breathes. "It flowed here once, hot as soup on the stove. Now it's stone. Take the picture, Rusty."

Rusty lifts his long neck. Click.

But the picture comes back red. The lava rock is dark — the picture shows it red!

"Something's on your lens," Dr. Maya says. Rusty swivels one camera eye and looks at the other. There it is: one tiny speck of red dust, stuck to the glass. He wipes it with his little brush. Click again.

Now the rock is dark and true.

Dr. Maya taps her chin. "The dust isn't just on the ground. It floats in the air. It lands on everything — even a camera."

You look at the first red picture, then the clean dark one.

"Is that the secret?" you ask. "Is Mars red because the dust is everywhere?"

"Maybe," says Dr. Maya. "Maybe." And the little speck of dust rides the wind away, looking for somewhere new to settle.

s3.text:
"Come and see," says Dr. Maya. She lays the new picture on the table, right beside the ones from before. "What did you two find out there?"

You tell her. All of it.

She listens. She nods. Then she reaches into her desk drawer and pulls out something small and ordinary — an old nail, the kind you might find in a garden shed. It is not shiny. It is not gray. It is red.

"Watch," she says.

She holds the rusty nail up to the screen, right next to the red dust of Mars. You lean in close.

They are the same color. Exactly the same.

"The nail is made of iron," says Dr. Maya. "When iron sits out in the air long enough, it rusts — and rust is red." Her eyes go wide and bright. "And Mars is covered in iron. Every rock. Every hill. The whole planet rusted, long, long ago."

The rusty secret of Mars.

Far away, a little rover's camera eyes blink. The speck of red dust settles softly on his shoulder, like it has heard the answer too, and is glad somebody finally said it out loud.

s4a.text:
"Then let's wait," you say. "Let's see what story the storm leaves."

Far away on Mars, the wind begins to blow. It starts as a whisper, then a whoosh, then a great rumbling tumble of red dust that swallows Rusty whole. The sky turns orange. The sun shrinks to a pale coin, then vanishes completely.

Rusty does not panic. Rusty hunkers down. He tucks his camera eyes close, folds his solar wings, and waits, quiet as a stone. The dust storm whirls around him for one day, two days, three.

Then, slowly, the wind grows tired. The sky opens like a curtain. The pale coin of sun comes back, and Rusty shakes himself — dust flying off in red puffs.

"Look at his panels," Dr. Maya says, pointing. The dust has settled in swirls and stripes, like the lines in a fingerprint. "The wind painted a map on him. It shows us exactly where the storm blew."

You lean in. The red dust on Rusty's back tells the story of the whole storm, written in rust.

"Even the storm carries the secret," Dr. Maya says softly. "It's all the same red."

And far away, a little rover lifts his camera eyes to the sky, and takes a picture of the sun coming back.

s4b.text:
"Then let's look here," you say. "Let's find something on Earth that wears the same red."

You turn from the screen, and there — on the windowsill, small as your smallest fingernail — sits a ladybug. Red shell. Dark dots. She has been there the whole time, quiet as a secret.

"Look," you whisper.

Dr. Maya looks. She smiles, and picks up the picture of Mars — the red dust, the red hills, the whole rusty planet — and holds it right beside the windowsill.

You lean in close.

They are almost the same red. Not exactly — the ladybug is brighter, shinier, alive — but close enough to make you gasp. Mars, the biggest red thing you know, and a ladybug, the smallest, wearing nearly matching coats.

"Rust is red," Dr. Maya says softly. "And so is she."

The ladybug opens her wings — one tiny flick — and flies away into the garden. But Dr. Maya does not put the picture down. She pins it to the wall, right beside a photo of a ladybug she took last summer.

"There," she says. "Now the secret has a friend."

Far away, Rusty's camera eyes blink. He turns them around — all the way around — and takes a picture of himself, the red plain stretching behind him like a great rusty blanket. A selfie.

Something small and red to take home.

c1.question: "Rusty can only visit one place next," Dr. Maya says, leaning toward the screen. "Should we follow the old rover's tracks into the crater, or climb the giant volcano to see the frozen lava?"

options.label: Follow the old rover's tracks into the crater
Climb the giant volcano to see the frozen lava

c2.question: "The mystery is solved," Dr. Maya says, smiling. "But Mars has one more gift for us. Should we wait for the dust storm to pass and see what story it leaves, or look for something here on Earth that wears the same red?"

options.label: Wait for the dust storm to pass and read its story
Look for something on Earth that wears the same red

stories.title: The School That Learned to Sway

s1.text:
On the first Monday of spring, Zoe ran up the hill to Hillcrest School and stopped so fast her shoes squeaked on the pavement. The gym had vanished. Well, not vanished — but it was wrapped head to toe in scaffolding, like a present in too much wrapping paper, and a big white notice hung on the door. CLOSED, it said. FOR EARTHQUAKE RETROFITTING. Zoe read it twice. Retrofitting. She knew earthquakes. She did not know retro anything. Every morning that week she pressed her face to the fence on her way in, peeking through the diamond-shaped gaps. She saw men carrying steel beams. She saw dust drifting in the sun like slow gold glitter. And once, she saw a woman in a welder's mask lift the mask, catch Zoe peeking, and wave — not a shooing wave. A come-here wave. So on Friday, Zoe went. The woman had silver at her temples and a voice that rose and fell like a song.

"You've been watching us all week, darlin'," she said.

"I am Granny Imani. I do the welding. And you — you must be the girl who loves this old school." Zoe nodded, and before she could stop it, her worry tumbled right out.

"Is the gym broken? It's my favourite. It's creaky and it smells like floor polish and I know every squeaky board. Why does it need fixing? What's a retrofit?" Granny Imani wiped her hands on a rag, smiling.

"Come, then. Stand here, on the safe side, where I can see you. Let me show you what we're doin' for your old friend."

s2a.text:
"Under the gym it is, then," Granny Imani says, and she lifts a heavy plastic flap on the side of the building.

Cool air comes out. Zoe ducks under the flap and stops. She is underneath her whole school. It floats above her on rows of yellow jacks, and she can see the bare dirt underneath.

"We lifted it," Granny Imani says, "just a little. Enough to slide some new feet underneath." She leads Zoe to a stack of giant black pads, thick as dinner plates and wider than dinner tables.

"Touch it," she says.

Zoe presses her palm flat. The pad is smooth, a little warm, and it gives a little, like the rubber on a shoe sole.

"Rubber and steel," Granny Imani says.

"Rubber, steel, rubber, steel. Like a stack of Oreos, yes? The rubber lets the ground slide sideways. The steel holds the school steady up and down." Zoe looks up at the underside of the gym, floating there.

"That's it?" she says. "Squishy pads?"

Granny Imani laughs, a low warm sound.

"Wait until you see what happens when the ground moves." On the way out, Zoe sees a poster on the site office wall.

A red line zigzags across a map. Beyond it, a little volcano puffs smoke.

"Same restless plates," Granny Imani says.

"They make the earthquakes here. They make the mountains there." Zoe looks back at the giant pads.

They seem too soft to beat a whole earthquake.

s2b.text:
"To the lab, then," Granny Imani says, and she drives Zoe across town to a big concrete building at the university.

Inside, her nephew Dev is standing next to a platform the size of a garage floor.

"This is the shake table," he says.

"It does earthquakes. Small ones. Safe ones." On the table sit two little buildings.

One is glued stiff to a wooden base. The other sits on tiny rubber pads, loose as a cake on a plate.

"Magnitude five first," Dev says.

He turns a dial. The table rumbles. The stiff building shakes so hard its windows pop out. The padded one just glides side to side, like it is skating on ice.

"Now six," Dev says.

He turns the dial one more number. The rumble gets much louder, much faster. The stiff building snaps in half and falls over. The padded one keeps gliding, back and forth, back and forth, like it has all day. Zoe laughs.

"It just rides it out," she says.

Dev nods.

"That's base isolation. The ground moves. The building doesn't have to." On his shelf, Zoe sees a little model volcano and a map with arrows pushing into each other.

"Same plates that shake us," Dev says, "they also build mountains." Zoe looks at the broken stiff building, then the smooth rubber pads.

She has an idea about what should work. She wants to try it herself.

s3.text:
All weekend, Zoe couldn't sit still. On Saturday morning she cleared the kitchen table, found the wooden blocks from the game cupboard, and pulled out the baking tray. She filled it with wobbly jelly, because Granny Imani had said the ground moves like something soft, not like a floor.

"Right," Zoe said.

"Let's build." She stacked the blocks tall and careful, one on one, until it stood like a little tower.

Then she had her big idea. Glue. She ran for the glue stick and stuck the bottom block hard to the tray, pressing it down with both thumbs.

"There," she said.

"Nothing's moving you." She held the tray with both hands and shook it side to side, the way the ground shakes.

The jelly wobbled. The tray rattled. And the tower — snap. It broke clean in half, blocks tumbling into the jelly with a soft plop. Zoe stared.

"But I glued it," she said out loud.

"I made it strong." She picked up the broken pieces, turning them over in her fingers, and then she remembered.

The thing she'd seen at the school. The way the building wasn't meant to fight the shake at all. It was meant to move with it.

"Oh," she whispered.

"You don't hold on. You let go." She pulled the rubber liners from the jar lids in the drawer — the grippy kind Mum used for opening stubborn jam — and laid them flat on the tray.

She rebuilt the tower on top, block by block, no glue this time. Then she shook the tray again. The jelly rippled. The rubber slid and shifted. And the tower swayed — a slow, gentle lean, side to side — but it did not fall. Zoe laughed so loud the cat jumped off the windowsill.

"You did it," she told the tower.

"You danced." She found a marker and wrote on the bottom block, in her best letters: Tower Zoe.

s4a.text:
On Monday morning, Zoe carried Tower Zoe up the hill in both hands, like a birthday cake. The scaffolding was gone. The gym doors stood wide open, and inside, Granny Imani was welding the very last steel X-brace, sparks falling like tiny orange stars. She lifted her mask.

"You came! And you brought a friend." "It's my tower," Zoe said.

"It survived the jelly. I wanted the crew to see." Granny Imani crouched down, and her lilt went soft and sing-song.

"Look here, darlin'. Every brace spreads the shaking, the way arms spread a hug — so no one wall carries it all. And every one I weld is a promise. A promise that a child in this room will be safe." Zoe set her tower on the floor, right above the hidden isolators she'd learned about, and the wood hummed faintly under her knees.

Somewhere below, the whole building was ready to glide. Granny Imani pressed a stamp onto a paper hard hat and held it out. JUNIOR RETROFIT CREW, it said.

"Welcome aboard," she said.

Zoe wore it all the way home, past the fence, past the pavement where her shoes had squeaked. Her school hadn't just gotten stronger. It had learned to dance.

s4b.text:
On Monday after school, Zoe carried Tower Zoe back to Dev's lab, and Dev grinned when he saw it.

"The official test," he said.

"Full dial. Magnitude seven. Are you ready?" Zoe swallowed.

"Ready." She set her tower on the shake table, on its little rubber pads, and stepped back beside him.

Dev turned the dial all the way. The table roared. It shook so hard the pencils danced in their cup. And Tower Zoe swayed — a slow, easy glide, side to side, like it was riding waves. It did not fall.

"Yes!" Zoe shouted, because she could not help it.

Dev slowed the table, and the printer hummed and spat out a long strip of paper.

"The wobble graph," he said.

He pointed to two lines. One was a wild black scribble, jagged as a mountain range.

"That's the stiff one — it fought the shake and lost." Beside it ran a tiny, gentle wave, smooth as bathwater.

"And that's yours." He taped the graph to the lab wall, right next to photographs of real towers that sway on purpose, and wrote her name underneath in thick marker.

Zoe carried a copy home folded in her pocket. That night she took it out and smoothed it flat. Proof, in black and white, that the best way to stand tall is to learn how to lean.

c1.question: "So, little engineer — you want to come under the gym with me and touch the real pads, or you want to go shake some buildings to bits at my nephew's lab?"

options.label: Go under the gym with Granny Imani to see and touch the actual base isolators
Visit Dev's university lab and watch models get rattled on the shake table

c2.question: "Your tower survived, so — do we carry it to the gym to show the crew, or do we take it back to the lab and crank the dial all the way up?"

options.label: Bring Tower Zoe to the reopened gym and show Granny Imani and the crew what she discovered
Take Tower Zoe back to the lab for the full magnitude 7 test and the printed proof

s1.text:
Maya had been drawing the same app for three weeks, and the kitchen table knew it. There were seventeen pages of sketches now, taped together in a long paper snake that curled off the edge and onto the floor. Screens, buttons, arrows. A little square drawing of a smiling snack bar that she had redrawn maybe forty times.

"Okay," said Leo, her best friend and official tester, scooting his chair closer. "Show me again."

Maya spread the pages flat. "This is {app_name}. You tap here to add what you ate. Then here to see your week."

Leo pressed his finger on the first drawing. "Tap." He moved to the second. "Tap." He got to the third page and stopped. His finger hovered over the paper, circling like a confused bee. "Wait. Do I tap the banana or the arrow?"

"The arrow," Maya said.

"But the banana is bigger."

"The banana is just there to look friendly."

"Then the banana is lying to me."

Maya opened her mouth to argue, then closed it. She looked at page three the way Leo was seeing it, and he was right. The banana was huge and tappable-looking. The arrow was tiny and shy.

Grandma Rosie set down a plate of oatmeal cookies, still warm. "How's the testing going, inventors?"

"The banana lied," Leo said, taking two cookies.

"Mm," said Grandma Rosie, like this was a serious engineering report. "Paper can only tell you so much, sweetheart. At some point you need real fingers on a real screen."

Maya looked at her paper snake, all seventeen pages of it, taped and re-taped and full of good guesses. A real screen. Real fingers. She could actually build this. She had the sketches. She had the feedback. She even had a banana that needed demoting.

"Leo," she said slowly, "what if I make a real version? Like, an actual app?"

Leo grinned through a mouthful of cookie. "Finally. I've been tapping paper like a pigeon for nothing."

Maya pulled out a fresh page and wrote at the top: Version One. Real one.

s2a.text:
Maya built Version One in one weekend, fuelled by toast and stubbornness. She moved the banana to the corner, where it could be friendly without lying. She made the arrow big and green and impossible to miss. By Sunday night, the little snack bar on the screen glowed like it meant it.

"Okay," Maya whispered. "Moment of truth."

She tapped Add Snack. The button worked. She tapped View Week. A chart appeared, slightly crooked but real. Then she tapped Save, and the app made a sound like a robot falling down a well.

Maya froze. "That is not the sound I picked."

She tried again. The robot fell down the well again. Louder this time.

"That is a horrifying sound," she said. But the snack was saved. The app worked. Ugly in places, terrifying in one specific place, but real.

Monday morning, Maya slid the phone across the table to Leo and watched his face like it was a test result.

Leo tapped. He frowned. He tapped again. The robot fell down the well, and Leo jumped so hard his knee hit the table.

"Why does it sound like that," he said. It was not a question.

"I don't know yet. But did it save?"

Leo looked at the screen. Then at her. Then back at the screen.

"It saved," he said, slowly. "Maya. It's real. The banana doesn't lie anymore, and it saved my snack."

He tapped Add Snack again, just to watch it work. Maya felt something warm spread through her chest, like the first bite of something still in the oven.

Version One was out in the world. It had one user, one terrifying sound effect, and seventeen pages of paper behind it.

It was a start.

s2b.text:
Maya built Version One in one weekend, fuelled by toast and stubbornness. She moved the banana to the corner, where it could be friendly without lying. She made the arrow big and green and impossible to miss. By Sunday night, the little snack bar on the screen glowed like it meant it.

"Okay," Maya whispered. "Moment of truth."

She tapped Add Snack. The button worked. She tapped View Week. A chart appeared, slightly crooked but real. Then she tapped Save, and the app made a sound like a robot falling down a well.

Maya froze. "That is not the sound I picked."

She tried again. The robot fell down the well again. Louder this time.

"That is a horrifying sound," she said. But the snack was saved. The app worked. Ugly in places, terrifying in one specific place, but real.

She found Grandma Rosie in the kitchen, rolling out dough. Maya held out the phone with both hands, like it might break or bite.

"Grandma? Will you test something?"

Grandma Rosie wiped her hands on her apron and took the phone seriously, the way she took all important things. She tapped Add Snack. She peered at the chart. She tapped Save.

The robot fell down the well.

Grandma Rosie did not flinch. She looked at the screen for a long moment, then at Maya.

"Well," she said. "That is a sound that has opinions."

Maya burst out laughing, and the knot in her stomach loosened for the first time all weekend.

"But Grandma, does it work?"

Grandma Rosie tapped Add Snack again, carefully, like she was planting a seed. "It works," she said. "The banana minds its manners now. And you made this. From paper."

She handed the phone back and pulled a warm cookie from nowhere, the way grandmas do.

"Version One," she said, like she was naming a ship.

Maya took the cookie. Version One was out in the world. It had one user, one opinionated sound effect, and seventeen pages of paper behind it.

It was a start.

s3.text:
The day came to test it on a real screen. Grandma Rosie brought cookies, as always. Mr. Chen from next door agreed to try it, holding his phone like it was a very old, very precious map. Maya held her breath. She was not allowed to speak.

Mr. Chen tapped. He swiped. He frowned. On the third screen, his finger circled, a lost bee looking for a flower that wasn't there. He sighed, a quiet, crumpled sound, and handed the phone back. "It's lovely, Maya," he said, "but I think I'm too old for this."

The words stung. She bit her tongue, tasting copper and frustration. She wanted to shout, "No, you're supposed to tap the little arrow!" But the rules were the rules. Later, Leo tried it on his older phone. The screen went black. Dead. Maya's heart did a slow, cold flip.

"What did you expect to happen?" Mr. Chen asked gently, not unkindly. "And what happened instead?"

Maya looked from her beautiful sketches to the blank, silent phone. The paper banana had been a liar. The real screen was a wall. The bug wasn't in her drawings. It wasn't in her head. It was out there, in the real world, only appearing when real hands tried to hold it. It was a problem she couldn't fix alone.

s4a.text:
Maya released Version One to five kids at school, and for six days her phone was quiet. Then, on the seventh day, Jasper sent a message. It had seventeen parts.

"Make it talk to my watch," read Maya. "Make it scan barcodes. Make it predict my future. Make the banana bigger." She looked up. "The banana is not the problem anymore."

Leo peered over her shoulder. "Number eight says, 'Add a button that tells my brother to stop touching my stuff.'"

"That's not a feature," Maya said. "That's a family argument."

Grandma Rosie arrived with cookies that smelled like cinnamon and decisions. She set the plate down and looked at the list, all seventeen items scrolling like a grocery receipt from a giant's house.

"You can't build everything at once, sweetie," she said. "Pick the two that matter most. The rest get a 'not yet.'"

Maya stared at the screen. Her finger hovered. Then she circled the crash fix—because Leo's phone still went black—and the bigger, clearer arrow, because Mr. Chen's finger deserved a target it could find. She wrote "not yet" beside the other fifteen. The words felt like closing a door softly, not slamming it.

Version 1.1 went out on a Tuesday. It had the fix. It had the arrow. And it had one secret thing nobody asked for: when you added a snack, the little icon did a tiny, happy bounce, like it was glad to see you.

Leo tested it first. He added a cookie. The icon bounced. He added another. It bounced again. "Did you make it... happy?" he asked.

Maya looked at her phone. The app icon—the one she'd drawn forty times on paper—now glowed a little brighter, like it had swallowed a small piece of sunset.

"I made it polite," she said. "It says thank you."

s4b.text:
Maya released Version One to five kids at school, and for six days her phone was quiet. Then Jasper sent the list. Seventeen requests. Maya read them twice, then a third time, her stomach tightening like a screw.

"He wants it to play music," she told Mr. Chen, who was fixing his fence next door. "And count steps. And translate dog barks. I don't even know how to do that. I don't know what this app is anymore."

Mr. Chen hammered once, then stopped. He looked at her over the fence, not unkindly. "What problem are you really trying to solve, Maya?"

She opened her mouth to say "everything," then closed it. She thought about the paper snake, the seventeen pages, the banana that lied. She thought about Leo's finger circling, lost.

"I want to help people remember what they ate," she said slowly. "So they can see their week. That's all."

"Then most of these," Mr. Chen said, nodding at her phone, "are for a different app. One you don't have to build."

Maya went inside. She circled two requests: the crash fix, and the clearer arrow. Beside the other fifteen, she wrote "not yet." The words felt like putting down a heavy backpack.

Version 1.1 went out on a Tuesday. It fixed the black screen. It made the arrow big enough to find. And Maya added one secret thing nobody asked for: when you opened the app, the little snack icon wiggled, just once, like it was stretching awake.

Leo noticed immediately. "It moved! Did it always move?"

Maya checked her phone. The icon—the one she'd drawn forty times—now glowed a little brighter, the colors sharper, like someone had cleaned a window.

"No," she said. "But it knows what it is now."

c1.question: "Who should test it first, Maya? Your best friend or your grandma?"

options.label: Test with Leo, the honest best friend
Test with Grandma Rosie, the unexpected tester

c2.question: "How will you decide which two features to build, Maya?"

options.label: Ask Grandma Rosie for advice over cookies
Ask Mr. Chen for guiding questions

s1.text:
The man at the door tears our tickets in half, and then we are inside the biggest room we have ever seen. Red velvet seats, row after row, soft as a cat's ear. Front row. Us.

On the stage, a hundred musicians are all playing at once, but nobody is playing the same thing. A horn goes brrrp. A drum goes bomp. The strings slide up and down like slow sirens, and the whole swirly cloud of it tickles our ears.

"Listen," says a voice. A woman with a violin tucked under her chin is leaning toward us from the stage. "I'm Wren. And this is Bumble." She holds out her violin. "Go on. Touch the wood."

We do. It hums under our fingers, warm and buzzy, like a bee in a box.

Wren grins. "Here's the strange part." She points with her bow. On a little box at the front stands a woman in a long dark jacket, doing nothing at all. Just smiling, with crinkly eyes, like somebody's grandma watching pancakes cook.

"Nobody is shouting orders," Wren whispers. "Nobody is counting. So how does everyone know when to play?"

We look at the woman on the box. She looks back at us, and her smile gets bigger.

"Come closer," says Wren. "Before the lights go down. Let's find out."

s2a.text:
We slip up the little stairs and into the string neighborhood, where music stands crowd together like houses on a busy street. Wren sits us down right beside her chair. "Watch," she says, and she pulls her bow across the strings. Bumble sings out, and the string under her fingers trembles blurry, like a tiny bee trying to get free.

All around us, bows are sliding. A cello hums so low we feel it in our ribs.

But then we notice something. Wren's fingers are busy, busy, busy — and still her eyes flick up. Between every phrase, up they go, quick as sparrows, to the woman on the little box. We look down the row. The violins are doing it too. And the cellos. And the big basses at the back, their heads tipping up like sunflowers.

"See?" Wren whispers, without stopping her bow. "All of us. Watching her."

"But she hasn't made a single sound," we say.

"Not one," says Wren, and her eyes flick up again. "So what are we all looking at?"

s2b.text:
We tiptoe past the horns, past the flutes, all the way to the very back of the stage, where the percussion corner sits like a toy shop after a tornado. Cymbals lean like golden plates. A xylophone glitters. And in the middle of it all stands a drum as big as a bathtub.

"Careful of the triangle," says a cheerful voice. A woman with her hair in a bouncy bun steps out from behind the giant drum. "I'm Tova. Want to hear my heartbeat?"

Before we can answer, she taps the big drum with a soft padded stick. Boom. Boom. Boom. It rumbles up through the floor and into our shoes.

"That's the sound the whole orchestra builds on," Tova says. "Like a house on its foundation." She points with her stick, way, way across the stage, to the little box at the front. "And from back here — the farthest seat there is — I can see her hands. Clear as anything."

We squint. We can see them too, small and white, waiting.

"She never makes a sound," Tova says. "So what do you suppose those hands are saying?"

s3.text:
Wren taps our shoulders. "Front row," she whispers. "Quiet as mice."

We settle into the red velvet. The lights go down, and Maestra Elena lifts her hands high, high, like she is reaching for a shelf.

The whole orchestra swells. A hundred instruments rise together, big as a wave, and the sound fills our chests like a deep breath.

Then her hands sink low, low, like she is patting a sleeping dog.

The music shrinks. It gets so small we lean forward. We hold our breath. The strings are whispering secrets, and the brass is humming softer than a cat's purr.

"Did you feel that?" Pip the clarinet player mouths at us from his chair. He wiggles his fingers on the shiny keys. "Her hands told us."

Then the small white baton flashes. It points down, sharp as a pencil tap.

Every instrument begins at exactly the same second. Bomp. Brrrp. A drum, a horn, all together, like one giant voice.

"It's a language," Wren breathes. "Her hands draw it in the air, and the music answers."

Maestra Elena turns. Her eyes crinkle at us, warm as toast. She beckons with one finger.

"You've been watching," she says, her voice cozy as a kitchen at breakfast. "Do you think you've cracked it? Would you like to test the language yourselves, before the real concert?"

We look at Wren. Wren looks at Pip. Pip grins.

"What do you say?" Maestra Elena asks. "Shall we see if the baton will listen to you?"

s4a.text:
"Test our ears!" we say.

"Then close your eyes," says Barnaby the trumpet player, sliding in beside us. "Each family plays alone. You guess who."

First: a humming, warm and smooth, like honey pouring. "Strings!" we whisper. Wren and Bumble are swaying.

Then a golden buzz, bright as sunshine through a window. "Brass!" Barnaby lifts his trumpet and plays one note so big and shiny it feels like breakfast.

Next, quick notes dart and tumble like birds. "Woodwinds!" Pip winks.

Last: Boom. Boom-boom. The floor shakes our shoes. "Percussion!" we shout, laughing.

Barnaby points to the side of the stage. "And that grand piano? Secret agent. Hammers hit strings inside. Both families at once."

Then Maestra Elena lifts her baton. The violins begin soft as rain on a roof. Her hands climb, and the storm climbs with them, brass rolling, drums cracking, until thunder fills the whole hall. At the very end she catches our eye and conducts the last soft note just for us.

Afterward, Wren signs our program. "The quietest person made the biggest music," she says.

We carry it home like a candle.

s4b.text:
"We want to try!" we say.

Maestra Elena opens a little case. Inside lies a spare baton, white as a piece of chalk. "A small flick means softer," she says. "A big sweep means louder. Show me."

Wren gathers her strings. Pip rounds up his woodwinds. We climb onto the little box, and our knees feel wobbly.

We lift the baton. We bring it down, crooked as a worm.

The musicians play. Together. Exactly together. Pip grins so wide his clarinet nearly slips.

We flick small. The music shrinks to a whisper. We sweep big, and it grows and grows, rumbling into a small thunder under our own two hands. Our hearts are pounding like drums.

Then the real concert begins, and we watch Maestra Elena do the same thing a hundred times bigger. Tova's timpani go Boom right on cue, and the floor rattles our shoes.

Afterward, Maestra Elena closes our fingers around the spare baton. "On loan," she says, eyes crinkling. "Until next time."

We carry it home carefully, like a candle flame. A leader's job, we know now, is helping everyone else shine.

c1.question: "The concert hasn't started yet, so we have time for one quick look before we must sit. Shall we visit my string neighborhood up front, or tiptoe all the way back to the percussion corner where the big drums live?"

options.label: Visit the string neighborhood with Wren
Tiptoe back to the percussion corner with Tova

c2.question: "So you've found my secret. Now, would you like to test your ears and guess each family by its sound, or would you rather borrow a baton and try the language with your own hands?"

options.label: Test our ears by guessing each family from its sound
Borrow the baton and try conducting a small group

stories.title: The Slowest Magic Trick in the Pond

s1.text:
We are standing at the warm, shallow edge of Grandfather Shell's pond, just us and the mist, when the old snail slides out from under his lily pad. "Come and see," he says. "Quickly, before the sun drinks the mist."

He points one long eye-stalk at a wobbling blob of jelly eggs. Inside, little black dots are uncurling, one by one, like commas waking up.

"That," says Grandfather Shell, "is where the whole road starts. Jelly to hop, all along this one pond edge. But you have to walk it slowly. One square of the pond-calendar at a time."

Something pops up beside us. Bloop.

A froglet — all legs and stubby tail, half finished and twice as bouncy. "Did somebody say expedition?" he says. "I'm Pippin. Legs: done. Tail: still loading. I am the greatest guide in the pond, and I have been waiting for recruits all morning."

He pats his little tail with one foot. "Don't mind this. It's not falling off. It's my lunch for later."

We look at the tiny black commas. We look at Pippin. How does something that small ever hop?

"One station at a time," says Pippin. "Follow me."

s2a.text:
Nix is waiting by the weed, quick as a blink. "Down here," she says. "Quietly now."

We slip below the surface, and the pond turns green and cool and full of little lives. Tadpoles hang in the weed like commas that never woke all the way up. Beside each small head, two feathery tufts wave and wave.

"Gills," whispers Nix. "Like a fish. They fan the water and breathe it. Watch."

We watch. The tufts flutter, flutter, flutter, and every wriggler hangs there drinking the pond through them.

"I hide in this weed too," Nix says, showing us a curled leaf, a hollow stem. "Because I'm mid-journey as well. One day I trade all this water for sky." She says it like a secret she's proud of.

"Will the gills go?" we ask.

"They go," says Nix, and her eyes shine. "The station closes early on this road. What replaces them?" She only smiles. "Next square. You'll see."

We come up dripping, with the green light still in our eyes, and Grandfather Shell chalks one more square on the pond-calendar: gills, seen, just in time.

s2b.text:
Pippin leads us along the warm stones, where the sun has made the shallow water bathwater-warm. "This," he says, "is my favourite station. The leg queue."

All along the stones, tadpoles are sprouting legs. Back legs first. Always back legs first. Then front. Nothing jumps the queue.

One tadpole pushes past us with two new back legs dangling, tail still doing all the work. It goes along like a boat with an engine and no oars, wobbling, determined, and we have to press our lips together not to laugh with delight.

"I remember that bit," says Pippin softly. "You have the legs, but nobody's told them what to do yet."

He plants himself on a stone. "Watch the order. Back legs." He waggles them. "Front legs." He waves one at us. "In the right order, every time. The pond doesn't rush." He wobbles, proud as anything, and nearly tips off the stone.

Grandfather Shell slides up beside us, slow as a cloud, and chalks two new squares on the pond-calendar. "Legs," he says. "Twice."

But the legged tadpoles still trail long tails, and not one of them can hop. Pippin taps his own stubby tail and grins. "Something has to happen first," he says. "Guess what's on the menu."

s3.text:
We scramble up the lily pad, and Grandfather Shell is waiting, slow and smiling. "Well?" he says. "What did you find?" We tell him, and he nods like he already knew.

"Now for the heart of the trick," he says. "Gather close." He taps Pippin's stubby tail with one eye-stalk. "This never falls off. Never. It melts back into the body — absorbed, like soup soaking into bread. A packed lunch a tadpole carries behind it. That is why a changing tadpole hardly eats. It is busy digesting its own tail."

We stare. Pippin pats his little tail with one foot, gently this time. "Thank you for the ride," he says to it. "You were delicious." Then he puffs out his chest — and keeps it puffed. "Feel that? Lungs. Two of them. Still loading, but nearly there. One more square and I breathe actual air."

Grandfather Shell sighs a happy snail sigh. "I have a cousin in Mexico," he says, "an axolotl, who keeps her feathery gills forever and never finishes the trick. That is one way to be." He looks at Pippin. "This is another."

Bloop. Pippin bounces. "Last square, recruits. Where should we watch it from?"

s4a.text: "Down here!" Pippin shouts, leading us along the muddy rim where the water laps at our toes. He plants his feet at the very edge, tail stub quivering, and turns to face us with an expression of utmost seriousness. "Witness positions, please. This is it." He opens his mouth wide, wider, widest — and gulps. His throat bobs. His sides swell like two balloons filling for the first time ever. Air. Actual air. "It tastes like outside!" he wheezes, delighted. Then he gathers himself: legs bent, lungs full, tail nearly gone, everything the whole journey was building. He springs. A wobbly, splashy arc through the air — and lands smack on a lily pad, arms windmilling, one foot dangling. "I meant to do that!" We cheer so loudly a dragonfly rattles off its reed. Grandfather Shell slides up beside us, and we pull out our smooth pond pebble. One chalk notch for every square, every stage, every small change — and now the last one, for the hop. Pippin hops down into our cupped hands, damp and warm and thrumming. "Same tadpole," he says softly, looking back at the jelly eggs glistening in the shallows. "Different page." We carry the pebble home in a pocket, heavy as a whole pond, light as a first breath.

s4b.text: "Up! Up!" Pippin cries, and we scramble onto Grandfather Shell's broad lily pad, which dips under our weight like a green trampoline. The old snail settles beside us, eye-stalks pointed down at the water. "Best view in the pond," he says. "I've watched a thousand first hops from this front step." Below us, Pippin takes position. We hold our breath. He opens his mouth — gulps — his throat bobs, his sides swell, air going in for the very first time. Then he launches. Up, up, legs kicking, lungs full, tail a memory — and he lands right beside us on the pad, which boings like a drum. The whole pond seems to wobble with applause. "Told you I'd make it," Pippin pants, grinning. Grandfather Shell reaches into his shell and pulls out the pond-calendar — squares of jelly, nubs of leg, shrinking tails — and turns to the last page. Blank. "For next spring's eggs," he says. "The road is a circle, not a line." We notch our pebble one final time — one mark for every stage we visited — and tuck it safe away. Grandfather Shell raises one slow eye-stalk in a slower wave. Pippin waves back with a foot. "Same time next year, recruits," he says. "I'll be the one with no tail at all."

c1.question: "The road has two lanes from here, little travellers," says Grandfather Shell, slow as a cloud. "Will you slip below with Nix to see how the wrigglers breathe, or walk the warm stones with our bouncy friend and watch the legs come in?"

options.label: Go underwater with Nix to see the gills at work
Stroll the sunny ledge with Pippin to watch legs sprout in order

c2.question: "It's nearly hop o'clock!" Pippin squeaks, quivering. "Where should my expedition stand for the big moment — down at the muddy water's edge, right in the splash zone, or up on Grandfather Shell's lily pad with the bird's-eye view?"

options.label: Crouch at the muddy water's edge for the first breath and first hop
Watch from the lily pad beside the snail and see the hop land beside you

s1.text:
The wind in Iceland has cold fingers. It pokes them down our collars and flaps our maps like flags, but we are a crew of young field-trip helpers, and we do not mind. We are standing in a great rocky valley, and Dr. Petra Hammerfall is grinning at us.

“Boots wide,” she says. “Wider. There.”

We look down. A long dark crack runs between our feet, deep and still. “Your left boot,” says Dr. Petra, “is on the North American tectonic plate. Your right boot is on the Eurasian one. Two enormous pieces of Earth’s crust — and you are standing on both.”

We wiggle our toes. Nothing. Not a wobble, not a hum.

“I can’t feel it move,” we say.

“No,” she says. “But it is moving. Right now, this second, those two plates are drifting apart — about as fast as your fingernails grow.” She holds up her hand and waggles her fingers. “That is the speed of continental drift. The slowest race on Earth, and it never, ever stops.”

We stare at our fingernails. Growing. Right now. So quietly we cannot hear a thing.

“Far below us,” Dr. Petra goes on, “the hot, soft rock called the mantle creeps along like porridge in a pot, and it carries the plates on its back, the way soup carries a noodle.”

Then, from down by the water, comes a voice like a wave with a laugh in it. “Ahoy the valley!”

An old sailor with a white beard waves from a jetty, beside a little boat with a glass bottom. “Captain Brio,” calls Dr. Petra, “and his great raft-pieces tour!”

“All aboard!” booms the Captain. “The plates won’t wait! Well. They will. But the tide won’t!”

s2a.text: "Maps it is!" Captain Brio thumps the wheel and {boat_name} swings out over the dark water. He spreads his old charts on the little table, one on top of the other, each one soft as a handkerchief from folding. "This one," he says, tapping it, "I drew on my first crossing, when my beard was black as tar. And this one last year. Lay your finger on the edge of Iceland, shipmates. Now the edge of Norway." We do. The gap between them is wider on the new map. Just a whisker. But wider. "The sea has stretched," says Brio, "a fingernail's width, every single year of my life. I have crossed this ocean forty times, and every time it was a little bigger." We look at our fingernails. Growing. Right now. Dr. Petra leans over the glass bottom. "Down there is where the new width comes from. The mantle — that hot, slow rock, thick as treacle — rises up between the two plates and hardens into brand-new seafloor." "A fellow named Wegener said the continents drift," Brio chuckles, "and they laughed him out of the room. Now look." He points down. Through the glass, far below, a faint red glow pulses in the dark, like embers under ash. "The ridge," whispers the Captain. "The seam where the world makes more world."

s2b.text: "The arrows, then!" says Captain Brio, and Dr. Petra flips open her tablet on the little table. A map of the whole world glows up at us — and all over it, tiny arrows creep. Every tectonic plate has one, sliding its own slow way. "It looks," we say, "like a puzzle being nudged." "That is exactly what it is," says Dr. Petra. "Once, long ago, all the land huddled together in one giant piece called Pangaea. Then the pieces drifted apart — continental drift — and they are drifting still." She taps our home. A little arrow points away from Iceland, slow as slow. "In 1915 a man named Wegener said this out loud, and everyone giggled at him. Continents, moving? Imagine." Captain Brio snorts into his beard. "Who's giggling now?" "Nobody," grins Dr. Petra. "These arrows are drawn by satellites. They prove him right, every day." We watch our arrow. Creeping. Fingernail speed. Through the glass bottom, the seafloor slides past below us, patient as porridge. "So," says Dr. Petra, and her finger lands on two arrows pointing straight at each other, "if all the raft-pieces are moving — what happens where they meet?"

s3.text:
The boat chugs around a great grey headland, and there, high above the water, a wooden platform clings to the mountainside. Bright flags snap and flutter on their ropes — red, blue, yellow, white, green — cracking like whips in the wind.

“Up we go,” says Captain Brio, tying the boat to a post that looks older than he is. “Someone here has been waiting to meet you.”

A woman in a warm striped apron waves us onto the platform. Her name is Ama Dolkar, and her eyes crinkle when she smiles. “You came,” she says. “Good. The cloud comes this afternoon, and I want you to see my mountain first.” She points up. The peak soars over us, white and enormous. “When I was a girl, that mountain was lower than it is now. Truly. I have measured. India is pushing into Asia — slowly, slowly, fingernail speed — and the land has nowhere to go but up.”

We look at our fingernails. Growing. Right now. So is the mountain.

Ama Dolkar presses something small and cool into our hands. A shell, curled like a sleeping cat, turned entirely to stone. “I found it on the mountainside,” she says. “It lived on the seafloor once. Then two plates pushed together — like two rugs shoved against each other — and the seafloor crumpled up into the sky.”

We turn the shell over and over. A sea creature. Up here, where the flags snap and the wind has cold fingers.

Captain Brio leans on the rail, glass-bottomed boat bobbing below. “So,” he says, “where do the great raft-pieces take us next?”

s4a.text:
“Down we go,” says Nix, and the submersible slips under the waves with a sound like a held breath. Down. Down. The blue turns to ink, and the ink turns to black, and Captain Brio’s voice crackles through the speaker: “Steady, little climbers. The great raft-pieces are pulling apart right beneath you.”

Then we see it. A glow, faint and red, like the last coal in a campfire. Nix kills the lamp.

“Look,” she whispers.

The glow grows. It is not fire. It is rock — hot, soft rock from the mantle, rising where the two plates tear away from each other. It bubbles up, slow as honey, and spreads out on the seafloor, and cools, and hardens, and becomes new land. Brand new. Black and shining and steaming in the cold water.

“New seafloor,” Nix says. “Being born. Right now.”

We press our hands to the cold glass. Our fingernails are growing. The seafloor is growing. Same speed. Same quiet, patient push.

The lamp flickers. “Battery says home,” says Nix, and up we go, up through the black into the blue, and there is the boat, and there is dinner, warm and steaming in the little galley. Petra hands us something small. A grey pebble with a white stripe, one half from each plate, picked up at the rift valley where we stood with our boots wide.

“It is riding a plate too,” she says. “Moving while you sleep.”

We put it in our pocket. It is still moving. So are we.

s4b.text:
The boat noses onto a beach of black sand, and Captain Brio drops the anchor with a splash. “Mind your step, little climbers,” he says. “This island is younger than you are.”

Petra is already off, striding up the beach, eyes on the ground. “The tide is coming,” she calls. “I want to find the youngest rock on Earth before it does.”

We follow. The sand is black because it is lava, ground up fine by the sea, and it is warm under our boots. Ahead, a crack in the ground breathes out steam that smells like struck matches. Petra stops us at the edge of a shallow crater, and we stand behind a ridge of old, hard rock, where the ground is steady, and look down.

“Here,” she says, pointing. “The plate edge opened, and the mantle rose up, and the island built itself — grain by grain, flow by flow.”

She kneels. She brushes black sand aside with her hand, and there it is: a ribbon of rock so dark it drinks the light, smooth and sharp-edged, different from everything around it. “This,” she says. “This is the newest. It cooled last week. Maybe yesterday.”

We touch it. It is warm. Our fingernails are growing. The island is growing. Same slow race.

Back on the boat, Captain Brio pours cocoa into thick mugs, and Petra gives us the pebble from the rift valley — grey with a white stripe, one half from each plate. “It is riding a plate too,” she says. “Moving while you sleep.”

We hold it tight. It is still moving. So are we.

c1.question: "Out the window or down through the glass, shipmates? Shall I show you my old maps and how the sea has stretched, or shall the doctor show you the dancing arrows that prove the great raft-pieces move?"

options.label: Captain Brio's worn maps and the widening Atlantic
The satellite map of sliding plates and old Pangaea

c2.question: "The plate edge runs two ways from here, little climbers. Down, where the ridge glows and new seafloor bubbles up — or across, to a young island still being built. Which shall it be?"

options.label: Descend in the submersible to watch new seafloor born at the glowing ridge
Stand on the black-sand island where a plate edge has torn open

stories.title: The Star That Danced with Nothing

s1.text:
Up on the roof of the observatory, the night smells like cold dust and rain that hasn't happened yet. Dr. Maya Reyes is here with us, and so is Professor Wobble, who is wearing one purple sock with Saturn on it and one green sock with a nebula. He is also talking to the telescope. "I see you, little star," he squeaks, in a voice that sounds like a mouse swallowed a walkie-talkie. "Oh yes I do."

We are watching a star near the middle of the Milky Way. On the computer screen it is just a dot of light, but this dot is *moving*. It is racing around in a tight little circle, faster than any star should, around absolutely nothing. Just dark. Just empty space.

"That," says Dr. Reyes, "is the strangest thing I have ever seen."

Professor Wobble leans over the keyboard. "What shall we call her?" he asks us. "She needs a name."

We look at the screen. The dot is zipping around like a firefly on a string. "{star_name}," we say.

"{star_name}," repeats Professor Wobble, and he types it in. "Welcome to the show."

He opens a tin and passes us {snack}. We eat them slowly, watching. The star goes around, and around, and around. But here is the thing that makes our skin feel fizzy: whatever she is dancing with, we cannot see it at all. Something is there. Something is pulling her in that fast, tight circle. But the middle of the dance floor is dark.

"What is she dancing with?" we ask.

Dr. Reyes smiles. "That," she says, "is exactly what we are going to find out."

s2a.text:
"Follow the dancer," says Professor Wobble. "Good choice. She's the one doing all the work." He pats the telescope. "Keep your eye on her, old friend."

We watch {star_name} race across the screen. Around she goes, and around again. She is not wandering. She is *lapping* — the same tight circle, over and over, like a race car stuck on a very small track.

"Time her," says Dr. Reyes.

Professor Wobble clicks a stopwatch. We hold our breath. Around. Around. Around. Click.

"She's fast!" he squeaks, in his telescope voice. "Oh, she is *very* fast!"

Dr. Reyes writes the number on a whiteboard, and then she does some maths underneath it. The numbers get bigger and bigger. Her eyebrows get higher and higher.

"Here is the rule," she says. "The faster a star moves, the heavier the thing pulling on it must be. Like a swing — the harder you pull the chains, the faster you go." She taps the whiteboard. "And {star_name} is moving so fast that whatever is pulling her weighs as much as *millions of suns*."

We look at the screen. Millions of suns. Our mouths fall open a little.

"But wait," we say. "Something that heavy should be enormous. Something that enormous should be easy to see."

"Yes," says Dr. Reyes. "It should."

We stare at the middle of {star_name}'s circle. There is nothing there. No giant star. No glowing mountain of anything. Just dark, ordinary, empty space.

Professor Wobble leans close to the screen and whispers, "Where are you hiding, heavyweight?"

The dark does not answer. But {star_name} keeps dancing around it, as fast as ever — and now we know she is dancing with an invisible heavyweight, millions of suns heavy, that refuses to be seen.

"First clue," says Dr. Reyes, and she writes it on the board: *Something enormous is there. We just can't see it yet.*

s2b.text:
"Let's peek at the dance floor," says Dr. Reyes. "Sometimes you learn more from the floor than from the dancer."

Professor Wobble nods so hard his glasses slip down his nose. "Move the telescope," he tells it, in his squeaky voice. "Not at the middle. *Beside* the middle. There's a good fellow."

The telescope hums and turns. On the screen, {star_name} slides off to one side, and we look at the space next to her path instead.

And there it is.

A ring. A huge, glowing ring of gas, orange and white, swirling slowly around the dark spot like water going around a drain. It is beautiful. It looks like someone stirred a pot of soup with a giant spoon and the soup caught fire.

"Oooooh," we say.

"That gas," says Dr. Reyes, "is falling toward the dark spot. And as it falls, it rubs against itself and heats up — like your hands getting warm when you rub them together, only a million times more. By the time it gets close to the middle, it is so hot it glows."

Professor Wobble presses both hands to his cheeks. "Dinner's cooking!" he squeaks. "But where's the cook?"

We giggle. But he is right. Something is heating up all that gas. Something is pulling it in and spinning it around and making it glow like a campfire. Something with a very strong pull.

"The gas can see it," says Dr. Reyes. "The star can feel it. Everything near it knows it is there."

"Everything except us," we say.

"Everything except our eyes," she corrects. "But our eyes are not the only way to look."

We watch the glowing ring swirl, slow and bright, around a middle that stays perfectly dark. Professor Wobble hands us another {snack}, and we eat it without looking away.

"Second clue," says Dr. Reyes, writing on the board: *The invisible thing is heating up everything near it — but it still refuses to be seen.*

s3.text:
Dr. Reyes pulls up a second picture on the screen, right beside the first. "What did you find?" she asks. We tell her. She nods slowly, and then she does something wonderful: she puts the two side by side, and they fit. They fit like puzzle pieces clicking together, like the last two socks in the drawer.

"There is something there," she says. "Something with gravity so strong that once anything crosses a certain line — even light itself — it cannot get back out. That line is called the event horizon. And the something is called a black hole."

A black hole. We say it out loud, because it is a magnificent thing to say. Professor Wobble says it in his telescope voice: "A black hooole."

"Is it going to grab us?" we ask.

"No," says Dr. Reyes. "It doesn't reach out and grab anything. {star_name} is simply orbiting it, the way Earth orbits the Sun. It is the same gravity that pulls a dropped ball to the floor. Just much, much more of it."

Professor Wobble passes the tin of {snack} around again. "And now," he says, "the best part. In 2019, telescopes all over the world worked together like one giant eye, and they took an actual picture of a black hole's shadow. An actual picture!"

"And tonight," says Dr. Reyes, grinning, "our telescope is joining the next big photo night."

Professor Wobble pats the telescope. "Did you hear that? You're going to be famous."

s4a.text:
We stay. We stay up past midnight, which already feels like a small adventure, and Professor Wobble passes the tin of {snack} around one more time. "Fuel," he whispers. "Astronomers run on it."

On the screen, nothing is happening yet. Dr. Reyes explains that our telescope is not working alone tonight. Dishes and domes all over the world — on mountains, in deserts, in the cold white bottom of the Earth — are all pointing at the same dark spot. Together they make one giant eye, as wide as the planet.

"Ten minutes," she says.

We wait. We eat {snack}. Professor Wobble narrates in his telescope voice. "I see you, little photons. Come along now. Nearly there."

"Three," says Dr. Reyes. "Two. One."

The screen flickers. And slowly, slowly, like a photo developing in a bath, a ring appears. Fuzzy. Orange. A glowing donut of light with a perfect dark middle.

"There," breathes Dr. Reyes. "That dark center is the shadow. The event horizon. The light around it is gas, heated up and glowing as it circles. We are looking at something no one can see — by looking at everything around it."

We cheer. We actually shout, because we cannot help it, and Professor Wobble shouts too, and the telescope gets a kiss on its cool metal side.

The printer hums. Out comes our very own copy of the ring, still slightly warm. We hold it carefully, the way you hold something that matters.

"The star that danced with nothing," says Professor Wobble softly. "And we caught the nothing."

We tuck the picture under our arm to take home. Proof that the dark has a shape — and that we helped find it.

s4b.text:
We step outside. The rooftop air is cold and smells like dust and rain that still hasn't happened, and the telescope hums quietly behind us, doing its long, patient work.

"Look up," says Dr. Reyes.

The whole sky is spilled with stars. The Milky Way runs overhead like flour dusted across a dark counter, and for a moment we just stand there with our mouths open, because we are small, and the sky is not.

"Now," says Dr. Reyes. "Finding one invisible point in all of that sounds impossible. So we cheat. We use the stars we can see."

She points. "There — the teapot of Sagittarius. Follow the spout. Now slide over to that bright pair. Now stop."

We stop. Between two ordinary stars there is a patch of nothing. Just dark. Just empty sky.

"There," she says quietly. "That is where {star_name} dances with her invisible partner. You cannot see the black hole. You will never see it. But you can find it — by the way everything around it moves."

Professor Wobble has gone very quiet, which for him is a kind of reverence. Then he squeaks, softly, "I see you, little nothing."

He hands us a star chart and a silver pen. "You do the honours."

We circle the dark spot. The pen scratches. The circle shines.

"Now you know the secret handshake," says Dr. Reyes. "Any clear night, you can find that patch of sky and know exactly what is hiding in it."

We fold the chart and tuck it into a pocket, close and safe. Somewhere up there, {star_name} is still racing around her partner in the dark.

"Goodnight, you two," we whisper. "We know you're there."

c1.question: "The star is dancing with something we can't see. Do we follow the dancer, or peek at the dance floor?"

options.label: Track the racing star itself and measure its speed
Look beside the star's path at the space around it

c2.question: "Photo night is here, friends! Do we stay glued to the screen for the big reveal, or step outside and find our invisible friend in the real sky?"

options.label: Stay inside and watch the worldwide telescopes reveal the black hole's shadow
Go onto the rooftop and locate the dark spot among the constellations

star_name.role: The fast-orbiting star we are watching

snack.role: The midnight snack Professor Wobble shares during the long telescope wait

s1.text:
Captain Marek has a boat with a name we get to choose. What shall we call her? The Moth? Good. The Moth it is. We are her crew tonight, and we are going sailing in the dark.

The harbor is sleepy. Ropes creak. Water goes plip, plip against the wooden sides. Captain Marek spreads out a big paper chart on his knees and holds the lantern close. His finger traces a dotted line across the paper, past the harbor, past the last buoy, to a tiny island with a tiny lighthouse drawn in ink.

"There," he says. "We will get there the old way. No compass. Just the stars."

"Just the stars?" we ask.

"Just the stars," he says. "Sailors did it for a thousand years. So can we."

He pushes off, and the Moth slides out into the black water. Behind us the town lights shrink smaller and smaller, like somebody turning down a lamp. And as our eyes get used to the dark, the sky begins to fill. First a hundred stars. Then a thousand. Then more than anyone could ever count.

"Now," says Captain Marek, "we find the one that stays."

s2a.text: Captain Marek points up, and there it hangs, bigger than we ever imagined: the Big Dipper, seven bright stars making a giant ladle in the sky. "Find the two stars at the end of the cup," he says. We reach up with one finger and trace the dotted line between them, just like on his paper chart, up and up past the edge of the Dipper's bowl. The line lands on a single star, not the brightest, not the biggest, but holding perfectly still while all the others seem to drift around it. "Polaris," says the captain. "The North Star. For a thousand years, sailors found their way across black oceans by that one steady light." We look at it a long moment, and it looks back, small and sure. "Now you know the secret," he says. "But the night is long, and the sky won't sit still for us forever."

s2b.text: "Lie back," says Captain Marek, so we stretch out flat on the deck boards, the wood still warm from the day's sun. "Watch." Down low, almost touching the horizon, one bright light shines steady and unblinking. "That's not a star," he says. "That's a planet. A neighbor waving hello." We watch and watch until our necks feel long, and slowly we see it: the whole sky is turning, wheeling like a giant slow top. Nobody says anything for a while. The water goes plip, plip. Then the captain points, and we trace the dotted line with our finger to the center of the wheel. Polaris. The one dot that stays put while everything else spins around it. "Now," says Captain Marek, "you feel it moving. But what is that still center for?"

s3.text:
A gentle hand shakes us awake. 'Come and see,' whispers Captain Marek. 'The sky has been busy while you slept.'

We sit up, blankets tight around our shoulders. The boat is quiet. The water is black glass. And the stars—oh, the stars have moved. But one star has not moved at all. It hangs exactly where it always was, steady and bright and sure. We hold still and look at it, and it holds still too.

'You found something out there,' says the captain, nodding at the sky. 'Now let me show you something sailors have trusted for a thousand years.'

From his coat he pulls a small brass tool on a loop of string. It glints in the dark. 'This is the curious one,' he says. 'It always wants to know exactly how high the North Star floats.'

He holds it up, arm straight, and squints along its edge. 'Your turn.'

The brass is cool in our fingers. We hold it up, and the string hangs down, and there—right at the top—sits the star that never wanders. We are navigators now, measuring the night with our own two hands.

'The island is still out there,' says Captain Marek. 'But now we know which way is north.'

s4a.text:
'North is ours,' says Captain Marek. 'Who wants to steer her in?'

We do. We do!

The tiller is smooth wood, worn by a hundred hands. It feels big in ours. 'Keep the star over my shoulder,' says the captain, sitting very still, 'and you cannot go wrong.'

So we steer. The Moth hums through the dark water. When the bow drifts, the star slides sideways—and we pull it back, pull it back, until it floats over the captain's shoulder again, steady as a button sewn on the sky.

'You're navigating,' he says softly. 'Truly navigating.'

Then—light. A great warm beam sweeps out from the island and finds us, turning slowly. It touches our faces, and we do not say anything at all. It goes on around, and comes back, and touches us again. The lighthouse and the North Star, shaking hands above the sea.

Inside, the keeper is waiting. Her name is Wren. 'Ships use my lamp close in,' she says, 'and the star far out. They're partners.' She presses something small into each of our palms—a brass star, stamped with an arrow pointing up.

We sail home at pink dawn, steering by the memory of the light. And whenever we hold our brass star up to the sky, the arrow points the way.

s4b.text:
The wind drops. The sail goes soft as a sleeping cat.

'Well,' says Captain Marek, listening. 'The wind has gone to bed. So we do what sailors do—we anchor in the cove and row.'

The little rowboat goes plip, plip across water black and still. The island waits, dark and quiet, and at the top of it Wren the keeper holds a lantern low. 'Quickly,' she whispers. 'The sky won't wait forever.'

We climb. Round and round the lighthouse stairs, up and up, while below us the great lamp turns slowly, doing its night's work.

At the top, Wren opens the door to the whole sky.

Oh. Stars everywhere, wheeling slowly above the sea, the whole great turning of it spread out like a map too big for any table. And there, in the middle of it all, the star that stays. We lean on the rail and watch it turn. Nobody says anything. We don't need to.

'There,' says Wren at last, pointing low across the water, 'is where the Sun will rise, and end the stars' shift.' Then she presses something smooth into each of our hands—a piece of sea glass, soft as a secret. 'A fallen star,' she says, 'that found its way home.'

We sail in at dawn, holding our stars, knowing the way north forever.

c1.question: "The sky's awake and waiting, crew. Do we hunt the North Star right now, with the Dipper as our arrow, or do we lie back on the deck first and let the whole sky show us its slow turning?"

options.label: Find the North Star now using the Big Dipper's pointer stars
Lie on deck and watch the sky slowly wheel before finding the star

c2.question: "North is ours, and the island's close. Shall we sail her straight in, one of you on the tiller steering by the star, or drop anchor in the cove and row ashore to see the sky from the top of the lighthouse itself?"

options.label: Take the tiller and sail to the island guided by Polaris
Row ashore and climb the lighthouse to watch the wheeling sky from the top

s1.text:
"Quick — she's about to start," says Theo, waving us down the street. Theo is the sculptor's apprentice, twelve years old, with grey dust on his eyelashes, and he has promised us something worth hurrying for: today, a statue gets born.

The street smells of rain and chalk. Our shoes tick on the pavement. And then we see it — a tall old workshop with windows the size of doors, and two doors the size of... well, doors.

Two of them. Side by side.

The first has a little wooden sign, spattered and finger-smudged with clay. It says: THIS WAY. COME AND GET MUDDY.

The second door is painted white, and its sign has no smudges at all. Just four words, carved deep into the wood: NO SECOND CHANCES.

"Why would one studio need two doors?" we ask.

Theo grins — but he doesn't answer. Not yet. He just pushes the clay door open, and the smell that rolls out is cool and earthy, like digging in the garden after a storm.

Inside, the studio is enormous. Shelves of tools. Lumps of grey clay wrapped in wet cloth. And in the far corner — something that makes us stop walking.

A block of white marble, taller than a grown-up, taller than two grown-ups, sitting on a wooden cradle. Nobody goes near it. Even Theo's voice drops.

"That," he whispers, "is the giant. It's been sleeping there all winter. Signora Alba says you don't wake a giant until you know exactly what you're doing."

The marble glows faintly in the morning light, smooth and pale and very, very patient.

"Wake it?" we say. "You mean she's going to carve it?"

"This morning," says Theo. "One chip at a time. And every chip that comes off—" he points at a bin by the door, brimming with pale stone flakes, "—can never, ever go back. That's what the white door means."

He picks up a lump of clay and presses it into our hands. It's cool. It's soft. It squishes between our fingers like it wants to become something.

"But this door," Theo says, "this door forgives everything. Watch."

s2a.text:
We push the muddy door wide.

"Good choice," says Theo. "This is where things get squishy."

Inside, Signora Alba is standing at a long table, sleeves rolled up, grey clay streaked across her apron like stripes on a badger. She doesn't say hello. She just holds out a lump of clay, cool and damp, and presses it into our hands.

"Squish it," she says. "That's the first rule."

We squish. It gives way between our fingers, soft as bread dough, and it feels wonderful.

"Now watch."

She takes a small lump and rolls it between her palms. Then — pinch — a nose. Press — a chin. A tiny squeeze with her thumbnail, and suddenly there's an ear. She isn't cutting anything away. She's adding on, bit by bit, building a little face out of nothing.

"That's modelling," says Theo. "You add. Clay always lets you add."

He points at a shelf behind him. On it sits a lumpy, cracked little figure with one arm much longer than the other.

"My first try," he says proudly. "Terrible, right?"

Then he picks up a dented figure from the table, squashes it flat with both hands, rolls it into a ball, adds a splash of water, and starts again. Just like that.

"See?" he grins. "Nothing wasted. Nothing ruined."

And we notice — the bin by this door is completely empty. Not one scrap of clay in it. Because every bit goes back. Every mistake gets another chance.

Signora Alba squints at our hand. Then at the clay. Then back at our hand. She's copying the exact bend of our fingers, one knuckle at a time.

"Hold still," she murmurs. "Your hand is teaching me."

We hold very still. Our clay is warm now, and it feels like it's waiting.

But through the wall — faint, sharp — we hear it. Tap. Tap. Tap.

The other door. The white one.

"What's happening in there?" we whisper.

Theo's smile goes quiet. "The giant," he says. "She's waking it up."

s2b.text:
We pull the white door open.

It's heavier than we expected. The hinges don't creak — they hum, low and serious, like the door itself is thinking about whether to let us in.

Inside, everything is pale. Pale floor, pale dust, pale light falling through a high window. And there, in the middle of it all, stands the giant.

Up close, the marble block is even bigger. Taller than the door we just walked through. Its surface is smooth and cold-looking, like the side of a river stone, but enormous.

Signora Alba stands beside it with a chisel in her hand.

"Feel this," she says, and holds it out.

We take it. It's heavier than it looks — the metal cool, the wooden handle worn smooth. A serious tool. Not a toy.

"Now watch."

She places the chisel against the marble. One tap with the mallet. Tink. A small white chip spins off and lands on the floor.

She picks it up and holds it in her palm.

"That chip," she says, "can never go back. Not with glue. Not with wishing. It's off. It's done."

She points at the bin by the door. It's brimming — overflowing with pale stone flakes, hundreds of them, thousands, each one a decision that can't be unmade.

"That's why the sign says what it says," Theo whispers behind us.

Signora Alba walks slowly around the block. One hand trailing along its cool surface. She stops. Tilts her head.

"There's someone inside," she says quietly. "There always is. My job is to find them — and not take away one chip too many."

We stare at the marble. And for a moment — just a moment — we think we can see it too. A shape. Waiting.

The whole studio feels like it's holding its breath.

Then, through the wall, we hear something completely different. A wet, happy squelch. Laughter.

"That's the other room," says Theo. "Want to know why it sounds so cheerful?"

s3.text:
We follow Theo across the studio, under a low stone arch hung with damp cloths, into a room we have not seen yet.

And there it is. The giant — right here, close enough to touch, glowing like snow that never got cold. And the sculptor herself stands beside it, one hand flat on the marble, as gentle as someone resting a hand on a sleeping dog.

"You found something," says Signora Alba, not turning round. "Tell me on the way. We are nearly ready."

On the workbench next to the giant sits something small and grey. A clay model — no bigger than a loaf of bread — and it is the giant's twin. Same pose. Same tilt of the head. Same everything, in miniature.

Theo leans close. "Wait," he says. "You made it twice?"

"Three times," says Signora Alba. "The first two were wrong. Clay does not mind being wrong." She picks up a strange tool — two metal legs, like a compass with no pencil — and touches one point to the clay model's shoulder, one to its chin. Then she lifts it across to the marble and checks the same two spots on the giant. "Calipers," she says. "They measure, so I do not have to guess. Clay lets me make every mistake first, where mistakes are free. Marble charges for every one."

She marks a spot on the white stone with a stub of chalk. Just a dot. The smallest beginning.

"So the two doors," says Theo slowly, grin spreading across his dusty face, "aren't rivals. One is for practising. One is for committing."

"Now you understand my studio," says Signora Alba, and she lifts her chisel.

But Theo is frowning at the little grey model, because a bigger question has just walked into his head. "Wait. If statues are this old — older than everything — then which came first, back at the very beginning? The forgiving one, or the one that never forgives?"

s4a.text:
"That," says Signora Alba, "is a question for the keeper of old stone." She leads us out through the quiet streets to the museum, where a woman with a magnifying glass is waiting among the statues.

"Come and see," the conservator says. Her gallery is cool and still, full of white faces watching from their pedestals. She stops beside a marble hand, five hundred years old, each finger smooth as soap. "Look close."

We lean in. There — on the thumb — a tiny extra groove, thin as a hair.

"The chisel slipped," she says. "One slip, half a second, five hundred years ago. The stone kept it. Stone keeps everything." She says it the way you'd talk about a friend who never forgets a birthday.

Then she shows us a Roman face, older than old, its nose chipped, its expression perfectly calm. "Two thousand years," she says, "and he is still exactly what his sculptor meant him to be. That is the other side of the secret. The same hardness that never forgives a mistake is what lets the finished statue last forever."

It clicks. We can hear it click. The white door isn't cruel — it's the reason anything survives at all.

Before we leave, the conservator presses something into our palm. A small marble chip, cool and smooth, from a restoration bin. "A piece of forever," she says. "It will outlive all of us."

On the walk home it sits in our pocket, heavy for its size, and Theo keeps reaching in to check it's still there.

"So clay is for finding the statue," he says, "and stone is for keeping it."

"And now," we say, "we're keeping a little piece of the keeping."

The chip stays cool all the way home. It will probably stay cool forever.

s4b.text:
"That," says Signora Alba, "is a question for the people who pour fire." She wraps our little clay figure — the one we squished and shaped ourselves — in cloth, and leads us down the street to the foundry.

We hear it before we see it. Roaring. Then the door opens and the heat rolls out like a giant's breath.

Inside, furnaces glow orange, and moulds stand in rows like sandcastles waiting for the tide. A foundry worker in a heavy apron waves us over. "Just in time," she says. "The furnace cools at four."

She presses our clay figure into a box of sand and lifts it out again, leaving a perfect figure-shaped hollow. Then — this is the clever part — she pours in hot wax, lets it set, and packs a new mould around the wax. "The wax melts out," she says, "and leaves a space exactly your figure's shape. Watch."

The crucible tips. Bronze pours out, glowing orange, liquid as soup, and runs into the space the wax left behind. We hold our breath and watch.

"Clay forgives everything," the worker says, "so you can get it right. Then the right one gets poured into metal, and metal never forgets. Your soft little lump is becoming a statue that could outlive its maker."

It clicks. The clay door isn't just for practising — it's the first step on the road to forever.

When the mould cracks open, there it is: our figure, in bronze, gleaming. The worker grins. "I made two. This one's twin is yours."

She wraps it in cloth and gives it to us. Cool at last. It took all night to stop being dangerous.

All the way home, Theo carries it like a baby bird. "It was mud," he keeps saying. "It was mud, and now it's forever."

"Squish first," we say. "Shine later."

And the little bronze horse — because that is what it turned out to be — warms our pocket the whole way home.

c1.question: "Two doors, two totally different sounds behind them — squelching on one side, chipping on the other. Which do we open first: the muddy one, or the one that says 'no second chances'?"

options.label: Open the clay-spattered door first
Open the 'no second chances' door first

c2.question: "The mystery's nearly solved, but there's one last clue, and it's split in two hiding places. Do we hunt it in the quiet museum with all the old stone faces, or in the roaring foundry where they pour fire into moulds?"

options.label: Follow the conservator to the marble gallery
Follow the foundry worker to the bronze pour

s1.text:
