Pip had pockets full of moon rocks and a plan that was not really a plan.

"Just one little peek," Pip whispered, and slipped through the open hatch of the Sun-Far Express.

Inside, everything hummed. A round navigation globe glowed on its stand, and an old woman in a star-covered shawl was settling into the pilot's seat.

"Well," said Mrs. Nova, not even turning around. "You must be my stowaway."

Pip froze. "I'm a moon-rock collector," Pip said, which was true, mostly.

"A collector." Mrs. Nova smiled at the window, where the Sun blazed huge and gold, filling nearly the whole glass. "Then you are in the right ship. I'm going to see Saturn's rings one last time. Every planet on the way. Rusty, say hello."

"Hello, hello!" chirped a little robot at the controls. "Welcome aboard, stowaway!"

The globe spun and glowed brighter. "Route confirmed!" it announced in a warm, round voice. "Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune! Eight planets, from nearest the Sun to farthest!"

Pip's eyes went wide. "A pebble from every planet," Pip breathed. "In order."

"In order," Mrs. Nova agreed. "Strap in, collector."

The engines rumbled. The huge Sun slid sideways in the window.

And they were off.

s2a.text:
Mercury!" announced the navigation globe, glowing brighter. "First planet! So close to the Sun, and almost no atmosphere to hold the heat!"

Mrs. Nova landed gently on grey, dusty ground. "Rusty," she said, "the shields."

Rusty zipped over with two shiny heat shields. "One for you, one for me!" he chirped. "Follow me, collector. I know the good spot."

Pip followed Rusty to where a tall rock cast a long shadow. "Stand right here," said Rusty, "where the shadow meets the light."

Pip stood with one foot in sunlight, one in shade. The sunny side of the shield grew warm as an oven. The shady side felt like deep winter, all at once.

"Hot and cold!" Pip laughed. "On the same planet!"

"Almost no air to carry the warmth around," said Mrs. Nova. "So the heat stays where the Sun puts it."

Pip bent down and picked up a small grey pebble, still warm on one side, cool on the other. Into the pocket it went.

In the window, the Sun was still huge, but not quite as huge.

"One pebble," said Pip.

"Seven to go," said Mrs. Nova.

s2b.text:
"Venus!" announced the navigation globe, glowing golden. "Second planet! Farther from the Sun than Mercury, but hotter — the hottest of all!"

"Hotter?" said Pip. "But it's farther away!"

"Wait and feel," said Mrs. Nova, landing softly under thick golden clouds.

Rusty brought two puffy white suits. "Cloud suits!" he chirped. "The air down there is thick as soup. These keep us comfy. Follow me, I know the clear patch."

Pip stepped out beneath the clouds. Everything glowed dim and gold, like evening inside a lantern. The ground was warm under Pip's boots — warm everywhere, all over, all at once.

"The clouds wrap the whole planet like a blanket," said Mrs. Nova. "The heat gets in, but it can't get out."

"So a blanket beats being close!" said Pip.

"On Venus, it does."

Pip found a smooth yellowish pebble, warm all the way through, like a stone left in the sun. Into the pocket it went.

In the window, the Sun had shrunk a little smaller.

"Two pebbles," said Pip.

"Six to go," said Mrs. Nova.

s3.text:
The Sun-Far Express sailed on, and a blue-green marble swam into the window.

"Earth!" sang the navigation globe, glowing bright. "Third planet from the Sun — and we are leaving the inner planets behind!"

Mrs. Nova slowed the ship. "Look back, collector. Really look."

Pip pressed close to the glass. White clouds swirled over blue seas and green land, soft as paint in water. "It looks alive," Pip whispered.

"It is," said Mrs. Nova. "Earth is the only planet with liquid water on its surface. The only one with an atmosphere we can breathe." She tapped the window gently. "Not too hot. Not too cold. Just the right distance from the Sun."

Rusty leaned against Pip's shoulder to see. "Lucky old Earth," he beeped.

Pip pulled out the pebbles from the journey so far and turned them over — grey one, yellow one, and now the newest find, still warm from being found. "They're all so different," Pip said. "Same Sun. Such different worlds."

"Distance changes everything," said Mrs. Nova. "And we are about to go very far indeed."

Pip looked at the window. The Sun was smaller now — no longer a huge blazing disc, but a bright gold coin, shrinking.

"What will it be like out there?" Pip asked. "So far from the Sun?"

"Cold," said Mrs. Nova, smiling. "And full of surprises. Strap in, collector. The giant planets are waiting."

The engines rumbled. Earth slid behind them, blue and bright and home.

s4a.text:
The Sun-Far Express dipped toward a world the color of brick dust. "Mars!" sang the navigation globe. "Fourth planet from the Sun — and getting chilly!"

Rusty popped open a hatch and pulled out three pairs of chunky boots. "Dust boots!" he beeped. "So we don't sink!"

The ground crunched underfoot, red as far as Pip could see. They climbed a dune that rose like a slow red wave, and at the top, Mrs. Nova pointed. "Olympus Mons. Tallest volcano in the whole solar system."

It didn't look like a mountain. It looked like the sky had hunched one enormous shoulder.

The Sun hung low, a small orange button. Around it, the sky turned blue — a deep, dusty blue, like twilight on Earth but thinner, stranger.

"Why is Mars red?" Pip asked.

"Rust," said the globe, glowing. "The dust is full of rusty iron!"

Pip picked up a pebble, dark red and rough. It felt cold even through the glove. The thermometer on Rusty's arm blinked: freezing.

"It's beautiful," Pip whispered.

"It is," said Mrs. Nova. "And it only gets colder from here."

Pip looked at the window as they lifted off. The Sun was smaller again — a bright seed, shrinking.

s4b.text:
The Sun-Far Express rose above a sea of striped clouds, and the ship tilted so everyone could see down.

"Jupiter!" sang the navigation globe, glowing so bright it hummed. "Fifth planet from the Sun — and we are very, very far now!"

Beneath them, the Great Red Spot rolled like a slow red ocean, wide as a world. Lightning flickered inside it, silent and deep.

"How big is that storm?" Pip breathed.

"Bigger than Earth," said Mrs. Nova. "Jupiter is so large, all the other planets could fit inside it."

Rusty pressed his face to the glass. "It's like a giant marble that never stops swirling!"

Pip watched the bands of orange and white curl and fold, slow as honey. The thermometer on Rusty's arm blinked: deep cold, colder than Mars, colder than anything.

"Can I collect a pebble here?" Pip asked.

Mrs. Nova smiled. "Jupiter has no surface to land on. Just clouds, all the way down. But—" She reached into a pouch and held out a smooth stone, striped orange and cream. "From the last time I was here. A gift, collector."

Pip held it up to the window. The Sun was a bright star now, small and sharp among other stars.

"We're really out here," Pip whispered.

"We are," said Mrs. Nova. "And Saturn is waiting."

c1.question: "First stop, young collector. Shall we visit Mercury, where the Sun is three times bigger, or Venus, where the clouds glow like gold?"

options.label: Visit Mercury first
Visit Venus first

c2.question: "We're far from the Sun now, and the cold is deepening. Would you rather see Mars, the red world with the tallest volcano, or Jupiter, the giant with a storm bigger than Earth?"

options.label: Visit Mars
Visit Jupiter

stories.title: The Tangle in the Hot Water

s1.text:
Down, down, down we go, in my trusty submersible, {submersible_name}. It's a good ship, mostly. The lights are bright, the buttons beep, and the kettle usually works. Outside the window, the water gets darker and darker, until it's blacker than the bottom of a well. But we are not alone. Look! A little fish with a light on its head, like a tiny reading lamp. It blinks at us. We blink back.

We're heading for the mid-ocean ridge, a long, long mountain range at the bottom of the sea. There are no trees, no snow, just stone pillows, soft when new, hard when cold, and always in the way. That's where my friend lives: Professor Pincers, the yeti crab. He's very clever. He wears a diving helmet made from a giant clam shell and carries three wrenches, even though he only has two claws. I never asked about the third wrench. It seemed rude.

Suddenly, the radio crackles. "Mayday! Mayday! Is that you?" It's the Professor. His voice is wobbly. "My garden! My beautiful, fuzzy garden is fading!" His garden is not flowers. It's a field of bacteria, tiny living specks that he farms on his own claws. They live on chemical energy, not sunshine. It's the only snack bar for miles. "Come quickly!" he squeaks. "Bring your biggest brain!"

We push the lever. {submersible_name} hums a little faster. Ahead, a shimmery glow rises from the seafloor, like heat rising from a hot road. The hydrothermal vent field. Whole neighborhoods of animals crowd around the hot vents in the dark, a bustling underwater city. But something is wrong. The tube worms are droopy. The water is cloudy. And there, on a pillow of stone, is Professor Pincers, waving all three wrenches in a panic.

s2a.text: "Follow my claw! Follow my claw!" shouts Professor Pincers, waving it so hard his helmet wobbles. "It's doing the wiggling!" We steer {submersible_name} after his pointing claw, bumping over the stone pillows. Bump. Bump. "Pardon me," I say to one particularly lumpy pillow. The water here is cloudy and thick, like soup left too long on the stove. The Professor scuttles ahead, his three wrenches clanking against his shell. We turn a corner, and there it is. A black smoker chimney, big as a house, has toppled over. It lies across the vent opening like a giant dropped a stone log across a doorway. The hot water that should be bubbling up is trapped underneath. "My bacteria!" the Professor wails. "They're starving! No chemical energy means no food!" The tube worms nearby are drooping, their red plumes pale as old socks. The water feels cold. Very cold. And getting colder.

s2b.text: "Quick! The thermometer!" Professor Pincers cries, tapping the glass of his helmet with a wrench. "We must know how much chemical energy we've lost!" I grab the long probe and stick it out the window of {submersible_name}. The numbers flash. Twenty degrees. Then fifteen. Then ten. "It's dropping fast," I say, my stomach doing a little flip. "Like a bathtub when the plug is pulled." The Professor scuttles over, his claws clicking on the seafloor. He points a wrench at the gauge. "Without the hot water, the chemical energy stops flowing," he says, his voice very small. "My bacteria can't make food. And if they can't make food..." He doesn't finish. He doesn't have to. We both look at the tube worms. Their red plumes are pale and droopy, like flowers that haven't been watered in a week. The whole neighborhood is hungry. And the water is getting colder by the minute. We have to fix this. Now.

s3.text:
"Right," says Professor Pincers, tapping his clam-shell helmet. "Time for brute force. Rosie, fetch!"

I push the lever. {submersible_name} glides forward, and out swings Rosie, my trusty robotic arm. She is very strong. She is not very clever. I aim her right at the lump of pillow lava blocking the vent, the one we need to move. "Grab it," I whisper. "Gently."

Rosie grabs. And squishes. The pillow is still hot and soft, like dough that has not finished baking. It oozes between her metal fingers and sticks there in long grey strings. "Oh, Rosie," I sigh. She looks embarrassed, or as embarrassed as a robotic arm can look.

"Plan B!" shouts the Professor, waving a wrench. "Blast it with water! Cold water! That will loosen it!"

I aim the thruster hose. Whoosh! The cold water hits the hot pillow, and we both watch it happen: the doughy rock freezes solid in an instant, harder than before, a great stone plug sitting smack on top of the vent. 

Thunk. That is the sound of two plans failing.

The Professor's claws droop. His fuzzy garden droops too. But then I notice something. The water above the vent is shimmering, wiggling, like the air over a hot road. The heat is still down there, pushing, shoving, trying to get out. The current itself is nudging at that plug, again and again, like a shoulder against a stuck door.

"Professor," I say slowly. "What did you just find out there? Because I think the water wants to help us." His eyes go wide. The third wrench twitches. "Tell me everything," he whispers. "And then... we stop pushing. And we let the mountain push for us."

s4a.text:
“Thrusters!” I shout. “Rosie, hold tight!”

I swing {submersible_name} around until our nose points with the shimmer, not against it. The water is already pushing, a warm river in the dark. We just have to add our voice to its song.

“On three,” says Professor Pincers, climbing onto the window ledge. His eyes are bright. “One. Two. THREE!”

I push the lever. WHOOSH! Our thrusters blast, and the shimmer current catches us, lifts us, carries us forward like a giant invisible hand. We are surfing on hot water! The Professor whoops and waves a wrench.

The current hits the plug. Pebbles and grey strings of hard lava tumble away like crumbs off a table. Smaller stones dance. And then—

POP!

The plug spins free, and hot water bursts up in a shimmering column, black and glittering. The vent is open!

The tube worms shoot up like red fireworks. The Professor leaps from the ledge and lands smack in the warm flow, claws waving, his fuzzy garden drinking in the chemical energy. He does a little dance, right there on the seafloor, three wrenches jingling.

Later, when the celebrating is done, he presses something into my hand. A small stone, cool and smooth, shaped like a lumpy pillow. “For your shelf,” he says. “Soft when new, hard when cold. Like all the best ideas.”

We wave goodbye and rise, rise, rise through the dark. In my pocket, the stone pillow sits warm against my leg. Or maybe that’s just me, still smiling.

s4b.text:
“Rosie’s turn,” I whisper. “Slow and steady.”

I ease {submersible_name} closer. Professor Pincers crouches by the window, one claw raised, ready to guide.

“Easy,” he murmurs. “Easy does it.”

Rosie’s metal fingers reach out, slow as syrup, and touch the first loose stone. Nudge. It rolls an inch. The shimmer current catches it, and whoosh—away it goes, tumbling into the dark.

“Again,” says the Professor.

Nudge. Whoosh. Another stone spins free. Nudge. Whoosh. One by one, the pebbles and grey strings drift off, carried away by the water that wants to help. The plug gets smaller. Lighter. The shimmer grows stronger, pushing harder, until—

POP!

The last chunk shoots upward, and hot water explodes out in a glittering black fountain! The vent is clear!

The tube worms stretch tall, tall, taller, their red plumes waving like flags at a parade. Professor Pincers throws both claws in the air and clicks them together so hard his helmet rattles. His fuzzy garden drinks deep, and I swear I see it grow fuzzier right before my eyes.

He disappears for a moment, down to the vent’s edge, and comes back holding something that glitters. A tiny crystal, clear as ice, formed in the hot water’s breath. “For you,” he says, dropping it into my hand. “Proof that gentle wins.”

We rise through the dark, the crystal cool in my pocket. Behind us, the vent shimmers and hums. Ahead, the whole ocean waits. But tonight, one small corner of it is warm and fed and dancing.

c1.question: "My garden is fading! Should we follow my wiggling claw to see what is blocking the hot water, or measure the temperature to see how much chemical energy we have lost?"

options.label: Follow the Professor's pointing claw to find the blockage
Use the sub's sensors to check the water temperature and chemical levels

c2.question: "The water wants to push the rocks loose! Should we ride the shimmer current with our thrusters, or gently nudge the stones with Rosie's arm?"

options.label: Ride the natural current and boost it with the sub's thrusters
Carefully push the stones into the current using the robotic arm

submersible_name.role: The deep-sea submersible the storyteller pilots

s1.text:
I remember being twelve, in the school library at 3:47 p.m., the week our class project page was due. The library smelled of old paper and rain on coats, and on Mrs. Okafor's desk sat the ancient globe lamp, a warm glass Earth glowing like a nightlight the size of a pumpkin.

"Watch this," Dev said, and pressed refresh.

The little circle spun. And spun. And spun some more, the way a ceiling fan spins after you switch it off, not doing anything at all.

"Maybe it's shy," I said.

Then something strange happened. Every screen in the library froze at the same moment. The catalog computer. The checkout screen. The big monitor by the encyclopedias. A dozen spinning circles, all at once, like the whole room had taken a breath and forgotten to let it out.

Everyone looked up. A first-grader by the fish tank said, very seriously, "The internet fell down," and nobody laughed, because honestly, we were all thinking it.

"It's not down," Mrs. Okafor said, tapping her own frozen screen. "It's just not answering. Your request went out there somewhere. The question is where it got stuck."

Out there somewhere. I looked at the glowing globe on her desk, all those little countries painted in faded gold, and it hit me: when you press enter, your question doesn't just float off like dandelion fluff. It travels. Real places. Real machines. Somewhere between this library and wherever {project_page} lives, a dozen computers we'd never see were supposed to answer in a blink — and one of them wasn't.

"Where does a request even go?" I asked out loud.

Dev grinned the grin that meant trouble, the good kind. "Let's trace it. Hop by hop."

Mrs. Okafor pulled a big sheet of paper from her desk drawer and spread it out right under the globe lamp, smooth as a map. "Explorers," she said, "start at the beginning."

s2a.text:
"Restart it," said Dev. "That's rule one. When in doubt, turn it off and on again. Everybody knows that."

"Everybody knows it because it works," I said, and we went looking for Baz.

Baz the technician kept his kingdom in a closet behind the photocopier, a room full of blinking lights and zip-tied cables. He listened to our whole theory, then said the best thing a grown-up can say: "Show me."

He opened a grey box on the wall. Inside sat the library's router, no bigger than a sandwich, covered in little lights. "This is where your request leaves the building," Baz said. "Hop one. Sometimes it just needs a nap."

He unplugged it. The lights blinked out, one by one, like windows going dark at bedtime. We counted to ten under our breath. He plugged it back in.

The lights came up. Red. Red. Yellow.

Green.

"Yes!" we both shouted, because we could not help it. Baz laughed and we sprinted back to the globe lamp, where our map waited. Dev pressed refresh with the ceremony of a knight drawing a sword.

The circle spun.

And spun.

"But the light was green," I said. "Green means go."

"Green means the router's fine," Dev said slowly. Then he looked up. "Wait. The catalog computers."

The catalog computers were humming along, happy as ever. Kids were typing in book titles. The school's network was fine. It had never been the problem at all.

"So hop one answered," Dev said, and he drew a little check mark on our map, right beside the library. "The request leaves here just fine. The broken link is farther down the road."

Farther down the road turned out to be a real road. Baz had followed us out, carrying a short piece of cable cut open so you could see inside it. No copper wires. A thread of glass, thinner than a hair.

"Fiber," he said. He clicked a laser pointer and shone it in one end. A red dot appeared at the other, bright as a ladybug. "That's how your request travels. Light. Cables of glass running under the streets, under the sea, all the way to wherever that page lives. Your question goes out as a blink of light, and the answer blinks back."

I looked at the globe lamp, at all that painted ocean between the countries. Light, swimming along the sea floor, carrying our question.

"So somewhere out there," I said, "a blink of light is getting lost."

"Hop two," said Dev, and uncapped the pen.

s2b.text:
"Test it gently," Dev said. "Before we blame anything, let's see what still works."

He opened a new tab and typed in a different site. Not {project_page}. Just some ordinary page, the kind nobody ever thinks about twice.

It popped up. Instantly. Blink and you'd miss it.

"Ha!" I said. Then, quieter: "Oh. That doesn't actually fix anything."

"No," Dev said, grinning the good-trouble grin. "But it tells us everything. Watch."

He typed a third site. Up it came. A fourth. Instant. Every page on Earth seemed to be answering except ours.

"So the school's network works," I said slowly. "The Wi-Fi works. The request leaves the building happy as anything."

"The network is innocent," Dev announced, and he drew a big check mark on our map, right beside the library. "Cross it off. Our broken link belongs to somebody far away."

Somebody far away. I looked at the globe lamp, glowing warm over our map, all those faded gold countries. Mrs. Okafor was at her desk beneath it, stamping returns, and she had been listening the whole time. Librarians always are.

"You know what a server is?" she said. "It's this desk."

We looked at her desk. It was a desk.

"All day long, everyone asks me things at once," she said. "Where are the dragon books. Can I have more time. Somebody spilled something in the biographies. And I answer, one at a time, as fast as I can. A server is a computer whose whole job is answering. Requests come in from everywhere, and it sends pages back, like me handing books across this desk."

"And if your desk is closed?" Dev asked.

"Then nobody gets their book," she said. "The request arrives at a dark desk, and it waits, and waits."

She tapped the little circle still spinning on our screen.

"Your question is out there right now," she said, "knocking on the door of some server you'll never see, in some building you'll never visit. And that server, for some reason, isn't answering."

I pictured it. Our question, folded like a paper airplane, sailing across the room of the world, and landing on a desk with the lights off.

"So how do we find out where it landed?" I asked.

Dev pulled the map closer. "Hop by hop," he said.

s3.text:
We spread everything on the table under the globe lamp, and the warm glass Earth glowed over our map like it was keeping watch for us. "Okay," Dev said, pulling the laptop close. "Time to follow it for real. There's a tool called a traceroute. It shows every stop a request makes, like a train timetable."

"A train timetable for our question," I said.

"Exactly. Watch." Dev typed, and lines began to appear, one by one. "Hop one, the library. Hop two, the school district. Hop three, some company in the city." Each hop was a different network, owned by a different company, handing our request along like a bucket brigade. Four. Five. Six. Seven. Eight. Nine.

Then the list just stopped.

"Where's ten?" I asked.

Dev leaned in. "That's the thing. There is no ten. Our request gets through nine networks in less time than a blink, and then — nothing. Footprints ending at a locked door."

Mrs. Okafor looked over our shoulders. "So the chain isn't broken in the middle," she said. "It's broken at the very end."

"But wait," I said. "The page is big. Pictures and everything. How does all of that even travel?"

"In pieces," Dev said. "Like a jigsaw puzzle. The server chops the page into little packets, one piece per envelope, and every envelope takes the trip. Right now our envelopes are landing on a desk where nobody's answering."

I closed my eyes and pictured it: our request as a paper airplane, folded neat, sailing across a huge dark room toward a librarian who had fallen asleep at her desk. It lands. It waits. No answer-plane comes back.

"So the server itself is the problem," Dev said slowly. "And we can't restart a machine we don't own."

The globe lamp hummed softly. Nine good hops, one silent one. Somewhere out there, past nine companies' worth of cables, a computer was sitting in the dark with our page inside it.

"Then we need another way to wake it up," I said. "Or another way around."

s4a.text:
"We knock," I said. "Politely."

Dev flipped the page over, and there it was, small as a postage stamp: a hosting address. An actual email. We wrote one sentence — please, our class page won't load — and pressed send, and our airplane sailed off into the dark one more time.

Then we waited. The globe lamp hummed. The clock said 4:15.

Ping.

"It's a person," Dev whispered. A real person, in a city we'd never visited, who owned the very server our page lived on. The machine had crashed, they wrote — just stopped, like a clock that needs winding — and they'd restarted it, and sorry about that, and good luck with the tide pools.

Dev pressed refresh.

The page appeared. All of it. In a blink. The same request that had failed all afternoon — the same words, the same airplane — came home answered, because the librarian had woken up.

"Nothing changed except the answerer," I said.

"Watch this," Dev said, and opened a panel at the bottom of the browser, a waterfall of tiny lines. "Look. That's not one request. It's dozens. One for the words. One for each photo. One just for the font." The lines filled in at different speeds, fast and slow, a whole fleet of answer-planes landing one after another.

I wrote back: thank you. Two words, to a stranger I'd never see.

We folded the map and put it in my bag, and Mrs. Okafor switched off the lamp, and the library went dim and gold at the edges.

I still think of that room of humming librarians, every single time a page loads.

s4b.text:
"Around," I said. "There has to be another road."

"While we think," said Baz, "look at this." He pulled up a video, and there it was: a ship in the middle of the black ocean, hauling a cable up from the deep, a glowing glass thread no thicker than a garden hose, rising past starfish and the shadow of an old wreck. A crew in yellow jackets spliced the broken threads together, patient as people mending a fishing net, so messages could cross the ocean again.

"That's the internet," I said. "A thread in the cold dark, and somebody fixing it."

"And here's the other road," Dev said, typing. "A cached copy. A library keeps a snapshot of pages it's seen before." Yesterday's version of our page appeared — a little faded, half the pictures missing, but there. "See? The server exists. The route around the broken link is real. Lots of roads run between the same two places."

We studied yesterday's tide pools under the glowing globe, and it was enough to go home on.

The next morning, Dev's phone buzzed before first bell. The server's owner had found the crash overnight and restarted the machine. We pressed refresh together, and the page — today's page, whole and bright — answered in a blink. The same airplane. The same question. This time, an answer-plane sailed back.

I remember thinking the internet isn't magic. It's a promise kept by people we'll never meet — and every page that loads is a thank-you note, waiting to be read.

c1.question: "Every guess crosses one suspect off the list," Dev says, spinning the laptop around. "So which suspect do we cross off first?"

options.label: Blame the Wi-Fi: get Baz to restart the router and watch the lights
Try a different website first and see what that proves

c2.question: "The footprints stop at hop ten," Dev says, tapping the screen. "The server's asleep and it's not ours to wake. Do we knock on the owner's door, or find another road around?"

options.label: Email the server's owner and ask them to wake the machine
Hunt for a cached copy and learn how messages route around breaks

project_page.role: The class project webpage that won't load

stories.title: The Thunder Sheet and the Sunset Gel

s1.text: "You two!" calls the stage manager. "You're on crew." She hands us a clipboard and a headset. Not a script. A headset. It smells like dust and old batteries. We follow her behind the curtain, where the air is cooler and the floorboards creak like they're telling secrets. Painted flats lean against the wall—one shows a castle, one shows a forest, one shows a giant sandwich. Ropes hang in loops like sleeping snakes. Up a narrow staircase we climb, into a little room that glows. This is the booth. A window looks down at the empty stage. Two people wait for us. One sits at a board covered in switches. One sits at a table covered in... things. Coconut shells. A metal sheet. A shoebox full of rice. "This is lighting," says the stage manager. "This is sound effects. They'll teach you." The sound effects person grins and picks up the metal sheet. It wobbles. It makes a noise like a garbage can falling down stairs. We laugh. "That," she says, "is thunder. Or it will be, once you learn how to ask it nicely." We look at the stage far below. We look at the switches. We look at the coconut shells. We are not in the spotlight. We are behind the curtain. But the stage manager taps the clipboard. "The show doesn't happen without you," she says. And the headset crackles, like it's listening.

s2a.text: "Thunder," we say. The sound effects person—her name is Mags—hands us the metal sheet. It's heavy and cold. "Hold it by the edge," she says. "Like a pizza. Now wobble it. Slow." We wobble. CLANG. It sounds like a garbage can rolling down stairs. It sounds like a trash truck hitting a pothole. Mags covers her ears. "Too fast," she says. "Old Rumble-Belly likes to take his time." We laugh. We try again. This time we hold our breath. We move our wrists slow, slow, like we're stirring a giant pot of soup. The metal bends. It shivers. Rumble. Rumble. The sound travels through the floorboards, up our legs, into our chests. It sounds like weather coming. It sounds like the sky is thinking about rain. Mags grins. "There," she says. "Now you're asking nicely." The headset crackles. "Cue-to-cue in five minutes," says the stage manager. We look at the sheet. It wobbles. It waits.

s2b.text: "Sunset," we say. The lighting operator—his name is Pip—spins his chair around. "Good choice." He points to the spotlight. "White light is boring. We fix that with gels." He opens a drawer full of colored squares. Thin plastic, like stained glass you can fold. He slides a red one into the slot in front of the lamp. Click. The white circle on the stage floor turns strawberry-red. "Too cold," we say. He tries orange. Fire-orange, like the inside of a pumpkin. "Closer," we say. He tries blue. The stage turns into a cold morning, the kind where you can see your breath. We shiver. "Not that one." Pip taps his chin. "Sunset over the sea," he says. "Needs to be warm. Needs to be pink and gold at the same time." He pulls out a square that looks like nothing special. He slides it in. Click. The stage turns the color of peach skin, of toast, of the sky right before the stars come out. We gasp. "That's it," we whisper. "That's the one."

s3.text: The stage manager lifts her hand. "Cue-to-cue," she says. "Standby lights. Standby sound." A pause. "GO." And the booth comes alive. The spotlight slides across the stage like a slow gold finger. Below us, someone shakes the thunder sheet—gently, gently—and it answers with a low, rolling growl. Not a garbage can this time. Real thunder. The fog machine hums awake. White mist curls onto the stage and starts to rise. It rises. It keeps rising. "Uh oh," says the lighting person. The fog swallows the actors' shoes. Then their knees. Then their whole bodies. Gone. Nothing but a white sea where our actors used to be. "Cut the fog!" calls the stage manager. The machine stops. Slowly, slowly, the mist sinks back down. Two actors reappear, blinking like surprised owls. We can't help it—we laugh. "The fog means well," says the sound effects person. "It just doesn't know when to stop." She shows us the trick. "Count it. One potato, two potato—then off." We try it. One potato, two potato. Click. The fog rolls out low and stays low, hugging the floor like a magic carpet. The actors wade through it, visible from the waist up, floating. "Beautiful," whispers the stage manager. The thunder sheet gives a small, proud wobble. Rumble. Just a little one. Like it knows.

s4a.text: Opening night. The booth is dark. Our headsets crackle. "Standby storm," whispers the stage manager. "GO." We take hold of the thunder sheet. Slow. Slow. We wobble it low, and it answers with a growl that rolls out over the seats. The audience gasps. A real gasp, all at once, like one big lung. The sound effects person grins and slides the spotlight wider. Rain crackles in the speaker. We wobble again, softer, and the storm wanders away over the hills. After the show, she presses something into our hands. A small square of the sunset gel. "For the crew," she says. That night we hold it up to the lamp in our room. The whole wall turns fire-orange. We sit in our own little sunset. "We made them gasp," we say. The gel glows on the dresser, warm as a coal.

s4b.text: Opening night. We stand backstage by the thunder sheet, peeking through a gap in the curtain. "Standby sunset," whispers the stage manager in our headset. "GO." Above us, the lighting operator slides the gel into the spotlight. Click. And the stage becomes a sea at dusk. Orange light spills across the painted waves. The actors glow like they're standing inside a peach. Out front, the audience goes very quiet—the good kind of quiet. The thunder sheet leans against us and gives one small, proud wobble. Rumble. After the show, the set painter beckons us over. She hands us a tiny painted flat—a miniature of the castle wall we braced. "For the crew," she says. It's light enough to carry with one hand. But it holds the whole show. We set it on our shelf at home, where it catches the morning sun. "That's ours," we say. "We helped build that."

c1.question: "You can only learn one tool before the cue-to-cue. Do you want to make the thunder, or paint the sunset?"

options.label: Learn the thunder sheet
Try the spotlight gel

c2.question: "Where do you want to stand when the show starts? In the booth with the sliders, or backstage with the noisemakers?"

options.label: Watch from the lighting booth
Stand by the thunder sheet

s1.text:
Nico counts everything. Stairs on the way up. Windows on the way down. So when we walk the shiny hallway of our old school, past the blue diamond tiles that march along the wall, it is Nico who stops dead.

"Wait," he says. "Count with me. Blue, blue, white. Blue, blue, white."

We count. Blue, blue, white. All the way down the hall, the same little song — until it isn't.

"There!" Nico's finger lands on one blue diamond, right at our height. It is flipped the wrong way. Its point aims at the floor, not the ceiling.

"Somebody set it crooked," I say.

"Mm, no." Mr. Okafor pokes his head out of the bathroom, where he is re-tiling the floor. He shows us how he works: he slides a tile along the ground, flips it like a pancake, turns it till it sits just right. "Tiles don't mind which way they point," he says. "That one wasn't set wrong. It was set differently."

Nico looks at me. I look at the tile. Its point aims at the floor like a finger.

"Who flipped it?" Nico whispers. "And why?"

s2a.text:
"The hall," Nico says. "Come on."

We stand in front of the flipped tile, and Nico runs his finger along the wall, the way Mr. Okafor slides his tiles. "Every flipped one is blue," he says. "And look — they only show up at corners."

We slide along the wall, slow, the way Mr. Okafor does it. Nico counts under his breath. One flipped tile. Then another. Then another.

"Left," Nico says. "Left again. Now right."

The flipped tiles make a trail of turns. We follow them down the old corridor, past the coat hooks, past the radiator that ticks like a clock. Six flips. Six turns.

Then the corridor ends. Blank wall. No door, no cupboard, nothing.

Nico stares. "That's it?"

I touch the wall. It's just wall.

"The flips point somewhere," Nico says. "But where?"

s2b.text:
We find Dee on the porch steps, tapping her foot. Clap, stomp, clap. Clap, stomp, clap.

"Dee," Nico says, "we found a flipped tile in the hall. It points somewhere, but we don't know where."

Dee doesn't answer. She just keeps tapping. Clap, stomp, clap. Clap, stomp —

Her foot comes down early. A stumble. She grins.

"You did that on purpose," I say.

"Did I?" Dee says. She taps it again. Clap, stomp, clap. Clap, stomp — stomp. Early again.

Nico tilts his head. "That's the same as the tile. A break right where you're listening for it."

Dee's grin gets wider. She taps the rhythm one more time, slow. Clap, stomp, clap. Clap, stomp — stomp.

"Six," Nico says. "The early stomp lands on beat six. Same as the hall."

Dee just taps and waits.

s3.text:
Dee is waiting on the school steps, and she does not even say hello. "Well?" she says. "What did you find?"

We tell her. All of it, talking over each other, and her eyes get rounder and rounder until she claps once, sharp. "Grandma Wren," she says. "Now."

Grandma Wren's sewing room smells like warm cotton. Her quilt lies draped over the frame, half finished, soft as a blanket fort. She does not ask what brought us. She just smooths the fabric with one slow hand and says, "What do you notice?"

We look. Nico looks longest.

"The squares," he breathes. "They're turned sideways. But only along this one edge."

He is right. All down one border, the little squares point the wrong way, one after another, like footprints in fabric. A trail. Somebody stitched a trail.

"And here." Dee's finger stops at the corner. One square. Then two. Then four. Each bunch doubling the one before, growing and growing, like the quilt is counting something bigger than itself.

Grandma Wren says nothing. She is smiling at the corner.

Nico grabs my sleeve. "The flipped tile in the hall. It was never the message. It was the arrow." His voice drops to a whisper. "The message is the doubling. It's telling us how big the hidden thing is. And how many breaks to count on the way."

Dee grins her widest grin. "Then we'd better start counting."

s4a.text:
"Inside," we say together.

So we count the breaks backward, out of the sewing room, down the hall. "One," says Nico, where the tiles change color. "Two," says Dee, clapping once at the corner. Three, four, five. At six we stop, and there it is: {hidden_spot}.

Dee pulls the door. Inside, behind a stack of old chalk, sits a tin box gone soft with dust.

Nico lifts the lid. Fabric squares. Dozens of them, the prettiest cloth I have ever seen — tiny flowers, tiny stars, one blue the exact blue of the hallway tiles. And a note, folded small.

"Read it," Dee whispers.

"For whoever counts," Nico reads. "The pattern was mine first. I copied it from the cracks in the dried garden mud, and set it in the wall so it would last. — Mama."

Grandma Wren has followed us, quiet as a cat. "My mother laid those tiles," she says. "Now each of you, pick one square. Keep it."

I take the blue one. Dee takes stars. Nico holds his square up against the wall, and the flipped tile points straight at him.

"It was never crooked," he says softly. "It was the most important tile in the whole building."

And for the first time all day, Nico stops counting.

s4b.text:
"The garden," we say.

So we count the doubling outward, across the playground, one step, two steps, four. Dee claps the rhythm. Nico stomps it. And the garden waits, dry and cracked from the long summer.

"Look at the mud," I say.

It has split into shapes. Six-sided shapes, pressed together like a honeycomb, like a quilt, like —

"The hallway tiles," Nico breathes. "They're the same. Somebody copied the ground."

We count the crack-clusters. One, two, four, doubling, doubling, until the sixth. Dee digs with careful fingers, and there, wrapped in waxed cloth, sits a tin.

Inside: fabric squares, dozens, tiny flowers and tiny stars. And a note. "For whoever counts. The pattern was mine first. I found it in the mud and set it in the wall so it would last. — Mama."

"Grandma Wren's mother," Dee whispers. "She laid the hallway tiles."

Back inside, we each pick one square to keep. Mine is blue as the tiles. And Nico runs his finger along the wall, slow, slower — and stops.

"The vines between the tiles," he says. "They're a maze. And it ends at that little painted door."

We look. We look at each other. Dee grins.

"Tomorrow," says Nico, pocketing his square. "Tomorrow we count that."

c1.question: "We could chase the flips down the hall ourselves," Nico says, "or Dee's on the porch tapping something weird — she might already know. Which way?"

options.label: Trace the flipped tiles along the hallway
Ask Dee about her stumbling rhythm

c2.question: "The doubling tells us how many breaks to count," Grandma Wren says, smoothing the quilt. "But you can count them back inside, or count them out into the garden. Where do you want to follow the pattern?"

options.label: Count the breaks back through the school to the hiding spot
Follow the doubling outside to the cracked-mud garden

hidden_spot.role: the place in the school where the message points and the tin of quilt squares is hidden

stories.title: The Tower That Learned to Wobble

s1.text:
"Did you feel it?" Ren whispers, before we've even knocked. "Last night. My whole bed went wobble, wobble, wobble."

We're standing outside Professor Zinnia Bolt's lab, which used to be a garage, halfway up a hill in Japan. The door is painted with wiggly lines. The doorbell goes ding-rumble-ding.

The door flies open. "Investigators!" cries Professor Zinnia Bolt. Her lab coat is covered in patches, and every patch is a wiggly line. "Come in, come in. The mountain has been talking all night."

Inside, the lab is crammed with homemade gadgets — springs, pendulums, a machine with a pen that scratches away at a long strip of paper. Scratch. Scratch-scratch. The pen is drawing wobbly lines right now, small ones, wobbling along like it's had too much fizzy drink.

"Last night," Zinnia says, tapping the paper, "a real earthquake shook this whole neighbourhood. The pen went wild! Look at these zigzags." The lines leap and jolt across the strip like a heartbeat gone bonkers. "But here's the magnificent mystery. The big shake stopped hours ago. So why is my pen still wobbling?"

Ren is very quiet. He stares at the wiggly lines. "I barely slept," he admits. "Does it mean another big one is coming?"

"A fine question!" Zinnia beams. "And you two are exactly the junior investigators I need."

Then she shows us something. By the doorframe there's a worn spot on the floor. "When the ground trembles, this is where I stand. Doorways are strong." She says it like it's the most ordinary thing in the world, and somehow that makes us feel steadier.

The pen wobbles on. Scratch-scratch. Wobble, wobble.

The mystery is waiting.

s2a.text:
"Interrogate the seismograph!" we shout, and Zinnia spins around like she's been waiting for exactly those words. "Excellent choice, investigators. The machine remembers everything."

She pulls the long paper strip from last night off the machine and spreads it across a table, weighting the corners with teacups. We lean in close. The strip is covered in one enormous zigzag mountain — the pen must have gone completely wild.

"That's the earthquake," Zinnia says, tracing it with one finger. "But look what comes after."

After the big mountain, the line settles into little bumps. Bump. Bump-bump. Smaller and smaller, like a heartbeat calming down.

"Those are aftershocks," she says. "The ground settling. Like hiccups after a sneeze — one big achoo, then hic, hic, hic, while everything finds its place again."

Ren stares at the little bumps. "So the hiccups aren't... a countdown? To something worse?"

"No," Zinnia says gently. "Aftershocks get smaller and fade away. And nobody — not me, not anyone — can predict exactly when one will come. So instead of guessing, we measure. We prepare. That's the whole job."

She crosses the room and pulls a giant rolled-up map from a cardboard tube. It unfurls across the floor with a fwump. "Now look at this. The Earth's outside shell is cracked into enormous pieces, called plates. They creep along about as fast as your fingernails grow."

"That's so slow," Ren breathes.

"Slow, but they never stop. And where two plates grind past each other — a plate boundary — the rock sticks, and strains, and then suddenly slips. That's an earthquake." She taps the map. "And here is Japan, sitting right where several plate boundaries meet. We live on the crack, investigators!"

Ren looks at the map, then at the little hiccup bumps on the strip. He's still quiet, but it's a different kind of quiet now — the thinking kind.

"We should keep this," we say, pointing at the strip.

"Take it," Zinnia says, rolling it up and pressing it into our hands. "A clue for your pocket."

s2b.text:
"The shake table!" we shout, and Zinnia actually applauds. "Follow the wobble-o-meter!"

The wobble-o-meter is a brass arrow bolted to the wall, wobbling back and forth, pointing down a corridor. We follow it — past a shelf of springs, under a hanging pendulum — into a room the size of a garage, where an enormous metal platform fills the floor.

"My shake table," Zinnia says proudly. Along the wall sit shelves of towers built from wooden blocks, and one beautiful model skyscraper with tiny windows. "Every tower I build, I test right here."

She pulls a lever. The whole platform starts to rumble, side to side, and the block towers tremble and sway. Rumble. Rumble-rumble.

Ren grabs our sleeve. "Whoa."

"Now — how mighty was last night?" Zinnia lifts a glass jar off a shelf. Inside are firecrackers. "This is how I think about magnitude. Magnitude is the size we measure a quake with. Imagine one firecracker — pop — that's about a magnitude five. But a magnitude six isn't a little bit bigger. It's about thirty firecrackers. Every whole number up, thirty times the energy."

"Thirty?" Ren's eyes go wide.

"Thirty. Last night's rumble was a modest pop, as pops go." She sets the jar down and her voice goes a little rueful. "But it knocked my best tower completely flat. Look."

On the end of the table sits a heap of scattered blocks. Zinnia pokes it with one finger. "Every design I've tried, the table beats it eventually. I need a tower that survives. And I need investigators to help me build it."

The table rumbles on beneath our feet. Ren watches the towers sway, and then he asks the question that changes everything.

"Wait," he says slowly. "Why does the ground shake here at all?"

s3.text:
"What did you find?" Zinnia asks, peering at us like we're specimens. "Show me."

We tell her. She listens, nodding so hard her goggles slip down her nose. "Yes! Yes, exactly!" she cries, and sweeps an arm toward the corner where a big map of the world hangs beside a low table. "Come. Time you saw the whole picture."

The map is covered in wiggly lines, of course. Zinnia taps one that runs right under Japan. "The Earth's shell isn't one solid piece," she says. "It's cracked into giant plates, like a jigsaw puzzle that's too big to see. And they move. Slowly. About as fast as your fingernails grow."

Ren leans over the map. "That's it? That's what made my bed wobble?"

"Not quite." Zinnia rummages in a drawer and pulls out two foam puzzle pieces. She presses them together, edge to edge. "Watch. The plates creep along, but their edges catch. They stick." She pushes harder. The foam bends. Strains. We hold our breath.

SNAP. The pieces jolt past each other, and the whole table rattles.

"That!" Zinnia shouts, delighted. "Stuck edges suddenly slipping. That's an earthquake. Last night's quake happened on a plate boundary right under us."

Ren's shoulders drop. He lets out a long breath. "So it has a reason," he says. "It's not just... angry."

"Never angry," Zinnia says. "Just stuck."

Then her seismograph pen gives a fresh hiccup. Scratch-scratch-WOBBLE. Zinnia grins. "But knowing why the ground shakes is one thing. My towers still fall down. So now—" she spins toward a strange platform in the corner, bristling with springs and clamps— "we build."

s4a.text:
"We build!" we shout, because we cannot help it.

Zinnia heaves a box of wooden blocks onto the shake table. "One tower. My table, full rumble. Build!"

Our first tower is tall and skinny, a proper skyscraper. Zinnia presses the big red button. Rumble. RUMBLE. The tower topples before the table even gets going. Ren snorts, then claps a hand over his mouth. "Sorry," he says, grinning. "It fell over SO fast."

"Splendid data!" Zinnia cries. "Again!"

So we build low and wide and stiff, every block wedged tight. Rumble. RUMBLE. This one holds for three whole seconds — then cracks right down the middle and collapses in two sad heaps.

"Too wobbly, then not wobbly enough," Ren groans. "What does this table WANT?"

Then he stops. On the shelf behind Zinnia sits a little model skyscraper, and its bottom isn't stuck down at all. It rests on bendy joints, like ankles. Ren touches it, and it sways, and sways back.

"Professor. Your tower wobbles."

Zinnia's eyes go huge. "It does, doesn't it."

We rebuild one more time, with wobble room in the base — loose joints, give in them, room to move. "Full rumble!" Zinnia roars, and slams the button.

The table shakes. The floor hums under our shoes. And our tower sways like a tree in wind, this way, that way, this way —

—and stands.

"IT WOBBLED AND IT STOOD!" Zinnia stamps our design into her notebook, WHUMP, like a passport. "Buildings survive by moving WITH the shake, not fighting it!"

As we leave, she snips the zigzag strip off the seismograph roll and presses it into our hands. "Last night's quake. You earned it."

Ren folds it carefully into his pocket. "Can I come back and help test the next one?" he asks. His voice doesn't wobble at all.

s4b.text:
"The hiccups!" Ren says. "I want to catch one in the act."

"Aftershock detectives!" Zinnia flings open a drawer and tosses us magnifying glasses. "The little shakes that follow a big one. Camp by the seismograph. Watch the pen."

We pull up stools. We watch. The pen scratches along, calm, calm, calm — then WOBBLE. Ren grabs my arm. "One! Write down the time!"

We wait. And wait. Nothing. Then two hiccups, bang-bang, right on top of each other.

"Seven minutes, then forty seconds, then... no pattern," Ren mutters, staring at our list of times. "Come ON. Pick a schedule."

The pen does not pick a schedule. It hiccups whenever it likes, like the ground has the giggles and won't say why.

"Nobody can predict them," Zinnia says gently, peering over our shoulders. "Not me, not anyone. The wiggles refuse all schedules. So scientists do something better. We measure. We prepare." She taps the strip. "Every wobble tells us how big, how deep, how the ground moved. We call the size of a quake its magnitude. And then—" she spins around— "we build for it. Watch."

She sets her little model skyscraper on the shake table, the one standing on bendy joints like ankles. Beside it she plonks a stiff block tower. "Full rumble!"

Rumble. RUMBLE. The stiff tower cracks down the middle and collapses. The skyscraper sways like a tree in wind — and stands.

"It wobbled and it STOOD," Ren breathes. "That's the trick. Move with the shake."

"That's the trick," Zinnia agrees.

Ren looks at the wiggly lines for a long moment. "You know what?" he says. "Knowing why the ground shakes makes it way less scary."

Zinnia snips the zigzag strip off the roll and presses it into our hands. "The planet's heartbeat," she says, "drawn in ink. Take it home."

c1.question: "Junior investigators, two trails of clues! Do we interrogate my seismograph and read what the wiggles are telling us — or do we fire up the shake table and measure just how mighty last night's rumble really was?"

options.label: Examine the seismograph and its wiggly paper strip
Power up the shake table and the firecracker jar

c2.question: "So the ground snaps and the ground hiccups — splendid! Now, do we build a tower that can out-wobble the shake table, or do we hunt those aftershock hiccups and catch them in the act?"

options.label: Build and rebuild a tower until it survives the shake table
Track the aftershocks on the seismograph like detectives

stories.title: The Tune That Stuck to Our Socks

s1.text:
Rain on the window. Drip, drip, drop. And inside our heads, all morning long, the same ridiculous tune: {stuck_tune}. We have hummed it at breakfast. We have hummed it at our socks. It will not leave us alone.

"A mystery," says the Tune Detective, and she flips open her notebook so fast her pencil nearly falls out. "Why does one melody stick like a burr on your jumper, and another one just slides away?"

"Burrs have hooks," we say.

"Exactly." She taps her pencil on the cardboard box we have been using as a drum. Boom. Boom-boom. "So a sticky tune must have hooks too. And I know how we find them. We build our own tune, from scratch, and we make it stick on purpose."

On purpose! We sit up straight.

She presses the big red button on the tablet. Recording. "Detectives," she says, "we need three notes and a pattern that repeats, then surprises you. That is the whole secret. Probably."

"Probably?"

"Detectives say probably," she says, and grins. "Ready?"

s2a.text:
"First, we take apart the tune that's stuck," says the Tune Detective. "Like detectives at a crime scene."

She taps the cardboard box. Knock-knock-knock. We know that part! Then — ding-dong! She makes a doorbell sound with her voice, and we laugh, because the knock-knock-knock suddenly turned into a doorbell ring.

"Did you hear that?" she says. "It repeats. Then it surprises you."

We listen again. Knock-knock-knock. Knock-knock-knock. Knock-knock-knock. Ding-dong!

"Same, same, same — DIFFERENT!" we shout.

She writes it in her notebook, big and proud: SAME-SAME-SAME-DIFFERENT. "That is the hook," she says. "That is why {stuck_tune} stuck to us like a burr. Our brains love a pattern — and they love it even more when the pattern does something sneaky at the end."

"Sneaky like a doorbell in the middle of knocking," we say.

"Exactly." She spins the pencil like a tiny baton. "Now we know the trick. Question is — can we build one ourselves?"

We look at the box drum. We look at each other. Our fingers are already wiggling.

s2b.text:
"First, we open the piano," says the Tune Detective, and she lifts the big wooden lid in the corner.

Whoa. Inside, the piano is a whole secret world. Long strings stretch across the bottom, thick as skipping ropes. Short strings sit up top, thin as spaghetti.

"Long strings, low notes," she says, and presses a key way down at the end. Bwooom. We feel it in our belly buttons. "Short strings, high notes." Ting! Like a tiny bell in our ears.

"It's a harp inside a box," we whisper.

"A harp that wears a fancy wooden coat," she says. Then she points at the black keys. "And look — groups of two, groups of three. Two, three, two, three, all the way along. That's how you never get lost."

We hum {stuck_tune} way down low, where the skipping-rope strings live. Then way up high, where the spaghetti strings ping. It's the same song — just wearing different colored shirts.

"So a melody can climb up and down," we say, "and it's still itself."

"Still itself," she says. "Now — what if we made one climb on purpose?"

s3.text:
"Well?" says the Tune Detective, pencil ready. "What did you find?" We tell her everything, and she writes it down in big swoopy letters. "Good. Because now we build. Three notes, like stepping stones." She taps the cardboard box. Boom. "Up." Boom. "Up." Then her hand hovers. "And down." Boom-boom.

Our turn. We climb the two stairs and slide back one, just like {our_melody}. Up-up-down. Up-up-down. It sticks already! We are humming it at our socks when the last note lands with a thunk. A tipped stone. A dropped pot rolling across the kitchen floor.

"There!" yells the Tune Detective, nearly snapping her pencil. "Did you hear that?"

"It wobbled," we say.

"It wobbled," she agrees, and her eyes go round and bright. "The repeat part is perfect. But the surprise? A surprise should feel like a doorbell ring, ding-dong, somebody wonderful arriving. Not like a pot hitting the floor." She flips her notebook to a fresh page. "So. Same three notes. Same climb, same slide. But the ending has to ring."

We look at the box. We look at each other. Up-up-down, we hum, and this time we stop right before the thunk.

"Again," whispers the Detective. "And this time, listen for the doorbell."

s4a.text:
"Swap it," we say. "The last note. Give it a new one."

"Which new one?" asks the Tune Detective, pencil hovering.

We hum the climb. Up-up. Then, instead of the thunk, we slide down just one small step, close and smooth, like the last stair home. Ding.

The Detective writes it down in big swoopy letters. "Same, same, same," she says, "and then—"

"Different," we whisper.

She taps the red button. Recording. We play the whole thing into the box: up-up-down, up-up-down, up-up-ding. Then we press play.

Out it comes. Same-same-same-DIFFERENT. The surprise lands like a doorbell ring, and we burst out laughing, because somebody wonderful has arrived, and it is our own tune.

"Again!" we shout.

We play it again. And again. The Tune Detective is laughing too hard to write. "Detectives," she says, wiping her eyes, "the melody has hooks. It is officially stuck."

She is right. We hum it all the way downstairs, up-up-down, up-up-ding, and the rain on the window hums along. Drip, drip, ding.

That night the tune comes home in our pockets, curled up warm like a penny we forgot we had. And whenever we want, we can take it out and ring it.

s4b.text:
"Keep the wobble," we say. "But move the whole tune up. Higher."

The Tune Detective raises one eyebrow. "The same tune? In a taller hat?"

"Higher," we say. "Like climbing two more stairs before you start."

So we do. Up-up-down, up-up-down, and then we step up, up, and play the whole pattern again from there. Same climb. Same slide. Same wobble at the end. Only now the wobble sits up high, and it does not sound like a dropped pot anymore. It sounds like a question.

And the tune answers it. Ding-dong.

The Detective taps the red button. Recording. We play it back, and there it is: our melody, wearing a higher shirt, and the wobble is the funny answer we did not know we were waiting for. We laugh so hard we have to sit down on the floor.

"The surprise was hiding," says the Detective, scribbling. "It just needed a lift."

"It repeats," we say, "and then it surprises you."

"Probably," she says, and grins.

We hum it all the way downstairs, low version, high version, low, high, and the rain on the window keeps the beat. Drip, drip, ding-dong.

That night the tune comes home in our pockets, both shirts and all, and the wobble turns out to be our favourite part.

c1.question: "Do we take apart the tune that's stuck, or open up the piano and see how notes work?"

options.label: Take apart the stuck tune to map its pattern
Open the piano and explore how notes go up and down

c2.question: "Do we swap the wobbly note for a new one, or move the whole tune higher and keep the wobble?"

options.label: Change the last note to a different surprise
Shift the whole melody higher and keep the wobbly note

stuck_tune.role: The nonsense song stuck in our heads at the start

our_melody.role: The three-note pattern we build and repeat
our_melody.default: Up-up-down, like climbing two stairs and sliding back one

s1.text:
"You're up. Good."

Ruth's voice comes out of the dark like gravel and coffee. She hands us each a thermos and points toward the marsh, where the sky is just turning the colour of a peach.

"Whooping cranes," she says. "We're counting them. Every last one."

We're standing on a wooden platform above the water, and the wind is doing that thing where it goes right through your jacket and says hello to your ribs. Below us, the marsh stretches out wide and silver, and somewhere in it are birds taller than we are.

Sam, Ruth's assistant, opens a notebook so worn it looks like it's been through a rainstorm. Because it has. Several.

"Look at this," Sam says, and turns the book so we can see. "Nineteen forty-one. The whole species. Every whooping crane alive on Earth."

The photograph is small and grainy. Twenty-one birds, standing in a line, like they're posing for a class picture.

"Twenty-one," Ruth says. "That's it. That's all there were."

We stare at it. Twenty-one birds. You could count them on your fingers and toes and have one left over.

"And now?" we ask.

Ruth smiles, and it's the kind of smile that has a whole story inside it. "Now we're over eight hundred. But we don't guess. We count. Every spring, every bird, by name and by number."

She pulls something from her vest pocket and presses it into our hand. A feather. White as the first snow, longer than our hand, soft along the edges.

"Carry that," she says. "It's the count feather. Whoever holds it calls the number."

Sam flips to today's page. "We've spotted twenty this morning. But the youngest chick, the new one, we haven't seen yet."

Ruth's eyes scan the marsh. "One missing," she says quietly. "In a family this small, one matters."

The feather sits in our palm, light as nothing, and the wind carries a sound across the water. A low, rolling call, like a question being asked far away.

"That's the parents calling," Sam says. "They're looking too."

We close our fingers around the feather. "Then let's find that chick."

Ruth nods once. "Now you're counting."

s2a.text:
"The reeds," we say, and Ruth grins like she was hoping we'd pick the wet one.

We climb down into the marsh, and the water finds our boots right away. Cold. Squelchy. The kind of cold that makes your toes sit up and pay attention. Ruth moves ahead of us, slow and low, one hand on the cattails, and we copy her exactly. Step. Wait. Step.

"Chick's smart," she murmurs. "But smarts don't help if you're stuck."

Then we hear it. A thin, peeping sound, scared and small, coming from the water's edge.

There. Tangled in a mess of old fishing line, half-hidden in the reeds, is a crane chick. Grey and fluffy, with legs like sticks and eyes like black beads. It sees us and peeps louder.

"Easy now," Ruth says, and her voice goes soft as flannel. "You're all right, little one."

She shows us how to hold a bird this big. One arm around the body, wings folded gentle against the sides, beak pointing away from faces. "Like hugging a football that bites," she says. We kneel in the cold water and work the line loose, finger by finger, while the chick's heart goes thump-thump-thump against our sleeve.

The line comes free. The chick stands, shakes itself like a dog, and stares at us.

"Go on," Ruth whispers. "Your folks are calling."

It runs. It flies. It's gone into the silver.

Ruth picks up the tangled line and holds it like it weighs a ton. "Third one this season," she says, and her voice has gone flat as yesterday's soda. "The marsh is full of this stuff."

We look at the feather in our hand. Twenty-one cranes, and now one more safe. But the water keeps secrets, and not all of them are kind.

s2b.text:
"The blind," we say, and Sam nods like that's the smart money.

We climb the wooden steps, quiet as we can, and slip into the observation blind. It's a little hut with a long window, and it smells like old wood and rain. Sam hands us binoculars that feel heavy and important.

"Leg bands," Sam says. "Like license plates. Every crane has one. Find the chick, read the band, log it. That's the job."

We scan the marsh. It's huge from up here, silver and green and full of secrets. A heron stands still as a statue. Two ducks argue about something. And then—

"There," Sam breathes.

Three cranes. Two tall ones, and between them, a fluffy grey chick with legs like sticks, pecking at something in the shallow water. We find the leg band. Red, with white numbers. Sam flips through the notebook, taps a page.

"That's her. Number twenty-one. Safe and feeding."

The relief hits us like warm soup. We didn't know we were holding our breath until it comes out in a whoosh.

Ruth climbs up behind us, quiet for her size. She looks through her own binoculars, and her shoulders drop an inch. "Good," she says. "That's good."

But Sam is staring at the notebook, and Sam's face has gone serious. "Ruth. The count."

"I know," Ruth says.

"Twenty-one is good. But if we lose three this year, or four—" Sam stops.

Ruth takes the feather from our hand and holds it up to the light. "Eight hundred birds," she says. "Sounds like a lot. It isn't. Not when the whole species fits in one marsh."

We look at the chick, small and busy and alive. Twenty-one today. But the math is thin as ice, and the water underneath is cold.

s3.text:
Back at the station, Ruth pours the last of the coffee into our thermos caps and pulls up a chair that creaks like it's telling its own story.

"So," she says, and her drawl wraps around the word like a blanket. "What'd you find out there?"

We tell her, and she listens the way she counts birds — every single one matters.

"Good," she says. "That tells us something." She reaches into her vest and pulls out the white feather, the one from this morning, and sets it on the table between us. "You want to know how we got from twenty-one to eight hundred?"

We nod.

"Incubators, first," Ruth says. "Scientists hatched eggs in machines, warm as toast. The chicks came out fine. But they looked at the first thing they saw — a human face — and decided that was Mom." She shakes her head. "They wouldn't follow other cranes. Wouldn't migrate. Just stood around waiting for a person to tell them where to go."

"So what fixed it?" we ask.

"Costumes." Ruth says it flat, like it's the most normal thing in the world. "Grown scientists in white sheets, holding crane puppets on sticks, never saying a word. The chicks imprinted on the puppets instead. Followed them everywhere." She taps the table. "That fixed the imprinting. But those birds still didn't know the route south. Nobody to teach them the way."

Sam leans against the doorframe. "Every failure told them exactly what to fix next."

"That's the thing about a population this small," Ruth says. "You don't get to give up. You just get to learn." She picks up the feather and turns it slowly. "Eight hundred birds now. Recovery is real. But this marsh, this year, these young cranes — including our chick — they still need a teacher. And winter doesn't wait."

She holds the feather out to us. "So. How do we teach them the way south?"

s4a.text:
The ultralight looks like a dragonfly that swallowed a kite. Its wings are painted white, with black tips, exactly like a whooping crane's.

"The birds think it's their mama," Sam says, patting the little aircraft. "Only way they'll follow."

Ruth zips her jacket. "Pilot wears a white costume, never speaks. Just flies. The chicks imprint on the plane, not the person."

We climb into the chase vehicle, a truck with a radio and a scope mounted on top. Our job: track the flock, keep the route clear, count every bird that rises.

The pilot taxis. The young cranes — seven of them, including our chick — lift from the marsh, wings beating slow and sure. They fall in behind the ultralight like they've done it a hundred times.

"They're following," we breathe.

"Every mile south," Ruth says into the radio, "they're learning the way."

For three weeks we leapfrog ahead, checking fields, clearing hazards, sleeping in motels that smell like chlorine and hope. The radio crackles updates: flock over Kentucky. Flock over Tennessee. Our chick's leg band, spotted and logged.

Then, one bright morning, the call comes. "All seven on the ground in Florida. Safe."

Ruth goes very still. Then she smiles, and her voice lifts like a bird taking off. "Eight hundred and one."

She presses the white feather into our hands. "You held the count. Now hold this. It went up by one you helped."

The feather is light as nothing. It feels like everything.

s4b.text:
We stay. Somebody has to mind the ground.

Ruth hands us binoculars and a clipboard thick as a sandwich. "Flyway team. We clear the path, log every bird, and watch the skies. The youngsters fly themselves — we just make sure nothing's in their way."

Sam shows us the marsh at dawn, where old fishing line hangs from reeds like silver thread. "Birds tangle in that," Sam says, snipping it free. "One piece at a time."

We work for days. We log cranes in the notebook — number, time, direction. We join volunteers on hilltops, thermoses in hand, eyes on the clouds. The white feather rides in our pocket, a quiet weight.

Then, on a cold morning that smells like snow coming, Ruth grabs our arm. "Look up."

Seven white shapes pass overhead, wings black-tipped, calling to each other in voices like rusty gates swinging. No plane. No costumes. Just cranes, flying south on their own.

"Leg band," Sam says, training the scope. "Blue over silver. That's our chick."

We count them as they pass. One, two, three — all seven, strong and sure.

Ruth updates the notebook, her pencil steady. "Eight hundred and one," she says, and her drawl wraps around the number like a scarf. "Recovery isn't a maybe. It's a count that keeps climbing."

Sam adds one more number to the spreadsheet. Ruth tucks the feather into our hands.

"Take that home," she says. "And remember — in Yellowstone, the wolves came back, and even the rivers changed. Save one species, you lift a whole world."

We close our fingers around the feather. It is warm from her pocket, and it feels like a promise.

c1.question: Ruth lowers her binoculars and says, "One bird short, friends. We can wade the far reeds and look for her, or climb to the blind and read leg bands till we find her. Which way?"

options.label: Search the reed beds on foot
Spot her from the observation blind

c2.question: Ruth taps the migration map and says, "These youngsters need a teacher. We can fly with them in the ultralight and lead them south ourselves, or stay here and make the whole route safe from the ground. Both matter. Which team are we?"

options.label: Join the ultralight team and lead the cranes south
Stay and protect the route from the ground

stories.title: The Wave at the Edge of Forever

s1.text: The first thing Sam ever did on The Long Fall was wave. It was a small wave, the kind you give when you are not sure anyone is looking, and Sam gave it to the black hole. Through the observation deck viewport, Abyss-7 burned like a ring of fire that had forgotten to burn out. The accretion disk, Horizon called it, the ship's AI, who spoke from the walls in a voice like slow honey. All that light, Horizon said, is falling. It has been falling for a million years, and it will never arrive. Sam pressed closer to the glass. Under their jacket, pinned flat so it would not crinkle, were the star charts they had drawn by hand, every station between home and here. The charts were the reason Sam was hiding in the dark behind a supply crate, and the charts were the reason, when Commander Yuki's boots stopped right in front of that crate, Sam did not run. You made these, Yuki said, holding one up to the light. Sam nodded. Yuki crouched down until her eyes were level with Sam's. She smoothed the crinkled corner of the chart with her thumb, gently, the way you might smooth a bird's ruffled feathers, and handed it back. Then you already know, she said, that we are going down. Behind her, Dr. Thorne held up two watches, ticking side by side, perfectly in step. One stays with the ship, he said. One goes to the edge. And when they come back together, they will not agree. Sam looked at the burning ring. Looked at the charts. Looked at the wave still fading on the glass. I want to see it, Sam said. Not read it. See it. Horizon hummed, pleased. Then welcome aboard, little stowaway. The geometry of forever is waiting.

s2a.text: The Long Fall climbed, and Sam watched the universe bend. We are entering the photon sphere, Horizon said, her voice rippling through the walls like rings in a pond. Here, light itself is trapped in circles. Sam pressed both hands to the viewport. Outside, the stars did something impossible. They smeared. They stretched into slow arcs of red and gold, curving around the darkness below like water circling a drain. And then Sam gasped. There, in the glass, was the back of their own head. Horizon, Sam whispered. I can see myself. From behind. Horizon was quiet for a moment. Yes, she said at last, and she sounded pleased. Oh, Sam whispered. Below them, the blackness was perfect and total, a hole punched out of the sky. But all around its edge, starlight poured over in a glowing waterfall, endless and silent. It is beautiful, Sam said. It is geometry, Horizon said. The geometry of forever. The ship trembled. Engines burning, Horizon said softly. We must not stop. Not here. Sam did not answer. They watched the waterfall of light fall, and fall, and fall, into the dark that never filled.

s2b.text: The Long Fall dropped, and everything began to stretch. Down we go, said Dr. Thorne, and his voice was calm, but his knuckles were white on the railing. Sam felt it first in their stomach, a pull like an elevator dropping too fast. Then the ship groaned. A long, low sound, like a cello string being pulled tight. Spaghettification, Dr. Thorne said. The gravity below us is stronger than the gravity above us. It is pulling the ship apart, atom by atom, like taffy. A pencil rolled off the console and hit the floor with a thud that sounded too heavy. Then a wrench. Then Sam's own boots felt glued to the deck. Watch this, Dr. Thorne said. He lowered a watch on a long cable, down toward the floor, toward the black hole. It ticked. Then it ticked slower. Then slower still. Sam listened to the spaces between the ticks grow wide. Time is stretching, he said. Down there, a second takes longer than a second up here. Sam stared at the two watches on the console. The one on the cable was falling behind. The one on the ship ticked on, ordinary and quick. They will never agree again, Dr. Thorne said. Not ever. The ship groaned again, deeper this time. Horizon spoke from the walls, gentle as ever. Window for return is narrowing, she said. But oh, little stowaway. Look how the light bends. Dr. Thorne put a hand on Sam's shoulder, steadying them against the pull. Feel that? he said. That's the universe pulling. Sam nodded, and did not step away.

s3.text: The Long Fall trembled as its engines burned at maximum thrust, fighting to hold position against the pull of the void. Sam gripped the railing, feeling the vibration in their teeth. We are at the edge, Horizon whispered, the AI's voice soft with awe. The event horizon. Sam looked out the viewport. There, suspended in the dark, was a figure made of stretched red light. {explorer_name}, Horizon said. They crossed years ago. To us, they are still falling, frozen forever at the threshold. The explorer's arm was raised, caught mid-wave, the gesture pulled into a long, crimson arc that spanned the darkness like a brushstroke. Sam said nothing. They pressed a hand to the cold glass and looked. The arc did not move. It did not fade. It simply hung there, patient as a held note, glowing red against the black. Somewhere below it, the engines hummed, and the ship trembled, and the dark went down and down. Are they okay? Sam asked at last. They are beyond our reach now, Horizon said gently. We cannot go closer. Sam watched the wave a while longer. What did they find? Sam whispered. What were they trying to tell us? Horizon did not answer. On the glass, the crimson arc hung in the dark, still waving.

s4a.text: We skim it, Sam said. Yuki's hands moved across the controls, and The Long Fall tipped forward into the dark. The engines screamed. Sam felt their body stretch, not painfully, but like dough pulled thin, and through the viewport the universe outside began to spin faster. Stars bloomed and died in seconds. Decades burned away like morning mist. Then they crossed. Inside the event horizon, there was no up, no down, only the singularity pulling every path toward its heart. Sam looked back and saw the entire future of the universe rushing toward them like a film running too fast. Look, Horizon whispered. The grid of spacetime projected across the glass showed every line converging. There is no direction that leads out. Every road ends at the center. Sam reached out and touched the cold glass where {explorer_name} still waved, frozen in red. They weren't trapped, Sam realized. They were greeting us. Across all that time. Yuki fired the engines, a precise burn that tore them away from the edge, and suddenly they were falling up, back toward the station. But when they docked, the station had changed. New faces. New children. Decades had passed outside. Sam stepped onto the deck, holding the recording of that endless wave. They looked for a face they knew. They did not find one. A small child approached, staring at the screen. What is that? the child asked. Sam smiled, feeling the weight of years in their pocket. It's a wave, Sam said. From someone who fell further than anyone. See how the light stretches red? That's time, bending. The child reached out, touching the screen where the crimson arc hung frozen. Were they scared? the child whispered. No, Sam said. They were saying hello. Horizon hummed from the wall, soft and warm. Hello, little stowaway, she said.

s4b.text: Turn back, Sam said. Yuki slammed the engines to maximum thrust. The Long Fall groaned, fighting the pull, and Sam felt their body stretch like taffy, thin and long, as the ship fought to escape. Hold on, Yuki shouted. The viewport showed the edge burning red, the frozen wave of {explorer_name} still hanging there, eternal. The ship shuddered. Metal creaked. Then, with a sound like a held breath released, they broke free. They fell up, away from the abyss, back toward the station where the lights were warm and familiar. When they docked, only hours had passed. Dr. Thorne met them, holding up the two watches. Look, he said. The watch that went to the edge ticked slower. It was permanently behind, out of sync with station time. Sam took the watch, feeling its weight. It was proof. Time itself had bent for them. That night, Sam stood at the observation deck, watching the black hole burn. Horizon hummed softly. You went to the edge, the AI said. And you came back. Sam held up the watch. Its second hand moved slower than the station clocks. Sam pressed the watch to their chest, and stood very still, feeling the slow tick against their heart. Dr. Thorne stood beside them, watching the watch tick against Sam's shirt. It ticks with you now, he said. Horizon hummed, pleased. Welcome home, little stowaway.

c1.question: "We can take the high road through the photon sphere where light bends in circles, or dive straight down to feel the stretching—what's your call, stowaway?"

options.label: Take the upper path to see light orbit the black hole
Descend immediately to feel gravity's pull

c2.question: "This is it—the point of no return. We can skim the edge and cross just enough to see every path lead to the center, or we can turn back now while we still can. What do we do?"
