options.label: Skim the event horizon to experience the point of no return
Escape now and return to the station

explorer_name.role: The name of the previous explorer frozen at the event horizon

stories.title: The Wheel in the Soft Red Dust

s1.text:
We have flour on our knuckles and bread dough back in the kitchen, and here we are on the back step with the backpack workshop between our boots.
We look up. The telescope is glowing again, and tonight it is making a sound.
"Beep. Beep beep."
"Somebody wants us," we say.
We climb through the little round door, and here we are on Mars.
The ground is red. Not fire-engine red. Rusty orange red, like cinnamon spilled everywhere. Even the sky is butterscotch.
We take one hop, float high, and come down slow.
"Beep."
Over by a low ridge sits a little rover, as big as a picnic table, six chunky wheels and a glass eye on a stalk. It turns and blinks at us.
This is {rover_name}, and {rover_name} is stuck.
One front wheel has sunk deep into dust as fine as the flour on our hands. We crouch down and look. The wheel turns and turns. The dust just swallows it.
{rover_name} is not scared, only stuck, and maybe a bit embarrassed.
We open the workshop on a flat rock. Springs and sticky tape. A bicycle bell. Two shiny tin lids.

s2a.text:
A ramp. Obviously.
"If it cannot climb out," we say, "we will build it a road."
So off we go hunting flat rocks, and hunting on Mars is the best job there is. One hop drifts us down beside a pile of red slabs, and we carry four at a time, because up here even the big ones feel like pillows.
Clack. Clack. Clack.
We put them down in a neat slope in front of the wheel and pat the last one flat.
"Ring it," we say, and we ring the bicycle bell. Ding.
{rover_name} rolls forward and puts a wheel on the first rock. It sinks. Then the next one. Our fine flat road goes down into the soft dust, one slab at a time, like biscuits left too long in the milk.
"Beep."
{rover_name} lifts that round glass eye. Not at the hole. It is looking past us, at the sky, where two tiny moons are chasing each other.
We look too, and we forget to be disappointed.
Then we stand up and dust off our knees. Pushing down on this dust does not work.

s2b.text:
A fan. If the dust is too soft to hold a wheel, we will take the dust away.
We put it together fast, the way inventors do. A squeezy rubber bulb from the side pocket. A paper cone taped on the end.
"Aim," we say. "Squeeze."
We hold the puffer in front of the buried wheel and squeeze. Poof. A cloud of red dust jumps straight up. Squeeze, squeeze, squeeze. Poof, poof, poof.
The dust climbs into a swirling orange cloud, and then it just hangs there. The air on Mars is very thin, so dust floats a long slow while before it comes down.
And down it comes, all of it. On our boots. In our hair. And all over {rover_name}, from top to bottom.
There is more dust in the hole now than before.
We look at each other, red from hoods to heels, and laugh until we sit down in it.
{rover_name} turns the glass eye on us and beeps twice, which is definitely a giggle.
Then we stand up and brush ourselves off. Blowing this dust around does not work.

s3.text:
We sit down on the flat rock beside {rover_name} and think.
Our {first_try} did not work. That is fine. Every good invention starts with one that flops.
So we look hard at the dust instead. We poke one finger in, and down it goes, easy as a finger into a bag of flour.
Then we lay our whole hand flat and press.
Our hand stays right on top.
"Oh," we say. "Oh. Again."
We do it again to be sure. One pointy finger sinks. One flat hand floats.
The dust is too soft to hold anything narrow. But wide and flat? Wide and flat it holds up fine.
"It is deep snow," we say. "A boot sinks. A snowshoe walks."
{rover_name} beeps and lifts the glass eye toward the ridge, where the wind has combed the dust into long soft ripples, row after row, and for a moment we both go quiet.
Then we open the workshop again. Two shiny tin lids and one long roll of sticky tape.
Two very good ideas.

s4a.text:
Snowshoes. Snowshoes for a rover.
We take the two tin lids and bend their edges up, like little dishes, then tape them onto the buried wheel, one each side, so the wheel wears wide flat boots.
Tape, tape, tape. Then three more strips, because inventors always add three more.
We stand back. {rover_name} looks silly and splendid.
"Ring it," we say. Ding.
The wheel turns. The lids press down on the dust, wide and flat, and they do not sink. They hold. The wheel climbs, slow at first, then up and out with a soft crunch.
{rover_name} is free.
It spins in a happy circle and beeps a little tune, and we hop up and float and come down cheering.
Then we walk with our friend to the top of the ridge, and the whole rusty world goes gold in the low sun.
{rover_name} points the round glass eye at us and takes our picture.
"Say cheese," we say.
We are red from head to boots, with flour still on our knuckles, and we are grinning like anything.

s4b.text:
A road. If the dust cannot hold the wheel up, we will put something on top that can.
We unroll the long strip of sticky tape, sticky side down, and press it flat across the soft patch. It makes a smooth silver road from the wheel to the firm ground.
Then we press small flat pebbles all along it, so the wheel has something to bite.
"Ring it," we say. Ding.
{rover_name} rolls forward, very slowly. The wheel finds the silver road. It grips. It climbs. And out it comes, with a soft pop and a puff of red powder.
{rover_name} is free.
It rolls back and forth on the firm ground, trying every wheel, and beeps a bright little tune. Then it pats its own flat back with one arm, which means climb on.
So we climb on. We trundle over the ripples, past a low pink hill, while the sun goes down and the two moons come out.
"Slowly," we say. "No hurry at all."
It is the slowest, best ride we have ever had.

c1.question: "Right," we say, and we crack our floury knuckles. "A ramp made of flat rocks, or a fan to blow the dust away? Ramp, or fan?"

options.label: Build a little ramp out of flat rocks
Build a puffing fan to blow the dust away

c2.question: "So," we say, holding one up in each hand. "Wide tin boots on the wheel, or a sticky road under it? Lids, or road?"

options.label: Strap the wide tin lids onto the wheel like snowshoes
Roll out a long tape road for the wheel to climb

rover_name.role: the little six-wheeled rover with the buried wheel

first_try.role: the fix we built on our first attempt

s1.text:
When I was younger, I ran a little research boat in a calm bay, with a hydrophone trailing in the water and headphones that smelled of salt. The summer Nico came to help, we heard something odd on the very first dawn.

The bay was still dark. The water went plip, plip against the hull. Nico had the headphones on, both hands pressed over them, tongue stuck out in listening.

Then it came. Weee-ooo-weee.

A sliding whistle, up and down and up again, like someone drawing one long curly line with sound.

Nico's eyes went round. "Did you hear that?"

"I heard it," I said.

And then — from far away, so far it was barely a thread — the exact same tune came back. Weee-ooo-weee. Same slide. Same curl. Same everything.

Nico grabbed the notebook and wrote it down, with a question mark so big it fell off the bottom of the page.

We listened all that day. We heard squeaks and clicks and one long burp that was probably a seal. But the sliding whistle did not come back.

Then, at dusk, when the water turned the colour of weak tea — weee-ooo-weee. And again, far off, the answer. Weee-ooo-weee.

Nico pulled the headphones off slow, like the sound might spill.

"Out of all the whistles in the whole sea," Nico said, "how does one dolphin find its one best friend?"

I did not know. But I knew we were going to fill that notebook finding out.

s2a.text:
We spent the whole next day being detectives, which mostly meant sitting on the deck with our ears sweating inside the headphones.

"Detectives need hats," Nico said.

"Detectives need snacks," I said, and passed the biscuits.

I keep my old recordings in biscuit tins, labeled in pencil. Summer of the Slapping Tail. The Month of Seal Burps. We played them one by one, slow and careful, one note at a time, and Nico checked each whistle against the notebook.

Click-click-click. No. Squeeeak. No. A long farting sound.

"Seal," we said together.

Then Nico sat up so fast the biscuits slid. "Wait. Wait. Back one."

The recording hissed. It was five summers old, from a tin labeled Rain, Rain, Rain. And out of the rain came: weee-ooo-weee. Same slide. Same curl. Same everything.

"That's IT," Nico whispered. "That's the one. Five years ago!"

"Five years," I said. "Songs don't last five years, Nico. Somebody has been keeping that whistle."

Nico wrote it down, and underlined it three times, and the pencil snapped.

That was when something splashed beside the boat. A young dolphin, barely bigger than Nico, popped up and whistled at us — a short, cheeky pip-pip-pip! Then it did it again. Pip-pip-pip! Then it spun in a circle and did it again.

"It's showing off," Nico said.

"Mm," I said. "Or it's saying its name. Dolphins do that. They carry their whistle like a name tag, and the whole pod knows them by it."

Nico looked at the notebook. At the dolphin. At the notebook.

"Then our whistler isn't singing a song," Nico said slowly. "It's calling somebody."

Pip-pip-pip! went the little dolphin, like a doorbell that had figured itself out.

s2b.text:
We rowed over to Old Sal at the harbor dock, where he mends nets and drinks tea strong enough to stand a spoon in. Sal has watched this bay for forty summers, and he swears he knows every dolphin in it by face.

"He does not," I said.

"I do so," said Sal, not looking up from his net.

Nico climbed onto the dock, took a big breath, and whistled it. Weee-ooo-weee. The whole tune, slide and curl and all.

Sal's mug stopped halfway to his mouth. Tea went over the side. He did not notice.

"Where," he said, very quietly, "did you hear that?"

"On the hydrophone," I said. "Dawn and dusk. Every day this week."

Sal set the mug down like it was made of eggshells. "I knew a dolphin who whistled exactly that. Young one, with a fin bent over like a folded corner of a page. Used to follow the boats and whistle that tune at everything. Gulls. Buoys. Me." He shook his head slowly. "Then one spring, gone. Just gone. Years back now."

Nico had gone very still. "Gone where?"

"Nobody knows. Pods travel. Dolphins have their own ways of talking, their own dialects, family to family — and sometimes a family moves on, and takes its voices with it." Sal picked up his net again, but his hands weren't mending. "But here's the thing, Nico. If that whistle is back in my bay..."

"It's not back," I said. "It's being answered. Every dawn. Every dusk. Somebody here has been calling it all along."

Nico opened the notebook and wrote, in letters that wobbled: the whistler used to LIVE here.

"Then somebody in this bay," Nico said, "is still waiting for their friend to come home."

Sal looked out at the water for a long moment. "Forty summers," he said, "and that is the saddest and the best thing I have ever heard on this dock."

s3.text:
Back on the boat, Nico held the notebook so tight the pages bent. "Play it," Nico said. "Play what we heard."

So we did. {playback_moment}.

Weee-ooo-weee. Out into the bay it went.

Then — quiet. The whole bay held its breath. No plip against the hull. No gulls. Just us, listening so hard my ears hurt.

"Maybe nobody's home," I whispered.

And the water beside the boat went WEEP — and up leapt a dolphin, high as the mast, with a fin bent like a folded corner of a page.

"Look at that fin!" Nico shouted. "That's — that's got to be —" Nico grabbed the pencil. "I'm calling you {dolphin_name}!"

The dolphin whistled. Weee-ooo-weee. Our tune. Our exact curly line, answered from ten feet away.

And right at that moment, round the point, came Grandma Riptide and her whole family — big black backs, white eye-patches, fins like sails. They were talking the whole time, loud and fast: click-click-buzz, whaa-whaa-whaa. Nothing like dolphin talk. Same ocean, different family language.

But tucked inside Grandma Riptide's slow calls — weee-ooo-weee.

Nico's mouth fell open. "She knows it too!"

"It's a name," I said, and it clicked together like a puzzle box. "A name you invent when you're young, and keep your whole life. They've been calling their friend by name, all these years. And the friend heard. And came home."

Grandma Riptide glided close, slow and certain, and looked at us with one dark eye, as if to say: took you long enough.

s4a.text:
"Let's just listen," Nico whispered, and tucked the pencil behind one ear. So we did. We sat on the deck with our knees up, and the dusk came down soft as a blanket.

Then — there. Two fins, side by side, sliding past the boat. One bent like a folded page-corner, one straight as a ruler. Old friends, swimming close enough to touch.

Weee-ooo-weee, went one. Weee-ooo-weee, the other answered. Back and forth, back and forth, like a catch-song — my turn, your turn, my turn, your turn. Saying each other's names the way you'd say hello, hello, hello, it's really you.

And Pip — oh, Pip. Pip the gull had been sitting on the mast all week, listening. Pip fluffed up, took an enormous breath, and went: "WEEE-OOO-SQUAWK."

Nico clapped both hands over their mouth. The dolphins did not even pause. They just kept trading names, slow and sure, like a pot that knows it has all day.

Pip tried again. "WEE-SQUAWK-WEE." Worse. Somehow worse.

Then Grandma Riptide rose beside the boat, slow and certain, and gave one long, low call. Her whole family answered — whaa-whaa-whaa, click-click-buzz — their own family language, singing the bay goodnight. The sound rolled over the water and through our chests, and Nico pressed a hand flat against the deck to feel it hum.

"They're singing them home," Nico whispered.

I still have that notebook. On the last page, in Nico's wiggly writing, it says: a name you keep is a friend you keep.

And somewhere on an old tape, there's one more whistle — the one Nico invented that summer, just for keeping. Weee-ooo-weee.

s4b.text:
"I want my own," Nico said, and grabbed the pencil. "If a dolphin can invent a name, so can I."

So all that dusk, Nico practiced. First try: "Wooo-weee-wooo." Too wobbly. Second try: "Weee-weee-weee." Too squeaky — Pip the gull copied it perfectly, which Nico said was cheating. Nico changed it a tiny bit each time, the way young dolphins do, sliding the middle note lower, stretching the end out longer.

Then, just as the water turned the colour of weak tea, Nico whistled one that settled. "Weee-ah-weee." Down in the middle, like a swing at the bottom of its swoop.

"That's it," Nico said. "That's me."

We played it out into the bay. Weee-ah-weee. Once. Then we waited, both of us holding our breath without meaning to.

The water went still. Plip, went the hull. Nothing else.

And then — from out by the point, clear as a bell — came one answer. Weee-ah-weee. Our bent-finned friend, saying it back, once, polite and pleased. The way you'd answer a new friend who says hello in your language.

"It worked," Nico breathed. "The bay knows my name."

Grandma Riptide rose then, slow and certain, and gave one long wailing call — a sound from her own family's dialect, old as the tides. We couldn't translate a word of it. We didn't need to. It rumbled through the deck and up into our ribs, and it was plainly, warmly approving.

Then she turned toward the dark channel, where the salmon run, and her whole family fell in behind her — following her memory, the way they always have.

I still have the notebook. On the last page, Nico's name whistle is drawn in wiggly ink, with a star beside it.

That whistle is still in the bay somewhere, I like to think. Names travel.

c1.question: "Well, detective," I said, tapping the notebook, "do we hunt through my old recordings to see how long that whistle's been around — or do we row over to Old Sal, who swears he knows every dolphin in this bay by face?"

options.label: Dig through the boxes of old tapes on the boat

sets_slots.playback_moment: slow and careful, one note at a time, the way you test an old tape

options.label: Row to the dock and ask the fisherman who remembers every dolphin

sets_slots.playback_moment: one bold clear call, the way Sal would hail an old friend

c2.question: "So," I said, as the bent-fin dolphin's whistle faded into the dusk, "do we just sit quiet and listen to the two old friends talk — or do you want to invent a name whistle of your very own and offer it to the bay?"

options.label: Sit quiet at dusk and hear the two friends call each other by name
Practice and settle your own name whistle, then play it to the bay

dolphin_name.role: What Nico names the mysterious whistler in the notebook before learning its real 'name' is its whistle

playback_moment.role: How the hydrophone playback happens in s3 — slow and careful, or loud and splashy — set by c1's branch choice
playback_moment.default: slow and careful, one note at a time

stories.title: The Wobbly Bowl and the Sleepy Balloon

s1.text:
I remember a smell that lived in Grandma's kitchen. Warm and yeasty, like a hug you could eat. Let me take you there, {child_name}.

"Mr. Abernathy next door has had a long, tired week," Grandma says, tying her apron. "So today, we bake him {loaf_name}. Real bread, from scratch."

She turns the radio on. Plinky music fills the kitchen.

From the crock by the stove comes a squeaky little voice. "Ahem! Stirring orders!"

That's Spoonilla, the good wooden spoon. Grandma insists she runs the whole kitchen.

"Big slow circles, please!" Spoonilla squeaks.

We stir the squishy dough, {stir_style}. It squishes between our fingers.

Then Grandma pats it into a bowl and covers it with a cloth.

"Now it sleeps," she whispers. "And while it sleeps, it grows. Like a sleepy balloon."

We peek. Under the cloth, the dough is already puffing.

Soon we will carry it to Mr. Abernathy, still warm.

s2a.text:
"Wake the yeast!" Spoonilla squeaks. "Tiny helpers, up and at 'em!"

Grandma sprinkles the yeast into warm water with a pinch of sugar. We lean close. We watch.

Nothing. Then — bloop. Bloop bloop! Little bubbles come fizzing up, like the water is giggling.

"It's alive!" we shout, because we cannot help it.

"It was just sleepy," says Grandma. "Like someone else I know before breakfast."

Now the flour. "Three cups!" orders Spoonilla. "One! Two! Three!" We scoop a tiny white mountain, and we stir, {stir_style}.

But oh — the bowl will not hold still. Every stir spins it round on the counter. Round and round it goes, and the dough sloshes half in, half out.

"Hold the bowl, chef!" Spoonilla squeaks. "HOLD THE BOWL!"

s2b.text:
"Slow and steady!" Spoonilla squeaks. "Mountain first!"

We scoop the flour, one spoon at a time, and level each one with a finger. Tongue out. Nice and flat. Grandma smiles and says nothing, because levelling is serious work.

Then she pours the warm water in, slow as honey, while we stir, {stir_style}.

And here is the funny part. The soft powder turns sticky. Then stretchy. Then it grabs hold of everything — our fingers, our knuckles, the spoon. It will NOT let go.

Spoonilla thinks this is hilarious. "Stuck!" she squeaks. "The chef is stuck to the supper!"

Grandma just nods. "Sticky is right," she says. "Sticky means it's working."

Is it working? It feels like glue with ideas.

"Keep stirring!" squeaks Spoonilla. "Show that dough who's chef!"

s3.text:
"Well, look at that," Grandma says. "What did you find?" We tell her, and she smiles. "Then we know just what to do."

She shows us the fix. We press and fold, press and fold, until the dough stops fighting and turns into a soft, smooth ball.

"Good squishing!" Spoonilla squeaks.

Under the cloth it goes. We watch it rise, slow and round, like a sleepy balloon. It peeks over the rim. "The yeast made tiny puffs," Grandma whispers. "They did their work."

Into the oven it goes. Before the timer even rings, the smell floats through the whole house. Warm and yeasty, like a hug you could eat.

"Soon," Grandma says, "we carry it to Mr. Abernathy, still warm."

s4a.text: Ding! The timer sings. Grandma opens the oven, and out comes {loaf_name}, golden and puffy, smelling like the whole kitchen is smiling. "Now, little baker," Spoonilla squeaks. "March!" We wrap the warm loaf with {gift_extra} tucked in, and we carry it across the yard, quick quick quick, before it cools. Knock knock KNOCK! Mr. Abernathy opens the door. He smells the bread. His whole face wakes up, like a lamp turning on. "For me?" he says. We share the first warm slice right there on his step. He lends us his butter knife, "for next time." And that is why, in my memory, bread smells like knocking on a door.

s4b.text: Ding! The timer sings. Out comes {loaf_name}, golden and warm. "Tiptoe time," Grandma whispers. We wrap it in a tea towel with {gift_extra} tucked inside, and a crayon card that says its name in big wobbly letters. We carry it across the yard, soft soft soft, and set it on Mr. Abernathy's porch. The card goes on top. Then we hide behind the bush and hold our breath. The door opens. We hear his surprised laugh float out the window, warm as the bread. Home again, I fold the empty towel under my arm. It is still warm. And that is why, in my memory, a warm towel smells like someone smiling.

c1.question: "Now, chef — do we wake up the sleepy yeast first and watch it bubble, or do we build our flour mountain first and pour the water in slow?"

options.label: Wake the yeast first and watch it foam
Measure the flour mountain first and mix gently

c2.question: "The loaf is ready, little baker. Do we march it over right now and knock on his door big and brave, or do we tiptoe it onto his porch like a secret surprise?"

options.label: Carry it over and knock on the door right now
Leave it on the porch as a quiet surprise

loaf_name.role: The silly official name of the bread

stir_style.role: How the child stirs during the playthrough

gift_extra.role: The small extra tucked in with the gift loaf

s1.text:
The week before the science fair, Grandpa Joss and I are crouched under the desks after school with a shoebox of tangled fairy lights. We are building a brain. A real brain has eighty-six billion neurons, which is too many, so we are doing a very impressive hundred.

"It needs a name," Joss says, holding up two bulbs like a doctor. "Something with pizzazz."

We call it {model_brain_name}.

The door bangs open. In bursts Professor Pippa Volt, the visiting brain scientist, with pipe-cleaner neurons sticking out of her satchel like a mad bouquet.

"Show me a reflex!" she cries, and before we can blink she taps my knee with a little rubber hammer she built herself. My leg kicks. I did not tell it to. It just kicked.

"See?" Pippa beams. "The signal jumped a gap called a synapse before you even decided anything. Your wrinkly cortex" — she flaps her hands at her own head — "is a whole sheet crumpled to fit the box."

Our model is meant to do the same thing: pass one spark down a chain of lights, leaping each gap, all the way to the end. Joss presses the big red button.

Flick. The first bulb lights. The spark reaches the first gap — and dies.

Pippa clasps her hands. "Recalculating!" she says, delighted. "How wonderful."

The fair opens in five days.

s2a.text:
"A great big SHOVE!" we shout together.

Pippa rubs her hands. "Excellent. Terrible. Let's begin."

We empty the science cupboard. Every battery in school — rectangle ones, fat ones, the bumpy one from the weather station. Joss wires them in a row, tongue stuck out in concentration, while I hold the ends and Pippa hums a tune that sounds like lightning.

"More power!" cries Pippa. "The spark won't jump? We'll give it a shove it can't refuse!"

Joss presses the big red button.

FIZZ.

One enormous fizz, blue-white and beautiful, and a smell like warm plastic, like a hot water bottle left too near the radiator. Every single light blinks on at once — a hundred tiny suns — and then, pop. All out. The whole {model_brain_name}, dark as a pocket.

"Oh," says Joss.

Pippa is delighted. She is actually clapping. "Recalculating! How wonderful!" She picks up a dead bulb and holds it to her ear like a seashell. "You see, my brilliant builders, your real brain never shouts louder at a synapse. Never. It practises. It sends the signal again and again, and each time the gap gets a tiny bit easier to cross — like a path worn through grass. You cannot bully a synapse. You have to build it."

Outside the window the sky is going plum-coloured. We have a hundred fried lights, four days left, and no idea what building a path looks like in wire.

"So," says Joss, brushing plastic off his sleeve. "Not louder."

"Not louder," Pippa agrees. "Cleverer."

s2b.text:
"The dome!" we shout together. "Skip the boring bits!"

"Magnificent instinct," says Pippa. "Catastrophic. Proceed."

We drag out the tinfoil. The cortex, Pippa told us, is a whole sheet crumpled to fit inside your head, so we crumple — great silver folds and valleys, squashed and patted and squashed again until it sits on top of our shoebox like a crinkly metal turban. Joss crowns it with the best bulbs, the swirly ones. It looks spectacular. It looks like a brain that has already won the fair.

"Behold," breathes Joss, "the thinking part."

"Press the button," says Pippa, eyes shining.

Joss presses the big red button.

Flick. Bulb number one lights. The spark reaches the first gap — and dies. The glorious dome sits there, silver and splendid, doing absolutely nothing. Not one of its fancy bulbs so much as flickers.

"It's not thinking," I say.

"It is a very beautiful hat," says Pippa. She taps the tinfoil gently, almost fondly. "Here is the thing, my brilliant builders. A brain cannot wire the fancy bit before the path leading to it exists. You wire what you repeat — and you have repeated nothing yet. Not one signal has ever crossed that first gap. So the dome has nothing to think with."

Joss slowly takes off the tinfoil turban and holds it like a sad cake.

Outside, the sky is going plum-coloured. Four days to the fair, one spark still stuck at gap one, and we don't know what building a path looks like in wire and lights.

"So," says Joss. "The boring bits first."

"The boring bits," Pippa agrees, "are the whole trick."

s3.text:
That evening we end up at Grandpa Joss's kitchen table, where he is dropping juggling balls for what must be the fortieth time. Plop. Plop. Plop-plop. And laughing every single time, which is not like him at all.

"What did you find out there?" he asks, scooping a ball off the floor. "Anything useful?"

"Maybe," I say. But I'm watching his hands. He throws all three balls at once, the same way, every time, only harder. Like if he just throws harder, his hands will get it.

And it clicks.

"You're doing what we did," I say. "Trying the whole thing at once."

Pippa, who has been quiet for a whole minute, which is a record, leans forward. "A brain laying track just ahead of a moving train is wobbly," she says, "because it is building as it goes. So. We build one piece. Then the next."

So we try the fix on both projects at once. One synapse, one ball.

Joss and I wire a single gap in {model_brain_name} and pulse it gently, again and again, until the spark leaps it every time. Then Joss picks up one ball. Just one. He throws it hand to hand, slow as syrup, until his hands stop thinking about it.

"Wearing the path smooth," Pippa says, almost softly. "Every throw tells the synapse exactly what to adjust. Mistakes too. Especially mistakes."

Then she shoos us upstairs, because, she says with a mad gleam, "Sleep is when the brain tidies its new paths. The builders work the night shift."

s4a.text:
Morning, and something odd. Joss picks up one ball to show me the slow throw, and it goes hand to hand, smooth as pouring tea. He stares at his own hands. "I wasn't even trying," he says.

"The night shift," I say. Pippa was right. Sleep tidied the path.

So all week we build, slow piece by slow piece. One synapse a day on {model_brain_name}, wired and pulsed until the spark leaps it every time. One ball a day for Joss. Two balls, hand to hand, plop, plop, until his hands stop thinking about it.

Then it's the fair. Our table has a crowd. Pippa is wearing a hat shaped like a neuron, which tells you everything about Pippa.

"Ready?" Joss says.

I press the big red button.

Flick. The first bulb lights. The spark reaches the first gap — and leaps. Then the next. Then the next, gap after gap after gap, faster and faster, all the way up to the cortex dome, and the whole hundred bulbs blaze at once. The crowd gasps.

And at that exact moment, Joss gasps too — but not at the lights. At his hands. While his mind was on the spark, his hands picked up three balls and started juggling all by themselves. Up, across, catch. Up, across, catch. No thinking. Just doing.

"Reflex!" Pippa shrieks, nearly falling off her stool. "The path fired on its own!"

Before we leave, she presses something into my hand. One pipe-cleaner neuron, bent and a bit wobbly.

"For the path you built yourselves," she says.

It lives on my windowsill now. And every time Joss juggles — which is constantly, show-off that he is — I look at it and think: that little spark learned to jump. So did we.

s4b.text:
Morning, and something odd. Joss picks up one ball to show me the slow throw, and it goes hand to hand, smooth as pouring tea. He stares at his own hands. "I wasn't even trying," he says.

"The night shift," I say. Sleep tidied the path.

Then it's the fair. Our table has {model_brain_name} on it, half-lit, half-dark, with gaps still waiting. Pippa says it looks distinguished. Joss says it looks like a hedgehog with a fringe.

And that's when I see her. A little kid, standing at our table, poking one of the dead gaps with her finger. Her own project is under her arm — a cardboard volcano, slightly squashy. Her eyes are doing the shiny thing that means tears are thinking about it.

"It just won't work," she says. "I tried and tried."

And before I even think, I hear myself say it. "Your brain is building it right now. You just can't feel it yet."

She looks up. "Really?"

"Really," says Joss, pulling out a chair. "Watch this."

We spend the whole fair showing her the one-synapse trick. One gap. Pulse it gently. Again. Again. Joss juggles one ball beside her, slow as syrup, to show her what wearing the path smooth looks like. Pippa keeps leaning over to whisper "recalculating, how wonderful" every time the spark dies, which makes the kid giggle every single time.

And then — flick. Her first spark crosses its first gap.

Her face lights up brighter than our whole model.

"I felt it!" she says. "I actually felt it!"

We never do light the whole brain. Nobody gives us a prize. But when we pack up, the kid presses something into my hand — one single fairy-light bulb, twisted off her volcano.

"So you remember where the spark started," she says.

It sits on my windowsill now, next to a photo of Joss mid-juggle. One bulb. One gap. One leap.

That's where every spark starts.

c1.question: "The spark won't jump, my brilliant builders! So — do we give it a great big SHOVE, or do we skip the boring bits and build the glorious cortex dome first?"

options.label: Wire in every battery we can find and force the spark across
Skip ahead and build the beautiful crumpled cortex ending

c2.question: "Friday's the fair, and our chain is only half-grown. Do we race to light the WHOLE brain for the big red-button moment — or do we stop and help that small scientist whose own spark is stuck at gap one?"

options.label: Spend the week finishing the chain for the grand button-press
Leave our model half-built and teach the one-synapse trick to the stuck kid

model_brain_name.role: The name we give our fairy-light brain model

s1.text: Moonlight spills across {hero_name}'s blanket in a long white stripe. Outside the window, the moon hangs over the rooftops, glowing like a big banana. "Good night, Moon!" says {hero_name}, and waves. The moon glows brighter! So {hero_name} waves both arms. Brighter! Both arms and one leg! Grandma windmills too, like a silly machine. Biscuit the cat meows at the window. "Grandma, look," says {hero_name}. "The moon is a banana. It must be hungry!"

s2a.text: "First, a cracker!" says {hero_name}, holding it up to the window. The moon just glows. "Then the banana, because it matches!" But when {hero_name} turns around, the plate is empty. Biscuit the cat licks his whiskers. Crumbs! "You ate the moon's snack!" giggles {hero_name}. Biscuit purrs. The moon hangs there, still hungry, still glowing. "The whole jar!" says {hero_name}. Grandma helps lift it, heavy and wobbly, up to the windowsill. "Eat up, Moon!"

s2b.text: "I'll catch it!" whispers {hero_name}. The moonbeam slides across the floor like a silver snail. Step on it! It slips away. Grab it with both hands! It wiggles free. Scoop it in the jar! The jar stays empty. But look - the moonbeam lands smack on Biscuit the cat. Biscuit glows! He purrs louder and louder, a soft rumbling cat-lamp in the dark. "The moon knows the softest spot," laughs Grandma. {hero_name} pats the warm, glowing cat. The moonbeam stays right there, on Biscuit's stripey back.

s3.text: Grandma pours more warm milk. "Here's the thing, little one," she says. "The moon's glow is borrowed. Every evening, the sun tucks its light into the moon's pocket, like handing over a night-light. The moon carries it all night, watching every house." {hero_name} gasps. "The sun and moon take turns?" Biscuit purrs. Then {hero_name} sits up tall. "Grandma! If the moon watches us all night... somebody has to tuck IT in!" Grandma raises her mug. "How do you tuck in something so big and glowy?"

s4a.text: "My blanket!" says {hero_name}. Grandma helps drape it over the windowsill, like the moon's very own covers. Then {hero_name} sings. Loud! "GOOD NIGHT, MOON!" Too loud for bedtime. Softer now. Softer. A whisper. "Good night, moon." The glow settles over the room like a blanket of its own. {hero_name} climbs into bed under one white stripe. "Good night, Sun, wherever you're sleeping." And one small moonbeam stays on the blanket. All night long.

s4b.text: "My pillow!" says {hero_name}, marching it to the window. On the sill it goes, so the moon has somewhere to rest its face. Biscuit claims half of it. Official pillow-guard. Pat, pat. "Good night, Moon. Good night, Sun, wherever you're sleeping." Grandma carries {hero_name} to bed, and look - the moonbeam has saved a stripe of glow across the blanket, tucked in neat. The moon watches every house on the street. So nobody sleeps alone. Not ever.

c1.question: "Well, little moon-keeper," says Grandma, sipping her warm milk, "if that banana moon is hungry, shall we feed it a bedtime snack - or shall we try to catch that slippery moonbeam sliding across the floor?"

options.label: Feed the moon snacks held up to the window
Chase and try to catch the moonbeam

c2.question: "The moon's doing the night watch, all right," says Grandma, setting down her mug. "So how do we tuck in something as big as the sky - with your blanket, or with your pillow?"

options.label: Drape the hero's blanket on the windowsill and sing a loud-to-soft lullaby
Prop the hero's pillow on the sill for the moon to rest its face

s1.text:
Let me tell you about the day I spent in the biggest warehouse you can imagine. Picture a building so long that the far wall looks hazy, like the end of a road on a hot day. Yellow lines crisscross the floor like streets, and robots zip along them between shelves taller than houses. Beep. Beep. All day long.

My friend Rae is the engineer there, and she met us at the door with a bright vest for you, {kid_name}, so everyone could see you coming. "Blue squares," she said, pointing down at the floor. "Stand on those and you're off the robot roads. The yellow lines are theirs." She said it the way you'd show someone where to stand at a crosswalk — just how things work around here.

Then she whistled, and around the corner came Zip.

Zip is the fastest robot on the floor, a squat little fellow on wheels with a light on top that spins when he's pleased with himself. And here is the thing about Zip: he used to be perfect. Every box, every shelf, every single time. But lately — well. Watch.

Zip rolled up to us with a box on his back, spun his light, and beeped like he'd just won a race. Then he dropped the box on a shelf, spun around, and zipped away.

Rae leaned over and read the label. She sighed.

"That's {wrong_delivery}," she said. "And that shelf is for winter coats."

We looked at the box. We looked at the shelf. Somewhere down the aisle, Zip beeped again — a proud beep, a job-well-done beep. And that's the strange part. Zip wasn't being lazy or broken-down. Zip believed, all the way through, that he'd put that box exactly right.

"The afternoon shipment leaves at four," Rae said, pulling a marker from her pocket. "I need my best robot back. And I have a hunch you're the one to find out what he's actually doing."

She flipped over a shipping label and started to draw.

s2a.text:
"The recipe," you said. "Let's read his recipe."

Rae grinned and popped open a laptop right there on a shelf, between the winter coats and a stack of hats. "Zip's brain is just code," she said. "And code is a recipe. If this happens, do that. If the shelf says coats, put coats."

We read it line by line, out loud, the way you'd read a cake recipe looking for the missing egg. If the camera sees a shelf number, beep. If the shelf number matches the box label, drop the box. It all made sense. Every line was sensible. Every line was right.

"There's no mistake," I said.

"No typo," said Rae. "No missing line. Huh." She tapped the laptop. "So let's try the oldest fix in the world. Turn him off and on again."

She whistled Zip over, pressed a button under his chin, and his light went dark. Then she pressed it again. Beep. His light spun, and off he went — and for two whole minutes he was perfect. Coats to coats. Hats to hats. Rae checked her watch. "See? Fixed."

Then Zip rolled past us, beeped his proudest beep, and dropped {wrong_delivery} onto the winter coat shelf. Again.

Rae pulled out {loop_drawing}. Three arrows in a circle: sense, think, act. She put a big check mark on think.

"The thinking is fine," she said. "The recipe's good. And do you know what that means?" She leaned in. "Broken code doesn't behave for two minutes and then break. Broken code is broken right away. So whatever's wrong with Zip... it isn't in his think."

The loop had one arrow checked. Two to go.

s2b.text:
"Test him," you said. "Like an engineer."

"My favorite kind of detective," said Rae. "Here's the secret, {kid_name}. Engineers don't wait for things to break. They break things on purpose, gently, and watch what happens."

She whistled Zip over, and he came zipping up, light spinning, pleased as anything. Rae tore off a strip of packing tape. "This is his camera eye," she said, pointing to a little dark circle on Zip's front. "His sensor. It's how he sees the shelf numbers. Watch."

She pressed the tape over the eye.

Zip stopped. Mid-roll, mid-beep, mid-everything. His light went still. He simply froze, like a statue of a robot.

"No seeing, no moving," said Rae. "His loop is stuck on sense. He can't think about a shelf he can't see." She peeled the tape off. Beep! Zip sprang back to life and zipped away as if nothing had happened.

"Your turn," said Rae.

Next time Zip rolled past, I held my thumb over his little eye — gently, the way you'd cover a camera on a phone. Zip froze under my thumb. I could feel a tiny hum in him, waiting. I lifted my thumb. Beep! Off he went.

"Now we reset him, so the test starts clean," said Rae, and she pressed the button under his chin. Zip went dark, woke, and ran perfectly — coats to coats, hats to hats — for two whole minutes. Then, beep, {wrong_delivery}, winter coat shelf. Again.

Rae pulled out {loop_drawing} and checked off think. "A reset wipes his thinking clean, and the wrongness survives it. So the mistake isn't in his think." She frowned. "But look — if his eye were dead, he'd freeze. He doesn't freeze. He delivers, confident as a postman. So his sense isn't dead either. It's... telling him something. Something wrong."

s3.text:
Rae flipped the label over and checked off the THINK arrow with a satisfied scratch of her marker. "Two down," she said. "If Zip's brain is working, then the trouble must be in his body. His actuators — the motors that make him go and grab."

She rolled out a cart of spare wheels, and we helped her swap them in, one, two, three, four. Zip spun in a delighted circle, his motors whirring smooth as bathwater running. "See that?" Rae said. "Beautiful."

Then she handed him a box. Zip beeped, zipped down the aisle, and parked it — we ran to look — right back on the wrong shelf. The proud beep floated back to us. Rae sighed and checked off ACT. "Two arrows down. One to go."

We stared at the drawing. Three arrows in a circle: sense, think, act. Only SENSE was left unchecked, and somehow that made us both go quiet.

"What did you find?" Rae asked you, {kid_name}. "Out there, just now."

You told her. And whatever it was, it made you both look up at the same moment — at Zip's camera eye, the little glass circle above his gripper.

"Can we look at that?" you asked.

Rae lifted you up on her shoulders. And there it was. A greasy smudge, right across the lens, thick as jam on toast. "Oh, Zip," Rae breathed. "You couldn't see."

She wiped it clean with a soft cloth from her pocket. Zip blinked — you could actually see the focus adjust — and beeped. A different beep. A surprised beep.

"Every robot runs that loop," Rae said, tapping the drawing. "Sense, think, act. Zip follows his floor lines. My old mentor Fen's rover on Mars has to think for itself — a signal takes twenty-two minutes to get there. But they all run the same three arrows."

Zip delivered the next box perfectly. His light spun gold.

s4a.text:
Rae clicked her pen. "Then a ride it is. Zip's cleared for passengers — supervised ones."

She walked us to a painted circle on the floor. "Feet inside this. My hand stays on the stop button the whole time. That's the deal."

Zip rolled up and lowered his cargo plate with a polite little chirp. You stepped on, {kid_name}, and I held the rail beside you. Rae's thumb rested on the red button. "Ready?"

Zip beeped. We moved.

The aisle slid past, smooth as skating. And here is what you could feel, right through your shoes: Zip's wheels never stopped adjusting. A tiny hum, a tiny turn, faster than a blink. His sensors read the yellow line ahead, his brain decided, his wheels obeyed — and then it happened again. And again. Sense, think, act. Sense, think, act. The loop wasn't a drawing anymore. It was under your feet, working.

"Feel that?" Rae called, jogging alongside. "That's feedback! He's checking himself a hundred times a second!"

Zip slowed, turned, and stopped at a shelf. He lifted the box of {wrong_delivery} — gently, carefully — and set it down. Rae checked the label. She checked the shelf. She grinned like I'd never seen.

"Toy aisle. Correct shelf." 

Zip's light spun gold, and his beep echoed down the whole long building. Proud, and this time, right.

Back at the workbench, Rae pressed something into your hand. The shipping label, with its circle of three arrows — every one checked off now, in her thick black marker.

"You earned that," she said.

I still have my copy, taped up by my desk. And whenever something in my house acts confused — the remote, the toaster, the cat — I check its eyes first. You'd be surprised how often that's the whole problem.

s4b.text:
Rae clicked her pen. "The museum shelf, then. My favourite corner of the whole building."

She led us past the workbench to a long shelf against the wall, and — well. It didn't look like much. Old grippers, scuffed wheels, camera eyes in a row like buttons. But Rae ran her hand along it the way you'd pat a good dog.

"Every piece here was somebody's invention," she said. "Somebody sat at a bench and dreamed it up, and tried it, and it failed, and they tried again."

She lifted down a camera eye and put it in your palm, {kid_name}. It was cloudy — fogged and dim, like Zip's smudged lens, except this one would never wipe clean.

"That's from the first warehouse robots, years before Zip. They bumped into everything. Shelves, walls, each other. Bonk, bonk, all day long." Rae tapped the cloudy lens. "They could see, but they couldn't check themselves. Then someone invented the feedback check — the loop looking at its own work — and suddenly a robot could notice it had gone wrong. That one idea changed everything."

You turned the little eye over in your hand. Somewhere behind us, Zip beeped — a crisp, correct, modern beep.

"He's standing on their shoulders," Rae said. "Every robot is. Even Fen's rover, out there thinking for itself on Mars. Somebody's wrong guess is underneath every single thing it does right."

Then she did something I didn't expect. She took the shipping-label drawing — all three arrows checked — and folded it around the little retired lens, and pressed both into your hand.

"Take them. The loop that fixed Zip, and the eye that started it all."

That lens sits on my windowsill now, where the morning light comes through it. A reminder that seeing clearly is the first job of every robot — and not a bad one for a person.

c1.question: Rae taps her marker on the loop drawing and says, "Two ways to hunt a bug, kid. We can read Zip's recipe line by line and look for a mistake — or we can poke his senses on purpose, the way engineers test, and watch what he does. Which sounds like your kind of detective work?"

options.label: Open Zip's code on the laptop and hunt for the mistake line by line
Test Zip like an engineer — tape over his camera and see what he does

c2.question: Rae clicks her pen and grins. "Zip owes you one. So — do you want to ride his route and feel that loop working under your feet, or should I show you the shelf of old broken parts, where every piece of him was somebody's invention first?"

options.label: Ride along on Zip's route and feel the sense-think-act loop in motion
Visit the shelf of old robot parts and hear how each piece was invented

kid_name.role: The kid character, the listener's stand-in

wrong_delivery.role: The silly wrong thing Zip keeps delivering to the wrong shelf

loop_drawing.role: The three-arrow loop diagram Rae draws, which gets one arrow checked off per failed attempt and returns in the endings
loop_drawing.default: drawn in marker on the back of a shipping label
